en: Preface to the Collected Explanations of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
The difficulty of thoroughly investigating the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* lies not merely in its condensation of a hundred [verses] into ten, nor simply in its concise phrasing and rich meaning.

While it is indeed a direct commentary on the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-kārikā*, it in fact subsumes the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, and the *Viṃśatikā-vijñapti-kārikā*.

There are approximately several hundred fascicles of various treatises, including the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Madhyānta-vibhāga*, the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Pañcaskandhaka*, the *Kārikā*, the *Tarkajvālā*, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Saptati-śāstra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra*, and the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*.
Although the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Vyākhyāyukti* are most numerous among them, they can only serve as corroboration for this treatise; they cannot, however, subsume it. Alas!

How profound and how vast! There is nothing that can surpass it. Moreover, its establishment of right principles and refutation of heterodox views within always employs the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-linga*), which is correct in every instance.
Yet, among the teachers of the present day, those who have thoroughly mastered *hetuvidyā* (logic) are exceedingly rare.

Furthermore, if one has not thoroughly investigated and fully integrated the various treatises into one's mind, yet hastily attempts to explain this treatise, it is rare that such a person would not be like one who writes characters by chance while dictating in Yan—making errors at every turn.
For instance, in the first fascicle, the two syllogisms (anumāna) refuting the three categories of substance, quality, and action according to the Vaiśeṣika school are presented.

These are based on their tenet that objects such as jars and garments are touched by the tactile faculty (kāyendriya) and seen by the visual faculty (cakṣurindriya), and thus constitute the objective domain of the five consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna). This is evident...

That which is obtained through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the body’s tactile sensation and the eye’s visual perception—is the reason (*hetu*). That which is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Form and sound are the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, by employing both the theses of "having resistance" (*sapratigha*) and "lacking resistance" (*apratigha*) as a single reason, one exposes the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

This argument does not appear in the *Daśanigraha-sthāna-śāstra*, but rather in the *Śata-śāstra*. Furthermore, it follows the sequence of the refutation of the three [views] in the subsequent fascicle.
Regarding the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), they are subsequently refuted by means of the three periods of time.

This is because the Hīnayāna adherents maintain that "arising" exists in the future, whereas the past and present possess no function of arising at all; therefore, he refutes this by treating the future as identical to the past.

This tenet does not appear in the *Śata-śāstra*, but rather in the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Qīngliáng Cháo*. Instances such as these are too numerous to enumerate; even with one's own eyes, one cannot... [end of fragment].
Upon arriving, if one were to hastily set pen to paper, there would be the fault of both self-misunderstanding and misleading others. Alas! How can one not be cautious?
Having devoted my heart to this treatise and examined various scriptures, I have made certain identifications, yet many points remain missing or doubtful.

Later, I heard that the masters Chao Song and Yuan Du had formed a fellowship at Mount Jiao to search throughout the Tripitaka, intending to comment upon this treatise; they sent a messenger to invite me.
The two masters arrived one after the other. I remarked, "Why do you not compose a supplementary commentary (*pùshū*) to serve as a guide for future students?
They replied in unison, "This cannot be done unless Master Yiyu arrives. I immediately dispatched a messenger to welcome Master Yiyu, but he failed to arrive due to being detained by other affairs.
As the years passed, it became extremely difficult to bring them all together, and I too had left the mountain. I have now sought out this...
It has been nearly ten years since Yuan Du passed away, becoming a person of the past, and I too am old and infirm, lying prostrate upon my pillow for two years with no sign of recovery.
Nevertheless, I have never ceased for a moment to study and savor this treatise. This summer, when the first rains fell, Master Shi completed his new commentary;

he sent me the printed edition of the first five fascicles, in which the book states: "In recent times, those who have commented on the Buddhist scriptures have each produced their own [interpretations]..."

Those who have already seen [the texts] are many. However, as the principles of the Nature School (Xingzong) are perfect and complete, there is no great harm in providing clever commentaries upon them.
The principles of the Characteristics School (Xiangzong), by contrast, are precise; even a single character added or omitted leads to errors by a thousand miles.

Although I, your humble servant, possess some personal views, I do not dare to include any interpretations for which my eyes have not personally examined the evidence or my mouth has not personally engaged in discussion. As for those who do provide such interpretations now:
I have merely compiled these words by gathering the sayings of the ancients; I do not know if they can satisfy your honorable mind.

Alas! This is precisely my own heart’s intent. I have always maintained that masters such as Dignāga and Dharmapāla were all sages who had attained the stage of fruition (phala-avasthā), counted among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Their composition of various treatises was the natural outflow from their minds of direct perception (pratyakṣa).

[They] emerge. We, however, employ our discriminating minds to conjecture and speculate, considering this to be *anumāna* (inference), yet we do not realize that these are all not valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*).
How could it be permissible not to verify them against the seal of the ultimate teaching? Therefore, I have titled my humble interpretation "Verification of the Meaning" (*Zhèngyì*);
my intention was precisely this. You, Master, may be said to have grasped what my mind agrees with. Upon reading it...

In his writings, whenever he encountered a point involving formal inference (*pramāṇa*), he would clarify it one by one; thus, even those who do not understand the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) will find everything perfectly clear upon reading them.
Regarding the various treatises scattered throughout the literature that fell within the range of his mind and eyes, the Master invariably addressed them first.
Furthermore, there are matters beyond the reach of other eyes. Only then did I realize that the Master’s dedication was so refined;
thus, how could the commendations of Chao Song and Yuan Du have been in vain? I heard the Great Master Zibo say that the transmission of the Abhidharma (Saṃmitīya) school has long been severed.
When the Dharma Master Luan Tai was traveling on pilgrimage and seeking shelter from the rain under the eaves of a house, he heard its—

Within, he heard the sound of Dharma being preached; upon listening, it was the teachings of the Abhidharma (the *xiàngzōng*). He entered immediately to see them, whereupon an old man was preaching to an old woman.
The Master then prostrated himself and requested instruction. He remained for over a month, after which he departed having fully transmitted their learning.
He suspected that this old man and old woman were not ordinary people, but rather manifestations of sages and worthies appearing in response to conditions. Master En Xuelang was the grandson of Luan.
Yuan Du was also the grandson of Xuelang, and both the masters Yiyu and Chaosong received the Dharma from Xuelang and were acclaimed as his foremost disciples;
thus, the source of their transmission has a clear origin. Having received the Master’s brief yet pointed instructions, I have benefited greatly.
However, he wished to eliminate all superfluous wording and preserve only a few words on the correct principles for protecting the Dharma.
He could not avoid the malady of being weary of complexity and delighting in simplicity; thus, the writings he produced throughout his life were extremely few.
Nevertheless, his disciples have continued the lineage from lamp to lamp, and their compositions now fill the world—how could these not also be the master’s own writings?
Having long neglected my pen and ink during this illness, I have taken up my brush to compose this preface upon the occasion of [his] joyous praise. I do not know whether it is truly fitting, yet...
Is it not a case of being self-opinionated?
On the fifth day of the first month of autumn in the Renzi year of the Wanli era, the lay practitioner Wang Kengtang, known as Nianxi,
wrote this preface to the *Weishi jishie* while struggling against his illness.

Although the teachings for a single lifetime differ in their accommodation of various capacities and vary in their specific approaches, if one examines where they ultimately converge, the two terms "nature" (*xing*) and "phenomena" (*xiang*) encompass everything without exception.
What is meant by "nature"? It refers to that which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, free from the four propositions, and transcending the hundred negations.
This is what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* calls the "quiescent single mind," and what the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* calls the "pure enlightened nature."
Furthermore, what is meant by "characteristics"? Within the fundamentally pure nature of awakening, there occurs a momentary lack of awareness;
this leads to the flowing forth of consciousness, the coagulation of form, the solidification of grasping, and the dispersion into emptiness.

Thereupon, the phenomena of form are divided into eleven, giving rise to the mutual production of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and so forth. The mental phenomena are divided into eight, and thus...

The characteristic of discernment (*vijñapti*) emerges. When the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are divided into fifty-one, the characteristics of contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), greed (*rāga*), ignorance (*moha*), and so forth emerge.

When the dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are divided into twenty-four, the characteristics of acquisition (*prāpti*), loss (*aprāpti*), arising (*utpāda*), cessation (*nirodha*), and so forth emerge.
When the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are divided into six, there are space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and so on.
The marks of equality emerge; the hundred dharmas proliferate; the myriad characteristics manifest transversely. Thus, the pure nature of awakening remains stifled and fails to flourish.

Consequently, ordinary beings perceive the marks but do not perceive the nature; they employ consciousness rather than wisdom. The three—sense organs, sense objects, and consciousness—gallop back and forth and escape one another.
At every turn they are bound by fetters; in every place they are stuck in attachment. The non-Buddhists and those of the Lesser Vehicle mistake [the head] for what they are lost to.

These shadows fail to realize that [all phenomena] are one's own mind; they erroneously cling to the notion that various dharmas exist as real entities external to the mind, and further cling to the idea that these dharmas possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, they distinguish between the light and dark hues upon flowers in the sky, and compare their length and brevity at the horns of a rabbit.
They form factions and divisions, contending with one another. It is for this reason that the meaning of establishing and refuting in the orthodox tradition of Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra was formulated.

Furthermore, this treatise takes Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) as its fundamental tenet. This means that the eleven factors, such as form (*rūpa*), are Consciousness-Only in terms of being the object-condition (*ālambana*);

the eight factors, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), are Consciousness-Only in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); the fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*) are Consciousness-Only in terms of association (*samprayoga*);
the twenty-four dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) are Consciousness-Only in terms of temporal states (*avasthā*); and the six unconditioned factors (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because this nature of consciousness is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), one understands that the five categories and one hundred dharmas are collectively termed *vijñapti-mātra*.

Since not even a fragment of a thing can be found apart from consciousness, the school is designated by the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*. Regarding the establishment of positions and the refutation of opponents:

for instance, when the eleven dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) are established as the objects of consciousness (*ālambana-vijñapti-mātra*), this serves to refute the views of non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna schools who maintain that mind exists externally [to its objects].

There truly exist all dharmas. The establishment of the eight consciousnesses as the self-nature of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) serves to refute the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) attachment to the six consciousnesses and the three poisons as the causes of birth and death;
it refutes the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools' reckoning of the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) and *pradhāna* (primordial nature) as the causes of birth and death;
and it refutes the attachment of certain classes of Bodhisattvas who deny that even consciousness exists. Thus, the fifty-one mental states are established.

Regarding the statement that "dharmas are merely consciousness in its associated state," this refutes the erroneous attachment of the Hinayana schools who maintain that mental factors (*caitta*) exist separately from the mind.

Furthermore, it establishes the twenty-four non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as being merely consciousness in its various states (*avasthā-vijñapti-mātra*).

To establish that true nature is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is to refute the Hīnayāna attachment to [attainments] such as *prāpti* and [elements] such as space as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, to posit the ten causes and four conditions as the causes for the arising of phenomena is to refute the naturalist non-Buddhists (*svabhāvavāda*) who claim that all phenomena arise without cause.
Therefore, if one seeks its essential purpose and investigates its beginning and end, it consists entirely of establishing and refuting.
This constitutes the meaning. Once the principles of establishing and refuting have been established, one knows that the myriad dharmas originally emerge from oneself and do not come from without;
they all arise dependently through conditions and are not substantially existent. Thus, the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths all lower their banners in surrender.
The eighteen schools of the Hīnayāna vied with one another to support the tracks of the Elephant (the Buddha), riding upon the openings he had initiated to lead others into the flawless state.

Bestowing new prescriptions, they drove away chronic ailments; thus, they gathered the hundred dharmas into the categories of characteristics and perception, and subsumed these characteristics and perceptions under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If one clings to a self or to phenomena based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one will sink into the river of ignorance.

If one realizes that the dependent nature is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one will move with ease within the ocean of awakening. Therefore, it is further clarified that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*), and these wisdoms are gathered to form the [Buddha] body.
Alas! After the ancient masters had seen their nature, some raised their hands, some shouted, some yawned, some stretched, and some brandished their staffs or held them upright.
They wave their sleeves; some protrude their tongues and raise their eyebrows, while others draw bows and nock arrows. Some dance with ceremonial tablets or roll balls;
some overturn meditation benches or kick over rice buckets; some bray like donkeys or bark like dogs—all of these are nothing other than the playful exercise of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*).

Those who elucidate Prajñā-Pāramitā do so without exception by striking out from within appearances and penetrating through consciousness. Thus, appearances are entirely nature, and consciousness is entirely wisdom;
only then can one attain true enjoyment, encounter the source at every turn, and find the sublime within the flow of phenomena.

Who would say that the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇavāda) is not essential? One knows this: that the nature (svabhāva) is not clarified because the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) have not been thoroughly penetrated.

Therefore, if one wishes to clarify the nature, one must first thoroughly penetrate the characteristics; only when the characteristics are thoroughly penetrated will the nature become clear of itself.

Now, since those who have realized the nature cannot be found, yet they further treat the characteristics as mere discarded hair, when questioned about the nature, they point to their chests or touch their tongues, or raise their arms and hold them aloft.

Quan said, "There is nothing that is not the Way. When asked about its characteristics, he replied, "The mouth is like a flat carrying pole; the eyes are like shooting stars. Quan said, "I have no use for such things.
To be crude and muddled, content to sit in self-deception—will the wisdom-lamp of the Buddhas not gradually go out because of this?
Is this not truly a matter of great lamentation? However, after Master Xuanzang had compiled this treatise, he orally transmitted it to Master Ji. Ji... [text continues]
The Master composed a commentary to explain its meaning. At that time, it was transmitted through direct instruction and personal guidance, becoming known throughout every household.
Consequently, from the Tang dynasty onward, those who propagated it became numerous, and those who realized their own nature were as plentiful as hemp and millet, found everywhere. Up until my...

Although the principles were clarified, their commentaries fell into obscurity; this treatise, too, was relegated to a high shelf. Consequently, the single lineage of the *lakṣaṇa* school (the Dharma-character school) remained dim and unmanifest.

Even those who attained the realization of nature (*jìng-xìng*) were as rare as the horn of a unicorn. Thus we know that while the realization of nature does not reside within characteristics (*xiàng*), it is in fact achieved by penetrating through characteristics to see nature.
Therefore, the *lakṣaṇa* school serves as the bright lamp for realizing nature, and is likewise the means for those wishing to reach Bodhi.
This is a single route map for the City of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-pura*). How could it be considered insignificant?

I, Run, having naturally shed my hair and donned the black robes, have improperly joined the ranks of those who lecture. Together with two or three like-minded companions, we have peered into its gates.

However, as my innate faculties are dull and slow, and my learning is further meager, when a single phrase from a passage easily understood enters my heart, it is like a thirsty person tasting nectar; it flows and overflows.
As for the flavor [of the teachings], whenever he encountered passages that were obscure, stammering, or convoluted, it was like chewing wax; thus, as soon as he read them, he would stop.
Later, upon opening the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), he finally succeeded in severing the barrier of his doubts and extracting the dark key.

From then on, he extensively explored such scriptures as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and others, as well as treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Vyākhyāyukti*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, along with the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the great sutras.

Among these, whatever was consistent with this treatise was immediately recorded by hand. Whenever my eyesight failed me, I invariably consulted those of recognized learning before finally taking up the pen.
Having accumulated these efforts over several years, I compiled them into this "Collected Commentary" (*Ji jie*).
Truly, I did not wish to mislead others with my own arbitrary speculations; therefore, I entitled it the "Collected Commentary. My sole hope is that future students may rely upon this commentary.
To thoroughly understand characteristics, to shatter characteristics, and to depart from characteristics—this would be fortunate.

If one relies on this interpretation yet remains mired in characteristics, then I shall have no words to offer against the reproach of being "like the extra legs of a snake. This commentary was first compiled in six fascicles during the winter of the year Jǐyǒu at Qiūshuī Ān in Yú;
it was subsequently completed in four fascicles during the summer of the year Xìnhài at Fúshān Lán'è in Hú.
The scroll was completed by the donation of funds and the request for its carving by the Yunshan Layman Jueshan.
Recorded on a summer day in the Renzi year of the Wanli era at the Cottage by the Tengg River.
*Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll One.
Composed by Bodhisattvas such as Dharmapāla and others;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled and annotated by the Śramaṇa Tongrun of Jinting Changshou Temple.

The Sanskrit term *siddhi* is translated in the Tang language as "accomplishment" (*cheng*). "Accomplishment" carries the meaning of being established and perfected; it refers to the establishment of the principles of the teachings and the perfection of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The Sanskrit term *mātra* is translated in the Tang language as "only" (*wei*). "Only" carries the meaning of "exclusive"; it signifies that there are no phenomena apart from the mind.
The Sanskrit term *vijñapti* is translated in the Tang language as "cognition" (*shi*). "Cognition" carries the meaning of discernment and differentiation; this applies to all eight consciousnesses.
Because it can discern its own object, the Sanskrit term *śāstra* is translated into Chinese as "treatise" (*lun*). A treatise has the meaning of "analysis";

it analyzes the five positions in order to instruct later students. The word "treatise" (*lun*) refers to the means of accomplishment, while "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) is that which is to be accomplished.

Since the means and the end are combined in this designation, it is called the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Demonstration of Consciousness-Only). This was after the World-Honored One beheld the stars.

He preached the Dharma for forty-nine years and expounded the sutras in over three hundred assemblies. To summarize: he took the one mind and the eight consciousnesses as the fundamental essence of his teaching.
Through the harmonious conjunction of causes and conditions, these manifest as the various phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Yet, the followers of the Lesser Vehicle and the non-Buddhists fail to realize that the triple world arises from one's own mind, and that the myriad dharmas are originally...

Regarding the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), they falsely conceptualize that there are real dharmas existing externally to the mind, and they falsely establish various divergent causes as the source of all dharmas.
Through such false teachings and erroneous understandings, they fall into ditches and pits.

Therefore, the great Bodhisattvas, giving rise to loving-kindness and compassion, rely upon the Mahāyāna sūtras to compose verses and commentaries, establishing the single school of Vijñaptimātra (Consciousness-Only) to guide and attract those of external paths.

The Hīnayāna emerges from the river of false views and returns to the ocean of nature; thus, this treatise exists. Now, these two characters "Vijñapti-mātra" (Consciousness-Only) possess ten meanings.

The first is the meaning of "discarding the unreal to preserve the real. This refers to the objects of the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature), which arise solely through false conceptualization and lack any substantial reality whatsoever.
They must be discarded because they exist only as mental projections and are non-existent in reality. That is to say, based on...
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is substantially real; it is the object of both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms and must be maintained.

This is because, in principle, sentient beings do not [truly] exist. It is truly due to the fact that all ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle have, since beginningless time, falsely clung to self and phenomena as being existent, while the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka falsely negated both principle and phenomena as being empty. Now, the Yogācāra contemplation...

In the middle [section], existence is dispelled by emptiness, emptiness is dispelled by existence, and both existence and non-existence are simultaneously dispelled by that which is neither existent nor non-existent;

therefore, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Second, the meaning of "discarding the mixed and retaining the pure": this refers to the two phenomena of object and mind, which arise in mutual dependence.

Because objects involve confusion and mixture, they are discarded as being unsuitable [for the ultimate sense]; since the essence of the mind is pure, it is called "consciousness-only. Thus, the subsequent passage states:
It is said: Consciousness exists only internally, whereas objects also extend externally. To avoid confusion with external objects, it is simply called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Third, this is in the sense of concealing the inferior and revealing the superior: that is to say, both the sovereign (the mind) and its attendants (mental factors) are capable of discernment; however, mental factors are inferior because they are dependently originated.

The mind-king (*cittarāja*) is superior because it is the substratum (*āśraya*). Since the subordinate factors are concealed and not taken up [as primary], it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "This teaching of consciousness-only merely reveals the superiority of the king; in principle, it includes the mental associates (*caitta*), just as when one says 'the king arrives.'"

It is not that there are no ministers or assistants; rather, it is the principle of gathering the branches back to the root. This means that the two divisions of the grasped (nimitta-bhāga) and the grasper (darśana-bhāga) are gathered back and returned to the essence of the self-cognizing division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) of the fundamental consciousness.
Therefore, it is called "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra). The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The objects of all consciousnesses..."

I. The Meaning of Manifestation by Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*). II. The Meaning of Abandoning Characteristics to Realize Nature (*lakṣaṇa-prahāṇa-svabhāva-sākṣātkriyā*). This means that while characteristics and functions are abandoned and not grasped, the essential nature is realized and not discarded;
therefore, it is called "Consciousness-Only. The *Saṃgraha* states: "Based on a rope, the cognition of a snake arises; seeing the rope, one knows it is non-existent.

When the perception of that [rope] is clearly realized, one then knows that the nature of clarity was a delusion. III. The Meaning of Objects and Consciousness (*viṣaya-vijñāna*). This refers to that which is observed...

Objects are manifested through the transformation of consciousness; since objects do not exist apart from consciousness, it is called "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra). The *Abhidharma-sūtra* states:

"That which is perceived by ghosts, humans, devas, and others differs according to each. Thus, the sevenfold teaching on the meaning establishes that the expressive teachings themselves proclaim consciousness-only.

The *Laṅkāvatāra* states: "Due to the attachment of one's own mind, the mind appears as external objects; that which is seen does not exist. Therefore, it is said to be 'mind-only' (*cittamātra*). **Eight.
The Meaning of Principle:** This refers to the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). The root verse says: "These various consciousnesses undergo transformation;
there is the subject of discrimination and the object of discrimination. Because these do not exist, everything is consciousness-only. **Nine. The Meaning of Practice:**

This means that when a bodhisattva is in the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), they perform the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and find that none of them are apart from consciousness (*vijñapti*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "When a bodhisattva is in the state of equipoise, they observe that the reflected image is nothing but mind. Regarding the meaning of the ten fruits:

this refers to the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) of the Buddha-fruit and all the merits possessed by a bodhisattva, none of which are apart from consciousness. As the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states: "True suchness (*tathatā*) is the objectless consciousness."

The pure, untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*)—as in the ten aforementioned meanings: nature, characteristics, objects, wisdom, teaching, principle, practice, fruit, tainted, and untainted—all these constitute the realization of the ultimate meaning of Vijñapti-mātra;
therefore, it is called the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Vijñapti-mātra). As for "volume" (*juan*), it carries the sense of unfolding and rolling up.
To unfold it is to peruse its text; to roll it up is to contemplate its meaning. Since this is spoken from the perspective of meaning, it is called a "volume."
"Also. "First" (dì) means "in sequence. "One" is the beginning of numbering. This treatise consists of ten fascicles; as this occupies the very beginning, it is called "the first."
Composed by Bodhisattvas such as Dharmapāla and others; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty by imperial decree.
This records the names of those who composed the commentary and translated it. Nine hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa...

The six heretical teachers vied with one another, and their false doctrines flourished. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu extracted the essential meanings of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and composed the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only).
Bandhuśrī, Sthiramati, and Pūrṇavardhana simultaneously composed commentaries upon it.
One thousand and one hundred years later, Dharmapāla, Guṇamati, Sthiramati, Nanda, Viśeṣamitra, Śuddhacandra, Dignāga, and Jñānacandra—these eight great [masters]...
The masters of the treatise (śāstrakāra) successively composed commentaries, each consisting of ten fascicles. Combining these earlier and later works, there were one hundred fascicles in total.
Consequently, later generations regarded Vasubandhu as the master of the root treatise (*mūla-śāstrakāra*) and the ten great masters of the commentaries (*vṛtti-śāstrakāra*) as the secondary masters.
Among these ten secondary masters, the four divisions of Dharmapāla were taken as the standard; thus, Dharmapāla was placed at the head. As for his...

Other masters, however, subsume [the preceding] under the term "etcetera" (ādi). Subsequently, Master Xuanzang synthesized these ten interpretations into a single work, compiling them into ten fascicles.
If one considers it the composition of a single master, it is this very treatise. As for the Tripitaka:

The Tripitaka consists of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma collections. A "Dharma Master" (fǎshī) is one who has thoroughly mastered these three collections and serves as a teacher and model for others.
"Translator" (yìzhě) means "to change"; it refers to changing the Sanskrit language into the language of the Tang dynasty.
I prostrate to the one who is perfectly pure in the nature of consciousness-only; I now explain that teaching for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

This single verse consists of two parts: the first half is the author’s expression of reverence toward the Triple Gem, and the second half is the author’s own statement of the intent for composing this commentary.
Regarding the word "prostrate" (*kai-shou*): *kai* means "to reach" or "to linger"; it refers to bringing the head down to the ground.
They remained for a short time to pay their respects. That which is the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) is the Dharma that is realized.

That which is "fully purified" refers to the Buddha, for he has exhausted the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) and forever extinguished the two types of death; thus, he is called "ultimate awakening.
That which is "partially purified" refers to the Sangha, for they have partially severed ignorance and partially realized the true principle; thus, they are called "partial awakening. This...
Both [the author and the commentator] are individuals capable of realization. Question: For what reason must one pay homage to the Triple Gem at the beginning of a treatise?
Answer: Because it is the most auspicious; because it is the true field of merit; because it possesses great power; because it gives rise to the superior mind;

and because it is able to bestow its grace—it is necessary to pay homage. Question: Since the two natures of essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mutually manifest and presented together, why do you show partial homage to only one of them?

Question: Its nature does not equal its characteristics. Answer: Because it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); because it is exclusively the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); because it is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because it is what is realized by the noble ones (*ārya*);
and because it is the basis for both delusion and awakening. For these reasons, one pays special reverence to it. Question: Why is it that the Dharma exists prior to the Buddha?
Answer: Teacher and disciple are mutually dependent; the Dharma comes first and the Buddha comes later. The Dharma is the mother of all Buddhas, for all Buddhas flow forth from within it.
When other sources speak of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they are explicitly explaining their mutual dependence.
The Buddha comes first and the Dharma follows, for it is man who can propagate the Way. A question is asked:

"Since the Master of the Treatise has already composed the thirty verses, by what causes and conditions did he further compose this commentary? The answer is: "The reason for commenting upon those thirty verses is as follows:"
Desiring to bring great benefit and great peace and happiness to all deluded and erring sentient beings, I have now composed this treatise [up to the point where it states]:
"By severing the cognitive obscurations that hinder understanding, one attains Great Enlightenment."

From this point until the section "Therefore, I have composed this treatise," the author personally recounts the causes and conditions for composing the treatise in order to clarify his intention to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

Regarding the "two emptinesses" (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), these are the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). These two emptinesses constitute the structural framework of this treatise;
therefore, they are mentioned at the outset. Regarding the term "delusion and error," it refers to those who do not understand, namely the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
It is said: "Delusion. The heterodox interpretations of the Hīnayāna are termed "error. Being both deluded and erroneous, the correct eye is obscured.
It is for this reason that the Master composed this commentary, so that those who possess false knowledge and erroneous understanding may attain true knowledge and authentic realization. Question:

Question: What is the benefit of generating understanding? Answer: Generating understanding serves to sever the two types of heavy obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). "Obstacle" has the meaning of covering and obstructing.
It covers the true mind and obstructs wisdom from arising. There are two kinds of obstacles: namely, the afflictive (*kleśa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya*).
What are the afflictions (*kleśa*)? They refer to the delusions of views and mental afflictions (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa*), which disturb sentient beings and cause them to dwell long in saṃsāra.
What is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)? It refers to all forms of ignorance (*avidyā*), which obstruct the objects of knowledge and prevent wisdom from arising.

These two types of obstructions are both comprised within the twenty-six root and derivative afflictions. Because these root and derivative afflictions possess the function of causing agitation and disturbance, they are termed the "affliction-obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*). There is...
The function of obscuration and hindrance is termed the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Therefore, if one wishes to sever this obstruction, one must first give rise to understanding;
once understanding has arisen, practice will commence; and once practice has commenced, the obstruction will be severed. Question: From what do these two types of obstructions arise?

Answer: The two obstacles arise together due to the grasping at a self and at phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*). "Grasping" (*abhiniveśa*) has the meaning of stubborn attachment and refusal to relinquish.

Because foolish worldlings stubbornly cling to the notion that all phenomena possess a real, sovereign self, and furthermore cling to the notion that phenomena exist as real entities external to the mind, these are called the two graspings at self and phenomena.
Due to these two graspings, the two obstacles subsequently arise. With the grasping at a self as their root, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are produced.

The hindrances take the clinging to phenomena as their root, giving rise to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). That is to say, when the notions of self and phenomena arise, the hindrances emerge. Question:
If this is so, by what means are these two types of hindrances severed? Answer: If one realizes the two kinds of emptiness, those hindrances are severed accordingly.

This means that when one is able to contemplate that within the phenomena of the five aggregates there is fundamentally no sovereign, asking "Who is this 'I'?", this is the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, when one contemplates that the phenomena of the aggregates are likewise not truly existent, asking "What is this 'dharma'?", this is the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Once one is able to realize and enter these two types of emptiness, those two obstacles should, upon mere thought, transform into unsurpassed awakening—namely, the [realization of] self and dharmas.

Emptiness is the exhaustion of hindrances. Because of grasping, hindrances are formed; through emptiness, hindrances are severed. Since one has fallen from the ground, one must rise back up from that very ground.
Question: What benefit and joy are there in severing hindrances? Answer: Severing hindrances is for the sake of attaining two supreme fruits.
Because the hindrance of afflictions obstructs Great Nirvāṇa, it causes all sentient beings to revolve in birth and death; therefore, it must be severed.

[The practitioner] attains rebirth and immediately realizes liberation. Regarding "attaining rebirth," this refers to the continuity of the linking of birth (*pratisandhi-saṃtati*), which is precisely the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-lobha-avidyā*).
Because the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obstructs great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), it prevents sentient beings from attaining perfect awakening;

therefore, by severing the obscuration to liberation, one attains bodhi. "Obscuration to liberation" refers to the non-forgetting of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); [the result is] the pure liberation that is realized.
This is because it constitutes an obstruction.

Furthermore, it is for the purpose of revealing and demonstrating the erroneous attachment to a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), so that one may know the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only) as it truly is.

This explains the delusion of worldly beings by specifically distinguishing between the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). "Revealing" (*kai*) means to open up; "demonstrating" (*shi*) means to point out. "Self" (*wo*)... [text continues].
The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent, yet it is falsely grasped; therefore, it is called "error. Consciousness-only is fundamentally existent, yet it is not known;

therefore, it is called "delusion. "Self" refers to what worldly people grasp as a sentient being or a life-principle; "knower," "seer," "agent," "experiencer," "thinker," and so forth, refer to what non-Buddhists grasp as such.
"Dharma" refers to what the Sāṃkhya teachers grasp as the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), beginning with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Superior...

The masters of the treatises maintain the six categories of meaning and so forth; all of these are delusions regarding the originally existent *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only), erroneously clinging to a fundamentally non-existent self and phenomena.
Therefore, these masters of the treatises loftily erect the banner of the Dharma, establishing true inference (*samyag-anumāna*) to demolish these two types of clinging.
This indicates the two kinds of emptiness so that those who are deluded regarding *vijñaptimātratā* may realize true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, because there are those who are confused and mistaken about the principle of *vijñaptimātratā*, this treatise was composed so that they may attain a correct understanding.

This is based on the four types of grasping, specifically clarifying the delusions regarding the sacred teachings. Previously, one grasped at a self and at phenomena within the [subjective] characteristics and views;
hence it was called "delusion and error. Here, one calculates existence or non-existence regarding objects and consciousness; hence it is likewise called "delusion and error.

Alternatively, if one grasps that external objects are not non-existent in the same way as consciousness—as in the "Realist" schools of the Hīnayāna who, relying on the teaching of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), grasp at the mind—[this is also such a delusion].

Regarding the coexistence of objects and consciousness: some maintain that internal consciousness, like its objects, does not exist—just as Bhāviveka, relying on the sūtras of intentional emptiness, negates the existence of consciousness itself.

Others maintain that while the functions of the various consciousnesses differ, their substance is identical—such as certain Mahāyāna bodhisattvas who claim that although the eight consciousnesses have different functions, their substance is but one, just as a single body of water or mirror reflects many waves or images.
Regarding those who hold that there are no mental factors (*caitta*) distinct from the mind, such as the Sautrāntika Buddhadeva:

they maintain that there is only the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and no mental factors at all. This is because a sutra states that for a person (*pudgala*), the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*)—both defilement and purification—depend upon the mind;

since there are no mental factors, although mental factors are mentioned among the aggregates (*skandha*), they are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*) for particular states (*avasthā*) within consciousness.
They do not exist as separate, real entities. As with the four aforementioned masters, some lean toward existence while others stagnate in emptiness;

some omit its function while others lack its essential basis. Their views differ and their attachments vary, yet none have been able to penetrate the subtle principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Therefore, these various commentators, in order to refute such attachments, [aim to lead them] to attain [realization] within the profound and subtle principle of consciousness-only.

I have composed this treatise because I seek to understand reality as it truly is. The preceding section concludes the explanation of the causes and conditions for composing the treatise; the following section provides the formal commentary on the thirty verses.
If there is only consciousness, how is it that the world—[from "arises" to] "transforms"—is said to exist? This means that differences are provisionally established in accordance with conditions.
Question: It may be granted that worldly people, not understanding *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), falsely cling to a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).
However, within the sacred teachings, those who do understand *vijñapti-mātra* also speak of a self and phenomena; how can this be? Next, a verse is cited as a general response.

The *Śāstra* states [below] that it explains the verse: that which is clung to by worldly people is called "worldly self and phenomena," while that which is established by the sacred teachings is called "sacred."
I shall teach you the Dharma. These two—self and phenomena—are both conventionally established; they do not possess an intrinsic nature.

Worldly self and phenomena are called "conventional" because they lack substantiality and follow mere conceptual attachment. The self and phenomena taught by the Noble Ones are also called "conventional" because, although they possess substantiality, they are provisionally designated.

Why are they called "conventional as lacking substantiality and following conceptual attachment"? Because they originally lack a real substance, yet are [grasped] through deluded conceptual attachment.

Regarding what is grasped: although there is no self or phenomena (ātman-dharma) as they are grasped, they are nonetheless called "self" and "phenomena" in accordance with the objects of the grasping mind.

This is termed a "provisional designation based on attachment despite the absence of a real entity. What, then, is meant by a "provisional designation established through force despite the existence of a real entity"? Although the entity of the phenomenon exists...

It is not that there is a self or dharmas; because the essence of dharmas is nameless, we forcibly designate them as "self" and "dharmas," yet these do not correspond to the actual essence of dharmas.

They are provisionally established in accordance with conditions. This is called a provisional designation of a self where there is no substantial entity. A "self" refers to a controller; "controller" implies the possession of sovereign power.
The "ruler" (*adhipati*) possesses the power of discernment and severance. The "master" (*prabhu*) is my essence, while the "ruler" is my function;

therefore, the master is the co-emergent self (*sahaja-ātman*), spontaneously sovereign and belonging to the seventh consciousness, whereas the ruler is the conceptualized self (*vikalpa-ātman*), because it possesses the power of discernment and severance.

The "self" and "dharmas" belonging to the sixth consciousness refer to what is called "guiding and maintaining. This means they can guide their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Both of these manifest with various aspects. The term "both" refers to the self and dharmas.
"Both have various aspects" means that there are many kinds of aspects of the self, and likewise many kinds of aspects of dharmas; hence it is said they are "both."

Regarding "my various characteristics," such as "sentient being" (sattva), "life-principle" (jīva), and so forth— the term "and so forth" includes "nourisher" (poṣa), "person" (pudgala), "born one" (jantu), "seer" (draṣṭṛ), "knower" (vedaka),
the "agent" (kartṛ) and "experiencer" (bhoktṛ) and "thinker" (mantṛ) postulated by non-Buddhists— this refers to a self that lacks intrinsic substance and exists only according to worldly convention.

Regarding "stream-enterers" (srotāpanna), "once-returners" (sakṛdāgāmin), and so forth— the term "and so forth" includes the three levels of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and the ten stages of the noble ones (ārya).

The three vehicles, the five natures, and the twenty-five states of existence—these are the phenomena with substantial reality (*savastuka*) that are provisionally established as "self" within the holy teachings.

As for the various characteristics of phenomena, such as substance, quality, and activity, the term "etc. includes the twenty-five *tattvas*, as well as Mahābrahmā, Īśvara, time, space, the primal limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), spontaneity, and the nature of things;
these are the phenomena without substantial reality (*avastuka*) that follow worldly convention. The aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*)...

"Elements and so forth" includes, by way of "and so forth," dependent origination, the faculties, the truths, the conditioned, the unconditioned, the contaminated, the uncontaminated, and all dharmas of skillful mastery;
these are dharmas established as having substantial existence. "Transformation" refers to the provisional designation of differences according to conditions;
this means that the various characteristics mentioned above are all provisionally designated in accordance with manifold conditions, each being distinct.
They differ; however, none of them designate the actual nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), as they are all merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

The above has generally clarified that both the self and phenomena within the two categories of worldly and noble teachings are merely provisional establishments, thereby explaining the first two lines of the verse.
Regarding these various characteristics, if they are established through conventional designation (upacāra), [it is because] those two—the self and phenomena—have no basis apart from this.

Question: If these various characteristics of the self and phenomena are all merely conventional designations following conditions, upon what do they rely as their substance to achieve their establishment?
Answer: Those two characteristics of self and phenomena both rely on the transformation of the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*) for their conventional designation.

This designation does not possess a real substantial entity. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to that which cognizes and distinguishes. "Cognizing" (*vijñā*) means thorough comprehension; "distinguishing" (*vi-jñā*) means differentiation.

This is because all consciousnesses are capable of thoroughly comprehending and differentiating their respective objects. Question: Mental factors (*caitta*) are also capable of cognizing and distinguishing.
Why is it not mentioned? The answer is: here, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) also includes mental factors (*caitta*), because they are necessarily associated with it.

The phrase "here" refers to what is stated in the verse. If one were to say that the verse mentions only that which is transformed by consciousness without mentioning mental factors, [it would be incomplete].
Because mental factors always arise in dependence upon the mind and are associated with it, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) alone necessarily includes the mental factors.

"Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) means that the substance of consciousness transforms and appears as two parts; both the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) arise based upon the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

By the phrase "the substance of consciousness," one refers generally to the self-witnessing parts of all eight consciousnesses, because within the self-witnessing part, there arises the appearance of the subjective perceiver.
That which is called the "seeing-part" (darśana-bhāga) manifests as if it were the object; that which is called the "image-part" (nimitta-bhāga) is the objective support.
These two parts are termed the "dependent nature" (paratantra-svabhāva), because they arise in dependence upon self-realization (svasaṃvedana). The deluded do not understand this;

based on this seeing-part, they posit the grasping of a self (ātma-grāha), and based on this image-part, they posit the grasping of phenomena (dharma-grāha). Therefore, it is said: "Based on these two parts, the [grasping of] self is posited."

This is the Dharma. Thus, the two divisions—the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga)—constitute the supported (āśrita), while the two attachments to self and phenomena (ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa) constitute the supporter (āśraya).
Since there is no supporter apart from the supported, it is said that "those two [attachments] have no support apart from these [two divisions]. Question:

Since a single self-witnessing consciousness (svasaṃvedana) transforms into the semblance of the two divisions, are the two types—the perceived and the perceiving—the same or different? Answer: They are both the same and different. They are the same...
As for "the same," it means that a single substance transforms and appears as two parts, just as a single snail manifests and produces two horns; therefore, they can be said to be the same.
As for "distinct," the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is a functional differentiation of the self-verifying part (svasaṃvedana-bhāga); thus, apart from consciousness, there is no separate seed.
The image-part (nimitta-bhāga) necessarily takes consciousness as its support; the seed of the image-part transforms and arises as something resembling the image. This is...

Therefore, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) arises from a distinct seed. Question: Since the objective aspect has its own separate seeds, why is it called a transformation of consciousness? Answer: Because it is not separate from consciousness;

for when internal consciousness undergoes transformation, the objective aspect subsequently arises. Thus far, it has been specifically explained that worldly self and phenomena arise from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

Alternatively, "internal consciousness transforms appearing as external objects" (up to) "conditioning this and grasping it as a truly existent external object" demonstrates that, according to our Noble Teaching, the self and phenomena arise from the transformation of internal consciousness.

Alternatively, the phrase "internal consciousness transforms appearing as external objects" precisely clarifies that the self and phenomena arise from the transformation of internal consciousness and do not exist as real entities external to the mind; therefore, they are said to be "appearing as objects."

Although these semblances of objects are transformed by internal consciousness, they are in fact produced through the power of the mutual perfuming of the seeds of the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*).
Therefore, when internal consciousness arises, it can transform itself into these semblances.

Sentient beings, failing to realize that these semblances of objects appear from internal consciousness and that their substance is fundamentally empty, instead falsely reckon these semblances to be real.
There is. It is just like a person afflicted by dreams who, through the power of their own dreaming, manifests various similar objects.
Failing to realize that the dream-scene is not real, they instead cling to these dream-objects as truly existent.
Yet they do not know that while in the midst of the dream, these objects have never been non-existent; nor do they know that after waking, these objects have never [ceased to exist].
It exists. Thus the Sūtra says: "It is like a person in a dream; while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, it cannot be found at all.
The above explains the third line of the verse.
Regarding the "real self and real dharmas" imagined by fools (up to the point where it says): "However, because they appear as such, they are said to be conventional.
This concludes that the self and dharmas of the world are worldly conventions, while the self and dharmas of the Noble Teaching are conventions of the Noble Teaching.
One is a designation based on deluded sentiment; the other is a transformation of internal consciousness. Therefore, they are [distinguished].
Because external objects are established in accordance with conceptualization, [they exist] as the basis for that [conceptualization]; thus, they also exist as ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sat*).

Beyond this, both external and internal objects are subsumed within consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). Question: For what reason do real persons (*pudgala*) and real phenomena (*dharma*) not exist at all outside of the mind, such that only internal consciousness exists?
Answer: External objects are the objects of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), being established in accordance with conceptualization.
Designations have no substantial reality whatsoever, being like the horns of a rabbit; they are not like the illusory existence of internal consciousness.

The substance of internal consciousness is *paratantra* (dependent), existing by relying on causes and conditions, like flowers in the sky; it is not like external objects, which are utterly non-existent.
Because the nature of external objects is non-existent and the nature of internal consciousness is non-non-existent, [this] negates the external.

Considering this, there is indeed an increase in attachment regarding objects separate from the mind, as well as a decrease in attachment through false emptiness—the erroneous grasping of emptiness by those with wrong views who negate even consciousness itself.
The meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) is made clear herein. Question:

If external objects are merely established by deluded mental constructions, they may be said to be provisional. However, internal objects are actually transformations of internal consciousness; for what reason are they also [considered provisional]?

[Question: Provisional. [Answer: Although internal objects are transformations of internal consciousness, they are not entirely non-existent; according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), they are called "provisionally existent.
Internal consciousness is the substance upon which these provisional objects depend; according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is called "substantially existent.

Thus, one should know that both the two kinds of self and dharmas in the world and in the sacred teachings are all provisionally existent and are entirely subsumed within Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Apart from consciousness, there is no separate phenomenon. Therefore it is said: "At the summit of the Peak of Profound Mystery, it is not of the human world;
outside the mind there is no dharma—before one's eyes are the green mountains."
How should one understand that there are truly no external objects? [This is because they] secretly transform within the body and perform their functions.
Question: The world consists of the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world (the environment), all of which are real objects external to the mind.

Why do those who advocate *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) claim that internal consciousness is what exists, internal objects are merely appearances, and external objects are non-existent? Answer: Because of what is perceived by the world...

Because the grasping at a real self and real dharmas is entirely without substance, one knows that there is only the manifestation of what resembles external objects, which is transformed by internal consciousness.
Question: Present-day people are able to know, see, speak, act, create, and experience.
"All these are truly existent presiding lords within this [body], who secretly bestow and silently direct [its functions]; only through them can [the body] be accomplished.
How then can a real self not be found? Answer: "Although the selves and dharmas clung to by the world are many, to speak briefly, there are but three types:
first, the self that is identical to empty space; this is the 'experiencer' self (*bhoktṛ-ātman*) postulated by the Sāṃkhya teachers."

The first is the self conceived as a creator, as posited by the two [schools]; the second is the self that is indeterminate in its expansion and contraction, as posited by the Lion-King (Mṛgārāja) and Vyāsa;
the third is the self as a minute atom (*paramāṇu*), as posited by the Ahrīka heretics and the Nirgranthas.
These are known as the three theories of the six teachers. The remaining ninety types do not, in total, transcend these.
First, this is not reasonable. Why? Because all dharmas that are cultivated and realized are conjoined with a self.
First, [the author] refutes the "self" that is identical to empty space. He first sets forth the external inference as follows: "The self is a real entity;

its essence is eternal and omnipresent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it performs actions and experiences their fruits in every location. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like empty space. This...

The thesis commits the fault of the "unestablished predicate" (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*); the reason commits the fault of the "contradiction with the specific characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddha-hetu*);

and the example commits the fault of the "unestablished locus of the property to be proven" (*asiddha-sādhyadharmika*). Therefore, the *Hetuvidyā* states: "Regarding the 'unestablished predicate,' it is as when a follower of the Buddha posits to a Sāṃkhya that sound is subject to destruction.
Regarding the 'reason contradictory with the specific characteristic of the property,' it is as when one says that sound is eternal because it is produced."

Because it is of the nature [of being a property], this reason exists only in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); therefore, it is contradictory (*viruddha*). Regarding the case where the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is not established:
for example, one might say, "Sound is eternal, because it lacks resistance, like an atom. Next, one establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute it as follows:

"The self (*ātman*) is a subject; its thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is eternal and omnipresent; the reason (*hetu*) is that it should not experience pleasure, pain, and so forth in accordance with the body; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like..."

Regarding "emptiness" (*ākāśa*): thus, the *Inmyeong so* (Commentary on Valid Cognition) states that when one presents a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to an opponent, if the three members [of the syllogism] are complete and clear, thereby enlightening the respondent, it is called a "true proof" (*sādhanābhāsa*).
To refute an incomplete inference or to point out errors in the text while enlightening the proponent, it is called a "true refutation" (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
When one presents an inference to an opponent but the three members are deficient or erroneous, failing to enlighten the opponent, it is called a "pseudo-proof" (*sādhanābhāsa*). To falsely refute...
It is not perfect. The critique contains errors and fails to realize the opponent's position;

thus, while it appears to be a valid refutation, because the opponent presents a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) that possesses faults in its three members, it cannot be complete. Therefore, I first expose those faults in their argument, and subsequently employ their own argument to refute it.
In this way, their position becomes a "pseudo-establishment" (*sādhanābhāsa*), while my position constitutes a "true refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*). This is what is meant by "seizing" (*apahāra*).
A thief kills another thief. Next, let us refute [the opponent's position] by examining its similarities and differences.

Furthermore, if the essence of the self (*ātman*) as you maintain it is identical to space and all-pervasive, then the essence of the self you maintain must be the same as the essence of the self maintained by those sentient beings.
