Question: Since the view of self does not take a real self as its object, what then does it take as its object?

[Question: [What is the object of this grasping? [Answer: It takes as its object only the internal consciousness that manifests the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) appearing as the semblance of a self.
Following one's own deluded sentiments, one universally conceptualizes these as a real self; however, there is no truly existent, real self that can be taken as an object.
However, all forms of self-grasping can only be eliminated by repeatedly cultivating the superior meditation on the emptiness of persons.

Below, this section briefly indicates the two types of self-grasping, their points of origination, and the manner in which they are abandoned through cultivation. Regarding "innate" (*sahaja*) grasping:
it arises simultaneously with the body and functions spontaneously. Regarding "conceptual" (*vikalpita*) grasping: it functions through deliberation and discursive calculation.

Because it arises [simultaneously]. The following section on "co-emergent self-grasping" (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) precisely clarifies that co-emergent grasping differs from conceptualized (*vikalpita*) grasping.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "It follows far behind the manifest activity as an object of non-intentional conditions; from beginningless time until now, it exists spontaneously.
It does not depend on intentional conceptualization, investigation, or analysis, just as a small child feels joy upon seeing its mother—this is co-emergent greed."
Seeing someone weeping is innate anger (*sahaja-dveṣa*), for it arises spontaneously without depending on external conditions. An ancient master said:

"The student of the Way does not recognize the Real, solely because they have recognized the 'conscious spirit' (*vijñāna*) from of old. This has been the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas;
the deluded call it the 'original person. It is what the *Mencius* refers to as the 'heart of the infant,' and what is called 'innate knowledge' (*liang-zhi*)."
All such capacities are subsumed under this category. This [consciousness] is of two kinds:

first, the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its substantial basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*), and transforms its own image as its objective division (*nimitta-bhāga*). Taking this objective division as its object, it clings to it as a real self.
This is called the innate grasping (*sahaja-abhiniveśa*). This grasping occurs uninterruptedly from moment to moment; thus it is called "constant continuity" (*nitya-santati*).

Second, this refers to the sixth consciousness taking the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) as its object, either grasping them collectively as a self or grasping them individually as a self.

Regarding "collective grasping," this means that the sixth consciousness relies on the appearance of the aggregates transformed by the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as its substantial basis (*ālambana-pratibhāsa*), while itself transforming an internal image to serve as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Taking this objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) as a basis, one clings to it as a real self. As for "clinging to something else," this refers to clinging to form (*rūpa*) as the self, or clinging to sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth as the self;
all of these take the reflected image (*pratibimba*)—which arises based on the underlying substance (*mūla*)—as their object, clinging to it as a real self.
This is also called "innate" (*sahaja*). Whether this clinging arises or ceases, it is termed "interrupted. These two types of innate clinging are difficult to sever because they are subtle.

Because it has operated spontaneously from beginningless time, it continues until the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), where one practices the superior contemplation of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*).

It is gradually severed stage by stage until, upon reaching the Vajra-like Mind (*vajropama-citta*), it can finally be completely eliminated. As for the term "superior emptiness of arising," it is called "superior" because it distinguishes this from the emptiness of arising realized during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Question: Why does it not speak of the "emptiness of self" (*ātma-śūnyatā*) or the "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)?
Regarding the statement "emptiness of beings" (*sattva-śūnyatā*): the answer is that if one speaks of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it does not encompass other realms of existence;

if one speaks of the emptiness of the self (*ātman-śūnyatā*), there are those who cling to external phenomena as being the self. Therefore, one speaks of the emptiness of beings to harmonize and integrate these perspectives.
The grasping at a self through discrimination (up to the point of its cessation) can be eliminated by contemplating the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of arising in all phenomena.
Regarding "external conditions": this is said in contrast to internal causes, referring to false teachings and false discrimination.

The characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the characteristics of a self as taught by false teachings refer to the real aggregates and real self external to the mind, which were previously clung to by non-Buddhists and followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). These two—

The grasping at a self is coarse and thus easy to sever; within the stage of the path of vision, at the initial moment of the first bhūmi, when the universal true suchness of the emptiness of persons manifests before one, it is severed all at once and instantaneously.
All such aforementioned forms of self-clinging—from [the clinging to] the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*)—erroneously grasp these characteristics as a self.
This concludes the two types of self-clinging. The phrase "all such aforementioned forms of self-clinging" refers back to the two types of self-clinging mentioned above.
Regarding the statement that the aggregates external to one's own mind may exist or not exist, the *Zongjing* says: "The subject that perceives..."
That which is not a point of attachment is termed the "distant object-condition external to the mind. The seventh [consciousness] conceives of a self;

the phenomena external to the mind may either exist or not exist, because as long as the seventh consciousness has not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it must necessarily rely upon an external objective substrate.

The sixth [consciousness] conceives of a self; the phenomena external to the mind may either exist or not exist, for this consciousness possesses a sharp and intense mode of activity (*ākāra*) across all states.
Because it can function with mastery. Regarding the statement that "all [factors] exist within one's own mind":
when the subjective cognition encounters an object and attains a point of attachment, this is precisely what is called the "intimate object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) within the mind.

Whether one considers it separate or not, that which is reckoned as the self must necessarily exist as the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga). Therefore, the following section provides a concluding demonstration.
However, because the characteristics of the aggregates arise from conditions (up to: all of them arise dependent upon the five aggregates of grasping).
Question: Among the characteristics of the five aggregates of grasping and the imagined self, which exists and which does not? Answering by means of a formal inference (*pramāṇa*):
The characteristics of the aggregates definitely appear to exist, because they arise by depending on causes and relying on conditions, just like a magical illusion.
Furthermore, the proof states: "The self as falsely grasped is definitively non-existent, because it is a mere arbitrary conceptualization, like that which is absolutely non-existent.

Thus, the sutra below provides scriptural evidence: "The five factors, beginning with form (*rūpa*), fully encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), because they are accumulations of various conditions and are produced by their collective action.
Since not even the slightest phenomenon is produced by a single condition, they are called 'aggregates' (*skandha*). Defilements are called 'grasping' (*upādāna*)."
Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*): they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*) because they arise from clinging, like fire from straw or chaff;

or, the aggregates belong to clinging, and are thus called "aggregates of clinging," like the subjects of a sovereign; or, the aggregates produce clinging, and are thus called "aggregates of clinging," like a tree that bears flowers and fruit.
If a real self (*ātman*) does not exist, how could these things be possible? [This applies] up to: "In this, you have committed an error, but it is not a fault in our own school.
This refutation of the self presents a difficulty regarding the three times. The objection states:

Because worldly people possess a self, they are able to remember the past, cognize the present, and study for the future; they experience benefit or harm to themselves, and engage in such matters as being benefactors or enemies. Now...
If you say that the self does not truly exist, then who is it that recollects the three periods of time? First, we shall refute this by means of its essential nature.
You claim that the self you grasp is permanent and unchanging, such that all three periods are identical.
Thus, the present would be the same as the past, and the past would likewise be the same as the present. If the present were identical to the past, then the essence of the self would be eternal.
If there were no [self], then the enmity and gratitude of the three periods of time would likewise be eternally non-existent; who then would perform recollection, recognition, and study?
If the past were identical to the present, then the substance of the self would be eternally existent. If the substance of the self were eternally existent...
Enmity and gratitude across the three periods of time should likewise be ever-present; what need is there to recall, recognize, or rehearse them? Why is this so?

Because the essence of the later [moment] is no different from that of the earlier. Next, [the argument] is refuted by means of its function: if it is claimed that the essence of the self is fundamentally without change, [then...]
Furthermore, it is logically untenable to claim that while my essence remains constant, its functions undergo change such that there are activities like recollection, cognition, and rehearsal;

for essence and function are not separate. If function were not separate from essence, and the essence were eternal, then the function would also have to be eternal, and thus my functions should not undergo change.
Conversely, if the essence were not separate from the function, then as the function changes, the essence should likewise change.

Then my substance (ātman) should not be said to be permanent. Upon investigating from both sides, one cannot say that it is "I" who remembers and recites matters such as the enmities and favors of the three periods of time. Next, the correct principle is revealed:

however, matters such as the enmities and favors of sentient beings are seeds of a single type, maintained within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), which continue in an uninterrupted succession. By means of these seeds...
My son, all phenomena act as causes for one another, being perfumed moment by moment; thus there arise memory, cognition, recitation, study, gratitude, resentment, and so forth.
This does not mean that a real self acts as the perceiver. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"In years past, you may have seen a strange object, and though many years have passed, you have neither remembered it nor forgotten it. Later, suddenly seeing that same extraordinary thing again,"
Memories remain as clear as ever, never lost; thus, within your essential clarity and profound stillness, you are perfumed by every thought-moment—how could there be any calculation?
Therefore, know that the true self does not take the three periods of time as its object.
If there were no real self (*ātman*), who could perform karma? (Up to: that one who performs karma and receives its fruit is not logically contradictory.
This refutes the objection that the self is the agent and the experiencer. The objection states: "If there is no real self, who performs the karma?

Who receives the fruit? First, he establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute it: "A real self cannot be the agent or the experiencer, because it is devoid of transformation (*avikāritvāt*), just like [space]."
[The opponent says: "Space. Furthermore, they measure [the argument] as follows: "If a real self were capable of acting and experiencing, it would be subject to change;

therefore, it must be impermanent. Next, the correct meaning is set forth: "However, those sentient beings who are capable of creating and experiencing are all the eight types of mind-kings (*citta-rāja*)."

Furthermore, through the power of the primary mind and its mental factors (caitta), the internal causes and external conditions that initiate karma and moisten rebirth, and the force of habitual perfuming (vāsanā), there arise matters such as the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma, including the beautiful and the ugly;
it is not a real self that acts or receives these results.
If there were truly no self, who would transmigrate through birth and death? (Up to: It is only the foolish who falsely grasp at this [process] as a self.
This refutes the difficulty regarding aversion toward and seeking after the self. The objection states: "If there is no real self, who is it that sinks into birth and death?
Who is it that realizes nirvāṇa? First, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute it: Since the essence of the self is permanent and thus lacks arising and ceasing, it is like space.
What is meant by wearying detachment? Since the self is eternal and free from suffering, it is like space;
what, then, is there to seek or pursue? Thus, their attachment to an eternal self is self-destructive. Next, the correct principle is revealed:

however, all sentient beings, driven by the power of afflictions, create various evil karmas and thereby undergo saṃsāra. Because they suffer from birth and death, they feel weary [of cyclic existence].

Because of the three realms, one seeks to attain nirvāṇa. From this, it is known that there is certainly no real self that can act as the agent of birth-and-death or nirvāṇa, nor of suffering, pleasure, cause, or effect.
There are only various consciousnesses that perish before and arise after, with cause and effect continuing in succession like the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale at equal times.
Thus, one knows that all causes and effects do not depart from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna). However, by...
Due to the perfuming of false conceptions, that which resembles the appearance of a self manifests. The deluded, being ignorant of this, grasp it as a real self.
For this reason, the masters of the treatises, at the outset, refute the grasping at a self and directly reveal the emptiness of the self; this truly has its underlying intent.
How can one know that external phenomena truly exist? (Up to: These are real and not merely conventional appearances obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The refutation of the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) is hereby complete. Below this, the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is formally refuted. The question is asked:

"If all various mundane and supramundane phenomena are all substantially existent apart from the mind, how can one speak of 'Cognition-Only' (*vijñaptimātra*)? Apart from consciousness, [what exists]?"

"Is there not a single dharma that can be apprehended? He replied: "Because when external dharmas clung to by non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles are investigated through reasoning, none of them exist.
Again he asked: "In what way do those things clung to by non-Buddhists not exist? First, below the section on the Sāṃkhya school, he provides their specific tenets.
In Sanskrit, *saṃkhyā*; here it is translated as "number" (*shù*). This "number" refers to the number of mental factors (*buddhi-saṃkhyā*). Number...

The fundamental basis for the designation of all phenomena is established through enumeration; thus, it is called Sāṃkhya (the Theory of Enumeration). Because this theory can produce enumeration, it is also termed Sāṃkhya.
Its original source was composed by Kapila. The *Saptati-śāstra* (Seventy Verses) was composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa.
Its system of reckoning consists of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). According to the *Śata-śāstra*, from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) arises Intellect (*buddhi*), and from...
From the arising of consciousness (*buddhi*), the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*) is produced. From the "I-consciousness," the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise;

from the five subtle elements, the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); and from the five gross elements, the eleven organs (*indriya*). The *puruṣa* (Spirit) is the sovereign, characterized by eternal consciousness. Abiding in the center, it is indestructible and imperishable, and it appropriates all phenomena.
Now, based on the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are summarized briefly into three categories. [The first category is] *prakṛti*.

The middle [classification] consists of four; the extensive, twenty-five. First, regarding the threefold summary: first, *svabhāva* (self-nature); second, *ahaṃkāra* (the "I-maker"); third, *vikāra* (transformation).
*Svabhāva* is the primary truth (*prathama-tattva*), also called *pradhāna* (the primal nature).

When it has not yet produced the *mahat* and other elements, but merely abides in its own state, it is called *svabhāva*. Once it produces the *mahat* and so forth, it is then called *pradhāna*, because its activity is preeminent.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The supernatural powers of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) extend to eighty thousand kalpas;
beyond eighty thousand kalpas, they are shrouded in darkness and know nothing, hence it is called the 'Dark Principle' (*mṛta-tattva*). From this, initial awakening and cognition arise.

Second, regarding the statement 'I know,' this refers to the twenty-fifth principle, the Divine Self (*ātman*). Third, as for 'transformation,' the intermediate twenty-three principles are its own..."

That which is produced by nature is called "transformation. Thus, there are three stages. Regarding the four [stages] situated in the middle: first, the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) is without transformation;

second, the great elements (*mahat*, etc. are both fundamental and transformed; third, the six [subtle elements] are merely transformed; fourth, the knower (*puruṣa*) is neither fundamental nor transformed.
The first means that the fundamental nature can produce the great elements and so forth; therefore, it is called "fundamental" (*mūla*). It does not arise from anything else. Therefore...
It is not a transformation. The two *mahat*s, the *ahaṃkāra*, and the five *tanmātra*s—these seven are both primordial (*prakṛti*) and transformations (*vikṛti*).

Because the *mahat* arises from the primal nature (*prakṛti*), it is a transformation; because it can produce the *ahaṃkāra*, it is a primordial cause. Because the *ahaṃkāra* arises from the *mahat*, it is a transformation.
Because they can produce the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), they are primary causes (*prakṛti*). Because the five subtle elements arise from *ahaṃkāra*, they are transformations (*vikṛti*);

because they can produce the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), they are primary causes. The three internal organs—the five organs of perception, the five organs of action, and the mind (*manas*)—arise solely from others;
therefore, they are only transformations. Since they cannot produce others, they are not called primary causes. The fourth knower is the Self (*ātman*).
Taking "cognition" (*vijñāna*) as its essence, it does not arise from another, nor can it produce another; therefore, it is neither original nor subject to transformation.
There are twenty-five categories in detail, as explained in the *Śata-śāstra*. However, there are nine positions in total. Within these, the twenty-three truths themselves comprise seven positions:
first, the Great One (*mahat*); second, the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*); third, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); fourth, the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); fifth...

Five are the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*). Six are the organs of action (*karmendriya*). The seventh is the organ of mental equilibrium (*sāmānyendriya*). Including the first and the last [of these categories], there are twenty-five. Question:
Since the primal nature (*prakṛti*) is invisible by its own nature, how is it known to exist? Answer:

Because the great elements (*mahat*) and other phenomena arise from the primal nature, and because it possesses the three qualities (*guṇa*). Question: How is it that the primal nature can serve as the cause of production for all phenomena?

Answer: Because of the conjunction of the three *guṇas*. The three *guṇas* are, in Sanskrit, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. In older translations these were rendered as "sorrow," "joy," and "darkness";

in newer translations they are rendered as "greed" (*rāga*), "hatred" (*dveṣa*), and "delusion" (*moha*). Because of this self-nature (*svabhāva*), through the conjunction of the three *guṇas*, it is able to produce the twenty-three principles (*tattvas*).
Self-nature is the agent; the *puruṣa* (Spirit) is not the agent. Question: If it is not the agent, what is the use of the *ātman*?
[Question: For what purpose? [Answer: For the purpose of realizing the object (*artha*). "Object" refers to the sphere (*viṣaya*); it is for the sake of realizing that sphere.
That is to say, the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) are what I know; I am the seer, not the agent, and others cannot know them. [Question:
If the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is the agent and the self (*ātman*) is not the agent, by what cause do they unite? [Verse Answer: "The self seeks to perceive the three qualities (*guṇa*)."
The *prakṛti* exists in isolation, like the union of a cripple and a blind man; from this principle, the world arises.
When it is said, "I seek to see the three *guṇas*," it means that I have such an intention: "I shall now see the *prakṛti* consisting of the three *guṇas*"; therefore, I am united with the *prakṛti*.
As for the statement that the *prakṛti* exists in isolation, it means: "I am a person in distress, possessing only [the capacity for]..."
Because it sees, the self-nature (*svabhāva*) acts as the other, enabling [the self] to exist independently. It is like the union of a cripple and a blind man.

The self-nature unites with the self (*ātman*), just as the blind man unites with the cripple; for the self is like the cripple because it cannot act, and the self-nature is like the blind man because it cannot see.
Through the union of these two, they are able to produce the world and provide enjoyment for the self, just as the cripple [provides mobility].
The blind each find their respective locations; each attains its own station. When I perceive the self-nature (*svabhāva*), I immediately attain liberation, such that I alone remain.

Question: It has already been stated that the conjunction [of elements] can produce the world. What is the sequence of this production? Answer in verse: "From self-nature, the sequence of production arises:
the Great [Elements], Ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and the sixteen. Within the sixteen, there are five; from these..."

The five great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise. That is to say, first the self-nature (*svabhāva*) arises; "great" (*mahat*) has the meaning of increase, because the characteristics of self-nature increase.

This "great" is also called awakening (*bodha*), also called perception (*saṃjñā*), and also called knowledge (*jñāna*). Following this "great," the grasping at a self (*ahaṃkāra*) arises. As for this grasping at a self:

The functioning arising from self-nature observes the "I" and knows it; because this knowledge of the "I" requires an object, it is also called *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") and is also named the beginning of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Next, regarding the sixteen that arise from *māna*: these are the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*), the five active faculties (*karmendriya*), and the mind-faculty (*manas*) as the faculty of equanimity. This passage generally clarifies that all sixteen arise from *māna*. Regarding the ten...
Among these six, first the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements) arise. From the five *tanmātras*, the five great elements (*mahābhūtas*) arise; from the five great elements, the eleven faculties arise.
First, regarding the arising of the five *tanmātras*: (1) sound, (2) touch, (3) form, (4) taste, and (5) odor. Each of these five possesses both substance and function.

They are called *tanmātra* because they possess a limited measure (*mātra*), because they are determinate (*tan-mātra*), and because they are determined to produce the five great elements through their specific functions. From sound...

Sound alone gives rise to the great element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*). Touch alone gives rise to the great element of wind (*vāyu-mahābhūta*). Form alone gives rise to the great element of fire (*tejas-mahābhūta*). Taste alone gives rise to the great element of water (*ap-mahābhūta*).

Fragrance alone gives rise to the great element of earth (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*). Next, regarding how the five great elements give rise to the eleven faculties (*indriya*): first, the five faculties of cognition (*vijñānendriya*) arise; next, the five faculties of action (*karmendriya*) arise;
and finally, the mind-faculty (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) arise. How do the five great elements give rise to the five faculties of cognition? It is as follows:
Sound arises solely from the great element of space; space constitutes the auditory faculty. Therefore, the ear hears sound. Tangibility arises solely from the great element of wind;
wind constitutes the tactile faculty. Therefore, the tactile faculty experiences tangibility. Visible form arises solely from the great element of fire.
The fire element constitutes the eye faculty; therefore, the eye faculty perceives visible forms. Taste arises solely from the water element; the water element constitutes the tongue faculty;
therefore, the tongue faculty perceives tastes. Fragrance arises solely from the earth element; the earth element constitutes the nose faculty;
therefore, the nose faculty does not perceive the earth itself, but perceives fragrance. Next, the five faculties of action arise: first, speech.
1. Possession; 2. Both hands; 3. Three feet; 4. Urination; 5. Defecation; as well as grasping, walking, playing, and laughing—these are excluded.

Regarding the faculty of mental equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), its essence is discrimination (*vikalpa*). Thus, the treatise says: "Discrimination is the characteristic of the mind. This characteristic is the mental object itself.
The sixth [faculty] possesses five [aspects] and is established as such because it universally takes all objects as its conditions. Regarding the twenty-fifth, "I know," it is by means of...
The intellect (*buddhi*) conceives of itself as the "I. How is it known that there is an "I"? Because the aggregate [of the elements] exists for the sake of another, that "other" is the "I.
Due to the three qualities (*guṇa*), which are the cause of saṃsāra, the "I" is agitated by their transformations; thus, liberation is not attained.

By knowing that the twenty-three principles (*tattva*) are subject to transformation and impermanent, one develops revulsion and cultivates the Path. When the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) withdraws its manifestations, the various [evolutes] cease to arise.
"Truth! I am liberated. Therefore, the verse says: "I am neither bound nor liberated; I do not transmigrate through birth and death.
This is because there is no possession of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), because there is no transformation, and because there is no agent. Question: If this is so, who is it that is bound?
Who is it that attains liberation? Answer: Saṃsāra and bondage; liberation is only the intrinsic nature (svabhāva). It is through the transformation of the intrinsic nature that there is bondage;
if one attains perfect universal knowledge (samyak-saṃbodhi), one immediately attains liberation.

This means that the twenty-three truths are understood as perfect universal knowledge, clarifying that bondage and liberation do not depend upon a self (ātman). To say "I am liberated" is merely a conventional designation based on the [intrinsic nature].
However, there is liberation. Here, the statement "the one who conceives 'I' is the thinker" refers to that boundless and unliberated *puruṣa* (spiritual self) which they postulate.
This *puruṣa* is able to experience the twenty-three principles, beginning with *mahat*, which are produced by primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the three *guṇas*.
While primordial nature and the three *guṇas* can only produce these twenty-three principles, [the *puruṣa*] cannot...

Regarding "enjoyment": the enjoyer is the *puruṣa* (the self). However, those twenty-three principles they postulate, such as the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, although composed of the three *guṇas*, are all substantially real.
They are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are directly experienced through enjoyment.
This is precisely what is currently conceived here [in China] as the primordial chaos (*hundun*), as Laozi described it: "profound and obscure. Its...
Within it is an essence, vague and indistinct; within it is a substance. Zhuangzi said: "The essence of the ultimate Way is profound and dark;
the pinnacle of the ultimate Way is obscure and silent. These all refer to the *mindingi* (the principle of darkness). This is the general recognition of a mass of ignorance as the ultimate Way.
To overturn this *mindingi*, one immediately realizes the Great Treasury of Radiant Light (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*).
That position is irrational; why is this so? [This section] first refutes it, then interrogates it, and finally employs a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to dismantle it.
It states that each of the twenty-three categories, such as the "Great One" (*mahat*), is entirely produced through the combination of the three qualities (*guṇas*).
Just as an army, a forest, a jar, or a chariot exist only through combination, they are not substantial entities (*dravyadharma*).

How can it be said that [substances] are apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Therefore, he first sets forth the external inference (*bāhyapramāṇa*), stating: "The subject (*dharmin*) is 'the great elements' (*mahābhūta*) and so forth;
the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are real and not nominal, and are apprehended by direct perception. He states the reason (*hetu*): "Because they are composed of the three things.
Since this thesis claims they are real and not nominal, yet the reason is that they are composed of the three things, the thesis and the reason are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, the opponent counters this thesis by refuting it. He establishes the following syllogism: "The subject (dharmin), 'wholes such as large [size],' must be nominal and not real;
this is the thesis (pakṣa). The reason (hetu) is: 'because they are composed of three things. The example (dṛṣṭānta) is: 'like an army, a forest,' and so forth."
Furthermore, if dharmas such as the Mahat were substantially existent (up to the point where they undergo transformation and are impermanent), the same logic would apply.
This serves to mutually refute the producer and the produced. The "original substance" (*prakṛti*) refers to the three *guṇas*.

The meaning is that if the twenty-three principles beginning with the Mahat were substantially existent, they would be identical to the three *guṇas* as producers; they could not be a composite of the three, nor could they be [distinct from them].

It is stated that [the principles] such as *mahat* are produced from the three *guṇas*. Since that which is produced is identical to that which produces it, he proceeds to refute this by means of formal inference (*pramāṇa*), saying:
"The various dharmas such as *mahat* are not composites of the three [guṇas], because they are substantially existent, just like the three primal substances (*prakṛti*).
If the three *guṇas* were themselves the twenty-three principles, then the three *guṇas* would likewise have to be composites of the three *guṇas*. Because...

Because that which is capable of producing is identical to that which is produced. He then sets forth a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to refute [this view], saying: "The three—sattva and the others—are also composites of the three;
since they are identical to the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, they should be like the Great Elements and so forth. Below this, he refutes by analogy regarding transformation:

if the primal matter (*prakṛti*) is capable of transformation, then the Great Elements and so forth should also be capable of transformation. He sets forth a formal inference to refute [this], saying: "The dharmas of the Great Elements and so forth are also capable of transformation."

[They] transform because they are substantially existent, just like the three primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Since the great elements and so forth are impermanent, the primary elements must also be impermanent.

To refute this, one establishes the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*): The triad of *sattva* and the others must also be impermanent, because they are identical to the great elements and so forth, just like the phenomena of the great elements themselves.

Furthermore, each of the three primary natures (*mūlaprakṛti*) possesses multiple capacities (up to the point where it is said that "the others should also be so," because there is no difference in their essence).
This is a refutation based on the identity of essence and function. "Capacity" refers to function.

If these three qualities (*guṇa*) were each capable of producing twenty-three phenomena, then these three qualities would each possess multiple capacities. Since the capacities are many, then these...
The substance of virtue (*guṇa*) should likewise be manifold, because substance and function are inseparable. Substance is identical to self-nature (*svabhāva*).

As the *Śataśāstra* states: "If this grasped self-nature were supreme, then one part would possess function and transform into [the elements such as] 'Great' (mahat) and so forth, while other parts would lack capacity and undergo no transformation.
This would mean that the very self-substance must become manifold. Because it becomes manifold..."
Concentration (*samādhi*) is impermanent. Furthermore, regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), each possesses numerous functions such as clarity, agitation, and dullness.
Since it is admitted that the substance (*svabhāva*) and its function are identical, if the nature conforms to the function, it would follow that there must be multiple substances.
Because the supreme nature (*parama-svabhāva*) is without differentiation, the supreme substance would likewise have to be multiple. If the substance were thus multiple, it would follow that...
Just as with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, [the three qualities] are necessarily impermanent.

If it is claimed that the substance of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), being all-pervasive in a single location, undergoes transformation when a function arises in that one location, then all other locations should likewise undergo transformation simultaneously;
for the substance of the three qualities is pervasive and without distinction.
It is granted that these three things have distinct essential natures and characteristics; therefore, one should not say that the three combine to form a single unity.

This is a refutation based on their distinct essential natures and characteristics. Even if it were granted that the three *guṇas* have distinct essential natures and characteristics and are not all-pervasive—

How could they combine to form a single characteristic? If it is argued that while they have not yet combined they remain three, but at the time of combination they transform into one—this principle is also untenable.
For there is no difference in the essence of the three *guṇas* whether they are combined or uncombined;

how could there be a principle whereby they remain three when uncombined but become one at the time of combination? If it is argued that although the essences of these three things are distinct, their characteristics...

This is the same [point]. Therefore, when they are in a state of conjunction (*saṃnipāta*), if they were to become a single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*), it would contradict your own tenet that the substance (*svabhāva*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) are one.
If you claim there is no such fault because the substance is different while the characteristic is the same, then the substance ought to become indistinguishably one, just as the characteristic is.
Alternatively, the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) should manifest as three, just as the substance (tattva) does.

If this were so, then a single substance would have to constitute a single characteristic, or the three characteristics would have to constitute three substances. One should not say that the three substances combine to form a single characteristic.

Regarding the two terms "single characteristic" (ekalakṣaṇa), if they are distinguished here in terms of substance and characteristic, then the "single characteristic" is the transforming agent (pariṇāmin).
If the subsequent text were to distinguish between the general and the specific, then the single characteristic would be that which undergoes transformation;
by means of this single characteristic, that [other] single characteristic is established. In reality, there are not two.

Furthermore, the three [guṇas] are the particulars and the Great One (mahat) and so forth are the universal; since the universal should likewise consist of three, how can one perceive it as a single entity?
This is a refutation based on the identity of the particular and the universal: the three guṇas are the particular characteristics, while the Great One and so forth are the universal characteristics.
Because the three guṇas together produce a single phenomenon, if these two—the universal and the particular—are mixed into a single location, then the "one" [cannot exist].
One is established, but the three do not establish three. How can the three *guṇas* combine to produce a single characteristic?

If it is argued that although the three *guṇas* undergo transformation, they do not actually combine to form a single characteristic, then at the time of their transformation, since they are not combined—[how could they produce one?]
It would be no different from the time when they are not changing. Furthermore, one should not say that they become a single color and so forth;

for how could one perceive three *guṇas* becoming a single color? If you claim that the three *guṇas* combine to form a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then the distinct characteristics of the three *guṇas* must necessarily be lost.
Once their distinct characteristics are lost, the very substance (*svabhāva*) of the three *guṇas* must also follow suit and perish along with those characteristics.
[The individual characteristics] are lost. Since the essential characteristics are lost, by what means could a single characteristic be formed?

If it is argued that each of the three qualities possesses both general and particular characteristics, and therefore, although they form a general characteristic, the particular characteristics are not lost—this is also not the case.

This is because it is impossible to say that each of these three *guṇas* possesses the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) such as "mahat" (the Great One) and so forth, as well as their own individual characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
This is because the general characteristics such as "mahat" are themselves the individual characteristics of the three *guṇas*.

If one were to claim that the general characteristic is identical to the individual characteristic, then upon each of the general characteristics such as "mahat," there would have to exist the individual characteristics of the three *guṇas* respectively; how could it be otherwise?

One perceives the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of color as a single unity, such as "greatness" (*mahat*), yet does not perceive the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the three constituents (*guṇas*).

How, then, can they be grasped as objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Yet, that treatise states that objects such as jars and clothing exist because of [the presence of] qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), substances (*dravya*), sameness (*sāmānya*), difference (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).
Because it is seen by the eye and touched by the body, it is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as an object of the sense-faculties. This is certainly not the case.
A cognition of a substance (*dravya*) induced by qualities (*guṇa*) is not subsumed under direct perception;

that is to say, a cognition of a substance induced by various qualities such as blue or warmth is definitely not subsumed under the direct perceptions of seeing or touching. It is not [induced] by karma, generality (*sāmānya*), or particularity (*viśeṣa*).
It arises because it is produced in dependence upon and following from the conjunction with other characteristics.

Just as the knowledge of reality induced by smell and taste, up to the knowledge of reality induced by sameness and difference, is not subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) such as seeing or touching—because it arises in dependence upon and following from the conjunction with other characteristics—it is like all cognitions of non-reality and so forth. Therefore, one should know that all [such cognitions] are likewise.
Cognition produced through the conceptual synthesis of words is not a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that truly apprehends its object;

rather, it is a cognition that takes what is real as its object, yet is not a true direct perception because it is produced through conceptual synthesis, like the cognition of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

In this way, even up to cognition that takes a composite whole (*saṃghāta*) as its object, it is also not a true direct perception that apprehends its object, because it is produced through conceptual synthesis, like the cognition of reality (*tattva*) and so forth.
Therefore, one should not maintain that among the six categories of meaning (ṣaṭpadārtha) there exists an object of direct perception (pratyakṣa).

However, all that is reckoned as direct perception by the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) is actually invalid cognition (apramāṇa); thus it is refuted by saying: "All these are merely false conceptual constructions (parikalpita), not true direct perception."
There are those who maintain that there is a single Great Lord (Maheśvara), [and so on], up to: "He should also produce [effects] instantaneously because He is eternal.
This ash-smearing outsider (kṣapaṇaka) forms this conception because he observes that sentient beings in the world do not act according to their own desires.
Why is this? It is because we see sentient beings in the world who, while at the stage of the cause, desire to cultivate pure karma but fail to achieve their wish and instead commit evil;
and while at the stage of the fruit, they pray to be reborn in a happy realm but fail to achieve their wish.
They subsequently undergo various sufferings. Seeing this, they think: "There must necessarily be another creator, a progenitor, and a transformer who acts as the father of those things;
namely, Īśvara, the cause of all things, who is able to produce all phenomena. To refute this, it is said: "If that Īśvara were able to produce [them]..."
That which is a conditioned phenomenon is necessarily impermanent; being impermanent, it is not omnipresent; and not being omnipresent, it is not ultimate reality.
If you claim that its essence must be eternal and omnipresent, and that because all virtues are inherently contained within that essence, it is therefore able to produce [all things], [then...]
Then it would follow that at all places and at all times, all phenomena would arise simultaneously, without necessarily depending on those [beings'] desires or the conjunction of various conditions.

If the Lord (Īśvara) must further wait for those desires and those various conditions before he can produce [phenomena], then he contradicts the doctrine of a single cause consisting of the Lord. If it is claimed that the Lord is omnipresent...

If all phenomena were produced such that desire and its conditions also arose from themselves without depending on anything else, then desire and its conditions would likewise arise instantaneously, because that single cause would be constantly present. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"If all things in the world were produced by a single cause, such as Īśvara, then everything would arise simultaneously; this is not the case."
They arise in succession. Since we observe that all phenomena arise in a sequential order, we know for certain that they are not produced by a single cause.
If one were to maintain that Īśvara causes these phenomena to arise and causes these phenomena to cease according to his own will, then he would not truly be "sovereign" (īśvara).
Furthermore, because they arise from the distinctions of desire (*icchā*), or rather, because the distinct desires would have to arise simultaneously—
since their cause, Īśvara, is without distinction— if these distinct desires do not arise together because they further depend on other causes,
then it is not the case that everything has the single principle of Īśvara alone as its cause; or else, those causes upon which they depend must likewise further depend on others.
If [the world] arises sequentially due to differences in causes, then the causes upon which it depends must be infinite.

If it is argued that although the will of Īśvara arises instantaneously, the various worlds do not arise simultaneously because they arise in accordance with his will, this is also logically untenable;
for that will of Īśvara is no different between its prior state and its subsequent state.
Other assertions that there is a single Great Brahmā who produces all phenomena are all refuted in the same manner.
Those who assert the existence of Mahābrahmā are the proponents of the fourth Veda and the fifth Ātman theorists.
The Vedas maintain that Nārāyaṇa can produce the four castes, while the Ātman theorists maintain that it is Brahmā.
It is capable of producing all things. The *Devanirvāṇa-śāstra* states: "From the navel of the god Nārāyaṇa, a great lotus flower arises;
upon this flower is the progenitor Brahmā. That Brahmā creates all living and non-living beings."
Brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā; Kṣatriyas were born from his two arms; Vaiśyas were born from his two thighs;

and Śūdras were born from his two feet. As for those who calculate time, they immediately dismiss the non-Buddhists who maintain that all things arise from time, because they observe that through the conjunction of various conditions—such as sowing seeds—fruit sometimes arises and sometimes does not. Time...
There is a functional activity that either expands or contracts, causing those stalks and so forth to flourish or wither accordingly.

Although this [activity] is not visible at the time, one knows that "time" exists by means of the seasonal nodes, flowers, fruits, and so on. As for the theorist of direction (dig-vādin), he is the fifth master of the treatises;
he maintains that humans are born from the directions, that humans arise within heaven and earth, and that after death they return to the directions. Therefore, the directions are...
The first is the eternal (*nitya*). This is the cause of *nirvāṇa*.

Those who calculate the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) are the teachers of the Āṇḍavāda school, who say that at the very beginning of the past, the world consisted only of a great mass of water, from which a great cosmic egg (*mahāṇḍa*) was produced, shaped like a hen’s egg.

His countenance was like the color of gold. Later, it split into two sections: the upper became heaven and the lower became earth, with a single Brahmā-deva in between, capable of creating all things animate and inanimate.
According to the *Sanwang li* (Calendar of the Three Kings), when heaven and earth were in a state of chaotic unity (*hundun*), Pangu was born within them.
In one day he underwent nine transformations; he became the spirit of heaven and the sage of earth. Heaven...
The sun was one zhang high; the earth was one zhang thick; and Pangu was also one zhang tall.

After eighteen thousand years had passed in this manner, heaven opened and earth was laid out. Pangu had the body of a dragon and the head of a human. His head reached to the extreme east and west; his feet reached to the extreme east and west;
his left hand reached to the extreme south, and his right hand reached to the extreme north. When he opened his eyes, dawn broke; when he closed his eyes, night fell.
Exhaling is called "summer" (shǔ); inhaling is called "winter" (hán). Blowing the breath forms wind and clouds; the sound "zhà" becomes thunder and lightning.

When Pangu died, his head became the character "jiǎ," his throat "yǐ," his shoulders "bǐng," his heart "dīng," his gallbladder "wù," his spleen "jǐ," his ribs "gēng," his lungs "xīn," his kidneys "rén," and his feet "guǐ.
His eyes became the sun and moon; his whiskers became the stars.
The eyebrows are the polar axis; the nine orifices are the Nine Provinces; the breasts are Mount Kunlun; the knees are the Southern Peak; the thighs are Mount Tai; the corpse is fish and turtles;
the hands are flying birds; the claws are tortoises and dragons; the bones are gold and silver; the hair is grass and trees;
the fine hairs are wild ducks; the teeth are jade and stone; sweat is rain; and the large intestine is the Yangtze River.
The ocean is [the kidneys]; the small intestine is the Huai and Si rivers; the bladder is the myriad streams; and the facial disc is Lake Dongting. Wei Zhao’s *Tongji* states:
"According to secular tradition, Pangu underwent seventy transformations in a single day: he overturned to become heaven and lay prostrate to become earth.
He died at eighty thousand years of age. This is also somewhat similar to the Western Regions' reckoning of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Therefore, it is recorded here. As for those who calculate [existence] as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*), they are the proponents of causelessness (*ahetuvādin*).
They maintain that all things arise spontaneously without a cause and perish spontaneously. This spontaneity is eternal and is the cause of all things. For example, thorns are naturally sharp;
the black color of a crow is not dyed, and the white color of a crane is not washed. At times a violent wind suddenly arises, and at other times it ceases.
[The breath] ceases. At times a violent river overflows, yet in a single moment it suddenly dries up completely;

at times fruit-bearing trees flourish, and at other times they wither. Because of this, the view that things arise without cause arises. This is roughly the same as the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi in this land.
As for "empty space" (*ākāśa*), it refers to the ninth school, the Ājīvikas, who reckon that empty space is a single entity.
"Permanence" is the cause of all myriad things. From emptiness arises wind; from wind arises fire; from fire arises warmth; from warmth arises water;
from water arises ice; ice becomes solid earth; from earth arise the five grains; the five grains give rise to life.

When life perishes, it returns to emptiness. As for "Self," it is identical to what was previously refuted; apply the same refutation as before, using the argument against the "Independent Creator" (Īśvara) as an analogy.
If one wishes to understand this in detail, one must consult treatises such as the *Śataśāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
There are others who hold the biased view that sound is eternal because it depends on various conditions, just like a jar or a garment.

The "treatises on knowledge" (*vidyā*) refer to the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*): namely, logic (*hetuvidyā*), inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), grammar (*śabdavidyā*), arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*), and medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*).
"Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) refers to that which is definitive and unchanging; it is the valid authority of the sacred word (*āptavacana-pramāṇa*).

This refers to the Grammarians (*Śabdika*), who exclusively maintain that among the five sciences, the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*)—which expresses and defines all phenomena—is eternal. Furthermore, they hold that the nature of all sound is...

The permanent does not arise from conditions; rather, it is manifested in dependence upon conditions. It is like a bell or a drum that resounds when struck by a mallet, or metal and stone that ring when tapped;
likewise, the meaning of a text is manifested through its verbal expression. Therefore, the *Hetuvidyā* states:

"If one establishes that sound is impermanent because it is produced, this reason is unestablished for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*) in a debate with a proponent of the theory that sound is manifest, for such a proponent maintains that sound..."
The phonemes (*akṣara*) are eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing; yet, it is only through their being articulated that they can be made manifest.
The following refutation states: both [positions] are irrational. Next, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute them:

"Furthermore, the sound of the *Veda* (the *Śruti*) must not be eternally abiding, because it is admitted to be expressive, just like any other sound. This is because the sound of the *Veda* and other sounds are identical in their nature as sound."
Next, the measurement [of the argument] states: Other sounds and the essence of sound are likewise not eternal, because they depend upon various conditions, just like jars, garments, and so forth.
There are non-Buddhists who maintain that although earth, water, fire, and wind are impermanent, their essence is substantially real.

There are two types of proponents who calculate [the world] in terms of atoms (*paramāṇu*). The first are the non-Buddhist Lokāyatika teachers, who calculate that both mental phenomena (*nāma*) and physical phenomena (*rūpa*) are composed of atoms.

However, among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), that which is most subtle and refined, and which possesses the capacity for objective cognition (*ālambana-cintā*), is what constitutes mental phenomena.
Just as all visible matter consists of the four great elements, yet only a lamp emits light while others do not, so too are the four great elements [distinguished].

Among these, there are those who can engage in objective reflection. Second, they reckon the atoms (*paramāṇu*) to be eternal because they do not understand dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as it truly is.
They claim that gross matter is produced from atoms; yet when gross matter is gradually analyzed, its very nature is that of the atom.

Therefore, while gross matter is impermanent, the causal measure [of the atom] is eternal. What is called "gross matter" refers to the "subordinate atom" (*putra-paramāṇu*), whereas the "causal measure" refers to...
The "parent atoms" (*pitṛparamāṇu*) are the most subtle initial atoms; they are called "parent atoms" because they aggregate to produce all material forms.
That which is produced is the "child atom" (*putraparamāṇu*). Although the child atom is impermanent, it does not transcend the parent atoms; therefore, it is substantially existent.
That too is irrational. Why? [From here until: How can it be said that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal?
First, the proof of the non-existence of atoms as a permanent cause is refuted. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated: The essence of the postulated atom must not be real.
Because they possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), like the trail of ants, and so forth. Next, the production of gross derivative matter (*rūpa*) by atoms is refuted.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "The atoms you assert must not collectively produce gross derivative matter, because they lack spatial dimensions, just like the mind and mental factors.
Third, the permanence of atoms is refuted. The formal argument is as follows: "The atoms you assert are certainly not permanent."
It is able [to produce], because it gives rise to a fruit, just like that which is produced.
Furthermore, the fruit produced does not exceed the measure of its cause; as with a coarse fruit, there is no distinction in the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Fourth, the refutation based on the effect-form not exceeding the magnitude of its cause. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

Furthermore, the produced effect should not be apprehended by the sense organs such as the eye, because it does not exceed the magnitude of its cause; it would be like an atom (*paramāṇu*), for they [the opponents] maintain that atoms are not apprehended by the eye.
Fifth, the refutation based on the confusion of cause and effect characteristics. First, the opponent’s counter-argument is restated: If it is claimed that the effect-form and...

Regarding the argument that "the effect is a coarse color because it is conjoined with a cause that is coarse, and it is certainly that which is apprehended by the sense organs," the refutation is established through formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows:

The grasped resultant color lacks the quality of coarseness because it is conjoined with a cause of the same measure; therefore, it must be like an atom (*paramāṇu*). Alternatively, it must be an atom itself.
Furthermore, it is consistent with being coarse because its location is not distinct [from its cause], just like coarse resultant form (*phala-rūpa*).
If one were to claim that resultant form pervades its own causes, then for this reason it would also not be apprehended by the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
Sixth, refuting [the opponent's view] by analogy with the cause. First, the counter-argument is restated:

If it is claimed that the resultant form (*phala-rūpa*) is omnipresent within its own causes, yet the substance of those causes is not unitary and may be termed "gross," this is refuted by establishing a formal inference (*pramāṇa*). The argument is:

The substance of the resultant form you maintain must be non-unitary, because its locations are distinct, just like the causes in which it resides. Since the result is just like the cause, even though it is gross...
It is also subtle. Therefore, gross matter is likewise not apprehended by the sense faculties.
If [you claim that] it becomes gross because many fruits are combined, then what you maintain is internally contradictory from beginning to end.
Regarding the refutation of the eight causes: first, the thesis is restated; then, it is refuted from below by means of multiple causes.

If it is claimed that gross matter does not arise from atoms, but rather that gross matter is composed of many parts and is apprehended by the sense faculties, then [this would imply] multiple causes consisting of atoms.

Furthermore, coarse matter can also be produced through synthesis; it is just like this. Thus, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) as causes, being material in nature, are sufficient to constitute an object and be apprehended by matter.
Why then wait for resultant matter to synthesize into coarse matter before it becomes an object of the sense faculties?

If coarse resultant matter is already composed of many parts, it must not be substantially real. Consequently, the causal relationship you maintain between prior and subsequent moments would be undermined.
This is contradictory.
Furthermore, the claim that the effect and the cause both possess material obstruction [is refuted] up to the point that it is merely a false conceptualization following worldly sentiment.

Ninth, the refutation is based on the fact that cause and effect cannot mutually contain one another; the formal syllogism (pramāṇa) used for this refutation can be understood from the preceding section. Next, the counter-argument is restated.

If it is argued that the effect enters the cause and the cause receives it, or that the cause enters the effect and the effect receives it—just as water enters sand and the sand receives it, or as medicine enters copper and the copper receives it—the following refutation is made: "Who allows that sand can receive water, or that copper can receive medicine?

Next, a refutation by means of concession and withdrawal (*anujñā-pratiṣedha*) follows: If it is claimed that cause and effect both mutually enter one another, then all their constituent parts would be separated.

If, like separate objects, they do not produce an effect together but instead transform themselves into coarse matter, then it follows that they cannot be considered a single, permanent entity, because the resulting matter would exceed the dimensions of its causes.
Furthermore, this is refuted by both the concessive and the apagogic arguments.

If you claim that although the characteristics of the cause are manifold, the characteristic of the effect is a single entity, then when one part is perceived, all parts should necessarily be perceived.
Because this and that are both one, and because the one is the all; if one does not admit that the one is the all, it contradicts reason.
If one admits that the one is the all, it contradicts facts. Therefore, what they grasp is merely a false conceptualization.
However, although the categories of non-Buddhists are numerous, [if their view were correct], there would be no distinctions such as blue or yellow among colors and so forth.
This [passage] generally refutes four types of attachments. First, the attachments are set forth: "existent phenomena" refers to derived phenomena;

"existence-nature" refers to the existence-nature of both the primary elements and the derived phenomena. These attachments are refuted below: let it not be that all phenomena are identical to existence-nature.
This is because phenomena (*dharma*) and principles (*tattva*) cannot be grasped as being identical; for while the principle is one, phenomena are diverse. Thus, the *Śataśāstra* states:
"If colors such as blue were identical to the nature of color (*rūpatva*), one should know that the essence of the nature of color would be the same for all.
If sounds such as pleasant ones were identical to the nature of sound (*śabdatva*), they should likewise have the same essence as the nature of sound. If the sense faculties and their..."
If their nature were one, then their substance would have to be identical according to that nature.

Consequently, each individual sense organ would have to apprehend all objects, and each individual object would have to confront all sense organs. In this way, the distinctions established by your own school would all fail to be established.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: If there is a phenomenon that shares the same nature as existence (*sat*), its essence must be identical;

its essence would be without distinction, just like the nature of existence itself. If this were so, it would contradict one's own tenets, contradict common worldly consensus, and contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because blue, yellow, and other such qualities are objects of direct perception.

Second, the attachment to the existence of dharmas and their nature as "existence" (and so forth). [This extends to] the point that they should not be objects of the eye and other faculties, just like sound and the like.

First, the attachment is set forth; it is refuted below. Regarding the phrase "lest all dharmas lack the nature of existence": this is because phenomena (*vastu*) and principles (*tattva*) cannot be divided into two.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated: If a dharma and its nature as "existence" were distinct in essence, then their essences would necessarily be different. Body...

It cannot be apprehended, as it would be non-existent like that which has already ceased. Since it would differ from the nature of existence, it would be identical to a non-entity; thus, it contradicts what follows below, and the refutation remains the same as before.
It should be like sound and other such things, which are not objects of the eye and so forth.

Just as sound and the eye do not come into contact at all, [the opponent's position] also contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As the *Śata-śāstra* says: "If blue and other colors were different from the nature of color, they should be like..."

Sound and so forth are not the objects of the eye; sound and so forth are likewise [not the objects of the other senses]. If they were of a nature different from sound and so forth, they would have to be like form and so forth—objects that are not the domains of the ear and the other senses.
In that case, all established categories of meaning would fail to be established, and one would be identical to the heretics who hold the false view of nihilism.
Third, the attachment to the existence of a "being-ness" (*sattā*) and other such universals as real principles is certainly not established.
This is the doctrine of the Leśavāda teachers; first their attachment is stated, and it is refuted below.

If "being-ness" and form (*rūpa*) were identical, they would share the same fault as the Sāṃkhya school. If they were different from form and so forth, they would incur the same error as the Vaiśeṣika school. Next, [the argument] is based on contradiction.
The identity [of essence] refutes both types of duality—oneness and difference. If one says the characteristics are different, then the essence must also be different; it cannot be said to be one.
If one says the essence is one, then it cannot be said to be different. In that case, the establishment of all sentient and insentient things would be impossible.
However, it is absolutely impossible for all phenomena to share a single identical essence; they must either be one or different.
This is stated to reveal that all phenomena are provisional and not real, yet you do not understand this and cling to them as being real.
If examined according to principle, such a position can never be established.
The four [positions] that maintain the existence of dharmas and their nature as "existent" (sattā)—let those who possess wisdom not mistakenly grant assent to them.
These are the tenets of the Vātsīputrīyas. First, the positions are set forth; they will be refuted below. Regarding the claim that "they are neither identical nor different":
this means that this position is the same as the previous one which maintained they are both different and identical. This is because being non-identical is...
They are not different, because that which is not different is precisely one. If you say that this constitutes a positive assertion (*vidhi*), it should not be a double negation;

for instance, establishing "not one" to manifest "one," or establishing "one" to manifest "not one"—this is called a positive assertion. Now, since both are negated, what could possibly be manifested?
If it were merely a negation (*pratiṣedha*), there would be nothing to be grasped; for example, establishing "not one" to negate "one," or establishing [the negation of] non-...
"Differentiation is used to exclude difference. Since this is established as a negation of error, one must not further harbor any attachment.
As for the claim that "negating and affirming should be mutually contradictory," if it is a negation, it is not an affirmation; if it is an affirmation, it is not a negation.

Regarding the claim that "neither affirming nor negating would result in frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)," since it is neither a negation nor an affirmation, what benefit could there possibly be? How would it differ from worldly jesting?
In discussion, you present fallacies and yet maintain another divergent characteristic that is universally recognized by the world;
you alone deny its existence. This contradicts worldly consensus and violates your own tenets. To make such a statement is merely an attempt at sophistry to evade fault.
These four propositions above are the basis upon which the non-Buddhists rely; relying on these four, they engage in contentious attachments and arbitrary fabrications. Apart from these...
The four positions and the hundred negations are both discarded. Therefore, after refuting attachments, [the text] concludes by summarizing them within these four positions.

This is because the objects grasped by other vehicles—ranging from those asserted to exist as real entities apart from consciousness to the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—do not exist in reality.

The refutation of the non-Buddhists' clinging to dharmas is now complete. Below this, the clinging to the vehicles of the remaining [Buddhist] teachings is formally refuted. First, there is a general inquiry; next, a general refutation.
"Form" refers to the eleven types of material dharmas. "Dissociated formations" refer to acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*).

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*), birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), decay (*jarā*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the sets of names (*nāma-kāya*),
phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), fourteen dharmas, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)— that is, the three unconditioned [dharmas].
Because the Hīnayāna does not grasp at mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), it does not include these.
Furthermore, regarding the form (*rūpa*) that is grasped, there are generally two kinds—[up to] how could they possibly aggregate to form things such as jars and robes?
First, the dharma of form is refuted. Form is of two kinds: namely, resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and non-resistant form (*apratigha-rūpa*).
Resistant form refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body; and visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects. Non-resistant form refers to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
It is visible form (*rūpa*) and non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). Because it repeatedly observes various forms and, having observed them, relinquishes them, it is called the "eye.

Because it repeatedly hears sounds as they arrive at this [organ], it is called the "ear. Because it repeatedly enables one to smell various fragrances by means of this [organ], it is called the "nose."
Therefore it is called the nose. Because it can eliminate hunger and thirst, frequently engages in speech, and manifests through calling and summoning, it is called the tongue.
Because it is followed by the various faculties and is accumulated throughout [the body], it is called the body.
For a long night, the foolish polish, adorn, conceal, and protect it, grasping at it as their own, reckoning it as "I" and "mine. Furthermore, all worldly people rely upon this conventionally...
Various designations and concepts are established, such as "sentient being," "person," "living being," "born one," "mind-born," and "māṇava.
Therefore, it is called "mind" (*manas*). Because it can be numerically manifested in specific locations, and its substance and qualities can increase, it is called "form" (*rūpa*).
Because it is repeatedly proclaimed and repeatedly fades away, following various increasing discourses, it is called "sound" (*śabda*). It departs from its substance and remains hidden in form.
Because it repeatedly turns with the wind, it is called "fragrance" (*gandha*). Because it can be tasted by the tongue, yet repeatedly invites illness and suffering, it is called "taste" (*rasa*).

Because it can be numerically categorized as belonging to the body and can be realized through attainment, it is called "tangibility" (*spraṣṭavya*). Because it is able to universally sustain [the body] and is exclusively of the nature of an object of the mind, it is called "phenomena" (*dharma*).
These eleven factors each possess one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight [subdivisions].

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* extensively analyzes their characteristics in [sections] ninety and so forth. The Sautrāntikas maintain that resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
They hold that the constituent atoms are real, while the constituted [objects], such as the sense organs, are provisional;

since the provisional is constituted by the real, the eye perceives coarse form and does not perceive atoms. The Sarvāstivādins maintain that both the constituent and the constituted are real. Therefore, [the author] first refutes them, saying:
That resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is certainly not substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because that which constitutes the atom (*paramāṇu*) is not substantially existent.

Next, it is refuted by distinguishing between that which possesses resistance and that which lacks resistance. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The various atoms are conventional (*prajñapti*) and not real, because they possess resistance;
they should be understood like jars and the like. Furthermore, how could these various atoms aggregate to form jars, robes, and so forth?
Because they lack resistance, they should be like non-form (arūpa).
Furthermore, if atoms possessed spatial dimensions, they would have resistance; thus, the real existence of resistant form (sapratigha-rūpa) is not established.

This is an analysis based on whether [the atom] possesses spatial dimensions (*sapradeśa*) or lacks spatial dimensions (*apradeśa*). "Spatial" (*dig*) refers to location; "dimension" (*pradeśa*) refers to parts or positions.
That is to say, if this atom possessed location and parts, it could be analyzed. Since it can be analyzed, it would not be substantially real.
If it lacked spatial dimensions, then this atom would not belong to the category of form (*rūpadharma*); how then could atoms combine to form [gross objects]?

How could coarse matter receive light and cast shadows? We observe in the world that when the solar disc first rises and illuminates a pillar or similar object, shadows and light appear on both its eastern and western sides.
As the sun moves, the light shifts; as the light turns, the shadow follows.
Since the reception of light and the casting of shadows differ according to location, the atoms you maintain must certainly possess spatial dimensions. If the sun...
When a wheel touches objects such as a wall, the light and shadow are necessarily on this side and not on that, or on that side and not on this.
Thus, one knows that atoms (paramāṇu) must certainly possess spatial dimensions (digbhāga).

Since pillars, walls, and so forth are composite entities, and all are composed of atoms, one knows that atoms must certainly possess spatial dimensions. Once they possess spatial dimensions, they lose their status as atoms.
"Subtle. In the first [case], the color of the fruit is borrowed to manifest that the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses spatial divisions;
in the second, it directly clarifies that the ultimate atom possesses spatial divisions. Furthermore, every ultimate atom must necessarily have spatial orientations according to its location.

If this were not so, it would contradict your own tenet that ultimate atoms aggregate together. If ultimate atoms lacked the property of aggregation, then every particle could [be considered an isolated atom].
This penetration is called the Tathāgata’s supreme and wondrous form; it cannot be termed a coarse, obstructive material form of the mundane world.

Since this is not the case here, we know that atoms must certainly possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*). Furthermore, you maintain that resistant matter is formed by the aggregation of various atoms.
If they lacked spatial dimensions, then mountains, walls, earth, stones, and so forth would all be able to pass directly through one another.

[If it were] to enter, there would have to be no obstruction. If that were so, it would be the form realized by the noble ones of the four fruits, which is certainly not comparable to mundane obstructive and resistant form.
Since this is not the case now, it must possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*).
Because it possesses spatial dimensions, it must be analyzable. Since it is analyzable, it is certainly not substantially real. Therefore, obstructive form is [not real].
There is no such non-establishment.

How could the five consciousnesses lack a supporting basis (*āśraya*)? As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), [it consists of] form (up to the point of being) that which has been transformed by one's own consciousness.
The following clarifies the correct meaning. It asks: If external resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is certainly not substantially existent, then how can the first five consciousnesses...
Is there a root that is without support, as well as a form that serves as its object? The answer is: although it possesses form, it does not come from the outside;
rather, it is manifested by the internal consciousness itself, and is thus called "internal form. The question is:

since consciousness is without material obstruction while form possesses material obstruction, how can internal consciousness transform into form? The answer is: it is said that internal consciousness gives rise to form.

At that time, these do not arise through their own power, but rather because the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) maintains the seeds of the objective parts (nimittabhāga), such as form and so forth;

through the power of this perfuming (vāsanā), it transforms into what resembles the five sense organs (indriya)—such as the eye—and the five sense objects (viṣaya)—such as form—which constitute the objective parts.

Thus, the sense organs and so forth, as objective parts, serve as the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) and support for the consciousness, while the objective parts of form and so forth serve as the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) of the consciousness. Question:
