Because this dharma is the true principle, it is called *dharmatā*. [This continues until: Therefore, the various unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are not definitively real entities.
The following conclusion clarifies that all six kinds of unconditioned phenomena are merely provisional designations. Because they are the true principle of all dharmas, they are called *dharmatā*.

Because they are vast, empty, and free from obstruction, and are not manifested by any material thing, they are called "space" (*ākāśa*). As for "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is also...

It is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). "Discernment" (*saṃkhyā*) refers to the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*). Because it takes wisdom as its condition, one discriminates and eliminates all afflictions;

since it can manifest the principle of cessation, the Tripiṭaka masters translated this as "cessation through discernment. That is to say, cessation obtained by the power of discernment is termed "cessation through discernment.

This has the nature of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*); by means of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one severs all obstructive defilements, becomes detached from bondage, and realizes [this state].

Liberation is conventionally designated as "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). As for "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is also called "cessation not due to analytical conditions.

It is not obtained by destroying afflictions through the faculty of wisdom; rather, it is manifested through intrinsic purity and the absence of conditions. Regarding the "absence of conditions," the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"That which permanently obstructs future arising obtains cessation not through deliberation; that is, it can permanently eliminate what has not yet arisen..."

When a dharma arises, its attainment (*prāpti*) differs from what preceded it; this is called cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This attainment does not arise through deliberation, but rather through the absence of conditions; hence it is called cessation not through deliberation.
For example, when the eye and the mind are focused on a single form (*rūpa*), other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass away.
The five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) that would have taken those objects as their spheres remain in the future state and never arise again; this is due to those [conditions].

It cannot take past objects as its cognitive object because the conditions for such cognition are incomplete; thus, it attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The commentary explains:

When the eye takes a visible form (*rūpa*) as its object, the ear and other faculties would also be capable of taking sound and so forth as their objects; however, because of the focused attention on the visible form, the ear and others do not take sound and so forth as their objects.
Since the sounds and other objects of that same moment have already passed away, the consciousnesses that would take sound and so forth as their objects no longer arise.
By means of the first five consciousnesses, one perceives only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as they do not perceive the past; therefore, it is called "immovable.

This refers to that which transcends the first three dhyānas and reaches the fourth dhyāna, being free from the three calamities and the eight unfavorable conditions, and which manifests the true reality revealed by a body and mind undisturbed by joy, pleasure, and the like;

this is termed "immovable cessation" (*aniñjya-nirodha*). As for the "cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*), it refers to having already transcended the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Desire. Having transcended the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of a temporary cessation of perception, the truth revealed by the cessation of all non-permanent mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as a portion of the permanent mind and mental factors, is called the Cessation of Perception and Feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
These five are all conventionally established based upon *tathatā* (suchness), yet *tathatā* itself is also a conventional designation; that is to say, it is a verbal expression.
This ultimate state is ineffable; therefore, it is provisionally named "True Suchness" (*tathatā*). However, the various sūtras establish different names for it:

some speak of existence and others of emptiness; some speak of truth and others of reality. These are all taught in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings (*yathā-yogya*) and consist merely of verbal designations;

they possess no substantial meaning whatsoever. For instance, the teaching of existence is intended to refute the denial of phenomena by Bhāviveka, while the teaching of emptiness is intended to refute the views of the Mahīśāsakas.
In asserting existence, it negates the reality of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the illusion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

In teaching True Suchness (*tathatā*), it distances itself from the perversions of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the delusions of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). It differs from other schools in that it does not posit [reality] as existing apart from form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

To separately grasp permanent phenomena as being substantially existent is called "True Suchness" (*tathatā*). Since True Suchness is itself a provisional designation, the preceding five [categories] may be understood accordingly.
As for the various phenomena grasped by non-Buddhists and other vehicles—even their grasping of external objects constitutes attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
First, establish a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute the objects of perception as being inseparable from consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). The formal argument is stated as follows:
**Thesis:** The phenomena (*dharma*) grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles are the subject; they do not have an intrinsic nature distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

**Reason:** Because they are objects of apprehension (*grāhya*). **Example:** Like mind and mental factors. Just as mental factors are not separate from the mind, so too are the objects of apprehension not separate from consciousness.
Furthermore, because it is not separate from the mind, the next [step] refutes the notion that the apprehending mind does not take as its object a real entity separate from consciousness.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: **Thesis:** The subject, the cognition that apprehends that [external object], does not directly perceive that [object]. **Reason:** Because it is an apprehending cognition. [Explanation: "That" refers to the external object. The five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), which are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), are the cognitions that apprehend those external objects.

"Cognition" here refers to the five sensory consciousnesses of direct perception. The thesis asserts that the apprehending five sensory consciousnesses cannot directly perceive an object that is separate from the mind. The reason given is that they are indeed apprehending cognitions.

It is like the analogy of taking this [object] as a condition for cognition (the word "this" refers to the five sense-consciousnesses of direct perception). It is said that the five sense-consciousnesses of direct perception cannot take an object separate from the mind, just as the mental consciousness cannot take the five sense-consciousnesses of direct perception as its object.
Therefore, the *Zongjing* asks: "If there are no external objects, there should be no mind capable of perceiving through direct perception.
If there is no direct perception capable of cognizing, how can people of the world say that such a cognition exists? I now personally realize it to be thus."

"Is this an object? He replied: "Present awareness is like a dream. This means that when the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) arise as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and cognize the five objects such as form, one can only cognize the object that is cognized;
one cannot be aware of the present cognitive mind that is capable of cognizing.
Why is this? The mental consciousness that is able to cognize dharmas arises only after the five sensory consciousnesses have already occurred;

since the mental consciousness does not yet exist at the very moment they arise, it cannot cognize the mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is only upon reaching the second moment that the mental consciousness actually arises.

When one is aware of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) in a preceding moment, both the direct perception of the five consciousnesses that is being cognized and the object of that direct perception have already ceased and perished;

this is because the various consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, and by the time the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, the direct perception of the five consciousnesses has already ceased and perished.
The question asks: regarding form (*rūpa*), the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), in all three states...

[Objection: There are no mental states or mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); they must necessarily be substantially real (*dravya-sat*). [Response: To this, one establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to answer:

"All mental states and mental factors are not truly existent, because they are dependently originated (*paratantra*), just like magical illusions. [Question: If all mental states and mental factors are not substantially real, for what reason is it further said that "there is only consciousness" (*vijñapti-mātra*)?
[Answer: It is in order to eliminate the grasping of those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and followers of other vehicles (*anya-yāna*) who maintain [the existence of objects] as separate from the mind.

Because mental factors have distinct, real objects, it is said that "all is consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). This negates the existence of objects external to the mind as being substantially real;
it does not, however, mean that consciousness-only itself is substantially real.

If one were to further cling to that consciousness-only as being substantially real, it would be no different from the non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles who cling to external objects as being substantially real; one would likewise fall [into error].

This is to be attached to the "Middle Way. What is called being attached to the Middle without skillful means is still equivalent to being attached to "one. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* asks:

"If one eliminates the object while preserving consciousness, it may be called 'consciousness-only. But if both object and consciousness are eliminated, what consciousness can be established? The answer is:

Those who establish the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) initially dispense with the object while retaining the mind; yet, when considered from the ultimate perspective, the dispensing with the object is intended to empty the mind.
Therefore, the simultaneous subsiding of both object and consciousness is their correct principle. This simultaneous subsiding of object and consciousness is itself the true nature (dharmatā).
The true nature (*tathatā*) is precisely the *amala-vijñāna*. One may also discuss this by way of its ultimate conclusion; it is indeed the *amala-vijñāna*.
However, there are briefly two kinds of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*): [up to] the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is like illusory phenomena and so forth.
This briefly demonstrates the two types of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and the manner in which they are abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding this attachment to phenomena and the previously mentioned attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*), if one distinguishes between the two attachments to self and phenomena according to the Mahāyāna, both are suddenly and simultaneously severed at the first moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

As for the innate (*sahaja*) attachments to self and phenomena, a portion of each is abandoned in every successive stage until, at the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi, they are suddenly and simultaneously [abandoned].

They are exhausted. Therefore it is said: "The conceptual grasping of self and phenomena is utterly absent in the Stage of Great Joy (*pramuditā*); that which arises simultaneously with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses is eliminated stage by stage;
the seventh [consciousness] eliminates both seeds and manifestations through the path of cultivation; and thereafter, in the Vajra Path and so forth, they are entirely non-existent.

If one refers to the Hīnayāna, at the time of the initial Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one suddenly severs the conceptual grasping of a self and realizes the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Having severed the simultaneous (*sahaja*) grasping of a self, one then realizes...
Regarding the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) is never present from beginning to end.
As for external phenomena that may or may not exist, these are the remote objective conditions (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*); the subjective cognition (*ālambaka*) may or may not exist.

As for internal phenomena that all exist, these are the immediate objective conditions (*sākṣālambana-pratyaya*); the subjective cognition always exists. Therefore, all grasping at phenomena takes as its object only what arises from one's own mind.

That which appears as a semblance of a phenomenon is grasped by the ignorant as being real. It is asked: "Between that which appears as a semblance of a phenomenon and that which is grasped as a phenomenon, which exists and which does not?
The answer is: "One is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and one is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); they differ regarding existence and non-existence."
The formal proof (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: All things that resemble [real] phenomena definitely exist, because they arise from conditions, just like illusory objects.
Those entities grasped as real definitely do not exist, because they are falsely conceptualized, just like absolute non-existence. Therefore, [the verse says] "in the world," and so forth.
Citing scriptural authority:
Thus, that which is grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles [is merely] the mind revolving as if resembling those [objects], because it is turbid with habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
This concludes the preceding discussion: that the real self and real dharmas grasped apart from consciousness do not exist as real entities; therefore, [it is] the mind...

Mental factors (*caitta*) certainly do not take as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) dharmas that are form apart from consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor dissociated dharmas (*viprayukta-dharma*), nor unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
This is because, apart from consciousness, form and the other [objects] lack any substantial reality (*dravya-sat*).

Since an immediate object-condition must necessarily depend upon a dharma that possesses substantial reality, if one does not transform form and other dharmas within oneself, they can never be an immediate condition. That is to say:

By analogy with present internal consciousness, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the visual aggregate cannot serve as the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the auditory aggregate, because their respective essential natures (*svabhāva*) belong to different categories.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the mind and mental factors of that [auditory] aggregate in the present.

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are not the direct objective condition for this [visual] aggregate of consciousness. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they are comprised within a different aggregate. As in [the previous example].

It is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Not only can that aggregate not serve as the direct condition for this aggregate, but even the mental factors (*caitta*) within the same aggregate cannot serve as the direct condition for the mental king (*cittarāja*) of that same aggregate.
This is because the king and its factors each possess their own distinct substantial entities (*dravya*). To establish this through formal inference (*pramāṇa*), it is stated:

The mental factors (*caitta*) that arise together [with a primary consciousness] are the subject (*dharmin*). It is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that they are not direct objects of cognition (*ālambana*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

because their own nature (*svabhāva*) is distinct [from the primary consciousness], just like other things that are not grasped [as objects]. If one follows the later text, there is the principle that various consciousnesses can mutually serve as objects;

for example, the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the first seven, and the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition for the first five consciousnesses.
The sixth [consciousness] takes two parts of the eighth as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). The seventh relies solely upon the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth as its object.
The first seven do not serve as object-conditions for the eighth.

The eighth relies solely on its own three types of objects as its object-condition, because it does not rely on the first seven as its objective basis (*pratibimba*). Why is this? If one considers it from the perspective of itself...

When consciousness transforms into reflected images as its conditions, then all phenomena can serve as direct conditions (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*). Therefore, between this collection [of mental factors] and that collection [of objects], there exists the sense of mutual conditioning.

If one considers indirect conditions (*parokṣa-pratyaya*), then all mental factors belonging to the same collection are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because each possesses its own objective essence (*bimba*).
Thus it is said: "Phenomena external to one's own mind may exist or not exist; those within one's own mind..."
The Dharma exists in its entirety. From "by this" below, he concludes; from "therefore" below, he cites scriptural authority.
Someone raises this objection: "If there is no [object] apart from consciousness, how can it be said that the mind evolves as if appearing as external objects?"

An external objection states: If the real self and real dharmas that we assert as being distinct from consciousness are not truly existent, then even the semblances of self and semblances of dharmas—which our own internal teaching asserts as not being separate from consciousness—would likewise be unobtainable. Why is this so?
This means that a conventional designation (prajñapti) must be established based on a real entity, a similar entity, and their common attributes.

This is because a conventional entity exists only after there have been a real object and a similar object. The following analogy clarifies this: the existence of a real fire represents the real entity;

the existence of a person who resembles fire represents the similar entity; and the fact that this person possesses qualities such as a red complexion and courage like those of fire represents [the common attribute].
This is a common [conventional] phenomenon (*sādhāraṇadharma*). It is only through these three factors that one metaphorically designates this person as "fire.

Now, since you do not admit the existence of a real self (*ātman*) or real phenomena (*dharma*), from what basis could you establish a conventional self or conventional phenomena? Since the conventional does not exist, the "semblance" (*pratibimba*) likewise cannot be established;
for it is only because there is a semblance that there can be a convention. Since the semblance is not established, yet you claim that the mind appears as an external [object], [this is untenable].
As for the objection that "the object undergoes transformation," is this not a contradiction of one's own words?

That criticism is irrational, because it fails to recognize that the self and dharmas are dissociated from consciousness; therefore, one should know that metaphorical designations do not arise based on [intrinsic] categories.
This refutes the notion that conventional entities are established based on similar things. As for the term "category" (*jāti*), it carries the meaning of "similarity.
While the red intensity of fire can burn everything, although the red intensity of a person resembles that of fire, it lacks the quality of being able to burn.

It does not belong to the category of fire. If a person who lacks the common property of being combustible could nevertheless be metaphorically designated as "fire," then one could likewise metaphorically designate water and other substances by names such as "fire.
If it is argued that [the designation applies] because of the quality of being red and intense...

Although they do not possess the inherent quality of burning like fire, it is nonetheless incorrect to metaphorically designate a person who is red and fierce as "fire," on the grounds that such a person stays close to fire and does not separate from it.
This is because we observe that even among those who are red and fierce, there are instances where they are separated from fire;
for example, a person who is currently brave, fierce, and red may never [have been near fire] at all.

It has been observed that fire and the person have coexisted. Thus, it is clear that the designation "fire-person" is not established based on a resemblance between them. Therefore, the conclusion states:

if one were to say that [the designation] is formed based on a category [of similarity], then since this person lacks the quality of being able to burn and is not intimately related to fire, yet there is still a figurative designation of this person as "fire" or "fire-element," we know that such designations are merely metaphorical.
It is established based on categories (*jāti*).
The principle that it is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) based on a substantial reality (*dravya*) is also not established;

because this conventional designation is not established based on a substantial reality, this refutation shows that the conventional entity is not established by depending upon a substantial entity. Therefore, it is said: "It is not so. Substantial reality (*dravya*) refers to the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
This is because the quality of fierce redness is not shared by both humans and fire.

While the quality of fierce redness can burn when it resides in fire, it causes mental agitation and feverish heat when it resides in a human. This is because the substance of fire is different from that of a human;
their bases—the insentient and the sentient—are each distinct. Thus, even though there is no common quality, one may metaphorically speak of "fire" and "human."
In that case, one should likewise apply the conventional designation "fire" to water and so forth.

If you argue that although a person and fire are different, they may be conventionally designated as "fire" because their quality of heat is similar, this is not correct; for when we speak of a "fire-person" here, we do not mean the quality of fire.
If one were to designate a person by the quality of fire, then every person would possess the quality of heat, and thus [every person] would be... [a fire].
One may thus be called a "fire-person. Therefore, we know that the conventional designation "fire-person" is established through the fire-element; it does not exist as a substantial reality.
Furthermore, since a conventional designation must necessarily be established based on a real entity, this objection [of yours] is not consistent with correct reasoning.
This refutation of conventional entities does not establish them based on real entities. As for "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena;
only non-conceptual direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) directly apprehends this essence.

Just as fire has heat as its specific characteristic and water has moisture as its specific characteristic, one must necessarily wait until one personally apprehends the essence itself before knowing that it is fire.
Warmth: that water is cold does not depend on verbal expression, for it is not an object known by conceptual cognition (*buddhi*). As for common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):
when one says "fire" or "water," everyone infers that the nature of fire is warmth and the nature of water is cold;
this is an object known by conceptual inferential cognition (*vikalpa-anumāna-jñāna*). However, at the moment one speaks of "fire" or "water," one does not [directly] apprehend warmth or cold.
Regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): these specific characteristics of cold and warmth are objects realized through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of body-consciousness.

Furthermore, when visual consciousness perceives blue color, it apprehends the specific characteristic of that blue color. However, when a subsequent conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises and forms the cognition "this is blue," this constitutes an inference based on a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
As soon as the mind forms such a cognition, it is already accompanied by names and conventions (*nāma-pada*).

Because they fall within the realm of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), this conventional cognition and its expression do not, apart from these common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), have any other means for establishing particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their basis.
Nevertheless, conventional cognition and its expression necessarily arise based on similar vocal sounds;
where sound does not reach, this conventional cognition and its expression do not circulate. This is due to the relationship between the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*).

Since neither [of these] can personally realize the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), we know that metaphorical designations do not rely on real entities, but rather function based on things that merely resemble them.

"Resemblance" refers to the superimposition (*samāropa*) of characteristics that are not actually existent; for both the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), as well as all five categories and one hundred dharmas, must depend upon causes and conditions to be able to manifest.
This is called the superimposition of things that merely resemble reality. If, by means of the real...
If one observes according to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), such a thing has never existed from the beginning; it is simply like placing a head upon a head.

Therefore, this is collectively termed "superimposition" (*samāropa*) and is not a characteristic of actual existence. Consequently, words and sounds necessarily function based on superimposed, semblance-like characteristics.
Thus, one cannot say that a provisional phenomenon must be established based upon a real phenomenon. For these reasons, the following conclusion of the objection is inappropriate.

However, in order to eliminate false attachments by means of the transformation of consciousness (up to this point), one provisionally designates the names "self" and "dharmas" to what is transformed by consciousness.
Question: Since these provisional phenomena do not rely on the ultimate reality for their establishment, from what do these provisional selves and dharmas arise? Answer:

Although they do not rely on the ultimate reality, they exist by virtue of being manifested through the internal consciousness. This is because non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles falsely conceptualize them.
There is a real self and real dharmas external to the mind;

in order to refute this attachment, it is said that what appear as a self and as dharmas are transformations of internal consciousness—this merely turns the case upside down. However, even this term "provisional" (prajñapti) is a forced designation.
This section concludes the present passage; more distantly, it concludes the previous verse which states: "Because of the provisional designation of self and dharmas, various aspects arise."
Regarding those three phrases based on what is transformed by consciousness, the following section cites scriptural evidence:
although the manifestations transformed by consciousness are of immeasurable kinds, [the term] "maturation" (*vipāka*) refers only to a portion of them and does not denote all of them.
This commentary on the verse states that these "transforming consciousnesses" are only three: namely, the three phrases "maturation," "intellection," and "consciousness that discriminates objects.

First, regarding the characteristics transformed by the internal consciousness—the terminology for these three types—there are one hundred dharmas in five categories in general, and infinitely many varieties in detail; yet, as for the types of transforming consciousness, there are only three. First:

Regarding "vipāka" (maturation): it is called maturation because it matures through transformation, matures at a different time, matures as something distinct from the noble ones, and matures as a different category.

Because it possesses these four meanings, it is termed "vipāka. This belongs exclusively to the eighth consciousness. Although the sixth consciousness also has vipāka, it constitutes only a single portion;
since this [eighth] consciousness possesses it predominantly, it is said to have the nature of being preponderantly vipāka. Second is volition (*cetanā*).
*Manana* (thinking) refers to deliberation; *māna* (measuring) refers to measurement.

These belong to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), because it constantly and critically deliberates upon the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as being the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). Although all consciousnesses possess the function of measuring, they are neither constant nor critical;

only the seventh consciousness is constant and critical in its deliberation. The third [function], "perceiving objects," belongs to the first six types of consciousness. Although the seventh [also perceives objects]...
The eighth consciousness also cognizes objects, but it functions by way of an internal door and cognizes only subtle objects.

Because these six [consciousnesses] can cognize objects with coarse characteristics, the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse indicates that the first six consciousnesses are combined into a single category;

this is because the five preceding consciousnesses that grasp objects must necessarily have a simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Next, the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is explained. First, regarding "transformation as cause": this refers to...

The two types of latencies—the latencies of the two kinds of grasping that are outflowing results (*niṣyanda*), and the latencies of various karmas that are maturation results (*vipāka*)—along with their two modes of manifestation, are called the "transformative cause" (*hetu-pariṇāma*).
Regarding the outflowing latencies: these are the seeds of the three natures belonging to the preceding seven consciousnesses, each of which produces its own manifestation.
It perfumes the eighth consciousness, causing it to increase; however, the eighth consciousness itself is excluded, as it is not a perfuming agent (*vāsanā*).

As for the seeds of maturation (*vipāka-vāsanā*), they are perfumed by the actualized functioning of the impure wholesome and unwholesome states of the first six consciousnesses, which perfume the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome maturation within the eighth consciousness, thereby causing them to increase;
the seventh consciousness is excluded, because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is not a cause of maturation.

Therefore, "growing and developing" herein has the meaning of "transformation. This refers to the transformation through successive stages until maturation is reached. Regarding the second, the "transforming agent that is the fruit":
by the power of the two aforementioned types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it draws forth the eighth consciousness along with its associated mental factors (*caitta*).

The perception of the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and so forth, as well as the various manifest fruits of maturation such as suffering and pleasure, are termed "fruit-transforming" (*phala-pariṇāma*).

Because the seeds that produce them directly are the preceding similar-type (*niṣyanda*) habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they draw forth the distinct essential characteristics of the eighth consciousness and its associated image- and perception-aspects;
these are termed "similar-type fruits" (*niṣyandaphala*). This is because the fruit resembles its cause, just as a virtuous seed of the perception-aspect produces a virtuous [result].
Manifest activity: from the seeds of afflictions arise evil manifest activities; from the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) arise neutral manifest activities.
Because the effect is concordant with its cause, it is called a "flowing-forth result" (*niṣyanda-phala*).

As for the "ripening result" (*vipāka-phala*), it is because the seeds of the six preceding wholesome or unwholesome karmas act as a distinguished dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to summon and induce the eighth [consciousness], which constantly continues as a retribution for the power of the projective karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*); therefore, it is so named.

Regarding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*): "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karman*) refers to "projection," meaning the drawing forth [of a result]. This means that karma possesses the power to project a general retribution;

thus, when wholesome or unwholesome karma is created by the first six consciousnesses, it projects the eighth consciousness to undergo wholesome or unwholesome retribution, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.

This is called the fruit of maturation. Regarding "fulfilling karma" (*paripūraka-karman*): "fulfillment" means making complete. This means that karma lacks the power [to project], but only fulfills [the details of the retribution].

Regarding individual retribution (*pratiniṣyanda-vipāka*): it refers to the performance of wholesome and unwholesome karma by the preceding six consciousnesses, which is able to fulfill the two types of results—wholesome and unwholesome—of the sixth consciousness.
Therefore, the eighth consciousness is called the "lord of total retribution," while the preceding six are called the "lords of individual retribution.

However, when the preceding evolving consciousnesses are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they arise from the total retribution of the maturation consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) and are thus termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*); they are not themselves termed "maturation" (*vipāka*). There is...
Because [the six consciousnesses] are interrupted; because the consciousness that projects the fruit pervades all three realms; and because it is constantly continuous.

The six consciousnesses do not pervade [all states], as they are entirely absent in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), during the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), and so forth, due to their being subject to interruption.

Only the eighth consciousness possesses these three characteristics and is therefore called the "true maturation" (*vipāka*). First, the characteristic of pervasion excludes the first five consciousnesses. Second, continuity...

The sixth [definition] excludes [those results] produced by the three types of karma. The seventh [definition] states that those possessing these three characteristics are called "true maturation" (*vipāka*).

That is to say, both the aforementioned "maturation" (*vipāka*) itself and that which is "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) are termed "fruits of maturation" (*vipākaphala*), because their causes are diverse:

while the causes may be either wholesome or unwholesome, the fruits are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Although this term "maturation" has many meanings, here it refers specifically to the seventh [definition].
It is called "vipāka" (maturation) because it is that which is cherished and stored by the self-grasping, that which can maintain the two kinds of causes for maturation— wholesome and unwholesome—

and that which can transform into the two kinds of fruits of maturation— wholesome and unwholesome. It is not a term that generally encompasses meanings such as being of a different time or being a transformation of a different noble one (*ārya*).

Although the three names for the "transforming" consciousnesses have already been briefly explained—from [the point] "it transforms constantly like a torrential stream" up to "it is abandoned at the stage of an Arhat"—the above has been a brief explanation of the three names of the transforming consciousnesses;
below follows a detailed analysis of the three characteristics of the transforming consciousnesses. First, the question is posed; next, the verse is cited as the answer.
First, the initial transforming consciousness is analyzed through twelve gates. The *ālayavijñāna* is the gate of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). It is distinct...

"Ripened" (*vipāka*) refers to the gate of its fruit-characteristic (*phala-lakṣaṇa*). "All seeds" (*sarvabījaka*) refers to the gate of its cause-characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*). "Inconceivable" (*acintya*) refers to the gate of its inconceivability.
"Appropriation and locus" (*upādāna-sthāna*) refers to the gate of its object-condition (*ālambana*). "Cognizing" (*vijñapti*) refers to the gate of its mode-of-apprehension (*ākāra*).

"Always associated with contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition" refers to the gate of its association (*samprayoga*). "Only neutral feeling" (*upekṣā-vedanā*) refers to the gate of its concomitance with feeling (*vedanā-sahabhū*). It is "unobscured and indeterminate" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)."

Commentary: The section on the three natures; the same applies to contact and the other [mental factors]. The section on mental associates following the analogy of the sovereign mind; the section on the constant revolution like a violent torrent;
the section on cause, fruit, phenomena, and analogies; and the section on the stages of subduing and abandoning [afflictions] up to the stage of Arhatship.
From this point until twenty-three and a half verses later in the text, the characteristics of Vijñapti-mātra are explained in detail.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the first transformative consciousness... because the fault of being a 'storehouse' (*ālaya*) is the most serious, it is specifically mentioned here.
This explains the gate of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the first transformative consciousness. Mahāyāna teachings refer to the *Abhidharma* and so forth.
Hīnayāna teachings refer to the *Ekottarika Āgama* and so forth. *Ālaya* is translated here as "storehouse" (*zàng*); because it possesses the three meanings of a storehouse, it is so called.
Ālaya-vijñāna means that which is capable of storing, that which is stored within, and that which is clung to as a self.
"Capable of storing" (nibandhana) has the sense of being able to hold; it is like a storehouse, for it can store all manner of precious treasures and the like.

Because this [consciousness] is able to contain and store the seeds of defilement (saṃkleśa), it is called "capable of storing. This is explained from the perspective of its function of maintaining the seeds. As for "that which is stored," it refers to...
The meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*) is like a treasury, because it is the basis for jewels and other such things;
this consciousness is likewise the locus that serves as the basis for all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśadharma*). This is explained from the perspective of its capacity to receive perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Regarding "appropriation" (*upādāna*), it means to hold fast and not relinquish, just as a treasury of gold, silver, and so forth is firmly guarded by people; this consciousness is similarly firmly grasped by the defiled *manas*.

Because it is that which is inwardly grasped by the self, it is called "appropriated" (*ālaya*). Furthermore, the *Qixinlun chao* states: "Regarding the meaning of the eighth consciousness as 'that which can store':
this refers to the fact that only this consciousness can contain and store phenomena such as the sense organs and the physical body, just as images are contained within a pearl.
Therefore it is said: 'If one wishes to seek all dharmas, they are all found within the ālayavijñāna; if one wishes to seek all images, they are all found within the maṇi.'"
Next, regarding the meaning of "that which is stored": it means that the substance of this consciousness takes form and mind as its locus of storage.

This is because form and mind constitute the two parts of this consciousness—namely, the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). It is like a pearl being within an image; therefore, it is said:
"If you wish to seek the *ālaya-vijñāna*, look only within form and mind; if you wish to seek the *maṇi* jewel, look only within blue and yellow."
"Internally" means that it can conceal its own essence within all phenomena, and it can also conceal all phenomena within its own essence.
This refers to the mutual functioning as conditions between the defiled and the pure; that is, the concealer and the concealed act as causes for one another in turn.
Therefore, it is called "mutuality" (*pāratantrya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "How is the establishment of mutual causality defined? It answers:
"The *ālayavijñāna* acts as two kinds of causes for those evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*): first, it is the generative cause as seeds; second, it is the causal basis.
Regarding the generative cause as seeds, this refers to all the evolving consciousnesses—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate."
At the time of birth, all [sensory cognitions] arise seated upon the seeds of the ālayavijñāna.

As for the causal basis of support, it means that the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) evolve by taking the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) grasped by the ālayavijñāna as their support;

they do not function without an object of perception. Furthermore, because this consciousness exists, the mental faculty (*manas*) comes into being, and by taking this mental faculty as its support, [the sixth consciousness evolves].

Because it ceases, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises. For example, just as the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) proceed by depending upon the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), such as the eye and so forth, and not without those five faculties;
so too is it with the mental consciousness—it does not occur without the mind-faculty (*manas*).

Furthermore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the *ālaya-vijñāna* act as two kinds of causes for one another: first, because they nourish their respective seeds within the present life; second, [because...]
In order to cause those [seeds] to arise in a future state by gathering and planting them, one nurtures those seeds in the present state.

This means that as various wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses) arise in dependence upon the *ālaya-vijñāna*, they do so in such a manner that they arise and perish simultaneously with that single basis. In this way, and in this manner...

This consciousness is perfumed; by reason of this causal condition, the subsequent evolving consciousnesses—whether virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate—become increasingly predominant, increasingly intense, and increasingly clear as they arise.
That which implants those seeds within future states refers to the category of that perfuming, which is capable of drawing forth and encompassing the future.

This very resultant *ālayavijñāna*—by virtue of being the cause of seeds, the cause of support, the cause of nurturing seeds, and the cause of gathering and planting seeds—is termed the "establishment of the mutual causality between the *ālayavijñāna* and the evolving consciousnesses" (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Regarding sentient beings who grasp it as their internal self: this explains the meaning of "appropriation and storage" (*ālaya*), by means of the seventh [consciousness].

Regarding those with consciousness: because it is never momentarily separated from the eighth [consciousness] as they continue in succession from moment to moment, this meaning of the three *saṃskāras* (or *skandhas*) constitutes the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the first transformative consciousness.
This is because that [first consciousness] takes the maintenance of cause and effect as its self-characteristic.

"Appropriation" (ā-dāna) means to gather and take in; "retention" (dhṛti) means to grasp and maintain. Appropriation has the sense of that which stores and that which is stored; retention has the sense of being grasped and stored.
This is because it can appropriate and store all phenomena—such as the causes and effects of defilement—so that they are not lost.

Furthermore, it serves as the seventh [consciousness] by being grasped and stored as one's own internal self. This consciousness has many states and many names according to its specific characteristics.

However, the fault in the first [case] among the three is grave; therefore, it is explained specifically. As the subsequent text states: "Because it is the first abandonment, and because the fault is grave.
Here, only one aspect is raised; the specific textual citations follow, while the middle section provides a detailed analysis.
This refers to that which can induce birth in the various realms and destinies; because it is the actual, uncommon [cause] of maturation (*vipāka*), it is explained specifically as such.

This explains the section on the characteristics of the fruit within the verse. By means of the six causes mentioned previously, one performs the karma of the five precepts, the ten wholesome paths of action, and so forth, thereby inducing the general and specific fruits of maturation—the happiness of gods and humans.
If, however, by those same six causes one commits the ten unwholesome paths of action...
Karma brings about the ripening fruits of the three miserable realms, both collectively and individually; for this reason, it is called "ripening" (*vipāka*).
Based on the seeds within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of this consciousness, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is metaphorically established.

Furthermore, based on the states of body and mind within this consciousness, the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is metaphorically established. If this consciousness did not exist, then all life-faculties and the various homogeneous characters would cease to exist.
Because it is impossible for a superior, distinct ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) to arise [from other causes]. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"That is to say, based precisely upon those factors belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), this consciousness continues to arise through beginningless perfuming (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, its ability to maintain that beginningless perfuming is called its 'characteristic as fruit' (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).
Although this consciousness has many characteristics of fruit, the ripened fruit exists only in this consciousness and is absent in other consciousnesses.
Therefore, it is explained partially.
This [consciousness] is able to grasp and maintain the seeds of all phenomena (up to: briefly stated, there are only these three characteristics.
This is the explanation of the "causal characteristic" (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) section within the verse. "Cause" (*hetu*) is precisely the seed. The *ālayavijñāna*—due to its being mixed with...
The specific functional capacities established through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of various phenomena belonging to the category of defilement serve as the causes for their arising;

this is termed the "characteristic of cause" (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*). Because this consciousness maintains the seeds of all phenomena in a manner that other consciousnesses lack, it is specifically designated as such.
The section beginning with "The first transformative consciousness" below is the conclusion.

The passage from "All seed-characteristics (*sarvabījaka*) should be further distinguished" up to "because provisional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*) are not causes or conditions" is a specific explanation of "all seeds.
As for the term "seeds," they reside upon the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
A portion of the manifesting functional capacity produced by the primary consciousness is called a "seed. This seed belongs to the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect).

It is neither identical to nor different from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the fruit it produces, because the fundamental consciousness is the essence (*svabhāva*) and the seeds are its function (*kāritra*).
The seed is the cause; the manifest activity is the fruit. Therefore, these two phenomena should logically be neither identical nor different.
If they were identical, one could not speak of them as having both essence and function, or as having both cause and fruit.
Now, since essence and function, as well as cause and fruit, are each distinct, they are not identical. If they were different, their separate parts should be observable.
The seed is capable of producing the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), just as a grain seed can produce beans and so forth.

Alternatively, it is only when its substance (*svabhāva*) ceases that it can possess function (*vṛtti*), because you admit that the substance and function of cause and effect are invariably distinct. Now, since the substance and function here are similar, the cause and effect must be identical;
therefore, they are not distinct. Although this seed is neither one with the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) nor with the fruit it produces...

It is not different [from those dharmas], yet it is a substantial, real dharma and not a provisional dharma; for a provisional dharma is ultimately non-existent and is not produced by causes and conditions.
This [resultant consciousness] is neither identical to nor different from all dharmas... (up to)... it is not comprised within the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) as a maturation (*vipāka*).

The objection states: "If the existence of dharmas as conceived by the Vātsīputrīyas—being neither identical to nor different from 'existence' (*sattā*)—is rejected as being merely conventional (*prajñapti*), then this seed, which is likewise neither identical to nor different from the various dharmas, should also be conventional. Thus, one may formulate the following syllogism:
This [seed] is conventional and not real with respect to the various dharmas, because it is neither identical to nor different from them; it should be like a jar and so forth."

If these seeds are merely conventionally existent, then True Suchness (*tathatā*) should also be merely conventional, because seeds encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
If True Suchness did not exist, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) would also not exist, and one would fall into the error of nihilism. The answer is:
However, all seeds are said to be substantially existent (*dravyasat*) within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), unlike True Suchness, because True Suchness...
Because it is free from the conceptual elaborations (*prapañca*) of identity, difference, existence, and non-existence. The following explains that the seed is real and not provisional:

although the seed takes the eighth consciousness as its substance, it is precisely the objective realm (*viṣaya*) of the eighth consciousness’s image-part (*nimittabhāga*), and is not a separate entity.
Because it is the object of the eighth consciousness’s seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), although it is neither identical to nor different from it, it is a substantial dharma with real existence;
it cannot be said to be non-existent. Question: If this is so, among the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), under which nature is this eighth consciousness and its various seeds subsumed?
Answer: If explained according to the perspective of the basis (*āśraya*) and its substance, these contaminated seeds [are of the same nature] as the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).

In their essence, they are without distinction, as both are subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This is because the characteristics are subsumed into the nature, and the functions are subsumed into the essence.
However, if explained according to the gate of the differentiation of functional capacity, both cause and effect are common to all three natures, by means of this seed.
It is capable of acting as the manifesting cause and capable of bringing forth the manifested fruit. Question:

Since the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) seeds already known are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, by what nature are the untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds subsumed? Answer: All untainted seeds are not subsumed within maturation (*vipāka*); they are not indeterminate.
Therefore, both cause and effect are subsumed under the nature of goodness (*kuśala*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the eighth consciousness-seeds generally comprise two categories:

first, those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) and subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature; second, those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), which are subsumed exclusively under the nature of goodness. An objection is raised:
since the uncontaminated is subsumed under the nature of goodness and does not belong to the indeterminate, it is not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*). Why, then, [is it said to be so]?
The *Vibhaṅga* (Analysis) states that all twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) and are born of maturation. Regarding these twenty-two faculties:

the six faculties beginning with the eye; the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); the male faculty (*purisindriya*) and female faculty (*itthindriya*); the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*); and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
The faculty of "desiring to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "having fully known. Answer:
Although it is said in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* that all [of these] are called "maturation" (*vipāka*), they are not of the same indeterminate nature as the eighth [faculty].

That is to say, these twenty-two faculties all rely upon maturation and are thus termed "maturation-seeds. Just as visual consciousness and the others are called "born of maturation" because they rely upon maturation, so too are these. All [are thus established].
This is a case of dependence between things of different natures, not of the same nature. To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*):

untainted seeds depend upon tainted consciousnesses as a dependence between things of different natures, just like the visual consciousness and others; or alternatively, untainted seeds exist by virtue of the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Because it is that which transforms and matures, it is designated by the term "vipāka" (maturation). It is not, however, the vipāka comprised within the eighth [consciousness] which is neutral (avyākṛta);
therefore, untainted seeds (anāsrava-bīja) are comprised exclusively of the nature of the wholesome (kuśala).
Regarding this, there is one interpretation that all seeds (up to) establish cause and effect in such a way as to avoid confusion.

This master Qingmu and others maintain that both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds are all inherently existent (*prakṛtistha*); they hold that there is no principle of new perfuming (*navavāsanā*).

Through the process of perfuming, it merely causes those that are inherently existent to increase and reach maturity. As cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* below, the sūtra provides scriptural proof for this. [End of] *Yogācārabhūmi*.
To cite scriptural proof: "All seeds are fully possessed" means that both the defiled and the pure types are inherently present from the beginning.
"Lacking the seed of *sambodhi*" means that although the pure seeds are present, they do not manifest. Regarding the five lineages (*pañca-gotra*):
The lineages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, tathāgatas, the indeterminate, and the icchantikas. The *Laṅkāvatāra* says: "How does one know the lineage of the śrāvaka-vehicle that is uninterrupted?
If, upon hearing [the teaching], one realizes the abandonment and knowledge of the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases..."

The pores of his entire body are radiant, joyful, and delighted; he delights in cultivating the wisdom of marks (*lakṣaṇajñāna*), yet does not cultivate the signs of awakening through the realization of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is called the unintermittent lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle. As for the unintermittent lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle:
If, upon hearing an exposition of the distinct conditions for immediate realization, their body hairs stand on end and they weep with flowing tears;
or if, upon hearing an exposition of non-proximate conditions, all forms of non-attachment, various bodily forms, various supernormal powers,
and various transformations of separation and union, their minds enter accordingly— this is called the immediate lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

Regarding those of the lineage of uninterrupted succession in the Tathāgata vehicle: this refers to the lineage of uninterrupted succession of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*), the lineage of uninterrupted succession of phenomena devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvadharma*), the lineage of uninterrupted succession of the noble self-realization (*pratyātma-ārya-adhigama*), and the lineage of uninterrupted succession of the excellence of external realms (*bāhyakṣetra-viśeṣa*).
If, upon hearing these four matters, one’s mind is not startled or terrified, this is called the uninterrupted succession in the Tathāgata vehicle.

Regarding the spiritual lineages (*gotra*): those of indeterminate lineage refer to those who, when the three [types of] lineages are taught, enter according to what is taught and thereby establish their respective distinct lineages;

these are the *icchantikas*. As for the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "having fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
"Knowing" refers to the meaning of the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). This is due to perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Below, the meaning of cause and effect is established: it is stated that the seeds inherently present within the eighth consciousness are increased by the perfuming of the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), rather than being produced by individual perfumings.
When these seeds arise and manifest, the seed is the cause and the manifest [consciousness] is the fruit.
When the manifest arises from the seeds, the manifest is the cause and the seeds are the fruit; it is by establishing it in this way that cause and effect remain unconfused.

If one were to allow for new perfuming—such as the perfuming of the uncontaminated by the contaminated, or the perfuming of the contaminated by the uncontaminated, or even the mutual perfuming of the wholesome and the unwholesome—then cause and effect would become disordered.
There is an interpretation that all seeds arise because they are perfumed (until: they depend on what is to arise, not on their own existing substance).
This refers to Nanda’s position that both tainted and untainted seeds are produced solely through new perfuming and do not exist inherently from the beginning.

The phrase "all arise because they are perfumed" means that even those [seeds] which are inherently present are produced through perfuming. As for the citation of the sūtra below, it serves as scriptural proof; the discussion in the treatise [below]...
Citing scriptural evidence: Regarding the existence of external seeds as perfumations (*vāsanā*), these constitute the *paratantra* (dependent) retribution of sentient beings;

they are induced by the collective karma of sentient beings and are also termed "perfumation. Regarding their non-existence, this is because one's own root-seeds (*mūla-bīja*) are transmitted through successive stages.
As for the three types of perfumation—namely, those of names and words (*nāma-pada*), etc.—there are two kinds of perfumation of names and words: first, the manifest...
There are two types of verbal expression regarding meaning: first, verbal expression regarding names; second, verbal expression regarding the manifestation of objects.

There are two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of self-grasping: first, innate self-grasping; second, conceptual self-grasping. There are two types of habitual tendencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*):

first, contaminated virtue; second, various non-virtues. These contaminated seeds are all produced by means of perfuming (*vāsanā*). Since this is the case for the contaminated, it is likewise for the uncontaminated. Question:
If untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) do not exist inherently from the beginning, why is there a distinction between spiritual lineages (*gotra-viśeṣa*)? Answer:
The distinction between spiritual lineages does not depend on the presence or absence of untainted seeds; rather, it is established based on the presence or absence of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).
As cited in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Awakening of Faith* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*) also states: "All sentient beings, by virtue of their fundamental craving and desire, manifest..."
Ignorance (*avidyā*) manifests the unequal distinctions among the five natures (*pañca-gotra*). It appears in varying degrees of depth and shallowness based on two kinds of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).

What are these two obstructions? First is the obstruction of principle (*tattvāvaraṇa*), which hinders correct knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*). Second is the obstruction of phenomena (*vastvāvaraṇa*), which perpetuates the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
What are the five natures? If these two obstacles have not yet been severed and extinguished, one is called "not yet a Buddha.

If sentient beings have permanently abandoned craving and desire, first eliminating the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) but not yet severing the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), they are only able to realize and enter the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
they are unable to manifestly abide in the realm of Bodhisattvas. If all sentient beings in the final age wish...
To float upon the Great Perfectly Awakened Sea of the Tathāgata, one should first make a vow to diligently sever the two hindrances.
Once these two hindrances are suppressed, one can then awaken to and enter the realm of the Bodhisattvas.

If the hindrances of phenomena and principle are forever severed and extinguished, one enters the subtle and wondrous Perfect Awakening of the Tathāgata, fulfilling both Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa. If sentient beings, though seeking...
"O virtuous friend, encountering those with wrong views who have not yet attained right awakening is what is called the lineage of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is due to the errors of false teachers, not the fault of sentient beings; this is known as the differentiation of the five lineages of sentient beings. Question:

"If that is so, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* further state that those in the hells possess the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)? Answer: "This is based on what will occur in the future..."
The arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) does not mean that the substance of untainted seeds already existed from the beginning.
According to one interpretation, seeds each have two types [of causes]; this [latter type] is what is called the seed produced through cultivation (*paribhāvita-bīja*).

This is the correct principle for protecting the Dharma: it establishes that both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds each consist of two categories—innate (*prakṛtistha*) and newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*)—and that these respectively produce their own corresponding manifest activities (*samudācāra*). These do not exist sequentially, nor are they confused with one another.

If a newly perfumed seed encounters the necessary conditions, it arises from the newly perfumed; if an innate seed encounters the necessary conditions, it arises from the innate. By accepting both principles, one accords perfectly with the truth.
Regarding the doctrine: Question. If seeds each have two types, do both types of seeds together produce a single manifestation? Answer.
Although all phenomena have two kinds—new and old—at the time they are about to arise or manifest, they may arise from the new or they may arise from the old;
these are what are called the "two types. This does not mean that both types arise and manifest as one within a single moment. If that were so...

This would entail the fault that many [distinct] types [of seeds] would coexist within a single sprout. Question: If they have not yet been permeated by hearing at all, from what does this innately existing seed arise?
Answer: It is said to arise together with the body from beginningless time, just like the seeds of external plants and trees.
If only the fundamental consciousness existed and the evolving consciousnesses did not, they could not serve as mutual effects nor would they constantly function as causes for one another.

If only the fundamental consciousness existed and there were no newly perfumed [seeds], then since the seven evolving consciousnesses—both the sovereign and their mental factors—would all possess the capacity to perfume, they could not serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the eighth consciousness.
The following verse is cited as proof: "All dharmas reside within the storehouse consciousness... The phrase "all dharmas" refers to...

"Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the aforementioned seven [consciousnesses]. "Cognition" (*vijñāna*) refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). "Storehouse" (*ālaya*) refers to the eighth [consciousness], which acts as the storehouse that can contain and holds all phenomena within it.
"Cognition is likewise toward phenomena" means that the former seven act as the storehouse that can contain, while the eighth acts as that which is contained.
They are mutually the nature of the fruit, and also constantly the nature of the cause; this refers to the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*).
The perfumed serves as the cause, and that which is perfumed serves as the effect; that which can produce serves as the cause, and that which is produced serves as the effect.
This precisely refers to the mutual perfuming and activation between the first seven consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness in their present manifestation.
The meaning of this verse is that [the claim] from "the ālayavijñāna" up to "therefore it is only the fundamental" contradicts both reason and scripture.
This explains the verse. Regarding the phrase "as the wick and the flame burn each other," it is like a bright lamp:
the flame and the wick arise and burn simultaneously and mutually. That is to say, in a single moment, the lamp-wick serves as the basis for the production of the lamp-flame. This is...
Thus, the wick is the cause for the arising of the flame; at that very moment, the flame is further able to burn its support, the wick.

In this way, the lamp-flame is the cause for the burning of the wick. The arising of the flame from the wick is analogous to the arising of the manifest [result] from the seed. The burning of the wick by the flame is analogous to the arising of the seed from the manifest [result].
Furthermore, the mutual dependence for their abiding, like bundles of reeds, is analogous to the arising of seeds from seeds. As it is said:
This demonstrates that there is a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), by which seeds and manifest phenomena arise and mutually depend upon one another for their subsistence;

only then do they constitute direct causes and conditions. Although the others are termed "conditions" (*pratyaya*), they are not "causes" (*hetu*). To establish this through formal logic (*pramāṇa*):

the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are the subject (*dharmin*); the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that at all times they are mutually cause and effect.

The reason is stated as follows: because they arise in a continuous succession, and because they abide in mutual dependence, it is like the relationship between a wick and its flame, or like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.

If it were said that seeds exist only inherently (*prakṛti-stha*) and are not produced by perfuming (*vāsanā*), how could the first seven consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness serve as mutual causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) for one another?
If one claims that seeds exist inherently and are merely made to increase through perfuming, [the objection remains].

Because it is long-lasting, it may be described as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). However, this does not mean that being perfumed and causing [the seeds] to increase is what constitutes a causal condition.

If one were to claim that being perfumed and causing [the seeds] to increase could be called a causal condition, then virtuous and non-virtuous karma that produces ripened results (*vipāka-phala*) would all have to be called causal conditions rather than dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Therefore, we know that although these [seeds] are inherently present, they also arise through perfuming. If one were to cling to [this view]...
If seeds did not arise through perfuming (*vāsanā*), it would contradict both scripture and reasoning.
If [uncontaminated phenomena] were merely newly arisen conditioned uncontaminated states, then uncontaminated phenomena would not be produced without a cause.
If there were only newly perfumed seeds and no innate seeds, then conditioned uncontaminated phenomena would be unable to arise, as they would lack causes and conditions.
Conditioned uncontaminated phenomena refer precisely to the four wisdoms of enlightenment below.
While self-nature *tathatā* may not be produced from seeds, the four wisdoms of enlightenment must necessarily have seeds. If innate uncontaminated seeds did not exist, [they could not arise].
The four wisdoms of enlightenment must arise from contaminated seeds, because contaminated [seeds] do not produce uncontaminated seeds.
If contaminated seeds could produce uncontaminated [phenomena], then uncontaminated seeds would likewise produce contaminated ones.

If one were to admit that the uncontaminated produces the contaminated, then it would follow that contaminated afflictions and virtues would arise again from within the uncontaminated seeds of all Buddhas.
The seeds [of the mind] should likewise give rise to unwholesome seeds.

According to the *Vibhajyavādins*, regarding such statements as "the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure" (*cittaprakṛtiviśuddhi*), it appears at first glance that the nature of the tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) itself can produce the untainted; thus, there would be no need for a separate untainted seed.

If one examines this minutely, the phrase "the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure" refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the emptiness of the mind, which serves as the cause for the four wisdoms of enlightenment.
Therefore, untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not arise without a cause;
they must certainly possess seeds within them.
Regarding the statement "the nature of mind," what meaning does that refer to? (Up to: Because the natures of seeds and active manifestations are identical.

This is a successive clarification of the single phrase "the nature of mind is originally pure. According to the Abhidharma school (lakṣaṇavāda), they define "mind" as arising from the accumulation [of seeds], and take the True Suchness revealed by the emptiness of the mind as its nature.
Therefore, it is asked in response: "As for the 'nature of mind' spoken of by those proponents of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpavādin*)," [what is meant?]

"Original purity. What meaning does this term signify? If one asserts that the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the nature of the mind, then the principle of emptiness cannot be the seed of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), because emptiness is an eternal phenomenon (*nitya-dharma*) and thus lacks transformation. Consequently, he sets forth the formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"The principle of emptiness is an eternal phenomenon; it is certainly not a seed, because it lacks transformation, just like space (*ākāśa*). It must be [the *dharmadhātu*]...
That [seed] perishes immediately; it is only when there is a superior capacity that it constitutes a seed.

If one were to say that the nature itself is the mind and serves as the cause for the untainted (*anāsrava*), this would be identical to the Sāṃkhya school. They hold that the three qualities (*guṇa*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) act as the productive cause;
although the characteristics of the three qualities undergo transformation, primordial nature remains eternally one and unchanging. Thus, he sets forth the formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
It is said: "Nature is identical to mind; although its manifestations undergo transformation, its essence remains eternally one, much like the Sāṃkhya school.
If it is asserted that nature is identical to mind, and this mind is the cause of the untainted (anāsrava), then [what of] the evil mind and the indeterminate mind?"

All [minds] should be wholesome. This is because contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) are subsumed under the category of maturation-neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), whereas uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are subsumed under the category of the wholesome.

If one does not distinguish between the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral, but speaks generally of "nature" as being simply the mind, then the single term "nature" would encompass the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the neutral;
consequently, unwholesome and neutral minds would necessarily become wholesome.
Regarding its nature: if one allows that an unwholesome or neutral mind could possess a wholesome nature, then it should be associated with the eleven wholesome factors, such as faith and so forth.
If one does not allow that an unwholesome or neutral mind possesses a wholesome nature, then this unwholesome or neutral state is not associated with wholesome factors.
Since even an unwholesome or neutral mind cannot be associated with wholesome factors, how [could it be otherwise]?

Can it be associated with untainted seeds? Furthermore, since an impure wholesome mind is termed "defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*) and its nature is not untainted, it is no different from unwholesome or neutral minds; it certainly cannot serve as a cause for the untainted.
Thus, he presents the formal argument (*pramāṇa*): An impure wholesome mind is not by nature untainted, because it is defiled, just like [an unwholesome or neutral mind].
Because of [the presence of] evil minds and so forth, wholesome *sāsrava* (outflowing) minds should not serve as causes for the *anāsrava* (non-outflowing).
This is to avoid the consequence that the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—would mutually act as causes for one another.

If it is argued that the real nature (*dharmatā*) of an outflowing mind is the seed of the non-outflowing, then the real nature of the non-outflowing mind would likewise be the seed of the outflowing. Within a single nature, one must seek...

Because a differentiating cause and condition cannot be found. If it were claimed that the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is an untainted seed (*anāsrava-bīja*), then all manifest activities (*samudācāra*) arising during the stage of an ordinary person would necessarily be untainted; they should thus be called "noble ones" (*ārya*) and not "ordinary persons.
If it is argued that although the actual nature (*dharmatā*) of the ordinary person's mind is untainted, yet the characteristics of an ordinary person...
If it is argued that [the state] still remains within the stage of defilement and is therefore not called "untainted" (*anāsrava*), this is also incorrect.
Since the characteristics of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) are already tainted, then both the mind and its seeds must necessarily be tainted.

For what reason does your treatise claim that there are ordinary beings who possess only the accomplishment of untainted seeds? If the seeds are accomplished, then the manifest activity [must also follow].

It is likewise so, because there is necessarily no distinction between the nature and characteristics of the seeds and their manifestations. Consequently, one in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) should be called a noble one (*ārya*).
However, it should be understood that when the sūtras speak of the "innate purity of the mind" (*cittaprakṛtiviśuddhi*), they are referring to the category of untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).

This clarifies the correct meaning. Regarding the purity of the mind’s nature (*cittaprakṛti-viśuddhi*): this refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the emptiness of the mind that arises through accumulation.
This *tathatā* is precisely the actual nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of this mind, which is immovable and unchanging.

This actual nature is without action, unconditioned, undefiled, and unstained; it is called "purity by nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*). Furthermore, it is said that the substantial reality of this mind is not...

Although it falls within the midst of afflictive defilements, it is called "pure by nature. This does not mean that the nature of the tainted (*sāsrava*) mind is untainted (*anāsrava*), which is what is meant by "pure by nature.

Because this mind-nature is pure by nature, all sentient beings have, from beginningless time, possessed untainted seeds that are spontaneously accomplished (*dharmatā-siddha*) without depending on perfuming (*vāsanā*).
