Subsequently, upon reaching the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), [these seeds are activated].

By means of the power of hearing and perfuming, [these seeds] are perfumed and caused to increase. Therefore, at the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one abandons the delusions of conceptual construction (*vikalpavāsanā*).
When the untainted (*anāsrava*) manifests, it necessarily takes these pure, untainted seeds of *tathatā* as its cause to become an actualized manifestation (*pravṛtti*).
Once the untainted manifestation has arisen, it successively perfumes and brings about all the seeds of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). For this reason, it is certain that [these seeds] exist.

Regarding the two types of seeds—the originally existing (*prakṛtistha*) and the newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*)—just as it is with the untainted (*anāsrava*), so should it be understood for the tainted (*sāsrava*).
Although various holy teachings speak of internal seeds [as being the seeds of the supramundane mind], this is merely a provisional explanation.
First, this responds to the previous position. Question: If that is so, why does the treatise state that internal seeds necessarily possess perfuming (*vāsanā*)?
Answer: Although the sacred teachings clarify that internal seeds necessarily possess perfuming, the meaning of "perfuming" here applies only to the sense of "augmentation" (*upacaya*).
Furthermore, it is not definitively taught that all seeds arise solely through perfuming; how then could one completely deny the existence of innate seeds?
Nevertheless, although they are innate, if they lack the power of perfuming, they cannot be increased or made to flourish, nor can they produce superior fruits.
They must undergo the process of perfuming and gradual cultivation until habituation merges with their nature; only then can they attain fruition. Therefore, it is said regarding the internal...

All seeds necessarily possess perfuming (*vāsanā*). When this perfuming of hearing occurs while listening to the True Dharma, it does not merely perfume and give rise to the seeds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas;
it is also able to perfume and give rise to the originally existing uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharma-seeds, which successively produce supramundane minds.
This perfuming of hearing has two kinds of conditions. If it perfumes the seeds of contaminated dharmas, the cause and effect are not forgotten, and it is able to induce [their maturation].
The superior matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the two vehicles serves as a potent dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for supramundane dharmas;

however, this seed can be severed upon reaching the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). If one perfumes the seeds of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas, these act as the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for supramundane dharmas;
this cause remains uninterrupted until the stage of Buddhahood, because it is innately present (*prakṛtistha*), and is not [severed].
[Included in] that which is to be abandoned. Question: If the hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*) is a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), why can it perfume the seeds of supramundane mind?
Answer: Because this nature of the direct cause and condition (*hetupratyaya*) of the untainted seeds is subtle, profound, and hidden, it cannot be fully understood.
Therefore, by relying upon the coarse and manifest nature of perfuming as a superior dominant condition, it is expediently described as "supramundane."

The seeds of the worldly mind are, in reality, the seeds of the supramundane mind; they are the intrinsically existing (prakṛtistha) primary causes and conditions for the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the establishment of the distinctions among lineages (*gotra*) based on obstructions, each possesses two types: the intrinsically existing and the newly arisen (*ābhisamskārika*).

This also applies to the previous position. Question: If that is so, why does the treatise state that the original distinctions among sentient beings' lineages (*gotra*) are established based on the presence or absence of obstacles, rather than by the presence or absence of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*)?
Answer: It is because the presence or absence of untainted seeds reveals whether the obstacles can or cannot be severed.

Regarding the meaning of "that which can be severed": if it were not by virtue of the presence or absence of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), upon what basis would those two types of obstructions depend for their severance or non-severance?
However, because untainted seeds are subtle, profound, and hidden, they are difficult to discern;
therefore, the distinctions among spiritual lineages (*gotra*) are manifested in relation to the two obstructions. This does not mean that untainted seeds are entirely non-existent.

Furthermore, if it is claimed that these two obstacles exist by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) and thereby establish the distinctions among the five natures (*pañca-gotra*), then the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-dharma-bīja*) must likewise exist by the very nature of things as distinct [from tainted seeds].
Why is this not admitted? If it is claimed that there are no untainted seeds at all, [then...]
In that case, the noble paths of the three vehicles would have no means of arising. Who could then sever the seeds of the two hindrances?
Yet you speak of establishing the distinctions between spiritual lineages based on those hindrances.

Since those noble paths would necessarily lack the possibility of arising, all untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) would become utterly severed and extinguished. To claim that they "can certainly arise" is logically impossible. Now, the following section generally refutes this [position].
No. From this point downward, the two [positions] have already been presented.
However, there are briefly six types of the meaning of "seed" (bīja), up to the point that one cannot say it possesses the capacity to produce [a result].

The following clarifies the six meanings of the seed (*bīja*). "Momentary extinction" (*kṣaṇika*) reveals that it possesses the characteristic of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and subject to transformation.
Only when it is in a state of transformation and capable of producing a manifest fruit does it constitute a seed.

This excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) over a long duration, and the eternal self (*ātman*) of the non-Buddhists from being seeds; for an eternal phenomenon lacks transformation and is thus incapable [of producing fruit].
Because it gives rise to all phenomena.
Second, "simultaneous with the fruit" means that [the seed] exists together with what it produces; therefore, one should simply say it is simultaneous with its fruit.
Question: If momentary cessation constitutes the seed, then should the preceding moment’s seed be regarded in relation to the subsequent moment’s seed? Or...
One should consider the past and future in relation to one another; all may serve as seeds. Answer: It is necessary that they coexist with their fruit.

That is to say, for this seed to be established as a seed, it must coexist and be in conjunction with the manifest fruit-dharmas that it is intended to produce. "Manifest" means present and currently existing.
"Conjunction" means existing within a single body at the same time. Only the production of the manifest from the seed occurs; different categories do not correspond in this way.
The two are not mutually contradictory. When a single entity at one time possesses the capacity for production, it is called "simultaneous existence with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*).
This excludes both temporal contradiction and necessary separation. If a seed were to produce a seed, this would be the mutual generation of its own kind;

such cases involve temporal contradiction and necessarily lack simultaneity. Question: Since the production of seeds from manifestations involves entities of different kinds, why are they simultaneous? If...

The seed that produces a seed is of the same category (*sabhāga*). Why do they not arise simultaneously? Answer: Although the seed, in relation to its manifest fruit, is of a different category, the two are not mutually contradictory;

therefore, they are admitted to be simultaneous. However, although the seed, in relation to a seed-fruit, is of the same category, their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are mutually exclusive, and thus they must necessarily differ in time.
Although the production of a seed from a seed is also called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), it lacks causal efficacy (*hetu-vyāpāra*) and is not [a true transformation].

"Simultaneous with the fruit" (phala-sahabhū) means that the seed and the manifestation must exist simultaneously in the present for there to be the causal function; this is what is termed "simultaneous with the fruit.
If [the seed] were future and not yet arisen, or past and already ceased, it would be a provisional phenomenon (prajñapti-dharma) and thus lack a real substantial entity (dravya-svabhāva).

Lacking the functional capacity to produce, it cannot serve as a seed. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "To produce a fruit after having already ceased is like a dead chicken crowing."

Question: Why is it that those of different categories do not contradict one another, while those of the same category do contradict one another? Answer: It is like a child in relation to its mother; the child is not the mother because they belong to different categories.

When the mother is related to herself, this is called being of the same category. They exist simultaneously and together. When the mother is related to herself, it is termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
Therefore, at any given moment, two bodies do not exist simultaneously. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"As for what is called 'coexistent,' it does not mean the past, nor the future, nor that which is separated [in time]. It is that which can serve as a seed. Why is this?
Because if the seed exists at this time, the fruit arises at that very same time. Now, based on its capacity to produce a manifest fruit, we establish the seed."
Regarding the name "seed" (*bīja*): it is not defined as that which arises from its own kind (*svajāti*).
Therefore, one should only say that it co-exists with its fruit (*phala-sahabhū*), and not that it co-exists with its cause (*hetu-sahabhū*).
"Third, it must persist continuously (*nitya-anuvartana*)," meaning that it must endure over a long period. This demonstrates that seeds produce their own kind (*sva-jātīya*).

Question: If a seed must exist simultaneously with its manifest fruit in order to be called a "seed," then why are the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the first seven consciousnesses not called seeds, since they too exist simultaneously with their fruits?
Answer: It must persist continuously; that is to say, it must endure over a long period. This means...

It continues in a long-term succession, its nature being of a single class, until the attainment of Buddhahood; it is only upon relinquishing the state of maturation (*vipāka*) that it is designated a "seed.
This excludes the case of the manifesting consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) when they perfume seeds, for although they coexist with the seeds and their fruits, they do not persist continuously.

Because consciousness arises intermittently and the three natures (trisvabhāva) arise alternately, rather than evolving as a single homogeneous stream over a long duration, it is incompatible with the nature of seeds.
Only the eighth consciousness possesses the status of a seed; it evolves continuously, which demonstrates that seeds produce their own kind.
Question: If you say it is a single homogeneous continuity, how can there be such a thing as "life-span" (āyus)?

[Question: What is the characteristic of exhaustion (*kṣaya-lakṣaṇa*)? [Answer: This refers to the characteristic of the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyuḥ-kṣaya-lakṣaṇa*), defined by the limitation of the fruit produced; however, the substance of the seed is not severed.

Regarding the determination of the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva-viniścaya*): it means that according to the power of the cause, there is the principle of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-artha*) whereby a fruit of a different nature is produced.

Question: If that which constantly evolves [in succession] is designated as a seed, then seeds of wholesome states (*kuśala*) and so forth that produce defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and other manifest states should also be called seeds.

Answer: It must be of a determinate nature; that is, a preceding cause gives rise to a subsequent manifest fruit, and the preceding and succeeding states—whether wholesome and so forth—are determinate and unmixed.
Only then is it called a seed. This excludes the case where a cause of a different nature produces a fruit of a different nature.
It is not called a "seed. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "That is to say, these seeds are individually determined;
they do not arise from everything out of everything. From this specific type of entity, only that same entity arises. Question:

If a cause of a different nature is not called a seed, how can it be said that while the cause encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Answer: That [text] speaks of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This explains the causal conditions; therefore, they are not identical.
The fifth [point], "depending on various conditions," means that this [seed] must depend on [the arrival of] conditions; thus, the seed does not constantly or simultaneously produce its fruit.

Question: If a self-nature cause that produces a self-nature effect is called a "seed," then this self-nature cause should produce this [effect] all at once at all times, and it too should be called a seed.
Answer: It must depend upon the convergence of various conditions and possess a preeminent capacity to give rise to the manifest state (*samudācāra*) before it can constitute a seed.
This refutes the non-Buddhist view of spontaneous and simultaneous production.

Regarding "fruition" and "multiple conditions": these refer to the four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*). For example, mental phenomena arise from the four conditions, while material phenomena exist through two conditions.

Furthermore, other schools of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) maintain that conditions are eternally existent; here, by stating that [phenomena] depend upon multiple conditions, it is precisely intended to refute the view that conditions are not eternally existent.
Therefore, seeds do not produce their fruits instantaneously. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "That is to say, these seeds must await their own specific conditions before they can produce a fruit;
they cannot produce everything at all times. When they encounter their own specific conditions in a particular place and at a particular time, it is then and there that their own fruit arises."
Sixth, "drawing forth its own fruit" means that [various factors], such as form and mind, are held to be mutual causes and conditions for one another.
Question: If a seed is defined as that which depends upon various conditions, then a single cause should produce all fruits;
or rather, a seed of mind should produce the fruit of form. Answer: It must draw forth its own fruit; that is, only when it draws forth its own specific fruit of form or mind is it called a seed.
Son, it is like a seed of form producing a fruit of form, or a seed of mind producing a fruit of mind, and so forth.

This refutes the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) calculation that a single cause produces multiple effects, and further refutes the other schools' (nikāya) insistence that matter and mind arise from one another.
Only those specific functional capacities within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna)— up to [the point that] they are fruits produced by seeds of common characteristics—
properly constitute internal seeds, provided that a portion of these specific functional capacities within the fundamental consciousness possesses the aforementioned six characteristics.
All others are incapable of achieving this. Question: External grains such as wheat and so forth can also produce sprouts, stems, and leaves;
they could thus be called seeds. Why then do they not qualify? Answer: Because rice and other such grains are all produced by the collective karma of sentient beings for common enjoyment;
in reality, they are transformations of internal consciousness. It is only according to worldly convention that they are metaphorically designated as "seeds."
Question: Why is it not real? Answer: Because the seed of form lacks resistance, whereas the seed of grain possesses resistance.
Furthermore, these internal and external seeds possess two functional capacities with respect to the fruit they produce, which constitute two types of causes:

first, the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), which refers to that which directly brings about the fruit at the initial moment; second, the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), which refers to that which possesses residual power to...
The produced fruit continues in a succession until its ultimate end;

therefore, just as the internal seeds are called "generative causes" (*janaka-hetu*) in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), so too, in relation to the six sense faculties, youth, vigor, old age, decline, and death—continuing until the remains of the corpse have not yet perished—all these are called "projecting causes" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
If external seeds are considered in relation to the sprout, they are called...

It acts as the cause of production (*janana-hetu*). Subsequently, it draws forth the stem, causes leaves to emerge, brings about the blossoming of flowers and the formation of fruits, and continues in succession until the time of withering;
all these stages are termed the cause of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In this context, internal seeds [continue] until the limit of the lifespan."
They serve as productive causes (*janaka-hetu*). External seeds act as productive causes until the fruit ripens;

internal seeds can draw forth the remains of the corpse after death, while external seeds can draw forth the continuity of the withered state after [the plant] has perished. By means of this drawing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), they persist for a long duration.
If these two types of seeds were merely productive causes, then once that cause is destroyed, the fruit should immediately perish, and it would not persist for even a brief moment.

Regarding the meaning of continuous abiding: if one claims that moments arise in a successive succession where the preceding moment acts as the cause and the succeeding moment follows accordingly, then the final moment at the end should not be subject to total cessation.
Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that there exists an "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*).
These two seeds are like a drawn bowstring: with the bent bow acting as the cause, the arrow does not fall but travels to a distant place. Upon release—
The arrow is the cause of its arising; the bending of the bow is the cause of its projection. Once released from the string, it travels to a distant place.
If one were to claim that the act of releasing the arrow alone is the cause and not the bending of the bow, then the arrow would not travel far.

If one were to say that the arrow of the preceding moment gives rise to the arrow of the subsequent moment, and thus the arrow reaches a distance, then there would be no possibility for the arrow to fall. [End of External]

The same applies to internal seeds: they wither and perish because their generative causes (*janaka-hetu*) have been exhausted, and they cease completely because their projecting causes (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) have been exhausted.
Internal seeds necessarily depend on perfuming (*vāsanā*); for instance, without the cause of the perfuming of extensive learning, the fruit of extensive learning will certainly not arise.
As for external seeds, the presence or absence of perfuming is not fixed; therefore, the word "or" is used, as in the case of rice or barley seeds.
They arise from rice and wheat; what need is there for perfuming (*vāsanā*)?

Furthermore, it is said that just as *karañja* seeds, blue lotus roots, and reeds arise sequentially from charcoal, cow dung, and cow hair respectively, it is not the case that the *karañja* seeds and the like co-arise and co-cease with the charcoal and so forth, mutually perfuming one another, and thus arise from them. Thus, external seeds, or...

There is no perfuming (*vāsanā*). For example, when sesame seeds (*tila*) and the like arise and perish together with flower garlands and the like, it is through perfuming that they produce fragrances and so forth.

Thus, some external seeds may possess perfuming; therefore, external objects must necessarily rely upon external seeds as their dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because these are the most preeminent.
If external seeds are to bring about their fruit, they must necessarily have internal causes as their [primary] cause.
Regarding their direct conditions: the external receptacle world is a common-characteristic seed-field produced by the collective karma of many beings.
Since these rice, wheat, and so forth arise from this common-characteristic seed-field, internal seeds are not distinct from the external; they are thus termed "conventionally existent."
Based on what meaning is the term "perfuming" (vāsanā) established? [It is so called] because it causes seeds to grow and develop;
thus it is named "perfuming. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "As for what is called perfuming: it is like the perfuming of sesame seeds by flowers.
The sesame seeds and the flowers arise and perish together; these sesame seeds are then produced bearing the cause capable of generating that fragrance. Furthermore, it is like...
For one who practices with craving and so forth, the perfuming of craving and so forth arises and ceases simultaneously with that craving;

this mind arises bearing the cause for its production by that [perfuming]. Or, for one who is well-learned, the perfuming of extensive learning arises and ceases simultaneously with the mental attention (*manasikāra*) based on hearing;
this mind arises bearing the cause for its designation by that [perfuming], because it is able to sustain and maintain those perfumings.
One who upholds the Dharma is so named. It should be understood that the principle of the perfuming of the *ālaya-vijñāna* is likewise. Question:
How many meanings do the perfumer (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*) each possess to receive the designation "perfuming"? Answer: Both the perfumer and the perfumed each possess four meanings.
Therefore, it is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*). Question: Among the eight consciousnesses, which are the perfumers (*kṣepaka*) and which are the perfumed (*kṣepya*)?
Answer: The first seven are all perfumers; the eighth alone is the perfumed. Question: Regarding the first seven, do all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) act as perfumers, or is it otherwise?
Answer: Excluding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, because it lacks superior functional capacity and cannot perfume seeds, the remaining wholesome and unwholesome [natures] [do perfume].
And those of an obscured nature—these are all capable of being perfumed. Question: For what reason is only the eighth consciousness alone the perfumable? Answer:
Because the four characteristics of the perfumable exist only in the eighth; therefore, the eighth alone is designated as the perfumable.
What are the four characteristics of that which is perfumable (*bhāvyatva*)? [Up to: because its nature is not stable, it is not perfumable. Question:
What are the four characteristics of the eighth consciousness as the perfumable? Answer:

That which serves as the perfumable consciousness must be of a single type, stable, continuous and uninterrupted, and capable of maintaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) so that they are not lost; only such a thing is the perfumable.
Now, the first six evolving consciousnesses are not stable because they are interrupted during the five states of mindlessness;

thus, they certainly cannot be the basis for perfuming (*vāsanā*). As for the seventh consciousness, although it is uninterrupted during the impure (*sāsrava*) state, it is nonetheless interrupted by liberation during the pure (*anāsrava*) state;
therefore, it is not the basis for perfuming. Although the eighth consciousness is impure while in the causal stage, its essence is free from interruption.

[Response: Although they are undefiled-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), this does not preclude their ability to maintain uncontaminated seeds (*anāsravabīja*) and thus to be designated as "perfumable" (*bhāvya*).

One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: The seven preceding evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are the subject (*dharmin*); they are not perfumable, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they lack stable persistence (*asthira*).
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like lightning, wind, sound, and so forth.
Regarding the second point, the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): if a phenomenon is equanimous [in its nature] (up to: it only carries old seeds and is not newly perfumed). Question:
If that which possesses a stable and enduring nature (*sthirabhāva*) is what is perfumable, then the eighth consciousness of the Buddha-fruit is also stable and enduring;
should it not therefore be called perfumable? Answer: To be designated as "perfumable," it must be of a single class and indeterminate; thus, [the Buddha-fruit consciousness] is not.
Only that which opposes the two natures of good and evil can receive their perfuming. Now, the eighth consciousness of the Buddha-fruit is of a virtuous nature;

therefore, it cannot accommodate the perfuming of unwholesome or neutral natures, as it is not something to be perfumed. This is because the virtuous nature of the eighth consciousness of the Buddha-fruit is already perfected.
If it were of an unwholesome nature, it would be affliction (*kleśa*), and furthermore, it could not accommodate wholesome qualities such as faith.
The nature (*prakṛti*) is not perfumed because its various aspects are mutually incompatible; thus, it cannot serve as the object of perfuming (*bhāvyatva*).

Only the eighth consciousness, being a vast and expansive mind, can accommodate all karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) of both good and evil. Because it possesses this capacity, it alone is designated as the "perfumable.

As it is said: "The wholesome and the defiled are like musk, civet, leeks, and garlic; therefore, they do not receive perfuming. The indeterminate is like plain white silk; therefore," [it receives perfuming].

[The eighth consciousness] is capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*). Question: Since the untainted (*anāsrava*) eighth consciousness does not receive perfuming, from where do the various untainted seeds arise?

Answer: If it concerns the untainted pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) of a Tathāgata’s eighth consciousness, these exist only as seeds previously perfumed while [the Bodhisattva] was still within the causal stage.
This carries its original seeds; it is not newly perfumed only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood. One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
The eighth pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) is not that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*), because it is comprised within the nature of goodness (*kuśala-dharma*), just like camphor and musk.
Third, regarding the nature of being perfumable (*vāsanīyatva*): if a phenomenon is autonomous (*svatantra*), or [if it is] dependent (*paratantra*) yet firm and dense, it is not perfumable.

Question: If that which possesses a firm nature and an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature is called "perfumable," then for instance, the eighth consciousness, the five mental factors (*caitasika*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) all possess these two characteristics; they should therefore be called perfumable. Answer: As for that which is perfumable...
It must possess mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*) and have a nature that is not firm or dense; only then can it be that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*).

Regarding "mastery," this merely excludes the position of Nanda, who allows the eighth consciousness to be perfumed by the five minds, because mental factors (*caitta*), being dependently originated, lack such mastery and thus do not possess the nature of being perfumed.
Regarding "having a nature that is not firm or dense," this specifically excludes the True [Nature] of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.

Just as [the other seven consciousnesses] receive perfuming, the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) does not receive perfuming because it is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), firm, and dense, like gold or stone.
Only the eighth [consciousness] has an essence that is empty and porous, and thus it can receive perfuming. One should establish the formal argument (prayoga) as follows:

The eighth [consciousness] and the five objects are not of a nature that receives perfuming, because they lack sovereignty; they are like ministers and so forth. True Suchness is unconditioned and is not [of a nature that receives perfuming].
The nature of being perfumed (*vāsanā-dharmin*). Because its nature is firm and dense, it is likened to gold or stone.

Fourth, the nature of being in common conjunction with the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*)—up to the point that it may be the object of perfuming (*bhāvya*) but is not a mental factor (*caitta*) and so forth.

Question: If it is said that that which possesses a stable nature, an indeterminate nature, and the capacity to be perfumed is the "perfumable," then this person’s eighth consciousness should be able to receive the perfuming of another person’s first seven consciousnesses, because this person’s eighth consciousness also possesses the capacity to be perfumed.
Answer: Only when [a consciousness] exists simultaneously and in the same location as its own perfuming agent can it be called "perfumable. Now, in this case...

The eighth consciousness does not receive the perfuming of the seven preceding consciousnesses of others, because they do not exist simultaneously in the same location and thus lack the sense of conjunction;

therefore, it is not that which is perfumed. This also refutes the Sautrāntika position that a preceding moment of consciousness perfumes a subsequent moment of consciousness, as these are likewise not simultaneous and thus cannot be perfumed.
One should establish the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows: The eighth consciousness is not perfumed by the seven preceding consciousnesses of others, because they are not in conjunction.
Because they are conjoined, like the eye and sound.
What are called the four meanings of being an "impregnator" (*vāsaka*)? [Up to: Because it lacks the function of producing growth, it is not an impregnator. Question:
What are the four meanings of being an impregnator for the first seven [consciousnesses]? Answer: That which acts as an impregnator must, moment by moment, [possess these qualities].
Only that which possesses arising and ceasing is designated as "capable of perfuming" (*vāsanā*). Now, the first seven consciousnesses are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);

they possess the sense of arising and ceasing and have active functions; thus, they are capable of perfuming. This excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which remains unchanged before and after, lacks the sense of arising and ceasing, and lacks the function of growth and production;
therefore, it is not capable of perfuming. One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: These unconditioned phenomena are not [capable of perfuming].
This is the perfuming agent; it remains unchanged before and after, like empty space.
The second [type of consciousness] possesses superior function, yet because it undergoes arising and ceasing—and its power becomes weak—it is not a perfuming agent.

Question: If that which possesses arising and ceasing is called a "perfuming agent" (*bhāvakatṛ*), then for instance, the mind and mental factors produced by the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, as well as matter (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), all possess the activity of arising and ceasing; they too should be perfuming agents. Answer: There must be a superior function. Now, the first seven consciousnesses possess all three natures (*tri-dharmatā*), their power is predominant, and they possess a distinguished function capable of inducing [the seeds]. Therefore, they alone are the perfuming agents. As for the maturation-born mind and mental factors, matter, and non-associated formations, although they have the activity of arising and ceasing, they lack such a superior function. Consequently, they cannot be perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to project its own fruit. Matter and non-associated formations cannot project their own fruit; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Moreover, the perfuming agent must be able to produce its own fruit. Matter and non-associated formations cannot produce their own fruit; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to transform its own fruit. Matter and non-associated formations cannot transform their own fruit; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to increase its own fruit. Matter and non-associated formations cannot increase their own fruit; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to decrease its own fruit. Matter and non-associated formations cannot decrease their own fruit; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to manifest its own fruit. Matter and non-associated formations cannot manifest their own fruit; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to conceal its own fruit. Matter and non-associated formations cannot conceal their own fruit; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to cause its own fruit to arise. Matter and non-associated formations cannot cause their own fruit to arise; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to cause its own fruit to cease. Matter and non-associated formations cannot cause their own fruit to cease; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to cause its own fruit to increase. Matter and non-associated formations cannot cause their own fruit to increase; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to cause its own fruit to decrease. Matter and non-associated formations cannot cause their own fruit to decrease; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to cause its own fruit to manifest. Matter and non-associated formations cannot cause their own fruit to manifest; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. Furthermore, the perfuming agent must be able to cause its own fruit to conceal.
