Vāsanā (habitual tendencies) is that which can act as a perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*). This excludes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) produced by the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma;

because their power is weak, they lack a potent function and are therefore not perfuming agents. Although material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) possess a potent function, they lack the capacity for objective apprehension (*ālambana*) and are thus also not perfuming agents.
Non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) lack both of these functions and are therefore not perfuming agents. It should...

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: The resultant mind and mental factors, material phenomena, and non-associated formations do not possess the nature of being perfumers (*vāsaka*), because their power is weak, like that of a person about to die.

If the three realms of existence (tridhātu) were subject to increase or decrease, and if they possessed functional efficacy, then the fruits of Buddhahood attained at earlier and later times would necessarily have degrees of superiority or inferiority.

Question: If that which possesses arising and ceasing, as well as superior functional efficacy, is designated as a "perfuming agent" (vāsanā), then [the seeds] of the first seven stages prior to the fruit of Buddhahood would be such agents.

Possessing these two meanings, they should be capable of being perfumers (*vāsanā*). Answer: There must be increase and decrease. Only the first seven [consciousnesses] possess such distinguished functions;
they can increase or decrease, they can be wholesome or unwholesome, and they can accomplish tasks. Only then are they capable of being perfumers.

The first seven consciousnesses in the state of Buddhahood are of the nature of equality (*samatā*); they neither diminish nor benefit. Therefore, they are not perfumers. This applies to the first seven at the stage of fruition as well.

If it were capable of perfuming, it would not be complete; there would have to be superiority or inferiority between preceding and succeeding Buddhas. One should formulate the formal argument (pramāṇa) as follows:
The first seven [consciousnesses] in the state of fruition are not of the nature of perfumers, because they are subject to neither increase nor decrease, just like space.
Fourth, it evolves in conjunction with that which is perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*). Only when these four conditions are present does something qualify as a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*).

Question: If that which possesses arising and ceasing, possesses superior efficacy, and possesses increase and decrease is called a perfuming agent, then the first seven consciousnesses of another person would also possess the aforementioned three conditions and should thus function as perfuming agents for the eighth consciousness of this person.

Answer: Only that which is in conjunction with what it itself perfumes can be a perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*). Now, the seven [consciousnesses] of another person, in relation to the eighth consciousness of this person, do not exist at the same time or place;
thus, they lack the sense of conjunction and are therefore not perfuming agents. One should formulate the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows:
"The seven [consciousnesses] do not perfume the eighth consciousness of another, because they are not in conjunction, just like the ear and visible form. Question: The preceding...
Question: Why are the seven mental factors (*caitta*) also capable of being perfumers (*vāsaka*), just like the king (the mind)? Answer: Because they possess four characteristics. Question:
Why are the mental factors of the eighth consciousness not also perfumed (*vāsya*), unlike the king? Answer: Because they lack the characteristic of sovereignty (*vaśitva*). Question:
If mental factors are not sovereign and are not perfumed, why are they capable of being perfumers despite lacking sovereignty? Answer: [Because...]
As causes, they possess power because mental factors (caitta) possess power; therefore, they are capable of perfuming. To receive perfuming, one must be the primary recipient (vipākadhātu);
since mental factors are not the primary recipients, they are not what is perfumed. Question:

If it is said that as causes they possess power and thus mental factors can perfume, then as effects they should also possess power, and thus mental factors should likewise be what is perfumed. Answer: Mental factors, as effects, [lack the necessary stability].

At that time, that which lacks power cannot be perfumed. If the eighth consciousness (the king) and its associated mental factors (the subjects)—a single aggregate—were all to receive perfuming, then for every single perfuming agent, six types [of seeds] would arise through perfuming.
When they encounter conditions, these six types should then suddenly produce six manifest states simultaneously.

If one sentient being were to suddenly produce six manifest states, it would result in six sentient beings, which contradicts the sacred teachings regarding the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*).

If there were neither increase nor decrease [in the seeds], it would constitute a great error. Question: When the eighteen mental factors (caitta) of the seventh consciousness, which act as perfumers (vāsaka), perfume the eighteenth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna) at one time, they collectively perfume the seeds of the eighteen objective realities (bhāva). Why is there no fault of eighteen fruits arising simultaneously?
Answer: Although the perfumers are many, they receive perfuming in a single location and produce only a single fruit, just as in the case of a single grain of barley.
Just as many particles of flour together produce a single sprout, so it is here: although the grain of barley is one while the particles of flour are many, they together produce a single sprout;
likewise, although the locus of support is one while the seeds are many, they together produce a single fruit.
Question: Of the four divisions [of the eighth consciousness], with respect to which division do the first seven perfuming agents perfume the eighth consciousness? Answer:

The first five perfume the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness; the sixth perfumes the seeds of both the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) and the *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness.

The seventh [consciousness] can perfume the seeds of the eighth [consciousness’s] seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). Question: Among the four parts of the preceding seven [consciousnesses], which part is capable of perfuming? Answer:
The seeing-part and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are capable of perfuming seeds, because these two parts possess functional activity.

Question: The image-part is material form (*rūpa*); how can it perfume seeds? Answer: It is merely the seeing-part that provides the power, enabling the image-part to perfume seeds. The seeing-part...
The division consists of the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) and the power [of the object].

Just as an owl attaches a clod of earth to produce its eggs, so too do the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumable consciousness (*vāsyavijñāna*). Because it is like the perfuming of sesame seeds (*tila*), it is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).

This is a general explanation of the meaning of *vāsanā* (perfuming). "Perfuming" (*vāsana*) carries the sense of providing nourishment, stimulating, and triggering; "habituation" (*abhyāsa*) carries the sense of growth, development, and maturation.
For example, a sesame seed (*tila*) is originally charcoal that has been buried in the earth for a long time and has transformed into a sesame seed—that is, a sesame plant.
Just as the sesame seed and the flower arise and perish together, through the process of perfuming, a fragrance is produced.
In the West, if one wishes to prepare oil for anointing the body, one first gathers fragrant flowers and *tila* seeds in one place and soaks them until they are thoroughly saturated.

Afterwards, one takes the *tila* seeds and presses them to extract the oil; the oil consequently acquires a fragrance. Since sesame seeds originally possess no fragrance, it arises because of the perfuming by the flowers.
This serves as a metaphor for how the perfumer (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*) come together in one place to produce [an effect].
Only when the perfuming agent and the perfumed [basis] perish simultaneously can the seeds being perfumed undergo growth. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
The perfuming agent and the perfumed basis arise and perish together, whereby the seeds increase; this is like flowers perfuming sesame seeds.
When the perfuming consciousnesses and so forth arise from seeds—this is called a brief explanation of the characteristics of all seeds.

This clarifies that the perfuming agent and the perfumed object are simultaneous in their conjunction, such that the arising of seeds and manifestations serves as the direct causal condition (*pratyaya*). First, establish the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows:
The two dharmas of seed and manifestation are the subject (*dharmin*); the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that cause and effect are simultaneous; the reason (*hetu*) is "mutually [dependent]."

Because they arise from one another. The concordant example is like the wick and the flame. The seed is the phenomenon (*dharma*); furthermore, its ability to produce a seed is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is:
"because they depend upon one another," as in the example of two bundles of reeds. The mutual production of seeds and manifestations is like the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Regarding the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*): as for the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), it functions in accordance with the mind, existing simultaneously [with it];

because the fruit and the cause exist together, it is called the co-existent cause. As for the "fruit of human effort," this refers to various agents, instruments, and so forth, which accomplish diverse activities;
this is called the fruit of human effort. If a seed produces a seed, such that things of the same category produce one another, this is like the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Regarding the cause that induces an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*): as for the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it does not follow other categories because the cause and effect are similar.
An outflowing fruit refers to when the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—act as causes to induce fruits of a similar nature; these are called outflowing fruits.
For example, the seeds of the eighth [consciousness] of the three natures each produce manifest activities (*samudācāra*) of the three natures; thus, the fruit is identical to the cause.

Therefore, as for these two being the direct causal conditions (*nidāna*) for their results, this establishes them as causal conditions. These two are the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Apart from these two causes, all others are predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*); even if they are designated as "causal conditions," one should understand that this is a figurative expression.
This concludes the summary of all types of characteristics. [The text] asks: "How do seeds produce the manifest, and how does the manifest produce..."

Question: Just as a father begets a son and a son begets a grandson, these are certainly direct causes (*nidāna*). By what reasoning can the production of a seed from a seed also be called a direct condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Answer: Since the preceding moment has already ceased and the succeeding moment has already arisen, the substance of the preceding moment directly induces the succeeding moment.

The preceding thought and the succeeding thought are of one essence; how could they not be most intimate? Question: Since the present induces the present, this is also a case where a preceding thought intimately induces a succeeding thought;
it ought to be a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Why, then, is it instead called a true outflow (*nisyanda*)? Answer: Because the seeds already exist.
That is to say, the seeds of the preceding thought give rise to the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of that same preceding thought; those seeds reach the second [moment].

When a thought arises, it gives rise to a second thought as its manifestation; therefore, one knows that the manifestation of a subsequent moment is not directly produced by the manifestation of the preceding moment.
It is like a person wearing a flower who walks forward: the flower itself never moves forward on its own, but merely follows the person as they go.
Thus it is said: "The third category consists of direct causes and conditions; the fourth category consists of true outflows."
One knows that defilement and purity have no intrinsic substance, being formed according to perfuming. If one is separated from the conditions of the perfumer, no dharma can be found;
if there were no substance to be perfumed, what dharma could be established? Thus, one knows that there is not a single dharma that does not arise from the mind.
Following good or evil, it is defiled and formed; through the power of perfuming, it becomes a seed, like paper wrapped with fragrance that is stained by it.
Its fragrant aroma rises and spreads like a cord used to tie fish; it emits a stench when it comes near foul odors.
How much more so for the *ālayavijñāna* of retributive maturation, which is the abiding true mind: when it is perfumed by wholesome dharmas, pure seeds increase;
when it arises from unwholesome dharmas, defiled seeds are fully realized. Thus, while the internal correct cause exists inherently, it requires external conditions to manifest.

Assistance must rely upon new cultivation (*navābhyāsa*) to enable the arising of the fruit; thus, taking cause as the basis for transforming the ordinary into the sacred is like the nature of fire within wood, which is the direct cause of fire.
Without encountering human labor, it does not fulfill the function of fire. Similarly, the Buddha-nature within the body is the direct cause of Buddhahood;
without encountering pure conditions, its wondrous function is difficult to realize. How can the merit of cultivation be neglected?
What are the modes of activity (*ākāra*) and the objects (*ālambana*) of this consciousness? (Up to: Because it arises in dependence upon its modes of activity.

This explains the "unknowable gate," the "gate of modes of activity," and the "gate of objects" within the verse. First, there is the inquiry; second, the verse is cited as the answer; third, the explanation follows.
"Apprehension" (*vijñapti*), meaning "to discern," refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness that acts as the subject of cognition. [The] "bases" (*sthāna*).
As for "the locus," this refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), which is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

The sense organs and the body, as well as the seeds, are likewise the objective aspects of the fundamental consciousness. Within the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, there is a portion that possesses the capacity to produce manifestations;
this is called "seeds. The body endowed with sense organs is termed the "organ-body" (*indriya-kāya*). The organ-body...

The world that serves as the basis is like a vessel; thus it is called the "vessel-world" (*bhājana-loka*). Regarding the phrase "the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of marks (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), and discrimination (*vikalpa*"):

these are the seeds of the Buddha. "Marks" refers to the habitual tendencies of karma; they belong to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). "Names" refers to the two kinds of habitual tendencies of verbal expression;

they belong to the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*). "Discrimination" refers to the two kinds of habitual tendencies of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*); they belong to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). These are three of the five dharmas.

Furthermore, "the material sense-faculties and the bases of the faculties" explains the body of the faculties. The "material sense-faculties" refer to the ultimate sense-faculties (*paramārthendriya*).

The "bases" refer to the locations upon which those material sense-faculties depend. Both of these are appropriated by consciousness and taken as its own substance, because they share the same security and peril.
These two specifically refer to the seeds and the body of the faculties. Appropriation (*upādāna*).

Each possesses two meanings. Regarding the two meanings of "grasping" (*upādāna*): first, the meaning of "gathering," and second, the meaning of "maintaining. That is to say, it gathers [the aggregates] as its own substance and maintains them so they do not disperse.

Regarding the two meanings of "feeling" (*vedanā*): first, the meaning of "experiencing," and second, the meaning of "perceiving. That is to say, it experiences [objects] and takes them as its domain.

It causes the arising of sensation and perception. When the eighth consciousness conditions seeds, it possesses two meanings: first, it grasps them as a single entity, maintaining them so they do not perish;

second, it receives them as a single entity, apprehending them as its object. When the eighth consciousness conditions the sense organs and the body, it possesses four meanings of grasping and maintaining:

first, it assimilates them into its own substance, because they share the same neutral (avyākṛta) nature; second, it maintains them so they do not disperse; third, the eighth consciousness itself is maintained [by the body]; and fourth, it maintains the seeds.
This body is taken as an object for three reasons: first, so that it does not rot or decay; second, because this root-body is the eighth consciousness’s own direct image-part (*sākāra-bhāga*);
and third, so that they may share the same security and peril, for when the eighth consciousness is secure, the root-body is also secure.

The eighth [consciousness] is precarious; its root-body is also precarious. If the eighth consciousness takes the receptacle world as its object, it experiences one aspect within that which is appropriated (*upātta*), taking it as its objective domain.
Because this is a remote image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, it is not subsumed as its own essence nor maintained so as to prevent its dispersal.
When the receptacle world undergoes formation and destruction, the eighth consciousness likewise does not remain stable along with it.

It is precarious; therefore, it also does not cause the arising of sensory perceptions (*vedanā*). Although hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth are close at hand, they are likewise like the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*);
they are not grasped as one's own self, nor are they maintained [as such], nor do they give rise to sensory perceptions.

For this reason, the eighth [consciousness]—whether as that which maintains (*dhāraṇa*) or as that which takes as an object (*ālambana*)—should possess four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). First: that which maintains but does not take as an object, namely, the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). Second: ...

It is supported but not taken as an object; this refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). Third, it both supports and takes as an object; this refers to the sense organs and their bodies (*indriya-āśraya*). Fourth, it neither supports nor takes as an object;

this refers to the seven preceding [consciousnesses] in their active manifestation (*pravṛtti*). Question: For what reason does the eighth consciousness not take the seven preceding consciousnesses in their active manifestation as its objects? Answer:

Because there would be many fallacies. For this reason, it does not take [the object] as its condition. If it were to take it as a condition by way of a transformed reflection (*pratibimba*), it would incur the eighth fallacy of taking a conventional construct as a condition.

If it were to take it as a direct condition, it would incur the fallacy that the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is not established, because it would directly apprehend the minds of others.

Furthermore, it would incur the fallacy of increasing the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), because two layers of the seventh consciousness would arise through the manifestation of the first seven [consciousnesses].
Regarding the phrase "ālaya-vijñāna, etc.": it is said that the eighth consciousness arises as its own substance through the power of causes and conditions;
it then transforms the objects of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) into its own objective referents (*ālambana*), which are then cognized by its aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).

Furthermore, this aspect of seeing arises in dependence upon these objective referents, the aspect of images (*nimitta-bhāga*). The above provides a general explanation; the following provides a detailed analysis.
Among these, "that which realizes" refers to the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) [up to] the point where the aspects of the grasper and the grasped each turn forth spontaneously.
This is the detailed explanation of the gate of mental aspect (*ākāra*). Below this is Dharmapāla’s definitive establishment of the meaning of Vijñapti-mātratā;

it must necessarily possess four parts. First, he refutes Sthiramati’s position that establishes only the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), thereby demonstrating the error of not establishing the image and vision parts (*nimitta- and darśana-bhāga*). An...
The *Huìjù lùn* states: "This self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) arises from conditions and is thus dependently originated (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

therefore, it is said to exist. The perceived and perceiving portions (*nimitta- and darśana-bhāga*), however, do not arise from conditions; they exist only due to the false grasping of the conceptualizing mind (*parikalpita-citta*).

These two portions are existent in terms of mental construction but non-existent in reality. Furthermore, they transform to give rise to the dual grasping of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), which are themselves non-existent."—*Guhyasamāja-tantra* (Miyin jing).

The verse says: "That which is discriminated by the ignorant—external objects—does not exist at all in reality. Because the mind is turbid with habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it evolves appearing as those [objects].
Thus, one should know that these are merely the two parts (*dvaya*) manifested through the false conceptualization (*parikalpa*) arising upon the real self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*);
in truth, the two parts have no substantial entity. It is only because the ignorant do not understand that they falsely cling to them."
[The interlocutor asks: "If you say that the perception of marks (*nimitta*) is provisional, then consider such things as mountains, rivers, and the great earth;

these are included within the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). Since they are perceived as real, how can you say they are provisional? [The respondent] answers: "Although the mountains and rivers are seen as real, they fundamentally exist only through deluded attachment.

When analyzed according to ultimate principle (*tattva*), they do not depart from self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: 'By means of the attachment of one's own mind...'"

[The verse states: "The mind manifests as if it were external objects; that which is seen therein does not exist. Therefore, it is said to be 'mind-only. Thus, one knows that apart from self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), there are no real two parts of subject and object.

Therefore, Dharmapāla refutes [this view], stating: "Within the part of self-cognition, the two parts of the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) must necessarily be present.
Hence it is said: "When the substance of a contaminated consciousness arises, it always manifests as if it were both the cognizing subject and the cognized object."

The objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) manifests. If the mind and mental factors lacked an objective aspect, then the perceiving seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) would not perceive its own respective object.
Regarding "its own respective object": for example, the seeing-part of visual consciousness takes form (rūpa) as its own respective object, while other things are not its own.
Since the perceiving seeing-part does not perceive its own respective object, then each [of the mental factors] individually...

It is able to take all objects as its cognitive domain (*ālambana*). Just as the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of visual consciousness takes [objects], it is also able to take the image-portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of auditory and olfactory consciousnesses and so forth as its domain.

This is because the image-portion belonging to the eye-system is identical to the image-portion belonging to the ear-system, and the image-portion belonging to the ear-system is identical to the image-portion belonging to the eye-system.

To establish this through formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one states: "If mind and mental factors are the subject (*dharmin*), then 'having no objective image' is the thesis (*pakṣa*); the reason (*hetu*) is..."
[The opponent] says: [If so,] it would be unable to take its own object as an object, or else each [cognition] would have to be able to take all things as its objects.
The analogy states: because one's own object is like others, and others are like one's own.

If the mind and mental factors lacked a "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) capable of taking an object, they would be insentient and devoid of cognition, like space and such, lacking the functional capacity to take an object. If you say that although they are like space, they nevertheless...
If that which possesses the capacity to cognize were [non-existent], then even space would have to be a cognizer. To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*):
mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) should not be able to cognize, because they lack the characteristic of being a cognizer, just like space and so forth.

Alternatively, space and so forth would also be cognizers, because they possess the characteristic of being a cognizer, just like mental states and mental factors. Therefore, one knows that mental states and mental factors must necessarily possess the capacity to cognize.

The two aspects of the objective condition and the subjective object. The following citation provides proof: "All things are merely the perceived and the perceiver; their objects are all non-existent.
This means that all phenomena are the manifestations of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Apart from consciousness, there are no real external objects.

As for the statement that "the divisions of the perceiver and the perceived each turn spontaneously," this means that although there are no real external objects outside the mind, [they nevertheless arise] of themselves.
The object-aspect (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) manifested by the self-verifying consciousness (svasaṃvitti) evolve spontaneously without requiring forced effort;
therefore, one knows that the self-verification truly possesses both aspect and seeing. One cannot allow that the self-verification alone is real while the aspect and seeing are non-existent.

Regarding those who maintain that there exists an object of cognition distinct from consciousness, [it follows that] the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) would be identical; thus, these three entities would have no distinction between them.
Next, the errors in Nanda’s position—which posits two parts but does not posit self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*)—are refuted, thereby establishing the correctness of Dignāga’s system of three parts.
First, the errors in Nanda’s position of two parts are set forth: he does not establish self-cognition.
As for "division": that which takes the external essence outside the mind as its objective referent (*ālambana*) is the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*);

the image transformed by the sovereign (*rāja*) and its retinue is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). Thus, the very substance of the sovereign and its retinue is named the seeing-part; these two—the substance and the aspect of the seeing-part—constitute the division into the seeing and the object parts.
Furthermore, it is explained for them: "Why does that [consciousness] take an external object as its objective referent? Just as...

He does not establish a self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). Instead, he takes the external object itself as both the supporting faculty (*āśrayendriya*) and the objective referent (*ālambana*).
As for those with "similar aspects" (*ākāra*), this refers to the *nimittabhāga* (image-portion) transformed by the sovereign [consciousness], because they are equally images.

Regarding the statement that "although the number of entities is equal, their aspects are each distinct, because the aspects of consciousness, sensation, perception, and so forth are each different," the "entity" (*vastu*) refers to the seeing-portion (*darśanabhāga*), while the "number" refers to...

This refers to the mental factors (*caitta*). Although the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and the mental factors are identical in taking the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as their essence and are thus equal and without distinction, their characteristics of discerning, experiencing, and reflecting upon objects are each different.
Therefore, while they share the same essence in the seeing-part, their aspects differ as the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
Since this system does not establish self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), the object does not emerge from within itself; rather, it proceeds directly by...
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the essential nature as its object; thus, the very substance and characteristics of the seeing-part itself constitute the seen-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Next, [the text] sets forth Dignāga’s establishment of the three parts (*tri-svabhāva*). Regarding the realization that there are no objects of cognition apart from consciousness and so forth:

because one realizes that outside of one's own mind there are no separate objects, and that objects are transformations of the internally cognizing part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of consciousness, one [realizes them] by means of what is transformed by oneself.
The image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) functions as the object-condition (*ālambana*), while the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) functions as the mode-of-apprehension (*ākāra*).

Since consciousness has "discernment" (*vijñapti*) as its mode-of-apprehension, the very substance that serves as the basis for both the image and the seeing parts is called the "substantial entity" (*vastu*). This substantial entity is the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
If Nanda were to establish only two parts and not the self-verifying part, then the seeing part would [be the mind and mental factors].
One cannot remember it oneself. Just as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind never again encounters its object, so too, this [object] can certainly not be remembered at a later time.
"Encounter" (*geng*) means to experience. For example, if a presently active form (*rūpa*) has been previously perceived by the seeing-part, it can certainly be recollected at a later time;
if it was not previously perceived by the seeing-part, it can certainly not be recollected at a later time.
Because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which acts as the cognitive faculty, at times past and present, cognizes only the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and never cognizes itself;
since a preceding mind that has already ceased has entered the past, for what reason could it recollect itself?
This is because, in the past, it never reflexively cognized its own seeing-part. Therefore, it is now asserted that at the present time, the mind and mental factors [cognize themselves].

One is able to remember [past experiences] because it is clearly known that, in the past, there was necessarily a self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that took the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, thereby verifying that [seeing-portion] which apprehended the external object and functioning as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
Therefore, one is now able to remember. To establish this through formal logic (*pramāṇa*), the syllogism is stated as follows: This self-cognizing portion is the subject (*dharmin*).

If it did not exist, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: [otherwise] one would not be able to remember the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) themselves. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is... [as follows].

It is said: Just as when one has not yet encountered an object, one clearly knows that at the moment the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of visual consciousness suddenly takes blue as its object, it does not take yellow;

and when it takes yellow as its object, it does not take blue. This is because self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) serves as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*), ensuring that the seeing-part’s engagement with the object is non-erroneous.
Therefore, we know that self-cognition must necessarily exist. As for the mind and mental factors sharing the same supporting faculty (*indriya*): [the text continues].

Just as visual consciousness relies upon the eye-faculty and so forth, regarding "similarity of the object" (*ālambana-sādṛśya*): because internal matter appears as if it were external, it is called "similar.
This differs from the former master’s position that the primary substance (*bimba*) serves as both the support (*āśraya*) and the object.

Regarding "distinctive aspects" (*ākāra-prabheda*): because the functions of the sovereign [consciousness] and its perceived portion are distinct, this differs from the former master’s position regarding the reflected image (*pratibimba*).

The modes of activity (*ākāra*) are similar. Although the number of entities is equal, their characteristics differ because the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of consciousness (*vijñāna*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth, are distinct.

This means that although the essential natures of the "kings" (the primary consciousnesses) and their "retinues" (the mental factors) are all equally [empty], the characteristics and functions of these kings and retinues each differ from one another, because the eight consciousness-kings and their respective retinues each possess their own distinct nature; thus, they are not the same as the former case.
The Master [Dharmapāla] maintains that while the characteristics of reception (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] each differ, they all share the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as their essence.
However, regarding the mind (*citta*), following Dignāga’s three-part model is correct. The earlier Śubhagupta established only one part;
it possesses the essence but lacks function. Nanda established two parts; it possesses function but lacks essence. Both are mutually deficient. Dignāga...

The three divisions [of consciousness] encompass both essence and function. Therefore, the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) is taken as the object of cognition (*prameya*), the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect) as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying aspect) as the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

This is illustrated by the analogy of measuring silk with a ruler: the silk is the object of measurement, the ruler is the means of measurement, and the wisdom that records the count is called the result of measurement.
Now, when the *darśanabhāga* perceives the *nimittabhāga* without error, and is able to recollect the mind itself—this is the self-verifying aspect.
All dharmas take self-realization (*svasaṃvitti*) as their fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). Therefore, it is known that each of the eight consciousnesses possesses three parts.
If there were no self-realization, neither the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) nor the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) would exist. If these two parts exist, self-realization must necessarily exist;
for self-realization is like a snail, while the image and seeing parts are like its two horns. As cited in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*.
Furthermore, if one analyzes the mind and mental factors in detail (up to this point), that which is here termed "seeing" (*darśana*) is the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*).
Below this, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla establishes a fourth portion to compensate for the deficiency in Dignāga’s system.

This is because, were there no self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), there would otherwise be a lack of a third result of cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*). Now, Dignāga takes the seeing-portion as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding the statement that the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is established as the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) because it possesses the function of cognizing an object:

if the self-cognizing portion also possesses the function of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that illuminates an object, then by what dharma would the self-cognizing portion itself be established as the result of valid cognition?

Therefore, it is said: "If this [self-cognition] did not exist, who would verify the third [portion]? Since the divisions of the mind are identical in nature, they should all be capable of verification. Thus, [the opponent argues that] the self-cognizing portion must also have another result of valid cognition.

Since the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is a part of the mind, there must be a self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). Since the self-verifying-part is also a part of the mind, there should be a verifying-part-of-the-self-verification (*svasaṃvittisvasaṃvitti*).
Therefore, it is necessary to take the fourth part, the verifying-part-of-the-self-verification, as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

If there were no verifying-part-of-the-self-verification, then the self-verifying-part would have no fruit, because all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily possess a fruit. If [this were not so]...
Self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is established as the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

The aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) should not be considered a third result, because the aspect of seeing is sometimes not subsumed under valid cognition; for the aspect of seeing is common to all three types of valid cognition.

At times it apprehends an object with clarity, at times it infers an object without error, and at times it infers without attachment. Because the self-cognizing aspect is the very essence of the mind, it attains [the status of the result].

It functions as the result of inference (*anumāna*) and non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). Since the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is not the essence of the mind, it cannot serve as the result of valid cognition for the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti*).

For this reason, the seeing-part does not cognize the third [part]; that which cognizes its own essence must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Next, the internal and external are explained:

the seeing-part and the appearing-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are "external" because they consist of the grasper and the grasped; the latter two [parts] are "internal" because they are exclusively self-cognized.
Therefore, next, the object and subject of cognition are explained. The *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) is the object (*ālambana*); the other three are all subjects (*ālambaka*).

This is because the second part, the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part), only takes the first part, the *nimitta-bhāga*, as its object and does not take the latter two; for those [latter two] are accessible through the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The third part, the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-cognizing part), is the subject that cognizes the preceding subject, the *darśana-bhāga*, and is itself the subject that cognizes the subsequent *svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga* (self-cognition of self-cognition). The fourth part is the *svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga*.

Regarding the realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*): it can only take the third [aspect] as its object. The self-realization (*svasaṃvitti*) does not take the second [aspect], the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), as its object because the self-realization is merely the essence of the mind and does not give rise to functional activity;

thus, it does not take the seeing-part as its object. The first two [aspects] are both inference (*anumāna*) and non-perceptual (*aprāmāṇya*), while the latter two are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, whether one posits a single part for the mind and mental factors, there is no loss of the distinction between subject and object; or, if one posits two parts.

There is no fault of lacking self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). If one were to posit only three parts, there would be the fault of lacking *tathatā*. Now, by positing four parts, both the subjective and objective aspects are complete;
there is the part of self-cognition and the essence of *tathatā*, and thus there is no fault of infinite regress.

Therefore, it is known that although the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are not identical to self-cognition, they are nonetheless not separate from the part of self-cognition. And although self-cognition is not identical to the cognition of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti*), yet...

Nor is it separate from the realization of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*). Next, the scriptural proof is cited: "The two natures of the sentient beings' mind consist of all internal and external divisions.
This means that the three internal [aspects] constitute one nature, and the aspect of the object (*nimittabhāga*) constitutes another nature;

taken together, these are the two natures of mind and object. Regarding the "entanglements of the grasper and the grasped" and the perception of various distinctions: the entanglement of the grasper...

The seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) that acts as the cognitive object is the bondage of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*); the grasped aspect (*grāhya-bhāga*) is the bondage of entanglements (*paryavasthāna-bandhana*);

and the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*). If analyzed according to the three internal divisions, the seeing aspect possesses various distinctions, whereas the latter two do not, because that seeing aspect pervades all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, these four parts may be subsumed into three (up to: the discernment (*vijñapti*) is precisely the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness.

This reconciles the preceding text’s subsumption of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) into their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Although four, three, two, or one are established, [the ultimate reality remains the same].
Although there are various differences, each has its own underlying intent. It is not that establishing only four [categories] is correct;

nor is it that establishing only one part is ever incorrect. As stated below, the scriptural citations prove this: since it is said that "it is solely one's own mind," external objects do not exist at all.
Due to attachment, they appear as if they were external objects, yet they are not substantially real. Thus, one knows that [they are] separate from...
Apart from the mind, not a single dharma can be found. Thus, it is taught in various places that there is only the one mind.

Since the one mind necessarily includes the mental factors (*caitta*), the preceding statement that "discerning" (*vijñapti*) is the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of consciousness refers to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
How could the aspect of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*) be designated as the mode of activity?
Regarding the "locus" (sthāna), it refers to the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) [up to] "like the light of many lamps, each pervading yet appearing as one.
This is a specific explanation of the gate of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), namely the first category: the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

That is to say, this receptacle world—the mountains, rivers, and great earth—is the objective realm of the *vipākavijñāna*. It consists of the substantial *bhāga* (part) of form (*rūpa*), which belongs to all sentient beings.

By the power of the maturation of the seeds of common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-bīja*), there arises a transformation resembling the appearance of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) composed of the eight factors—form, sound, odor, taste, earth, water, fire, and wind.
These consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that act as creators and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) they produce.

Because these exist within the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*), they are called "external great elements. They do not exist apart from the mind. Furthermore, there are generally two kinds of seeds: the first is...

There are two types of characteristics: common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and uncommon characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding "common characteristics," this is because they are experienced by many people. Question:
Since this receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is produced by the collective karma of all sentient beings, they should experience a single result together within this receptacle world.
Yet, while all sentient beings reside within a single realm, there are distinctions between defiled and pure, coarse and subtle, and suffering and pleasure. How is this so?
The enjoyments are different. How can they be said to be produced by common karma? Answer:

Although all sentient beings are produced by common karma and thus arise together within a single realm without difference in location, they nevertheless necessarily follow the power of their own individual, uncommon karma.

Therefore, the objects of enjoyment—whether suffering or pleasure, defiled or pure, coarse or subtle—which are transformed [by consciousness], each differ for every individual. However, as for the receptacle world...
In their characteristics, there is nothing that is not identical; therefore, they can be said to be produced by common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*).
To say that "the locations are no different" refers to the common within the common. To say that "the transformations are each distinct" refers to the uncommon within the common.

An analogy for this is the light of a lamp, which appears as a single whole while pervading everywhere: the lamp represents sentient beings, and the light represents the fact that the locations are no different. Each...
The analogy is that while the transformations are each distinct, they appear as one and their characteristics are similar. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:

**Thesis:** Although all sentient beings are the subject (*dharmin*), they do not differ in location. **Reason:** Because their individual transformations are distinct yet their characteristics are similar.
**Example:** Like the light of many lamps, which, though distinct, appears as one. Question: Are mountains, rivers, and the great earth the collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*)?
What is the basis for that which is experienced? Answer: A sutra says, "For example, a trichiliocosm is not accomplished by a single condition nor by a single event;
it is only through immeasurable conditions and immeasurable events that it is accomplished.
That is to say, the great earth rests upon the water-circle; the water-circle rests upon the wind-circle; and the wind-circle rests upon the space-circle."

The wheel of space has no basis; all such things arise from the collective karma of sentient beings and the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas, enabling all sentient beings to enjoy them according to their respective needs. It further states:
"Because the seeds of the sovereign karmic power of all sentient beings have matured, clouds of golden treasuries arise within the great void," and so forth.
The worlds are successively established; they are defiled or pure, coarse or subtle, and each is experienced individually according to the power of shared karma.

Furthermore, it is said that by severing the great elements of false conceptualization, the internal and external earth-elements and so forth are produced. It is also said that when enlightened clarity and empty dullness interact, they create agitation;
thus, there is a wind-circle that upholds the world and its realms. Therefore, one should know that these are all [the manifestations of] sentient beings.
It is produced by karma. If there were no distinct phenomena apart from the mind, what would transform into these appearances?
(Up to: because those whose karmas are identical all transform [them] in common.
Question: Since the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) manifests the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), by whose ripening is this appearance of the receptacle world manifested?
One interpretation holds that "all" refers to the common manifestation of both the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); this is the meaning of Candragarbha.

Why is this so? This is the inquiry. "As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*" below cites the scripture as proof. "There is a certain interpretation" below represents the correct position of Dharmapāla.

If this receptacle world were transformed by all sentient beings, then holy ones in pure lands should be able to transform them into impure lands, and ordinary beings in impure lands should be able to transform them into pure lands; for the term "all" encompasses both the holy and the ordinary.
Furthermore, the noble ones of the three fruits, weary of and detached from the realm of form, enter into emptiness and are reborn in the formless realm;
they will certainly never again return to be born in the desire or form realms. Even if this land were to transform, what further use would there be for it?

Reasoning through this in detail, all these statements refer to the transformations of the maturation (*vipāka*) of those currently dwelling in this land and those who are destined to be born here in the future.

Regarding the present abode: because ordinary beings dwell in the defiled while Buddhas dwell in the pure, there is no fault of Buddhas transforming the defiled or ordinary beings transforming the pure.
Regarding the future abode: there is thus no fault of noble ones in the formless realm transforming the lower realms.
The sūtra speaks of "all" based on a partial scope; it does not mean that it encompasses all things, including both the noble and the ordinary.

According to one interpretation, if that were so, then at the time when the vessel-world is about to be destroyed, [the perceptions] of ghosts, humans, devas, and so forth would differ from one another.

Candragarbha further questioned: "If all such statements refer only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and do not include noble ones (*ārya*), then at the time when the three calamities are about to destroy the world, all sentient beings will reside in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Since there would be no one currently dwelling here or destined to be born here, whose karmic maturation (*vipāka*) would transform into this world? If you claim that it is the person of the formless realm who transforms it..."
Regarding this land: since ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have already grown weary of having form and have been born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they currently lack a physical body.
What, then, would be the use of transforming this land of form?

Even if those in the formless realm were to transform themselves into physical bodies to enjoy the form realm, the form realm and the formless realm are separated by vast differences in coarseness and subtlety; they do not [correspond].
Regarding the support: for those who are formless, transforming into a material world—what benefit does this provide to the body? Dharmapāla replied again:
"However, the world that is transformed is fundamentally intended as a support and object of enjoyment for the material body; therefore, it manifests in such a way.
If there is a support and enjoyment for one's own body, and it is beneficial to oneself, then it transforms into that. It is by virtue of this principle."
When a person of the formless realm is born in another region of the formless realm, their ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) likewise transforms into the formless realm of its own level,
thereby obtaining support and experience. If that land is one of mixed habitation,
or if they are born in this land of mixed habitation, that consciousness likewise transforms into this land of mixed habitation, thereby obtaining support and experience.

Therefore, when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed or is first being formed, although there are no beings currently dwelling within it or destined to be born there, this receptacle world nonetheless exists as a present reality.
This is explained with reference to what is commonly experienced by all; however, regarding individual experience:
Regarding the instruction "one should know according to this": although beings are born into this same realm, the karmic fruits they experience are each distinct.

This is called "common karma with distinct retribution" (*sādhāraṇa-karma-vipāka-bheda*). It is just as with a single body of water: gods see it as lapis lazuli, humans see it as water, hungry ghosts see it as a river of pus, and fish see it as their dwelling place.
Because other realms and other individuals do not share these experiences, they are not common.

"Various seeds" refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—up to "just as the nature of *tathatā* does not contradict *vijñaptimātra*"—which is a separate explanation of the aspect of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This concerns the second category: the objective realm (*svabhāvaviṣaya*).

As for the seeds of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) being subsumed within the nature of consciousness, this is because they are subsumed within the eighth [consciousness], which is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). As for the seeds of uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) not being subsumed within this nature:
Because they are subsumed under the nature of goodness (*kuśala-dharma*), and because they are not objects perceived by a consciousness that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Although they are not the objects perceived by this [specific] consciousness, they are never dissociated from it, just like the nature of *tathatā*. This is the true nature of consciousness and does not contradict *vijñapti-mātra*.

To state the formal argument (*prayoga*): The seeds of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are the objects perceived by consciousness, because they are subsumed within the nature of consciousness, just like matter (*rūpa*).

...and so forth. The seeds of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas do not contradict *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Although they are not [direct] objects of cognition (*ālambana*), they are nonetheless inseparable from it, just like the nature of *tathatā* (suchness).
Regarding the "body with faculties" (*sendriya-kāya*), this refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*). Otherwise, there would be no sense of experiencing others.

This explains the gate of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). It refers to the third category, the objective realm. Because it is the body possessed of sense-faculties, it is called the "root-body" (*indriya-kāya*).
The aforementioned receptacle world is produced by the collective karma of all sentient beings and is enjoyed collectively; therefore, it is called the "common seed."
This physical body is formed by the individual karmic seeds of all sentient beings; therefore, it is called the "non-common characteristic seed.

That which transforms into the semblance of the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) consists of the purified great elements (*mahābhūta*) and refers to the ultimate sense organs (*paramārthendriya*).

This is called "the non-common within the non-common. These ultimate sense organs are transformed solely by one's own consciousness and are thus termed "non-common," as they are experienced exclusively by oneself.

Furthermore, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). As for the "basis of the faculties," this refers to the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) which serve as the support for the ultimate sense organs (*paramārthendriya*);
these are termed "the shared within the unshared. From the eighth transformation onward, they are termed "unshared. That which others may also utilize is termed "shared.
Although this body of faculties is composed of unshared seeds, yet within those unshared seeds, there is further...
By the power of the maturation of a portion of the seeds of common characteristics,

one is able to transform even the external sensory organs (*buddhāyatana*) of another person’s body so that they appear as such for one's own enjoyment. Otherwise, there would be no sense in enjoying the objects of others.

Regarding this, there is an interpretation that [the *ālayavijñāna*] also transforms into something resembling the sense organs (*indriya*) [extending] to those other corpses, such that their continuity is still perceived.
Question: Does the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) transform its own respective organs, or does it also transform the organs of others? One master says:

It not only transforms its own organs but can also transform the organs of others, because the treatise states that the five organs of one's own and others' bodies appear as if they were real. Since...

It is said that the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) of another’s body are precisely what transform for oneself the others’ *tuccha-indriya* (physical sense organs) and *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organs).

A master, setting forth the correct principle, says: "This fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) can only transform into something resembling the others’ *tuccha-indriya* as an object of my own enjoyment;
it can by no means transform the others’ *paramārtha-indriya* into an object of my own enjoyment, because [the latter] cannot be [appropriated by another]."
Because one experiences the superior objects of others. Question: If that is so, how can it be reconciled with the statement that the five sense organs of both oneself and others appear?

Answer: When the treatise says that the five sense organs of oneself and others appear, it means that the *ālaya-vijñāna* of oneself and the *ālaya-vijñāna* of others each transform themselves into those organs;
it does not mean that one transforms the organs of another. If one were to claim that one could transform the organs of another...
If the sense-faculties (*indriya*) were [the cause], then why would those who have already died not have their five sense-faculties remain as they were, instead of allowing them to rot and decay?

Therefore, the fact that the remaining physical remains of those born in other realms or who have attained nirvāṇa are still seen to persist in continuity rather than immediately collapsing all at once is due to the power of the drawing-in cause of their own consciousness (*svasaṃtati-vijñāna*), and not due to the transformation by others. Thus, it is known that [consciousness] alone is capable of transforming.
Regarding the semblance of a basis (*āśraya-sadṛśa*): it is absolutely impossible to transform the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of another.

Thus far, we have discussed that which is transformed by the power of karma (*karmabala*), up to the point of [discussing] the actual matter-form (*rūpa*) included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

The previous statement referred to the environmental body (*bhājana-kāya*) transformed by the power of karma; this present statement refers to the environmental body transformed by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is precisely the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
Up to this point, we have discussed only the environmental bodies transformed by the karmic power of sentient beings across various realms, levels, and individuals.
Each has its own distinctions and cannot be altered, because they are produced by the fixed karma of those sentient beings.

If, however, it is a holy one, the vessel-world, the lands, and the earth may be transformed through the power of their concentration, wisdom, and supernormal faculties; or their own body may become another.
In some cases, another's body is taken as one's own; in others, one's own realm is taken as another's; and in yet others, another's realm is taken as one's own—thus, there is no fixed certainty.
If we consider the bodies and lands that are transformed for the sake of self-enjoyment, they continue uninterruptedly for a long duration, being inexhaustible until the end of the future.
If we consider activities such as emitting light and shaking the earth for the sake of benefiting others, they proceed in accordance with sentient beings.

Because they are initiated by the power of conditions and causes, they are for the most part temporary; therefore, they are indeterminate. Below, the four types of objective spheres (*viṣaya*) are summarized.
Briefly stated, the objects transformed by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are: first, the seeds of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) nature; second, the body possessed of sense organs;
third, the five sensory objects and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*); fourth, the manifest forms (*rūpa*) that appear within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This is because the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhiphala-rūpa*) is also subsumed under the matter of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).

It is also called "matter produced by mastery over meditative concentration" (*samādhi-vaśitā-ja-rūpa*). For example, the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanas*), up to mountains of fish, rice, and meat, great rivers of ghee and curd, the great earth, gold, and so forth—all are included within this category of matter.
Why is it that this consciousness cannot transform into something resembling those [other] consciousnesses, even though they also take this form as their object?
This clarifies that, between the two types of transformation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), this refers to the transformation as causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Question:

Since this consciousness is already able to transform into something resembling the locus (*āśraya*) as its objective support (*ālambana*), why does it not also transform into something resembling the mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), associated phenomena (*samprayukta*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)?

Are these taken as objects? Answer: The transformations of contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) are, in brief, of two kinds. First, transformation by causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*).

This refers to the spontaneous arising of the mind through the latencies of verbal designations (*nāma-vāsanā*) and the latencies of prior karma (*pūrva-karma-vāsanā*), without depending on deliberate attention (*manasikāra*).

The objects transformed in this way are called "transformation by causal conditions"; these are the first five consciousnesses and the eighth [ālaya-vijñāna], which follow their respective seeds of verbal designation.
The immediate cause (hetu-pratyaya) is the condition for [the object], while the seeds of karmic maturation (vipāka-karma-bīja) serve as the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).

The objective realm manifested through the power of these causal conditions constitutes the substantial reality; this is the "objective sphere" (svabhāva-viṣaya), from which one obtains genuine experience.

Second, regarding "conceptual transformation" (vikalpa-pariṇāma): this refers to the objective realm manifested by the mind that arises through the deliberation of mental attention (manasikāra); such a realm is termed "conceptual transformation."

These refer to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Because they arise following their own respective conceptualizations and mental attentions (*manasikāra*), the objects transformed by the power of these conceptualizations serve as the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
These may be "images-only" (*kevala-chāyā*) or "those bearing substance" (*sadravya-chāyā*);

they can only function as objects and lack real efficacy. Regarding these two gates: the first is arising through production, and the second is arising through transformation. Now, this fundamental consciousness—

This transformation of causes and conditions transforms only real matter (*rūpa*), not the reflected images (*pratibimba*) or the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), because those objective parts of the mind and mental factors lack practical utility.

Question: Since the transformed mind and mental factors are merely provisional objective parts (*prajñapti-nimitta-bhāga*) and the eighth consciousness does not take them as objects, why do the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) not likewise transform and serve as objects? Answer: If they were truly non-existent...

Because it has not yet been realized during the stage of a cause (hetu-avasthā), if it were to transform into an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta), it would likewise lack practical utility; therefore, it does not take them as objects.
Non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) are merely conventionally established based on states (avasthā-prajñapti) and likewise lack practical utility; thus, they also do not become objects.

Consequently, the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) does not take mind and mental factors as its objects, but takes only real matter (bhūtarūpa). However, this is stated with reference to the stage of outflows (sāsrava-avasthā); in the stage without outflows (anāsrava-avasthā), [it is otherwise].

Eighth, this matured consciousness (vipāka-vijñāna) transforms into the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna). Although it is devoid of conceptual discrimination, the substance of the mirror is limpid and pure;
thus, although the various images lack actual utility, they nonetheless manifest from it. Otherwise, the Buddhas would not be termed "Perfectly Omniscient" (samyak-saṃbuddha).
Therefore, during the stage of outflows (sāsrava), this matured consciousness—whether in the desire realm or the form realm—takes as its objects all three categories of objective natures.
If it is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it takes only the seeds of outflows (*āsrava-bīja*) as its object, and does not take the body or the vessel-world as its object.

Because there is aversion to form, and because there is no form resulting from karmic fruit (*vipākaja-rūpa*), the ten types of outflowing form—including the sense-faculties, the body, and the vessel-world—are not its objects.

Only the substantial form that is the result of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-vastu-rūpa*) falling within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is its object. Since the maturation (*vipāka*) of that realm takes this form as its objective field, it also possesses [form].
There are three conditions.
That which is "unknowable" refers to this aspect of activity (*ākāra*) [extending] up to the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), and it should be understood that other such states are likewise so.

This explains the gate of unknowability. "Aspect of activity" (*ākāra*) refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*). "Internal appropriated objects" (*ādhyātmikopātta-viṣaya*) are like the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).

This refers to the three types of objective spheres (*viṣaya*). Because these two divisions—the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*)—are subtle, hidden, and difficult to know, why is this so?
It is because the *ālayavijñāna*, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), takes as its object a limited sphere of appropriation (*upādāna*);

within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it takes as its object an extensive sphere of appropriation; and within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)...
In the Sphere of Infinite Space, it takes as its object an immeasurable apprehended realm; in the Sphere of Nothingness, it takes as its object a subtle apprehended realm;

in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, it takes as its object an extremely subtle apprehended realm. Because this consciousness takes such subtle objects, it is difficult even for those of worldly wisdom and sagacity to discern;
therefore, it is said to be "unknowable. The phrase "How [is it] below? is an inquiry. It is like [the state of] cessation.
Below, the state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is used to demonstrate that [the mind] is unknowable.

This is because within the cessation of perception and feeling, both the ever-active mental factors (*nitya-pravṛtta-caitta*) and the occasionally active mental factors (*anitya-pravṛtta-caitta*) have completely ceased; yet it is still said that "consciousness does not depart from the body," as if there were a mind present.

Thus, one knows that the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses are subtle, profound, hidden, and extremely difficult to comprehend. Therefore, the formal argument (*yukti*) is set forth regarding the cessation of perception and feeling.
There is consciousness, because it is comprised within sentient beings, just as when there is a mind. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra* says:

"When a practitioner enters the samādhi of dhyāna, subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) continue to evolve, yet they do not perceive this. They then think, 'Consciousness has ceased,' and subsequently enter the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
In reality, consciousness does not cease before entering the absorption, for the seeds of habitual tendencies have not [been extinguished]."

It ceases; therefore, it does not cease. Because the objective realm shifts and the grasping is incomplete, it ceases. This may be understood by analogy with the lower stage of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*).
Thus, the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Essence) says: "This essence cannot be described; it is subtle and most difficult to know.
It pervades the entire dharma-realm yet has no dwelling mind. It sustains all things without manifesting any signs, like a bird flying through the sky, which comes and goes."
Soaring aloft and spreading wide, it cannot be traced; it is like the pupil within the eye, which, though it illuminates the myriad phenomena of the universe, the eye itself never sees.
Like the moon containing a single hue that manifests the forms of ten thousand images, it is equal to the sun radiating a thousand beams of light.
It shines universally upon the four continents. Like a *maṇi* jewel, it rains down treasures without thought;
it extensively saves all living beings, just as a magnet moves iron without awareness. It revolves throughout the six realms of existence. A verse from the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
"The storehouse consciousness sustains the world, like a thread threading beads, or like a chariot with wheels, turning according to the winds of karma. Like a potter...

The wheel of fortune and the staff; when the vessel is formed, it functions according to its use. Within the various realms, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) acts with collective power such that nothing is not accomplished.
Throughout all internal and external worlds, it pervades and encompasses them entirely. It is like the images of the many stars, arrayed throughout the void.
Sustained by the power of the wind, its movement never ceases; like the tracks of a bird in the sky, though sought, they cannot be seen.
Yet the bird does not leave the sky as it flaps its wings and advances or retreats. The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise: it does not leave one’s own or another’s body.
Like waves arising from the sea, like the sky containing the myriad forms, the storehouse consciousness is likewise: it contains and stores all things.
The various habitual tendencies are like the pupil in the eye; the eye can never see itself.

The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) dwells within the body, storing all seeds and universally sustaining life, warmth, and consciousness. Like clouds covering the world, its karmic activities never cease.

Sentient beings are unable to perceive it. Furthermore, it is said: "O virtuous ones, all objective forms are the ālayavijñāna, which transforms in association with the habitual tendencies of form, appearing as their images;
they do not possess a separate substance. This is identical to the false conceptualizations of the ignorant.
O virtuous ones, whether all sentient beings are sitting or lying down, walking or standing, they are in a state of stupor, intoxication, or sleep."
From sleep to even running about in a frenzy—all these are nothing other than the ālayavijñāna.
Just as the power of a magnet causes iron to move, such that although it has no mind, it appears to have a mind, so too is the ālayavijñāna:
sustained by the phenomena of birth and death, it wanders through the various realms of existence; it is not the self, yet it resembles the self. Furthermore, there is a verse:
It is said: It is able to sustain the causes of the world, namely the ālaya, the eighth *puruṣavijñāna*.

It moves through all things, like a wheel turning many pots; like oil pervading sesame seeds; and like the salty taste within salt, as well as the nature of impermanence, which is omnipresent throughout all forms.
Therefore, whether it be the bodies of ordinary beings or sages, or lands that are pure or defiled, they are all—
Manifesting from consciousness.

With how many mental factors (*caitta*) is this consciousness associated? (Up to: Because it is subsumed under the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*).

This explains the section on association (*saṃprayoga*), namely the five universal mental factors. First, the question: "Always with... and so forth. Next, the verse provides the answer: "Ālaya... and so forth. Next, the explanation:
As long as the *ālayavijñāna* has not been emptied, it is called "not yet transformed. This term encompasses both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*). It is named...

Regarding the phrase "pervasive in all states": it is called pervasive because it can function throughout all four types of universality—namely, throughout the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses, the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), and at all times.
The above provides a general explanation; the following is a detailed exposition.

Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the differentiation of transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three. (Up to: Just as its nature is not identical to the conjunction of the three, like feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.

Contact is explained below. First, the essential nature and function are presented; then, the term "conjunction of the three" is explained. "Conjunction of the three" refers to the sense organ (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because their essences are distinct, they are called "three. Because they do not oppose one another but rather accord with one another, it is called the "conjunction of the three. Now, regarding contact...
It arises based on those three types [of phenomena] and can also cause those three to harmonize and unite in a single place;
therefore, contact (*sparśa*) is said to function at that stage of their conjunction. As for "transformation" (*vikāra*):
because contact exists, it enables these three to all possess the capacity to give rise to all mental factors (*caitta*); thus, it is called transformation. Transformation is precisely arising.

Furthermore, just as all phenomena arising from the mind are termed "transformations" (*vipariṇāma*), so too that which is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refers to contact (*sparśa*)—which resembles the functional capacity of the three preceding [factors] for producing mental states—and is thus designated as discrimination. "Discrimination" is merely a synonymous term for "resemblance.

Following the phrase "the transformation of the faculty," this specifically highlights that the power of the faculty's transformation is superior to that of consciousness and its objects. Question: For what reason?
The triad of conditions is common to all, yet the sense organ alone is preeminent. The answer is: first, because it is primary; it possesses a superior capacity. Second, because it is proximate;
it can directly produce the mental factors (*caitta*). Third, because it is pervasive; it does not merely produce mental factors, but can also produce the mind (*citta*) itself.
Fourth, because it is continuous; it is always uninterrupted. The object and consciousness are not so. Although the substance of the object is capable [of producing cognition],...

The mind and mental factors that arise [from them] do not possess the status of being "superior" because they lack two of the three required meanings: they are neither the primary cause nor are they proximate.
Although the mind is the primary cause and is proximate to the arising of mental factors, it cannot produce the mind itself; thus, it lacks one of the necessary meanings and is likewise not superior.
Both the object and consciousness share the characteristic of impermanence and continuity. Consciousness arises from the object, and the object...
Because it exists due to consciousness, the sense faculty alone is preeminent. Therefore, in the section on the "Aggregation" (*saṃnipāta*), he cites scriptural evidence:

that which brings all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) together to cause them to encounter their respective objects is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of contact (*sparśa*). Thus it is said: "Its nature is to cause the mind and mental factors to encounter their objects.
Since it possesses a function similar to that of the mental factors that arise in succession, the [mental factors] such as feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) depend upon it.
Therefore, its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth. Below, the sūtras and śāstras are reconciled.
The *Utpādanirodha-sūtra* states that the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) all arise with contact (*sparśa*) as their condition.
