For this reason, it is said that consciousness arises from the conjunction of two; contact arises from the conjunction of three; and feeling, perception, and formations arise from the conjunction of four. Why is volition (*cetanā*) not mentioned?
It is because the single term "formations" (*saṃskāra*) subsumes all seventy-three factors.
As the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states: "The aggregate of formations consists of seventy-three items. Among the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*), excluding feeling and perception, the remainder...
The forty-nine factors, as well as the twenty-four formations dissociated from mind, are all termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Therefore, it is said that "all [mental factors] have contact (*sparśa*) as their condition. Although the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states only that contact is the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*), it does not mention the aggregate of formations;
this is because volition is the primary and most predominant factor within the aggregate of formations. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* also says: "Formations..."

It is called "volitional formation" (*saṃskāra*). Since volition (*cetanā*) is the nature of karma, and its meaning as "formative activity" is predominant, it is the most excellent. Therefore, the Buddha said:

"That which can form the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). By mentioning only this single factor of volition, the entire aggregate of formations is subsumed. Question:

Why, among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), are feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) excluded, while all others are included in the aggregate of formations? Answer: Because feeling involves attachment (*abhiniveśa*).

Regarding the various desires: one becomes attached to them through the power of the relish for perceptions; regarding the various views: one becomes attached to them through the power of distorted perceptions.
Furthermore, among the phenomena of birth and death, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are the most predominant causes; for it is by being addicted to sensation that [one clings].

Because of the arising of inverted perceptions, one wanders through the cycle of birth and death. For these two reasons, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as distinct aggregates.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that contact (*sparśa*) is the basis for feeling, yet it does not mention perception or volition (*cetanā*).

This is because contact gives rise to feeling more proximately and potently; that is to say, what is grasped by contact and what is grasped by feeling are extremely close to one another in their causal induction.

Because it is superior. Question: Since contact (*sparśa*) can cause the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness to come together, this contact is merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) for that triad;

how could it have a real substance? Answer: However, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of contact is real and not provisional, because it is a mental factor (*caitta*) among the six sets of six dharmas.
The *Śarīra-pāda-śāstra* states: "The six sets of six refer to the six consciousnesses and the six contacts."
The six feelings, the six perceptions, the six volitions, and the six cravings.
This is because there are feelings produced by eye-contact up to feelings produced by mind-contact, and cravings produced by eye-contact up to cravings produced by mind-contact;

furthermore, because these constitute the nature of the nutriment of contact among the four nutriments; and furthermore, because all seventy-four factors have contact as their condition; and furthermore, the ten...

Because, among the two conditions [of contact and feeling], contact is the condition for feeling; thus, like feeling and perception (*saṃjñā*), each has its own distinct nature and is not identical to the triad of the meeting [of sense-faculty, object, and consciousness].

If it were identical to the triad of the meeting, it would be the same as acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the intrinsic nature of contact is not identical to the triad of the meeting.

Among the six groups of six dharmas, [mental factors] have the nature of being mental concomitants (*caitta*). Because they are subsumed under "nutriment" (*āhāra*) and because they can act as conditions (*pratyaya*), their nature is like that of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth.

As for attention (*manaskāra*), its nature is defined as that which arouses the mind; [if it were not distinct from concentration], it would follow that it is not a universal factor (*sarvatraga*), as it would not differ from concentration.
Regarding "Mental Application" (*manasikāra*), its essence and function are first presented. The following section provides the explanation. There are two meanings of "alerting":
first, causing the mind that has not yet arisen to arise; second, causing the mind that has already arisen to be drawn toward its object. Question:

Does mental application alert the mind while it is in the state of seeds (*bīja-avasthā*), or when it is in active manifestation (*pravṛtti*)? Answer: It is in the state of seeds, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is clear and sharp; even though...
While in the state of seeds, if there is an object that reaches it, it can alert the mind and cause [the seeds] to arise as actual manifestations.

This is illustrated by the analogy of many people sleeping together in one room; when an outsider comes as a thief, one person among them whose nature is to sleep lightly is able to awaken the others.
Although this person has not yet risen themselves, they are able to awaken the others and cause them to rise.

Mental attention (*manasikāra*) acts as a seed that can both awaken those seeds of the various minds to produce manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), and can cause the manifest activity of the mind to move toward its objective sphere (*ālambana*).
The former is its essential nature (*svabhāva*); the latter is its functional activity (*karma*). Question:

Why does mental attention only awaken the mind to give rise to manifest activity, rather than awakening the mental factors (*caitta*)? Answer: Although it also induces the mental factors, the mind is the primary [agent].
This merely speaks of drawing the mind and does not mention mental factors (*caitta*). Some say that this expresses a partial meaning.
Others define *manasikāra* (attention) as causing the mind to turn toward a different object; others define it as holding the mind to a single object. Both views are irrational.

If it means causing the mind to abide, it would be no different from the mental factor of concentration (*samādhi*), which also causes the mind to abide without shifting to another object. If one says it means turning [the mind], then...

Because it is not subsumed under the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*). Regarding the phrase "turning toward a different object," this means that while one is correctly taking this object as a focal point, one subsequently shifts to take that other object as a focal point.
"Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the experiencing of what is agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral; it is called "feeling of the object" (*viṣaya-vedanā*) because it is not shared with others.
First, the essence and function [of sensation] are presented. "Receiving" (*ling*) means to take in; "accepting" (*na*) means to contain.
If one receives an adverse object, the mind arises with the desire to separate from it; if one receives a favorable object, the mind arises with the desire to unite with it;
if one receives an object that is neither adverse nor favorable, the mind remains neutral—neither desiring to unite nor desiring to separate. This is the nature of sensation (*vedanā*).

Because it serves as the basis for desire, it is able to give rise to craving; this is "experiential enjoyment" (*paribhoga*). [The text] states "there are some who say" below to describe divergent views:

first, "objective experience" (*viṣaya-vedanā*) refers to that which was previously described as the apprehension of the disagreeable, the agreeable, and that which is neither; second, "experiential nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*) refers to...

This refers precisely to that which they grasp as the "contact co-arising with experience" (*anubhava*). Because contact gives rise to feeling (*vedanā*), and feeling is itself the act of experiencing, it is called "co-arising.
This feeling does not experience external objects; it experiences only the contact that arises simultaneously with it.

Since it takes contact as its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is termed "intrinsic feeling" (*svabhāva-vedanā*). Only this intrinsic feeling is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object of feeling.

The object (*viṣaya*). Because it does not share a common object with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), if the feeling of the object were shared by the king, then that which takes the object as its condition would be called "feeling of the object," and that which takes the contact co-arising [with it] as its condition would be called "feeling of self-nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*).

Below, first, there is a general refutation of this as irrational, because feeling certainly does not take the simultaneously arising contact as its object; for there has never been a case where a father gives birth to a son and the son...
Because it would entail the fallacy of [the cause] being identical to its effect. Next, we shall refute the claim that contact (*sparśa*) is not the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of feeling (*vedanā*).

If you argue that this feeling arises resembling contact, and therefore feeling is called "self-nature feeling" because it can experience contact, then contact would be the "resembling cause" (*sādṛśya-hetu*) and feeling would be the effect.
In that case, would every effect that resembles its cause be the self-nature of feeling? Furthermore, since contact is the cause of feeling and gives rise to feeling...
It should be called "feeling produced by causes," and cannot be called "feeling by its own nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*), because contact (*sparśa*) is not the intrinsic nature of feeling.
If it is argued that this is like a king consuming various kingdoms and towns, then the king is a metaphor for feeling, and the kingdoms and towns are metaphors for contact.

To say that the king eats the kingdom and the towns is like saying that feeling (vedanā) is the sensation itself; it is the sensation produced by that very sensation which is called the self-nature of feeling.
To claim that contact (sparśa) is not its self-nature is also incorrect, because they maintain that the simultaneous contact of apprehension constitutes its self-nature.
Now, if one defines the self-nature as the feeling produced by contact, then feeling would be non-existent [as a distinct entity].
There is an object of self-cognition, for they maintain that the contact itself is the object of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If it is argued that although feeling (*vedanā*) experiences contact, it does not abandon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of feeling and is thus called "feeling by way of its own nature," then all phenomena do not abandon their own intrinsic natures;
would they therefore all be the intrinsic nature of feeling? Thus, what they have said merely deceives infants. Next, [the text] clarifies...

The experience of an object (*viṣaya-vedanā*) constitutes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of feeling. Now, this experience of an object is the specific characteristic of feeling, not a common characteristic shared with others.
This is because it is called the "experience of an object" solely because it is able to apprehend its own corresponding object;
it does not apprehend all objects, nor is it an object of common perception for a king or others.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) has the nature of grasping the image of an object; [it continues] until it is able to subsequently give rise to various names and expressions.

First, its essence and function are presented: that is, one must first... [The text continues: To explain "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*), it refers to the meaning of grasping the image; that is, this mental perception (*manasaḥ saṃjñā*).
First, one establishes the boundaries within objects such as forms and sounds and grasps their images.

Because of this grasping of images, one subsequently gives rise to verbal designations, such as "this is sound" or "this is form. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "Wherever location, shape, color, and images appear, these are called 'characteristics' (*nimitta*).
When there is such a characteristic, it is designated as a 'vase' and so forth; yet this [designation] is not [the reality itself]."
The remainder is called "name" (*nāman*). To designate various names and manifest various characteristics is called "conceptual construction" (*parikalpa*).
"Volition" (*cetanā*) has the nature of causing the mind to engage in activity; it is called "associated" (*samprayukta*) because it [functions] toward the objects of perception and so forth.

First, the essence and function are presented. Regarding the commentary on "that which is capable": "volition" (cetanā) has as its intrinsic nature the deliberation over whether an object is a correct cause or a false cause, and whether it is fit to be undertaken or not.
Its functional activity consists of driving and employing one's own mind to create good or evil, and to achieve the correct or the false.
Question: What is the difference between attention (manasikāra) and volition? Answer: Attention is like a horse.
Action is like a rider; if the horse were to travel only straight ahead, it would be unable to avoid the treacherous and seek the level.

It is because of the rider that the horse is made to avoid the one and seek the other. Contemplation (*cintā*) is likewise: it causes the mind to not wander aimlessly, but to abandon the deviant and resort to the correct.
This is what is meant by "no deviance in thought" (*si wu xie*). Furthermore, it is said: "Be careful in your thoughts," and again, "Act after threefold reflection. These are the five.
Below: This explains that the five [mental factors] are determined to be associated with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because they are omnipresent within all minds.

The section on "contact" (*sparśa*) below explains the meaning of association (*samprayoga*). Question: Since both the mind and its mental factors each possess their own specific modes of activity (*ākāra*), what is meant by "association"?

Just as the eighth [consciousness] has discernment (*vijñapti*) as its mode of activity (*ākāra*), while feeling (*vedanā*) has experiencing (*anubhava*) as its mode of activity, and so forth—the answer is:

although these five factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), differ from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) in their modes of activity, they necessarily arise simultaneously, share the same sense-faculty as their support (*āśraya*), have the same object of perception (*ālambana*), and possess similar intrinsic natures; therefore, they are called "associated" (*samprayukta*).
The mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this consciousness is extremely indistinct... [up to] ...just as neutral states (*avyākṛta*) invite both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

This explains the section on its association with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*). There are three interpretations. First, it is determined that the feeling is equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) based on its mode of activity.

There are three kinds of feeling: suffering (*duḥkha*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity. If it were any other consciousness, it would be associated with the feelings of suffering or pleasure, which are definitely distinct and clear; this is not the case here.

Because it experiences suffering and pleasure, it is not clear and distinct. If it were any other consciousness, it would necessarily be able to differentiate between the characteristics of favorable and unfavorable objects;

however, this [consciousness] is non-conceptual because its apprehension of objects is fixed. If it were any other consciousness, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) would necessarily be coarse and it would necessarily be easily distracted.

There must necessarily be interruptions; however, this [state] proceeds as a single, uninterrupted continuum. Therefore, it is known that it corresponds exclusively with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Next, regarding the karma that draws forth the neutral feeling of the meditative absorption: the maturation (*vipāka*) is the primary retributive fruit for the entire duration of a single lifetime, and it is the response to the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*).
All of these are summoned and induced solely by the power of past wholesome or unwholesome karma, without depending on present karmic conditions.

Therefore, it is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). As for the two feelings of suffering and pleasure, they exist only as the maturation-born (*vipākaja*) within the first six consciousnesses;
because they depend on present conditions, they are the primary subjects of retribution (*vipāka-svāmī*) and are the results of completing karma (*pūrakakarma*).

They are not associated with this [ālaya-vijñāna] feeling. Thirdly, regarding its determination through the aspect of being "appropriated and stored," this consciousness is the manas, which uniformly grasps [the ālaya-vijñāna] as its self.
Because it takes the internal self as its object, there is no transformation. If it were associated with the two feelings of pleasure and pain, there would indeed be transformation.

However, the manas-consciousness abandons the grasping of an internal self; since the seventh consciousness is also characterized by the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is therefore associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity.
Question: Among these five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), why is the factor of feeling (*vedanā*) singled out and distinguished, while the other four are not? Answer: Feeling...
Although its substance is one, its functional meanings are threefold; therefore, it is distinguished separately. The other four are not so.
For example, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is likewise distinguished because its functional meanings differ as being obscured (*nivṛta*) or unobscured (*anivṛta*). Question:

Since this consciousness is associated with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), how can it also be the maturation (*vipāka*) of evil karma? Answer: Because the sensation of equanimity is not incompatible with either the wholesome or the unwholesome. Since...

Deceptive wholesome karma can bring about [retribution], and unwholesome karma is likewise. If suffering and pleasure did not coexist, there would be no pleasurable fruits among humans and devas, nor would there be any painful fruits within the three miserable realms.
To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*): this ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is brought about by both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it is not contradicted by suffering and pleasure, just like neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena. Therefore, it is known that the eighth true consciousness is eternally as such.
The characteristic of relinquishment resembles a spontaneous condition and accords with the path of constancy. It is not defiled by impure dharmas;
how could it be governed by pure dharmas? It is not fettered by birth and death; how could it be stilled by nirvana?

For this reason, it is called the lord of consciousness; thus it is titled the King of the Mind (*citta-rāja*). It is solely due to a single thought of ignorance that the waves of the seven consciousnesses arise.

Once the mental factors (*caitta*) have been produced, the King of the Mind is consequently lost. All of this stems from the forceful awakening of the luminosity of awareness, which differentiates the subject and establishes the object.
A clear understanding arises, and the objects of the mind appear distinctly. One then mobilizes the emotions of discrimination, such that self and other become manifest.

Thus, within the minds of sentient beings, enmity and kinship are formed according to hatred and love; within the realm of insentient things, forms and obstructions are manifested following one's perceptions and thoughts.
Consequently, externally, mulberry fields turn into seas and seas turn into mulberry fields;
internally, the close becomes the cause of enmity and the enemy becomes the seed of kinship. They alternate between high and low status, responding to one another in turn. From this point on...

The fruits of karma are ever renewed; the conditions for suffering are unceasing. If one desires to return to the truth and revert to the source, to turn back from delusion and merge with the Real, it requires only that a single thought does not arise.

When the boundaries of past and future are severed, the mind of discrimination ceases, the karma of saṃsāra perishes, retribution ends and the faculties wither, and causes being empty, effects are lost.
The defilements of emotion, objects, and consciousness that have no beginning will vanish entirely in an instant. As for the primordial...
The Buddha-eye and the eternal body manifest instantaneously in accordance with reality.

How could this consciousness not be a distinct object-consciousness (*viṣayapratiniyatavijñāna*)? [From "because it is interrupted" up to: because it is subject to interruption, it is certainly not the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

Question: For what reason is this ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) associated only with the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), and not included among the five categories of object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*)?

Answer: Because the object-specific factors and the others are mutually contradictory. Question: In what way are they contradictory? Specifically, regarding the desire (*chanda*) of the object-specific factors:

*Chanda* (desire) is the longing for an object that one finds pleasing; this consciousness, however, evolves according to the force of wholesome or unwholesome karma and lacks such longing, and therefore it is not associated with *chanda*.
*Adhimokṣa* (resolve) is the act of certifying, maintaining, and determining an object;
this consciousness is dull and obscured, incapable of certifying or maintaining anything, and lacks determination, and therefore it is not associated with *adhimokṣa*. *Smṛti* (mindfulness)...

This [storehouse consciousness] clearly remembers past experiences previously cultivated so as not to forget them; however, this consciousness is dull and inferior, unable to remember clearly, and therefore is not associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the mind’s ability to focus one-pointedly on a single object without any other distractions;
since this consciousness spontaneously and separately perceives three types of objects, it is not associated with concentration. Wisdom (*prajñā*) functions solely to discern and analyze.
Regarding the matters of virtue and non-virtue: this consciousness is subtle, obscure, and brief, and thus lacks the capacity for discernment; therefore, it is not associated with wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, as for the "object-specific" mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*), they arise by taking various distinct objects;

since this consciousness is exclusively a single type of continuous stream, it is not associated with the object-specific factors. This consciousness is exclusively the maturation (*vipāka*) and is ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*); it is not...

Because it is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*), it does not associate with the eleven virtuous [mental factors]. Because it is not of an unvirtuous nature (*akuśala*), it does not associate with the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth.
Although the four factors beginning with regret (*kaukṛtya*) can be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they do not always exist in a continuous succession;

therefore, they certainly do not associate with maturation (*vipāka*). However, this does not preclude their being born of maturation (*vipākaja*); among those born of maturation, these four may be present.
Therefore, dharmas are of four kinds, namely: wholesome, unwholesome, [neutral], and so forth; because this is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
This explains the gateway of the three natures. There are four types of indeterminate: first, the indeterminate of transformation, which refers to the indeterminate mind.
Mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Second, the indeterminate that is transformed [by them], namely all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and all seeds (*bīja*).
Third, the situational indeterminate (*avasthā-avyākṛta*), namely the nominal indeterminate phenomena among the twenty-four types of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Fourth, the ultimate indeterminate (*paramārtha-avyākṛta*), namely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena of space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Furthermore, within the first type of indeterminate, there are further...
There are four types: first, the neutral of maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*); second, the neutral of deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, the neutral of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*);

and fourth, the neutral of transformation (*nairmāṇika*). Regarding the "neutral of maturation": "disparate" (*vi*) refers to difference, meaning a distinction between cause and effect in terms of their nature;

this is because the cause may be either wholesome or unwholesome, whereas the fruit is exclusively neutral. "Maturation" (*pāka*) means ripening, which pertains solely to the fruit. When cause and fruit are spoken of together, it is termed "maturation" (*vipāka*). Question: [What are] the four?
Within the Dharma, under which category is the ālayavijñāna subsumed? Answer: This consciousness is subsumed exclusively under the category of non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) dharmas.
Because this consciousness is of the nature of maturation (vipāka), and since it is maturation, it is certainly not subsumed under either the wholesome or the defiled natures.
If this consciousness were wholesome or defiled, the processes of saṃsāric flow and cessation would be impossible to establish.
Because it is neither virtuous nor defiled, it can follow along with virtue and defilement to undergo both the process of transmigration and the cessation of suffering.

This explains its indeterminate nature by way of its being the maturation (*vipāka*). This consciousness is the basis for both the virtuous and the defiled, yet it is itself neither virtuous nor defiled.

If it were virtuous, it could not be the basis for the defiled; if it were defiled, it could not be the basis for the virtuous. Because it is neither virtuous nor defiled, it is able to serve as the basis for the virtuous.

"The basis of defilement" (*saṃkleśāśraya*). This indicates that it is neutral (*avyākṛta*) by way of being the support for both the wholesome and the defiled. This consciousness possesses the nature of being perfumable (*bhāvyatva*);

because it is neither wholesome nor defiled, it is able to receive the perfuming of the wholesome and the defiled. If it were itself wholesome or defiled, it would not be capable of receiving perfuming.

If it did not receive perfuming, then the causes and effects of the wholesome and the defiled would all result in annihilation. This indicates its neutrality by way of its being the object of perfuming.
Thus, by possessing the three aforementioned meanings, it is established that the eighth consciousness is comprised solely within the category of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding the term "non-obscured" (*anivṛta*): "obscuration" (*nivṛti*) refers to the quality of being obstructed by defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*), which carries the sense of covering.

It acts as an obstruction such that the Noble Path cannot arise, and it acts as a veil such that the true mind cannot attain purity. This consciousness lacks these two qualities; therefore, it is so named.
It is "unobscured" (*anivṛta*). Regarding the term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*): wholesome causes produce desirable results, while unwholesome causes produce undesirable results;
both of these possess a distinct and powerful nature that can be defined and distinguished.
This consciousness lacks these two characteristics, and is therefore called indeterminate.
"Contact and so forth are also like this" (up to) "because the six eye-consciousnesses and so forth arise simultaneously.

This explains the category of mental factors (*caitta*) by analogy with the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*). It has three points: first, it states that the *ālayavijñāna* is comprised within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature;
the five [mental] factors are likewise indeterminate by analogy; and all associated dharmas must be identical in nature to the sovereign mind.

Because of its nature, this interpretation is correct. Furthermore, below the section on "Contact" (*sparśa*), the second master maintains that the five factors beginning with contact—like the *ālayavijñāna*—are also of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).
They are also such that their aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) are both unknowable;

they take as their objects the three types of natures; they are associated with the five mental factors; and they are subsumed under the category of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). There is another interpretation [which holds otherwise].

[The Master] below [the third teacher] says: "The five [factors], such as contact (*sparśa*), like the *ālayavijñāna*, are also maturation (*vipāka*) and possess all seeds (*sarvabījaka*), up to being non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
for by using the phrase 'likewise,' there is no distinction made from the *ālayavijñāna*.
Dharmapāla refutes both teachers in general, saying: "Their explanation is irrational, because the consciousness upon which the five factors such as contact depend..."

Yet it exists; it is like a minister who relies upon a king, but does not possess the king’s sovereign autonomy. Furthermore, the five [sensory consciousnesses], such as touch and the rest, are identical to the various wholesome and defiled mental factors (*caitta*);
how then could they receive perfuming (*vāsanā*)? How could they, like the [store] consciousness, be able to maintain seeds?

Therefore, we know that that which receives perfuming and maintains seeds must necessarily be the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), and the five sensory objects are not included therein. Thus, he sets forth the formal argument (*pramāṇa*):

Contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] cannot receive perfuming (*vāsanā*), because they lack independence (*asvatantra*) in relation to consciousness, just like craving (*rāga*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth.

If each of the five objects were able to receive perfuming and maintain seeds, then a single sentient being would possess six distinct substantial entities (*dravya*). Since there would be six such substantial entities for the seeds, from which seed would the fruit arise?
Ultimately, one must not say that six seeds produce a single fruit, nor that multiple seeds produce a single sprout.
Because it has never existed before. If one were to claim that the fruit arises from a single seed, then the remaining five seeds would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the six fruits arise sequentially and gradually from within each individual seed, because they are simultaneously perfumed by the sovereign [seed] and their potencies are equal, lacking any sequence. Nor can it be said that the six [seeds] exist simultaneously.
Six fruits arise simultaneously; however, it must not be thought that six eye-consciousnesses and so forth arise at one and the same time within a single sentient being.
Who says that contact and the others can also receive perfuming? [The text continues] up to: "it should be explained according to what is appropriate; it does not mean all [factors do so]."

The opponent offers a defense, saying: "Who said that contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] can receive perfuming (*vāsanā*) or maintain seeds (*bīja*)? He then counters with a reductio ad absurdum:

"If they do not receive perfuming or maintain seeds, how can you say that contact and the others are like the *ālayavijñāna*—that is, that they are also maturation (*vipāka*) and possess all seeds (*sarvabījaka*)?
Again, he defends his position, saying: "When I say that contact and the others are like consciousness and its seeds, I mean that they are... [the text continues].

When the ālayavijñāna takes seeds as its object, the associated factors such as contact (sparśa) manifest in the likeness of the aspect of those seeds and apprehend them as their cognitive objects; this is what is called "possessing all seeds" (sarvabījaka).

This is not like the eighth consciousness [the ālayavijñāna] which can maintain the actual seeds themselves. This is because the five factors beginning with contact share the same objective referent as the ālayavijñāna.

Furthermore, upon reaching the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), although contact and the others do not manifest, the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world [the physical environment] still exist as their objective referents.

The objective referent (*ālambana*) also takes that which resembles the seed as its object. Since a direct objective condition (*sākṣād-ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily exist, he then sets forth the formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"This [cognition] characterized by a resemblance to a seed is the subject (*dharmin*). It is not the support (*āśraya*) of consciousness; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

because it does not function as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the production of manifest consciousnesses and so forth. It is like the resemblance to the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) within touch and other [sensations], and likewise [like other examples]."
It is like fire that lacks the capacity to burn. Refuting this, he says: That defense is irrational.

Because the objects of perception such as contact (*sparśa*), which resemble seeds and resemble sense-faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, must depend upon the *ālayavijñāna* having already been perfumed; only after that can there be the grasping and experiencing of seeds, faculties, and so on.
Only then can contact and the others be analogous to consciousness. If the eighth [consciousness] has never yet grasped [them], [the analogy fails].
If it is the appropriation of the true seeds, then upon what do the [factors] such as contact depend for their transformation into that which resembles the seed?

For this reason, the previous verse stated "all seeds," which certainly refers to the two meanings of being able to receive the perfuming and maintaining the seeds; it does not state that the object-condition (*ālambana*) is the "all-seeds.
If it were otherwise, since the seeds previously mentioned are already the object-condition, this [appropriation] would again be described as the locus of the seeds.
If [the term] "object-condition" (ālambana) were included, the root verse would incur the fault of redundancy. Furthermore, the subsequent refutation makes no such distinction.

If you argue that all cases should be treated as analogies because the phrase "likewise" (tathā) also lacks a specific distinction, then it would follow that while the ālayavijñāna is capable of discerning (vijñapti), contact (sparśa) and the other [mental factors] are also capable of discerning;
and while the ālayavijñāna is associated with five objects, contact and the others are also associated with five objects. There is...
Is this the principle? For this reason, it is known that the phrase "it is also thus" is stated according to what is appropriate to be said;
it does not mean that everything is to be treated as a universal analogy.
The *ālaya-vijñāna* is neither annihilated nor eternal (up to: it is like a torrential stream), for such is the nature of cause and effect.
This is the explanation of the method of cause, effect, phenomenon, and analogy. Question: Is the ālayavijñāna subject to annihilation or is it eternal? Answer:

It is neither annihilated nor eternal, because it is "constantly revolving" (*nitya-parivṛtti*). This is the essential crux of the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) school; by means of this, the tenet is established, and by means of this, attachments are refuted.
It rests solely upon these two characters, "constant" and "revolving. To say "constant" means that this consciousness continues as a single, homogeneous stream.
It is constant and uninterrupted. Because this consciousness serves as the fundamental basis, it is able to establish the three realms, the five destinies, and the four modes of birth.

As for why it is able to establish these, it is because that ālayavijñāna is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and is capable of firmly grasping and maintaining all tainted seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*), preventing them from being lost. "Transformation" refers to the mentation of this consciousness.
One should contemplate that arising and ceasing occur such that there is no abiding from moment to moment. The cause ceases as the fruit arises; the fruit arises as the cause ceases.

There is transformation between the preceding and succeeding moments; they are neither permanent nor identical. Because they are neither permanent nor identical, they are able to receive perfuming. Thus we know that by virtue of being constant (*nitya*), there is transformation (*pariṇāma*);

and by virtue of transformation, there is constancy. By virtue of constancy, it can maintain the seeds; by virtue of transformation, it can receive perfuming. "Constancy" is spoken of in terms of its essence.

Turning this to the application of the syllogism: one constantly uses the view of annihilationism to negate [the extremes], and turns that negation to negate the views of determinate death or permanence.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: The ālayavijñāna is the subject (*dharmin*). It is neither annihilated nor permanent; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it evolves continuously (*nitya-anuvartana*).

The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is like a torrential stream. For in that torrential stream, the characteristic of the waves and the characteristic of the water are never separated from one another.
Therefore it is said: "The ādāna-vijñāna is extremely subtle; its habitual tendencies and seeds are like a torrential stream.
Just as the flow of a torrent is neither interrupted nor permanent, this consciousness is said to revolve perpetually like a stream."
First, this consciousness is likened to a violent torrent as the fundamental basis for rebirth within the three realms.
Because of this consciousness, sentient beings are caused to drift and drown in the ocean of birth and death, unable to achieve liberation. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it can universally produce all modes of rebirth, just as an actor transforms [his appearance]."
It manifests the various realms of existence. Next, it uses the metaphor of a torrential flood to illustrate the perfuming of impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"The winds of external objects cause the ocean of the mind to surge, so that the waves of consciousness are uninterrupted. Third, it uses the metaphor of a torrential flood to illustrate the maintenance of seeds.
Because of this consciousness, one is born either in the heavens or among humans; yet the various seeds and the five factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), have never been separated from it.
Just as aquatic grass follows the current up and down without ever abandoning its nature as water-plant, so it is here. This concludes the double application of the dharma and the analogy.

Regarding the term "beginningless": because this consciousness arises as a fruit while its cause ceases, and its cause ceases while its fruit arises, it is profoundly subtle and without any discernible starting point;
hence it is called "beginningless. This dharma and analogy specifically refer to the present eighth [consciousness].
In a single moment, it functions as both cause and effect; by negating [the extremes of] annihilation and permanence, it establishes the meaning of dependent origination.
Therefore, it is said that this consciousness perpetually revolves like a flowing stream, rather than being defined in terms of the three periods of time.
Since the past and future are not substantially existent, how could they be conventionally established as non-annihilated?
This refutes the doctrines of the Sarvāstivādins, the Mūlasarvāstivādins, the Haimavatas, and others, who maintain that while all phenomena exist, the self does not.
They assert that the three time periods and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are all substantially existent, yet none of them possess a self.
First, let us present that objection. The objection states: "The principle of cause and effect is established only when it continues uninterrupted throughout the three periods of time.
The past serves as the cause and the present as the effect; the present serves as the cause and the future as the effect.

Now, since the Mahāyāna teaching of cause and effect takes the cessation and arising of a single lifetime in the present as the meaning of cause and effect, it does not establish the past [as a cause]."
[The opponent asks: "No. If the past and future are not real dharmas, then the present is likewise [not real], and thus one could establish that they are impermanent (*anitya*).

Since they are called impermanent, they would then become subject to annihilation (*uccheda*). How could they not be annihilated? How can annihilation possibly constitute the correct principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? The Mahāyāna replies:
"You say that the past and future are both substantially existent (*dravyasat*), and thus you may call them non-annihilated. Since you have said they are non-..."

To sever [the continuity] would be the permanence of death; how could one then attain the state of non-permanence? Furthermore, how could such permanence ever constitute the correct principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
The Master further states: "It is not that I delight in engaging in polemics to refute the errors of others in order to establish my own position.

Rather, it is because I have no choice but to act so, lest false doctrines remain unsubdued and the correct principles fail to manifest. Moreover, you do not understand the Mahāyāna doctrine of present causes and effects."
Regarding the correct principle of the dependent origination of the continuum, some maintain that it is subject to annihilation. I shall further clarify the general outline for you once more.

However, when I previously stated that "the effect arises upon the cessation of the cause," this was with reference to the present moment: at the very stage when the preceding cause ceases, the subsequent effect already exists.

This does not mean that the fruit arises only after the cause has been extinguished through dependence upon its cessation. If the fruit were to arise only after the cause had ceased, one could conclude that there is annihilation.
Now, however, cause and fruit are simultaneous; as the seed and the manifestation arise together, there is no longer any sequence of before and after.

How, then, could annihilation occur? It is just like the two ends of a scale, where the lowering and raising occur at the same time. The scale represents the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and the two ends represent [the cause and the fruit].
Cause and effect: the variations in height serve as a metaphor for arising and ceasing; "time" and so forth serve as a metaphor for the lack of difference between moments (*kṣaṇa*).

Thus, present cause and effect are like a violent torrent, flowing without interruption. Why then would one need to rely on past and future causes and effects for them to be established as non-interrupted?
Because the subsequent fruit has not yet arisen while the present cause exists, those who possess wisdom should practice accordingly.

The Hinayana school further objects: "If cause and effect are not established across the three time periods, but are instead defined solely by the cessation of the present cause and the arising of the fruit as constituting causality, then if one claims that the cause is a 'present cause' while the subsequent fruit has not yet arisen, this present..."
Regarding that which acts as the cause: if one claims the effect is a present effect, then since the preceding cause has already ceased, whose effect would this present effect be?
Since there is no effect within the cause and no cause within the effect, this results in annihilationism (*uccheda*).
How then can it be said to be free from both annihilation and permanence? The Mahāyāna replies: "If the cause does not perish simultaneously [with the effect]..."

The fruit arises, yet you maintain that the subsequent fruit already exists at the time of the cause. If the fruit already exists inherently, it must be eternal; why then wait for a preceding cause before the fruit comes to be?
Furthermore, the cause originally serves to produce the fruit; since the fruit does not depend on a cause, from what would the fruit arise?

Since both cause and fruit are thus non-existent, how can one avoid the extremes of nihilism and eternalism? Therefore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "If one claims that [the fruit] exists within the cause..."

Regarding the effect: I now ask you, are the two characteristics of cause and effect different or not different? If they are not different, then there would be no distinct entities for cause and effect;
since these two characteristics would be indistinguishable, it would be illogical to claim that the effect exists within the cause.
If they are different characteristics, then as for the entity of the effect within the cause, is it of an unarisen nature? Or...

Regarding the characteristic of having already arisen: if it were the characteristic of not yet having arisen, then while the effect has not yet arisen within its cause, to say that it "exists" would be unreasonable.
If it were the characteristic of having already arisen, then the essence of the effect would have already arisen; for it to arise again from a cause would be untenable.
This is not logical. Therefore, the effect does not pre-exist within the cause. Nevertheless, since a cause must exist, [the effect] arises in dependence upon conditions.

By this reasoning, your position is not established. If you wish for the relationship between cause and effect to be established, it must be demonstrated by relying on the functional activity (*kāritra*) of existing phenomena in the present.
Thus, as I stated previously, the effect arises and the cause ceases in a continuous succession (*saṃtāna*).
It is like a flowing stream, or like the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale, which are equal at all times. Now, you raise objections based on the causality of the three periods of time;
this does not accord with our Mahāyāna orthodoxy of Dependent Origination and Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). Why is this so?

Because you cling to the view that both essence and function, as well as causes and conditions, are all substantially existent from the very beginning; thus you fall into the extreme of eternalism, wherein there is no transformation.

Transformation. Cause and effect are definitively non-existent [in an ultimate sense]. Therefore, one should believe in the correct principle of dependent origination as present arising and ceasing within the Mahāyāna.
Yet, this correct principle is fundamentally beyond verbal expression; how could there be cause and effect?

Even those causes and effects are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*), unlike your own view that they are definitively real entities. How are they provisionally designated? It means observing that present phenomena exist.
The function of producing a subsequent fruit is metaphorically designated as a "future fruit" in relation to a present cause;
the observation that a present phenomenon possesses the characteristic of responding to a prior cause is metaphorically designated as a "past cause" in relation to a present fruit.
Thus, cause and fruit are not separate from the present—so why establish the three time periods as fixed entities? Question: This [designation of] a metaphorical cause...
Upon what basis is the fruit established? Answer: It is said that it is based on the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which manifests with the appearance of cause and effect;
however, these are not truly existent causes and effects existing outside the mind.

If one were to establish cause and effect separately from the arising and ceasing of the evolving consciousness, this would constitute grasping at phenomena as external to the mind, thereby falling into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "For example..."
A bright mirror manifests all forms and images; the manifestation of the manifesting consciousness is likewise so.

Such cause and effect are clear in their principle, remaining far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and perfectly accord with the Middle Way. The wise should study this; it consists, in brief, of two meanings.

The Hīnayāna explains the causes and effects of the three periods of time as occurring at different times; the Mahāyāna explains the causes and effects of a single present thought-moment as being simultaneous.
This is similar to the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena mentioned in the preceding text. However, regarding these two meanings:
Neither [position] may be discarded. If one refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), cause and effect are determined to be simultaneous;
if one refers to material phenomena (*rūpa*) and other such dharmas, it is not incorrect for cause and effect to span the three periods of time.
Other schools (nikāyas) assert that although past and future [dharmas] do not exist, the principle that they coexist with the present cannot be established.
This refutes the doctrine held by the Mahāsāṃghikas, Kaukkuṭikas, and the other seven schools, which maintain that dharmas do not exist in the past or future.

They reckon that present dharmas and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas truly exist, whereas for past and future dharmas, both substance (svabhāva) and function (kāritra) are entirely non-existent. Although [they do not exist],...
Regarding the past and future: within the single substantial entity of a present phenomenon, there exist the two temporal phases of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, there is the principle of the constant continuity of cause and effect. This means that even for phenomena that are extremely rapid in the present—such as sparks from a flint or flashes of lightning—they still possess the two phases of initial arising and subsequent cessation.
The moment of initial arising responds to a past cause, and by means of the subsequent...
At the time of cessation, it draws forth a future fruit. Although there are these two moments—the initial and the final—they do not depart from the single entity of the present.

As the prior cause is in the process of ceasing, the subsequent fruit is in the process of arising. Although the characteristics of the entities of arising and ceasing differ, they are substantially existent.

This is not like the provisional designations of past causes and future fruits found in the Mahāyāna. Since their substance is one, one is thus free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
The two times exist simultaneously, and thus the aforementioned difficulty does not apply. How could any wise person abandon this [system] to believe in the assertions of other schools?
This school establishes that the single substance of the present exists substantially in both times (past and future) for two reasons:

first, to avoid the fault of the other vehicles [Hīnayāna] which hold that the three times lack substantiality; and second, to transcend the provisional [status] of the past and future as asserted in the Mahāyāna.

How could one know that they will ultimately fall into the view of annihilationism and be unable to escape it? "That which exists" [refers to] the refutation. "How can it be permitted" [refers to] the sublation.
First, the present single moment is refuted as being devoid of two temporal dimensions, because the present single moment belongs to arising and not to ceasing.
If it were claimed that the cessation of a moment belongs to the present, then the arising of a moment should likewise belong to the future. If...
If it is claimed that existence within a single moment is called "arising" and thus constitutes the present, then non-existence within a single moment should be called "cessation";
how could this not be the past? If you claim that the cessation of the past belongs to the existence of the present, then the arising of the present should belong to the non-existence of the past.
If you claim that the time of arising is called the existence of the present, then the time of cessation should likewise be called the present.
In non-existence, it follows by this reasoning that a single present moment possesses both the two phases of arising and ceasing; such a principle is certainly impossible.
Furthermore, [the text says] "the two," etc., next refuting that arising and ceasing, being contradictory, cannot constitute a single entity.

Since the two characteristics of arising and ceasing are diametrically opposed, the characteristic of arising would lack cessation, and the characteristic of cessation would lack arising. How, then, could they be said to be a single entity?

There are two characteristics: arising and ceasing. If we discuss this in terms of worldly suffering and pleasure, then at the time of suffering there is no characteristic of pleasure, and at the time of pleasure there is no characteristic of suffering.
How could it be permissible for both characteristics of suffering and pleasure to coexist within a single present moment?
Third, the two times and the one essence cannot be established as identical. If one were to claim that arising and ceasing are one, then [arising...]
Cessation is not different [from arising], and cessation is not different from arising; one should not establish two distinct times.

If one were to claim that arising and cessation are different, then arising would belong to the present and cessation would belong to the past, such that they could not be said to be of a single essence. Therefore, the *Xianyang lun* states:
If it is claimed that the past and future exist substantially, then are the two characteristics of the past and future different from or not different from the characteristic of the present?

If they are not different, then establishing the characteristics of the three times is unreasonable. If they are different characteristics, then for their nature and characteristics to exist substantially is unreasonable.
Furthermore, are these phenomena of the three times permanent or impermanent? If one says they are permanent, [it is unreasonable].
It is not logical that [an entity] should fall into the three times. If it were impermanent, it would be logically impossible for it to exist as a real entity throughout the three times.
Therefore, the following section is introduced to refute [this position].
The Sautrāntikas and others [expound] the correct principle of dependent origination as the continuity of cause and effect.
This refutes the Sautrāntika position established by the Prajñaptivādins,

which asserts that present phenomena are real in terms of the aggregates (*skandha*) but conventional in terms of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), being established solely in dependence upon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons.
The continuity of the causes and effects of defilement and purity is uninterrupted; for they do not admit that the ālayavijñāna maintains the seeds.
Nevertheless, for the continuity of cause and effect to be logically possible, there must necessarily be seeds: from seeds, the manifest arises; from the manifest, seeds arise.
This is what is called "continuity. How could there be the production of a fruit without a seed? Since cause and effect do not exist, who would constitute continuity?
Therefore, it is said that this principle is also untenable. From here below, the conclusion exhorts one to give rise to faith.
This consciousness has been revolving continuously since beginningless time like a flowing stream, until it becomes an Arhat and a Tathāgata.
This explains the gateway of the stages for subduing and severing [afflictions]. First there is the question, then the answer. There are five stages of the cause and fruit of an Arhat:

first, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), wherein one cultivates the five stabilizing mind-observations (*pañca-sthāpana-vipaśyanā*), the observation of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*), and the observation of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*). It says:

The five *sthāpanā-cittas* (stabilizations of the mind) refer to stabilizing the mind in five locations. That is to say: for sentient beings with excessive greed, one practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*);

for those with excessive anger, the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*); for those with excessive delusion, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*);

for those attached to a self, the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhāga-bhāvanā*); and for those with excessive discursive thought, the contemplation of the nature of one's own mind (*svacitta-parikalpa-bhāvanā*). These are called the five.

One abides in the contemplation of the settled mind (*sthāpanā-citta*). Regarding what is called "distinct mindfulness" (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*): this refers to contemplating the body as impure, contemplating sensation as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as non-self.

Because one gives rise to distinct perceptions regarding these four dharmas, it is named "distinct-characteristic mindfulness. Regarding "general characteristic mindfulness" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*):
this refers to contemplating the four dharmas collectively as all being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. This is named "general-characteristic mindfulness."

Second is the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), which consists of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*). Regarding "Heat":

following the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there arises the first root of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) that is conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); this is called the dharma of Heat (*uṣmagata-dharma*). It is named "Heat" because it can burn the fuel of afflictions and serves as the precursor sign (*pūrva-nimitta*) to the fire of the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
It is like a person drilling for fire; since heat is produced at the beginning, it is called "Heat. This is a portion of the root of virtue of Heat.
Because it is the foremost stage, one first contemplates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Four Noble Truths. Since there are four aspects for each truth, they total sixteen.

Regarding the four aspects under the first truth, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), they are: impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*). First, as for impermanence:
This means that "suffering" refers to contemplating the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as arising and ceasing in every new moment due to causes and conditions;

"emptiness" refers to contemplating the five aggregates as being devoid of any characteristic of identity or difference; and "non-self" refers to contemplating that within the five aggregates, neither a self nor anything belonging to a self can be found.
Regarding the four modes of practice under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), they refer to origination...

It arises through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*). First, "accumulation" (*samudaya*) means contemplating that contaminated afflictions (*sāsrava-kleśa*) can summon the fruit of suffering.

Second, "cause" (*hetu*) means contemplating that the six causes (*ṣad-hetu*) can produce the fruit of suffering. Third, "condition" (*pratyaya*) means contemplating that the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*) can produce the fruit of suffering.

Fourth, "arising" (*jāti*) means contemplating the subsequent reception of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a body. Regarding the four modes of practice under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*):

This refers to exhaustion (*kṣaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and detachment (*niḥsaraṇa*). "Exhaustion" means observing that all various [defilements] have been exhausted in *nirvāṇa*.
"Cessation" means observing that the fire of afflictions has been extinguished in *nirvāṇa*. "Excellence" means observing that *nirvāṇa* is the foremost of all things.
"Detachment" means observing that *nirvāṇa* is free from the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). These are the four [aspects] under the Truth of the Path.
"Practice" (yoga) refers to the vehicle of the path and the right tracks. It is called the "path" because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can lead one to nirvāṇa.
It is called "right" because the thirty-seven factors are not inverted dharmas. It is called "tracks" because the thirty-seven factors are the places where all noble ones have gone.
It is called a "vehicle" because the thirty-seven factors are capable of transporting one along.

Because one attains the three liberations through these sixteen modes of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), the three grades of wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*)—inferior, medium, and superior—are established.
By contemplating the two upper realms together, thirty-two modes of contemplation are formed. Regarding the term "Summit" (*mūrdhan*):

when these wholesome roots of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) have gradually increased through their inferior, medium, and superior stages and reach the point of full completion, a further wholesome root arises which is called the Dharma of the Summit. It is a dharma that is still subject to regression.

Because it is the most excellent among [the stages], this level involves contemplating the three grades of the wholesome roots within the preceding thirty-two aspects for the sake of their maturation.

Regarding "patience" (*kṣānti*): as these peak wholesome roots (*mūrdhan*) gradually increase through the lower, middle, and upper grades until they reach full completion, a wholesome root arises which is called the dharma of patience (*kṣānti-dharma*).
It confirms the principle of the truths; because this is the most preeminent, it is so named.
This patience (*kṣānti*) is of three kinds: namely, inferior, medium, and superior. The inferior and medium patiences are identical to the stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*);
that is, they possess the observation of the objects of the Four Noble Truths and are capable of possessing the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).

The superior patience, however, observes only a single object—the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the desire realm—for a single moment. This is because it is immediately contiguous with the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). For this reason...

Therefore, the meaning that the roots of goodness, such as *ūṣmagata* (heat) and the others, are all able to take the suffering and so forth of the three realms as their objects is already established, because there is no distinction made [in the scriptures].
Immediately following the highest degree of *kṣānti* (patience), the *laukikāgradharma* (supreme mundane dharma) arises.

Like the highest degree of *kṣānti*, the *laukikāgradharma* also consists of a single moment of intensive contemplation (*anuprekṣā*) upon the single object of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the desire realm. Because this is still contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is called...

Because it is the most excellent in the world, it is called "the foremost. Since these contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are supreme within the world, they are therefore termed the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Regarding the third stage, the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*):

following the mind of the Supreme Mundane Dharma, the True Clarity of the Patience regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) gives rise to the eight patiences and eight knowledges with respect to the eight truths of the upper and lower realms. Specifically, the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-kṣānti*) resides therein.
In the desire realm, while the subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) and subsequent patiences (*anvaya-kṣānti*) pertain to the higher realms, there are sixteen minds in total.

That is to say, during the preceding "gate of entry," at the time of the fifteenth mind, which is the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*), one is called a "candidate for stream-entry" (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*). At the time of the sixteenth mind, which is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), [one becomes a stream-enterer].

The sudden severance of the afflictions of view and the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Regarding the four stages of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*):

the sixteenth moment of mind within the gate of emptiness of the first fruit is called the True Path of Seeing. Progressing from the first fruit toward further cultivation is termed the Stage of Cultivation.

If, among the nine grades of afflictions of cultivation in the desire realm, one has severed up to the sixth grade—consisting of six paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and five paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)—this is called...
The candidate for the first fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin-patipanna*) is called the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*).

When one has abandoned the latter three [categories of defilements] during the three paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one is called the candidate for the non-returner (*anāgāmin-patipanna*). Upon reaching the third path of liberation, one is called the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*).

If one abandons the seventy-two categories of defilements belonging to the eight higher stages, up to the seventy-second path of immediate succession, [one is the candidate for arhatship]. At the seventy-first...
When one is on the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for this stage, one is called an "Arhat-candidate" (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).

From the time of abiding correctly in the first fruit (*phala*) and proceeding with further cultivation thereafter, up until this moment of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), it is the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Regarding the five stages of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*):

upon reaching the seventy-second path of liberation, when the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) are completely severed and the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) is realized, it is called the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).
Furthermore, within this context, the ālayavijñāna is finally and completely relinquished only upon reaching the stage of an arhat.

This is because that arhat has severed the afflictions of view and cultivation belonging to the three realms, such that both the seeds and the manifest forms of both discriminative and innate self-grasping have been entirely exhausted.
The stage of arhatship described here does not refer solely to the śrāvakas; it comprehensively includes the adepts (aśaikṣas) of all three vehicles, because there are three types of arhats:
namely, the slayer of thieves (vadhaka), the worthy of offerings (arhat), and the one who does not arise again (anuppāda). These are the adepts of the three vehicles.
All [of these] possess this meaning and thus collectively receive this name. Question: How is this known? Answer:

The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* cites evidence that those in the three vehicles who have attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) all abandon the ālayavijñāna. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* cites evidence that bodhisattvas are called "Arhats.

This is because when a bodhisattva ascends to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), they eliminate the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of afflictions; it is only at the time of attaining enlightenment (*bodhi*) that they eliminate their seeds (*bīja*).
If that is so, then even regarding the seeds of affliction in a bodhisattva, this [text] also refers to them as an arhat.

Question: If, when a bodhisattva attains enlightenment, the afflictions and the objects of knowledge are severed simultaneously and instantaneously, then prior to realizing enlightenment, the seeds of affliction have not yet been permanently severed; thus, the ālayavijñāna must exist.
This does not refer to an Arhat. Why, then, is it stated in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* that even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas do not possess the ālayavijñāna?
Answer: This "non-retrogressive Bodhisattva" refers to those of the two vehicles who have already severed their afflictions and turned their minds toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
They are called "non-retrogressive" because they will certainly not retrogress by giving rise to afflictions. Because of this...

Because they advance toward enlightenment, they are also called "non-retrogressive. These non-retrogressive bodhisattvas are included within this category of arhats; thus, it does not contradict the meaning of the treatise.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas from the Immovable (Acalā) stage upward—such as those at the stages of Good Intelligence (Sādhumatī), Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā), and so forth—are all non-retrogressive, because their innate afflictions never manifest again. This is due to the innate nature of the phenomena...

[The Buddha] replied: "Because it functions spontaneously, its practice is inexhaustible and uninterrupted; because he cultivates progress in every thought-moment without indolence, it is called 'non-retrogression.

Furthermore, although this Bodhisattva has not yet completely severed the seeds of affliction within the *vipākavijñāna*, the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of self-view, self-love, and so forth directed toward this consciousness have already been suppressed, and he no longer clings to an internal self."
Therefore, they also permanently relinquish the name "ālayavijñāna" and are called arhats.
According to another interpretation, bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at that time.
This expresses a specific meaning. Some masters maintain that Bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward have already realized the emptiness of both the conceptualized self and phenomena;

they have already attained the two kinds of subsequent knowledge (prsthalabdha-jñāna) regarding the faculties; and they have already severed the two kinds of obstacles consisting of the conceptualized self and phenomena.
Having already cultivated both the single practice and all practices, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, although they may manifest afflictions, they are without fault.
Such bodhisattvas are also called "non-regressive. Nevertheless, these bodhisattvas have not yet abandoned the innate [afflictions].

Having already severed conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), one thereby also attains the relinquishing of the name "ālaya" and is called an Arhat. Thus, in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*, it is cited as proof that one does not commit the fault of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The spell and medicine serve as metaphors for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), while the various poisons serve as metaphors for the afflictions.

The Master of the Treatise first refutes [the opponent's view] and subsequently breaks down [their position]. Although conceptual discrimination has been severed prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) still remains.
They grasp the eighth consciousness as their internal self; how, then, can it lose its name of *ālaya*?

If it is said that "abandoning" means the cessation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then since Stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and others also cease conceptual construction, they too should be said to have abandoned it. Next, the text explains further:
Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) attain superior wisdom and possess correct knowledge; therefore, even though they give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), [they do not lose their status].
This does not constitute a fault. How could one possibly compare this to those such as the Stream-enterers? Furthermore, it is refuted [by others] thus:

although Bodhisattvas on the grounds have severed the delusions of conceptual discrimination and do not give rise to various views, they are able to give rise to correct cognition within the sixth consciousness.

No fault arises [from this]. However, since the innate [affliction] within the seventh consciousness remains unsevered and functions as spontaneous grasping and concealment (*ālaya*), how could it not be the same as that of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)?
Therefore, know that [your position] is irrational. Furthermore, an objection is raised:

"If an Arhat is said to have 'abandoned' [the afflictions], he should attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder). Why is this not the case? The answer is: "However, what is meant here by 'abandoning' refers to that..."
The seeds of innate afflictions have all been completely severed and exhausted; no longer grasping them as a self, one realizes arhatship, which is termed "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

This does not mean that the substance of the eighth consciousness is entirely abandoned, for its maturation (*vipāka*) has not yet become empty, as it still maintains the seeds of innate clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
If one were to claim that an arhat has abandoned everything, then [the arhat] would [necessarily be...]
If there were no seed-bearing consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), one would immediately enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; why then need this further objection?
Nevertheless, although the eighth consciousness has these various names—[from "all sentient beings" down to] "these various names"—they apply throughout all states.

The following section discusses the names of the eight consciousnesses, which have both general and specific applications. Because it was previously stated that "the substance of the eighth consciousness is never abandoned," this topic is addressed here.
Regarding the "general" application, it pertains to all ordinary beings and sages alike. Regarding the "specific" application, it refers to their individual abandonment [of the state].
First, the general status is explained: it is called *citta* (mind) because it can accumulate and store the seeds of all phenomena (*dharma*).
It is also called *ādāna* (appropriation), which has three meanings: first, *dhāraṇa* (sustaining), meaning it can sustain the seeds of all phenomena;
second, *upādāna* (appropriating), meaning it can appropriate the physical sense organs and their bases; third, *grahaṇa* (grasping), meaning it can grasp the continuity of rebirth.
It is also called the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeya-āśraya*), as it is the locus for the various phenomena of both defilement and purity, such as the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Because it is the locus [of all phenomena], and because it is that which those training in the Mahāyāna must know, it is called the "seed-consciousness" (*bīja-vijñāna*), as it contains and accumulates the seeds of all dharmas.
That is to say, in the causal stage it maintains both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*); in the resultant stage, it maintains only the non-out-flowing.
These four names apply universally to both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*).
Alternatively, it is called *ālaya* (up to) being associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom that is liberated from all hindrances.

Next, the specific stages are explained: it is called *ālaya*, which exists only for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*), but does not extend to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) or non-regressive Bodhisattvas;
or it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*), which extends from ordinary beings up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), as it exists in all of them.
This name is used exclusively for the Tathāgata; alternatively, it is called the *amala-vijñāna* (stainless consciousness).

This means that when this consciousness reaches the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, it suddenly severs the seeds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome states, as well as the uncontaminated seeds perfumed by inferior neutral states.
It transforms the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) into the stainless, which is named the pure white fruit (*amala-śukla-phala*).
This consciousness, being purely untainted (*anāsrava*), does not contain the seeds of any defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) nor the seeds of any tainted wholesome phenomena (*sāsravakuśaladharma*);
it is solely the substratum for the seeds of the most supremely pure untainted phenomena.
This name exists only in the stage of the Tathāgata and does not extend to other stages.

This is because within the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and Bodhisattvas, there is always the maturation (*vipāka*) that sustains seeds and receives perfuming (*vāsanā*), as they have not yet attained the thoroughly pure eighth consciousness.
Only in the stage of the Tathāgata does this consciousness exist. As it says in the citation below, this is established by scriptural proof.
The name *ālaya* is used because its faults are grave; [this continues] until: "because it is common to the mind and so forth, it should be explained according to one's preference.
The preceding section clarified that the stages have both general and specific aspects; this section clarifies that there is a sequence in their relinquishment. Question:
