The fruit should not be a rebirth-state (*gati*), because it lacks the essential nature of a maturation-rebirth-state. Regarding "defiled and wholesome minds":
that which is capable of relishing [the object] is called "defiled," while that which possesses meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) is called "wholesome.

Even if one were to concede that the essence of the rebirth-state includes the seeds of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) [dharmas], when one who has been born in the formless realm suddenly gives rise to [a mind] within an outflowing state of consciousness...
It is untainted (*anāsrava*). At that time, all those worldly minds are extinguished;

thus, the basis for birth in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) would have to be abandoned without effort, and one would spontaneously realize *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), because the maturation (*vipāka*) it encompasses would be empty.

If one were to allow that the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is empty in the formless realms, this would contradict the fact that only the Buddha alone is without a realm of rebirth (*agati*).

Regarding the essential nature of birth (*jāti*): if one does not establish *vipāka* (maturation) as the essential nature of the realms of rebirth (*gati*), one incurs the aforementioned faults of being neither pervasive nor constant, and furthermore, one incurs the fault that there would be no realms of rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). If, however, one establishes it as *vipāka*, none of these faults apply.

It is explained below that only the Buddha alone is not of the essential nature of the realms of rebirth, because his maturation is empty; likewise, the Tathāgata is not comprised within the three realms.

[Included] because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted; because suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*) have been abandoned; and because the seeds of conventional designation (*nāma-vyavahāra-bīja*) have been severed.

Therefore, the Tathāgata does not belong to the realms of rebirth (*gati*). All others are comprised within the substance of the realms of rebirth. Thus it is known [from the following]. This concludes the explicit demonstration.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that there is a body with sense organs (*rūpīndriya-kāya*)... [up to] "that mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.
Because the destinies and births are not intermingled due to the presence of appropriation (*upādāna*), it is mentioned next. First, the scriptural proof is cited: "If there were no... and so forth.

Next, the eighth consciousness is established as the appropriating mind (*upādātṛ-citta*). This means that sentient beings possess the body of the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*), because these are the direct objective parts (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness;
thus, only the eighth consciousness is capable of appropriating them. If it were any other consciousness, it would lack this capacity.

This is because the five material sense-faculties and their physical bases are past or future—having already perished or not yet arisen—and therefore [cannot be appropriated by those other consciousnesses].
There is no appropriation (*anupātta*). Because it exists as a substantial entity only in the present life, it must necessarily involve appropriation (*upātta*).

Since there is appropriation, there must certainly be a mind that appropriates. Having previously established that the maturation (*vipāka*) is the appropriator, one concludes that it is exclusively the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*).
This is because it is induced by the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—from previous lives; it is ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*), not wholesome.

Because of [factors] such as defilement (*kleśa*), within the realms of good and evil destinies, a single class [of consciousness] is able to pervasively maintain the continuity of the appropriated body possessing material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).

The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness, lack the quality of being appropriated. Question: If only the maturation (*vipāka*) is a single class that maintains continuity, [how is this so]?
Regarding the "appropriation of the material body," the Buddha has no *vipāka* (maturation). It would follow that the material bodies of all Buddhas lack appropriation. Answer:

This statement is intended as a reductio ad absurdum to clarify that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness, do not possess the nature of appropriation; it does not mean that appropriation belongs exclusively to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*).

This is because the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) material bodies of the Tathāgatas are also appropriated by the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*). Therefore, the term "appropriation" [is used].
This applies to all stages; however, it is only the *vipāka*-consciousness that can appropriate (*upādāna*) the contaminated physical body (*rūpakāya*), and thus this statement was made.

It does not mean that the uncontaminated physical bodies of the Buddhas lack appropriation. Next, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute the position that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) lack appropriation.
The formal inference states: "The various evolving consciousnesses and so forth are incapable of appropriating the contaminated physical body."

Because they arise through present conditions. For example, things such as wind and sound arise through present conditions; that is, they are produced by relying on present conditions, such as the nine conditions for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Next, [the text] refutes the grasping of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as being appropriated. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated:

Those [states], whether virtuous or defiled, cannot be appropriated because they are not projected by karma, just like non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). This is because the three natures are... [self-... *(Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end. The translation reflects the available portion.)*
It is produced by power and is not induced by karma, just like the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

It is pure by its very nature (*svabhāva-viśuddha*) and is not manifested by the abandonment of afflictions through the power of wisdom. Third, it destroys that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and is non-appropriated (*anupātta*).

The formal proof (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which is born of maturation cannot be appropriated, because it is not of the nature of maturation, because it is not a universal basis, and because it is not continuous.
[The argument] is like a flash of lightning and so forth. Fourth, the refutation of the mental factors (*caitta*) as being non-appropriated (*anupātta*).

The formal proof (*prayoga*) is as follows: All mental factors cannot be appropriated, because they are necessarily associated with the primary consciousnesses (*citta*), just as in the case of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Since the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) themselves cannot be appropriated, their mental factors likewise cannot be appropriated. Fifth, the refutation of matter (*rūpa*) and its non-associated [factors]...
The formations dissociated from the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) should also not be appropriated (*anupātta*). To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*):
All formations dissociated from the material sense-faculties cannot appropriate [objects], because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like space and so forth.

They lack an object of cognition because those formations dissociated from the material sense-faculties are not cognizing minds; therefore, they cannot take an object of cognition. Since they cannot take an object of cognition, [they are not appropriated].
Because it is capable of grasping [the body], it must be placed below [the other two]. This concludes the demonstration.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that there are three—vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—and that this very consciousness is the eighth consciousness.

It is said that this consciousness not only sustains the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*), but also sustains vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*); therefore, it is discussed next. First, a scriptural proof is cited: "If [it] were absent... and so forth.
Next, it is established that the eighth consciousness is that which sustains vitality, warmth, and consciousness. Regarding the phrase "vitality, warmth, and so forth":

warmth is a form-dharma (*rūpa-dharma*) that is a portion of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (object-aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, because it is apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*). The seeds of this consciousness are called "vitality" (*āyus*), because...

It can produce consciousness; therefore, the active manifestation is consciousness. By means of these three factors relying upon and supporting one another, they are able to abide in a continuous succession.
If the eighth [consciousness] did not exist, there would be no consciousness capable of sustaining vitality and warmth for a long duration.

Thus, [the author] refutes the notion that the evolving consciousnesses possess the function of constant sustenance, as they do not sustain vitality and warmth. He establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "As for the various evolving..."

Consciousness is an existent phenomenon. It cannot be established as the thesis that it "sustains life-force, warmth, and consciousness," because the reason is that it possesses intervals and transitions, and thus lacks the function of constant sustenance;
this is illustrated by examples such as sound and wind. Next, one infers that the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) possesses constant sustenance.
[It has] the function of being able to maintain vitality (*āyuṣ*) and heat (*uṣman*). To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*):

Only the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) can definitely be established as the consciousness that maintains vitality and heat, because it functions continuously and without interruption, just like vitality and heat.

Question: The Sūtra states that vitality, heat, and consciousness mutually support one another. Does this perhaps refer to a consciousness that functions with interruptions? By what means can it be definitively known that [the Sūtra] refers to [the *vipākavijñāna*]?

Regarding "uninterrupted transition," the answer is as follows: The Sūtra states that the three factors of vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) mutually support one another.

If vitality and warmth were of a single class and continued in uninterrupted succession, while consciousness alone underwent interrupted transitions, how could this possibly accord with the principle of these three factors mutually supporting one another?
Therefore, by inference through reasoning, it must be an uninterrupted transition.

[This refers to] consciousness (*vijñāna*). He asked again: "Since you state that these three factors are of a single class, continue in succession, and mutually support one another, then these three factors must either all be pervasive and all proceed without interruption, or all be non-pervasive and all possess interruptions.
Why do you allow that 'warmth' (*uṣman*) is not pervasive throughout the realm, yet not allow that consciousness has interruptions? This, when examined by reason, is not [tenable].

Objection: This leads to a logical difficulty. Response: It is said that in whatever locus these three factors are present, there must necessarily be a single category that is uninterrupted, non-transformative, and constantly upholding [the body], which is the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
If this consciousness were absent, it would lack the function of constantly sustaining vitality and warmth.
Based on the preceding reasoning, one can definitively know that the consciousness described in relation to these three factors must belong to a single, continuous category.
Regarding "immediate maturation" (*ānantarya-vipāka*): this does not refer to the fact that the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses) arise with intervals.

Even if one were to raise the objection that warmth (*uṣman*) is not omnipresent throughout the three realms, how could this undermine the preceding principle? This is because when warmth is relinquished, the other two [life-force and consciousness] are not relinquished;
and if the other two were relinquished, warmth would necessarily be relinquished along with them. Therefore, I maintain that what sustains life-force and warmth is the immediate maturation.

This principle is fully established. If it is argued that among these three factors, that which sustains vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) must necessarily be the intermittent evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and not the uninterrupted one, then since both warmth and vitality among these three factors are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), that evolving consciousness must also be contaminated and certainly not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This would be the case even if, suddenly, one were born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where the sixth evolving consciousness [would likewise be so].
When an uncontaminated mind arises and transforms into the uncontaminated state, at that time, which consciousness maintains that contaminated seed of life?
From this, it is known with certainty that there exists a maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) capable of maintaining life and warmth.
Furthermore, the sūtras state that among all classes of sentient beings [up to]... therefore, we know that this eighth consciousness definitely exists.

While there may still be confusion regarding its present maintenance of the sense organs, the body, warmth, and life-force, there is no ambiguity whatsoever concerning its departure at the time of birth and its arrival at the time of death;
it cannot be borrowed from or substituted for by anything else. Therefore, it is explained next. First, the sūtra is cited as proof: if it did not exist...

Below. Next, the eighth consciousness is established as the "scattered mind" (*vikṣipta-citta*). As for the term "scattered mind," it refers to the state of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), wherein all [other] minds are dispersed;
this consciousness alone exists therein, and is thus called the scattered mind. It is not the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), because it is a state possessing mind.

If the eighth consciousness did not exist, the scattered mind of birth and death could not be obtained; that is to say, when one is born below [in the lower realms], at the time of inferring the process of birth and death, [the other consciousnesses] are absent.

Regarding the transformation of consciousness (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*): this refers to the state of birth and death, wherein the clear and distinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is entirely obscured and dull.

This is because, as in the case of a person in deep sleep or at the moment of extreme fainting, the clear and distinct mental consciousness necessarily does not arise. To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*), one states:

"At the stage of birth and death, the clear and distinct mental consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*); it is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that it necessarily does not manifest. The reason (*hetu*) is: because the body and mind are extremely obscured and dull."

Because of fainting, it is like being asleep without dreams. "The clearly manifest mental consciousness" refers specifically to the sixth [consciousness]. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
In this state, the six types of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are the subject (*dharmin*); they definitely do not manifest is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason is stated: "Because the aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) are unknowable, it is like the state without mind (*acittaka*). The question is asked:

"For what reason are the aspects and objects of the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) all unknowable during the state of birth and death? The response is established by means of formal logic (*pramāṇa*):
"Furthermore, if the six evolving consciousnesses were definitely manifest in this state, their aspects and objects would necessarily exist."
Because it is cognizable, as in other times. "Other times" refers to ordinary times, when the six consciousnesses arise habitually;

at such times, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of perception (*ālambana*) are all fully cognizable. However, during the state of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they certainly do not manifest;
therefore, their modes of activity and objects of perception are all incognizable. Thus, one can infer that the mind in the state of birth and death must certainly be...
Regarding maturation (*vipāka*): Question. At the moment of death, since the sixth consciousness cannot discern its mental aspects (*ākāra*) or objects (*ālambana*), it is termed "non-existent.
Yet, at the moment of death, the aspects and objects of the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) are likewise unknowable; why, then, is it not non-existent? Answer.

Because the true maturation-consciousness is extremely subtle, both its aspects and objects are indiscernible. This does not mean that it is called "non-existent" because it is a state of no-mind (*acittaka*).

It cannot be fully understood. By means of this *vipāka* (maturation), it serves as the sovereign lord of the general retribution for the six preceding karmas of good and evil that project [a new existence], continuing through a single period of birth and death (*ekajāti*) without ever undergoing change. Therefore, while the physical form and mind disintegrate, this consciousness does not perish;

it is called "consciousness during the state of dissolution" (*saṃskāra-citta*), not a state of unconsciousness. An ancient master asked: "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth, the great trichiliocosm..."
Both are destroyed. I do not yet understand whether this [consciousness] is destroyed or not. He replied: "It is not destroyed. [The questioner asked: "Why is it not destroyed? He replied:

"Because it is identical to the great trichiliocosm. This is precisely that meaning. Below, he refutes the Hīnayāna attachment to the existence of a non-diffuse mind (*avipraṇāśa-citta*) at the stage of taking birth.
Since they regard the sixth consciousness as the non-diffuse mind, he first sets forth their calculation. Some say that at the moment of taking birth...

Within this state, the five consciousnesses are definitely absent. Why is this? Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) apprehends objects either by relying on the first five [consciousnesses] as doors of clarity before it can apprehend them, or by relying on the verbal instructions of others before it can apprehend them, or by relying on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to apprehend them.
These are all causes for the mental consciousness in its state of arising; thus, there are three causes for its arising in this state.
Since [the object] cannot be apprehended, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) at the stage of taking birth is likewise non-existent.
How then can it be said that one who takes birth and passes away must necessarily abide in a distracted state of mind? The following refutation states:

If there were no mental consciousness at the stage of taking birth, then when sentient beings are born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), since the five sensory consciousnesses are absent and there is no external instruction, the mental consciousness would never subsequently arise.

They arise again. If it is argued that although the five consciousnesses are absent during another teaching, they can be induced by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this is also not the case.
Even the mind of meditative concentration is only able to be induced by means of a distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Now, during another teaching, there is no formless concentration, and thus there is no distracted mental consciousness from which [the five consciousnesses] could arise. Since the distracted mental consciousness is absent, the mind of meditative concentration [cannot arise].
It is also non-existent because the concentrated mind is absent; thus, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is likewise non-existent.
However, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) now manifests from time to time during both concentrated and distracted states of mind. How can it be said that it does not exist?

If you argue that those [formless states] are not induced by a distracted mind, but rather arise spontaneously (*sateram*) in that realm after the power of concentration—habitually cultivated over a long period through the mental consciousness—is subsequently produced, [we reply:]...
Then, when one is first born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the habituated consciousness should likewise arise immediately upon its occurrence.

Since this is the case for the formless realm, it should also follow that when one is first reborn in the desire or form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*), the habituated mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should likewise arise. Why is it not so in this instance alone?
If you argue that at the time of initial birth, the habituated mental consciousness does not yet manifest because it is obscured by confusion; [we reply:]...
As for the former point: this very state of obscurity is precisely that which cannot be clearly known—the distracted mind within the cycle of birth and death. Why labor to explain it separately?

If one claims that within the state of birth and death there is a distinct category of subtle mental consciousness whose mode of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of perception (*ālambana*) are both unknowable, one should know that this is precisely what the Tathāgata spoke of cryptically as the eighth consciousness. It is not [the seventh].
Sixth: Because the objects of the sixth mode of activity can all be clearly cognized, this is an established meaning and not one that is unestablished.

Below, it is refuted that there is no non-discursive mental consciousness at the time of death. If there were no discursive mind at the moment of passing away, then the sensation of coldness in the upper and lower parts of the body would gradually arise;
for instance, in the case of wholesome karma, coldness proceeds from the bottom up, whereas in the case of unwholesome karma, it proceeds from the top down.
It is cold. This is because those who perform wholesome deeds will certainly ascend, while those who perform unwholesome deeds will certainly fall downward.

Furthermore, such numerous meanings as "the crown of the head is for the sages, the eyes are for the gods, the human heart is for the hungry ghosts, the belly is for the animals, the kneecaps are for the [hungry ghosts], and the soles of the feet are for the hells" would all fail to be established;
for at that time, although the evolving consciousnesses are attached to this body, they do not [function as such].

Because it clings to the physical body, at that time the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, may not function. Consequently, the sixth mental consciousness does not abide in this body;
the objects it perceives likewise lack any fixed standard, as they are all distracted conditions.
Since that [consciousness] dwells throughout this body exclusively and is constantly continuous, it cannot act as the master, nor does it grasp or maintain [the body]; thus, it should not be cold.
Contact arises gradually from that. The following clarifies that only the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) serves as the mind at the moment of death.

Only the maturation-consciousness, through the power of the wholesome and unwholesome karma of previous lives, constantly and universally continues in a stream, appropriating the physical body. It is by virtue of this appropriation [that contact arises].

The body possesses the tactile sensation of warmth. When the locus of appropriation (*upātta*) is relinquished, the tactile sensation of cold arises; for life-force (*āyus*), warmth, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are inseparable from one another.

Once the sensation of cold has arisen, although it is still a sentient being, it becomes an insentient object. This is because the eighth [consciousness], though it undergoes transformation and takes objects, does not appropriate them.
Thus, the following section concludes by revealing that the eighth [consciousness] is the "mind in a state of dispersion" (*vikṣipta-citta*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states that "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (up to the full formula). Thus, the term "that consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness.
The previous [passage] concerned the stages of actual birth and actual death; this concerns the stage of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) entering the womb.

This stage occurs after the end of life and before the taking of birth. First, the scripture is cited as proof. Then, the passage beginning with "If there were no... establishes the eighth consciousness as the "name."
Regarding "consciousness external to form" and "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form": "name" refers to the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
"form" refers to the physical matter such as the *kalala* at the moment of initial conception. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Within the first seven days, that which has already coagulated from the previously thin internal [fluid] is called *kalala*. Within the second seven days, it is like curd on the surface and inside, though it has not yet reached the stage of flesh."
The stage is called Arbuda; within three weeks it is termed "Internal. If it has already become flesh yet remains extremely soft, it is called Peśī.
Within four weeks, if it has already become firm and thick and is somewhat capable of being touched, it is called Ghana.
After five weeks, all belong to the stage of physical form; as this mass of flesh increases and the characteristics of the limbs appear, it is called Praśākhā.
From this point onward, when hair, body hair, and nails appear, it is called the stage of hair, body hair, and nails (*keśaromanakhāvasthā*).

From this point onward, when the sense faculties such as the eyes arise, it is called the stage of the faculties (*indriyāvasthā*). From this point onward, when their respective bases become clearly manifest, these are collectively called the stage of form (*ākṛtyavasthā*).
This name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) abides in mutual dependence with consciousness (*vijñāna*), never being separated from it. [To establish] the formal argument (*prayoga*):
It is said: Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and consciousness (vijñāna) serve as mutual conditions for one another, abiding in dependence upon each other, like two bundles of reeds.
This consciousness is precisely the eighth [consciousness]. Question: How is it known that this consciousness is the eighth and not the sixth? Answer:

Because the first six evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) are subsumed within "name" (nāma). If it were not the eighth, then the statement that "consciousness takes name as its condition" would be untenable.

Regarding "form" (rūpa): who is said to be the consciousness (vijñāna)? If it is claimed that the consciousness within the "name" (nāma) refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya), while the [consciousness] itself is the sixth [mental consciousness], this is also not the case.
Because at the stage of the kalala, the sense faculties are not yet complete and objects have not yet appeared before them, the five sensory consciousnesses do not exist.
Therefore, it is known that the consciousness within the "name" is precisely the sixth [consciousness]; whereas outside of the "name,"...

This consciousness is precisely the eighth. Even if one were to concede that the consciousness within the "name" (nāma) refers to the first five [consciousnesses] while the consciousness outside the "name" refers to the sixth, since the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are intermittent, they lack the power to constantly sustain name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
How, then, could it be said that they serve as the condition for name-and-form? Therefore, that which is able to sustain name-and-form must certainly be the eighth consciousness.
Thus it is.
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Three;
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Four.
Composed by Bodhisattvas such as Dharmapāla;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled and annotated by the Śramaṇa Tongrun of Jinting Changshou Monastery.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that for all sentient beings... [up to] "that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.
The previous [passage] was based on the state of arising and ceasing; this is based on the state of abiding, which is why it is mentioned next. First, a sūtra is cited as proof;

next, the eighth consciousness is established as the *vijñānāhāra* (consciousness-nutriment); next, a sūtra is cited for explanation. Regarding "morsel food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*): "morsel" (*kavaḍī*) means divided portions; "food" (*āhāra*) has the function of providing sustenance.

It has the meaning of "sustaining through nourishment," because it sustains and benefits the physical body and its material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*). Regarding "having transformation as its characteristic":

this is because the edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) of the desire realm must undergo transformation through the three types—odor, flavor, and tangibility—at which time it can then nourish and develop the sense faculties and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Because it is characterized by transformation, edible food is not included within the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*), since it is a form that undergoes transformation.
Because they lack utility. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is that which undergoes transformation;

by means of this transformation, it benefits the physical basis (*āśraya*). Contact as nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*) has the characteristic of contacting objects; that is, tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*).

As soon as it contacts an object, it can produce sensation (*vedanā*), which experiences joy and pleasure, thereby nourishing and increasing the material body and functioning as nutriment. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* [continues].

It is said: The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) is that which grasps objects; for by momentarily perceiving objects such as form (*rūpa*), it causes the basis [of existence] to flourish and increase.
The Buddha told Aniruddha: "All phenomena subsist by depending on nutriment.
For example, the eye has form as its nutriment; the ear has sound as its nutriment; the nose has fragrance as its nutriment; the tongue has taste as its nutriment."
The body takes fine and smooth [sensations] as its nutriment; the mind takes mental objects (*dharma*) as its nutriment, and so forth. Question: With which consciousnesses is this contact associated?

Answer: Although this contact is associated with all consciousnesses, it is the [contact] belonging to the six consciousnesses that possesses the predominant sense of being "nutriment," because it can touch coarse and manifest objects and can produce the two feelings of joy and pleasure, as well as a beneficial feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*), thereby providing nourishment.

This is due to the superiority of the six consciousnesses. Because the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] can both contact subtle objects, they are entirely unable to produce the two sensations of joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*);
they produce only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Although this does not cause harm, it likewise provides no benefit. As for the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*):

The characteristic of nutriment is the hope and desire [for objects]. Just as when a person hopes for things in the world that are lovely and desirable, they may consequently neglect sleep and forget to eat;
this can function as the act of nourishing. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā*) is the capacity for hoping.
By means of this hope, it benefits the basis [of existence], just as one preserves life by looking toward a bag of ashes or gazing upon a mass of foam."

Regarding "prolonging time" and so forth: although this mental food (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) is associated with all consciousnesses, it is the aspiration of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone that is most predominant;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned. As for the consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*), its characteristic is grasping and maintaining.

While the aforementioned edible food (*kavaliṅkāhāra*) sustains the body, and the two foods of contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*) nourish the mind, there is furthermore an eighth power of grasping and maintaining which causes [the continuity].

The power of body and mind increases, enabling it to function as the food of sustenance (*āhāra*). The *Abhidharma-samuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "The food of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*) is that which appropriates and maintains (*upādāna*).
Because of this appropriation, the basis (*āśraya*) endures for a long time. Were it not so, it would be like a corpse, soon to rot and decay.
This consciousness applies to all types of consciousness, yet the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is preeminent in its function as food. It is of a single, uniform nature.
Because the power of continued maintenance is supreme, this treatise explains that the four nutriments (*āhāra*) and the three aggregates (*skandha*) are mutually inclusive.

Regarding the inclusion within the four nutriments and the three aggregates: edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) consists solely of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*manasikāra*) are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and the eight [types of] kings are subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Regarding the inclusion within the four nutriments and the five sense bases (*āyatana*): edible food consists of odor, taste, and tangibility; contact and volition consist solely of the mental object base (*dharmāyatana*). The eight...

Regarding the King’s return to the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and its inclusion within the four nutriments (*āhāra*) and eleven elements (*dhātu*): The edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) consists of odor, flavor, and tangibility;

the nutriment of contact (*sparśa*) and the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā*) consist solely of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). The eight kings return to the seven minds, which are the six consciousness-elements (*ṣadvijñānadhātu*) and the mind-faculty element (*manas-indriyadhātu*).

The first six mental kings correspond to the six consciousness-elements, while the seventh and eighth consciousnesses both return to the mind-faculty element. Although these four types [of nutriment] above...

Each is distinct; yet all are capable of sustaining the bodies of sentient beings so that they do not perish or disintegrate, and are therefore collectively termed "nutritive in nature" (*āhāra-svabhāva*).
Below, [the text] refutes the [notion that] the first three nutriments are not constant and not universal, and thus are not the support for sentient beings.

Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is functional only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); since this edible food is not utilized in the higher realms, it cannot be universal or constant. As for contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*), the two...
Although food pervades the three realms, it is subject to interruption; therefore, it cannot be constant.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the eye and so forth," it refutes that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) can constantly sustain [existence] or serve as the support for sentient beings, because they are interrupted during states of mindlessness (*acittaka*).

Even when in states with mind, they follow their respective supporting faculties (*indriya*) and objective conditions (*ālambana*), and thus vary according to the three natures, the three realms, and the nine stages.
At all times there is change and transformation; it is neither pervasive nor constant, nor is it the support for sentient beings.
You followers of the Lesser Vehicle maintain that there is no eighth consciousness. Upon what, then, do the various sūtras rely when they state that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment?
If you claim that in the state of mindlessness there is no present consciousness, and that [beings] subsist by taking past and future consciousness as nutriment—
Regarding the proponent [of the opposing view], the refutation is formulated as follows:

Consciousnesses of the past and future do not serve as nutriment during the state of non-consciousness, because they are neither present nor permanent and lack both substance and function, like flowers in the sky and so forth. Furthermore, the formal argument (pramāṇa) states:

Consciousnesses of the past and future do not serve as nutriment during the state of non-consciousness; even if they possessed substance and function, they would not be subsumed under the present, because they do not possess the nature of nutriment.

It is like space and so forth. If it is argued that in the state of mindlessness, the meditative absorption-mind (*samāpatti-citta*) and other factors serve as nutriment for sentient beings and cause them to abide, this is refuted by the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):

The meditative absorption-mind and other such factors do not serve as nutriment for sentient beings in the state of mindlessness while they are abiding in that mindless state, because at that time they have already ceased. That which is past is not nutriment, as this is already fully established, just as [space is].

Because they have already ceased and no longer exist, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "The various minds and mental factors at the time of entering meditative absorption cannot be called 'nutriments,' because they have already ceased and do not exist.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth are included within the category of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), such that they serve as the sustenance for beings in the state of non-conception;
the four nutriments, such as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) and the rest, do not include the attainment of non-conception.

Because they are equal [in nature], and because they lack substantiality (*asvabhāva*). When analyzed in this way, it is certain that there are no six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) that can serve as nutriment for those sentient beings.
Your insistence that they exist is utterly irrational.

If you claim that in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and other states, there is a sixth consciousness that serves as nutriment for sentient beings, this will be refuted extensively below. Furthermore, regarding their statement that one is born into the two higher realms...
When one is in a state of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-citta*) within the realms, what serves as nutriment?

If it is claimed that untainted consciousness and so forth serve as nutriment, then since untainted consciousness and so forth destroy the tainted (*sāsrava*), they cannot function as nutriment for that body and life.

If it is argued that there are tainted seeds within untainted consciousness, and that these tainted seeds serve as its nutriment, [the response is that] untainted consciousness and so forth are incapable [of supporting them].
[The opponent claims that] uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds maintain contaminated (*sāsrava*) seeds; yet since even such seeds do not exist, how could they serve as food for them?
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Uncontaminated consciousness and so forth cannot maintain contaminated seeds, because they destroy existence (*bhava*), just like *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that sentient beings of the higher realms maintain their life-force with the body, or maintain their body with the life-force, or that body and life-force mutually sustain one another.
They would thus become food for one another; for among the four types of nutriment, bodily sustenance and life-sustenance are not included.

If it were claimed that body and life sustain each other as mutual food, then in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there is no material body to sustain life, life itself would have nothing to sustain it and would consequently undergo cessation.
How then could it function as nutriment? Furthermore, it cannot be argued that they are food for one another by virtue of belonging to the same group. [The assembly...]
Since the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) and so forth lack substantial reality, how can they function as nutriment?

From this, it is definitively known that there exists something distinct from the evolving consciousnesses—a maturation (*vipāka*)—which sustains the body and life-force, preventing them from being severed or destroyed.

Therefore, it is said that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment. Question: If all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment, the Tathāgata is also one [who subsists thus]. Is he not also a sentient being?
"Are sentient beings also sustained by nutriment? Answer: "Sentient beings are established solely based upon the aggregates of grasping (*upādāna-skandha*).
For the Buddhas, the aggregates of grasping are empty; they do not fall into the outflows (*āsrava*) and are not included within the category of sentient beings.

Even if the Buddhas were to appear as classes of sentient beings, they would still be sustained by nutriment. One should know that these are all manifestations of great compassion; they are not actual sentient beings and are not sustained by nutriment."
This differs from what follows below, which serves as a concluding summary.
Furthermore, the sūtra states that one who abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) can be known to have entered this state through consciousness.

Whereas the preceding section revealed the eighth [consciousness] by way of the process of phenomenal evolution (*pravṛtti*), this section reveals it by way of the process of cessation and return (*nivṛtti*). First, the sūtra is cited as proof.

In one who dwells in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the three types of formations (*saṃskāra*) are all extinguished, yet vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) do not cease.
This clearly demonstrates the existence of an eighth [consciousness] that maintains them. Next, the eighth is established and named "the consciousness that does not depart from the body.

If this consciousness did not exist, then for one dwelling in the attainment of cessation, since mental formations have already ceased, the visual and other sensory consciousnesses would likewise not be able to exist. If one does not admit the existence of this one...

Regarding the subtle, pervasive, and constant grasping that sustains life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as being present: on what basis is it said that consciousness does not depart from the body? The Hīnayāna school asserts:
"This consciousness that does not depart from the body is that which arises again at a later time after the state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);

it is not the eighth consciousness. They then formulate a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "The consciousness abiding in the state of cessation is the subject (*dharmin*). 'It is named that which does not depart from the body' is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*)..."
[The opponent] says: Because it arises again at a later time, it is like a tertian malaria. The Mahāyāna proponent says:

If that were so, the Sūtra should not have stated that mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) cease; for according to your claim that consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises again at a later time after having ceased, mental formations would not have ceased.
At a later time, it should also arise again, because consciousness and mental factors such as perception arise and cease together.

If one claims that consciousness arises again at a later time after having ceased, then vitality (*āyu*), warmth (*uṣman*), and the sense faculties (*indriya*) should likewise arise again at a later time like consciousness;

this would constitute a great error. To refute this by means of formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one states: Vitality, warmth, and the sense faculties are the subject (*dharmin*); they are designated as not being separate [from the body].
The body is the subject (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it arises again at a later time. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should likewise be like consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Have you ever seen anyone whose warmth, life-force, and sense-faculties have already ceased and yet arise once more? Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that the consciousness abiding in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is called "not separated from the body.
There must certainly be an eighth [consciousness] named the "consciousness not separated from the body. Next, [the argument] refutes [this claim] by means of insentient things. Furthermore—
In this state, since the first six [consciousnesses] have already ceased, if there were no eighth [consciousness] to maintain this body, it would become an insentient object.
How could such a being be called a noble one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? To refute this, the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established:

"One who abides in the absorption of cessation, if entirely devoid of consciousness, would not belong to the category of sentient beings and would be like a piece of rubble. Next, [the argument proceeds] by way of the absence of grasping (*upādāna*).

This refutes [your position]. If you claim that the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) does not exist in the state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), we shall refute this by means of a formal inference (*pramāṇa*).

[Thesis]: In the state of cessation, the sense faculties, life-force, and warmth must all perish. [Reason]: Because they lack a sustaining agent (*dhāraka*). [Example]: Just like a corpse. If that were so, [what would follow?]
In that case, the consciousness of a later time—like a tertian malaria—is certain not to arise again.
Since it does not arise again, what thing could be attached to that [body] such that consciousness would be said not to be separated from the body?

This is because once that *vipāka-vijñāna* has abandoned this [body] and transferred to another, there is no further rebirth. Next, [the argument] is refuted by means of the lack of a sustaining support. Furthermore, if...
In this state, there is no consciousness that maintains the seeds (*bīja*); consequently, subsequent consciousness would not arise, as it would lack its seeds.

There must necessarily be an eighth consciousness that maintains the seeds, after which [subsequent states] can arise, like a tertian fever. Furthermore, one may infer that dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) do not possess a real substance and cannot maintain seeds.
Form (*rūpa*) and so forth, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and mental concomitants (*caitta*)—all apart from consciousness—are non-existent.

It cannot maintain the seeds; therefore, we know that there must certainly exist a retributive consciousness (vipāka-vijñāna) called the "seed-maintaining consciousness. To state this in a general formal inference (*prayoga*):

Within the mindless states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there must truly exist a consciousness, because it possesses the faculties, vitality, and warmth, and is comprised within the category of sentient beings, just like a state with a mind.
By this reasoning, one knows for certain that within the state of the attainment of cessation, there exists a distinct [consciousness] that is not separate [from the body].

The body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) is the eighth. A follower of the Hīnayāna objects: "In the state of meditative absorption in cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), only the first five consciousnesses are extinguished;
one does not depart from the body-consciousness, which is the sixth. Why then must it be the eighth? [The author] refutes this, saying:

"This too is irrational, because this absorption is also called 'mindless' (*acittaka*). Once one has entered this absorption, the ever-active mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*) and the non-ever-active mental factors..."

Because all [consciousnesses] are completely extinguished therein. If one were to claim that the absence of the first five consciousnesses constitutes "mindlessness," then the four dhyānas and eight meditative absorptions (samāpatti) would all have to be called "mindless concentrations" (*acittaka-samādhi*), since all these concentrations are likewise devoid of the body of the five consciousnesses.

Furthermore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is included among the six evolving consciousnesses; therefore, in this state of cessation where the five consciousnesses are absent, the mental consciousness must also be absent. Thus, [the state of cessation] is established [as being without mind].

The *Pramāṇa* states: "In the state of cessation, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not exist, because it is included among the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), just like the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*).

Furthermore, in this state, there is a consciousness that is not separated from the body; it is profoundly deep and subtle, and its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and object of perception (*ālambana*) are both unintelligible.
Therefore, one knows that the remaining consciousness in the state of cessation is certainly not the sixth. He establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute [the opponent's position]:

The consciousness within this state is not the sixth consciousness, because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and object of perception (*ālambana*) cannot be known, just as with vitality (*āyuṣka*), warmth (*uṣman*), and so forth.
If there were any knowable consciousness present in a mindless state, it would have to be included among the four dhyānas or the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
it is not subsumed under this [mindless] state. Why? Because those who enter these meditative attainments do so fundamentally for the purpose of ceasing all discernible consciousness.
It is not for the purpose of desiring to fully understand this consciousness that one enters meditative absorption. To refute this, the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established:
"This state of cessation is not included within this [conscious] state, because it possesses cognitive aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) that can be known, just like other states."
Furthermore, if the sixth consciousness were present in this state, [it would follow that] it is not of the nature of mind, just as dharmas such as visible form are not.
Below this, the presence or absence of the sixth consciousness is demonstrated by means of the presence or absence of mental factors (*caitasika*).

Since the mind and its mental factors must necessarily be associated (*samprayukta*), if there were mental factors in this state, the Sūtra should not have stated that for one abiding in this meditative absorption, "mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) have ceased."

All [mental factors] are extinguished. Since all mental concomitants (*caitta*) are subsumed under formations (*saṃskāra*), it would also be incorrect to call this the "attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception" (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-samāpatti*), because feeling and perception are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
To defend this position, one might say that within this state of meditative equipoise there are three types of preparatory application (*prayoga*):

first, physical application, which refers to inhalation and exhalation; upon entering the fourth dhyāna, these bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) are severed. Second, vocal application, which refers to...

When one enters the second dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra cease; thus, verbal formations are cut off. When one enters the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), three mental formations cease—namely, feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā);
thus, mental formations are cut off. The preparatory application for this attainment involves only the cultivation of weariness toward feeling and perception;

therefore, within this attainment, only feeling and perception are extinguished. This is because these two mental factors, feeling and perception, provide strong support to the mind among all mental concomitants.

It is only "mental formations" (*citta-saṃskāra*) that are so named; now, when feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) are said to cease, it is called the cessation of mental formations. Since other mental factors (*caitta*) still remain, what contradiction is there?
This is truly like someone caught red-handed with stolen goods crying out in distress. The refutation states:

If you claim that one merely detests feeling and perception, and thus only these two categories cease while the first six [consciousnesses] do not, yet this is called "cessation," then in the state of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), one merely detests perception; [how could this be distinguished from your case?]

Furthermore, one should maintain that only perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are extinguished, while the first six [consciousnesses] are not extinguished; this is what is called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

Yet, why do you not admit that the six consciousnesses exist within this attainment of non-perception? Moreover, since you already recognize that the two factors of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) provide strong support for the mind, when these feeling and perception are extinguished, the mind should likewise be extinguished.
Why then do you dogmatically insist that while perception and feeling are extinguished, consciousness (*vijñāna*) remains?
"It depends. This is precisely "using one's hand to perform a fist-punch" (a metaphor for using a means to achieve an end). He turns the argument to save his position, saying:

"When applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)—the formations of speech (*vāk-saṃskāra*)—cease, speech itself does not cease. If the bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) cease while the body still remains, then by this analogy, although feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) may cease, the mind (*citta*) still remains.
Why, then, must the mind and its mental formations necessarily cease simultaneously? Thus he refutes [the opponent].

He said: "If it is as you say—that when the bodily formations of inhalation and exhalation cease while the body still remains—then it should follow that when the verbal formations of vitarka and vicāra cease, speech likewise remains.
Yet you do not accept this; why is that? However, the three types of formations—bodily, verbal, and mental—are both pervasive and non-pervasive;
one must not discuss them with rigid dogmatism. If they are pervasive formations, then when they cease, the phenomenon [of their basis] is necessarily fixed."
When the universal factors cease, but the non-universal factors do not, then although the formations have ceased, the phenomena still persist. What are the non-universal factors?
They are the inhalation and exhalation of breath. Because this breath does not pervade all bodily phenomena, there are cases where the breath has ceased while the body remains.
Vitarka and vicāra are universal factors with respect to speech; therefore, when vitarka and vicāra cease, speech necessarily ceases as well.
If one applies the analogy of vitarka and vicāra to vedanā and saṃjñā, then since vedanā and saṃjñā have ceased, the mind (citta) should also cease;
for vedanā and saṃjñā are universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-sarvatraga-dharma). To refute this by means of formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one says:

Vedanā and saṃjñā are also included among the universal factors of the mind, because they are mahābhūmika-dharmas, just like cetanā and so forth. How could it be that vedanā and saṃjñā have ceased while the mind still remains? Furthermore, with...

The mental factors (*caitta*) are refuted by analogy. Since you admit that volition (*cetanā*) and the others are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), when feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) cease, volition and the others must also cease.
If volition and the others have ceased, then states such as wholesome (*kuśala*) or defiled (*kliṣṭa*) would all be absent at this stage.

How then can you say that although feeling and perception have ceased, the other mental factors still remain? You do not realize that if they are non-existent, they are entirely non-existent. It must be so for you...

If one maintains that although feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth have ceased, the mental factors (*caitta*) still remain unceased, then it would follow that feeling, perception, and the rest should not be subject to cessation.
This is because feeling, perception, and volition are all *mahābhūmika-dharmas* (universal mental factors).

Since there must be contact (*sparśa*) whenever there is volition and the like—because contact is the root of all mental factors—and since there must be feeling whenever there is contact, [it follows that these factors cannot cease]. Because of contact...
Because it is able to take feeling as its object, wherever there is feeling, there must necessarily be perception; for these two dharmas, feeling and perception, are not mutually exclusive.
What is meant by "existence" is existence in its entirety. To offer a further defense:

regarding the link of craving conditioned by feeling within the twelvefold chain of dependent origination, this feeling only conditions craving after one perceives an object that is desirable or pleasant; whereas if one perceives an object that is loathsome or repulsive...
This state of receiving the prediction does not take craving as its object. How could all feelings (*vedanā*) be capable of taking craving as their object?
By this analogy, it is the same for the arising of feeling from contact (*sparśa*). When contact encounters an agreeable object, a pleasant feeling arises;

when contact encounters a disagreeable object, how could a feeling also arise [in that way]? Therefore, your assertion that contact is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) is logically untenable.

[The opponent’s position] is established. [The author] refutes it below, saying: "That explanation is not correct; they cannot be cited as analogous examples, because the two dharmas of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) possess distinct differences.

This refers to the Buddha’s own specific distinction: "Only among the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), when ignorance (*avidyā*) and contact serve as conditions, do various feelings arise;

with feeling as condition, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is produced. This [passage] specifically distinguishes that craving arises with feeling as its condition, and does not imply that there is craving without such a condition.
There is no instance where contact gives rise to feeling such that there is feeling for one and not feeling for another. Therefore, wherever there is contact, there must be feeling;
wherever there is feeling, there must be perception. This principle is certain, as these are the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

Thus, it is known that feeling and perception do not cease, and volition and the others likewise do not cease. To refute this by means of formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one states: "In this state of cessation..."
Feeling and perception are also not extinguished, because volition and other mental factors are present, just as in other states of consciousness.

If you admit that there is consciousness in this state, it would contradict the statement that "mental formations have ceased" in this state; furthermore, the extinction of feeling and perception could not be established [if consciousness were present].

If there are no mental factors (caitta) in this state, then consciousness (vijñāna) must also be absent, because mental factors and the mind (citta) are inseparable. This is because they belong to the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).

When the Dharma perishes, the mental factors also perish; for if the universal factors were to perish while the dharma did not, then sensation and the others could not be termed "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*).
If the mental concomitants were to perish while the mind did not, then this consciousness would likewise not be an associated phenomenon (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
If one were to admit that the mind and its mental concomitants are not associated phenomena, then this consciousness would [not be established].

If it were said that [this consciousness] shares the same basis (āśraya), the same object (ālambana), the same time, and the same function as the mental factors (caitta), then it would be like form (rūpa) and so forth.
One may formulate the syllogism as follows: "This consciousness should lack a basis, an object, and so on, because it is not a mind (citta), just like dharmas such as form."

Furthermore, a sūtra states that "mind and mental objects serve as conditions" (extending to the point where it says) "the state of non-perception and so forth should be understood by analogy with this.

The preceding section refuted the primary mind (*citta*) by means of mental factors (*caitta*); the following section refutes mental factors by means of the primary mind. First, a sūtra is cited to prove that wherever there is mind, there must necessarily be mental factors:

because wherever there is mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there must necessarily be contact (*sparśa*); and wherever there is contact, there must necessarily be feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth.

Therefore, it is said that when one has not yet entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness possesses sufficient power to form contact (*sparśa*) and give rise to contact;

because of this contact, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth can arise. Consequently, by the power of the mental factors (*caitta*) that cultivate aversion prior to concentration, these three factors lack efficacy while one is in the state of concentration;
they cannot produce contact. Since contact does not arise, there is likewise no feeling and the other mental factors.
It is not meant that consciousness (*vijñāna*) also ceases [in this state] for it to be called the "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*). [The opponent] refutes this, saying:

"If that were so, this absorption should be named 'the cessation of mental factors' (*citta-saṃskāra-nirodha*). Why then is it said only that feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) cease? [The proponent] offers a further defense:

"Because at the time of entering the absorption, one feels only aversion toward feeling and perception; when these two cease, all mental factors cease. It is based on this prior aversion toward feeling and perception that [the name] is established."
Regarding the designation of the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute [the opponent's view] as follows:

If that were so, the mind abiding in the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) should also cease simultaneously [with its mental factors], because it is associated with those [factors] that are to be suppressed, just like other mental states (*citta-caitta*). If feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) were to cease while the mind did not cease, how could it be called a "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*)?

Generally, this absorption of cessation possesses these two names: "cessation of the mind" because there is no sovereign [mental factor], and "cessation of feeling" because there is no objective basis [for sensation].
Therefore, by means of these two concentrations, the King’s position is refuted together. Below, the refutation is made in terms of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Furthermore, if there were a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within this concentration, under which nature would it be subsumed? It could not be of a defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature; for among all wholesome concentrations, these two natures do not exist.
If these two were present, there would necessarily be mental factors (*caitta*), yet the primary intention [of this concentration] is aversion [to such factors].
One may be defiled while practicing virtue, but one should not give rise to defilement out of a distaste for virtue.

One’s original intention is to weary of distraction and seek tranquility, but one should not give rise to distraction while seeking tranquility. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "This meditative concentration is inseparable from bodily consciousness;

it certainly cannot be mental consciousness, because [mental consciousness] cannot be established as being either virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate. If it is not non-virtuous, it must certainly be...

Because it is virtuous. Even within the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the existence of any unvirtuous state is not permitted; how much less could there be an unvirtuous state in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?
Nor is it indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one were to allow that this [consciousness] therein is of an indeterminate nature, it would result in the establishment of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Furthermore, this mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) is definitively virtuous and not unvirtuous; as for this virtue, it is...

Why? If it were associated with the wholesome, it would have to be associated with shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), and the three roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in every instance of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in order to constitute a wholesome nature. If it were not so associated, its wholesome nature would not be established.

Furthermore, it is also incorrect to claim that this consciousness does not associate with the three roots of goodness, yet associates with what is wholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*) or ultimate goodness (*paramārtha-kuśala*); for such a view contradicts [the established principles].

According to our own school, it is intrinsically wholesome (*svabhāva-kuśala*) because only shame (*hrī*), embarrassment (*apatrāpya*), and the three roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are included in this category;
their essential nature is wholesome, just like potent medicine, as they do not depend on association (*samprayoga*) or origination (*samutthāna*).
As for ultimate wholesomeness (*paramārtha-kuśala*), only suchness (*tathatā*) and nirvāṇa qualify, because they are definitive. That is to say, true liberation is [nirvāṇa]. Because of [nirvāṇa]...
It is the most ultimate peace within the cycle of existence, for all sufferings are forever stilled, just as one who is free from illness.

If it is claimed that this mind is not virtuous by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*) or ultimate reality (*paramārtha-kuśala*), but is virtuous through its motivation (*samutthāna-kuśala*), being induced by the roots of virtue of application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*) rather than by the power of the roots of virtue such as non-attachment (*alobha*), this is also not the case. As for what is meant by "virtuous through motivation," it refers to...

When noble beings within the fruit-stage initiate supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and other such matters through their preparatory application (*prayoga*), it is called "virtue by way of origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*). Regarding "virtue of application" (*prayoga-kuśala*):

it refers to relying upon and associating with virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*), hearing the true Dharma (*saddharma*), attending to it correctly (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), cultivating pure wholesome dharmas, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharma-pratipatti*); this is called virtue of application. The author of the treatise says: "If that is so..."

This also contradicts your own tenet. According to your own tenet, the mind in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is free from the coarse movement of perception (*saṃjñā*) and other mental factors due to aversion toward them;

it is not induced by the application of formative attention (*manasikāra*) or by roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). If it were induced by the roots of goodness through such application, then, like other wholesome minds, it would not be designated as "arising simultaneously" (*samutthāna*).
To refute this, one may formulate a syllogism: "The mind abiding in the attainment of cessation is a wholesome state arising simultaneously [with its cause], because..."
Because it is induced by the cultivation of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and because it would contradict one's own tenet (*svasiddhānta*). It is like other wholesome minds (*kuśalacitta*).
Regarding the arising of minds of the three natures immediately after a wholesome mind, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Just as nine minds arise immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm—namely, the four minds of its own realm, and two minds of the form realm: a wholesome mind and a defiled mind at the time of entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and at the time of rebirth (*pratisandhi*)."

In the formless realm, there is one [type]. At the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), a defiled mind of that realm arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, but a wholesome mind of that [formless] realm does not arise, because it is extremely remote.

Furthermore, regarding the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), since a wholesome mind can give rise to minds of the three natures, how could a wholesome mind—being prompted by a preceding [moment]—be something induced by the roots of merit of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*)? Therefore, the mind is...
"Excellent. It must indeed be by the power of association with wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

'Alternatively, some maintain that because it is induced by the wholesome roots of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*), the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) is called wholesome, and not by the power of association with wholesome roots.
This contradicts the definition established in that treatise according to which the mind becomes wholesome through the power of association. If that were so, then this concentration—"

The mind must necessarily be associated with the three wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*). Since it is associated with the wholesome roots, it must also necessarily be associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), for there is no other cause [for this].
Therefore, it is said that it is not without mental factors (*caitta*). If there were no mental factors, the mind itself would also not exist.

Investigating in this manner, one concludes that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness, are definitely separated from the body in the state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Its...

Regarding "not being separated": this definitely refers to the eighth [consciousness]. This is because when entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one is precisely ceasing the previously active, distracted evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) such as the eye-consciousness;
it is not for the purpose of ceasing the extremely quiescent appropriating consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*). Question:

If, at the time of entering the meditative attainment of cessation, only the distracted evolving consciousnesses are ceased while the extremely quiescent appropriating consciousness is not ceased, then since there is still a mind present in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), why is it called [the state of] cessation?

"Mindless. Answer: The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Formation of Karma) states: "There are two kinds of mind: first, the *saṃgrahaka-citta* (collecting-arising mind), because it is the locus where immeasurable seeds arise;

second, the *vicitra-citta* (variegated mind), because it evolves through the distinctions of objective conditions (*ālambana*) and modes of activity (*ākāra*). In states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the second kind of mind is absent;
therefore, it is called a 'mindless state. It is like a four-legged horse that is so named because one leg is missing. It is also called...
There is no basis for it. Since this is the case for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one should know that the same applies to the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*).
Furthermore, because the Sūtra states that the mind is defiled [and so forth], until: "since this is not established, the latter is also not established."

This summarizes the meaning of the preceding nine chapters. Since the preceding nine do not go beyond [the processes of] saṃsāra and its cessation (nivṛtti), [this chapter] first cites scriptures as proof.
Next, it establishes the eighth consciousness as the basis of defilement and purity. First, it provides a general explanation:

because the mind is the cause of all dharmas of defilement and purity, and because it is that upon which all dharmas of defilement and purity depend, the mind is able to receive those states of defilement and purity.
The active manifestations of all phenomena (*dharmas*) perfuse [the mind], and because it can also maintain the seeds of those defiled and pure phenomena, [it is established].

Next, the defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are specifically explained as being of three kinds: namely, afflictions (*kleśa*), the performance of karma (*karma-kriyā*), and the experiencing of results (*phala-upabhoga*).

Since these three types of phenomena are distinct from one another, they are divided into three. If there were no eighth consciousness to maintain the seeds of the afflictions, then within the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*), [afflictions would not persist].
Once the evolving consciousnesses have ceased and their subsequent retribution is exhausted, one is reborn in a lower realm.

There, the evolving consciousnesses associated with the afflictions of that lower realm arise again as active manifestations (*samudācāra*). These manifest consciousnesses would then lack seeds and arise without cause, because prior to this state, there was no consciousness capable of maintaining the seeds.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If one passes away from the higher realms, such as the Realm of Non-conception..."
When one is born in this world, the initial consciousness that is defiled by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) would, at the moment of its arising, be without a seed.
This is because both the basis (*āśraya*) and its perfuming (*vāsanā*) have already passed away and lack any present existence.
If these afflictions were to arise without a cause, then the afflictions of those in the three vehicles who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would have been severed long ago.
If [the storehouse consciousness] were non-existent, then all things would likewise arise without cause. Since this is not the case, how could that be so?

If this consciousness did not exist to sustain the seeds of karmic fruits, then the uninterrupted cycle of wandering through the three realms and nine stages—such as the various karmic retributions of humans, devas, ghosts, and animals, characterized by hair, horns, needle-like throats, and bloated bellies—would also have to be without cause.

Because other consciousnesses cannot maintain seeds and cannot serve as causes, if defiled karmic fruits could arise without a cause, then for those who have entered the remainderless nirvāṇa, karmic fruits and afflictions would necessarily arise again. Is there any such principle?

Next, [the text] refutes the absence of the twelve links of dependent origination: if this consciousness did not exist to maintain the seeds, then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) would lack their condition.
Consciousness would not be able to be established. "The practitioner" refers to one who correctly performs wholesome or unwholesome karma that leads to future lives;

this perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and forms the seeds of direct maturation (*vipāka*) for the future, which persist in a continuous succession within the fundamental consciousness.

Upon entering the mother’s womb, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is formed. Now, if it is said that consciousness (vijñāna) is the sixth [consciousness] and not the eighth, then, in the absence of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), there would be no dharma capable of sustaining the seeds of karma and the seeds of consciousness;
consequently, the conditionality of formations (saṃskāra-pratyaya-vijñāna) could never be established.
Since this is not established, the defiled consciousness that links rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) also cannot be established.

Because the sixth consciousness cannot be perfumed and does not maintain the seeds of karma, and since these karmic seeds are absent, what would give rise to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)? Question: Why is it that the defiled consciousness linking rebirth does not have volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) as its condition?

Answer: Because the defiled consciousness linking rebirth is not produced by the impelling force of volitional formations. Even if it were produced by the impelling force of volitional formations, [it would still not be so].
What fault is there? Answer: Because there would be no sense of connection due to the vast temporal distance. The twelve links of dependent origination are divided into the three periods of time:
two causes in the past, five fruits in the present, three causes in the present, and two fruits in the future.
