Regarding those oppressive feelings associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, they are always termed "suffering.

Regarding those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one master states that they are associated exclusively with the feeling of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and lack the feeling of physical suffering (*duḥkha*), because they oppress the mind; thus, there is mental distress.

There is no suffering [in the sixth consciousness]. Below, he cites scriptural evidence: various holy teachings state that the mental distress experienced on the level of the mind-base (*manobhūmi*) is precisely what is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "In the hell realms, immediately following the eighth maturation (*vipāka*), there arises a sixth maturation-born [consciousness] characterized by a continuous stream of suffering and grief.
Therefore, we know that suffering belongs to the first five [sensory consciousnesses], while grief belongs to the sixth. It further states that in the hells, discursive thought (*vitarka*)...
Vicāra (sustained thought) is associated with a portion of the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*). The same applies to the realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*).

Regarding hell-beings (*naraka*), it is said that their vitarka and vicāra are associated with a portion of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and a portion of the faculty of sorrow, because they are triggered by contact with unpleasant objects and are associated with sorrow and suffering. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

"The vitarka and vicāra of hell-beings are exclusively of a dejected nature; they are induced by contact with undesirable objects and are associated with sorrow and suffering, just as in the case of hell-beings."
Investigation and analysis (vitarka-vicāra) experience painful feeling; the same applies to all investigation and analysis in the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.

Thus, we know that even extremely heavy mental distress is not termed "pain" (duḥkha), but is still termed "sorrow" (daurmanasya); how much more so for other, lighter forms of it, which cannot be anything but sorrow?
There is an interpretation that [this] applies to both humans and devas (until: ...); fearing that the text would become overly prolix, it is not described in detail here.
This second master maintains that the *bhūmi* (stage) contains the two feelings of suffering (*duḥkha*) and grief (*daurmanasya*), referring to those born in the two realms of humans and devas.

It is always termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) and not termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*), because it is not exceedingly heavy. If one is born in the two realms of animals and hungry ghosts, it is termed both sorrow and suffering.
For those among animals who experience a mixture [of sensations], it is light; therefore, it is termed sorrow. For hungry ghosts who experience it purely, it is exceedingly heavy;
therefore, it is termed suffering. If one is in hell, it is termed only suffering, because it is experienced purely and is exceedingly heavy.
Because of discrimination (*vikalpa*), pleasure reaches its limit in the third dhyāna, and suffering reaches its limit in the hells; therefore, in all [other realms], there is no discrimination.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is cited as evidence that there is feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) in the sixth [consciousness].

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that a certain class of innate self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the sixth [consciousness] are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It further explains of its own accord, according to the treatise: [The text continues: ...because it is based on the treatise...
Regarding what was stated: this co-nascent painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) associated with the mental level (*manobhūmi*) is comprised within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is certainly not the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), because the treatise states that the faculty of grief is by nature afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and is not indeterminate.

Furthermore, it is said that regarding the faculties in the hells, the remaining three definitely do not manifest or are not possessed; it further explains itself: "The remaining three are definitely the three faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and grief (*daurmanasya*). This is because...
When one undergoes the retribution of suffering in those hells, there is only the indeterminate faculty of suffering (*avyākṛta-duḥkhendriya*);

there can never be the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the faculties of pleasure, joy, or sorrow. This is because that indeterminate faculty of suffering is invariably associated with the manifest faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Yet, how could it be that the manifest faculty of equanimity is not known? It is simply that in that treatise, the sixth [consciousness] is definitely not established as the faculty of equanimity.
An objection is raised: "Do you not know that the treatise merely speaks of 'receptivity' (*āśrayatva*)?

It is not necessarily the case that because receptivity does not constitute the sixth [consciousness], it definitively establishes the mental faculty (*manas*). The response is: "Those six [faculties] are receptive to consciousness only intermittently;
they certainly do not correspond with receptivity. Since receptivity does not correspond with the sixth [consciousness], it definitively establishes the mental faculty."
This is the root [of the argument]. That treatise should not claim to speak only of "receptivity" (āśraya) while failing to establish the mental faculty (manas-indriya).
Since it speaks of receptivity, it necessarily refers to the mental faculty as well, because both that receptivity and the mental faculty are of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).

If it is argued that the treatise only states that the mental faculty (*manas*) is established as being capable of receiving [feeling] and not as being definitively established [as such], why does that same treatise further state that the manifest seeds of hell-beings (*naraka*) are definitively established as possessing eight faculties?

The mention of "eight faculties" specifically refers to the eighth consciousness, because it is also associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Below, [the text] provisionally refutes that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is the sixth [consciousness].
It is not the eighth. If it is argued that because the five consciousnesses do not continue in succession, the sorrow faculty (*daurmanasyendriya*) certainly does not exist in the hell realm;

yet, because the eighth [consciousness] is of a single type, uninterrupted, and constantly continuous, it must certainly be the sorrow faculty—then at the stage of extreme fainting during death and birth, when the six consciousnesses have already ceased to function, from where would the sorrow of the eighth [consciousness] arise? Thus, one knows for certain that it is the sorrow faculty.
It does not belong to the eighth [consciousness]. The same applies to the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

If it is argued that the eighth consciousness is the sovereign lord of the total retribution (*vipāka*), and therefore the faculty of suffering in hell must necessarily belong to the eighth, then when one is experiencing suffering within hell, what exactly is designated as the "eighth"?
Even if one maintains that the inhabitants of hell manifest in male or female forms, whichever form is taken would have to be considered the eighth.
Eighth, this reasoning is also incorrect. The bodies of those in the hells are sometimes large and sometimes small, as they lack a fixed form;
however, the fruit produced by the eighth [level of] karmic maturation possesses a fixed form. Furthermore, the body summoned and manifested by that evil karma—

Because formless beings have no physical shape. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In the case of those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture, at the initial stage of receiving birth, they obtain only two ripening faculties (*vipākendriya*), namely the body and life.
In the initial stage of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*), they obtain six, seven, or eight.
Specifically, those without form initially obtain six faculties, as was the case at the beginning of the eon. What are these six? They are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life. If...
Those with one set of sexual organs initially obtain seven faculties, such as the various devas and others. If they possess both sets of sexual organs, they initially obtain eight faculties.

How could there be those with two sets of sexual organs who undergo transformational birth? This is because it is possible for those in the miserable realms to be born by transformation with two sets of sexual organs.
Question: Since they lack physical form, what experiences suffering? Answer: By the power of their past evil karma, [suffering] arises naturally within them.
At the gates of the five sense organs, they constantly undergo suffering, as described in the section on the "Sixfold Reciprocal Retributions" and elsewhere.

If one were to claim that the bodies in hell must necessarily possess eyes and other faculties, and must therefore have fixed male or female forms rather than being merely transformed manifestations—even if such fixed forms did exist, what use would they serve?
For within the Great Avīci Hell, there can be no longing for sexual desire.
Regarding such matters, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "All sentient beings in the various hells (*naraka*) are entirely devoid of sexual activity.

Because they have for a long time continuously experienced various kinds of extremely intense suffering, by virtue of this cause and condition, those sentient beings—whether male, do not give rise to desire for women;
and whether female, do not give rise to desire for men. Why is this?
How much more so when they are combined through mutual union? Since the physical bodies of ghosts, animals, humans, and others involve a mixture of suffering and pleasure, sexual desire exists.

By this reasoning, it is known that the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is necessarily established as the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], because both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are associated with the feeling of equanimity.

In the case of the hells, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is necessarily established as the sixth [consciousness], because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are both associated with the feeling of equanimity. This is the analogy for the lower realms.
The mental level (*manobhūmi*) lacks the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*). Your claim that the mental level in the hells possesses the faculty of sorrow is likewise incorrect.

Just as the third dhyāna, a realm of extreme bliss, lacks the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one should know by analogy that the hells, being places of extreme suffering, certainly lack the faculty of sorrow.
Therefore, the remaining three [faculties] mentioned must be understood as sorrow, joy, and pleasure. Question: Since within the hells...
There is only the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); there is no feeling of pleasure (*sukhavedanā*).

Why does the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* state that in the Avīci hell there is no interval of pleasure between sufferings, and thus it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*), whereas in other hells pleasure arises intermittently? Although there is no [feeling of pleasure] resulting from karmic maturation (*vipākaja*), there is that which is of similar outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
Answer: As stated in the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*, when people feed their six domestic animals, they provide them with food and drink that are both warm and cold.
In the hot hells there are cool intervals, and in the cold hells there are warm intervals. These warmth and coolness resemble their preceding causes;
they are conventionally designated as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*). One should understand that this is a heuristic device (*anuvartana-yukti*) for the sake of explanation.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states that within the Saṃjīva hell, at times a cool breeze blows and the flesh and blood are restored; at other times, [they emerge...]
A voice cries out, "Reviving! and those sentient beings suddenly come back to life.

Because they experience painful sensations during the time when such flesh and blood regenerate, and because they experience a brief interval of joy and pleasure, this realm is not called "Uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).

Furthermore, this is a method of explanation according to the underlying principle (*anuvartana-yukti*), or it is a general statement that in this place of mixed sensations there is no ripened pleasure (*vipāka-sukha*); thus, it is metaphorically said to possess "pleasure of outflow" (*niṣyanda-sukha*).
Because the locus of mixed sensation (*miśra-vedanā*) is also entirely suffering. As for "mixed sensation," it refers to the mixture of cold and heat sensations. Question:

Since there is no faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) on the mental level (*manobhūmi*), why does the holy teaching state that the dejected sensation on the mental level is called the faculty of sorrow?

Answer: This is stated based on a partial perspective; for the most part, it is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). This can be understood through the general discussion in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Part II.
[The Buddha] replied: "It is known. Furthermore, that which is described in the *Yogācārabhūmi* as the continuity of suffering born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is, in fact, suffering.

Because this suffering belongs to the same category as other forms of grief (*daurmanasya*), it is metaphorically designated as 'grief' based on its categorial similarity; in reality, however, it is suffering.

Alternatively, because that faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) can impair both body and mind, although it is subsumed under the faculty of suffering, it is also termed 'grief. It is called 'suffering' specifically because it impairs the body."
It is called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) because it harms the mind. For example, the joy (*prīti*) of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) benefits both body and mind;

thus, although it is a faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*), it is also called "pleasure" (*sukha*). It is named "joy" because it benefits the mind, and "pleasure" because it benefits the body. However, this has not yet reached the third dhyāna.

There is certainly no true pleasure; thus, because there is no faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), it is said that the first and second dhyānas possess only eleven faculties and lack the faculty of pleasure.

Regarding these eleven faculties: this is stated in relation to the desire realm and the first two dhyānas. The first five consciousnesses exclude the faculty of pleasure and possess the four [faculties] beginning with suffering (*duḥkha*).
The sixth consciousness is likewise. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses each possess only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). As for the hells...

Since both body and mind are associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), there are eleven [faculties] [in that realm]. Just as one knows that the place of ultimate bliss lacks the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one should know that the place of ultimate suffering lacks the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

From this point downward, the conclusion is shown: the place of pure suffering is comprised solely of the faculties of mental suffering (*manoduḥkhendriya*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and does not include the faculties of grief, joy, or pleasure.
There is an interpretation that the six consciousnesses and the three feelings do not coexist (up to: because the Buddhas have already severed the causes of sorrow and suffering).

This explains whether the first five [consciousnesses] and the sixth [consciousness] coexist with the three natures or not; this is consistent with the previous explanation in the section on the three natures.
Regarding the six categories of mental factors briefly indicated previously (up to the point where it says): "The meaning of the others not being universal will be explained later.

This explains the first category, the five universals (*sarvatraga*). First, a question is posed; next, a verse is cited as the answer; and below that, the treatise provides the explanation. It states:
"These five mental factors have already been explained in detail within the first transformation (*pariṇāma*); they will not be analyzed further here. Question: How so?
One should know that these universal [mental factors] exist. Answer: Because scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*) serve as the authoritative criteria (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding this, first, the scriptural proof is cited: when the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness comes together, contact (*sparśa*) necessarily exists; only after contact arises do feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) occur.
Because they are thus invariably present, all four are termed "universal. Next, the proof for attention (*manasikāra*) is cited: if the faculty...
Although the object is present, consciousness can only arise when attention (*manaskāra*) is manifest; if there is no attention, consciousness cannot arise.

Therefore, at the moment consciousness arises, attention must necessarily be present. This is because one discerns (*vijñapti*) within the sphere of attention, and attention occurs within the sphere of discernment.
Thus, it is known that attention is also a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). Next, this is inferred through reasoning: namely, when consciousness arises...
At that time, there must be a triad of conditions. Wherever this triad exists, contact (*sparśa*) necessarily arises, because that triad of conditions exists only by virtue of contact.
If there were no contact, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) could not be brought into union to touch upon a single object;
therefore, we know that contact must exist. Even though the locus of contact exists, if there were no attention (*manasikāra*) to draw the mind toward its respective object, then the mind...
The King’s senses are in disarray and he does not know where they are headed; thus, contact (*sparśa*) and attention (*manasikāra*) arise mutually.
When there is correct attention, contact resides within that attention; when there is correct contact with an object, attention resides within that contact.

As the various consciousnesses take objects as their conditions, these two mental factors always serve as the primary function. It is by being led toward the object by the former two that the mind subsequently experiences this [object].

Regarding objects as good or evil: when an object is good, one feels compliance and thus gives rise to a mind of attachment; when an object is evil, one feels aversion and thus gives rise to a mind of hatred;
toward neutral objects, one neither hates nor loves, remaining simply equanimous. This feeling (*vedanā*) is subsumed under one of these [three] within the state of non-cognition (*acittaka*).
Therefore, it arises in the state of non-cognition; were this [feeling] not present, one would not perceive a state of consciousness (*sacittaka*) devoid of these [mental factors].

First: once *vedanā* (feeling) has already experienced the pleasant and the unpleasant, giving rise to attachment and aversion, it subsequently distinguishes boundaries and demarcates spheres upon those pleasant and unpleasant objects;
it categorizes right and wrong and evaluates worth and worthlessness. This *saṃjñā* (perception) is also subsumed under one of these [mental factors] within the state of mindlessness;
therefore, in the state of mindlessness, this "one of them" does not exist. One does not see a state of mind that lacks this "one of them."

Once one has established the boundaries within one's own objective domain, one then perceives the characteristics of correct causes, incorrect causes, and so forth within that delimited domain, and performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds.
This volition is also subsumed under "one of the [two] concomitants" (*anuvartin*) within the state of non-cognition;
when non-cognition arises, this "concomitant" is absent, for no state of cognition is seen that lacks a concomitant.
Therefore, these five are called the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). Whenever there is a mind, these five must necessarily be present.
The mind-king is like a sovereign, while these five universal factors are like supportive ministers.

If the enlightened sovereign embodies the Way and dwells in the correct position, then the supportive ministers will reverently obey his commands, not daring to arrogantly exercise their own power or confer favors. However, as for an incompetent ruler...
One is thus being toyed with by the great ministers upon the palms of one's hands. Therefore, when the mind-king is upright, mental attention (*manasikāra*) is upright;
when mental attention is upright, all that is contacted is upright; since all that is contacted is upright, that which is experienced therein is also upright.
Once that which experiences within is rectified, then all that is perceived and conceived will invariably return to correctness.
Therefore, when the sovereign mind (citta-rāja) is correct, all mental factors (caitta) obey its command and function accordingly;

if the sovereign mind is not correct, the mental factors will divide their authority and cause disorder. Thus, the practitioner first takes the stage of volitional attention (manasikāra) as the point of entry for practice.
One must not be careless in one's efforts.

Next, regarding the "object-specific" (viṣaya-viśeṣa) factors, these refer to the five mental concomitants from desire (*chanda*) up to wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, the treatise states that their function is to serve as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*).
Below this, the second category—the five object-specific mental factors—is explained. First, the general name is explained: they are called "object-specific" because...

This is because the objects of the five mental factors (*caitasika*) are each distinct; they do not, like the universal factors (*mahābhūmika*), share a single common object, and are therefore called "distinct" (*pṛthag*).
As for "desire" (*chanda*), its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the longing and expectation for an object of preference, and its functional activity (*karma*) is to rely upon diligence (*vīrya*).
There is no mundane or supramundane phenomenon that does not arise through it.

Because one delights in something, it is accomplished; thus, by delighting in worldly dharmas, one accomplishes worldly fruits, and by delighting in world-transcending dharmas, one accomplishes world-transcending fruits.
How profound is this! One must not fail to rectify one’s inclinations. Zhaozhou said:

"For this old monk, apart from the two times of rice gruel and meals, which are occasions for miscellaneous mental engagements, there is nowhere else where the mind is engaged in such diversions."—Ancient Record.
For those who have donned the armor of humanity and seek to realize unsurpassed *bodhi* within a fixed period, it is the power of their aspiration and delight.
It is precisely because this aspiration and delight reach their ultimate intensity that they can labor tirelessly from dawn until night, never for a moment succumbing to indolence.
Were it otherwise, in a single *kṣaṇa*, they would turn back a thousand or ten thousand times. A certain master said: "That which one delights in is what can be attained."
Regarding objects of delight: because one desires to see or hear them regarding such objects of delight, and because there is something hoped for, one asks. Regarding objects of aversion:
when they have not yet come together, one does not hope for their union; when they have already come together, one hopes for their separation.
This too is a matter of great happiness; how could it not be desire? Why must one wait for an object that is inherently delightful before calling it desire?
Answer: As you say, this merely involves seeking what is incompatible with an object that is loathsome, or hoping for separation from it.
It is simply because one feels a sense of relief and exhilaration within oneself that this occurs; it does not mean that a sense of attachment arises toward the loathsome object itself.
A mind that delights—how could it be called "desire"? Therefore, with respect to both objects that are loathsome and those that are neutral, there is absolutely no fondness or delight.
Even when directed toward an object that is pleasing, if a mind of longing does not arise, there is likewise no fondness or delight. The second master says:
That which is "delighted in" is the object sought; one seeks union with an object that is pleasing, and seeks [separation] from an object that is loathsome.
[The opponent] says: "It is excluded, because there is aspiration toward both objects. The third master says: "That which is desired is the object of observation.
One gives rise to a fondness for all objects, whether wholesome or unwholesome, and only after careful examination and detailed investigation does one have aspiration;
therefore, it is called 'desire' (*chanda*). If one does not desire to examine and investigate carefully, one follows like a person's stumbling foot."

Regarding those objects that arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), none enter the mind; thus, there is a complete absence of desire. By this principle, desire is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).
All three explanations are valid, but the latter is especially so. To distinguish it from others, one master says:
"Desire necessarily depends on the power of hoping for an external object before the various minds and mental factors can apprehend their respective objects. Therefore, when the mind arises..."
This must certainly be so; therefore, the Sūtra states that desire (*chanda*) is the root of all phenomena (*dharma*). This [opponent] erroneously takes attention (*manasikāra*) to be desire.
First [the author] refutes this, and then dismantles it, saying: "When the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) apprehend external objects, they do so entirely by means of attention;

what bearing does desire have on this? The Sūtra states that consciousness (*vijñāna*) can only arise when attention is present; it does not say that the mind and mental factors arise by means of desire."

Furthermore, he refutes this by analogy: "If you say that desire (*chanda*) is the root of all phenomena (*dharma*) and that all mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise because of desire, then since the Sūtra states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the root of all phenomena, do not all mind and mental factors likewise arise from craving?
Question: "Since mind and mental factors and so forth do not arise from desire, why does the Sūtra make such a statement? Answer: "However, the Sūtra..."

When it is said that desire (*chanda*) is the root of all phenomena, this refers to the fact that all undertakings arise from the inclination toward them; therefore, it is said that desire is the root.
Alternatively, this desire is a wholesome desire (*kuśala-chanda*) that is capable of inciting diligence (*vīrya*) and assists in the accomplishment of all virtuous deeds;
thus, the treatise states that its function is to serve as the basis for exertion, while the sutra states that desire is the root. This does not mean that desire [itself] is capable of...
The arising of the mind and mental factors takes this as their basis.
How so? If resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) were [required] toward a determined object, this would in turn require something else, leading to the fault of infinite regress.
First, the essence and function are presented. This refers to the explanation beginning with "false" and "inferior.

Regarding the statement, "decisively sealed and maintained so as to be unshakable," this means that by relying on the power of the evidence provided by false teachings and correct teachings, as well as false principles and correct principles, one remains fixed upon the object of apprehension.

Investigating thoroughly and with clarity, one reaches a definitive conclusion and maintains it steadfastly; because other conditions cannot then pull it away or seize it, this is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*).
As it is said: "Form is like a mass of foam; feeling is like a bubble on water; perception is like a mirage; mental formations are like a plantain tree."
Consciousness is like a magical illusion; thus, it is decisively superior and cannot be led astray. As the saying goes:

"An army of three divisions may seize its commander, but a single man’s resolve cannot be taken away. An ancient sage said: "Even if you claim 'neither mind nor Buddha,' I remain 'this very mind is Buddha.
If one is half-doubting and half-believing, as if existing yet non-existent, this is called hesitation (*vicikitsā*).

Regarding the object (*ālambana*), there is certainly no resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). Even if one maintains a mental impression, if there is no mind that decisively resolves upon it as "one stroke, two pieces," there is likewise no resolute conviction.
For this reason, resolute conviction is not included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*). [The following] distinguishes it from others. One master says:
When the mind and its mental factors apprehend their respective objects, there is no place of obstruction; yet all possess *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction).

This is because [the opponent] mistakenly identifies pervasive application (*vibhūta*) as *adhimokṣa*, and thus it was previously refuted. Later, it is further dismantled as follows: "That which is capable of being unobstructed is the object itself;
that which is not obstructed is the mind and its mental factors. Before a thought is raised, the mind and its objects are fundamentally unobstructed."
At the moment a superior mind arises for even an instant, it is entirely due to the power of the sense faculties and mental attention (*manasikāra*);

what has this to do with resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)? If such a superior arising were not dependent on the sense faculties and mental attention but instead awaited resolute conviction, then that resolute conviction could not arise of itself and would require something further upon which it depends.
If resolute conviction requires something further upon which it depends, then that [further thing]...
That which awaits must itself await something else; thus, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress.
Why is this? Because one attends to an object previously experienced [until] it serves as the cause for recollection at a later time.

First, the essence and function are presented, namely that which is below the teaching. Next, the explanation follows: "That which has been previously practiced" refers to matters that have been repeatedly cultivated.

"Clearly remembering without forgetting, taking this as the basis for concentration and making it one's work" means being alert and not dull, being vividly clear and distinct, keeping the object of mindfulness present before one, without even a moment’s loss.
To apply effort in this manner so that distracted thoughts naturally settle is called "right mindfulness."—The Ancients.
Dechun said: "A single thought is ten thousand years; ten thousand years are a single thought. This is precisely it.
Among the ancients who practiced nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name) and Chan meditation, there were none who achieved realization without relying on the power of this correct mindfulness.

Therefore, regarding the myriad affairs of daily life, they never gave rise to a thought concerning things they had never encountered before; and even regarding those they had previously encountered, they let them pass like the wind by their ears, without a mind of focused attachment.
Because it cannot clearly remember and no recollection arises, this [mental factor] is also not subsumed under the universal (sarvatraga) factors.

To distinguish it from others, one master says: whenever the mind arises, it must necessarily be accompanied by mindfulness (smṛti), because through mindfulness, the object is clearly remembered and not forgotten.

It can serve as the cause for recollection at a later time. This too is refuted by the previous [argument] that it is a misconception to hold that mental application (*manasikāra*) is memory (*smṛti*).

Later, it is further demolished: "If you claim that a preceding thought-moment is the cause of a succeeding one, then there should be no delusion or faith in the succeeding moment, since the preceding moment also possessed delusion and faith.
However, the cause of the preceding mind and mental factors does not reside in existence.

[Response: Indeed, it is because the power of the currently occurring universal mental factor of perception (*saṃjñā*) is so strong that it is sufficient to serve as the cause for recollection at a later time;
there is no need for a separate mindfulness.
How could this be established? Because the object of observation [is not the mind itself], just as mindfulness and wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth are not identical to the mind.

First, the essence and function are presented; next, they are explained. Regarding the phrase "the objects of observation," this refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth, as well as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "focusing the mind without distraction, taking meditative concentration as the basis for activity," this means that within the ordinary environments of daily life, one applies the mind to observe:
what is form (*rūpa*), what is sensation (*vedanā*), and so on? What is this form? What is this sensation?
And so forth. By thus concentrating the mind with single-mindedness and without distraction, there will naturally arise a point of entry.
Thereby, the original luminosity reveals itself and the wisdom of definitive discernment is born. One need no longer wait for the "wisdom after the tooth" to be sought from the lips of others;
all the great ancestral masters of the past employed this very method. When it is said that the mind is concentrated, it indicates that this mind desires—
Regarding the phrase "abiding in what object": this means that one is able to cause the mind to abide in this object; it does not refer exclusively to a single object.

If it referred exclusively to a single object, then since the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) contemplates the eight truths across the upper and lower realms with distinct objects before and after, there would be no focused concentration, and thus no meditative absorption (samādhi).
Therefore, the term "focused concentration" does not imply a single object alone. Even if it were a single object, [the same principle would apply].
If the mind is not focused with one-pointed concentration, meditative absorption (samādhi) will not arise; therefore, it is not included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Below follows a refutation of this [opposing] view. One master says: "Even when the mind is not focused one-pointedly on a single object, meditative absorption still arises at that time;
however, its characteristics are subtle and hidden, and those with coarse minds simply do not perceive it. This is truly a universal factor; it is no idle talk. Below...

The refutation states: If it is claimed that this concentration (*samādhi*) causes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to harmonize and converge upon a single object, and is therefore a universal factor (*sarvatraga*), this reasoning is also incorrect.
For the function of contact (*sparśa*) is to cause the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness to harmonize and proceed toward a single object;
this is not the function of concentration. If it is further claimed that this concentration can cause the momentary mind to be free from heterogeneous objects of focus...

This reasoning that [mental factors] are universal (*sarvatraga*) is also incorrect. Since a momentary mind is the shortest possible duration of time, it naturally lacks any variation regarding its object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Why must it wait for concentration (*samādhi*) before becoming free from variation?

If you claim that it is by means of concentration that the mind grasps its object and thus becomes universal, this reasoning is also incorrect; for it is concentration that causes the mind to grasp [the object] equally.
As for the object of focus (*ālambana*), it is the mental attention (*manasikāra*); it is not the concentrated mind itself.

If it is argued that the essence of this concentration is the concentrated mind—on the grounds that the Sūtra states concentration is a training of the mind and is identical to one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*)—this reasoning is also incorrect.
It is by relying on concentration that the distracted mind is withdrawn and focused intently upon a single object. Therefore...
The Sūtra speaks of "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*). This one-pointedness of mind is a discipline for gathering and calming the mind;

therefore, it is not identical to the mind itself. This is because this concentration is included among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Concentration (*samādhi*) is certainly not identical to the mind, because it is subsumed under the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), just like mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Since mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth each possess their own distinct intrinsic nature, this concentration is likewise so; how then could it be identical to the mind?
What is wisdom (*prajñā*)? Regarding the objects of observation... (up to)... it is certainly not omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), unlike faith, craving, and so forth.

First, its essential nature and function are presented; next, it is explained. "Discriminating and severing doubt" means that regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, as well as the objects of gain and loss, one first employs the mind of wisdom to investigate and differentiate them, and only thereafter reaches a definitive conclusion, such that the mind is free from doubt.
Therefore, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird; neither can be dispensed with.
One must give rise to wisdom through concentration, and attain certainty through wisdom. Thus it is said: "With a single mind unmoving, one is called 'entering the various dhyānas';
realizing that objects are non-arising is called 'prajñā. If, within a state of ignorance regarding what is not the object of contemplation...
If there were discernment (*pravicaya*), then this wisdom (*prajñā*) would not exist; therefore, it is not subsumed under the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

To distinguish it from the inferior [view], some masters say that even in a state of delusion where discernment is absent, wisdom still exists within the mind, though its characteristic is subtle and hidden.
Because the ignorant mind is prevalent, [this faculty] remains hidden and does not manifest. It is not that this wisdom (*prajñā*) does not exist;

rather, it is because this wisdom is a "great receptacle" (*mahābhyupagama*) of phenomena. How do we know it is a great receptacle? Because within the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is described as a "universal mental factor" (*mahābhūmika*). As the verse of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), attention (*manaskāra*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), and concentration (*samādhi*)—these are universal throughout the one [mental continuum]."
"Take this to heart. These ten are all called 'universal mental factors' (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). [The opponent] refutes this, saying:
"The Abhidharma treatises of the various schools contradict one another and lack a fixed standard; they cannot be adhered to as a definitive system.

For example, the *Abhidharmakośa* names six types—delusion (*moha*), negligence (*pramāda*), indolence (*kausīdya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—as the 'great afflictive universal factors' (*kleśamahābhūmika-dharma*). Therefore, desire (*chanda*) and contact (*sparśa*), and so forth..."
If compared in terms of their scope (*bhūmi*), both are pervasive throughout all levels; thus, desire and the others may also be termed "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

However, if desire and the others are compared with contact and the other universal factors in terms of their function as pervasive concomitants, they are not of equal status; how then could they be called "universal mental factors"?

Because the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) pervade all four categories of universality, whereas the object-specific factors (*viniyata*) pervade only two; furthermore, the Sūtra states that the five beginning with contact (*sparśa*) are universal.

If one were to claim that ten are universal, it would contradict the Sūtra, and thus one should not dogmatically insist on such a view. To refute this, the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is presented:
"The five beginning with desire (*chanda*) are certainly not universal, because they are not like contact and the others, just as greed (*rāga*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth are not."
There is one interpretation that these five [consciousnesses] necessarily support one another and coexist with the *ālayavijñāna*, as there are many such instances.
The following passage generally describes the various states (*avasthā*) in which these five manifest. One master says:

"These five definitely arise together because they mutually assist one another. Another master says: "The five objects do not necessarily arise together, for they exist within the four [mental states]."
Among all [factors], they pervade all natures and all stages, yet they do not pervade all times nor all [mental] concomitants.
Since they do not arise simultaneously, there is no sense of their co-arising. Furthermore, it is said that these five arise in dependence upon four objects;
because the objects are indeterminate, the subjects [the consciousnesses] are also indeterminate. Therefore, one should say that these five may at times arise as one, or at times arise...
Two arise; three arise; four arise; or they arise together, or they do not arise together.

Regarding the statement that "one arises," this means that with respect to a desired object, desire arises, resolve arises, mindfulness arising from prior habituation arises, and concentration arises through contemplation. Question:

Since both concentration and wisdom arise with respect to the object of contemplation, why is it said specifically that "concentration arises"? Answer: It is because for those of a dull or ignorant disposition, the mind...
It is highly disordered, flowing and racing about. In order to stop this distracted mind, one may focus intently on the object of observation to prevent the mind from scattering;
yet, being unable to discern right from wrong or gain from loss, it is called "deluded concentration" (*mūḍha-samādhi*). This is termed "having concentration but lacking wisdom.
Question: Since there is no discernment within a state of delusion, how can it be said that the mind takes an observed object as its focal point?

Regarding the object (*ālambana*): The answer is that when one reaches the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), even a slight degree of the power of wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī- and cintāmayī-prajñā*) enables one to take an object as a focus;

therefore, it is said that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) takes the observed object as its focus. Alternatively, based on the predominance [of one factor over the other], it is said that there is concentration without wisdom, as in the passage "like a play" (*yathā krīḍā*), which cites evidence for the existence of concentration without wisdom.
Or, in the passage "or at times," it explains the existence of wisdom without concentration, or that both arise at certain times.

This refers to the simultaneous arising of pairs with respect to four objects. In total, there are ten such pairs: first, desire and resolve; second, desire and mindfulness; third, desire and concentration;
fourth, desire and wisdom; fifth, resolve and mindfulness; sixth, resolve and concentration; seventh, resolve and wisdom; eighth, mindfulness and concentration.
9. Mindfulness and wisdom; 10. Concentration and wisdom. At times three [factors] arise together, meaning that these three arise simultaneously with respect to four objects.

Altogether there are ten sets of three: 1. Desire, understanding, and mindfulness; 2. Desire, mindfulness, and concentration; 3. Desire, concentration, and wisdom; 4. Wisdom, desire, and understanding; 5. Wisdom, understanding, and mindfulness; 6.
Wisdom, mindfulness, and concentration; 7. Understanding, mindfulness, and concentration; 8. Understanding, mindfulness, and wisdom; 9. [The ninth set is as follows:]...

Regarding the recollection of the desire for liberation: there are ten types of recollection involving concentration and wisdom. As for "sometimes arising as four," this means that the four arise simultaneously with respect to four objects.

There are five sets of four: first, the desire for liberation, recollection, concentration; second, the desire for liberation, recollection, wisdom; third, wisdom, the desire for liberation, recollection;

fourth, wisdom, liberation, recollection, concentration; fifth, liberation, recollection, concentration, and wisdom. Or they may arise together, namely: the desire for liberation, recollection, [concentration, and wisdom].

Regarding concentration and wisdom: when these four objects give rise to the five [mental states] beginning with desire, there are thirty-one categories in total, comprising both general and specific instances.

That is to say, when each of the five beginning with desire arises individually, there are five categories; when two arise together, there are ten for each pair; when three arise together, there are ten; when four arise together, there are five; and when all five arise together, there is one category.
Alternatively, there may be mental states where none of these five arise, such as when they do not arise in the absence of these four objects. This refers to the state of confronting the objects.

Because it arises only at specific times; because it does not arise even during moments of sudden, impulsive mental activity (*sauratya-citta*), as such states lack conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*);
and because it does not arise simultaneously with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), as it is not omnipresent within the mind.

The seventh and eighth consciousnesses, as well as these five specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*), and even the five sensory consciousnesses, all possess the wisdom of accomplishing tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

The preceding section clarified that the objects of the [five] sense-consciousnesses do not pervade all times; this section clarifies that the objects of the [five] specific mental factors do not pervade all [mental states] simultaneously.

Regarding these five [mental factors], their presence or absence in the seventh and eighth consciousnesses depends on the stage: in the eighth consciousness when it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are definitely absent;
in the seventh consciousness when it is contaminated, there is only wisdom (*mati*). If it is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are associated with all five.

The six consciousnesses, such as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whether in their transformed or untransformed states, are all associated with the five factors, as there is no exclusion of them.
Regarding the first five transforming consciousnesses, one master says that these five are entirely non-existent;

another master says that these five may exist, meaning that although they lack predominance (*adhipati*), they possess a subtle and inferior presence, rather than being completely absent. [The text] excludes those that are equal or inferior. The question asks: "The five..."

Since the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are distracted and lack focused attention, how can there be meditative concentration (*samādhi*)? For it is only by drawing the mind into equanimity that one enters concentration.
The answer is: if we discuss the moments of emerging from or entering concentration, the distraction of the five consciousnesses certainly cannot exist.

However, if they apprehend objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) while in a state of concentration, they must necessarily agree with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); therefore, concentration is possible [for them]. Yet, regarding the five consciousnesses...

Regarding "without concentration" (*asamāhita*): this merely excludes *samāpatti* (equipoise), but does not exclude *samādhi* (meditative absorption). *Samāpatti* refers to the moments of emerging from and entering into meditative equipoise; *samādhi* refers to the period of remaining in equipoise.
For this reason, the Noble Teaching states that those possessing the supernormal powers of the eye and ear [possess them] while in a state of non-concentration;

this clearly demonstrates that the first five [consciousnesses] also possess wisdom (*prajñā*), because this wisdom is the cognition associated with the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear. It is also [the case for] the nose...
Because they are associated with the consciousnesses of the tongue and body. Below, the five mental factors are summarized by way of two stages.
If one considers the stage of non-mastery, these five mental factors may sometimes not be present; however, when mastery is attained, these five are necessarily present.

Because one contemplates suffering, its origin, the path, cessation, the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*), and the non-established truths (*avyavasthāpita-satya*) and so forth, one's desire does not diminish.

Because one understands the immeasurable within the one and understands the one within the immeasurable, one's resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) does not diminish. One contemplates that which is remote.
It is just as it is today; thus, mindfulness does not diminish. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is nothing that is not samādhi; thus, concentration does not diminish.

Since all five consciousnesses possess the wisdom of performing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, opening the mouth, moving the tongue, looking about, or frowning—all these are nothing other than Buddha-activities;
thus, wisdom does not diminish. By virtue of these five dharmas, within the state of mastery, the eight...
All consciousnesses can be associated [with these].

Regarding which feelings (*vedanā*) these five object-specific mental states (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) are associated with—from [the question] "which feelings" up to the various analytical categories—one should reflect according to reason.

This statement concerns the five [mental factors] and their association with feelings. One master says: "Desire (*chanda*) is associated with the three feelings of joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)."

[They] correspond [to the feelings]. With the exception of the two feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*), because the objects of those two—sorrow and suffering—do not give rise to desire for pleasure (*chanda*).
The remaining four mental factors (*caitasika*) all correspond to the four feelings, with the sole exception of the feeling of suffering.

This is because investigation (*vitarka*), decision (*vicāra*), clarity (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), and discernment (*pravicaya*) are absent from the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*); furthermore, the five consciousnesses are subsumed under the feeling of suffering. Since the five consciousnesses...

It is not associated with the four [mental factors]. The same applies to painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*). One teacher says: "The five factors, such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth, are all associated with the five feelings.

Because one gives rise to sorrow and distress while seeking to realize enlightenment, and because one seeks liberation from a realm of pure suffering—both the aversion to suffering and the aspiration for pleasure are forms of desire—therefore, desire is also associated with both the feelings of grief (*daurmanasya*) and pain (*duḥkha*)."

This [explanation] applies to the previous master’s position that desire (*kāmacchanda*) does not associate with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) or suffering (*duḥkha*). This is because it has already been stated that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) exists within the mind.

Thus, it applies to the previous four factors (*dharmas*) that do not associate with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*). Below this, the treatise cites the *Śāstra* to prove that desire does indeed associate with both mental distress and suffering.
Below the section on the faculty of suffering, it further proves that these four factors associate with the faculty of suffering. This is because...
The former master said: "The five consciousnesses lack the functions of deliberation, determination, clarity, and mindfulness; therefore, these do not associate with the five consciousnesses.
To this, [the author] replies: If the sense organs already associate with the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), what fault is there in these four factors associating with suffering?
Moreover, although the first five consciousnesses lack the four predominant factors (*adhipati-dharma*), they do possess subtle functions such as the sealing of objects (*viṣayamudraṇa*).
4. How can it be said that they do not exist? Because of this, these five are definitely associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*).

Below, other categories are clarified to distinguish these five, which further pervade the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three realms (*tridhātu*), and the states of training and no-more-training (*śaikṣa-asaikṣa*), among others.
Since these five pervade all natures and all stages, it is known that the three natures and the three realms are all pervasive. The sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functions as its basis.
Since non-retrogression does not exclude any [of these], one should know that those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and so forth, should likewise all possess it.
Such categories may be inferred by applying this analogy.
