"Some harmonize the spirit and nourish the breath to preserve spontaneity (*ziran*); some torment the substance and emaciate the form to achieve the Ultimate Way (*zhidao*);
some cling to non-attachment while establishing themselves before external objects; and some seek meditative stillness (*jinglü*) to suppress the deluded mind."
Some carve away their emotions and extinguish the Dharma to congeal in emptiness; some cling to shadows and conditions to embrace appearances;

some lose the true illumination of the spiritual source; some destroy the right cause of the Buddha-seed; some concentrate their consciousness within pure cognition to receive retribution in an insentient realm;
some clarify the mind and obliterate form to abide in the fruit of rebirth in the heavens of the eight difficulties; or some become attached to existence.
Yet they guard the city of *śūnya* (emptiness), or negate all existence as being like a rabbit’s horn;

some remain in a dark room having cut off all views, while others persist in the objects of knowledge despite having severed all illumination; some mistake the presence of cognition for the very form of the True Buddha, while others imitate a state of ignorance.
They are of the same category as wood and stone. Some cling to delusion while grasping for the ultimate fruit, as if thinking that the mud itself is the jar.
Others forget conditions while seeking the gate of liberation, like trying to find water by striking away the waves. Some project outwardly and vainly give rise to dream-like affairs;
others guard within and sit upright, harboring their ignorance. Some take "oneness" as their principle, claiming that all phenomena are identical to suchness; others see...
They differ in their respective establishments of dharmadhātus: some maintain that ignorance and non-discrimination constitute the Great Way;
some, adhering to views of emptiness, reject good and evil as true cultivation; some understand the inconceivable nature to be a necessity for emptiness;
some take the true, good, and wondrous form to be substantially existent; and some cultivate a sunken faculty while severing all thought, becoming like the gods of the outflows.

Some study contemplation through vitarka and vicāra, following the realm of their own emotional estimations; some fail to exhaust the nature of delusion, forming the view of a primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*);
some are ignorant of the illusory substance, establishing a doctrine of empty nothingness; and some mistake reflected images for reality.
Some abandon the illusory to seek the real; some designate the objects of seeing and hearing as "living things," while others point to illusory transformations as "insentient.
Some give rise to mental constructs that deviate from quiescent awareness; some sever mindfulness and thereby impair the Buddha's functioning.
Some are deluded regarding the qualities of intrinsic nature and give rise to the view of a physical body; others rely on ultimate emptiness and fall into the view of annihilationism.
Some cling to the Great Principle while abruptly discarding the adornments; some are confused by the teachings on gradual progression and engage solely in contrived activity;
some rely on the essence as being detached from conditions and stubbornly cling to a fixed nature; others forget that all things are extinguished and merely preserve their own ignorance.

Some fixate on the nature of persons and phenomena as being inherently such, thereby falling into the view of causelessness. Some maintain that objects and cognition arise together in a union, resulting in a common perception.

Some hold that mind and objects are indistinguishably mixed, confusing the distinction between subject and object. Some cling to the differentiation between the ultimate and the conventional, binding themselves with the ignorance of cognitive obscurations.
Some adhere to the notion of a single, unchanging reality, thereby falling into eternalism. Others fixate on the four characteristics of conditioned existence as the agents of transformation.

They sink into nihilism and sever [the roots of goodness]. Some cling to the notion that there is no cultivation and thus reject the stages of the sages; others claim to have attained realization and thereby turn their backs on the natural truth (*t’ien-chên*).
Some indulge in attachment to the environment and its inhabitants, following the cycle of worldly rebirth;

others loathe birth and death and thereby lose true liberation. Some are deluded regarding true emptiness and revere causes while clinging to fruits; others savor the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and rejoice in Buddhahood while detesting Māra. Or they are attached to...
Some cling to the literal words of whatever they have heard as the ultimate truth; others lose sight of the true nature of sound and seek silence by rejecting speech.
Some adhere to their own religious vehicles while loathing the meditative concentration of their own minds; others propagate dhyāna contemplation while disparaging the definitive teachings.
Some vie for eccentricity, looking only to themselves, only to suddenly sink into the ocean of consciousness; others purify their conduct to the point of ostentatious cleanliness.

Yet, seeking only the profound and esoteric, one instead falls into the city of the aggregates (*skandha*). Some give rise to extraordinary intellectual understandings, which fester as sores upon their flesh.

Some abide in the original purity of their nature, yet cling to that bliss and thereby incur illness. Some seek out texts and extract meanings, drinking only the "guest water" of external interpretations.
Some maintain stillness in secluded dwellings, yet sit amidst the "dust of dharmas. Others give rise to a mind of attainment while discoursing on the signless (*animitta*).
In the Mahāyāna, some employ conceptual schemata to probe the profound principles beyond external phenomena; some abandon discourse to give rise to views that transcend words;
some preserve the means of expression and thereby incur the reproach of clinging to the pointing finger; and some recognize only active function, remaining within the source of birth and cessation.
Some dwell exclusively on memory, remaining at the limit of consciousness and perception; some arrange their practice and lose the nature of Perfect Enlightenment;
some indulge themselves and fail to enter the gateway to the Path; some give rise to physical and mental diligence and become stuck in conditioned phenomena;
some maintain a state of effortless naturalness and sink into the fetters of wisdom; or some focus exclusively on calculation and diligent reflection, thereby losing right concentration (*samādhi*).
Some imitate unimpeded mastery and thus abandon their cultivation; some follow along with their fetters and defilements while relying on the emptiness of their original nature;
some cling to entanglements and hindrances while falsely attempting to eliminate them; some cherish what they value and thereby give rise to craving for dharmas;
some are arrogant and disparage the causes of Buddhahood; some advance in their practice but deviate from their fundamental mind; and some regress and fall into negligence.
Some contradict the evidence through their words and thus impair the ground of reality; some treat essence and function as separate entities and thereby deviate from the Buddha-vehicle.
Some rejoice in quiescence and dwell in emptiness, losing the nature of great compassion; some obliterate conditions and loathe the conventional, violating the gate of suchness.
Some cling to the view of self and remain oblivious to the emptiness of persons; some are deluded regarding direct perception and stubbornly maintain attachment to phenomena. Or...
Some understand without possessing faith, thereby nourishing false views; others possess faith without complete understanding, thereby fostering ignorance.
Some claim that while the person is correct, they cling to the dharmas; some say that while the object is profound, their wisdom is shallow. Some grasp at things and thus lose sight of Buddha-nature;

some abandon them and thus deviate from the reality of suchness. Some distance themselves and thus contradict the cause; some identify with it and thus lose the fruit; some deny it and thus slander it.
Some cling to the Real while disparaging the provisional; some loathe ignorance while turning their backs on the gateway of immovable wisdom (*aniñjya-jñāna*);
some detest diverse objects while harboring attachment to the samādhi of the dharma-nature; some rely on the principle of identity while giving rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*);

some deprecate specific characteristics while destroying the gateway of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*); some regard [the teachings] as bodhi while slandering the True Wheel of Dharma; or they deny the existence of sentient beings.

Thus, they destroy the essence of the true Buddha; some cling to fundamental wisdom while rejecting expedient wisdom; some are confused by the primary teaching and instead adhere to the gates of transformation;
some stagnate in principle and sink into the pit of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*); some cling to phenomena and cast themselves into the net of empty illusions;

some sever extremes and obliterate traces, thereby violating the gate of dual illumination; and while preserving the primary and maintaining the mean, they lose the intent of skillful means (*upāya*).
Some, through the one-sided cultivation of concentration or wisdom, scorch and wither the sprouts of the Way; some, practicing in isolation, sink and bury themselves in the Buddha-way.
Some perform non-active practices while cultivating conditioned bodhi; some cling to a mind of non-attachment while studying a semblance of prajñā.
Some give rise to pure marks and thus become deluded regarding the true nature of defilement; some abide in the stage of correctness and thereby lose the fundamental emptiness of the mundane.
Some establish the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) and thereby obscure *tathatā*; some give rise to a mind that cognizes awakening and thus contravene the *dharmatā*.
Some cling to the true expositions and give rise to views based on words; they consume nectar yet die prematurely. Or, while emphasizing the perfect principle, they give rise to a mind of attachment;
they drink the *amṛta* (clarified butter) yet turn it into poison. The above is a brief enumeration of one hundred and twenty kinds.

All of these are delusions regarding the fundamental tenets and losses of the essential meaning. They turn their backs on profound stillness and deviate from the truth; they are like pressing one's eyes and seeing flowers, or mistaking a head for its reflection in water.
It is as if striking water to seek fire, or climbing a tree to catch fish; it is like fearing one's shadow while fleeing into emptiness, or feeling the wind and grasping at lightning.
Suffering is not the seed of sweetness; how could sand be the cause of rice? None of these can be harmonized through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), nor unified under a single principle.
Thus, one becomes deluded regarding skillful means and entirely ensnared by views; failing to reach the true teaching, one casts oneself into the net of views.
Therefore, the celestial Māras and external paths originally have no such seeds; it is only through losing mindfulness in practice that their source branches out. Hence, we know that—

If there is anything held as weighty or relied upon, establishing knowledge or establishing understanding—even if one does not forget a single hair’s breadth of such views—all of these become the ways of external paths (*tīrthika*).

As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-existent, there is nothing that can be known. To understand the nature of phenomena in this way is ultimately to have nothing to understand.
Since all things lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), upon what could one rely to form an understanding? It is like debating the horns of a rabbit."
To discern the size of the Great and the Small, or to determine the length of a tortoise’s hair—where both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are empty, one may well be laughed at by the world.
When the dust of emotion (*qingchen*) creates its own separation, one truly loses the Way right before one's eyes.

Therefore, even for one who has truly awakened to the essence (*zong*), they cannot yet maintain views of non-existence or hold onto non-understanding; how much less could they follow words to cling to meanings and give rise to views of existence?
Do you understand? If so, what is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)? The *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "That which is called right view is without high or low; it views all phenomena with equanimity. Furthermore, right view is the absence of all views;
this is called right view.
The three types of wrong views refer to the denial of cause, effect, function, and substantial reality (up to) all such categories as these, which are subsumed under wrong view.
This view acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for those not included among the four [specific] views, they are all subsumed under this [general] view.

Regarding the denial of cause, effect, function, and substantial reality, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "It refers to seeing worldly giving based upon the various mundane meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*)."
"Lord, suppose there is one who practices giving throughout their entire lifespan without interruption.
After passing away from that life, they are reborn into a low-born family, impoverished and destitute. They think to themselves: 'There was certainly no giving, nurturing, or sacrificial offering.
Yet, they see another person who, throughout their entire lifespan, consistently practiced either sublime conduct or evil conduct; they see that person pass away."
They fall into the evil destinies and are born in the hells, or they go to the happy destinies and are born in the blissful worlds of the heavens.
They think to themselves: "There certainly are no wholesome deeds nor unwholesome deeds, nor is there any maturation of the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions.
Furthermore, they see a member of the kṣatriya caste who, after his life has ended, is born among the brahmins.
Among the various castes such as the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, or when a Brāhmaṇa has passed away and is born into a caste such as the Kṣatriya, he thinks:
"Certainly, there is no one in this world who comes from a Kṣatriya or other caste in that [previous] world;
nor is there anyone in that world who comes from a Kṣatriya or other caste in this world."
He observes that those of the kṣatriya and other castes pass away from their respective lineages; furthermore, he sees those who have abandoned desire being reborn in lower realms.
He also sees that after a mother’s life has ended, she is born as her daughter, and after the daughter’s life has ended, she becomes her mother again;
the father dies to become the son, and the son returns to become the father. Having seen that parents are not fixed, he reflects upon this.
This is their thought: "In this world, there are certainly no fathers and no mothers.

Or else, seeing that when a person's body perishes at the end of life, they are either reborn in the realm of non-perception, or reborn in the formless realm, or enter into nirvana, they seek their place of rebirth but are unable to see it.
They think to themselves: "There are certainly no beings born by transformation, because their place of origin cannot be known.
Or, having developed the overweening pride of an Arhat regarding themselves, they see signs of rebirth at the time of death and think:
"In this world there are surely no true Arhats; there is no giving and no receiving. Nor...

To deny the existence of sacrificial offerings is called the denial of causes (*hetu-viparyāsa*). To deny the existence of wholesome and unwholesome conduct is called the denial of activity (*prayoga-viparyāsa*).
To deny the existence of the maturation of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions is called the denial of results (*phala-viparyāsa*).

To deny the existence of father and mother, to deny the existence of beings born by transformation, and to deny the existence of true arhats who have eternally exhausted all outflows—to deny all such things is called the denial of reality (*bhūta-viparyāsa*).

Regarding the matter: as for the two types of "causelessness" concerning the past, first, there are those who, having passed away from the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and been reborn in this world, lack the supernormal power of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Consequently, they are unable to remember all the stages prior to the moment their minds emerged [from that state].

They then maintain that all phenomena originally did not exist and arose [de novo], thinking, "As it is with me, so it is with others. Thus, they maintain that both the self and the world are entirely without cause. Second...

Due to discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), one does not remember previous lives and thus forms this attachment: that [the self] arises without cause. Regarding the claim that the four realms of existence (*bhava*) are finite:

first, because one is able to recollect everything from the Avīci Hell below up to the fourth *dhyāna* above, and perceives the self as completely filling all within them, one then thinks: "Beyond this there is a self; I ought to be able [to perceive it]."

1) Because one perceives [a limit], one knows there is a limit. 2) Because one can recollect exclusively [in one direction] while there is no limit laterally, and because one clings to the self as being all-pervasive, one clings to it as being limitless.
3) Because one can recollect [the limits] above, below, and laterally, one clings to both having a limit and being limitless.

Fourth, by recollecting the stage of the destruction of the eon (*kalpa*), one gives rise to the perception that [the world] is neither finite nor infinite, because the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) cannot be apprehended.

Regarding the "fourfold equivocation regarding immortality" (*amarā-vikṣepa*): the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that heterodox paths (*bāhyaka-mārga*) reckon that the heavens are eternal, which they call "immortality.
They further reckon that by answering without equivocation, one will be reborn in those heavens; therefore, the Buddha rebuked them.
[The Buddha] said: "What you call 'secrecy' and so forth is merely evasive equivocation. Regarding the four types [of equivocation]:

first, fearing that one might appear ignorant by saying 'I do not know what is wholesome or unwholesome,' when others question me, I am unable to give a definitive answer; for if I were to give a definitive answer..."
1. Fearing that he might perceive my ignorance and mock me, [one] thinks: "The secret meanings of those devas should not all be explained.

This is the first form of crookedness. 2. Thinking: "It is not the case that my pure deva permits the disclosure of all secrets—namely, what has been personally realized and the path of purification"—this is the second form of crookedness.
3. One refrains from answering out of fear, fearing [that one will be exposed].
"I am dull and inferior; I am known as such by others. Due to these causes and conditions, I do not attain liberation. Taking this as my dwelling, I abide therein.
Fourth, there are those who are foolish and obtuse, who practice only the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) without any true understanding.
If anyone questions me, I instead cross-examine them and then assent to everything they say, following their words without contradiction. This is called "nirvāṇa in the present life."
There are three types: first, one who sees the fivefold sensual pleasures currently experienced by gods or humans and considers that to be *nirvāṇa*.
Second, although they feel aversion toward the five desires, they take the current abiding in the first dhyāna to be *nirvāṇa*;

because this state is induced within their own bodies, they perceive it as having attained bliss, and they see others currently abiding in dhyāna in the same way. Third, because they feel aversion toward vitarka and vicāra, they currently attain the second dhyāna.

One regards it as *nirvāṇa*. Fourth, because one grows weary of all discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and investigations (*vicāra*), one regards dwelling in the present moment within the third dhyāna as *nirvāṇa*.

Fifth, because one grows weary of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), and even of inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), one regards dwelling in the present moment within the fourth dhyāna as *nirvāṇa*.
Because it awaits the past, it is called the "future limit" (*aparānta*). Furthermore, this [view] conceives that since the self currently possesses happiness, it will also possess happiness later;

thus, it is subsumed under the future limit. Alternatively, those who conceive that Īśvara and so forth are the cause of all things do so because they observe that sentient beings in the world do not act according to their own desires. Why is this? Because we clearly perceive in the world...
At the time of those causes, when they wished to cultivate pure karma, their original intention was not fulfilled; instead, they committed evil.
At the time of those results, when they wished to be reborn in a favorable realm, their desire was not fulfilled; instead, they underwent various sufferings.
They then thought: "Regarding all things in the world, there must necessarily be another creator or progenitor who acts as the father of those things—namely, Īśvara."

This refers to those who desire purity yet are biased toward defilement, who prefer what is correct yet remain stubbornly attached to what is perverse; who do not reflect upon themselves but attribute their faults to Heaven;
and furthermore, who attribute everything—life and death, existence and non-existence, fortune and misfortune, nobility and meanness—to Heaven alone.
All these are subsumed under this view. There are those who falsely speculate regarding various false liberations, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:

"There are certain non-Buddhists for whom there is the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*); they are detached from sense objects, perceive the impermanence of phenomena, and see that the categories of mind and mental factors do not arise.
They hold that the objects of the past, future, and present, as well as all sensations and the aggregates, are exhausted like a destroyed seed, such that deluded conceptualization no longer arises."
These people conceive the notion of nirvāṇa regarding this [state]. Some define liberation as the transition from one direction to another.
Others, whose wisdom has been scorched by the evil of external paths, perceive a distinction between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*);

they hold that what is produced by the person is called "primordial nature," just as the *pradhāna* (the unmanifest) is compared to darkness. Furthermore, they maintain that the *guṇas* undergo transformation, and that the *guṇas* are the agent.
They conceive the notion of nirvāṇa; or they perceive Īśvara as the actual creator of saṃsāra;
or some perceive the twenty-five *tattvas*; or there are kings who protect their kingdoms and receive the *Ṣaḍdharmaka-śāstra*, regarding it as nirvāṇa and so forth.
There are various such deluded imaginings spoken of by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which fail to establish what ought to be established and are rejected by the wise. Or again—
Regarding those who falsely conceive of what is not the Path as the Path: there are certain non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who hold such views.
They claim that if sentient beings bathe their limbs in the river Sundarikā, all their evils will be entirely extinguished and they will attain supreme purity.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who observe the cow-vow, the dog-vow, the pig-vow, the pheasant-vow, the chicken-vow, and the deer-vow.
The precepts of the *ujjuka*, or those who observe the precept of holding ink and brushes, or the precept of nakedness, or the precept of smearing ashes,
or the precepts of self-mortification such as fumigating the nose, plucking out hair, lying on thorns, or lying on pestles, or the precept of using excrement and filth—
reckoning all such things as purity— are entirely subsumed under wrong views.
The fourth is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which has the function of serving as the basis for all disputes.

Adherence to views means grasping another's view as one’s own; that is, regarding three types of views and their associated aggregates, one clings to them as being supreme, excellent, and capable of bringing about purification. Because of this, each person mutually clings to their own [view] as superior. All [of these]...
Strife arises because of this; therefore, it is said that its function is to serve as the basis for all strife.

Regarding the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), when it pertains to [views] that accord with [the path], it is described as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and is not subsumed under the two types of clinging.

Regarding "prohibitions and observances" (śīla-vrata): this refers to practices such as those of the cow-herders and dog-keepers, as well as plucking out one's own hair, fumigating the nose, and the meditative concentrations and wisdom of the Sāṃkhya school.
Because they grasp at these causes and effects as being superior, pure, liberating, and leading to transcendence, they practice accordingly;
yet it yields no benefit, and they undergo toil and suffering in vain. Therefore, it is called "fruitless toil and suffering. Formerly there was...
There were two non-Buddhist practitioners: one named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who observed the cow-vow;
the other named Ajita Keśakambalin, who observed the dog-vow. On different occasions, these two went to the place where the Buddha was staying.
After exchanging various kind words and greetings with him, Pūraṇa asked the World-Honored One: "This Keśakambalin observes the dog-vow and practices the path."
"It is complete. Where shall he be reborn? The World-Honored One replied, "Desist; do not ask.

Although he requested the Buddha a second and a third time, the Buddha then said, "If you have observed the dog-precepts without any transgression, you shall be reborn among dogs. If there has been any transgression," [he shall be reborn elsewhere].
"You shall fall into hell. Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, he wept bitterly with a choked voice, unable to restrain himself.
The World-Honored One said to him, "I told you previously that you should stop and not ask; now you have indeed harbored resentment.
Then Pūraṇa said, "It was not my intention for this man to be reborn in the realm of dogs, and that is why I weep. Nevertheless, throughout the long night, I have observed the cow-vow."
"Will it be so in the future as well? I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will explain this for me.

The World-Honored One replied, "In accordance with the previous 'dog precepts,' these [views] all arise from failing to understand the True Path and falsely clinging to erroneous causes. Vāśpa then asked again:

How is it that undertaking the precepts of the pig, the cow, or the dog is called being without deficiency or transgression? Answer: If one acts in accordance with the laws of the cow or the dog, it is called being without deficiency or transgression.
Thus, the *Xiányáng shèngjiào lǎoshì jīng* (Exposition of the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings) states: "One attains purity by grasping and receiving pure things."

Is one purified by grasping impure things? If one were purified by grasping pure things, then since dogs and the like are universally acknowledged in the world to be impure, your claim that one attains purification by observing the precepts of grasping dogs and the like would be unreasonable.
If, on the other hand, it were by grasping impure things, then [the self-essence] would not be...
It is not logical that one who is already pure could cause others to be pure; would this not be to undergo toil and suffering in vain? Question:
Within these two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*), there is the grasping for something as supreme and capable of bringing about purification.

Elsewhere it is said that grasping for something as supreme is called the "grasping for views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), while grasping for that which can bring about purification is called the "grasping for precepts and vows" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). What is the meaning of this? Answer: [The text continues with the response.]

This is a brief explanation of the shadow [of the full meaning], or it is explained according to the principle of following [the conventional]. If one wishes for the meaning to be complete, one must necessarily reckon both cause and effect as being attained.

Otherwise, why would reckoning what is not cessation as cessation and what is not the path as the path be subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) rather than under the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*)?
This is because wrong view reckons cause and effect individually, whereas the two types of grasping reckon cause and effect together. Therefore...
They are simply different.

Thus, among these ten afflictions—both general and specific—from [the point of] being either innate (*sahaja*) or conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*), this is a classification according to alternative categories (*paryāya*).
First, regarding the innate and the conceptually constructed, as for the "general and specific": the first five are the general.
Because they are not further analyzed, the latter five are treated separately, as the first [of those five] is divided into five types.

Among these ten afflictions (*kleśa*), greed (*rāga*), anger (*pratigha*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) all pertain to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) types, because those six can arise both spontaneously and through deliberate reflection.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are only...
It arises through discrimination; it does not extend to that which is innate.

This is because it can only arise through the power of two external conditions—an evil friend and false teachings—and furthermore, through the power of one's own internal causes of deep reflection and subtle investigation. Thus says one master.

The innate (*sahaja*) form of the view of extremes is exclusively the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). The view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is coarse in its characteristics and lacks the quality of being innate;
it arises only through the power of evil friends, false teachings, and the like. The following citation provides proof. The *Yogācārabhūmi* asks: "Which view of extremes is innate? It answers:
"That which is subsumed under the view of annihilationism is innate. It asks again: "By what means is this known? It answers: [as follows].

This refers to those who, prior to the Path of Seeing, have practiced the six types of realization (*abhisamaya*) and have already suppressed the conceptually constructed afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*), leaving only the innate ones (*sahaja*).
Yet, they give rise to such fear, thinking: "Now, where is my self?
Is this not an association with the innate view of annihilation? Thus, even animals and other such dull-witted beings, when encountering adverse conditions...
All [beings] fear that I might cease to exist and thus give rise to alarm and dread; therefore, we know that the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) encompasses the innate (*sahaja*).
One master says: "The statement in that treatise that the innate view pertains only to the view of annihilation is said according to its coarse characteristics.

If discussed according to the actual principle, the innate also extends to the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*); for instance, among birds and beasts, there are only those who cling to the self as eternally existing."

Furthermore, they fervently engage in activities that provide for their needs over a long period of time—such as building nests to avoid wind and rain, or gathering fruits and gourds to nourish their bodies—is this not precisely the grasping at a self as eternally existing?
Therefore, the *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), in its lower section, cites scriptural evidence [to prove this].

Regarding these ten afflictions, which ones are associated with how many others? (Up to: Since the arising of all afflictions necessarily depends on delusion (*moha*), this clarifies that they cannot be associated with themselves.
Greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—these three definitely do not arise together, because their objects are either objects of attachment or objects of aversion.

Because they are mutually contradictory, they do not resolve upon an object; because they do not give rise to attachment, greed (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*) may or may not be associated.
The word "or" is a term of uncertainty. Because the objects of what is loved and what is despised are distinct, these two do not arise simultaneously.
However, because the objects of what is defiled and what is relied upon are identical, their association can be asserted. Regarding greed, it [is associated] with all five views...
Because it gives rise to attachment (*rāga*), it is necessarily associated with [the mind]. Hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) may sometimes arise together;

however, because the object of hatred and the object of pride are different, they are not associated. Since the object of contempt (*avamanyanā*) and the object of aversion (*vidveṣa*) are the same, one may say they can arise together.

At the initial moment of hesitation, the mind of aversion has not yet arisen, so one may say that hatred and doubt do not coexist. However, when one reflects for a long time without reaching a decision, [they do coexist].

One then gives rise to a mind of indignation; it can be said that anger (*dveṣa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) arise together. If the object of doubt is a favorable matter, the mind of anger does not arise;

however, if the object of doubt is an unfavorable matter, then resentment and hostility also arise. Therefore, anger is necessarily not associated with the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*), because one who clings to [wrong views] as supreme does not give rise to hatred.
Anger may, however, be associated with the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), or false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). It is pleasant...
When one clings to the aggregates as permanent, aversion does not arise. When one clings to the aggregate of suffering as permanent, resentment and anger subsequently arise.
If the arising of the aggregate of suffering is severed, anger ceases; if the arising of the aggregate of pleasure is severed, anger persists.

Anger is not produced toward evil deeds that are slandered by false views, yet anger can indeed arise toward good deeds that are so slandered. Pride possesses a fixed view, whereas doubt is characterized by indecision; therefore...
They are not associated. Pride is not incompatible with any of the five views; however, it certainly does not arise simultaneously with the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

The same applies to pride’s relationship with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and a portion of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). When the view of a self-identity clings to an aggregate that is pleasant, and wrong view slanders a bad thing, they can be said to be associated.
However, when the view of a self-identity clings to an inferior aggregate that is suffering, and wrong view denies a good thing, [they are not associated].
Furthermore, they are not associated. Doubt lacks definitive resolution, whereas views possess settled conviction; thus, they are certainly not associated.
The five views are necessarily not associated with one another, because there cannot be multiple instances of wisdom (*prajñā*) within a single moment of mind.
Delusion (*moha*), however, can be associated with all nine types [of afflictions], for it is by means of this that the afflictions arise.

With which consciousnesses are these ten afflictions associated? Because pride and the others arise through deliberation (*tulanā*) and so forth, these [ten] afflictions are associated with eight consciousnesses in this treatise.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) lacks them entirely, because it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

The manas possesses four: delusion (*moha*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and attachment (*tṛṣṇā*). The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses all of them. The five sensory consciousnesses possess only three: namely, greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).
Question: Why is there no [conceit or doubt] in the remaining [five consciousnesses]? Answer: Because conceit, doubt, and the five views arise from weighing, hesitation, and seeking;
the five consciousnesses lack such weighing. Therefore, they are not associated with conceit. They lack hesitation; therefore, they are not associated with doubt.
Because they lack investigation (*vitarka*), they are not associated with the five views (*dṛṣṭi*).

As for which of these ten afflictions are associated with which feelings (*vedanā*)—from [which feeling] up to their arising together with other feelings—they should be understood according to the principle.

This treatise concerns the association with feeling (*vedanā*). These ten afflictions—namely, the three of greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*)—whether innate (*sahaja*) or discursive (*vikalpita*), are all associated with the five feelings.
Question: Greed is a state of attachment; how can it be associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*)?

Hatred is by nature mere resentment; how could joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) arise from it? Answer: When greed encounters adverse conditions, it also gives rise to sorrow and suffering. When hatred encounters favorable objects, joy [arises].

Pride associated with pleasure is common to both [types of pride]. One master says that the pride arising from both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptualized (*vikalpita*) [ignorance] is associated with four feelings, excluding only the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).
Question: How can pride be associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*)? Answer: Because one relies upon inferior aggregates (*skandha*) characterized by suffering, it is associated with sorrow.

One master says that innate *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") is also associated with the feeling of suffering, because in the realms of pure suffering (*ekāntaduḥkhagati*), the mental faculty (*manas*) possesses suffering. If [one were to] divide...
The distinct type of pride (*māna*) does not coexist with suffering, because that pride is absent within the realms of pure suffering (*ekānta-duḥkha-gati*).
The reason it is absent is that within the realms of pure suffering, there is no permeation by false teachers or false teachings;

consequently, those beings do not create karma that leads to rebirth in the evil destinies, for such karma must depend upon discrimination (*vikalpa*) to be activated, and discrimination is absent within the realms of pure suffering. This also applies to doubt (*vicikitsā*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

The two grasps (*upādāna*) consist of four feelings (*vedanā*), excluding suffering (*duḥkha*). They arise solely through conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and lack the quality of being innate (*sahaja*).
Question: How can joy (*prīti*) arise when the mind is characterized by hesitation (*vicikitsā*)? Answer: If one suspects that a desired object is unattainable, there is neither suffering nor sorrow;

thus, the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) arises. Question: The two grasps regard various views and precepts as superior. Why, then, are they associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*)? Answer: The two grasps... [text ends].

If one takes as objects views associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*) or precepts associated with sorrow, as well as the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which they depend, [they are associated with sorrow] because they are associated with sorrow.
This is because even various unbeneficial and painful activities—such as rubbing the nose or plucking out hair—are accompanied by sorrow. One teacher says:

"The two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise simultaneously with the three feelings of joy (*sukha*), pleasure (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); they do not coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses, and therefore there is no suffering (*duḥkha*)."

Feeling (*vedanā*) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, there is no feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*). If one distinguishes [the feelings] associated with the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), there are four feelings, excluding suffering (*duḥkha*).
Question: Why is there sorrow? Answer: Because grasping at the aggregates of suffering and pleasure as either permanent or annihilated both gives rise to sorrow.

One teacher says that the co-arising views of self-identity and extremes are also accompanied by suffering; for in places where one experiences pure suffering, these views take that extreme [suffering] as their object.
Regarding the "aggregate of suffering" (*duḥkha-skandha*): because it is necessarily associated with suffering, the treatise states [this] below, citing proof as previously done.

As for the phrase "the rest is as explained before," this refers to the "discriminative views" (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*). All that has been discussed above is an investigation based on the actual meaning (*tattvārtha*), not an explanation based on coarse characteristics (*sthūla-nimitta*).

If categorized by their coarse characteristics, greed (*rāga*), conceit (*māna*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are all associated with three feelings, excluding the two feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*).
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is associated with only three feelings, excluding the two feelings of joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*). Ignorance (*moha*) is associated with all five feelings.
False views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are associated with four feelings, excluding only the feeling of physical pain. If greed and ignorance arise together...
Pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) extends throughout the four lower stages, namely from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the third dhyāna, because it is associated with all six consciousnesses.

However, pleasant feeling that arises concomitantly with pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) excludes the desire realm and extends only through the [upper] three dhyānas, because it is associated solely with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

As for doubt and independent ignorance (*avidyā*), in the desire realm they are associated only with the two feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*); they do not reach [the feeling of] aversion (*dveṣa*), as such does not exist in the higher realms.

Therefore, regarding the statement that "the other feelings arising together should be understood according to principle": it means that among the nine afflictions (*nava-āghāta-vastūni*) and the four feelings (*catasro vedanāḥ*), some exist and others do not within the three realms;
the same applies to the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
With how many of the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*) do these [afflictions] correspond? (Up to:

Because views are not distinct from wisdom when they arise together with it, this treatise maintains that they correspond with the object-specific factors. Greed, hatred, delusion, and pride may arise together with all five [object-specific factors]. Question:

Since their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and agitated, how can there be concentration (*samādhi*)? Answer: Because greed and the others arise by focusing intently on a single object, concentration can indeed be present. Doubt...
Furthermore, the five views may coexist with four [of the other mental factors]. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) excludes resolve (*adhimokṣa*), because doubt is characterized by indecisiveness.
Views do not coexist with wisdom (*prajñā*), for a view is itself wisdom; there cannot be multiple instances of wisdom within a single moment of consciousness.
To which natures are these ten afflictions subsumed? Although they frequently manifest, because they do not obstruct the wholesome, this treatise maintains that they correspond to all three natures.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) alone is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), because when hatred arises, it causes harm and distress to oneself and others.
The remaining nine are common to both the unwholesome and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If these nine belong to the two higher realms, they are exclusively...
They are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), not the unwholesome (*akuśala*), because they are suppressed by the power of the meditative absorption of the two realms.

If these nine [afflictions] are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and arise through discrimination (*vikalpaja*), they are not indeterminate; they are exclusively unwholesome, as they are capable of giving rise to evil karma.
If these innate [views] give rise to unwholesome conduct, they are also unwholesome; if they do not give rise to unwholesome conduct, they are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Why is this? Because they are subtle and do not obstruct wholesome states, and because they do not give rise to unwholesome [conduct].

One should know that among the nine [types of views], only the two innate views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) do not give rise to unwholesome karma and do not obstruct the wholesome. Only...
They are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
To which realm (*dhātu*) do these ten afflictions belong? [The answer is: They are taught according to their predominant occurrence or their specific objects;
this treatise concerns their correspondence with the realms. Among these ten afflictions, hatred (*pratigha*) belongs only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it does not exist in the higher realms.
Therefore, the remaining nine [afflictions] all pertain to the three realms. First, it is explained that lower-realm afflictions give rise to upper-realm afflictions.
If one is born in a lower stage and has not yet abandoned the afflictions of that lower stage, the afflictions of the upper stages do not manifest.

It is only when one suppresses the coarse innate [afflictions] of the lower stage and attains the fundamental meditative concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of that upper stage that the afflictions of the upper stage may all manifest.

Question: Why is it that the various contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) do not subdue conceptualized (*vikalpa*) and subtle innate (*sahaja*) afflictions, but only subdue the coarse innate afflictions, thereby attaining the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of those stages? Answer:

Although the various contaminated paths cannot subdue conceptualized and subtle innate afflictions, they are able to subdue and eliminate the coarse innate afflictions, whereby one gradually attains the fundamental concentration.

Because those innate gross afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) operate by way of an external orientation and are capable of deluding objects, and because their distracted and coarse agitation directly obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they must first be suppressed before that concentration can be attained.
Once that concentration has been attained, the discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-utpanna-kleśa*) and the subtle innate afflictions of the higher realms (*ūrdhva-dhātu*) are then able to manifest.
Next, it is explained how afflictions of a lower stage arise in a higher stage. If...
In a higher realm, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realms—both those arising from discrimination and those arising spontaneously—are all capable of manifesting.
For example, when one born in the fourth *asaṃjñi-sattva* heaven has exhausted its celestial retribution and abandons that celestial form, a *antarābhava* body manifests.

At that time, one who slanders an Arhat and must undergo a future existence falls into hell; at that moment, the *asaṃjñi-sattva* being, though their body remains in the higher realm, [experiences these states]. Five.

The signs of decline appear; as one is about to be born into a lower realm, one immediately gives rise to the craving and defilement that moistens birth in that lower realm, thereby attaining birth in the lower realm.
Question: Since it is said that those in a higher realm can give rise to afflictions of a lower realm, why is it said that one born in a higher realm does not give rise to those of a lower realm?

Answer: This is stated according to the majority of cases—that [the higher levels] do not give rise to [defilements of] the lower. In reality, however, they do occasionally give rise to the defilements of the lower.

To clarify this, it is explained that the upper and lower levels serve as mutual conditions for one another; first, those of the lower levels take the upper as their object, and the afflictions of the lower levels also take the upper levels as their objects.

The treatise states that when the affliction of craving in the desire realm seeks rebirth in a higher plane, it does so because one relishes the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of that higher plane.

Since hatred (*vyāpāda*) loathes both cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), it likewise loathes the detachment from desire (*vairāgya*). Thus, we know that both craving and hatred take the higher planes as their objects.

If one discusses them in terms of taking all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the higher realms collectively as their object, then the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) clings to "self" and "mine," while the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) clings to annihilationism or eternalism.

The conceit of self (*asmimāna*) causes the mind to be uplifted; thus, it is able to take what is superior as its object. Since this is established, the principle that the other five [types of conceit] also take what is superior as their object is fully proven. Question:
If it is said that lower stages can take higher stages as objects, why does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* state that greed and so forth of the lower realms do not take the higher as objects?
Answer: This is either stated based on coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*), or it is stated based on specific objects of focus (*viśeṣālambana*). It is based on...

Regarding the explanation based on coarse characteristics (*audārika-lakṣaṇa*): it is because one does not perceive the dharmas of this stage while grasping at the dharmas of another stage as "self" or "mine.

Regarding the explanation based on specific conditions (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*): it is because the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) necessarily arises dependent upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

For these two reasons, it is said that the lower stages do not take the higher stages as their objects. Question: Why is it that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages also take the lower stages as their objects? Answer: Because...
Those born in a higher realm, relying on their own superior virtues, look down upon and despise sentient beings of the lower realms; therefore, they are able to take the lower realm as an object.

If one discusses the general taking of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the lower realm as an object, then the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—which clings to "self" and "mine"—the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—which clings to annihilation or permanence—and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which causes the mind to become stained and attached, can all take the lower realm as an object.
Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the latter three views, it should be understood that they likewise function in this manner.
It is the same here. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is not mentioned because there is no hatred above; delusion (*moha*) is not mentioned because it is definitely present.
As for the statement "below," the resolution of the objection is as previously explained.
Regarding these ten afflictions, by what are they subsumed among the categories of "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth?
They are not subsumed under "in training" or "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), because those [two] are exclusively wholesome. This treatise corresponds to the sequence of stages:

these ten afflictions are not included within the stages of being in training or beyond training, because being in training and beyond training subsume only the nature of the wholesome, and do not subsume the unwholesome. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "The meaning of 'skillful means' for one in training is one."

One portion of all [phenomena] is "in training" (*śaikṣa*), which refers to the meaning of the excellence of those in training. One portion of all [phenomena] is "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), [referring to those who have reached the ultimate].
All wholesome, afflicted, and neutral phenomena other than these two types constitute one portion that is "neither in training nor beyond training" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
What do these ten afflictions abandon? (Up to: Because they do not contradict the contemplation of the truths (*satya-darśana*), they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

In this treatise, they are [treated as] suppressed and abandoned. These ten afflictions are not non-abandonable; in the state of Buddhahood, both their manifest forms and seeds are exhausted, as such defilements no longer exist there.
They are associated exclusively with the wholesome and so forth. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "When one realizes the truths..."
Regarding the meaning of what is to be abandoned through the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of wisdom: one portion of all [factors] is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).

Regarding the meaning of what is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) subsequent to that clear realization: one portion of all [factors] is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the meaning of the permanent abandonment of all defiled factors as their antidote, as well as the meaning of those already abandoned: one portion of all [factors] is not to be abandoned (*aheya*). Now, it is said that they are "not non-[to-be-abandoned]."

"Those to be abandoned" explicitly indicates that these are abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Regarding these ten [afflictions] that arise from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), they have already been suppressed prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*);
at the time of the true path of seeing, both their seeds and their manifest activity are severed. Therefore, it is said that they are "abandoned solely by the path of seeing.

Of these ten afflictions, four are exclusively conceptual, while six are both conceptual and innate (*sahaja*). As for those that are innate, they consist of attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), ignorance (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
This refers to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). It may occasionally arise during the seven stages (*bhūmi*), but it is permanently suppressed in the eighth stage.

Upon the manifestation of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), it is severed all at once; therefore, it is said to be abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for the ten types of conceptual discrimination abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they are severed all at once because, at the time of the true path of seeing, one takes [the Truths] as a collective object.
The Four Truths. Therefore, it is a single, perpetual abandonment. Question: Why do the abandonments of afflictions involve both general and specific objects? Answer:

Because when one is deluded regarding the characteristics of the Truths, there are both general and specific modes of delusion. Regarding "general," this means that the ten afflictions generally delude one regarding the Four Truths.

This is because the two truths of Suffering and Origin are the causes and effects of the mundane world, and thus serve as the basis and locus for the ten afflictions; therefore, they are deluded [regarding them].

Yet they do not cease. The two truths of cessation and the path are the causes and fruits of supramundane reality; they are objects feared by the ten afflictions. Therefore, being deluded, one does not cultivate them.

It is precisely because of this general delusion that there is general objectification (*samantālambana*). As for the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*), it means that the ten afflictions arise from specific delusions regarding the four truths.

For example, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are deluded only with respect to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and are not deluded [with respect to the other truths].

Regarding the three truths, the remaining eight [afflictions] are deluded regarding all [truths]. Why, then, are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) deluded only regarding the truth of suffering?

It is because they do not know that this body is the fruit of suffering; instead, they cling to this fruit of suffering as "self" and "mine," and they cling to it as being either annihilated or eternal.

Therefore, it is said that these two arise only with respect to the fruit. Since their object of delusion is so firm, when practicing contemplation, one must specifically employ the two [aspects of] emptiness and non-self.
The Dharma serves as the antidote to the view of a self and the view of extremes. This antidotal Dharma also belongs to the Truth of Suffering, because it contemplates only the object of suffering.

Why do eight [of the ten afflictions] pertain to all four truths? It is because doubt, the view of a self, the view of extremes, and false views directly delude one regarding the principle of suffering.

Regarding the phrase "intimate delusion": it refers to the failure to realize that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are fundamentally without a self (*anātman*), yet giving rise to the twenty modes of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

This is the view of a personal identity that is deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha*). Taking this very view as its basis, one clings to the five aggregates of clinging as either annihilated or eternal;
this is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) that is deluded regarding suffering. Furthermore, there are various wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), such as the claim that there is no giving.
...and so forth, up to the actions of good and evil conduct, their karmic fruits, and their maturation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, to deny the existence of parents or spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka*) is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha*). If one is unable to reach a certainty regarding the Truth of Suffering and instead gives rise to hesitation, this is doubt (*vicikitsā*) deluded regarding suffering.
If there is a grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that falsely takes all views deluded regarding suffering to be [supreme], [this is also a misconception].
First, to hold that one can attain purity, liberation, and transcendence through this is the adherence to views regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Furthermore, to falsely grasp and follow such a view, and to regard the prohibitions and precepts associated with that view as being foremost for attaining purity, liberation, and transcendence, is the adherence to rules and observances regarding suffering (*duḥkha-śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Due to this clinging, regarding the views one has produced for oneself...

To cherish and be firmly attached [to views] is delusion regarding suffering as greed (*lobha*). To give rise to views toward others and, suppressing them, cause harm and resentment, is delusion regarding suffering as hatred (*dveṣa*).
Furthermore, relying on these views and giving rise to arrogance and inflation toward their kin is delusion regarding suffering as pride (*māna*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is twofold: first, that which is associated with various views, doubt, greed, and so forth; second, that which is solitary.
Regarding those who give rise to delusion concerning the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), both of these are ignorance (*avidyā*) that is deluded regarding suffering.

The preceding section clarified that all ten afflictions are deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The following section clarifies that eight [afflictions] are deluded regarding the latter three truths; among them, doubt (*vicikitsā*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) directly delude regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya*) and so forth.

As for the two graspings (*parāmarśa*), craving (*rāga*), and so forth, they should be understood by analogy with [the afflictions] regarding suffering. This refers to various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas...

[This is] the gate. To slander [the truth of suffering] by means of wrong views—calculating that Īśvara and so forth are the cause of all things and that there is no other cause—is the wrong view arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

If one holds to those various views as supreme and capable of attaining purification, this is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Origination. If, with respect to those things that conform to such views...

To regard the precepts and prohibitions received from one's own dharma as supreme and capable of bringing about purification is the attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

The rest is as previously explained. Thus, these eight kinds of afflictive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are delusions regarding the Truth of Origination and are abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, if various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas reckon that the world is finite, infinite, or resort to the "evasive equivocation" (*amarāvikkhepa*) regarding immortality—[these are likewise abandoned through the vision of origination].

A portion of the various views, as well as those who propound the theory of *nirvāṇa* in the present life, deny the quality of abandonment possessed by Arhats and slander the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), recklessly imagining a false liberation; this is a false view arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation.

Furthermore, if there is the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) that takes those various views to be supreme and capable of attaining purity, this is [likewise] delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation.

One gives rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). If, regarding those dharmas that accord with such views, one regards the precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) undertaken therein as supreme and capable of bringing about purification, this is the grasping of precepts and observances arising from delusion regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Due to this adherence, one cherishes and becomes attached to the views one has personally generated; this is greed for cessation arising from delusion. Regarding the views generated by others, one suppresses, opposes, and harms them.
And one gives rise to hatred. This is delusion regarding cessation and hatred. The rest is as previously explained.

Thus, these eight kinds of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are delusions regarding the Truth of Cessation and are abandoned through the vision of cessation. If one denies the existence of the true worldly fruit of Arhatship, [this constitutes a view of non-existence].
Taking all-knowledge as the guide, yet regarding the conditioned and the untainted as "immortal equivocation" (*amarā-vikṣepa*), this is one portion of wrong view that slanders the Truth of the Path.
It is not a true departure; it is the false reckoning of what is not the path as being the right path, [claiming] it can exhaust and transcend all suffering.
This is called the wrong view of being lost on the path. If there is the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), one grasps that which is erroneous.
To regard [such views] as supreme and capable of bringing about purification is called the adherence to views regarding the path (*mārga-dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

If one regards the various dharmas that accord with those views, as well as the prohibitions and precepts undertaken therein, as supreme and capable of bringing about purification, this is called the adherence to precepts and observances arising from confusion regarding the path (*mārga-utthita-śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The remaining afflictions of confusion regarding the path, such as craving and so forth, should be understood as previously explained.
These eight kinds of afflictive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are deluded regarding the Truth of the Path and are abandoned through the vision of the Path (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*). Question:

How can hatred (*pratigha*) be associated with Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*)? Answer: Hatred can indeed directly delude one regarding Cessation and the Path, because one gives rise to aversion and jealousy out of fear of them.
That is to say, being deluded regarding Cessation and the Path, one gives rise to a mind of fear, a mind of harm, and a mind of resentment.
The mind. In this way, hatred is also associated with delusion regarding the Path to Cessation (*nirodhamārga*). Therefore, the subsequent summary states:

"The relative proximity and distance of delusion regarding the Truths is as follows in its coarse characteristics. To speak of "distance": it arises by means of transformation, mediation, reliance, and attachment to reflections.
To speak of "proximity": it is like tongs grasping an object, or like the sun radiating light. All of these are subsumed under what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*). If...

To explain in detail: these are generally abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If greed, hatred, pride, doubt, and the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) arise in association with false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), they are associated with the six consciousnesses and are abandoned accordingly as those [afflictions] are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
As for innate self-view (*sahaja-satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and the craving, pride, and ignorance associated with those two views—although they are delusions...

The Truth of Suffering is associated with the seventh [mental consciousness], arising spontaneously; because it is subtle and difficult to sever, it is severed only through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Question: Since the ten afflictions, such as hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, are all deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths, why are these six [afflictions] said to be abandoned through the Path of Cultivation?
Answer: Although these [afflictions] such as hatred and attachment arise without being deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths, they arise from being deluded regarding specific objects;

nevertheless, they do not contradict the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, and are therefore to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). For example, although one does not give rise to craving for worldly causes and effects, one may still crave the realization of *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
and although one does not give rise to hatred toward worldly causes and effects, one may still feel hatred.
Although they have not yet attained *nirvāṇa* without remainder, they do not cling to the two worldly views of annihilationism and eternalism;

yet they may cling to the two supramundane views of existence and emptiness. Although they do not rely on conceptual discrimination to give rise to pride, they may nevertheless rely on the notion of a "self" in phenomena (*dharmātman*) to give rise to pride.
Although all afflictions possess objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), the distinctions regarding other categories should be contemplated according to reason;
this is the correspondence with the objects of focus (*ālambana*) in this treatise. These ten afflictions all possess objective aspects.

Those that arise simultaneously (*sahaja*) have a real basis (*dravya*), whereas those that arise through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*) lack a real basis. These are termed "afflictions that take as their object both entities and non-entities."

However, although those directly perceived objects (*sākṣāt-ālambana*) are all with-outflow (*sāsrava*), the essential substance (*svabhāva*) upon which they rely may also be without-outflow (*anāsrava*).

This is because afflictions take the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as their essential substance; therefore, they are said to be "afflictions that take both the with-outflow and the without-outflow as their objects.

If they take the afflictions of their own stage as their object and directly grasp their substance, then the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) resembles the substance; this is called "taking a portion as the object" (*bhāgālambana*).
Regarding the phrase "objects arising from other sources": as for the term "objects," this is because they possess substantial reality (*dravya*).

However, when taking the two truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as objects, or when taking the afflictions (*kleśa*) of other stages (*bhūmi*) as objects, one is unable to directly apprehend their substantial reality; therefore, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the original essence (*bimba*) do not resemble one another.
These are called "objects arising from conceptualization" (*vikalpa*). Regarding the term "named objects" (*nāma-viṣaya*): they lack substantial reality and yet exist.

Regarding the names, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "The objects of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are briefly of five kinds: first, objects that arise from false conceptualization, which refers to the objects of the ten conceptualized afflictions;
second, objects of views, which refers to the objects of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
third, objects of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which refers to the object of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth, objects arising from one's own conceptualization..."

These are named "objects" (*viṣaya*). They are the objects of apprehension for the two types of grasping (*grāha*). The fifth [category] consists of spontaneously occurring, stable objective entities;
these are the objects of the innate afflictions (*kleśa*). This concludes the indication under the remaining headings.

The characteristics of the six root afflictions have already been explained [up to the point where they] universally defile the mind; therefore, they are called the "great secondary afflictions" (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*).
This explains the fifth category of secondary afflictions. First, a question is posed; next, a verse is cited as the answer. The *Śāstra* states:

first, the general name is explained. Regarding the term "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), it refers to the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*), as well as forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), and...
The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as restlessness and the like, are merely distinctions in the states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).

Alternatively, although the five factors—lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—possess distinct substantial entities (*dravya*), they are all of the same category as the root afflictions;
because these arise with the root afflictions as their cause, they are termed "secondary" (*anu*). However, as for the ten [afflictions] beginning with anger (*krodha*)...
When compared with their own respective categories, these two arise only individually within unwholesome minds; if they were to arise simultaneously, there would necessarily never be a second.
Therefore, they are called "minor. In contrast, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) function together within their own category and pervade all unwholesome natures.

They do not pertain to the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*), but are merely termed "intermediate. The eight factors, such as restlessness (*auddhatya*) and so forth, are termed "concomitant" (*sahaja*) within their own class;

they pervade both types of defilement and arise simultaneously with their acquisition (*prāpti*). Because they cannot be termed "minor," and because all defiled states are pervasive, they cannot be termed "intermediate.
Since these two meanings are distinct, these eight are termed "great."

What is anger (*krodha*)? It is that which arises based on an object present before one. Since there is no distinct characteristic or function of anger apart from hatred (*dveṣa*), anger is defined as follows:
it is the outburst of wrath. Its nature consists in the arousal of fury toward an object currently present that is harmful;
its function consists in grasping weapons. That is to say, anger predominantly gives rise to violent and malicious bodily manifest actions (*kāya-vijñapti*).
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If one is bound by the obsession of hatred (*pratigha-samyojana*), it can cause the facial expression to become fierce and agitated.
If one is bound by the obsessions of the afflictions (*kleśa-samyojana*), it can cause one to take up swords and staves, engage in combat, litigation, and conflict;
thus it is called 'fury' (*pradāsa*). It is subsumed under a portion of hatred. If, in a single moment of anger, one forgets both oneself and one's kin, such anger must not exist."
If one can bring peace to the world through a single outburst of anger, or transcend the mundane world through a single fit of indignation, then this anger cannot be dispensed with. Why?
Because resentment (*upanāha*) is preceded by anger; for apart from anger, there is no distinct characteristic or function of resentment.

Because one previously harbored anger and malice without relinquishing them, they eventually became a festering resentment. Whenever one reflects upon this, the body becomes feverish and the mind is distressed;
for those who harbor such hatred, it arises from an inability to maintain forbearance and endurance, burning the heart like fire and causing constant heat and affliction.

Thus, it is subsumed under a portion of *dveṣa* (hatred). This resentment must not exist. If resentment has not yet been entirely eliminated by the power of the Path, one should [abandon] it once it has arisen.
It is not equal to that of the sages and worthies; this regret cannot be absent.
Why would one conceal the transgressions one has committed oneself? (Up to: it cannot be maintained that these are merely a portion of greed.

Concealment (*mrakṣa*) is protection. It refers to the nature of hiding and shielding over the transgressions and evils committed throughout one’s life, fearing that they will result in the loss of material support and reputation;
one acts solely out of dread that others might discover them. If one conceals a sin and fails to disclose it, one will inevitably experience regret and distress later on and will not attain peace.

Therefore, regret and distress constitute its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*). Thus, the Great [Treatise... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "是以大". This indicates the sentence is incomplete. The translation reflects the available text.)
The human mind is like a bright breeze and a clear moon; it has nothing to conceal or protect. When one commits a fault, everyone sees it;
when one reforms their faults, everyone looks up to them. If one conceals another's evil, this covering must not be absent. Thus said a teacher.
This concealment (*mrakṣa*) is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*). One who conceals their faults looks only to the present and refuses to disclose them;

because they do not fear the suffering of hell in the future, such a person is characterized by delusion. One master says that this concealment is subsumed under portions of both greed (*lobha*) and delusion:
because one fears losing present gains and offerings, it is driven by greed, while the act of hiding and protecting [the fault] is due to delusion.

Liu (the "exposed") is driven by delusion (*moha*). The treatises explain its coarse characteristics as being solely a portion of delusion, just as it is said that restlessness (*auddhatya*) is subsumed under the category of greed (*rāga*);
this too is based on its coarse manifestation rather than it actually being a portion of greed, because restlessness pervades all defiled minds.
What is *pradāsa* (malice)? It is preceded by anger (*krodha*) and resentment (*upanāha*).

Since there is no distinct characteristic or function of malice apart from hatred (*dveṣa*), this malice likewise arises with anger and resentment as its antecedents. Thereupon, one recollects past evils and encounters present adverse conditions;
the mind gives rise to violent heat, becoming fierce, perverse, and contrary. One frequently utters clamorous, violent, coarse, vulgar, and base speech.
Because it stings others, it is called a *jū* (蛆), meaning a *chich-jū* (蝍蛆), which is a centipede. "Stinging" (*shaku*) refers to the exertion of its venom.
This, too, is subsumed under one part of hatred (*dveṣa*).

What is meant by "jealousy" (*īrṣyā*)? It refers to sacrificing oneself for personal fame and profit. [This continues until: because there is no distinct characteristic or function of jealousy apart from anger (*dveṣa*).
To follow after external objects with one's person is called "sacrificing oneself" (*xùn*).

This refers to a jealous person who, upon hearing of or seeing the prosperity and nobility of others, constantly harbors deep sorrow and distress within their heart and finds no peace.
