Therefore it is said: "Among women, whether beautiful or ugly, once they enter the palace, they are envied; among men, whether..."
When the worthy and the unworthy enter court and are met with jealousy, this too is subsumed under a portion of *dveṣa* (hatred).
Why is it considered *mātsarya* (avarice)? Because it is an attachment to wealth and the Dharma; for apart from greed (*lobha*), there is no separate characteristic or function of avarice.

*Jian* (miserliness) means guarding and cherishing. *Tan* (addiction) refers to being submerged and intoxicated. *Zhu* (attachment) refers to stubborn adherence. *Cai* (wealth) refers to material resources. *Fa* (Dharma) refers to the teachings of the Path.
To possess wealth yet not relinquish it is called being a "slave guarding money. To possess the Dharma yet not bestow it is called being a "mute sheep-monk."

"Secret" (mi) means to conceal in a hidden place. "Miserly" (lin) means to harbor [attachment] within this. As for the "base hoarder," it is because they are base and stingy that they are able to accumulate.
This is subsumed under one portion of greed.
What is deception? It is for the sake of profit and reputation... [omitted] ...because there is no difference between the two in terms of the characteristic and function of deception.
Deception (*māyā*) is to delude others with words. Pretending (*kuhana*) means feigning. Guile (*lapanā*) refers to being crafty;

fraud (*naimittikatā*) refers to being deceitful. As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are five kinds: first, pretentious distinctiveness (*kuhana*), which occurs because of greed for gain and offerings.
Practicing the twelve *dhūta* ascetic virtues, he forms this thought: "Others have performed these practices and have already obtained veneration and offerings;
I too shall perform these practices and perhaps obtain them as well. For the sake of gain and offerings, he alters his deportment and feigns the possession of virtue.
Second, regarding intimacy with others: because of greed for gain and offerings, he goes to the homes of donors and says to them, "You all are like..."
My parents, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen are no different from you. If you have anything you require, I can provide it;
if there is anything that must be done, I can do it, regardless of distance. When you come to inquire after me, my staying here is solely for your sake.
It is not for the sake of seeking gain or offerings, nor out of greed for patrons, though I am capable of eloquent discourse.
They entice the minds of others through three types of agitation. That is to say, there are those who disregard the fault of greed and, desiring to obtain material goods, manifest signs of craving.
They say to a donor: "This robe, bowl, and sitting mat are excellent; if I were to obtain them, I would be able to make use of them.
A person capable of giving such things as they please is difficult to find. Furthermore, they say to the donor: "You..."
The family’s soup, rice, cakes, and fruits are fragrant and delicious; their clothing is also excellent. If you constantly provide for me, I shall surely give these things to you through my kinsmen.
This is the fourth form of flattery: because of greed for gain and offerings, one says to a donor, "You are extremely stingy;
you cannot even give to your parents, brothers, sisters, wife, children, or relatives—who else could you possibly give to?"

If someone were able to obtain your property, the donor would feel ashamed and, bowing his head, would bestow it upon you. When he reaches other households, he says to those people, "You possess great merit;
your human existence is not in vain. Arhats and others constantly enter your home, sitting and rising with you and conversing with you.
He does this so that the donor will certainly think, "I am a great Arhat. These are the five causes.

Seeking gain through gain means: using items for one’s livelihood—such as robes, alms bowls, saṃghāṭī cloaks, and sitting mats—to show them to others and say, "These were brought and given to me by the king, donors, or other noble persons."
This causes the donor to think: "If even kings and nobles provide offerings to him, how much more should I do so?
Thus, by means of this benefit, one seeks further gain; it is for this reason that it is called [wrong livelihood]. Regarding those who practice wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*):

it refers to seeking to sustain one's body and life through falsehood and deception, rather than through the food of right livelihood (*samyagājīva*); hence it is called wrong livelihood. Wisdom (*jñāna*).
The treatise states: A bhikṣu is called a "mendicant" (bhikṣu) because he maintains his life through purity.
As it is said in a sutra: Śāriputra entered the city to beg for food; having obtained it, he sat down to eat. A brahmin named Viśuddhanetra asked him, "Are you eating?"

He replied, "I eat. Viśuddhamati asked, "Do you eat with your mouth turned downward? He replied, "No. "Do you eat with your mouth turned upward? He replied, "No. "Do you eat with your mouth turned to the side?
He replied, "No. "Do you eat with your mouth turned all around? He replied, "No. Viśuddhamati said, "There are four ways of eating.
I have now questioned you on these, and you have answered 'no' to each. I do not understand this; you should explain it to me."

"What are 'downward-facing mouth' food and the others? Śāriputra replied: "There are renunciants who compound medicines, sow grains, plant trees, and so forth, sustaining their lives through such impure means;

this is called 'downward-facing mouth' food. Those who gaze upward at the stars, the sun, the moon, the wind, the rain, thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts, sustaining their lives through such impure means;
this is called 'upward-facing mouth' food. Those who fawn and curry favor with those of power..."

Acting as a messenger to the four quarters, using clever speech to seek much, and sustaining one's life through impure means—this is called "food from the mouth of the directions" (*disā-mukha-bhojana*).

Learning various incantations and divinations to calculate good and bad fortune, and sustaining one's life through impure means—this is called "food from the mouth of the intermediate directions" (*vidisā-mukha-bhojana*).
I do not fall into these four types of food, for I sustain my life by begging for pure alms. These, moreover, are each [rooted in] greed and delusion.
It is subsumed under one part.

What is meant by *śāṭhya* (deceit)? It refers to the act of deceiving others for the sake of self-gain. (Omitted) Because there is no distinct characteristic or function of deceit apart from these two.
*Śāṭhya* is defined as the use of clever speech to flatter others. Deceiving others (*vañcana*) is defined as misleading them regarding what they do not know or see.
"Feigning extraordinary deportment" means falsely manifesting a peculiar and marvelous manner of bearing, such that one's movements and stops differ from those of ordinary people.

"Risky" refers to what is dangerous and evil; "crooked" refers to what is deviant and perverse. "Deceitful and audacious" means to deceive others by taking advantage of their ignorance and to entrap them through fabrication.

To deceive others by concealing one's true nature is to hide oneself from view. To bend and comply with the exigencies of the times is to adopt the fawning countenance and servile posture of a slave, shifting one's conduct like a reed in the wind.
To act for the sake of winning another's favor is to strive to please people and flatter them.
To conceal one's own failings is to suppress one's unwholesome deeds while highlighting one's virtues. A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (the *dharma-pada*). This is...

The Buddha spoke these sincere words: "To act with a deceitful and crooked mind is to contravene the correct instructions of one's teachers and friends. This [deceit] is also subsumed under one portion each of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).

As for what constitutes harm toward sentient beings—[the definition of which extends from] "harming" up to the specific characteristics of malice (*vyāpāda*)—these should be explained by analogy with their opposites, the wholesome states.
"Inflicting harm" (*hiṃsā*) refers to severing the life-faculty of a being. "Afflicting" (*vihethana*) refers to causing alarm, fear, and oppression.
For example, it is like setting out bows, arrows, nets, and snares to drive them away, causing birds to flutter in disarray above and fish to struggle in disarray below, so that they find no peace;
all such acts are termed "afflicting."
What is *mada* (intoxication/presumption)? It refers to being haughty and self-reliant regarding one's own prosperity (*sva-sampatti*).

Regarding "one's own prosperity," this means being satisfied with oneself, such as wealth, nobility, talent, eloquence, administrative affairs, literary skill, fame, and power. Through these various factors, one gives rise to deep defilement. (Note: This is because there is no distinct characteristic or function of *mada* apart from the absence of greed. *Mada* is the act of being conceited and relying upon oneself.

Regarding "one's own prosperity," it refers to those who are content with themselves—such as those possessing wealth, status, ability, speech, governance, literature, reputation, and influence. Due to these factors, one develops a profound attachment.

They become attached. Some use wealth and status to treat others with contempt and act with arrogance; others use their literary talent, fame, or power to treat others with contempt and act with arrogance.
Their eyes look down upon the four seas, as if no one else existed beside them, like a drunken man who is being toyed with by his liquor.
Therefore it is said that intoxication and arrogance constitute its nature, and all defiled phenomena arise based upon it. The *Book of Documents* says:

"Do not be like Danzhu’s arrogance. The *Analects* says: "Even if one possesses the excellence of the Duke of Zhou’s talent, if they are arrogant and stingy, there is nothing further to be observed in them.
Arrogance is precisely the obstacle to humility; this too is subsumed under a portion of greed, arising from attachment to oneself.
This is because one gives rise to arrogance when things go well. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are seven such types:
namely, pride of health, pride of youth, pride of longevity, pride of noble lineage, pride of physical strength and beauty, pride of wealth and status, and pride of extensive learning, and so forth.
What is the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)? It refers to disregarding one's own Dharma. [It acts as] an obstruction to the growth of shame and the proliferation of various unwholesome deeds.
Regarding "disregarding one's own Dharma": when a person reaches a state of shamelessness, they do not even regard their own person; how much less so the Dharma of the Path?
Consequently, regarding all matters that are unbenevolent and unrighteous, they have no hesitation at all, and there is nothing they will not do for their own sake.
Thus, when one encounters those who are worthy, virtuous, and possessed of merit, one treats them with contempt and rejects them, refusing to associate with them;

this is the nature of shamelessness (*ahrīkya*). Since one does not draw near to the worthy or honor the virtuous, one will inevitably become intimate with ignorant associates and factions, thereby engendering evil conduct; this is the function of shamelessness.
What is the lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) that disregards the world? It obstructs the growth of shame and causes the proliferation of various unwholesome actions.
To disregard the world means that those who take pleasure in committing evil do not even care for themselves;

how then could they have the leisure to heed the censure, reproach, or rebuke of the people of the world? Thus, a sutra says: "There are two white dharmas capable of saving sentient beings: first, shame (*hrī*)."
Second, the two types of shame (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*). *Hrī* (self-respect) is not committing an offense oneself; *apatrāpya* (dread of blame) is not instructing others to do so.

*Hrī* is feeling internal shame; *apatrāpya* is confessing one's faults to others. *Hrī* is being ashamed before the devas; *apatrāpya* is being ashamed before human beings. One who possesses both *hrī* and *apatrāpya*—
One may be called a human being; one who lacks shame and dread of blame is called a beast. Therefore it is said: "The shameless have shame.

To be shameless means not to feel shame for one's transgressions and evils. This is a common characteristic shared by both [humans and beasts]; it is their outflow (*niṣyanda*), not their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

The following section clarifies that not being ashamed of one's faults and evils is a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), not a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). It is the direct opposite of the previously mentioned *hrī* (moral shame) and *apatrāpya* (moral dread). How so?
*Auddhatya* (restlessness) causes the mind to engage with its objects [in such a way that] it is not tranquil; this is not its specific characteristic.

Excitement (*auddhatya*) refers to being restless and flighty, leaping about across the four seas and traversing the nine provinces in an instant, such that the mind cannot attain even momentary tranquility;
this is its essential nature. Its function is to obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*) and calm abiding (*śamatha*).
The first teacher says: "Excitement (*auddhatya*) is subsumed under the category of greed (*rāga*), because it arises by recollecting past pleasurable experiences.
The second teacher says: "Excitement pervades all defiled minds and is not subsumed under greed alone;

furthermore, it is said that excitement has no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being instead subsumed under the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) shared among these ten afflictions. The third teacher establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute this:

Restlessness (*auddhatya*) has its own distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It pervades all defiled minds and is not subsumed under the category of "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the afflictions, such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth.
It is not the case that something lacks substantial reality simply because it is said to be subsumed under another category; for lack of faith and the like are also not merely nominal (*prajñapti*).
Question: If this is so, why do the treatises state that the afflictions are subsumed under common characteristics and are conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*)?

Answer: As with sleep and so forth, it is said that [restlessness] exists conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*). This is spoken in accordance with its dependent characteristics. Below, its intrinsic nature is set forth:
"The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of restlessness (*auddhatya*) is clamor and false agitation, which prevents co-arising factors from attaining tranquility;

this is its specific characteristic. If one were to claim that it has no separate self-nature apart from the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), then it should not be mentioned separately as an obstacle to serenity (*praśrabdhi*).
*Ma-tha* (mada) is its functional activity. Since there must be an essence before there can be activity, non-quiescence is not a distinct characteristic from this;
rather, agitation is its very nature.
How is it that *styāna* (sloth/torpor) acts as a direct obstacle to *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) regarding the object of the mind, rather than being mere delusion or darkness?
*Styāna* refers to a state of obscurity and heaviness.

It is a mental factor (*caitta*) that causes the luminous and non-obscured nature of the mind to gradually become obscure and gradually sink, rendering it incapable of function and unable to bear its burden. This is it.
This is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Consequently, the body fails to attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the mind cannot enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

One master says that torpor (*styāna*) is subsumed under the category of delusion (*moha*). A second master says that it is not merely a part of delusion, but is subsumed among all ten afflictions (*kleśa*).
A third master says that torpor has a distinct intrinsic nature, namely, a state of mental dullness (*jaḍatā*). He asks: what is this dullness?

What is the distinction between *styāna* (torpor) and *mūḍha* (delusion)? Answer: Delusion has the characteristic of confusion and darkness (*sammoha*), while torpor has the characteristic of mental dullness and heaviness (*staimitya*).
That which has the characteristic of confusion and darkness refers to a state of total lack of knowledge and awareness.

That which has the characteristic of mental dullness and heaviness, although not a state of total lack of knowledge and awareness, is nevertheless caused by a state of stupor and heaviness that renders the body and mind incapable of [functioning].
One attains mastery over pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Therefore, these two differ in essence.
Why is it that lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) regarding reality, virtue, and capability [is the cause], while this [pliancy] is the fruit, and not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Lack of faith means the absence of sincerity. Since there is no truthfulness, one consequently cannot accept any actual fact or principle;
one does not give rise to a fondness for true and pure virtues, nor does one arouse a desire for wholesome capacities.
Furthermore, one does not believe that one’s own mind can become a Buddha, nor that one’s own mind can become a Yao or a Shun.
It is solely because of a lack of faith that one does not diligently cultivate and purify [the mind].
Being negligent and superficial, it causes the field of the mind to become increasingly overgrown and defiled, until weeds, wild grasses, and thistles fill its midst.

Now, while all mental factors such as anger are called "defiled dharmas," the single dharma of lack of faith is a defilement even more extreme. It not only defiles oneself but also defiles others; for example:
It is like a pig wallowed in mud or a dog with the mange. Therefore it is said: "If a person lacks faith, one does not know what they can do.
How could one be indolent regarding the categories of good and evil? [This extends] to that which is neither pure nor defiled, and neither faithful nor faithless.
One who is indolent does not cultivate what is wholesome and does not abandon what is unwholesome; this refers to the dissolution of all faculties and the failure of all undertakings.
Therefore, it is said that its nature is laziness. Because such a person is unwilling to exert effort toward the wholesome in their daily life, it causes all defilements to gradually increase.
Therefore, it is said that its function is the augmentation of defilement. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "That is to say, one clings to..."
Taking sleep and reclining as one’s pleasure, one wastes day and night, abandoning all categories of wholesome qualities. Question:
Is it not diligence for one who goes out under the stars and returns under the stars, striving earnestly for profit and zealously pursuing fame?

Answer: Although this involves exerting effort toward defiled matters, it is nonetheless indolence; for while one is diligent regarding defilements, one is negligent regarding what is wholesome. This is the nature of defiled phenomena.

Furthermore, because wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) would otherwise decline, it is only when one applies oneself diligently to the good throughout the day that it can be called "exertion" (*vīrya*).
If one exerts oneself in neutral (*avyākṛta*) or trivial matters, while making no progress nor regressing in the category of the wholesome, this is also termed "laziness.

This [exertion] is subsumed under "desire" (*chanda*) and "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*); if one desires the good, it is subsumed under the nature of the wholesome, whereas if one desires the unwholesome, it is...

It is subsumed under the nature of unwholesomeness (*akuśala*). If there is no specific record [of its nature], it is because one’s acceptance, desire, and inclination reside in the interval between faith and lack of faith, or purity and impurity; therefore, it has no distinct nature.
How is heedlessness (*pramāda*) categorized among the defiled and purified categories? One should investigate its characteristics in the same manner as heedfulness (*apramāda*).
"Relaxation" (*fang*) means dissipation; "indulgence" (*yi*) means license—that is, a lack of self-restraint. As the Sūtra says: "To be absent for even a moment is like being a dead person.
How, then, can one afford to be dissipated? There is nothing else to study than seeking the lost mind. How, then, can one afford to be indulgent?

As soon as one lets go of restraint, one can no longer practice defense and cultivation; thus, evil increases while goodness diminishes. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that non-negligence (*apramāda*) is its nutriment.
This [non-negligence] is not a separate entity apart from the three unwholesome roots of laziness.
What is the loss of mindfulness regarding all objects of focus? The treatise further states that this pervades all defiled minds.
"Loss of mindfulness" means the forgetting of right mindfulness. As the Sūtra says: "If one can concentrate [the mind] in a single place, there is no task that cannot be accomplished.
Zhuangzi said: "When the will is undivided, the spirit becomes concentrated. When right mindfulness is forgotten, there is no sovereign within; thus...

[The topic] is subject to dispute. One teacher says that forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) is subsumed under a portion of mindfulness (*smṛti*). Another teacher says that forgetfulness is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*).
Yet another teacher says that mindfulness and delusion are each subsumed under their own respective portions.
What is distraction regarding various objects of focus? ... Thus, restlessness (*auddhatya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*) both pervade all defiled minds.
That which has "wandering" as its nature is like the flow of water that never turns back, or like the tossing of waves that never ceases.
Therefore, it is able to obstruct right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Since right concentration is absent, faulty wisdom (*daurprajñā*) arises based upon it. [End of] Collection.

The treatise states: There are six kinds of distraction. First is the distraction of mental attention (*manasikāra-vikṣepa*), which refers to when bodhisattvas abandon mental attention associated with the Mahāyāna and regress to practicing inferior mental attention associated with the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.

Second is external distraction (*bahirdhā-citta-vikṣepa*), which refers to when, while correctly cultivating virtue, one seeks out the five excellent sensual pleasures and the signs of clamor and bustle from the outside.
1) Distraction toward external objects, wherein the mind is allowed to wander and disperse amidst external conditions;

2) internal distraction, which occurs when, during the cultivation of virtue, the mind is disturbed by dullness, sleep, or inferiority, or by attachment to meditative absorptions, or by various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) within those concentrations; 3) distraction of mental signs, which refers to—based on...
Ceasing external signs, one directs the mind to contemplate the internal objects and their characteristics.
Fifth is distraction of gross heaviness, which means that with internal attention as a condition, various feelings arise; due to a body of gross heaviness, one conceives of "I" and "mine.
Sixth is distraction of intrinsic nature, which refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness; by their very nature, they lack the capacity for internal meditative concentration.
Therefore, one master says that this distraction (*vikṣepa*) is subsumed under the category of delusion (*moha*).

A second master says it is subsumed under the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) and has no separate substantial entity. A third master says that this distraction has its own distinct self-nature, namely restlessness (*auddhatya*);
because of that agitation and disturbance, it causes all co-arising phenomena to wander and dissipate. Question: [Regarding] restlessness and distraction...

What is the distinction between the two functions of agitation (*auddhatya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*)? Answer: Agitation causes the mind to be easily released; distraction causes the mind to easily shift its object.
"Easy release" means that as soon as it is joined [to an object], it is immediately released. "Easy shifting of objects" means that as soon as it is released, it immediately shifts to another object.

The term "easy" refers to the fact that [the mind] undergoes transition and change from moment to moment. Question: Since a single momentary mind (*ekakṣaṇika-citta*) fundamentally lacks transformation, how can this [distraction] be admitted therein?

"Regarding the ease of understanding and the ease of objects: Answer. Although there is no change in the understanding or the object within a single moment, there is a sense of transformation during the continuity of that understanding and those objects.

Why is this? When a defiled mind arises, it is entirely due to the power of restlessness and distraction that it must constantly change its understanding and objects from moment to moment, without abiding for even a single kṣaṇa. Or, by means of mindfulness and concentration..."
It is constrained by the power of wisdom, like a tethered monkey that remains still for a moment. For this reason, it is said that *auddhatya* (restlessness) is co-extensive with all defiled minds.
As for *asaṃprajanya* (lack of clear comprehension), regarding the object of observation... [as stated] in the treatise, it further states that this is also co-extensive with all defiled minds.
Those with erroneous understandings are like those who point to a deer and call it a horse, or address a tortoise as a turtle; they mistake a thief for their own son.
Because of these erroneous understandings, they take what is right to be wrong and what is wrong to be right.

Consequently, they violate prohibitions and transgress precepts, doing so for no other reason than for their own sake—claiming, for instance, that "wine and meat do not obstruct the path to Bodhi," or that one may seek Maitreya in brothels and taverns.

The inclusion of the words "and" (*ca*), "as well as" (*vā*), and "also" (*hi*) serves to indicate that there are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). This should be understood accordingly according to their respective categories.
These three words explain the three terms in the verse. By these three terms, it is clearly shown that secondary afflictions do not merely consist of twenty;
there are further defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) as well. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "These various afflictions..."

They are also called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), because they all follow the mind in performing the function of causing disturbance. Furthermore, there are others distinct from the primary afflictions (*kleśa*);
because these secondary afflictions arise as defiled mental factors subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they are also called secondary afflictions.
They are not called primary afflictions because they are not fundamental. Moreover, regarding those various things spoken of by the Blessed One in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*:
Regarding the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): as explained at length, these include sorrow, lamentation, grief, joy, and other such secondary afflictions.

As for what is called "secondary affliction" in the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, it refers to the unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as anger, enmity, and so forth—extensively described as various defiled matters.
The term "secondary affliction" also encompasses the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), as these are of the nature of being outflows (*niṣyanda*) from those aforementioned afflictions.

Therefore, other defiled phenomena that are of the same category as the afflictions (*kleśa*) are merely termed "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), because they are not subsumed under the primary afflictions, because they are of many kinds, and because they include both the afflictions and other defilements; thus, they are not limited to only twenty.

As for why only twenty are mentioned here, it is because the primary afflictions and those that pervade all three natures have not been included, and because these [twenty] are coarse and manifest. These remaining defilements...
The dharmas are either states (*avasthā*) or outflows (*niṣyanda*), as they are all subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Regarding the instruction to "reflect according to reason upon their respective categories," the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"All such afflictions are merely distinctions among these four characteristics; one should understand that they are subsumed accordingly. As for the "four characteristics," the first is...
1. Arising in all unwholesome minds; 2. Arising in all defiled minds; 3. Arising in specific unwholesome minds; 4.
Arising in wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral minds—namely, the two intermediate [mental factors] that accompany [the latter].
8. The eight great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), with the addition of wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and wrong resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*). These ten secondary afflictions are pervasive.
All arise from a defiled mind. The ten minor derivative afflictions, such as anger and the rest, each arise individually from an unwholesome mind;
when one occurs, a second necessarily does not. The four indeterminate [mental factors] arise universally from wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral minds.
As for these secondary afflictions, if they exist in the desire realm, they briefly operate within twelve bases (*āyatana*): namely, attachment, aversion, and delusion.

They operate by relying on the basis of attachment to misconduct, extending from anger (*krodha*) up to guile (*śāṭhya*). They operate by relying on the basis of quarreling, litigation, contention, and rivalry.

Shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) operate by relying on the basis of violating ethical discipline (*śīla*). Deceit (*māyā*) and so forth, up to malice (*vihiṃsā*), operate by relying on the basis of following and practicing the unwholesome ways of ignoble persons.
Hypocrisy (*kuhanā*) and so forth, up to evil companionship, operate by relying on the basis of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). Not...
Tolerance for indulgence and so forth, up to and including unbalanced attachment, proceeds based on attachment to various objects of desire.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*), and the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*) proceed based on the place where one reflects with the mind upon the meaning of the Dharma as it has been heard.
From sensual desire up to non-attention, it proceeds by way of the internal pacification of the mind based on the objects of thought;
it proceeds by way of being preoccupied with and clinging to the enjoyment of material wealth and the Dharma through successive stages;
and it proceeds by way of not abiding in a state that is upright, gentle, or conformable to its own kind, but rather by way of dwelling in a state of discordance.
The investigation of sensual desires and so forth, up to the investigation of attachment to family life, proceed based on secluded bedding, lodgings, and dwellings.
Sorrow, lamentation, and so forth, proceed based on places where manifold sufferings are accumulated.
Among these twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), those characterized by small, medium, and great degrees may all exist within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
Below this, the classification according to alternative systems is explained; first, the distinction between the nominal (*prajñapti*) and the substantial (*dravya*) is discussed.

Of these twenty, the ten minor secondary afflictions—namely, anger (*krodha*) and so forth—and the three major secondary afflictions—namely, heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)—are certainly nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), being merely states of mental factors.

Because they are by nature [afflictions], the four beginning with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) are definitely substantially existent (*dravyasat*). The three beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*) apply to both the nominal (*prajñaptisat*) and the substantial.

Regarding the twenty [secondary afflictions] below, next we discuss the co-nascent (*sahaja*) and the conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*). These twenty, when arising in accordance with what is co-nascent, are called co-nascent secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
when arising in accordance with conceptual construction, they are called conceptually constructed secondary afflictions. Regarding these two below, next we discuss their own categories.
They arise together. Among these twenty [mental factors], the minor derivative [factors] do not mutually correspond with their own kind, because they are not mutually compatible;
their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and violent, and each functions as a primary factor. As for the two intermediate [derivative factors], since they accompany all unwholesome minds...

Therefore, among the great and small [secondary afflictions], they can all arise together. Since the eight great [secondary afflictions] pervade all defiled minds, they necessarily arise in mutual conjunction with those of the small and medium categories.

Question: If the eight great [secondary afflictions] pervade all defiled minds and are all capable of arising together, why is it stated in other places that six or five are pervasive? Answer: When torpor (*styāna*) is predominant, restlessness (*auddhatya*) does not arise.

When restlessness (*auddhatya*) is predominant, lethargy (*styāna*) does not coexist with it, as their mental aspects (*ākāra*) are contradictory; therefore, these two are said not to be pervasive of all defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that five are pervasive, these are lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*);

because they do not conflict with any defiled mind, they are pervasive. These [five] exist only in the lower [stages]. Next, the association with the various consciousnesses will be discussed; first, concerning the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) in the small [category]:

The great [objects] lack both [small and medium]. The seventh [consciousness] has eight great [objects]. Some say there are five pervasive [objects] and six pervasive [objects], as explained in the meaning of the preceding text.
The six consciousnesses possess all three—small, medium, and great; the five consciousnesses lack the small [objects] and the ten [pervasive objects].
By this, the five great [afflictions] associated with the five feelings—up to the middling and great universal [afflictions]—are also according to their actual meaning;

this treatise concerns the association of these with the various feelings. Since the two middling [universal afflictions] and the eight great [universal afflictions] are common to the five sensory consciousnesses, they are associated with the five feelings.

One master says that among the ten minor [afflictions], anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), parsimony (*mātsarya*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) are associated only with the feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*).

They are associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*). The three—flattery (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*)—are associated with four feelings, excluding only the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).

One teacher says that the seven [afflictions] beginning with anger (*krodha*) are associated with four feelings, excluding only the feeling of pleasure (*sukhavedanā*); whereas flattery, deceit, and pride arise together with all five feelings.
The characteristics of these [secondary afflictions] arising together with feeling are all as previously explained in the section on the root afflictions.
Since the actual meaning is thus, it was stated before that greed, hatred, and delusion—whether innate or discriminative—can be associated with the five feelings;
since these secondary afflictions are all outflows from the states of those [root] afflictions, and since those are already associated with the five feelings, these too should likewise be so.

Thus it is. Among these, the four [afflictions] beginning with anger (*krodha*) are associated with all feelings (*vedanā*) except for pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*). However, if one considers their fundamental nature, they also pertain to pleasant feeling;

for it is said that when hatred (*dveṣa*) encounters a favorable object, it is accompanied by joy and pleasure. Therefore, we know that the small, medium, and great [degrees of these afflictions] all pertain to the five feelings.
If, however, one speaks according to the coarse characteristics of their specific manifestations, then anger, resentment, vexation, envy, and harmfulness are all [associated with unpleasant feeling].

The root affliction of hatred (*pratigha*) is subsumed under one part [of its own category]; it is associated exclusively with the two feelings of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), and is devoid of the feelings of joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*).

Concealment (*mrakṣa*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are subsumed under parts of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*); they are associated exclusively with the two feelings of joy and equanimity. Regarding the three—flattery (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*)—[they are as follows]:
It is also subsumed under a portion of greed and delusion. It is associated with the three feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity.

The "middle two" and the "eight great ones" are explained according to their coarse characteristics as they are conventionally distinguished; however, in accordance with the ultimate meaning, it is associated with all five feelings.

Thus, these twenty [mental factors] and the five object-specific factors (viṣaya-viniyata) [can coexist]; therefore, there is no fault in their association with distraction (*vikṣepa*) and concentration (*samādhi*).
This treatise concerns their association with the object-specific factors. All twenty and the five object-specific factors are capable of arising together. Question:

How can forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) be associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*)? Answer: Although they are not associated with right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*), [they are associated with their general counterparts].
They are associated; for they are also associated with deluded mindfulness and deluded wisdom. Question: Mindfulness takes the past as its object, while anger confronts the present.
How can they be associated? Answer: Although mindfulness takes the past as its object, it can also take as its object a present phenomenon that resembles what was previously practiced.
Although anger confronts the present, it can also take as its object a phenomenon from a past moment. This...

Because there are two [types], they can be associated. Question: Concentration (*samādhi*) consists solely of one-pointed focus, whereas distraction is characterized by a lack of uniformity; how, then, can they be associated? Answer:
When defiled concentration arises, the mind is likewise agitated; therefore, they are also associated.
The two intermediate [greeds] and the eight great [greeds] are associated with all ten afflictions; this is because they do not conflict with the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of greed and delusion.
This treatise concerns the association of afflictions. The two intermediate and the eight great [greeds] are associated with the ten afflictions.

The ten minor [afflictions] do not arise simultaneously with views or doubt, because the characteristics of the ten minor ones are superficial and coarse, whereas the characteristics of views and doubt are subtle and refined.

Anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) are associated with resentment (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and delusion (*moha*), but they do not coexist with greed (*lobha*) or hatred (*dveṣa*).
This is because these five factors are subdivisions of hatred; thus, hatred does not coexist with itself, just as a sword cannot cut itself or an eye cannot see itself.

Furthermore, they do not coexist with greed, because the two are mutually contradictory. Stinginess (*mātsarya*) is associated with delusion and pride, and likewise does not coexist with greed or hatred.

Since stinginess (*mātsarya*) is a derivative of greed (*lobha*), greed does not coexist with greed, nor does it coexist with hatred (*dveṣa*). Arrogance (*mada*) coexists only with delusion (*moha*); it does not coexist with greed or pride (*māna*).
Because pride involves intoxication and haughtiness, causing one to be uplifted and self-exalted, and because arrogance and pride have distinct definitions, they do not coexist.

Arrogance is subsumed under the category of greed; since greed does not coexist with greed, [arrogance likewise does not coexist with greed]. Concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*śāṭhya*), and guile (*māyā*) [coexist] with greed and delusion.
They are associated with pride. Since these three are all subsumed under the two portions of greed and delusion, they belong exclusively to the portion of greed;

they are not associated with greed but are associated with delusion. If they belonged to the portion of delusion, they would not be associated with delusion but would be associated with greed, as there is no contradiction in their modes of activity (*ākāra*).

Among the seven minor [afflictions], two are subsumed exclusively under the unwholesome (*akuśala*): flattery (*māyā*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*). Arrogance (*mada*) does not take lower realms as its object, because it is not based upon them.
This treatise discusses their association with the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). Among the seven minor [afflictions], two are exclusively of an unwholesome nature;

the triad of flattery, deceit, and arrogance, along with the eight universal secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), are subsumed under both the unwholesome and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) natures. Below this, the treatise discusses their connection to the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*).

It is so. Among the seven minor [afflictions], two are comprised solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); namely, anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).

These are comprised within the category of hatred (*dveṣa*), because hatred does not exist in the upper realms, and because those in the upper realms practice the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśaladharma*), they are without stinginess (*mātsarya*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*).

Thus, the middle two do not exist there. Deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) are comprised within both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*), as they are categories of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*). Arrogance (*mada*)...

Together with the eight [mental factors] associated with great delusion (*mahāmoha*), these all pervade the three realms. First, regarding their manifestation in the lower realms: if one gives rise to afflictions of a higher realm while born in a lower stage, it is possible to give rise to the first ten [afflictions] of the higher realms.
This is because, while being attached to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one may give rise to pride (*māna*), deceit (*mada*), flattery (*śāṭhya*), and guile (*māyā*) toward others.

Regarding the statement that afflictions of the upper realms arise from the lower realm: this is because one craves the flavor of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the upper realms, and because within this [lower] realm there are those who are arrogant, deceitful, and fraudulent, saying, "I have attained this absorption, whereas others have not," and so forth. Regarding the arising of afflictions of the lower realm from the upper realm:
in the upper realms, only the latter ten [afflictions] arise; this is because there are six or seven [types of] craving that co-arise with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which are about to be produced.

When descending, it is possible for the innate craving (*upapattyaṃśika-tṛṣṇā*) of the lower realm to arise; however, when one is born into the higher realms, there is no basis for the arising of [craving] belonging to the lower realms.

This is because such craving does not function as the primary moisture for rebirth, and because it would constitute a denial of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*). That which functions as the primary moisture for rebirth is innate craving, and that which directly denies cessation is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Next, the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are explained. First, the case where the lower [realms] take the upper [realms] as their object is clarified: among the intermediate [fetters], two; among the great [fetters], eight.

The lower [stages] also take the higher as their object. Because they take the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as their object, they arise in association with craving and other afflictions belonging to the higher realms.

Since these ten types [of mental factors] universally defile the mind, one master says that the ten minor [factors] of the lower realm do not take the higher realm as their object, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and proximate, and thus they cannot reach out to grasp the meditative absorptions of the higher realms.
Another master says that even the ten minor [factors] can take [the higher realm] as their object.
Above. One may also give rise to envy and other such afflictions toward the dharmas of a superior stage. Next, it clarifies how those in a higher stage take a lower stage as an object:
the flattery and deceit of the "Great Eight" and "Small Ten" can also take a lower stage as an object in the upper realms.

Because those in a higher stage rely on their superior meditative concentrations and become conceited toward the lower realms, these states arise in association with pride and other afflictions of the lower realm. Thus, Brahmā gave rise to flattery and deceit toward the Śākya son (the Buddha).

As for "the former": it is like the Great Brahmā King, who within his own assembly concealed his true state and manifested deceptive signs to mislead the bhikṣu Aśvajit, acting with feigned self-praise and so forth in order to avoid being questioned by him.
The reason that the pride of the upper realms does not take the lower realms as its object is that the pride of the lower realms is not something upon which one can rely.

All twenty are not included within the categories of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). (Up to: regarding their taking contaminated objects (*sāsrava*) as conditions, it should be understood according to the above.
As for their inclusion in the stages of the treatise: all twenty are neither included in the stage of training nor the stage beyond training.

This is because these twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), whereas the stages of training and beyond training consist solely of the pure (*anāsrava*). Therefore, they are not [afflictive] mental factors (*caitasika*).

They are associated [with afflictions]. Regarding the ten [afflictions] of the lower [realm], the treatise states they are abandoned by both [paths of seeing and cultivation]. The two intermediate [afflictions] and the eight great [afflictions] are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation;
they are not non-abandonable, because they are associated with both innate and discursive [afflictions]. As for those that arise discursively:
These are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Those that arise simultaneously with them are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

As for those abandoned by insight, they follow along with the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*) in their delusion regarding the characteristics of the Four Truths; whether deluded in a general or specific manner, they all arise simultaneously with the root afflictions.

Therefore, following the root afflictions, they all pertain to the four categories (*catuḥ-skandha*). Regarding the intimacy or distance of their delusion toward the Truths, they are all like the afflictions themselves.
Therefore, they pertain to both types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). One master says:

"The first ten minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they arise spontaneously (*svarasena*) by taking coarse, vulgar, and base worldly matters as their objects, and thus lack conceptual discrimination (*avikalpaka*). Another master says:

"The ten minor [afflictions] also pertain to both types of abandonment, because they arise through the power of both innate (*sahaja*) and discriminative (*vikalpita*) afflictions, and take the faculties of others as their objects."

Because the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and so forth give rise to anger (*krodha*) and other such afflictions, those [afflictions] abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) take as their objects—either collectively or individually—that which is to be taken as an object by their respective fundamental [views]. One master says:

"Anger and the others arise only from the fundamental delusions that directly obscure the Four Truths; they do not themselves directly obscure the Truths, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and superficial."

Because they are able to give rise to deep attachment. One master says that even the ten minor [afflictions] can directly delude one regarding the Four Truths, because they directly give rise to envy and so forth toward cessation, the path, and the others.

Below, the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) and their underlying realities (*vastu*) are explained. However, the ten [afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) only take existent objects as their conditions;
they must rely upon an underlying reality (*vastu*) in order to arise. Although all of them possess a direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),...

Regarding the outflowing [dharmas], the essential natures upon which they rely may be either outflowing or untainted; all these cases are to be understood according to what was explained in the section on the root afflictions.
*Cheng weishi lun*, Fascicle Six.
*Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), Fascicle Seven.
Composed by Dharmapāla and other Bodhisattvas;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The śramaṇa Tōng-rùn of Jīntíng Chángshòu Temple has completed the commentary on the twenty secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
[This concludes the section] up to the establishment of the name "unfixed" because they do not pervade all stages of meditative concentration.

This explains the sixth category: the indeterminate mental factors (*aniyata-caitta*). First, the question is posed; next, the verse is cited as the answer; then, the general name is explained. Regarding the term "indeterminate":
factors such as the wholesome belong to the wholesome state, while those such as the defiled belong to the defiled state.

Factors such as contact (*sparśa*) are necessarily universal to the mind, and factors such as desire (*chanda*) are necessarily universal to the ground. These four are called "indeterminate" because they are not fixed within either the wholesome or defiled mental grounds; thus, they pertain to all three.
Because it is by nature [indeterminate], it is designated as "indefinite" (*aniyata*).
"Regret" (*kaukṛtya*) refers to the mental state that thinks, "I have performed an evil deed; such an action was a mistake for me.
As for its nature being "remorse," there are two meanings. The first is that one did not know [the consequences] beforehand and only later, having already committed an evil deed...
One reflects with regret, thinking, "Why did I do this? This kind of regret must not be absent.
Second, regarding that which one has never previously committed as an evil deed, one later regrets it, thinking, "Why did I not do this?

This kind of regret must not exist. For wholesome deeds, the opposite is true. Therefore, *kaukṛtya* (remorse) has the nature of subsequent regret. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "That is to say..."
Its essence consists of a state of regretful distress regarding wholesome or unwholesome deeds already performed or yet to be performed, whether defiled or undefiled;

it is also simply a mind of remorse. Therefore, it is largely indeterminate. Its function is to obstruct meditative stillness (*śamatha*). Remorse is the result, while the act of misconduct is the cause.
Now, as for what is called "remorse," this is merely using the effect to clarify the cause.

"Sleep" refers to drowsiness, which renders the body unresponsive; [this continues] up to: it is designated as conventionally existent (saṃvṛti-sat) in accordance with its characteristic of delusion (moha).

"Drowsiness" (*middha*) refers to the state when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is dull and sluggish. "Sleep" (*svapna*) refers to the darkness and obscurity of the five sensory faculties (*pañca-indriya*). "Obscurity" (*mūḍha*) means being dim-witted;

"abridgment" (*līna*) means contraction. This indicates that when this mental factor arises, it causes the limbs and joints of this body to become slack and weary, such that one falls asleep even while sitting, and does not perceive even when others move them.
Furthermore, it causes this mind to become obscure and contracted.

It is capable of being clear, sharp, and discerning; such is the essential nature of this sleep. Because it is characterized by dullness and brevity, it functions as an obstacle to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
As for the phrase "because the mind revolves through a single door, being extremely dark and inferior," "dark and inferior" explains the character *mei* (dullness).
The first section explains the abbreviated terms. This refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) operating through both internal and external gates during the waking state;

however, if it is in this particular state, it operates solely through the internal gate. Below, the meaning of "dark," "feeble," and "single gate" is further explained: namely, when one has not yet arisen from sleep.
When this mind is precisely in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is alert and vivid, never clouded or darkened.

As soon as sleep arises, this mind becomes obscure and one knows nothing. Therefore it is said: "While in concentration, one is clear and simple; before sleep has arisen, this mind is in a state of wakefulness.
At that time, the myriad sounds and ten thousand forms all come rushing toward it. But as soon as sleep arises, this mind—
It is merely abbreviated and cannot be fully elaborated upon; therefore, it is said that this briefly distinguishes the state of waking.
Examining it in this manner reveals that sleep is not without essence or function, but must depend upon the mind.

Although sleep is established as a state of "no-mind," this is merely a provisional designation of a "state of no-mind" used to show that sleep is not itself the absence of mind, yet it is capable of—
That which reaches a state of non-mentation is sleep; therefore, sleep is taken as non-mentation.

However, this is not because actual sleep is non-mental, for sleep must necessarily be associated with the mind. This is because, like other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), it is associated with the mind.

As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Hindrances refer to the five hindrances: first, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); second, the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda*); third, the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness (*styānamiddha*)."
Namely, the four hindrances of restlessness and remorse, and the fifth hindrance of doubt. The "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*) refer to the ten envelopments:

lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*middha*), lethargy and restlessness (*styāna-auddhatya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*). To formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*): torpor is characterized by dullness and contraction.
It is not that they lack substance and function, for they are associated with the mind, just like other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).

Since the hindrances and entanglements are associated with the mind, sleep (*middha*) is likewise associated with the mind. One master says that regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep have only delusion (*moha*) as their essential nature.
There is no separate intrinsic nature [for these two]. This is because they are said to be subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and the portion of delusion (*moha*).

One master says: "These two are not only associated with the defiled; they are also associated with the wholesome. Therefore, they are not subsumed under the secondary afflictions and the portion of delusion.
It should be said that their defiled portions have delusion as their essence, while their pure portions have non-delusion (*amoha*) as their essence. Another master says: "Not so."
Sleep is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); it is not subsumed under either the nature of delusion (*moha*) or the absence of delusion.

It should be stated that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) has volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence, while sleep has thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) as its essence. To refute this by means of formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one says:

Defiled latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are said to be portions of delusion; they are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of delusion, just like lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth. These two [remorse and sleep] are indeterminate; therefore [the opponent's position is untenable].
[It is] not a part of delusion (*moha*). One teacher says: "This explanation is also incorrect.

If it is claimed that the conceptualization of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) constitutes the nature of regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*), how could it be that the fetter of wisdom becomes the nature of remorse, or that the fetter of conceptualization becomes the nature of sleep?
There is no such principle. The *Cheng-wei-shi-lun* (Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī) states: "One should explain that these two [regret and sleep] each..."

It possesses a distinct substantial entity (*dravya*). Its nature is not that of conceptualization through wisdom (*cintāmayī prajñā*), because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is distinct from that of other mental factors (*caitta*).
As for the treatise stating that it exists as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*), this is said in accordance with its characteristic of delusion;
it does not mean that it lacks a distinct substantial entity and is therefore merely conventionally existent.
"Vitarka" (investigation) refers to seeking that causes the mind to be hurried; [this continues] until one cannot perceive the distinctions among their essential natures and categories.
"Seeking" means searching coarsely by pursuing external objects. "Vicāra" (analysis) means examining minutely by scrutinizing internally.
"Hurried" means being rash and urgent. "Mental discourse" (manojalpa) refers to the objects apprehended by the mind, for these mostly depend upon names and expressions.
Regarding "having the nature of coarse and subtle movement": "coarse" is a term for something provisional or superficial; "subtle" refers to that which is dense and meticulous.
To speak of both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) means that these two natures are established by distinguishing between the coarse and the subtle within a single object.

These two, with respect to an object of mental discourse, are called "volition" (*cetanā*) when there is deep investigation, and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) when there is shallow investigation. When the investigation is deep, the spirit becomes concentrated; thus, the body...
When the mind is uplifted, it is at ease; when it is shallowly applied, it becomes restless. Thus, body and mind are not at peace.

If one were to separate them from reflection (*vitarka*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), these two distinctions could not be established. Question: That which is slow and subtle is reflection; that which is rapid and coarse is wisdom.

What is meant by "using them together"? Answer: If one employs correct mindfulness (*smṛti*) slowly while wisdom (*prajñā*) follows that slow mindfulness, it can cause both body and mind to be at peace.
If one employs correct wisdom quickly while mindfulness follows that quick wisdom, it can cause both body and mind to be unsettled.
Therefore, they may be used together.
Regarding the phrase "each of the two has two," there is a sense in which it refers to vitarka and vicāra; thus, the inclusion of these words is profoundly useful.

There are three interpretations for the statement "each of the two has two. The first master says: "The two dharmas, vitarka and vicāra, each possess the distinction between the two categories of defiled and pure;
this is called 'each of the two has two. A second master refutes this, saying: "It is not so. If one claims that vitarka and vicāra each [possess...]"

Regarding defilement and purification: remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) should also be understood as pertaining to both the defiled and the purified. One should explain these two as being like the previously mentioned primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Therefore, it is said "two. Because each of these possesses the two natures of unwholesome (*akuśala*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is further said "each two.
Alternatively, "two" and "each two" may refer to the fact that each possesses both active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*). A third master further refutes this, saying: "Nor..."
However, because these two pairs are stated following the "four indeterminate factors," one should say "two" twice;
this precisely indicates that there are two kinds of pairs. The first kind of pair refers to regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*); the second kind of pair refers to vitarka and vicāra.
Since these two pairs are distinct in their respective categories, the repetition of the word "two" serves to indicate that each of these two [categories] consists of two types.
This means they are both defiled and non-defiled; for they are not exclusively wholesome like faith and so forth, nor are they exclusively defiled like greed and so forth.

Alternatively, it is to exclude only the defiled, as the former masters describe them as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). This is to demonstrate that the indeterminate [mental factors] possess the nature of both [wholesome and unwholesome].
Therefore, it is said that each of the two [categories] has two [subdivisions].

Among the four, *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) are certainly nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*); since the treatise also describes them as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), this treatise [distinguishes between] the nominal and the real.
Among the four, only the two types, *vitarka* and *vicāra*, are certainly nominally existent. As for *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and *middha* (torpor)...

Regarding the seeds: one school asserts they are provisional, while another asserts they are real. Question: If that is so, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that they exist as conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*)?
Answer: This is stated in accordance with their dependent characteristics; it does not indicate that they lack intrinsic substance. Just as internal seeds possess a real substantial entity.

Yet the treatise also states that [these] exist as conventional realities (*saṃvṛtisat*). How could it be that internal seeds are likewise merely nominal? One may formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
Remorse and drowsiness are real entities, because they exist as conventional realities, just like internal seeds.
Among the four [dhyānas], vitarka and vicāra are definitely not associated [with one another];

this is because they are of the same category, though they differ in their coarseness and subtlety. This treatise maintains that they are associated with their own respective classes. Regarding the four [dhyānas], the two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra are definitely not associated [with each other].
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Vitarka is seeking; vicāra is examining. Or...

Vitarka (applied thought) is either volition or wisdom; it is defined as the coarse stage of investigating an object. Vitarka and vicāra (sustained thought)—these two—are defined as the subtle stage of examining that same object.
These two factors do not coexist in a single moment, because they differ in their respective natures of coarseness and subtlety, occurring sequentially.
Based on these two, the three stages [of the first dhyāna] are established. According to one interpretation, these three are established based on the sequential association of these two.
Establishment refers to the level of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna.

Because the coarse mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in their continuous succession are necessarily associated with both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), it is called the level "with *vitarka* and *vicāra*" (*savitarkasavicārā bhūmiḥ*).

In the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the coarse mind and mental factors in their continuous succession are definitely without *vitarka*; they can only be associated with *vicāra*. Therefore, it is called [the level]... [without *vitarka* but with *vicāra*].

The stage of "without vitarka and with only vicāra" refers to the mental states and mental factors of all stages from the second dhyāna upward, which, in their continuous succession, are definitely not associated with vitarka and vicāra; this is called the stage "without vitarka and without vicāra.
As for the subtle mental states and mental factors of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, as well as those of the intermediate dhyāna, they do not share the characteristics of vitarka and vicāra.

That which is associated [with vitarka and vicāra], as well as all material phenomena (rūpa), dissociated formations (viprayuktasaṃskāra), and all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) that are not associated with vitarka and vicāra, are also said to be the stage without vitarka and without vicāra (avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ). Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:

"The stage with vitarka and vicāra (savitarkasavicārā bhūmiḥ) and the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra (avitarkovicāramātrā bhūmiḥ) are exclusively stages possessing mind (sacittikā bhūmiḥ); the mindless sleep and the mindless..."
Fainting, the attainment of non-perception, birth in the realm of non-perception, the attainment of cessation, and the nirvana-realm without remainder are called the "mindless stages.
Question: If the three stages are established based on whether their seeds or manifestations arise, would this not lead to confusion?

Answer: In the desire realm and the first dhyāna, prior to entering meditative absorption, one has not yet abandoned the defilements associated with both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).

It is called "with vitarka and with vicāra. At the time of attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if *vitarka* is free from defilement while *vicāra* is not yet free from defilement, it is called the stage "without vitarka and with only vicāra" (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*).

From the second dhyāna upward, up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), if both *vitarka* and *vicāra* are free from defilement, it is called the stage "without vitarka and without vicāra" (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ*).
These three stages are based on the distinction between being free from defilement and not being free from defilement; they do not depend on those [other criteria].
Because it is spoken of as having vitarka and vicāra or being without vitarka and vicāra according to their respective modes of manifestation, there is no confusion. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"In this context, it is called 'without vitarka and without vicāra' by way of the principle of being free from the desire for vitarka and vicāra, not because they do not manifest.
Why is this so? Because for one who has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), due to the differences in the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of instruction..."
It is distinct. Therefore, even at one and the same time, there is the manifestation of mental activity (*manas*) that is without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Furthermore, for one who has already abandoned desire for applied and sustained thought, there is still the manifestation of applied and sustained thought, such as when emerging from that meditative absorption or being born in that stage. Question:
When one is born in the second dhyāna or in a higher stage, if consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness manifest while they are accompanied by applied and sustained thought...
When there is neither vitarka nor vicāra, [the consciousness] does not manifest. How, then, can it experience the objects of that stage through the material sense-faculties?

Answer: Because the seeds of the consciousnesses accompanied by vitarka and vicāra follow along with the samādhi devoid of vitarka and vicāra, once [the practitioner] has arisen from that state, this [consciousness] manifests. Furthermore, once this has arisen, the consciousness...
At the time of its manifestation, it is further pursued by the seeds of the concentration (samādhi) that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Therefore, this stage is not exclusively without vitarka and vicāra;

because those sentient beings have naturally become detached from all vitarka and vicāra, and are thus detached, that stage is called "without vitarka and without vicāra," even though this [state] manifests again here.
[This] practice is not an error. According to the true meaning, these three are established solely in terms of realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*).

That is to say, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna constitute the "first stage," because within them both vitarka and vicāra are obtainable among all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
In the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there is no vitarka among the contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena.
Because there is only *vicāra*, it is called the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*).

Because all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the stages above the second dhyāna lack both *vitarka* and *vicāra*, it is called the third stage. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
Among these, the desire realm and the first dhyāna—whether in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) or as a birth (*upapatti*)—are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
The intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), whether in absorption or as a birth, is called the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra.

From the second dhyāna upward, the entire form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are called the stage without vitarka and without vicāra. This includes the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned [states] of the first dhyāna.
This meditative concentration is also called the stage with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarkā savicārā bhūmiḥ*).

Because one enters this concentration by relying on dharmas that serve as the basis for vitarka and vicāra and taking *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, it does not proceed through the active manifestation of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

If one were to establish three stages based on association (*saṃprayoga*) and detachment from desire (*vairāgya*), the inclusion of all dharmas would be incomplete and there would be great confusion, even when speaking of the stage with vitarka and vicāra and so forth.
It is exclusively possessed of mind. This is a rough explanation of the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) from a single perspective.

Within this perspective, it is taught that in the stages from the second dhyāna upward—where there is neither vitarka nor vicāra—there exist the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), birth in the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

It is called the "mindless stage" (*acittaka-bhūmi*). Even when one is asleep without mind or in a state of unconscious fainting, it is still called "possessing mind," because the [mental factors] seven and eight are present.

Although it is said that this stage is called the "stage free from applied and sustained thought" (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*) because of the departure from desire for applied and sustained thought, [it is not entirely devoid of mind].
However, it is only said that from the second dhyāna upward, all stages have necessarily already abandoned the desire for vitarka and vicāra;
it is not said that those who have already abandoned the desire for vitarka and vicāra [necessarily belong to] the higher stages.

If that were the case, then even the dharmas of the lower stages would be called "without vitarka and without vicāra" by those who have not yet abandoned the desire for vitarka and vicāra belonging to the lower stages. Furthermore, regarding the dharmas of the higher stages...
If one were to say that they are "with vitarka and vicāra" and so forth, establishing them in such a manner would result in great confusion.

Therefore, these three are established solely in relation to the upper and lower realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*). Consequently, these *vitarka* and *vicāra* may be associated with the previously mentioned *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and *middha* (drowsiness), and *kaukṛtya* and *middha* likewise have the sense of being mutually associated.

All four [mental factors] are not associated with the seventh and eighth consciousnesses (up to: ...). For this reason, the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) certainly lack *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
This treatise concerns the association of the eight consciousnesses. These four are all not associated with the two consciousnesses—the seventh and the eighth.

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are associated only with the sixth consciousness, and not with the first five; for they are not among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) that necessarily pervade [all states of mind].
Because of the mind. One master says that the two dharmas of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are also associated with the five consciousnesses.

Furthermore, it is said that vitarka and vicāra are themselves the seven types of discrimination (*vikalpa*). As for the seven discriminations: first is spontaneous discrimination (*svarasa-vikalpa*), which refers to the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) that do not discriminate differently from the appearance of their objects;
they proceed spontaneously within their own respective domains. Second is discrimination with signs (*nimitta-vikalpa*)... [text continues]

It is distinguished [from the others]. That is to say, there are two kinds of discrimination based on intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), because they grasp the various characteristics of objects in the past and present.
Third is discrimination of signlessness (*animitta-vikalpa*), which is the discrimination of activity (*caryā-vikalpa*) that seeks after future objects.

All remaining types of discrimination take conceptual construction (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) as their intrinsic nature. Why is this? Because they involve mental deliberation (*vitarka*). At times, they involve investigation (*vicāra*).
Seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*), sometimes investigating (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), sometimes defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and sometimes undefiled (*akliṣṭa*); these are the various types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Conceptualization of seeking" refers to the conceptualization that arises from observing and seeking among all phenomena.
"Conceptualization of investigation" refers to the conceptualization that establishes what has been sought and observed by oneself through further investigation.

It gives rise to conceptualization. Regarding "defiled conceptualization," this refers to all conceptualizations that proceed in association with longing for the past, in association with desire for the future, or in association with attachment to the present;

whether they be conceptualizations of sensual desire, conceptualizations of malice, or conceptualizations of harmfulness, or those associated with any of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) or secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Regarding the arising of discrimination (*vikalpa*): non-defiled discrimination refers to that which is wholesome or neutral (*avyākṛta*).

This includes discrimination of renunciation (*naiṣkramya*), discrimination of non-ill will (*avyāpāda*), and discrimination of non-harmfulness (*avihiṃsā*); or it is associated with any one of the wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth;

or it consists of the discrimination pertaining to the modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*), the fields of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and various transformations (*nairmāṇika*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* speaks of spontaneous discrimination (*svarasa-vikalpa*).

Because these are distinct from the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). Since all seven types of discrimination belong to vitarka and vicāra, it is known that vitarka and vicāra are associated with the five consciousnesses.
One master states: "The two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and do not extend to the first five [consciousnesses]."
The treatises state that these vitarka and vicāra are unique dharmas of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna); therefore, they do not correspond with the five sensory consciousnesses.

Furthermore, it is taught that vitarka and vicāra are associated only with the two feelings of sorrow (daurmanasya) and joy (saumanasya), and it has never been stated that they are associated with the two feelings of suffering (duḥkha) and pleasure (sukha).
