The characteristics of the three types of transformation have already been extensively analyzed (up to the point where it says): "it is not that the mental factors and other dharmas are not inseparable from consciousness.
From the verse in the first fascicle: "By means of conventional designations of self and dharmas, various manifestations arise;

these depend on what is transformed by consciousness; these transformations are only three. Having proceeded thus with various analyses, the discussion of the three transformations is now just completed.

Regarding the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), the question is asked: Since the characteristics of these three types of transformation have already been extensively explained above, it is known that the two divisions of the grasped (*nimitta*) and the grasper (*darśana*) are transformations of one's own consciousness and do not possess real substance.

However, it is still not yet known that the self and phenomena, which are conventionally designated based on what is transformed by consciousness, lack real substance. Is it therefore the case that all things are merely consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)?
Next, the verse is raised as a response, and the treatise provides the commentary below. First, it is explained by way of the two divisions of the seeing and the seen aspects.

The phrase "these consciousnesses" specifically refers to the three transforming consciousnesses previously mentioned, along with their associated mental factors (*caitta*). Regarding the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*):

since both these sovereign [consciousnesses] and their mental factors can transform and manifest as the two divisions of the seeing and the seen aspects, the name "transformation" is established based upon this.
The transformed seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), because it is able to grasp that image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

The transformed image-part is called the "object of discrimination" (*vikalpya*), because it is the aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) apprehended by the seeing-part. By means of these two parts—the seeing and the image—...
This is a transformation of consciousness, yet they do not know this; they falsely conceptualize and cling to it as a real self and real dharmas.
This also arises from the pervasive conceptualization based on the two divisions of the seeing and the seen.

Apart from the seeing and the seen, there is certainly no other separate, real entity, because no real entity exists apart from the seeing and the seen. Therefore, all form, mind, and mental factors...
...the [six] bases, as well as the conditioned phenomena that are dissociated [from mind], up to the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena;
whether they be present phenomena possessing real functional activity, or past and future phenomena lacking real functional activity—all are not separate from consciousness.

However, when it is said "only" (*vijñaptimātra*), it is intended to negate the existence of real objects external to the mind; it does not negate the aspectual divisions (*nimittabhāga*) that are not separate from consciousness. And...
These are the mental factors (*caitta*) and other such phenomena.
Alternatively, "transformation" refers to the various internal consciousnesses [up to] the establishment of the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), which accords with the Middle Way.

Next, it is explained in terms of the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*). Regarding the term "transformation," it refers to the various internal consciousnesses, as well as their associated mental factors, the self, and phenomena.
Due to the power of the habitual tendencies of discrimination, at the time of their arising, they manifest as if appearing as external objects resembling a self and phenomena;
thus, the name "transformation" (pariṇāma) is established. It is these very minds and mental factors that are able to transform external objects so that they appear as a self and as phenomena.

This is called "the discriminator" (*vikalpa*). That which is grasped as external objects—appearing as a self and appearing as phenomena, and being taken as a real self and real phenomena—is called "the discriminated" (*vikalpita*).
By means of this, the discriminator transforms itself into the semblance of external objects and the characteristics of a provisional self and phenomena.
Furthermore, the real self and real dharmas that are conceptually constructed therein are definitively non-existent. Thus, the *Zongjing* says:

"For instance, when the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) transforms to give rise to the two portions of the object-phenomenon (*nimittabhāga*) and the perceiving-subject (*darśanabhāga*), it is just like tying a cloth to form a rabbit; the handkerchief itself is existent."

This is analogous to the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). Tying a handkerchief into the shape of a rabbit’s head—wherein no rabbit’s head originally existed on the handkerchief, but it arises through the act of tying—is therefore called "provisional" (*prajñapti*).
Likewise, the self-verifying portion originally lacks the two portions of appearance (*nimittabhāga*) and seeing (*darśanabhāga*);

yet, because reality is not realized, something resembling these two portions arises. Therefore, it is called "provisional. Furthermore, to grasp these two portions of appearance and seeing as a self is likewise provisional.

Regarding the Dharma: just as a cloth tied to form the head of a rabbit is already one layer of conceptual construction (*prajñapti*), tying it further to form two ears constitutes another layer of construction.

Likewise, from the self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) there arise the two divisions of the seeing and the seen; this is already one layer of construction, and to further grasp these two divisions as a self and phenomena constitutes yet another layer of construction.
Thus, although the two divisions of the seeing and the seen are themselves merely conceptual fictions, they are so.

There are [entities], because they arise from seeds. The two types of grasping—grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena—are definitively non-existent, because they are false imaginings (*parikalpita*).
Thus, one knows that all phenomena within and without the three realms are entirely devoid of intrinsic substance; there is only internal consciousness, which is false discrimination.

Since this principle is thoroughly established, it merely negates external objects apart from consciousness, but does not negate those phenomena that are not separate from consciousness. Therefore, [this is] the truth.

Dharmas such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) also possess existence. By virtue of this meaning, one remains far removed from the two extremes of superimposition and denial.

Through the term "only" (*mātra*), the superimposed attachment to external objects as substantially real is negated; through the term "consciousness" (*vijñapti*), the denial of the internal mind as being substantially non-existent is excluded.
Since one is thus free from both existence and non-existence, and free from both superimposition and denial, this is the true meaning of Vijñaptimātra.
The Middle Way principle is established.
By what teaching and reasoning is the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñapti-mātra) proven?

[From here until] "one is able to accordingly awaken to and enter into Consciousness-Only without external objects," the text below cites nine difficulties from the Hīnayāna to elucidate the principle that there are no phenomena outside the mind. First: The Causes of Consciousness-Only.
[Objection: The various Hīnayāna schools raise this objection: "Apart from the mind, we directly perceive that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) exist as real entities.
For what reason do you reduce them all to consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)? Upon what scripture and reasoning is the doctrine of consciousness-only established? [Response: The Mahāyāna replies:

"Did we not previously set forth the scriptural authority and reasoning at great length? Have we not already explained this to you? [Objection: The Hīnayāna says: "Although it was previously explained, our minds have not yet understood it."
However, if you insist on refuting the positions of others and establishing your own, you should provide me with a more precise and definitive exposition;
only then can the doctrine and reasoning of Vijñaptimātra be established. The Mahāyāna first cites scriptural authority for proof, as stated in the Sūtras:
"The triple world is mind-only. This means that the phenomena of the triple world are manifested solely by the transformations of a single mind.
Apart from the mind, there is not a single thing that exists. Question: In the realms of desire and form, there are external material objects and environments;
how can these be said to be transformations of the mind? It may be said that it is "mind-only" in the same way that the formless realm possesses only internal mind and no external material objects.
How can it also be said that "it is mind-only"? Does this not commit the fault of contradicting what is already established? Answer:
It is not only by stating that the object of form is not separate from the mind that it is called "representation-only" (vijñapti-mātra).

This also serves to negate the grasping mind—such as craving and so forth—that exists in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). For even in the formless realm, one gives rise to a deluded mind by craving the object of space; therefore, the formless realm is also [mind-only].

It is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). When one attains the untainted state (*anāsrava*), those supramundane, untainted forms (*rūpa*) and so forth—which are the objects of supramundane minds and mental factors—are also consciousness-only.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The objects of all consciousnesses are manifestations of consciousness-only.
Regarding the term "objects," this refers to both direct objects (*sākṣāt-ālambana*) and indirect objects (*paramparayā-ālambana*). Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra [Sūtra]...*

It is taught that all phenomena do not depart from the mind. As for "all phenomena," these refer to form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Vimalakīrti further states that sentient beings follow the defilement or purity of the mind;

as for "sentient beings," this refers to the four types of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings. Thus it is said: "If the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure; if the mind is defiled, the Buddha-field [is defiled]."

This refers to the "stains. Furthermore, it is said that a Bodhisattva who has accomplished the four types of wisdom and is able to progressively awaken to and enter the realm of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is a Bodhisattva prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds (*bhūmi*).

Although such a person has not yet realized the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*, by relying on the Buddha’s teachings and by observing Bodhisattvas on the grounds, they accomplish these four kinds of wisdom regarding *vijñapti-mātra* and subsequently enter into contaminated contemplation (*sāsrava-bhāvanā*) to contemplate those ten...
Regarding such matters as the mountains of fish, rice, and meat [manifested by] Bodhisattvas on the tenth stage, one immediately realizes:

"All such transformations do not depart from the transforming mind of the Bodhisattvas on the tenth stage; there is no external object whatsoever. Having performed this contemplation, one is also able to accord with and realize entry into *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).
First, the cognition of contradictory perceptions: if the object were real, how could this be established?
This explains how Bodhisattvas realize and enter into consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). For instance, regarding a single river of Ganges water:

hungry ghosts perceive it as a river of pus and fierce flames; humans perceive it as clear, cool water; devas perceive it as a ground adorned with jewels; and fish perceive it... [as their own environment].
This is their dwelling place. Because the transforming consciousnesses of these four classes of sentient beings are mutually distinct, the objects they transform are likewise mutually distinct;
therefore, it is called "the characteristic of mutually distinct consciousnesses. As for the term "wisdom," it refers to the wisdom of the Bodhisattva that takes these as its object.
The Bodhisattva says: "These four types of objects all arise from the individual karma of the four classes of sentient beings."

They are different. Although they occupy the same location, their respective transformations are distinct. If the object were substantially real, how could this be established? Furthermore, the treatise states:
"Just as humans see filth and excrement, while animals see it as pure and excellent food;
and what humans see as pure and excellent food, the gods see as foul-smelling and impure. Thus, one knows that merit follows the difference in perception. This refers to defilement.
The mind alone is pure; karma itself creates distinctions. Food has neither coarseness nor refinement. It is like a beautiful woman:
a lustful man sees her as pure and exquisite, and his mind gives rise to defiled attachment. An impure person views her as various foul secretions, with not a single clean spot.
A wife sees her with jealousy, glaring at her with hateful eyes. A lustful man views her as pleasure, while a jealous person sees her [as an object of envy].

This constitutes suffering. A practitioner of purity contemplates it and thereby attains the Way; it is not something for ordinary people to contemplate. Being without preference and without bias, these two are without objective referents.
When consciousness and wisdom reach that realm, since that object no longer exists, the other [the subject] should likewise be so.
Regarding those who possess the wisdom that cognizes objects of consciousness as non-existent: these are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Taking their own sixth, independent, and distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they project false objective images (*nimittabhāga*) by taking as objects such things as past water-moons, mirror-images, tortoise-hair, or rabbit-horns.
These objective images are merely constructed by the sixth consciousness of ordinary beings; they do not exist at all in reality.
Because the object does not exist, it is called "the cognition of an objectless consciousness.
That is to say, the Bodhisattva explains that these *nimitta-bhāga* (objective portions) transformed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not depart from their own transforming consciousness.
By this same analogy, all real objects do not depart from the perceiving consciousnesses of all sentient beings. Apart from the mind...
Externally, there are no real objects whatsoever.
Third, one’s own cognition should naturally be non-erroneous (until: through effort, liberation should be attained). Regarding "one’s own cognition should naturally be non-erroneous":

this refers to the fact that ordinary fools falsely cling to their own bodies as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure; [if cognition were naturally non-erroneous,] such ignorance would not exist.

This refers to the mind of the bodhisattva that takes [these] as its object. The Bodhisattva says: "This is merely the deluded mind of foolish people who, through inverted views, calculate [the dharmas] as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Apart from this grasping mind, there is in reality no permanence, bliss, self, or purity.
If permanence, bliss, self, and purity were necessarily existent entities, then these would naturally be non-inverted states, and one would not need to rely on spiritual practice to attain them."
[This leads to] liberation. If it were not so, it would be clearly understood that there is only deluded consciousness.
Fourth, regarding the transformation of the wisdom that accords with the three [knowledges]: if the objects were truly existent, how could they be transformed?
The first three knowledges observe the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the latter three knowledges observe the realm of noble ones (*ārya*).
This means that when Bodhisattvas of the nine stages attain mastery over the mind, they are able to spontaneously transform the great earth into gold and churn the long rivers into cream and curd.
This causes all sentient beings to truly obtain and enjoy [these things]. These objective spheres do not exist apart from the Bodhisattva’s mind that performs the transformation.
If these objects were substantially real, how could they be transformed? Question: For instance, when the great earth is transformed into gold—
Is it that the earth-element is extinguished so that the gold-element may arise separately, or is it that the earth is transformed into gold? The answer is:

It is said that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by means of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wondrous Observational Wisdom as their sovereign influence, are able to cause the earth-element of sentient beings not to arise and manifest the gold-element;
it does not mean that the earth is transformed into gold. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
It is said: "By taking contemplative practice as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), one causes other consciousnesses not to undergo transformation. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"When a Bodhisattva practices such Great Nirvāṇa, they contemplate man as gold, and contemplate gold as earth;

earth manifests the appearance of water, and water manifests the appearance of earth. These are accomplished according to their will, without any falsehood. Even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are capable of this."
To transform fire into water or to transmute iron into gold—this is the wisdom in which the objective realm shifts according to the activity [of the mind].
Furthermore, consider the Vaiśeṣika masters who maintain the six categories of existence; yet they can transform their bodies into massive boulders.

If objects were fixed and substantial realities, one should not be able to transform one's body into stone according to the mind. Therefore, we know that within all things there exists the principle of transformation. As the Saṃgha...
When one protects the perception of the body as a bed or a jar, one should know that all phenomena (dharmas) transform in accordance with consciousness.
Because all phenomena lack fixed characteristics, earth can be transformed into the appearance of water, and water can be transformed into the appearance of earth.

For instance, substances such as ghee, resin, and wax—which belong to the category of earth—melt when they encounter fire, becoming water and thus manifesting the characteristic of moisture; likewise, when water encounters cold, it solidifies into ice.
Yet they possess the characteristic of solidity. Mineral exudate becomes gold, gold deteriorates into copper, or returns to stone;
thus we know that good can become evil and evil can become good, for neither possesses a fixed nature.
Second, regarding the transformation of wisdom through subsequent observation: if the object were truly real, how could it transform according to the mind?

That is to say, when Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have attained superior meditative concentration and achieve correspondence with the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, as they observe even a single phenomenon, there immediately arise [the perceptions of] impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, and so forth; these are not [inherently present in the object].
These meanings, such as impermanence and so forth, exist within the very nature of phenomena; they are merely established in accordance with the observing mind.
If the object were truly real, how could it possibly shift according to the mind?
Third is the wisdom that functions in accordance with non-conceptual wisdom. There are numerous such scriptural authorities as proof for this:
when Bodhisattvas attain fundamental wisdom and realize *tathatā* (suchness), wisdom and *tathatā* are equal and identical;
internally and externally they are stilled and serene, with no further distinct objects. If an object were real, how could it fail to appear? Thus, the Bodhisattva...
"Below: Exhortation to believe. Furthermore, 'the verse below': Citation of proof. 'These, etc., below': Conclusion.

Because they are any one of the five consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness, which is universally established, they do not directly perceive objects separate from their own form, just like the others."
The following cites logical proofs. First, it establishes by reason that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the five sense objects is not separate from the five consciousnesses.

For now, we shall establish that the *nimitta-bhāga* of visual consciousness is not separate from visual consciousness; the other four are to be understood accordingly. The formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is visual consciousness as commonly established (*prasiddha*).

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it certainly does not directly perceive a form (*rūpa*) separate from itself. The reason (*hetu*) is "because [it is] among the five [consciousnesses] as commonly established..."

Because it is subsumed within one [of the categories] among consciousnesses, just like the other four consciousnesses that are universally established (*prasiddha*). The first position relies upon the two characters "universally established" (*prasiddha*) to exclude two types of eye-consciousness that are not so established.
For instance, the Mahāyāna accepts the existence of the eye-consciousness of Buddhas in other directions.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s untainted eye-consciousness (*anāsrava-cakṣurvijñāna*) is not admitted by the Hīnayāna, and is therefore excluded.

Within the Hīnayāna school, it is maintained that the Buddha possesses tainted eye-consciousness (*sāsrava-cakṣurvijñāna*) and that the defiled eye-consciousness of a Bodhisattva in his final birth exists; these are not admitted by the Mahāyāna, and are therefore excluded.
Generally, those points not accepted by both schools are "unestablished dharmas" (*aprasiddha-dharma*). Here, we simply adopt what is accepted by both schools.

It is only when the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) is accepted as commonly established (*prasiddha*) that it can serve as the basis for a thesis (*pakṣa*). Therefore, the term "commonly established" is placed before the word "visual consciousness.

Question: If the two characters "commonly established" were not included, what fault would there be? Answer: The subject of the thesis (*pūrvapakṣa*) would then incur the fault of being only partially established for either oneself or the opponent;
likewise, the reason (*hetu*) would also commit the same fault of being only partially established for oneself or the opponent.
This is the fallacy of the locus being unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*), because the subject of the thesis (*pūrvapakṣa*) lacks an established locus. Thus, the *Hetuvidyā* states:
"Space is substantially existent, because it is the locus of qualities. For one who argues against the non-existence of space, the locus is unestablished.

As for the subsequent statement—that the thesis is that [the object] is definitely not directly perceived as a form separate from its own consciousness—this merely refers to something outside the range of the visual consciousness's own manifestation.
All essential forms (*svabhāva-rūpa*) and the other four objects (*viṣaya*), when separated from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), are not directly perceived.

Within the Mahāyāna school, there are two kinds of form: essential form that is separate from visual consciousness, and form as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) that is not separate from visual consciousness.
If one were to debate with an opponent, the dispute would concern only the essential form; however, if the Mahāyāna school establishes its own position regarding the eye...

Consciousness directly perceives its own objective part (*sākāra-bhāga*). Question: Why do you not say that it definitely and directly conditions a form that is not separate from its own consciousness, rather than saying it does not directly condition a form separate from itself?

Answer: For fear of committing the fallacy of the non-establishment of the qualifier (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*), since the Hīnayāna schools do not admit that form is not separate from visual consciousness.
Next, the reason is stated: "Because it is subsumed under one or another of the five universally established sensory consciousnesses."
The term "established" (*prasiddha*) serves both to establish the reason and to exclude the non-established five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

If one did not say "established" and merely stated that it is "included within any one of the five consciousnesses," then this reason would incur the fallacy of being unestablished for either oneself or the other party, or for both.

As the *Hetuvidyā* states: "For example, if one were to establish that sound is impermanent because it is produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), [this reason] would be unestablished for a proponent of the Manifestation of Sound (*śabda-ābhivyakti-vādin*)."

The locus of the argument (*āśrayāsiddha*) is not established. Regarding the example, "like the other four consciousnesses which are universally established" (*prasiddha*), the term "universally established" also serves to exclude phenomena that are not so established.
If one were not to say "universally established," one would commit the fallacy of having either the reason (*hetu*) or the thesis (*sādhya*)—or both—unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
Thus, the *Hetuprakaraṇa* states: "When the property of the reason is not universally established, it is as when one says: 'Sound is eternal, because it lacks resistance.'"
Therefore, those things that lack material resistance are seen by them to be eternal, just like atoms (*paramāṇu*).

However, regarding those atoms, the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*)—eternality—is present, while the property that establishes it (*sādhanadharma*)—the absence of material resistance—is absent, because atoms possess the nature of material resistance.
As for the case where the property to be established is not proven, this is explained as being like consciousness (*buddhi*). Yet, all consciousness... [is] capable of establishing...

Regarding the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*): that which exists as non-obstructive matter is the property to be established; it lacks the nature of permanence, because all cognitions are impermanent.

Now, since it has been established that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of form-dharmas is not separate from visual consciousness, the remaining [objects]—sound, odor, taste, and touch—should be understood accordingly.
Question: The basis of the thesis must be admitted by both parties. What then is the body of the thesis (*pakṣatattva*) now being stated? The establishment...

The proponent maintains that [the visual consciousness] does not directly perceive objects apart from its own form (*rūpa*). The opponent maintains that it directly perceives the substantial form (*svabhāva-rūpa*) apart from its own consciousness.

How can this be said to be universally established (*prasiddha*)? Answer: Even the Hīnayāna schools maintain that visual consciousness does not directly perceive the other four sense-objects (*viṣaya*), because they are distinct from visual consciousness.

Thus, while one merely causes the opponent to accept the principle of non-direct perception, the "form apart from its own consciousness" (*sva-vijñāna-vinirmukta-rūpa*) is precisely the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*).
This is self-evident.
Since other consciousnesses are also cognitions, like visual consciousness and the others, they likewise do not directly perceive phenomena that are separate from themselves.

Second, by means of reasoning, the sixth consciousness is established, while simultaneously implicitly establishing the seventh and eighth consciousnesses. The formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
It is established that other consciousnesses are existent phenomena (*dharmin*). Furthermore, it is not the thesis (*pakṣa*) that they directly perceive phenomena apart from their own consciousness.

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they are of the nature of consciousness. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is, for instance, the five well-established sensory consciousnesses. This applies if one posits the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as the existent phenomena.

Since he does not accept the existence of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, he commits the fault of "non-establishment for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*) regarding the specific property being distinguished.

If one posits the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the subject (*dharmin*), and the opponent takes the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as the dissimilar examples (*vipakṣa*), then the fallacy of "uncertainty within the common locus" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) occurs within the argument.
The opponent points out this flaw, saying: "Is it because the mental consciousness is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*)?"
Do you prove that your other consciousnesses do not directly perceive phenomena distinct from themselves?

Or, because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are also of the nature of consciousness, do you prove that your other consciousnesses necessarily directly perceive phenomena distinct from themselves? Now, while speaking generally of "the others," the specific reference is to the sixth;
however, the intention includes the seventh and eighth as well. Thus, it implicitly establishes that the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are distinct from the other consciousnesses.
Regarding the phrase "likewise not directly perceiving" (*na pratyakṣam ālambate*) in the subsequent statement: "likewise" (*api*) means "the same as.

It is the same as the preceding five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) in that they do not directly perceive phenomena other than their own. The reason given is: "because this has the nature of consciousness" (*vijñānatvāt*);

that is, it is the same as the five consciousnesses in having the nature of consciousness. This is illustrated by the well-established example of the five consciousnesses themselves, which likewise do not directly perceive objects other than their own forms (*rūpa*).

This explains that the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is certainly not separate from this [consciousness], because it is neither existent apart from it nor non-existent apart from it; thus, it accords with the Middle Way.
The third [section] establishes by reason that the first six types of direct object-conditions all ultimately reduce to self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).

However, since the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) also functions in dependence upon self-cognition, only the aspect of the image (*nimitta-bhāga*) is established here, as the aspect of seeing is already universally accepted.

Therefore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows: The immediate objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the six consciousnesses is the subject (*dharmin*). It is necessarily not separate from the essence of the six consciousnesses; this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

because it is subsumed under either one of the two parts, the "seeing" (*darśana-bhāga*) or the "image" (*nimitta-bhāga*), just like the aforementioned "seeing" part which is the subjective perceiver.

Since the Hīnayāna schools admit that the seeing part is not separate from the essence of the mind, this is used as the concordant example (*sapakṣa*). This fourth [point] establishes [the position] through reasoning.
The remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*) is likewise not separate from the mind, for it is the direct objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

In relation to the first six consciousnesses, it is called the remote object-condition; since the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) does not admit an eighth consciousness, one does not mention the "objective aspect" but speaks only of the "remote object-condition.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: "All objects of perception corresponding to their respective consciousnesses" is the subject (*dharmin*). It is certain that...
The thesis is that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not separate from the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The reason (*hetu*) is stated:

"Because it is a dharma that serves as an object of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*)," with the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) being "like associated dharmas" (*saṃprayukta-dharma*). Following these [sections], there is the conclusion and proof; following that, there is the exhortation to have faith.
The Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya), relying on this, spoke two verses [extending to...]. In reality, there is also a pure portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
These verses serve as a testament that while the self and phenomena do not exist, emptiness and consciousness are not non-existent either.

What is called the "nature of a real self and phenomena" grasped by the ignorant is merely something that exists through the deluded discrimination of their confused minds; it refers to the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) manifested upon this consciousness.
The two divisions, as well as the two natures of self and phenomena, are ultimately and entirely non-existent. This consciousness possesses only the emptiness of the two kinds of selflessness;
regarding those two divisions of subject and object, as well as the two natures of self and phenomena, there is likewise nothing but emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that all dharmas are neither empty nor non-empty, because self and phenomena do not exist, unlike [the view that] they exist unilaterally.
The Hīnayāna considers consciousness to exist as emptiness, rather than being exclusively empty, much like Bhāviveka;

this accords with the sublime principle of the Middle Way, which is neither existent nor non-existent. This verse, for its part, states that [the dependent nature] is entirely non-existent based on its defiled aspect (*kliṣṭa-āśraya-paratantra*);
however, from the perspective of ultimate reasoning, the pure aspect (*viśuddha-āśraya-paratantra*) is definitively and truly existent.
If it is the case that only internal consciousness arises appearing as external objects—up to [the point where it is said] "like dream-objects and so forth"—this should resolve such doubts.
This explains the second objection regarding worldly affairs contradicting the tenet. The Sautrāntika masters raise the objection:
"If you say that there is only internal consciousness and no external objects, how is it that we currently perceive in the world various entities, both sentient and insentient?"

There are cases where the place is fixed, the time is fixed, but the body is not fixed, and the function is not fixed. The Master of the Treatise cites the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to answer this.
"The fixity of place and time is like a dream; the lack of fixity regarding the body is like when hungry ghosts collectively see a river of pus.

Just as in a dream, [an object] can perform a useful function. Within this context, there are four objections: first, the objection regarding the fixity of place. The objection states: "If you say..."

Regarding the principle that "all is consciousness-only and there are no external objects": for instance, when ordinary people direct a perceptual consciousness (*pratyakṣa-vijñāna*) toward the Southern Mountain, both that consciousness and the mountain are simultaneously present.
Since the Southern Mountain does not exist apart from the consciousness, one may say it is "consciousness-only.

However, if that same perceptual consciousness suddenly turns to direct itself toward the Northern Mountain, although the mountain remains in the south, it does not follow along with the perceiving mind.

They all turn toward the north together. Since this occurs when they are oriented toward the north, and the Southern Mountain does not move, it is clear that there exists an objective realm of the Southern Mountain external to consciousness;
how, then, can this be established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? The Master of the Treatise replies:
You yourself must admit that when sentient beings are dreaming, they sometimes see villages, gardens, men, women, and other such things located in a single place. That very place...
[The opponent] says: "It is certain. Sometimes that sentient being’s dreaming mind suddenly takes another object as its condition and does not see things such as villages, gardens, men, or women;
at such times, the dreaming mind is not fixed. Do you concede for the time being that all of this is mere consciousness (vijñaptimātra)? The Hīnayāna proponent replies:
"In our school, although the objects within a dream are fixed while the dreaming mind is not, nevertheless, none of them exists apart from the sentient being’s dreaming mind."
It is always *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). The Master of the Treatise says: "The objective forms perceived by me during the waking state are likewise so.
Although mountains and such remain constant, the sentient beings' minds that perceive them are not constant; nevertheless, none of them exist apart from the presently existing perceiving mind.
They are all consciousness-only. He establishes the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows: "The objective forms manifested during the waking state in my own school are the subject (*dharmin*)."
This is definitively the Vijñānavāda school. The reason is stated: "The object is fixed while the mind is not. The analogy is like objects in a dream.
Second is the objection regarding the fixity of time: it is argued that when one is correctly perceiving the Southern Mountain, both consciousness and the mountain appear simultaneously.

[Objection: One might argue that this establishes *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). For instance, when consciousness does not take a southern mountain as its object, the southern mountain still exists;
it does not perish along with the consciousness. Thus, there is an object that exists apart from the mind. How, then, can this be established as *vijñapti-mātra*? [The Mahāyāna proponent] counters:
Consider, for example, the villages, gardens, men, women, and other objects perceived by sentient beings within a dream. When the dreaming mind takes these as its objects, are they [real]?
"Regarding consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*): if it does not take an object as its condition, is it still consciousness-only? The Hīnayāna proponent replies:

"In our school, as for dream-objects, when the dreaming mind takes them as its condition, they are consciousness-only; even when the dreaming mind does not take them as its condition, they are also consciousness-only, because they are not separate from the dreaming mind.
The Master says: "The objective forms (*rūpa*) of my waking state are likewise so. I am now taking them as an object for a long duration..."

The Southern Mountain: the mountain does not depart from the mind; it is certainly *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). At times when one does not take the Southern Mountain as an object, the Southern Mountain still remains and does not perish along with the mind;
this too is *vijñapti-mātra*. Therefore, the verse says: "The determination of place and time is like a dream.
Third, the objection regarding the indeterminacy of the bodies of sentient beings: the objection states, "If you say that everything is *vijñapti-mātra*, then for a start..."
Suppose there are many sentient beings together in one place;
among them, half have eye diseases such as cataracts, whereby some see floating flowers, some see hanging hair, some see flies, and some do not see objects at all.
All of these are transformations produced by the consciousness of those with diseased eyes;

the perceived objects (nimitta-bhāga), such as hair and flies, do not exist apart from the mind of one suffering from cataracts, and are thus indeed "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra). For instance, consider one who does not suffer from cataracts in one eye.
When many are together in one place, what they perceive is the same. Since it is the same for all, it is clear that there exists an object external to the mind;

how, then, can this be established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? The Master of the Treatise counters with a question: "Consider, for instance, when a great multitude of hungry ghosts (*preta*) are together in one place.
Among them, those three or five who share similar karma will invariably see a river of pus together. Furthermore, there are another three or five who, according to their own [karma]..."
The hungry ghosts may see a fierce fire, or filth and excrement, or see people holding clubs to block their way; what they perceive is not fixed.
Thus, while these hungry ghosts occupy the same location, half perceive a fixed environment and half perceive one that is not fixed.
Is it permissible to say that all of them are merely consciousness-only? The Hīnayāna school says: although there are similarities and differences in what is seen, none of it...

Apart from the transformations of the consciousness of hungry ghosts through their own karma, all are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). The Master of the Treatise says: "My school’s doctrine of mere consciousness is likewise so.
Although those of one class who suffer from cataracts see things differently, those of another class who do not suffer from cataracts see them identically;
yet neither is apart from the transformations of the consciousness of these two classes of sentient beings."
All these are merely consciousness. Thus, the verse says: "The body is not fixed, as when hungry ghosts collectively see a river of pus and so forth.
This is the fourth objection regarding the indeterminacy of function. The objection asks:

Furthermore, by what cause is it that the hair, flies, and so forth seen by one afflicted with ophthalmia have no practical utility, whereas the hair, flies, and so forth seen by others not afflicted with ophthalmia do possess practical utility?
Furthermore, for what reason do things such as a city of gandharvas lack practical utility, while a city made of bricks and earth possesses practical utility?
Moreover, for what reason do sentient beings perceive swords, staffs, clothing, food, drink, and so forth within a dream?

Then it would have no practical efficacy. As for the claim that it acquires efficacy upon awakening, if your school maintains that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), then there ought to be practical efficacy at all times.
Since there is no practical efficacy, how can they be established as mere consciousness?

The master of the treatise interrogates, saying: "Do you also admit that the swords, staves, food, drink, clothing, and so forth obtained by sentient beings in dreams lack real functional efficacy and are merely consciousness? He answers: "Indeed.

Furthermore, for example, in a dream one may engage in sexual union with a woman and emit impurity, or be bitten by a snake and fall into a swoon; although there is no real external object, there is a real [result].
[The opponent asks: "Do you also admit that these [dream objects] are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*)? [The respondent] answers: "Yes. The Master of the Treatise says:

"Since you admit that both those with real causal efficacy and those without real causal efficacy within a dream are all merely consciousness, one should know that for those afflicted by cataracts and those not so afflicted, for what is obtained in a dream and what is obtained upon waking, for a false city and a real city, there is no reality."
Regarding function: all that possesses real function is but consciousness-only. Thus, the verse says: "Like a dream, it has functional utility.

Therefore, one knows that the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only; dreaming and waking are identical. That which is seen within the waking state is precisely the manifesting mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
What is seen within a dream is precisely the mental consciousness of the dream state. Since the discerning consciousness is identical, how can the differentiated objects be different?
If such is the case regarding delusion and awakening, why harbor any doubt? If such is the nature of sleep and waking, one may penetrate this clearly.
For what reason did the World-Honored One teach the twelve bases (up to the point of) making known that external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*) also do not exist?

This constitutes the objection regarding contradiction with the characteristics of the Threefold Knowledge (*traividyā*) and the Noble Teachings (*āryaśāsana*). The objection states: If the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) asserts that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), [then this contradicts the aforementioned teachings].

If there were no external objects, the Blessed One would have taught only the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); it would not be appropriate for him to teach that there are ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).

Yet, all the sūtras state that there are twelve bases. This clearly demonstrates that, apart from the sense-base of mind and the sense-base of phenomena, there are separately ten bases of form which truly exist external to the mind.
If one claims that all these are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), this does not contradict [the existence of external objects].
Regarding worldly conventions, would this not contradict the holy teachings? The Master of the Treatise answers by citing the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"Consciousness arises from its own seeds and evolves appearing as the aspect of an object; in order to establish the internal and external bases, the Buddha taught them as ten.
This means that the self-verifying portions (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses each arise from their own respective seeds of the five consciousnesses. And...

It can manifest as two divisions. The manifested *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-division) is called the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). The manifested *nimitta-bhāga* (image-division) appears as if it were an external object;
these are called the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*). In reality, all ten bases (*daśāyatana*) of the faculties and objects are not separate from consciousness.
This is a provisional answer given to the Sautrāntika masters using the seeds of the five consciousnesses, because they admit that seeds exist within the six consciousnesses.

Because it is held within [the aggregates], this Buddha’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) was intended to destroy the non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) attachment to the body as a single, unified self (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇātman*).
Therefore, he distinguished the ten bases (*āyatana*) of sense faculties and objects. The wise person, relying precisely upon the Buddha’s teaching, then performs this contemplation:
"Throughout immeasurable eons, driven by evil wisdom, I have sought [this self] while shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, falsely clinging to my own and others' bodies as..."
The notion of a "unified self" causes one to sink and wander through birth and death.

Now, by observing according to the teachings, one realizes that within the bodies of oneself and others there are only the ten bases—roots and objects—which constitute their substance. Within each of these bases, there is absolutely no function of a sovereign, independent, permanent, or unitary entity.
How, then, could there ever have been a self? By this means, one is able to awaken to and enter into non-self.

This principle establishes the contemplation of the emptiness of self; therefore, it is said that for the purpose of entering the emptiness of self, the twelve factors of existence (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) are taught.
It is just as if there were someone who denies the existence of future lives and falls into the pit of the view of annihilationism.

To prevent this, it is taught that all sentient beings, casting off one life and proceeding to another, are like a whirling firebrand that never ceases. Therefore, it is said that, in order to refute the view of annihilationism, the continuity of existence is taught.

Furthermore, there are those who, although they have realized the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and have already attained liberation, have not yet reached the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Consequently, they are unable to advance toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*). In order to lead them into the emptiness of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-śūnyatā*), it is taught that "the three realms are all consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*);
this is so that they may know external phenomena also do not exist, thereby swiftly entering the emptiness of phenomena and realizing [enlightenment].

Regarding supreme enlightenment, as for the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), although it is said that if this were so, then for instance, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the five sense-objects—which is the form transformed by the five consciousnesses—can be called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*);
yet it remains uncertain which consciousness constitutes the "consciousness-only" nature of the fundamental substance (*mūlapratibimba*) of the five objective realms.

This is because neither the five consciousnesses nor the sixth consciousness directly perceive the fundamental substance of the five objects; rather, it is this very fundamental substance [that serves as the basis].

Question: Are not the five objects real entities existing external to the mind? How, then, can they be established as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*)? Answer: They exist by virtue of being transformations of consciousness and do not exist separately.
It is said that the essential nature (*bhāva*) of the five sense-objects is the direct objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; it is not separate from the eighth consciousness.
This too is mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and not something existing separately.
Does this mere consciousness itself not also lack intrinsic nature? It is for this reason that the Lord Maitreya spoke the two preceding verses.
The fourth [verse] addresses the objection that mere consciousness is established as empty. The objection states: "If it is said that all phenomena are empty, then this very mere consciousness..."
"Is its substance not likewise empty? He replied, "No. Again he asked, "How can it be that while all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not empty?

He replied, "Because it is not that which is grasped as an object. He continued, "What was previously called 'empty' refers merely to the emptying of the imagined attachment to the existence of a substantial nature, a superior essence, and so forth, within all phenomena transformed by consciousness.
This is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*); logically, it is not [the case that consciousness itself is empty]."

Because it exists, it is said to be empty; yet it is not non-existent, for it is the pure dependent nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) realized by non-conceptual wisdom beyond words, and is thus termed the "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This nature of consciousness-only is the sublime conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

If this were non-existent, there would be no conventional truth; and if there were no conventional truth, there would likewise be no ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Why is this so? Because the ultimate...
Because conventional reality is established in dependence [upon ultimate reality], to negate the two truths is a "misapprehension of emptiness" (*durgṛhītaśūnyatā*).
Therefore, the Buddhas declare such persons to be incurable. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Buddhas teach the dharma of emptiness in order to transcend existence;
yet those who perceive emptiness as a [substantial] entity cannot be transformed by the Buddhas. One should understand that all phenomena possess both emptiness and non-emptiness based on this.
The Compassionate Honored One spoke the first two verses. [He asks:
"If all bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) also have consciousness as their essence... and if non-material consciousness were also absent, then [the former] would not exist either.
This is the fifth objection regarding the characteristic of form being non-mental. The objection states: "If it is claimed that all ten bases have mind as their essence, because of the mind..."
Regarding the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) manifesting as if it were the object-part (*nimittabhāga*):
why is it that the aspect of form (*rūpanimitta*) appears while the transforming mind itself does not appear?

Why is it that the transformed aspect of form proceeds as a uniform continuity and persists for a long duration, whereas the transforming mind is unstable, changing and not continuous? Now, since external form does not...
If it is clearly understood that external, real forms exist apart from the mind—just as they appear within the mind—why say that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*)?
Answer: Because all sentient beings, since beginningless time, have mutually perfumed one another through false conventional designations (*abhilāpa*).
By the power of this [consciousness], there appear manifestations resembling external objects such as form, all of which take the nature of consciousness as their basis.
Sentient beings, being deluded regarding this, conceive the notion that these are external, solid, stable, and continuous; however, they do not truly exist. Question:
If that is so, why must they manifest as resembling external objects? Answer: If they did not manifest by resembling external objects, then [the following would occur]: ...should [be supplied].
There is no inversion, nor is there defilement or purity. For instance, all ordinary beings, due to their prior delusion regarding objects such as form, engage in inverted and false attachments;

through this, they give rise to further defilements. If one does not admit that consciousness transforms and manifests in the likeness of external objects, then sentient beings would not give rise to inversions, and if inversions do not arise, then defilement would not exist.

If defilement (*saṃkleśa*) does not exist, how could pure phenomena (*viśuddhadharma*) exist? Therefore, the various consciousnesses also manifest as resembling form (*rūpa*). Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* verse states: [and so forth].

Regarding the "confused appearance" (*bhrānti-nimitta*), this refers to the appearance of form that is transformed by [consciousness]. Regarding the "confused substance" (*bhrānti-vastu*), this refers to the substance of the mind that performs the transformation.
If one grants that the confused appearance is a consciousness of form, it is because it is what is transformed by consciousness; however, the confused substance is not form.
Consciousness is not a transformation of matter. If there were no substance of consciousness, all defiled and pure phenomena would be non-existent.

Therefore, although the various consciousnesses can transform and manifest as the semblance of external objects, they do not depart from the mind; they are all in essence *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
The external objects such as form are clearly perceived; [this continues] until: they cannot be grasped as being real external forms.

This is the objection based on the contradiction with the tenet regarding the sixth type of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The objection states: For instance, the five sensory objects are clearly and directly realized by the five consciousnesses;

this is obtained through direct perception, a point fully established and agreed upon by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. If [you claim these objects] are not [directly perceived], it would contradict inference.

The two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arise from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), being produced by forceful reflection, deliberation, and mental fabrication; thus they can be established as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
Now, since the five sensory consciousnesses directly perceive (*pratyakṣa*) the five external, real objects (*viṣaya*), why is it said that these too are all merely consciousness? Answer:

Furthermore, for example, when the five consciousnesses of direct perception (pratyakṣa) apprehend the five objects, they grasp the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena without being accompanied by names or words;
there is no mind of deliberation, no arising of conceptualization (vikalpa), and no grasping [of them] as external.

It is only that the subsequent moment of mental consciousness (manovijñāna) conceptually discriminates and falsely clings to them as external, saying that real objects exist. Question: For instance, regarding the five objects of direct perception apprehended by the five consciousnesses—
[Question: Is this real or provisional? [Answer: It is real, not provisional. [Question: If that is so, then there would be five objects existing substantially apart from the mind.

Why, then, do you say "consciousness-only"? [Answer: When the five consciousnesses perceive the five objects, although they are all real, these are merely the objective parts (sva-lakṣaṇa-bhāga) transformed by the five consciousnesses themselves;
they do not exist apart from the five consciousnesses. However, when the subsequent conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises...
The false attachment that mental phenomena possess real external objects is itself non-existent, because they are known without corresponding to the actual nature of those objects.

Furthermore, objects such as form are not actually external forms; they appear as if they were external forms, just like the dream-objects perceived by a dreaming mind, which are certainly not real and cannot be grasped as being real external forms.
"If all forms during the waking state are like dream-objects" (up to) "thereby one has not yet understood that form-objects are mere consciousness.

This is the seventh objection regarding the contradiction between dreaming and waking. The objection states: "If all forms during the waking state are exactly like those manifested in a dream," [then how can there be a distinction between them?].
Regarding "not being separated from consciousness": for example, when a person awakens from a dream, they know that the objects of that awakening are merely manifestations of the mind.
Why, then, do they not realize at the time of waking that the visual objects manifested by their own consciousness are also "consciousness-only"?
It is just as when a person is in a dream and has not yet awakened; they cannot know for themselves that the dream-objects are merely the mind, but only upon reaching the state of waking...
Only then can one retrospectively contemplate the dream state, realizing that it was entirely a manifestation of the mind.

Since this is the case for dreams, one should know that the objects and forms perceived during the waking state are likewise so. Before reaching the stage of awakening, one does not know that the three realms are mind-only;

only upon reaching the stage of true awakening does one realize that all things manifest from the mind. This is what is meant by: "Only after attaining great awakening does one come to know this Great [Awakening]."
It is a dream. Because those who have not yet attained the stage of true awakening constantly dwell within a dream, the Buddha taught that it is the "long night" of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
For this reason, as long as one does not realize that objective forms are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), it is called the "long night" of birth and death;

specifically, the seventh [consciousness] is the root of this long night of birth and death, capable of causing the arising of afflictions, the creation of karma, and the cycle of the three realms. Directly...
When this consciousness is completely severed, it is called the stage of true awakening.
External forms are in reality non-existent and cannot be objects of internal consciousness; this is just as when one takes the mind and form of another as an object, and so forth.

The eighth objection concerns the external apprehension of another's mind. The objection states: "If it is the case that external forms are non-existent and are not the objects of internal consciousness, that may be so.
However, for instance, the mind of another person is a real existent; how could it not be the object apprehended by one's own consciousness?
If this person’s mind directly apprehends and grasps the mind of another person, then [that other mind] must be distinct from this person’s mind."
[Objection: There exists a separate mind as an object [of cognition], which would contradict the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

If this person cannot directly perceive the minds of others, how can they possess the "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*)? [Response: Although it is said that the minds of others are not the objects of one's own consciousness, we do not say that they are not the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Therefore, while one does not directly perceive the other's mind [in the sense of grasping its substance], the knowledge of others' minds is nonetheless established. If...
There is also a knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that takes the mind of another as its essential nature and perceives it through its own transformed aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
That is to say, one knows that the aspect of the other's mind is not separate from one’s own mind; thus, it too is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Although this person’s mind transforms and gives rise to an aspect when perceiving another person’s mind, it lacks any real functional activity. It is not like the hand or other limbs directly grasping an external object, nor is it like...
The sun and other luminaries emit light that directly illuminates their respective objects; yet these appear as if they were external objects, like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water.

Therefore, it is called "knowing another's mind," though it is not a direct cognition. It must be an object consisting of the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-part) transformed by one’s own consciousness that is directly cognized.
Thus, the following passage is cited as proof: "There is not even the slightest dharma that can grasp another dharma. This is because...
Because both the grasper and the grasped are mind, it is like the case of taking another's mind as an object; the same applies to form and so forth.

This means that when one takes the mind of another person as an object, one merely relies upon it as the substantial essence (*bhāva*) while transforming it into an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

As for the "object," this refers to the other person's sense-faculties (*mūrtendriya*); these too are merely relied upon as the substantial essence, and one transforms them into an objective aspect to perceive them, not apprehending them directly, just as in the case of the mind.

When consciousness takes the color of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) transformed by the eighth consciousness as its object, it likewise merely relies upon that [transformation] as a substantial basis (ālambana-pratyaya) and transforms its own image-part (nimitta-bhāga) to perceive it;
it does not directly apprehend it. This is just as when the five consciousnesses take the substantial objects transformed by the root-consciousness as their objects;
they do not directly apprehend them. Although they do indeed apprehend them, this only constitutes a remote objective condition (parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya).
If there are indeed distinct external objects, how can they be called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*)? [This leads to] the ninth objection:
that there are distinct objects which are not consciousness. The objection states:

If the meaning of "consciousness-only" is that there is not a single thing existing apart from the mind that could be termed "consciousness-only," then if another person's primary object (*mūla-pratibimba*) is not perceived by one, it would necessarily be separate from that person.
If external objects have the minds of others as their essential nature, how can they be established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? To refute this, it is said: "How strange!

Such stubborn attachment gives rise to doubt at every turn. Although the essential nature exists apart from one's own consciousness, it does not exist apart from the transformative mind of another person.
This does not contradict the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). If [the world] were separate from one's own mind, it would not be *vijñapti-mātra*.
How could the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra* possibly claim that consciousness belongs to only a single person? Question: If it is not the consciousness of a single person, then how is it so? Answer:

If the holy teachings spoke of the consciousness of only a single person, then the distinctions of rank and cause-and-effect among the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones would be impossible.
If all these were entirely non-existent, who would seek the Dharma and who would teach the Dharma?

However, because each sentient being possesses their own consciousness, these matters are established. If there were only a single consciousness, such things as these would not be accomplished at all.

Therefore, the single phrase "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) carries a profound significance. As for the term "consciousness," it does not mean that all people collectively possess one single consciousness.
This collectively reveals that sentient beings within the three realms each possess eight consciousnesses, each possess six categories of mental factors (*caitta*),

each possess the two divisions of the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), each possess twenty-four types of dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), and each possess six types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding "each has eight consciousnesses": because they are the self-nature of consciousness, the eight types of mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) are the most preeminent;

therefore, they are explained first. Regarding "each has mental factors (*caitta*)": because they are associated with consciousness, compared to the preceding mind-kings, they are superior first and inferior later;

therefore, they are explained next. Regarding "each has the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*)": because these two are transformations [of the mind], these two cannot arise by themselves; they require...
Relying on what was manifested by the two preceding kings—first the subject and subsequently the object—they are explained next.

Each has its own non-corresponding [factors], because they are states of consciousness; the twenty-four dharmas cannot arise independently, but are provisionally established based on the distinctions among the three preceding stages—first the real and subsequently the provisional—and thus they are explained next.
Each has its own unconditioned [element], which is the true nature of consciousness.
Therefore, while the preceding four [categories] are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Because it exists first and then ceases to exist, it is explained next.

Since all such phenomena do not depart from consciousness, they are collectively designated by the name "consciousness. The word "only" (*kevala*) serves merely to exclude the objects of the false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) of fools—namely, that there truly exist forms, non-associated formations, unconditioned phenomena, and so forth, which are distinct from consciousness. Thus, it is called "Cognition-Only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

The statement that "one is prohibitive and one is affirmative" possesses profound significance. As explained below, it reveals the benefits of the two kinds of benefit [self and others] in order to encourage faith;
therefore, it says: "The mind can become a Buddha; the mind creates sentient beings; the mind creates heaven; the mind creates hell."

When the mind is divergent, a thousand differences arise in competition; when the mind is equanimous, the Dharma-realm is level and vast. When the mind is ordinary, it is entangled by the three poisons;

when the mind is sagely, the six supernormal powers are mastered with ease. When the mind is empty, the single path is pure; when the mind exists [as a subject], ten thousand objects appear in纵横 (zōnghéng—transverse and vertical) array.
It is like a valley responding to sound: the voice is bold and the echo is sharp. It is like a mirror reflecting an image: the form is curved [and the reflection follows].

Yet when the shadow is concave, one thereby knows that the myriad practices arise from the mind; everything resides within oneself. To tread upon clouds and mists and drink the nectar of immortality is not bestowed by another;
to lie amidst flames and consume pus and blood is entirely something one can do for oneself. It is neither born of heaven nor produced by earth;
it depends solely on that first thought-moment which brings about this ascent or descent. If one desires external peace and harmony, [one must look no further].

Yet within there is tranquility; the mind is empty and the environment is still. When thoughts arise, phenomena are born; when water is turbid, waves are murky; when the pool is clear, the moon is bright.
The essentials of spiritual practice do not exceed this. It may truly be called the gateway to all wonders and the treasury of all spirits.
This is the root of ascent and descent, the source of misfortune and fortune. Simply rectify your own mind; why doubt external objects?
If there is only consciousness and no external conditions at all, [it is because] pure seeds manifest as activity and arise conditioned by them.

A general objection is raised: If there are only consciousnesses and no external conditions whatsoever, then since there are no external objects to draw the mind toward them, by what means could discrimination arise?
This is because "with the arising of the mind, dharmas arise; with the arising of dharmas, the mind arises.
Next, the verse is cited as a response. The commentary states: "The consciousness containing all seeds" refers to that within the fundamental consciousness which is capable of producing its own...
Regarding the differentiation of the functional capacity of the fruit: "functional capacity" refers to the eighth consciousness’s seeds being able to produce actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

By means of this functional capacity, it can produce four types of fruits; thus, it is called "all-seeded" (*sarvabījaka*). This excludes the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*), because this fruit is not produced from the seeds of consciousness.
It must arise through the actual manifestation of the truly uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and is realized by severing the afflictions; it does not [arise] from...
Regarding "arising from seeds": although this presently arising path does not arise directly from seeds, it possesses an indirect relationship with respect to its fruit;
however, this is not what is being discussed here, because this section speaks only of the seeds that produce the manifest activity of discrimination.
Because that is the seed of untainted purity. Question: If that is so, one should speak of "all seeds";

why then do you say "all-seed consciousness" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*)? Answer: Because these seeds take the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as their substance, it is called "all-seed consciousness.
These seeds are precisely the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness; apart from the fundamental consciousness, they have no separate existence.
Because it is the nature [of the storehouse consciousness]. Furthermore, the two terms "seed" (*bīja*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) serve to exclude that which is not a seed-consciousness.

This is because while the first seven [consciousnesses] are all called "consciousness," they are not seed-consciousness; and although external seeds are called "seeds," they are not seeds of consciousness.

Moreover, the term "seed-consciousness" indicates that this is the seed *within* consciousness, rather than the consciousness that *holds* the seed. This distinction in meaning shall be explained in the subsequent text. As for the word "like" (*yathā*):

Regarding the phrase "it transforms in such and such a way": within this consciousness, the seeds further obtain the immediate, sovereign, and auxiliary power, whereby they immediately transform and mature in such and such a manner.
Because it is shown that the seeds of transformation are not singular, the term "such and such" is repeated;
that is to say, all seeds encompass the entirety of designations, the grasping at a self, and the common seeds of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
"Common seeds, etc. refers to the fact that because they possess the power of mutual assistance, the eight manifest consciousnesses and so forth are said to be "mutually dependent" (*kṣaṇa*).

"The arising of various discriminations" refers to the manifest consciousnesses, as well as their associated aspects—the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect)—which are collectively termed "discrimination," because they all have false discrimination as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is the division.

Because there are many distinct types, it is said "this and that. For example, there are the three kinds of discrimination (*vikalpa*), the seven kinds of discrimination, the eight kinds of discrimination, up to the ten kinds of discrimination, and so forth.

Regarding the three kinds of discrimination: first is discrimination by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), which is the discrimination that functions solely with respect to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that serve as its present objects.
These objects of action are the specific characteristics of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); for instance, [the specific characteristic] of form (*rūpa*).
Taking "blue" as its mode of activity (*ākāra*), when visual consciousness arises, it also operates spontaneously with the mode of activity of blue.

Second is recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*); it is a conceptualization that follows after and recollects various conditioned phenomena previously experienced, and it takes only the past as its object.

Third is the conceptualization of deliberation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*). This refers to the mental activity of conceptualizing that which is not presently manifest across the past, future, and present;

it consists of imagining existence where there is no existence, and its objects are not those of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). There are five types of conceptualization as previously cited, and furthermore, there are seven types of conceptualization.
As previously cited, there are eight types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*): 1. Conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*):

This refers to the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of all things, such as form (*rūpa*), based on the perceived objects (*nimitta*) of form and so forth. 2. Conceptualization of distinctions (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*):

This refers to the various conceptualizations arising with respect to those very same perceived objects of form and so forth, such as: "this has form" or "is formless," "is visible" or "is invisible," "is resistant" or "is non-resistant. And so forth.
These are the immeasurable varieties [of discrimination]. Regarding the objective basis for the discrimination of intrinsic nature, they discriminate various distinct meanings.
Third is the discrimination of total grasping (*parāmarśa-vikalpa*), which refers to the "self" established upon the perceived objects such as form and so forth.

Furthermore, "sentient beings," "beings," and so forth, are conceptual designations (*prajñapti*) resulting from the activity of discrimination (*vikalpa*) induced by the grasping of a collection of many phenomena as a whole.

Because discrimination proceeds based on this cause of collective grasping, there are four types of discrimination regarding a self (*ātman*). That is to say, if a phenomenon is with outflows (*sāsrava*), [it is the object of these discriminations].

There is a false discrimination arising from the conditions of objects that are the locus of one's own views, which have been repeatedly cultivated through the long-term habituation of grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) involving appropriation (*upādāna*).
It consists of five types of discrimination regarding "mine" (*mama-kāra*):

namely, those objects which are tainted (*sāsrava*), involve appropriation, and have been accumulated through the long-term habituation of grasping at "mine," and which arise from the repeated cultivation of false attachments to objects that are the locus of one's own views.

There are six types of conceptualization arising from conditions that constitute the discrimination of craving: first, conceptualization based on objects that are pure, excellent, and agreeable; second, conceptualization based on objects that are impure, non-excellent, and disagreeable; third, conceptualization based on objects that are both pure and impure, agreeable and disagreeable. [The remaining five are: fourth, conceptualization based on objects that are exclusively agreeable; fifth, conceptualization based on objects that are exclusively disagreeable; sixth, conceptualization based on objects that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable. Seventh, conceptualization of non-craving, which is conceptualization based on objects that are impure, non-excellent, and disagreeable. Eighth, conceptualization that is neither craving nor non-craving, which is conceptualization based on objects that are both pure and impure, agreeable and disagreeable. [The remaining three are: ninth, conceptualization based on objects that are exclusively agreeable; tenth, conceptualization based on objects that are exclusively disagreeable; eleventh, conceptualization based on objects that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable. These are the eleven types of conceptualization. Furthermore, there are four types of conceptualization regarding the aggregates: conceptualization of the self, conceptualization of what belongs to the self, conceptualization of permanence, and conceptualization of pleasure.
