The mental [consciousness] is dissociated from the objects of sensory domains and from conceptualization. Thus, briefly stated, there are two kinds:

namely, the nature of conceptualization itself, and the objective bases and objects upon which conceptualization relies. Among these, there are three types of conceptualization: conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), conceptualization of distinctions (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), and conceptualization of grasping as a whole (*piṇḍagrāha-vikalpa*).
These three types of conceptualization give rise to the objective bases for the conceptual proliferation of discrimination. Conceptual proliferation...

Regarding the objects of focus (*ālambana-vastu*): because they rely upon and take as conditions the entities designated by such concepts as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, they are comprised within conceptualization, verbal expression, and discursive proliferation (*prapañca*).
Within these very entities, one engages in immeasurable, manifold, and diverse forms of conceptual construction and deliberation.
Among these, the conceptualization of "self" (*ātman*) and the conceptualization of "mine" (*ātmīya*)—these two types of conceptualization—serve as the root that gives rise to other views.
The root of pride, which is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), which is the root that gives rise to other forms of pride—
within these, the conceptualization of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and that which is neither, give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion as appropriate.

Therefore, these eight kinds of discrimination give rise to these three types of entities. If one wishes to briefly explain the essential nature of discrimination, it refers to all minds and mental factors within the three realms.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* describes ten kinds of subtle discrimination regarding the faculties and their objects:
first, fundamental discrimination, which refers to the ālayavijñāna; this is the basis for the others.
1. Distinctive discrimination (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*): because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is also discriminative. 2. Discrimination of the characteristics of conditions (*nimitta-vikalpa*):

that is, discriminating that form and so forth possess such characteristics of conditions. 3. Discrimination of the manifestation of function (*kāritra-vikalpa*): namely, the visual consciousness and so forth, which manifest together with their supporting consciousnesses, appearing as if they were those very objects of perception.
4. Discrimination of the transformation of the characteristics of conditions (*nimittavikāra-vikalpa*): namely, that which appears like a reflection of form and so forth.
There are six types of discrimination arising from the transformation of consciousness: First, transformation by aging and so forth;

that is, the consciousness of form and so forth manifests the appearance of aging and so forth, giving rise to various transformations, because internal and external forms and so forth all possess the characteristics of transformation such as aging.
The phrase "and so forth" includes the transformations of illness and death. Second, transformation by pleasant feeling and so forth; this is due to pleasant feeling.

The transformation of physical appearance (*kāyavikāra*). As it is said regarding those who experience pleasure: "the facial features are upright and majestic," and so forth. The phrase "and so forth" includes [those experiencing] pain and neither-pain-nor-pleasure sensations.

The three types of transformation caused by greed and so forth mean that the physical appearance undergoes transformation due to greed and the like. The phrase "and so forth" [includes hatred and delusion].
[This refers to] hatred, delusion, anger, and so forth; as it is said regarding anger and the like, [there are] ugly physical forms and so forth.
There are four types of transformation caused by affliction and the shifting of seasons: namely, killing, binding, and so on, which cause the characteristics of the body to transform;

and the shifting of seasons, which likewise causes the internal and external forms of the body, trees, colors, and so forth, to change. As it is said, when one is oppressed by cold and the like, [these transformations occur].

The transformations of the body and so forth; the transformations of the various destinies, such as the five *naraka*s (hells) and so forth—the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) including all evil destinies;

the transformations of the six desire realms and so forth—the term "and so forth" including the form and formless realms, meaning that within the various heavens and the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), there are likewise sentient beings, as well as various transformations of material objects and the like, such as [the palace of] Māra.
The *ni-zhu* (monastic jewel). Due to its majestic spiritual power (*vīrya-śakti*), various pure and wondrous colors and forms undergo transformation.
This is the fifth [category], the discrimination of the transformation of manifest characteristics (*nimitta-vikāra-vikalpa*).

That is to say, by means of the sense organs (*indriya*) such as the eye which serve as supports, images resembling form and so forth are made to appear, and the consciousnesses such as visual consciousness undergo various transformations. Within this very process, various discriminations arise, just as in the case of aging and so forth previously mentioned.
There is transformation. Transformation occurs in accordance with arising, just as the sense organs, such as the eye, may be sharp or dull, so too consciousness may be clear or dim.
The transformations of pleasant feeling and so forth are likewise. As it is said: for one who experiences pleasure, the mind is settled; for one who experiences pain, the mind is distracted.
This extends even to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there are also various discriminations of consciousness produced by the transformations of feeling and the like.

Sixth is discrimination induced by others, which refers to discrimination arising from associating with those who are virtuous or non-virtuous, as well as that which arises with the hearing of the true Dharma as its cause.
Seventh is irrational discrimination, which refers to the discrimination of various non-Buddhists resulting from hearing teachings that are not the true Dharma.
Eighth is rational discrimination, which refers to the discrimination resulting from hearing the true Dharma within the true Dharma. Ninth...
Adherence to conceptualization refers to the category of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), which has the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as its root.
It consists of conceptualizations associated with the sixty-two types of views and the ten types of distracted conceptualizations— namely,
those verbal expressions produced by bodhisattvas that are induced by others and do not accord with reality— which disturb non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Therefore, the meaning of this verse is to demonstrate that although external conditions do not exist, all various conceptualizations arise through the power of transformation of all seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), as well as the reciprocal power of the eight manifesting consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Why, then, would one rely on external conditions for conceptualization to arise? Regarding "all pure [phenomena]" and below, it is explained by analogy.

Having explained the distinctions of seeds and manifestations arising through conditions (up to their being mutual causes for one another), the following clarifies the meaning of the four conditions (*pratyaya*) for the arising of consciousness.
First, the question; second, the answer. First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): it refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) directly producing their own results.
This causal condition is of two kinds. The first is the seed (*bīja*), which refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). Three...

The realms, the nine stages, the three types of feeling, the characteristics of views and so forth, and the distinctions in their functional capacities, are able to project seeds of their own kind and give rise to the manifest results of their own kind.
Thus, these seeds in relation to those seeds, and these seeds in relation to those manifestations, are all termed "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Second, regarding the two types of manifestation: this refers to the first seven evolving consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, as well as that which is transformed by them.

The mutual perception of signs, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three realms (*tridhātu*), the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), the three measures (*tripramāṇa*), and the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) states are all termed "active manifestations" (*samudācāra*).

With the exception of all wholesome dharmas within the state of Buddhahood and the most inferior indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas—which are not capable of perfuming—these remaining seven bases, as well as the natures, realms, and so forth, are all able to perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and produce seeds of their own kind. This is precisely what is meant by these active manifestations.
[This refers to] the practice. Looking toward those seeds, they are also called "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*). [The following is] a detailed analysis. Question:

For what reason do only the first seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) perfuse the eighth consciousness, and not the mental factors of the eighth consciousness?

Answer: Because the mental factors of the eighth consciousness are not that which is perfused (*bhāvya*). Question: Why are the aspects such as the "perceived" (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the "perceiving" (*darśana-bhāga*) termed "perfusing agents" (*bhāvaka*)? Answer: This is not a matter of excluding that which is perfused.
Because they can act as perfumers independently. Question: Why are the wholesome states of the Buddha-fruit and the inferior indeterminate states excluded, as neither can act as a perfumer?
Answer: Because the Buddha-fruit is extremely perfected and the indeterminate states are extremely weak, they do not perfume to form seeds.

Question: Why is it that similar phenomena appearing in the present are called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) and not "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*)? Answer: Because a later manifestation does not arise from a preceding manifestation;
rather, it arises from its own seed. *Zhengjing* (Mirror of the Essential Teachings) asks: If a seed induces another seed, why is this called a "direct causal condition"? Answer:
When the preceding moment has already ceased and the succeeding moment has already arisen, the very essence of the preceding moment directly induces the succeeding moment.

Therefore, it is called the "direct cause" (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Question: Since the present induces the present, and the preceding moment also directly induces the succeeding moment, why is it described as a "similar outflow" (*niṣyanda*)?
Answer: Because the seeds already exist. That is to say, the seed of the preceding moment gives rise to the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) of that same preceding moment;
then, that seed of the preceding moment flows forward to produce the manifest activity of the second subsequent moment. Thus it is known.
The manifestation of a subsequent thought-moment is not directly produced by the preceding thought-moment. Question:

Why is the manifestation of a different category (vijātīya) considered a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)? Answer: Because it is not directly produced [by it].

Regarding the term "different category," this refers, for example, to the manifestation of form (*rūpa*) in relation to the manifestation of mind (*citta*), or the manifestation of mind in relation to the manifestation of form, and so forth. However, where it is stated that such a relationship constitutes a causal condition, it should [be understood as referring to an indirect or secondary cause].

Know that all these are merely provisional designations as skillful means. In some places, it is taught that only the production of seeds from seeds constitutes the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the production of seeds from manifest phenomena is not mentioned.
However, the statement that manifest phenomena produce seeds is spoken from the perspective of emphasizing what is prominent; it is not a discourse that exhausts the full extent of the principle.

Why is this? Because the Noble One has taught that the evolving consciousnesses and the *ālayavijñāna* stand in a reciprocal relationship, acting as mutual causes and conditions for one another, just like a wick [and its flame].
A flame arises; just as a flame arises and burns, so too the nature of causes and conditions is definitively the mutual production of seeds and manifest states.
How could one insist that it consists solely of seeds and not manifest states?

Second, regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), this refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses, because it is said that these very [consciousnesses] constitute the equal-and-immediate condition for one another.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the eight kinds of manifest consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) of the preceding moment, which,
without any interval, equally yield way and guide the subsequent moments of their own respective classes of mind and mental factors so that they necessarily arise.

The term "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses; this identifies their objective basis (*ālambana*). It excludes matter (*rūpa*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as these do not possess the nature of such a condition.

By specifying that a preceding aggregate serves as the condition for a subsequent one, it excludes simultaneous or subsequent states from being conditions for what precedes them. By specifying "of its own kind," it clarifies that they are not conditions for other types of consciousness.
"Immediately preceding" indicates that although the former serves as the condition for the latter, there is no interval between them. "Equal" means that which can induce [the subsequent state].
The forces of attraction are equal. That is to say: one attracts one aggregate, and one aggregate responds to one; one aggregate attracts one, and one responds to one aggregate;
one aggregate attracts one aggregate, and one aggregate responds to one aggregate; one attracts one phenomenon, and one phenomenon responds to one.
Although there are such variations in type, their power is entirely equal. "Opening" (*kai*) means to avoid; "guiding" (*dō*) means to summon and lead.

"Meaning" (artha) refers to the preceding dharma moving away to avoid [the subsequent one] while inducing the subsequent dharma to arise. The above clarifies dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As for "causing that to necessarily arise," this clarifies that even though a subsequent fruit may be separated by a vast duration of time, it is nonetheless conditioned by this very cause.
For example, an eye-consciousness from eighty thousand *kalpas* ago is also a condition for what follows, because that subsequent fruit is destined to arise.
It is specifically excluded from arising within the fruitless meditative absorption of nirvana without remainder; therefore, it is not this [equal-immediate] condition.
Although there is the sense of "opening," there is no sense of "inducing. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"With the exception of the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat at the moment of entering nirvana, all other previously arisen minds and mental factors are equal-immediate conditions. Question: When the eight consciousnesses arise...
"What is the use of these conditions? [The answer is: "Because within one's own single consciousness, the preceding moment does not cease and the succeeding moment does not arise;
since the self-substance of the preceding moment occupies its own path, when consciousness arises, these conditions must be employed. [Question:

"The eight kinds of manifest consciousnesses mostly evolve simultaneously with their corresponding seeds of the same class. Why is it that those consciousnesses do not possess [the relationship of] mutual equality (sahabhū-hetu) with one another?"
[Question: Regarding the intervening condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). [Answer: Because they are not mutually associated (*asamprayukta*), it is not subsumed under this condition.
For this reason, although the eight consciousnesses may arise simultaneously, because they are not mutually associated, they cannot serve as intervening conditions for one another in turn. [Question:
Since the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are not of the same category, like the seeds of the eight consciousnesses which always arise together yet differ in essence and function, as...

What is the meaning of their arising together and acting as mutual conditions? Answer: Although mental factors and the mind always arise together, because they are associated (*saṃprayukta*), they are like the light of many lamps;
being conjoined, they appear as one, and it is impossible to designate them as separate or distinct.

Therefore, they are able to act as mutual conditions for one another. As for the phrase "conjoined and appearing as one," this means they share the same basis (*āśraya*) and the same object (*ālambana*).
They arise simultaneously, are subsumed under the same nature, and are necessarily co-arising and co-ceasing. When one [consciousness] acts as a precursor, the others likewise act as precursors;
therefore, they function as mutual equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

This is not the case for the eight consciousnesses, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*), bases (*āśraya*), and objects (*ālambana*) are each distinct and unequal, and thus they do not serve as mutual conditions. Question: Since all eight consciousnesses possess this condition, when entering the state of non-...

Other minds should also possess this [quality]. Why is it that they definitely do not? Answer: When entering the mind of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (the state without remainder), the mind is extremely subtle and weak;

because there is no preceding [mind] to provide guidance, the subsequent [mind] does not necessarily arise, and thus it is not subsumed under these conditions. Question: How is this known to be so? Answer: There is a clear statement in the treatise:
"If this preceding consciousness ceases, and there is an interval of equal non-interruption in between, it causes that subsequent consciousness to certainly [arise]."
Regarding the fruit born of meditative concentration, it is said that a preceding consciousness serves as the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for a subsequent consciousness.
Since there is currently no other mind present, this principle does not apply; therefore, it is not such a condition.
Based on this meaning, one should state as follows: (up to) "the Sūtra does not state that they give rise to the great resolve.

This clarifies that the eighth [consciousness] exists throughout all three realms and nine stages, for at the time of death in a lower stage, it acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind at the time of birth in a higher stage.
Thus, death and birth in the lower and upper stages mutually induce and guide one another, all being equal.
Because they are equal. Question: When a present impure (sāsrava) mind is necessarily ceasing, does it act as this condition for a future pure (anāsrava) mind?
Answer: When an impure mind ceases, it causes that pure mind to arise with certainty.
However, when a pure mind ceases, there is certainly no arising of an impure mind; this is because the eighth pure mind arises as a mental complex (citta-varga).
It is transformed into the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Since this wisdom, once arisen, is never interrupted, there is no such condition [for its cessation].
The same applies when comparing the wholesome and the neutral: that is, when a defiled neutral mind ceases, a non-defiled wholesome mind necessarily arises.
When an undefiled wholesome mind ceases, it certainly does not give rise to a defiled or neutral mind. Question: From which realm and stage can this untainted (anāsrava) mind be induced?
Answer: It is said to be from both the form and desire realms. "The various lower [stages]" explains its induction from the form realm;
"the two vehicles' lower [stages]" explains its induction from the desire realm. Some maintain that "lower" refers to the sound-hearers (śrāvaka) of the form realm.
There are also instances where hearing acts as a projecting cause (*ākṣepaka*).

Regarding the seventh transformative consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), it does not arise in those [realms] for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) who have transcended the nine stages of the three realms;
thus, the seventh manas-consciousness exists throughout all nine stages of the three realms. This is because it follows along with whatever is produced by the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
Because they are bound together, those in the higher and lower realms who die and are born provide mutual guidance to one another, all as in the eighth [bhūmi].

Both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) possess this condition, allowing them to arise from one another. This is because, in the *manas*, wisdom transforms within the cause (*hetu*), unlike the eighth [consciousness], which exists only at the level of the fruit (*phala*).
Therefore, throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), both the contaminated and the uncontaminated are able to mutually induce one another. This is excellent.
The indeterminate and the defiled or undefiled also mutually induce one another, because the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons can lead from a preceding stage to a subsequent stage.
Question: In these realms of desire and form, the contaminated and the uncontaminated may arise from one another;
does this mutual arising also occur in the formless realm? Answer: This mutual arising occurs in the realms of desire and form, but not in the formless realm.
Because Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) are not born into this realm, there is no sense of the arising of signs;
for the sixth evolving consciousness and the [seventh] manas differ in their clarity or obscurity regarding their objects across the three realms and nine stages.
The sixth consciousness exists as an object-condition throughout the three realms and nine stages, because its evolving wisdom (*pravṛtti-jñāna*) also belongs to the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

Within the stage of nourishing birth (*janma-paripuṣṭi*), they mutually induce one another. When this consciousness first arises as untainted (*anāsrava*), it occurs only in the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), because the four wholesome states of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*) exist only in the form realm.
The three faculties of eye, ear, and body exist only in the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*).
The stage of the five destinies abiding together and the stage of the rapture and bliss born of seclusion in the form realm also possess this condition.
However, the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue possess this condition only within the desire realm. In the three stages above that, none of the five consciousnesses possess this condition.

According to a certain master, the five consciousnesses—whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—are all capable of arising alternately; prior to attaining Buddhahood, they are capable of arising alternately.

Therefore, one master says: "From contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*), uncontaminated [consciousness] arises; however, from uncontaminated meditative concentration, contaminated [consciousness] does not arise.

This is because uncontaminated fivefold sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna*) exists only in a Buddha; prior to attaining Buddhahood, those five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are necessarily contaminated.
The contaminated material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are subsumed under the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

This is because the five contaminated faculties are necessarily co-existent with the first five consciousnesses; because they necessarily share the same object; because it would be illogical for contaminated faculties to produce uncontaminated consciousness;
and because the objects of uncontaminated consciousness must be clearly manifest, whereas the objects of contaminated consciousness are necessarily obscure. Question:
Why is it that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), arise from one another, whereas the fifth and eighth do not? Answer:

The sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess three grades of evolving cognition (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*): in the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is the inferior grade; in the eighth stage, there is the middling grade.

In the case of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the superior grade transforms first; in the case of the inferior grade, the initial transformation has not yet become purely untainted (*anāsrava*).

Therefore, it co-arises with and mutually induces the tainted (*sāsrava*). However, if the five or eight [consciousnesses] transform only in their superior grade, then at the moment one attains the untainted, the tainted will no longer arise.
Because they arise simultaneously with wisdom, they are necessarily uninterrupted.
Third, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) refers to those phenomena (up to) which, even in the absence of external objects upon which the mind relies, [cognition] can still arise.
That which is called "existent phenomena" refers to those phenomena that possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*).

This excludes provisional phenomena (*prajñaptisat*) as well as the non-substantial phenomena of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and its objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*), because these do not give rise to the consciousness that takes them as objects.

For something to function as a condition (*pratyaya*), it must be a phenomenon possessing substantial reality and causal efficacy (*samartha*); only such a thing can draw forth and produce consciousness. Thus, the actual dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is a phenomenon possessing substantial reality.

Regarding the phrase "carrying its own characteristics" (*svākāra*), there are two meanings to "carrying": First is "transformative carrying" (*pariṇāmākāra*). This refers to the seeds of the eight consciousnesses.

It is the objective essence (*ālambanapratyaya*) of the remote object-condition. Because it relies upon this substantial entity as its objective essence, a semblance arises that appears like that essence;
this is called transformative carrying. Second is "clinging carrying" (*sākṣādākāra*). This refers to the actual image-part (*nimittabhāga*) of all direct object-conditions.
This is so. For this reason, the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) does not depart from the cognizing mind. That cognizing mind directly grasps this objective aspect while performing its cognition;

this is termed "grasping and carrying" (sahagata). Regarding the phrase "one's own aspect" (sva-nimitta), there are also two meanings. First, it is spoken in reference to the transformation and the remote object of cognition;
that is, the "own aspect" which is the semblance of the substance transformed by the cognizing mind—namely, the objective aspect resembling the original [object].

Taking its own substance as the essence: this characteristic is the characteristic of the phenomenal aspect (*nimitta*). Second, it is explained in terms of the immediate apprehension of the objective condition:
that is, the cognizing mind immediately apprehends the aspect of the object, which constitutes its own characteristic. This is the characteristic of the objective realm (*ālambana*).
Question: If it is that which carries its own characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), I do not yet understand whose characteristic the cognizing mind carries. Answer:
If it is a remote object (*viprakṛṣṭālambana*), it undergoes transformation and carries the characteristic of the original object (*bimba*). This is carrying a semblance of the original object.

If it is an immediate object (*sannikṛṣṭālambana*), it carries the characteristic of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). This is because the cognition immediately grasps the characteristic of the object.

Regarding the phrase "because of being an object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the statement that "the mind may be associated" (*samprayukta*): Ziyun says, "This distinguishes the result of the object-condition. Taking the object as the condition is the cause;
the resulting mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are the result. As for the term "mind," it refers collectively to the eight sovereign consciousnesses (*citta-rāja*).
As for the term "associated," it refers to the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*). There are those that arise and those that do not. Thus [it is said].

It is said: "The 'or' (perhaps) refers to that which is contemplated and that upon which consciousness relies. Because it is the object-condition (*ālambana*) of consciousness, it is called 'that which is contemplated.
Because it can induce the arising of consciousness, it is called 'that upon which it relies. This has a substantial nature (*dharmatā*) and is either proximate or remote.

If its substance is not separate from the substance of the perceiving portion (*darśana-bhāga*), it is what is internally contemplated and relied upon by the perceiving portion; this is termed a 'proximate condition.'"
This excludes what is transformed by other consciousnesses as well as the distinct objects of the eight consciousnesses themselves.

If, although separated in substance from the perceiving subject, it serves as a substantial basis that can give rise to the internal object of cognition, this is called a "distant condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*); that is, what is transformed by other consciousnesses.

Furthermore, that which is transformed by a distinct consciousness within one's own continuum and serves as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*) is the direct object-condition (*sākṣād-ālambana-pratyaya*).

This exists invariably in all cases of the subjective faculty (*ālambaka*), because no mental state such as consciousness can arise without the appearance of an object (*viṣaya-nimitta*) upon which it internally relies and depends.

As for the indirect object-condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*), its presence or absence in relation to the subjective mind is not fixed; this is because [it pertains to] that which is external to the mind.

Because of the nature of phenomena (dharma). Just as when one clings to a substantially real self or phenomena, although they lack an underlying essence (svabhāva), the mind nevertheless arises in dependence upon them;
likewise, there is a view that the eighth category of consciousness exists only by taking past and future objects as its conditions, for it lacks external substance.
This explains that distant conditions (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*) are indeterminate. First, regarding the eighth [consciousness], its distant conditions are indeterminate. One master says:

"The eighth consciousness possesses only direct conditions (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*), for it can transform itself according to the power of karmic causes; thus, it does not rely on distant conditions. Another master says:
"It definitely has distant conditions, for it must rely on another as a substrate (*ālambana*) before it can transform itself. A third master says: "Neither is the case."

In principle, if the eighth consciousness takes the *buddhadhātu* (sensory organs) and the physical world (*bhājanaloka*) of others as its objects, it must rely upon the *buddhadhātu* and the physical world of others to transform its own *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) for the purpose of cognition;
thus, there is mutual enjoyment, and there must necessarily be a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*).
If it were not the seeds of others that are mutually transformed and taken as conditions, then one's own seeds would have no sense of being enjoyed by others. This is not the case.
Because all sentient beings—whether wise or foolish, noble or base—possess seeds that are entirely equal.
Furthermore, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there exists the physical environment (*bhājanaloka*) as a support, such that remote conditions (*parokṣapratyaya*) may exist.

If it were the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there are no physical sense organs, bodies, or the material world, there would be no remote conditions. If, within the causal stage, one takes these three types of objects as conditions, they are exclusively...
There are direct conditions (*pratyaya*). When one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, all [cognitions] take their own objects as conditions and also take *tathatā* (suchness) as an object;
furthermore, when taking all past phenomena that lack substantiality as objects, there are no indirect conditions (*parokṣa-pratyaya*).

However, when taking the bodies of others or Buddha-fields as objects, they do so by means of reflected images (*pratibimba*), and thus there are indeed indirect conditions. Therefore, it is said that in the causal and resultant stages of the eighth consciousness, there are indirect objective conditions.

The presence or absence [of this condition] is not fixed. Regarding the eighth consciousness and the five mental factors, they definitely possess a remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*) during their causal and resultant stages, because they take the three substantial entities of the eighth consciousness as their basis for cognition.
Below, in the section on the seventh consciousness, it is explained that its remote object-condition is not fixed.

If the seventh consciousness has not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), its nature is innate (*sahaja*) and it lacks spontaneous power; it must therefore rely upon the eighth consciousness.
It takes [the ālayavijñāna] as its essence and serves as the condition for the self-manifestation of images. It grasps the eighth consciousness as its internal self.

In the state where the basis has already been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), when the seventh consciousness’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, there is no indirect condition (*parokṣa-pratyaya*); however, when its subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) takes suchness as its object, there is an indirect condition.
If it is the untainted (*anāsrava*) seventh consciousness taking past phenomena and all non-substantial dharmas as its objects, in all such cases, there is no [indirect condition].

Distant conditions (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). Therefore, the status of distant conditions for cause and effect is indeterminate. Section Six, Part Two: Clarifying that the sixth [consciousness] has indeterminate distant conditions.

If the aspect (*ākāra*) of the sixth consciousness is sharp and intense, then within the states of cause and effect, it may arise either through discrimination (*vikalpa*) or as innate (*sahaja*), and it can function with sovereign autonomy.
Thus, at all times, there are instances where it arises supported by a substantial object (*sālambana*) and instances where it does not.

Therefore, the sixth [consciousness] has indeterminate presence or absence regarding its remote objects (*viprakṛṣṭālambana*). The first five [consciousnesses] are below; this clarifies that the remote objects of the first five consciousnesses are indeterminate.
In the state where the basis has not yet been transformed (*aparivṛttāśraya*), the remote objects of the first five mental complexes are definitely present.

In the state where the basis has already been transformed (*parivṛttāśraya*), these are not definitely present, because when taking the past and so forth as objects, there is no external substantial entity (*bāhyadravya*).

"Obstruction" refers to its predominant function (*adhipatipratyaya*), distinguishing it from that which is not a cause-condition (*hetupratyaya*).

"Able to provide [conditions] for other dharmas" clarifies that it differs from the previously mentioned object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). "Whether favorable or adverse" clarifies that both concordant and discordant dharmas can serve as conditions.

Furthermore, "acting as a condition for subsequent, distinct dharmas, and not for preceding, ceased dharmas" distinguishes it from the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Four. First, favorable dominant conditions (*anuloma-adhipati-pratyaya*). For example, earth and water serve as favorable dominant conditions for green grass and the like;

as the eye obtains the condition of light; and as the six *pāramitās* serve as favorable dominant conditions for the fruit of Buddhahood, or as the two branches of "appropriation" (*upādāna*) and "existence" (*bhava*) serve as favorable dominant conditions for the five fruits, and so forth.
Second, adverse dominant conditions (*pratiloma-adhipati*). This refers, for instance, to frost and hail [acting upon] green [grass].
1. Contrary predominance (*virodha-adhipati*): For example, as when the eye encounters darkness; likewise, as when wisdom acts as a contrary predominance toward delusion.

Furthermore, at the very moment a single thought-moment acts as a contrary predominance toward delusion, it simultaneously acts as a concordant predominance toward the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

2. Potent predominance (*balavat-adhipati*), also called direct predominance (*pratyakṣa-adhipati*): For example, as the five sense faculties give rise to the five consciousnesses, and so forth. 3. Non-potent [predominance]...

Regarding predominance (*adhipati*): when the five faculties (*indriya*) of this person are considered in relation to the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) of that person, they constitute a "powerless predominance" and are also termed "remote predominance.
This is like the gold, silks, wife, and children of another person. Furthermore, it is like when a lamp flame is just arising;
all dharmas such as the great earth do not obstruct the arising of this flame, yet one takes only the aspect of non-obstruction and names it "predominance."
Question: Is this superior function not also present in the first three [conditions]? Answer:

Although the first three conditions are also sovereign (*adhipati*), the fourth is distinguished from them by excluding those and taking up the remainder, in order to manifest that each condition has its own specific distinction.

This superior function of conformity and opposition operates across four locations, because the four matters—arising, completion, acquisition, and attainment—are each distinct. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi*...

It is said: By virtue of seeds, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established; by virtue of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is established;

by virtue of the object (*ālambana*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is established; and by virtue of the support (*āśraya*) and the companions (*sahāya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is established.

Below, the dominant condition is specifically explained through twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). These refer to the five previously mentioned ultimate faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*), namely, the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and so forth.
They have as their nature the pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) transformed [by consciousness]. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"The five faculties are established based on the sense of being the basis for physical beauty and excellence. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The five faculties, beginning with the eye, possess predominant efficacy regarding the consciousnesses that discern their respective objects.
The two faculties of male and female have as their nature a portion of the body faculty. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Based on..."

The meaning of predominance regarding birth establishes two faculties. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The male and female faculties are established separately from the body faculty because they possess predominance within the categories of male and female.
This refers to the differences in physical form, voice, activity, and inclination between males and females, which constitute the distinction between the two sexes.
Because these distinctions exist by virtue of the male and female faculties, they are designated as the male and female faculties. Regarding this:

The two natures are predominant. The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is merely a provisional designation based on the state of the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"Based on the meaning of support, establishment, and predominance, one faculty is established. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), the life-faculty has a predominant function.
As for the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), its nature consists generally of the eight consciousnesses, since all eight manifesting consciousnesses...
Because it functions according to one's will, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "A single faculty is established based on the sense of predominance in functioning according to mastery.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The sixth mental faculty (*manas*) has predominant power over the consciousness that discerns all objects.
Regarding the five faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*), each has its own specific feeling as its intrinsic nature. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Based on the predominance of benefit and harm..."

Because of the sense of superior meaning (*adhipatārtha*), the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are established. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Among the defiled states (*saṃkleśa*), the five feelings such as pleasure (*sukha*) have a predominant function (*adhipatya*).
The five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) take faith itself and virtuous mindfulness (*smṛti*) and so forth as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The five faculties are established based on the sense of predominance regarding worldly purification (*laukika-vyavadāna*). The *Abhidharmakośa* continues: "By this..."
Because they subdue the various afflictions through their power and induce the Noble Path, there are nineteen faculties in total; when the final three faculties are added, there are twenty-two.
Regarding these final three faculties, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: first is the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

It possesses predominant efficacy in the attainment of the path not yet known. Its substantial status consists of three stages: first, the stage of the fundamental [path], which refers to being on the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Excluding the subsequent moment, the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) consists of three moments of mind: the entering mind, the abiding mind, and the emerging mind. "Excluding the subsequent moment" refers to the emerging mind;
since this belongs to the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it must be excluded.

This is because, although the great matter has already been clarified and the fundamental reality has already been seen at the time of the Path of Seeing, there remains a state of "that which is yet to be known" (*ajñeya*).
[It] transforms. Therefore, it is called "that which is yet to be known. Second, the stage of application (*prayoga*) consists of four [levels].

Because in this stage one exerts effort and practice, it is proximate to being able to induce the fundamental path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This is the definitive analysis of the wholesome. It exists within the four dhyānas.

Third, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), which refers to the three stages of the virtuous ones (*kalyāṇamitra*): namely, the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmana*). That is to say:

For one who has not yet attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the truths and desires to attain such realization, they generate a superior and wholesome desire for the Dharma (*dharmecchā*), such as the three types of mental training (*nirmarṣa*).

Until the time they have entered the stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*) and have not yet attained the wholesome roots conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya kuśalamūla*), all such wholesome roots are called the stage of equipment (*sambhārāvasthā*). This is because they serve as a remote support for the growth and development of the fundamental stage.

This refers to the meaning of one who travels a thousand *li* gathering provisions for three months. In these three stages, the nature of this faculty is collectively comprised of the nine untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties.
Within the stage of application (*prayoga*), the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is also present; the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*) likewise possess this faculty.
The "first three" refer to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

This is because there are those who attain it through superior insight (*darśana-mārga*) as well as those who attain it through collateral cultivation (*pārśva-bhāvanā*). The three formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*) also possess this faculty.

Furthermore, those of the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), although they already fully understand the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), give rise to this faculty even during the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi (*bhūmi-pūrva*) in order to seek the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This continues until it is subsumed within the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumati-bhūmi*).
The untainted [roots] born of emptiness are all subsumed under these roots of the Bodhisattva.

Although these roots also exist at the time of the Bodhisattva’s Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are mentioned only in relation to the stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*) and not in relation to the Path of Seeing itself, because that period is brief.

That is to say, at the time of the True Path of Seeing of the First Ground, it is manifested in a single moment of thought and does not belong to the three [preparatory] minds; as illumination arises, darkness departs. Thus [it is said].

It is said that time is short; for if it were the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it would then belong to only three moments of mind. Thus, beginning from below, the second faculty, the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*), is explained.
Since the essence of the path of seeing has already been realized, if one is in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is nothing previously unknown.

However, for the sake of abandoning the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one repeatedly and fully cognizes those same objects; this is called the faculty of "having known. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This..."

The faculty of one who possesses perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) has a predominant function within the path of attainment. Regarding those who have no lower [realms], this explains the faculty of one who possesses perfect knowledge:

it refers to a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who realizes the fruit of one beyond training, thinking, "Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been fulfilled. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"In the path of one beyond training, one knows 'I have known,' and therefore it is called 'knowledge' (*jñāna*). One who possesses this knowledge is [the possessor of the faculty of one who possesses perfect knowledge].

It is called "possessing full knowledge" (*ājñātāvī*). Alternatively, one who has practiced this knowledge until it becomes their very nature is called "possessing full knowledge," meaning they have attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Thus, they know for themselves as it truly is: "I have fully known suffering; there is nothing further to be fully known.

Furthermore, it is said that this faculty (*indriya*) has a predominant function in the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. Moreover, it is said to refer to the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).

Among the cessations, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has predominant efficacy; among the cessations of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) has predominant efficacy;

and regarding the dwelling in happiness in the present life, the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) has predominant efficacy, because by means of it one experiences the joy and bliss of liberation. Question: If they are established as faculties (*indriya*) on account of their predominance...

Furthermore, the nature of ignorance and so forth should be established as faculties (*indriya*), because the causes such as ignorance each possess a distinct and predominant efficacy (*adhipatya*) with respect to their respective effects such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Moreover, the vocal apparatus and so forth should also be established as faculties, because the vocal apparatus, the hands, the feet,
and the organs of excretion and generation possess predominant efficacy, respectively, in the matters of speaking, grasping, walking, and the discharge of pleasure.
Answer: Such matters as these should not be established as faculties (*indriya*), because the characteristics of what is accepted as a faculty are as follows. The verse says:
The basis of the mind, its differentiation, its persistence, its defilement, its provisions, and its purification—it is by these measures that the faculties are established.

Regarding "the basis of the mind": the six faculties, such as the eye and so forth, which constitute these six internal bases (*āyatana*), are the foundation of sentient beings. This is their characteristic.
There is differentiation by means of the male and female faculties; furthermore, by means of the life-faculty, this duration of a single lifetime is established, and this constitutes defilement.

By means of the five feeling-faculties, the equipment for purification is established; by means of the five beginning with faith, this constitutes purification; and by means of the final three faculties, [the state of being an Arhat] is established.
By this, the establishment of the faculties (*indriya*) is fully accomplished.

Therefore, one should not admit that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, or the vocal apparatus and so forth, are also established as faculties, because they lack the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*) in this context. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"The faculty of 'desiring to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the fifteen mental moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)."

All the faculties (*indriya*) herein refer to those included within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) subsumed under the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), as well as all the faculties present during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);

these constitute the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). Regarding the term "all the faculties," this refers to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*);
they are so designated due to the distinctions in their bases (*āśraya*), such as the stage of the threshold (*anāgamya*) and others. As it is said:
Regarding what is appropriate: there are the faculties of pleasure, joy, sorrow, and equanimity.

As for "one [instance of] the faculty of sorrow," this refers to that which is comprised by grief and dejection when, following the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), one seeks and desires to realize higher liberation.

These ten faculties, because they are practiced and turned toward the desire to know what was previously unknown, are called "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

Regarding the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*): from the sixteenth moment of the mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards, all faculties present within the various paths of those in training (*śaikṣa*) constitute the essence of the faculty of having known. Why is this?

It is because the aforementioned ten faculties, from the sixteenth moment of the mind of the path of seeing up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), [function] in such a manner...
Within the path of one in training (*śaikṣa*), there is no object to be known that has not already been known; therefore, it is called the faculty of "that which is already known" (*ājñātendriya*).

The "one who possesses full knowledge" (*ājñātāvin*) refers to the six faculties, such as the eye. These six internal bases (*āyatana*) are the foundation of sentient beings. Their differentiation is due to the male and female faculties.
Furthermore, by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), this [existence] persists for a single period. This defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is established by the five [faculties].
The faculty of feeling (*vedanendriya*) is the pure accumulation (*śuddhasambhāra*). It becomes purified by means of the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*);

it is perfected by means of the final three faculties. Because the task is thus brought to completion, one should not admit that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, nor the vocal organs and so forth, are established as faculties, for they lack this sense of predominance (*ādhipatya*) within this context.
Fascicle Seven.
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
Composed by Dharmapāla and other Bodhisattvas.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree;
compiled and annotated by the Śramaṇa Tongrun of Jinting Changshou Monastery.
Thus, these four conditions rely upon fifteen locations (up to) the point where it is revealed that this cause and effect is the locus of speech.
Below this, ten reasons are further provided to explain the four conditions (*pratyaya*) in detail. "Reason" (*hetu*) refers here to the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
For example, the basis of speech is precisely the basis of speech as one of the four conditions. First, regarding the basis of speech, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"It means that with respect to phenomena belonging to the three realms or those not so bound, there is the designation 'name. Because name precedes, conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) proceeds; because conceptualization precedes, speech proceeds. By means of...
Because of these words, one gives rise to various verbal expressions according to what is seen, heard, sensed, and known.

Therefore, based on speech and its locus, the "cause of conventional expression" (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) is established. This refers to the speech that expresses, which serves as the cause for that which is expressed; for it is through the speech as cause that meaning arises.
A treatise states that this cause of conventional expression is the basis for the two kinds of attachment: to names (*nāman*) and to characteristics (*nimitta*).
One sees; then, by following names and grasping at signs through attachment, one subsequently gives rise to verbal expression.
This shows that the view of attachment to names and signs is the cause of subsequent discourse, and thus reveals that this cause is the basis for speech.

The second is the basis for experiencing (*anubhava-adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to that which is depended upon (*apekṣya*). This is the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*). "Experiencing" (*anubhava*) means to undergo;
"feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*). All five feelings have the nature of undergoing experience. As for "dependence": [it is that which is depended upon].

Regarding "dependence" (*apekṣā*): it is established as a cause by means of that which is depended upon, both the agent and the object of dependence. Herein, "acceptance" (*parigraha*) is the cause and "dependence" is the result.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Those who desire the pleasure associated with the desire realm, or pleasure not so associated, depend upon this;
because this serves as their cause, they either seek to acquire or seek to accumulate the various requisites of desire."
Some seek enjoyment; some have desire for those who seek the pleasure associated with the form and formless realms.
Because they contemplate this, they either seek to acquire or seek to enjoy those various conditions.
Those who have desire for unconditioned pleasure, because they contemplate this, either seek to acquire or seek to enjoy those various conditions. All those who...

Regarding those who do not desire suffering: because they depend upon this, they either seek to distance themselves from or seek to experience the conditions for obtaining it or the conditions for its cessation.
Therefore, based on the basis of experience (*anubhava-adhiṣṭhāna*), the condition of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*) is established.
For it is because of this that one seeks or grasps at those various things; just as one depends on the hand, taking the hand as the cause, [action] arises.
Grasping depends upon action; with action as its cause, the activity of coming and going arises. It depends upon the joints;
with the joints as its cause, the activities of bending and extending arise. It depends upon hunger and thirst; with hunger and thirst as its cause, the pursuit of food and drink arises.
Following such infinite principles as these, one should know that all are termed "conditions of dependence" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
The basis for the three types of habitual tendencies refers to internal and external seeds (up to) their ability to draw forth their own distant results.
Habitual tendencies are precisely the ignorance that initiates karma. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"Due to the perfuming of pure and impure karma, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) of the three realms are able to induce desirable or undesirable personal existences within desirable or undesirable destinies. Furthermore, it is precisely...
By the power of this predominance (*adhipati*), external material resources either flourish or diminish.

Therefore, based on the locus of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of pure and impure karma within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there are three causes of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*). As the *Zongjing* states:

"Regarding all internal and external seeds in their unripened state, they are established as the cause of projection in relation to their subsequent respective fruits. This is because... [the first...]
Before the seeds of the eight types of outflows have been irrigated by the water of craving, although they do not yet immediately manifest as active states (*samudācāra*),
these seeds nonetheless possess the capacity to project and induce the fruit of future manifestation. This is because,
by virtue of this cause, they are able to bring about maturation (*vipāka*).
The fourth is the basis for seeds that possess moisture (*sābhisyandana-bījāśraya*). This refers to the capacity to give rise to their own proximate fruits.
"Seeds that possess moisture" refers to the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-avidyā*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"All phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as those bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), each arise from their own seeds. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called 'that which moistens,' and the seed is..."
That which is moistened. Because of these seeds thus moistened, the respective individual existences previously projected shall arise.
As the Sūtra says: "Karma is the cause for the production of birth; craving is the cause for the arising of birth.
Therefore, based on the locus of the moistened seeds, the cause for the arising of birth is established. The *Zongjing* states: "With respect to all seeds, in relation to the initial..."
The self-result is called the "arising cause.
The five bases of immediate cessation refer to the mind and mental factors (up to) because they fully encompass and sustain the six accomplishments of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the mind that has just ceased acting as a condition, serving as the basis for the subsequent momentary collection of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Since those subsequent moments of mind and mental factors arise depending on that preceding moment as their conditional locus, it is called the "basis of immediate cessation.
It is precisely upon this basis that the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*) is established. The "basis of the faculties" (*indriya-āśraya*) refers to the six...
The faculties (*indriya*) are the bases for the six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*). They are also established as the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*).
Regarding the "basis of activity" (*karma-adhiṣṭhāna*), this refers generally to the activity of both the agent and the instrument.

As for the "agent" (*karman*), this refers to the skillful intelligence of sentient beings capable of constructing various objects such as palaces, boats, carts, and other implements. As for the "instrument" (*karaṇa*), it is...
These are the various worldly implements, such as axes, saws, chisels, and so forth.
Excluding internal and external seeds, all auxiliary conditions that assist in accomplishing various activities are bases for functional activity (*kāritra-adhiṣṭhāna*).

In this context, the "appropriating cause" (*parigrahahetu*) is also established. As for the basis for human effort (*puruṣakāra-adhiṣṭhāna*), it refers to the aforementioned basis for functional activity.

Regarding the basis: it takes only the function of the agent, the *puruṣa*. With the exception of internal and external seeds, all other things that act as manifest conditions are bases for *puruṣakāra* (human effort).
This basis is also established as the *parigraha-hetu* (appropriating cause); this cause is able to bring about the fruit of *puruṣakāra*.
Regarding the basis for the vision of reality: this refers to all untainted (*anāsrava*) vision; because it is not false, it is so named.
True seeing (*bhūta-darśana*) serves as the basis for all untainted unconditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-asamskṛta*) and untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).
This state is also established as the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*); this cause can bring about the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).

"Appropriating" signifies the sense of mutual interrelation between cause and effect. With the exception of the direct causes and conditions (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*), it includes all other remote auxiliary conditions (*parokṣa-sahakāri-pratyaya*).
All such [conditions] are subsumed under this cause. The Abhidharma-śāstra states:

"Just as sunlight, water, and fertilizer, in relation to rice sprouts and the like, although produced from their own seeds, augment those [seeds'] power and are thus called 'appropriating causes' (*parigraha-hetu*). Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:

"Because all phenomena bound by desire are appropriated by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), appropriated by the sense-faculty condition (*indriya-pratyaya*), and appropriated by the object condition (*viṣaya-pratyaya*)."
Due to the five types of appropriation—namely, appropriation by function (*kāritra*), appropriation by human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and so forth—those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) proceed.

This is just as it is for the conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm; the same applies to those bound to the form and formless realms. Alternatively, through appropriation by the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), other unbound phenomena proceed.

Therefore, [the mind] arises based on the immediately preceding cessation (*anantaraniruddha*), the object (*ālambana*), the sense faculty (*indriya*), function (*kāritra*), and human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
The basis for the true view establishes the cause of appropriation.
Regarding the eleven bases of conformity (upaniṣad-sthāna), they extend to the point that they can induce and lead to unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

As for the "bases of conformity," this refers to the seeds of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) within the eighth consciousness, as well as their respective manifest activities (*pravṛtti*), each of which possesses its own conformity.
Regarding the function of conformity: each [seed] is capable of inducing superior categories of dharmas.

Just as uncontaminated seeds serve solely as the causal basis for their own superior uncontaminated conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, and do not serve as causes for inferior, lower-grade uncontaminated dharmas;
so it is with contaminated seeds. Therefore, the *Zongjing* says: "This is the initial seed."
The fruit produced by a [prior] seed is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) in relation to the subsequently drawn-out fruit of the seed.
This is because it is able to project and bring about the arising of the fruit; that is, one wholesome factor projects many wholesome factors. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"Wholesome factors bound to the desire realm can project various superior wholesome factors bound to the desire realm, and can also project those bound to the form and formless realms, as well as the unconditioned."
The wholesome dharmas bound to the form realm can induce the superior wholesome dharmas of the form realm, as well as the superior wholesome dharmas of the formless realm and those that are unbound.
The wholesome dharmas of the formless realm can also induce the superior wholesome dharmas of their own level, as well as the wholesome dharmas that are unbound.
The wholesome dharmas that are unbound can induce all the superior wholesome dharmas that are unbound.

Dharmas, as well as unconditioned dharmas; furthermore, unwholesome dharmas that can induce superior unwholesome dharmas—namely, such as sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), which can induce hatred, delusion, pride, views, doubt, and misconduct of body, speech, and mind. As it is with sensual desire, so it is with the others.
Furthermore, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas that can induce wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas—namely, those capable of sustaining the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the...
The indeterminate seeds, namely the *ālaya-vijñāna*, as well as other indeterminate phenomena, can induce similar and superior indeterminate phenomena;
that is to say, various types of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) can induce already-born sentient beings to remain without decay, and can induce the power of their satisfaction to increase.
Because they accord with those [beings], it is precisely based on this point that the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) is established.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "As for the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it refers to similar dharmas acting as a similar cause for similar dharmas.

Within their own category (*nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*), they act as causes for those of their own category and level; when compared across different levels, there is no sense of causality whatsoever. This cause applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This cause is capable of producing a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*)."

The twelfth [section] concerns the basis for the differentiation of functional capacities (vibhāga-śakti-pratiṣṭhāna), up to the point that each is able to obtain its own fruit within its respective realm.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because the intrinsic functional capacities (*svabhāva-śakti*) of all phenomena belonging to the desire realm are differentiated, they are able to produce various phenomena with distinct essential natures (*bhāva-viśeṣa*).
As it is with phenomena bound to the desire realm, so it is also with phenomena bound to the form and formless realms, as well as those that are unbound."
It is so. Therefore, based on the locus of distinct functional capacities, one establishes the cause of "distinctness" (*viśeṣa*).

As for the differentiation of intrinsic functional capacities, it is like form, mind, the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth; each possesses the power of its own seeds to project and produce [its result], and is thus called "distinct.

For example, wholesome karma such as the five precepts or the eight precepts definitely projects rebirth in the human or celestial realms as the eighth [consciousness], but does not project rebirth in the three miserable destinies.
8. If the ten unwholesome karmas necessarily lead to the three miserable realms and do not lead to the human or celestial realms, it is because they are incongruent [with those states].
If a phenomenon belongs to its own realm, it serves as a cause for that same realm. All such contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the three realms are likewise.
Each possesses its own distinct functional capacity as a cause, just as the one hundred and twenty official positions each have their respective duties as causes corresponding to those they oversee;
therefore, it is called "determined difference" (*pratiniyama*). "Determined" (*niyata*) means that cause and effect correspond to one another.
It is called "difference" (*viśeṣa*) because it is not shared with others.
Thirteen: The Basis of Conjunction (upapatti-saṃprayoga-sthāna). [This continues] until: "Because they are all identical in their arising and so forth, and in their single common activity.
Regarding the basis of conjunction, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "It is only by obtaining the conjunction of its own arising that dharmas bound to the desire realm arise.
As it is with dharmas bound to the desire realm, so it is with those bound to the form realm, the formless realm, and those that are unbound. This is as with arising."
It is likewise in this way that they attain conjunction, establish conjunction, accomplish conjunction, and exercise the function of conjunction.
Therefore, based on the locus of conjunction, the cause of common purpose (*sahabhū-hetu*) is established.

This [cause] collectively subsumes the six causes and eleven loci as the essence of this locus of conjunction; that is, each of the aforementioned eleven loci, in relation to its respective [object], [constitutes this].
Because within the production of the result from that which has been acquired by oneself, there is always the power of conjunction, it is called the "basis of conjunction.
It is precisely in this context that the cause of common purpose (*sahabhū-hetu*) is established—namely, the six causes ranging from dependence (*apekṣā*) to specific determination (*pratiniyama*).
Since these six causes each collectively accomplish a single effect, let us take one phenomenon as an illustration to clarify this. For instance, when visual consciousness arises:

Depending on conditions such as space and light, this is established as the *apekṣā-hetu* (contingent cause). Due to the two types of seeds—the new and the original—there arise, respectively, the *ākṣepa-hetu* (projecting cause) and the *janana-hetu* (generating cause).

Next, taking the immediately preceding [moment] (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the sense faculties and objects (*indriya-viṣaya*) as the *parigraha-hetu* (appropriating cause), these serve as the *āvāhaka-hetu* (inducing cause) in relation to the subsequent arising from the former. By means of the seeds of conventional expression (*nāma-kāya*), it is...
The cause for sequential occurrence is the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyama-hetu*), by which each [condition] produces its own respective fruit; other phenomena are likewise so.
Regarding the fourteen bases of obstruction (*āvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*): [this refers to] the fact that they do not contradict such matters as arising and so forth.

Regarding the "basis for obstruction," the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If there is an obstruction when a phenomenon bound by desire (*kāmadhātu*) is about to arise, it will not manifest and cannot emerge.

As it is with phenomena bound by desire, so it is with those bound by form (*rūpadhātu*), those bound by the formless (*ārūpyadhātu*), and those that are unbound (*anāpta*). Just as it is for the sake of arising, so it is for the sake of establishing, for the sake of accomplishing, and for the sake of perfecting."
The same applies to their function. Therefore, based on the locus of obstruction, one establishes the "contradictory cause" (*virodha-hetu*). The *Zongjing* states:

"Regarding the dharmas to be produced, that which can obstruct the cause is called the contradictory cause. As for the term "contradictory," it refers to how afflictions (*kleśa*) obstruct wisdom (*jñāna*), and darkness obstructs light, and so forth;
this constitutes a contradiction with increase. Regarding the locus of non-obstruction, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "If..."
When a phenomenon bound by desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) is about to arise, if there is no obstruction, it immediately manifests and comes into being.

As it is with phenomena bound by desire, so it is with those bound by form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), those bound by the formless (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and those that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*). The *Zhengjīng* (Mirror of the Doctrine) states:

"If this obstructive cause is deficient or absent, it is called the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*); this is precisely the concordant dominant condition (*anukūla-adhipati-pratyaya*). This clarifies [the point].

Yang says: Regarding "conditioned by" (*pratītya*), it means that if, with this as the precursor, this as the basis, and through the conjunction of these, various phenomena arise, or perform a function, or are established, or are accomplished, or are obtained—know that this is said to be their cause.
Question: With what as the precursor? By what is it established? Through the conjunction of what?
Therefore, what dharma arises? What dharma acts? What dharma is established? What dharma is attained? Answer:
Preceded by its own seed, with the exception of the seed of the support itself, it is established by means of the remaining supports—whether material or non-material—as well as karma;
and through the conjunction of its companions and objective conditions, it arises accordingly, bound by desire or bound by form.
The arising of all phenomena—whether bound to the formless realm or unbound—is preceded by their own seeds;
it is established by those very same preceding births, and accomplished through the conjunction of their conditions for arising. Regarding "one's own action" (*svakṛta-karman*):
it is the activity performed by oneself that achieves completion. As with the act of seeing by the eye, so it should be understood for the remaining sense faculties.
One should know that each performs its own specific function: for example, earth can support, water can moisten, fire can burn, and wind can dry.
Such categories as these are called the specific functions of external phenomena.

Based on the prior inclination and desire for the objects of knowledge, one establishes [the argument] through the thesis, reason, and example, in accordance with an assembly free from contradiction and the opposing debater.
For the sake of conjunction, the intended thesis can only be established. Preceded by knowledge of craftsmanship (*śilpa*), it is established according to the exertion applied therein;
because the various implements for the sphere of craft (*śilpakarmasthāna*) are conjoined, those respective spheres of craft are accomplished.
Furthermore, preceded by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is established by means of the support of one who dwells through nutriment (*āhāra-sthitika*). (4)
Food serves as a condition for the preservation and maintenance of sentient beings who have already been born.
Based on the predispositions of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Tathāgata lineages, it is established through internal causal power and brought into harmony through external causal power.

The attainment of nirvāṇa through the dissociation from afflictions and so forth—these ten causes are subsumed within two [primary] causes; the inclusion of other skillful means should be understood accordingly, as explained above.

Next, the mutual inclusion [of causes] is explained. First, it is stated that two causes subsume the ten causes. The section beginning with "The Bodhisattva... cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* as proof.
The section beginning with "Regarding this explanation... is where the Master elucidates the meaning within the *Yogācāra*.

That is to say, the single cause of "productive capacity" (*janaka*) does not merely subsume the two causes of "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and "actualizing" (*abhinirvartaka*), because it is also capable of projecting and actualizing the remaining four causes.

Regarding the seeds of all causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), those in the stage of non-maturation are termed the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), while those in the stage of maturation are termed the "arising cause" (*janaka-hetu*).
Among those six causes, the seeds of all causal conditions are subsumed within two causes, because both of these belong to the single category of the "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*).
Question: Since it is admitted that the four [causes], such as the "inducing cause" (*āvāhaka*), are productive, why is it stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*...

[The interlocutor] says: "It is not mentioned. [The author] answers: "Although these four causes do arise manifestly and are productive causes, they are like the first, second, fifth, and ninth [causes], which produce their own seeds;
however, because they are frequently interrupted, they are omitted from the explanation. Question:

Since they are frequently interrupted, why are they also designated by the name 'seed' (bīja)? Answer: Because they can directly bring about the fruit of manifest activity, they are also designated by the name 'seed.'"
