As it is said regarding those who take currently manifesting grains or barley as seeds: these too are designated as "seeds" because they are directly capable of producing manifest results.

Furthermore, among the remaining causes—not only those categorized as the conditions of dependence (*apekṣā*), appropriation (*parigraha*), and opposition (*virodha*) which serve as contributory causes (*upāya-hetu*)—but also within the six causes such as the projecting (*ākṣepaka*), the arising (*abhinirvartaka*), and the drawing-forth (*āvāhaka*), there are those that do not possess the nature of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

This is subsumed under the cause of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*). Question: On the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, two causes are designated as the "producers" (*janaka*) and the remaining eight as "skillful means.
Why, in this context, are six causes designated as the "producers" and the remaining four as "skillful means"? Answer:

It is not that the projecting (*ākṣepa*) and the actualizing (*abhinirvṛtti*) [causes] belong exclusively to those two as the producers; rather, the others [the remaining causes] also function as the projecting, the determining (*pratiniyama*), the homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and so forth.
Within the section on the non-contradiction of phenomena (*aviruddha-vastu*), there are also causal seeds; thus, it is not only those eight [causes] that are termed "expedient causes" (*upāya-hetu*).
For those two causes—namely, the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the actualizing cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*)—also possess expedient causes.

Furthermore, citing a treatise to prove that the ten causes are subsumed within these two causes, it is stated in the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi* (the three stages including the stage with vitarka) that only the single actualizing cause is capable of producing [phenomena].
The remaining nine are all skillful means (*upāya*). The Master of the Treatise elucidates their meaning, stating:

"In this text, among the six causes, those seeds that are currently active and function as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are all termed 'arising' (*utpatti*). As for the four remaining causes, those factors that are not causal conditions consist of the seeds of maturation and so forth;
these are all subsumed under skillful means. Question: In the stages such as those with vitarka (*savitarka-bhūmi*), only "arising" is mentioned.
Question: Why is it said here that the six causes constitute the productive [cause], while the remaining four constitute the contributory conditions (*upāya*)?
Answer: It is not the case that this arising belongs exclusively to those productive causes, for there are also causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the other five causes.
Nor is it the case that the remaining nine are called contributory conditions; rather, it is precisely that single arising [which is the object].
Because causes also possess skillful means. Alternatively, from the perspective of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), the first point is explained by emphasizing what is predominant.
From the perspective of the manifest, the second point is explained by emphasizing what is hidden.

Although within the process of origination there are also seeds that are not causal conditions, they are nonetheless proximate to their fruit, because they are capable of producing their own immediate results. This is because they produce [the result] directly.
Because the meaning of manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) is prominent, it is specifically stated that "arising" (*utpāda*) is the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
Although the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) also contains seeds as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is distant from its fruit, insofar as it projects its own fruit at a distance;
because the meaning of directly producing manifest activity is obscured therein, the projecting cause is not said to be the productive cause. This also applies to the preparatory means (*upāya*).

As for what you have said regarding the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*), upon what basis are they established? (Up to: "The first [condition], the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), includes [the others] with variations as previously described.

This clarifies that the four conditions are established based on fifteen bases and subsume ten causes (*daśa hetavaḥ*) and two causes. First, the question is posed; next, the treatise (*śāstra*) is cited.
Answer: First, it is explained that the four conditions are established based on fifteen bases. Regarding the establishment of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) based on seeds:

this refers to the aforementioned seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) and the seeds for moistening birth (*janma-sneha-bīja*). Regarding the establishment of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) based on the remaining [bases]:
this refers to the eleven bases (*āśraya*). Below this, the Master of the Treatise presents the meaning of the treatise, stating: "In this context, the seed is precisely the projecting [cause]."

Among the six bases—arising (*utpatti*), inducing (*ākṣepa*), determination (*pratiniyama*), commonality (*sahakārya*), non-contradiction (*avirodha*), and the four bases of reliance (*pratiṣṭhā*)—the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is subsumed under "seeds" (*bīja*). Although the conditions of subsequent discourse (*anuvyavahāra*), dependence (*apekṣā*), appropriation (*parigraha*), and contradiction (*virodha*) also possess causal conditions, they are not mentioned because they are intermittent. Alternatively, the term "seed" may apply exclusively to the fourth [basis], arising; this distinction between the immediate and the remote, the manifest and the hidden, is as follows:

[The text continues with an analogy: Just as when a king has gone abroad, his ministers govern the kingdom; yet, although the ministers act, the people say, "The king rules. Similarly, while the seeds produce the fruit, one says, "The field produces the grain," or "The rain produces the harvest.

Furthermore, just as when a king’s son is born, people say, "A king is born," so too, although the seeds produce the fruit, one says, "The field produces the grain," or "The rain produces the harvest. Moreover, just as when a king’s son is born, people say, "A king is born," so too, although the seeds produce the fruit, one says, "The field produces the grain," or "The rain produces the harvest. Finally, just as when a king’s son is born, people say, "A king is born," so too, although the seeds produce the fruit, one says, "The field produces the grain," or "The rain produces the harvest. Thus, the distinction between the immediate and the remote, and the manifest and the hidden, is established.

This is explained within the section on vitarka and vicāra. When it says "uninterrupted" and "objective sphere," one should understand that these terms collectively indicate two conditions (*pratyaya*), rather than merely five or six.
That is to say, the remaining thirteen bases (*sthāna*) also possess these two conditions; although they exist elsewhere, they are few and thus remain hidden.
I shall not elaborate on this further. Below, it is explained how the four conditions subsume the ten causes and two causes.

The treatise states that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) consists of the two causes among the ten—namely, the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the producing cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*)—and is collectively subsumed under the single cause of "that which brings about production" (*janaka-hetu*).

The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) consists of the remaining eight causes among the ten, and is collectively subsumed under the single cause of "expediency" (*upāya-hetu*). As for the intermediate [condition], the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and...

The objective field (*viṣaya*) as the basis (*āśraya*) is the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*). Question: Since the latter three conditions are included within the cause of expedient means (*upāya-hetu*), why is it alone designated as "predominant" (*adhipati*)?
Answer: Although it includes the three conditions, its meaning as "predominance" is manifold; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.

Furthermore, while other causes also possess the condition of immediate proximity (*anantara*) and the objective field (*ālambana*), the cause of appropriation is particularly manifest; therefore, it is specifically mentioned. It is the first [cause] that is able to produce [the effect].

Regarding the causes, whether advancing or retreating, they are all as previously explained. That is to say, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, both the cause of attraction (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the cause of production (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) serve as the productive causes;
whereas in the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi*, only the cause of production serves as the productive cause.
The causes and conditions that have been explained must necessarily have results (up to: "referring to the results obtained other than the four previously mentioned").

Next, the inclusion of results within the causal conditions is clarified. First, a question is posed; second, the answer is given. The first is *vipāka* (maturation). There are four types of maturation: first, maturation at a different time.
The cause resides in the past, while the resultant fruit is in the present; therefore, it is called "at a different time. Second...

It is "ripening as a different nature," meaning that past cultivation of the five precepts and ten wholesome paths of action brings about the ripening fruits of wholesome general and specific retributions for devas and humans;
whereas past cultivation of the ten unwholesome karmic paths brings about the ripening fruits of unwholesome general and specific retributions for the three miserable realms.
Because these are summoned by the natures of the wholesome and the unwholesome respectively, they are called "different natures. This is the third [category], "different types."

It ripens. Because one creates karma of a different class and undergoes birth in a different class, with the five destinies being distinct from one another, it is called "of a different class" (*visabhāga*).

Fourth, it ripens as something "different from the noble ones" (*visamyukta-ārya*); that is to say, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) depends on two kinds of obstructions and functions to differentiate the destinies and births.

Since these no longer exist for the noble ones (*ārya*), it is called "different from the noble ones. This refers to impure wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) which bring about birth in the happy destinies.
Regarding the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*): tainted unwholesome dharmas bring about the fruit of maturation in the miserable realms;
that which is neutral within one’s own continuum is the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); that which is born of maturation and is neutral is the sixth consciousness.

If one speaks of "maturation" alone, it does not include specific retributions; if one says "born of maturation," both the general and the specific are included. Second, regarding the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), there are two types: first...
"True outflow" (nisyanda) refers to the similar-type fruit (sabhāga-phala) produced by causes of the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
Just as seeds of the three natures give rise to the manifest activity (samudācāra) of the three natures, or as mental seeds give rise to mental manifest activity, [the fruit is so named].
The seeds of form produce the manifestation of form; contaminated seeds produce contaminated manifestations;
uncontaminated seeds produce uncontaminated manifestations, because there is no distinction between the nature of the fruit and the cause. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:

"If, due to the habituation of unwholesomeness, one delights in abiding in unwholesomeness, unwholesomeness increases. By cultivating wholesomeness, one delights in abiding in wholesomeness; thus, wholesome dharmas [increase]."

The increase [of merit] is called the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Second is the nominal result of outflow: this refers to cases where, for instance, due to killing in a previous life, one suffers a premature death in this life;
because there is a sense of similarity, it is termed "nominal. In reality, it is a dominant result (*adhipati-phala*). The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) states:

"When the subsequent result follows in accordance with its similarity to the preceding karma, it is called the result of outflow. Third is the result of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*): this arises from being freed from the bonds of afflictions and conceptual proliferation.
Dharma. The realization of this fruit is attained only by noble ones (*ārya*); it does not belong to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"If the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished by means of the Noble Eightfold Path, this is the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).

If ordinary worldlings extinguish the various afflictions through conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), this is not a definitive transformation and is not subsumed under this fruit. The *Zongjing lu* states: "By means of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*..."
Its essence is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is that which is realized through the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) path of abandonment. There are four fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*):

"human" (*puruṣa*) refers to a person (*puruṣa*), and "effort" (*kāra*) refers to activity. The causal phenomena act as the agent, and the conditional phenomena act as the instrument. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"If, in the present life, various worldly people engage in any kind of craft or occupation, they initiate human effort..."
"Puruṣakāra" (human effort) refers to such activities as farming, commerce, studying writing and arithmetic, and making seals.
Because of these human efforts, results such as harvests and wealth are accomplished; this is called the "puruṣakāra-phala" (fruit of human effort). Fifth is the "adhipati-phala" (dominant fruit).

This means that because they are predominant, superior, and preeminent: just as visual consciousness and the others are the predominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*) of the eye faculty and so forth, likewise, up to mental consciousness, it is the predominant fruit of the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*).

Furthermore, the non-disintegration of the bodily parts of sentient beings is the predominant fruit of the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Excluding these four fruits, all other twenty-two faculties are each distinct.

Because it possesses superior power (*adhipati-bala*), the fruit is able to arise; one should know that all such fruits are subsumed under the category of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, regarding the bestowing or not bestowing of power, as well as the concordant or discordant factors, these are all as previously explained.
This fruit is the most extensive, just as the dominant condition is among the four conditions, or as false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) is among the five views.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state that the locus of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) [is such]... (up to) "having already revealed the remainder, this alone is specifically taught.

In the lower section of the *Yogācāra*, the treatise is cited; under "habitual tendencies," the meaning of the commentary is explained. Generally, when the term "all" (*sarva*) is used, it refers to one instance while encompassing all fifteen.
That which is too broad refers to the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); that which is too narrow refers to the remaining four conditions. Alternatively, under "habitual tendencies"...
Because they are intended to highlight their preeminence, each is mentioned individually. Latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) belong exclusively to the third cause, the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).

Conformity (*anuvartana*) belongs exclusively to the eleventh cause, the producing cause (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*). True vision (*tattva-darśana*) belongs exclusively to the tenth basis, the basis of reliance (*niśraya*).

The activity of the agent (*puruṣakāra*) refers exclusively to the ninth basis, the basis of the agent’s activity (*puruṣakāra-niśraya*). The remaining [factors] belong exclusively to the other eleven bases. The other four bases have already been explained.
There are four fruits; therefore, these eleven are specifically said to be predominant.
Thus, it is stated that among these five fruits, everything from [the ten causes] to the four conditions is capable of being obtained.
This assigns ten causes and four conditions to the five fruits: five causes and one condition produce the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*);

seven causes and two conditions produce the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*); five causes and one condition produce the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*); and four causes and one condition [produce the dominant fruit].
Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*): some claim that there are eight causes and three conditions, but this is incorrect.

This is because the basis for prior human effort lacks seeds; therefore, it cannot possess the three causes—projecting, arising, and drawing forth—nor can it possess the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As for the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), all ten causes and four conditions may obtain it. Thus, the *Zongjing* asks: "Now, regarding the eight consciousnesses..."

[Question: Regarding each individual consciousness, how does each one possess four fruits? [Answer: For instance, when visual consciousness arises from a seed, it is a fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

The eye-faculty serves as its basis; this is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). The alerting of the mind by attention (*manaskāra*) associated with visual consciousness is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Alternatively, the fact that visual consciousness can take real form and so forth as its object is also a fruit of human effort. The eye-faculty...

This is the eighth [category], the immediate (*samanantara*) object-part (*ālambana-bhāga*). It is a maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*). The four consciousnesses, such as the auditory consciousness and so forth, are all to be understood by this same principle.

If the sixth [mental] consciousness arises from seeds, it is a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). Because the preceding moment of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) acts as the inducer, or because it can induce the first five consciousnesses, it is a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Furthermore, because it can take objects of the three times and internal or external realms as its conditions, it is called "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*).

Regarding the fruit of utilization (*niṣpatti-phala*): that which is capable of producing future retributions, both collective and individual, is called the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*). Furthermore, because it serves as the cause for maturation, it is also termed the maturation fruit.
If the seeds of the seventh consciousness arise as the manifest state, this is called the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

The preceding moment of the seventh consciousness acts as the support for the subsequent moment; this is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). It takes the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object.

The internal self is the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort). Its ability to serve as the support for the true *vipāka-vijñāna* (maturation consciousness) is termed the *vipāka-phala* (fruition of maturation).

If the seeds of the eighth [consciousness] manifest, it is termed the *niṣyanda-phala* (flowing-out fruit). Its serving as the support for the seventh [consciousness] is the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit).

Its ability to take the three objects as its cognitive domain, as well as its sustaining of seeds and receiving of perfuming (*vāsanā*), is termed the *puruṣakāra-phala*. Its essential nature is the true maturation.

The matured is called the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). These four conditions, ten causes, and five fruits encompass the entire path of both ordinary beings and sages, and constitute the gateway through which the teachings are established.
If these are lacking, not a single dharma is complete; if they are misunderstood, one will ultimately remain an outsider to the truth.
Furthermore, regarding the four conditions: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) directly produces its own fruit within the gateway of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) functions as the meaning of opening and guiding, whereby all phenomena arise. The objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is established only when it possesses the basis for mental attention.

These are established together based on the distinction between the immediate and the remote. As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it possesses a superior power that does not obstruct other conditions. Regarding the ten causes:
The "cause according to description" (yathā-abhilāpa-hetu) is the gateway that precedes all phenomena. The "contingent cause" (apekṣā-hetu) clarifies and manifests the activity of functions;
it draws forth and accomplishes its own fruit, gathers and encompasses all conditions, gives rise to and enables the production of all categories, and induces the actualization of various results.
As for "distinctness" (pratiniyama), the types are each separate. As for "commonality" (sāmagri), the essence is...

The characteristics are identical and uniform, yet they constitute a gateway for the arising of mutual opposition; they do not contradict the principle of arising through favorable conditions. Regarding the five fruits:

as for the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), the cause produces the fruit and it ripens at a different time; as for the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), the nature of the cause and the fruit is identical.
Their respective categories do not overlap. *Adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit) possesses superior power and function, capable of assisting other conditions.

*Puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) is that which is accomplished through one's own exertion, capable of obtaining wealth and profit. *Visaṃyoga-phala* (fruit of disjunction) involves severing obstacles and realizing the truth, thereby transcending all fetters.
As explained above, these causal conditions result in the five fruits. Thus, we know that cause and effect reciprocate, and that the transformation of consciousness is certain, like a mirror.
Manifestations appear like shadows following forms. Whether one partakes of jade-like delicacies and wears brocade robes, or wears robes of quail feathers and eats of wild herbs;

whether one dwells in a humble mat-door house or a golden palace, or possesses a thousand horses or but a single ladle—these conditions are never excessive, and their karmic retributions are without error. Thus, the *Treatise on Talent and Fate* says:
"The poor have no land even for a standing needle, yet Dao Yi possessed fields exceeding ten thousand *qīng*; the hungry have no store of even a *dān* or a *shí*, yet Li [Bo]..."

In the case of Xiang, his trees were called "thousand slaves. Furthermore, it is not only wealth and poverty that are determined by the transformations of consciousness; lifespan is likewise so determined.
Because of the causes of compassion or killing created by one's prior mind, one now definitely receives the fruit of longevity or brevity as a subsequent retribution.
If it is said that those who lack propriety must perish, why did Jie Zhitui alone live a long life? If practicing goodness brings auspiciousness, upon what basis could [the wicked] rely?
[This treatise] ends here. All wise people should believe and accept it.

Having concluded this digression, one should now address the main argument [extending to the point where it is shown that] the five consciousnesses rely solely upon the eighth consciousness as their objective support.
In this further explanation of the verse, it is shown that through the power of mutual interaction, various conceptualizations arise.

First, it clarifies how seeds and manifest activities serve as conditions for one another: the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) can function as three types of conditions to produce manifest activity.

Specifically, those seeds that directly produce [the activity] are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the manifest activity. Once the consciousness has arisen, the consciousness then takes the seeds as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

It serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). If various seeds possess the power to assist in the production of the consciousness that arises from them and the power not to obstruct it, they constitute the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

This statement—that a single seed possesses all three conditions for producing manifest conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—excludes the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because at the time a seed is produced, once it has arisen, there is no principle of it being produced again. [This applies to] defiled manifest [consciousness].
This being so, the same applies to pure manifestations (*viśuddha-nirbhāsa*). Next, the mutual functioning as conditions among active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) is explained.

The eight consciousnesses in their active state can mutually serve as three types of conditions when compared with one another: if they are compared across different [streams of] self and others, they possess the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

if they are compared as preceding and succeeding moments within the same category, they possess the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition. They lack the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), because active manifestations are not seeds.

This refers to the classes of sentient beings. When the eight consciousnesses of oneself and others are compared with one another, they can serve as two conditions—namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)—but excluding the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This is because consciousnesses of different categories do not mutually induce or lead one another.

When the eight consciousnesses within one's own aggregate are compared with one another, they possess mutual supportive power; thus, they definitely possess the dominant condition. Because they do not depend upon one another for their existence, they lack the immediate condition.

Regarding the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*), as for the statement that it "either exists or does not exist," this means that the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition for the preceding seven.
This is because when the seventh consciousness takes the eighth as its object, it relies upon the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth as its substantial essence (*svabhāva*).

The seeing-part of the seventh then transforms the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) which it takes as its object. The preceding seven do not serve as object-conditions for the eighth, because the eighth [does not rely on them].

Because it takes the preceding seven as its objects, and because it does not arise by depending on the preceding seven as its substantial basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*), and because it takes only the three types of objective spheres (*viṣaya*) as its objects,
it is said that "the eighth exists with respect to the seven, while the seven do not exist with respect to the eighth. Regarding the seventh [consciousness] and the six [consciousnesses],

it is said that "five do not exist and one exists," meaning that while the sixth consciousness takes the seventh as its object, the first five consciousnesses function only toward external objects and cannot [take the seventh as their object].

Because it takes the internal as its object, it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*). Among those, the first six evolving consciousnesses are all not object-conditions for that seventh [consciousness], because the seventh only takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as its object.
The sixth [consciousness] does not have the five [sensory objects] as its object, because the first five only take the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as their object.
The remaining five [evolving consciousnesses] do have it as their object, because the sixth is able to take both internal and external form and mind as its objects.

Regarding the sixth consciousness, it can serve as three conditions for its own preceding and succeeding moments, because it perfumes and thereby establishes the seeds of both the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*).

Third, concerning the mutual relationship between preceding and succeeding moments of the eight consciousnesses within their own respective categories: the sixth consciousness can act as three conditions.

That is to say, when the preceding moment ceases and the succeeding moment arises, it serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); because it takes the preceding thought-moment as its object, it also possesses the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

As for the conditions: because the various consciousnesses assist in its formation, they possess the condition of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The five, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses may function as two conditions [predominance and object], as they each apprehend present objects and do not take prior appearances as their objects;

therefore, the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is excluded. This is granted provided that the first five consciousnesses and the subsequent seeing-consciousness (the sixth) are held to take prior appearances as their objects.
The five [consciousnesses] and the seventh [manas], when viewed sequentially and reciprocally within their own respective categories, all possess three conditions, just as the sixth does.

Although the eighth consciousness does not take the preceding seven as its objects, the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) of the eighth are all perfumed by the preceding seven;

therefore, the preceding seven can serve as the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition) for the eighth. Specifically, the first five consciousnesses perfume the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth.

The seventh [consciousness] perfumes the seeds of the eightfold *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect), while the sixth [consciousness] perfumes both the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) and the *darśana-bhāga*. Therefore, it is said that the perfuming agents produce the seeds of those respective aspects.
Although they coexist as distinct entities, when viewed in relation to one another, this is explained only in terms of their mutual functioning as conditions for their actual manifestation.
The four explanations state that those of the same collection are of different entities.

This means that when mental factors (caitta) of the same collection are viewed in relation to one another, they possess only the *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition) and lack the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition), because each mental factor has its own distinct self-entity (*svabhāva*). This interpretation is partial;

for if it is based on the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mental factors, they are said not to take one another as objects. However, if based on the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*), there is indeed mutual taking as objects. That is to say, all...

The image-aspects arise with mutual substance as their basis, because they also serve as objects for one another. This is just like the seeds held by the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), which serve as the substantial bases for the image-aspects that resemble seeds—such as contact (sparśa) and so forth.
Since contact and the others must necessarily have a direct objective condition (sākṣātālambanapratyaya) in relation to consciousness, [this mutual relationship] must exist.

If those seeds which are the common objects of the five [consciousnesses] are not admitted, then since the formless realm lacks both body and the physical vessel, there would be no object of perception;
for in the formless realm, consciousness perceives only seeds and does not take transformed matter as its object.

Even if one were to admit that transformed matter serves as an object, it must necessarily be the substantial entity that resembles the seed, lest there be a case where the objective part (nimitta-bhāga) is not distinct from the object.

Because it is the substantial basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Touch and the other [mental factors] must necessarily arise as transformations resembling their objective counterparts (*nimitta-bhāga*). Therefore, all objective counterparts (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise mutually as their own substantial bases.

It is explained that the four parts (*catur-aṃśa*) are of the same substance (*ekadravya*): if the objective counterpart of the same substance serves as the object for the two aspects of the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), the objective counterpart is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) because it can induce that subjective aspect;
and since the subjective aspect is precisely that which takes the objective counterpart as its object, it is the... [condition].

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) has only a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) with respect to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), because that image-part does not take the seeing-part as its object;

thus, there is no object-condition. Regarding the relationship between the seeing-part and the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti*): it is likewise. The seeing-part, through its conceptualization, induces the self-cognizing part;
this is a dominant condition. The self-cognizing part takes the seeing-part as its object; this is an object-condition. As for the self-cognizing part in relation to that [seeing-part]...

There is only a predominance [of the self-witnessing part]. Since direct perception is not a non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) and cannot take its own self-witnessing as an object, it lacks an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

As for the other two parts acting as both conditions for one another, this refers to the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the witness-to-self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga*), because they mutually induce each other and serve as each other's objects.
In this root verse, by the power of their mutual interaction, each is produced from the other; none of them...
Based on the aspect of seeds (*bīja-lakṣaṇa*), it is said that only the manifest aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) have the sense of being mutual conditions for one another.
Regarding the pure assembly of the eight consciousnesses, their mutual interaction between self and others is analyzed in full detail in other treatises.
Fifth, regarding the pure assembly of the eight consciousnesses, when self and other are mutually related, all three parts possess objects of cognition (*ālambana*). That is to say:

the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the verifying-of-self-verifying-part as its object; the self-verifying-part takes the seeing-part and the verifying-of-self-verifying-part as its object;
and the verifying-of-self-verifying-part takes the seeing-part and the self-verifying-part as its object. Only the seeing-part itself is excluded from being an object.

Regarding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): Question. Since [the mind] arises by taking seeds and manifest phenomena as its objective conditions through present conceptualization, then seeds should likewise arise by taking manifest seeds as their objective conditions.
Now, how many conditions can a manifest phenomenon act as for a seed? And how many conditions can a seed act as for a seed? Answer:
If it is in the state of being a seed, it fully acts as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but not by way of immediate succession (*anantara*).

Because it is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). By means of these two conditions, these manifest minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are established. If one regards the manifest [factors] in relation to their seeds that produce them directly, they possess both conditions:
namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). In relation to seeds that do not produce them directly, [they possess only the dominant condition].

It is merely for the purpose of assisting and completing [the process]; thus, there is a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Since there is no sense of direct production, there is no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). The same applies to seeds in relation to seeds.

Based on this reciprocal power of internal consciousnesses, they mutually function as conditions and give rise to one another; thus, the analysis of cause and effect is established both by scripture and by reasoning.

Furthermore, when citing scriptures to establish this principle, it is clear that there are no external conditions. Even if external conditions were to exist, they would ultimately prove to be non-existent.
How much more so when it contradicts both scripture and reasoning—why persist in such dogmatic adherence?

Although the preceding verse distinguishes between two [categories], it generally indicates the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the three realms; yet, according to their predominance, they are presented as different gateways to demonstrate their specific distinctions.
Thus, they are spoken of as being two, three, four, five, and so forth. As the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Regarding the discrimination of afflictions (*kleśa-vikalpa*), some establish one..."

Regarding their types: they are so called by virtue of the meaning of afflictive defilement (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*). Alternatively, they are divided into two kinds: those abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*).

Alternatively, they are divided into three kinds: those bound to the desire realm (*kāma-pratisaṃyukta*), those bound to the form realm (*rūpa-pratisaṃyukta*), and those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpya-pratisaṃyukta*). Alternatively, they are divided into four kinds.

That is to say, there are the indeterminate factors associated with the desire realm, the indeterminate factors associated with the form realm, the indeterminate factors associated with the formless realm, and the indeterminate factors that are maturation.

Alternatively, they are divided into five kinds: those to be abandoned by seeing suffering, those to be abandoned by seeing the origin, those to be abandoned by seeing cessation, those to be abandoned by seeing the path, and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Alternatively, they are divided into six kinds: greed, hatred, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt. Alternatively, they are divided...
There are seven types, namely the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): first, the underlying tendency of sensual desire; second, the underlying tendency of ill will;
third, the underlying tendency of desire for existence; fourth, the underlying tendency of pride; fifth, the underlying tendency of ignorance; sixth, the underlying tendency of views;

and seventh, the underlying tendency of doubt. Alternatively, they are divided into eight types: namely, greed, ill will, pride, ignorance, doubt, views, and the two kinds of grasping (*upādāna*). Alternatively, they are divided...
There are nine types, namely the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*): first, the fetter of craving; second, the fetter of aversion; third, the fetter of pride;
fourth, the fetter of ignorance; fifth, the fetter of views; sixth, the fetter of grasping; seventh, the fetter of doubt; eighth, the fetter of envy; and ninth, the fetter of avarice.

Alternatively, they may be divided into ten types, namely the five dull and the five sharp. Or they may be divided into one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*). As there are thus many varieties of afflictions, [so it is].

The mind is likewise. Just as with "falling into the mental faculty" (*manas*) and "not falling into the mental faculty," so it is with mind, mentation, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), and the four natures such as the wholesome and so forth.
Although there is internal consciousness, there are no external conditions, because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) constitute their very nature.

Question: If there are only internal consciousnesses and no external objects, how is it that sentient beings transmigrate through the six sense bases and the cycle of birth and death remains uninterrupted?
Next, a verse is cited in response: "Due to the habitual tendencies of various karmas... and so forth. Regarding the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*):

it differs in name from "seeds" (*bīja*) but is identical in substance. Habitual tendencies are discussed in relation to seeds, while seeds are discussed in relation to manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).

There are three meanings for the term "established" (*sthāpana*). First, seeds are called "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). "Habitual" (*vāsa*) refers to perfuming (*bhāvanā*); "tendency" (*anā*) refers to a portion or residue.

Because these manifest activities perfume [the mind], they acquire this portion or residue. Second, manifest activities are called "habitual tendencies," meaning that manifest activities are produced by seeds;
thus, manifest activities are the portion or residue belonging to the seeds. Third, habitual tendencies are called "habitual" (*vāsanā*).

"Vapor. It is like the scent of incense, which possesses a portion of fragrance and so forth. The commentary below explains: "Meritorious karma" has the nature of contaminated wholesome volition (*cetanā*).

Because both its own essence and its fruit are desirable and its characteristics are preeminent, it is that which brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of happy realms and is the wholesome karma conducive to experiencing [rebirth] within the five destinies.
"Non-meritorious karma" is [contaminated...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.*

It has unwholesome reflection as its essence. Because both its own nature and its fruit are unpleasant and characterized by inferiority, it is that which brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of the miserable realms (*apāya*), as well as the unwholesome karma conducive to experiencing [rebirth] in the five destinies. Regarding immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*):

because such karma—whether great or small—abides in one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) and does not waver, it refers to the karma of the two higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) belonging to the levels of those realms. This is because...

Because concentration (*samādhi*) is able to cause the mind to abide in a single object, it is the ripening (*vipāka*) that brings about rebirth in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), as well as the wholesome karma conducive to feeling in those realms.
Volition (*cetanā*) constitutes its essential nature; all other [factors] of body and speech are termed its "retinue" (*parivāra*).

Since they collectively project and fulfill the fruit of ripening, they are all given the general designation of "karma. Question: Karma arises and then immediately perishes; how can it project [a result]?

[Question: Regarding the fruit: [Answer: Although this [action] perishes immediately upon arising and flows into the past, unable to summon a true ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) in the future, nevertheless, by the power of this karma, it perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and gives rise to a functional capacity for its own karma.
This very capacity is called "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*), because it is formed through the perfuming of the karmic residue. Since it is by means of this...
It arises through perfuming (*vāsanā*). This excludes what has previously existed. Since it serves as a seed, this excludes what is currently manifesting; therefore, it is termed merely "perfuming.
Such perfumings mutually perfume one another until they reach the time of maturation, at which point they summon the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*).

This karmic perfuming is precisely the superior dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for its future fruit; it is the aforementioned projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*), because it is capable of projecting [the fruit] from afar.
Because it is its own fruit. Regarding "the habitual tendencies of the two types of grasping": first, grasping at signs and views, which refers to the duality of subject and object;
second, grasping at name-and-form, which refers to the clinging to the five aggregates; third, grasping at mind and mental factors, which refers to all phenomena comprised within the five aggregates.
Because one does not depart from these two, there are the two retributions of the four graspings (upādāna), both in their general and specific aspects.

Those four graspings are all subsumed under the two graspings of conceptual proliferation (*nāma*) and self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*); these are the two graspings as active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

The capacity within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) that is directly produced by what has been perfumed by those [graspings] is called the "habitual tendencies of the two graspings" (*dvaya-upādāna-vāsanā*). These two graspings are precisely the future minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
It is the direct generative seed; that is, it is the cause of origination from a previous life, because it is capable of producing its own immediate result.

Regarding the term "simultaneous" (*saha*): it means that the karmic seed coexists with the seeds of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*). This is because the karmic seed is a remote dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), whereas the two graspings are the direct conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Although they differ in being remote and direct, they possess the sense of mutual assistance; therefore, they must necessarily coexist. Question: Karma...
Since the seeds are remote conditions, why are they mentioned first in the verse? Answer: Although the seeds of karma are remote, their actual manifestation in drawing forth retribution is evident;
therefore, they are mentioned first in the verse. Question: Why must all three types [of causes] be present for maturation (*vipāka*) to be established? Answer:

If there were no karmic seeds acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for maturation (*vipāka*), what would draw forth the arising of superior or inferior, pleasant or unpleasant states?
If there were no dualistic grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) acting as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), what would act as the proximate producer of seeds to give rise to the various consciousnesses?
Even if they were to arise, they would be subject to interruption and lack the quality of continuity; therefore, one must necessarily rely upon the three kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The vital energy (*vāyu*) acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); only then do birth and death continue in succession, and the retribution of good or bad fortune is received.
The preceding section differs from the following. This explains the latter two lines of the verse. Question:

Regarding the three fruits—maturation (*vipāka*), outflow (*niṣyanda*), and dominance (*adhipati*)—how can it be that while the fruits of outflow and dominance are inexhaustible, the karmic fruit of maturation is exhaustible? Answer: Although these two [types of] grasping...

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that receive their fruit are inexhaustible, whereas the karmic habitual tendencies that receive their fruit are exhaustible. Nevertheless, there is another distinction. Why is this?

Because of the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*): first, its nature is distinct; it differs from the nature of the karma and does not correspond with it in many respects. Second, it is difficult to summon;
although karma may summon it, the fruit only ripens when it is necessarily a different lifetime away. As for the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*)...
The predominating condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is twofold: first, identity of nature (*svabhāva-samatā*), because their essential natures are mutually compatible;

second, ease of production (*sukha-utpāda*), because they arise simultaneously, such that once this mindfulness has been perfumed (*vāsita*), it is immediately capable of producing its fruit. Question:

Since the fruits of the outflowing condition (*niṣyanda-pratyaya*) and the predominating condition are not the same, why must the arising of an outflowing fruit necessarily be accompanied by a predominating condition? Answer: The conditions for an outflowing fruit are narrow, whereas the conditions for a predominating fruit are broad. There is only...
That which is an outflow-natured result (*niṣyanda-phala*) necessarily possesses a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Regarding the term "outflow":

it refers to the relationship between seeds and their actual manifestations, as well as the fact that seeds of the same category act as simultaneous homogeneous causes (*sahabhū-sabhāga-hetu*) for one another. A dominant condition has no separate essence, as it is of the very nature of the outflow.

Furthermore, with respect to actual manifestations, seeds function as dominant conditions; with respect to seeds of their own kind, they function as outflows; and because they are the results of such outflows, they are termed "outflow-results. Thus, [the outflow-result] necessarily possesses the dominant condition.

The nature [of the cause] is identical; this is therefore the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), and thus it is easily produced. If, however, the karmic seed is considered in relation to its manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) and its own seeds, they are of different natures;
consequently, it is merely a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and does not concurrently function as a flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Therefore, when the enjoyment of the prior ripened fruit is exhausted, the retribution should also be exhausted, and it would be unable to produce further ripened fruits again. It must necessarily await other [conditions] in the future.

When the seeds of birth, occupation, and so forth have matured, and the actual ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is exhausted through experience in this present body, those karmas destined for maturation can again independently produce other ripened fruits.
By means of this, birth and death do not cease, and the cycle of transmigration continues without end.
Why, then, would one require external conditions for its continuity? This stream of consciousness has no time of interruption.
Therefore, the *Zongjing* says: "All birth and death are entirely products of deluded sentiment. If one suspects a snake and falls ill, how could there be a real object dwelling within the mind?
It is like hanging sand to satisfy hunger; it is merely a thought arising from one's own mind. One need only realize that all is mind-only."
"Spontaneously there is no fault. This verse concludes with a general explanation of the meaning of the preceding verses.

Furthermore, regarding the text from "The continuity of birth and death arises from various habitual tendencies" (至) to "together with," etc., the meaning of the remaining passages is as explained previously.
This is a detailed explanation of the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). First, regarding the habitual tendency of names and expressions (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*):

when grasping the images of objects and establishing names and expressions for them, all phenomena—whether characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing, or comprised within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—take that which is known through names and expressions as their direct seeds.
This is of two kinds. First, the designation that expresses meaning (*abhilāpa*). Only the sixth consciousness can take its name as an object and can produce it;
therefore, it is called "expressing meaning. All others neither take it as an object nor produce it.

That which is the specific differentiation of sound capable of expressing meaning excludes sounds that lack such expression, for the latter are not names and are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature, incapable of perfuming [the seeds].
The seeds of form, mind, and so forth are termed "distinctions" (*vyañjana*) within the context of names (*nāman*).

However, because of these names, the mind conforms to them and transforms into appearances resembling the dharmas of the five aggregates, the three natures, and so on, thereby perfuming and forming seeds. Because seeds arise due to names, they are designated as "name-and-word seeds" (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*).

Second, regarding the "name-and-word that manifests objects," this refers to the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the first seven consciousnesses, which are the seeing-parts (*darśana-bhāga*). It is not...
This is the objective part (nimittabhāga). Because the objective part cannot cognize objects, all perfumed seeds arise from the mind and mental factors.

If the seeds of the mind and mental factors depend upon something external, they are called "expressive linguistic conventions" (*abhilāpa-vyavahāra*); these are the sounds that express meanings because they are the objective part.

If they do not depend upon something external, they are called "manifesting linguistic conventions"; these manifest the sovereign mind and its mental factors, which constitute the subjective part (darśanabhāga).

Therefore, by virtue of these two kinds of seeds perfumed by verbal designations (*nāma-vikalpa*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) each possess their own specific seeds that directly produce them.

As for what is called the "habitual tendency of self-grasping" (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*), it refers to the seeds of the false grasping of "self" and "mine" regarding oneself and others within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses;
these are the seeds of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*). Innate self-grasping pervades the six [consciousnesses].
The seven consciousnesses involve the discrimination of self-clinging; this refers exclusively to the sixth consciousness.

Regarding what is called the "habitual energy of the links of existence" (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*), it refers to the two links of *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) and *bhava* (existence) among the twelve links of dependent origination. Because the two links of *saṃskāra* and *bhava* belong to the path of karma, they are not referred to as "karma-formations" (*saṃskāra*) here.

This is because those [past] formations belong to the past, whereas this [present link] manifests the perfuming of seeds that invite future fruits. Thus it is said: "Water mixes with scattered earth to form [clods]."

A lump of clay. Karma summons names and words, thereby giving rise to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Following this verse, the three preceding types of habitual tendencies are harmonized and explained.
The *Zongjing* says: "As for the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*), for example, Nanda possessed the habit of desire due to his repeated births in the past."
As a king, because he was closely attached to the five desires, Śāriputra had the habit of anger;
because in many past lives he had been born as a scorpion, Piṅgalavatsa had the habit of pride;
because in many past lives he had been a great brahmin who was widely learned and talented, yet possessed the arrogance of looking down upon others, even [the case of] the bhikṣu Paṇḍaka.
There are the habitual tendencies of delusion and so forth. Regarding the habitual tendencies of karma: for example, the bhikṣu Gomayakhāda (the Cow-Chewer) was formerly a cow.
While running through the forest, he brushed against and tore his *kāṣāya*. Due to these causes and conditions, although he attained the fruit of the Path, his residual habits were not yet purified.
Furthermore, it is like Kāśyapa who danced upon hearing the lute, or Ānanda who was always fond of singing;

both were formerly musicians in past lives, and because they possessed the remnants of such karmic habits, they experienced *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death). This arises from the *kleśa-āsrava* (outflows of affliction) and refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
If one experiences *pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth and death), it arises from *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) and refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yānika*). This is because...
Although the followers of the Two Vehicles have severed the manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), they have not severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from affliction, karma, and suffering, up to old age and death, as explained at length in the treatise.
Below, the three paths are correlated with and explained as the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The single link of ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed "initiating karma" (*karmotpādaka*);

the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are termed "moistening birth" (*janmārdrīkaraṇa*). These three afflictions (*kleśa*) are collectively termed "delusion" (*moha*). The two links of formative action (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), which are capable of inducing [rebirth], are termed "karma.

The five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) that are projected by karma, along with the two links of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), are collectively termed... [the result].

This is suffering. These seeds of affliction, karma, and suffering encompass the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). That is to say, the two members of existence (*bhava*) and becoming (*bhava*) are the habitual tendency of karma;
the remaining ten are the habitual tendency of the two graspings (*upādāna*). Therefore, they are collectively termed "habitual tendencies.

The two habitual tendencies of affliction and karma serve as the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the suffering of birth and death, while the habitual tendency of suffering serves as the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the suffering of birth and death. (Verse)

There are three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which correspond respectively to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*). Alternatively, "suffering" may be termed "appropriation" (*upādāna*):
herein, the afflictions are the two types of grasping and are called the "appropriator" (*upādātṛ*); suffering is the fruit of suffering and is called the "appropriated" (*upādāna*).

Both the appropriator and the appropriated are termed "appropriation" because they involve clinging. Karma is not termed "appropriation" because it lacks such clinging. Thus, there are these three: afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Regarding the subsumption of the twelve links: as the verse says: "Ignorance, craving, and grasping—these three are the path of afflictions;

the two links of formative action and existence belong to the path of karma; from consciousness through sensation, together with birth and aging-and-death, these seven factors share the name 'the path of suffering.'"
Nevertheless, the twelve links are briefly subsumed into four [categories] (up to: because at the time of being moistened and not yet moistened, they necessarily do not coexist).

Hereafter, based on two lifetimes and one cycle of cause and effect, it is explained that the projecting [cause] and the actualizing [cause] are distinct. First, the projecting link (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*).
Ignorance initiates the process and is able to draw forth the seeds of the five fruits, such as consciousness and the rest;

therefore, ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the "projectors. Here, "ignorance" refers exclusively to that which can initiate karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—for future lives.

That very karma initiated for future lives is what is termed "volitional formations. Since these formations induce results in future lives, they are not "conducive to the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the direct fruition (*sākṣād-vedanīya*). Furthermore, it is not an auxiliary factor.

For this reason, all karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*), as well as karma to be experienced in the future that serves as an auxiliary, are not the member of "formative action" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).

This is because, among those who initiate karma, there are those whose member of ignorance (*avidyā-aṅga*) has the capacity to universally initiate both general and specific retributions; those who initiate only the general retribution; and those who initiate only the specific retribution. This...
The first two [links] are taken as being originated by the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) and are subsumed under the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

The third is not subsumed under the link of volitional formations; therefore, it is distinguished by saying that it "only induces individual retribution" and is not included within the link of volitional formations.

"Volitional formations" refers specifically to meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations (*puṇya-apuṇya-āneñjya-saṃskāra*). As for the "two projected links," these are projected by the preceding ignorance and volitional formations.

Because it is produced [by conditions], it is called "that which is induced. To say "directly producing" is to reveal that the five members which are induced are the seeds that directly produce the future maturation (*vipāka*).

That is to say, once ignorance has set the formations (*saṃskāra*) in motion, these formations further perfuse the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), enabling this fundamental consciousness to attract the fruits of future birth, old age, and death; these are termed "seeds. If there were no formations...

The perfuming does not ultimately result in seeds. This is because the five factors, beginning with consciousness, are accumulated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) within a single moment; they lack temporal sequence.

They serve as the seeds for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as the maturation (*vipāka*), and as the seeds for contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*). This is designated as the limb of the six sense bases.
This refers to the members of contact and sensation. Herein, "the seeds of consciousness" refers to the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);

this means that the seeds of the eighth consciousness serve as the direct causal condition for future maturation (*vipāka*). Excluding the latter three causes, these are the seeds of all other maturational aggregates (*skandha*).
All are subsumed within the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). As for the latter three causes, they are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
Some say that the single link of name-and-form subsumes all five causes; however, this is merely a designation based on what is predominant, establishing four distinct categories.

Others say that the single link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) subsumes the six sense bases; however, this is merely a designation based on what is predominant, establishing five distinct categories. Question: In this context, as for consciousness...
Question: Why does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* state that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is a projecting factor (*ākṣepaka*)? Answer:

When the *Samuccaya* states that the member of consciousness is a projecting factor, it is because it takes the seeds of karma (*karma-bīja*) as the member of consciousness. Since volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) perfume the mind and thereby summon the consciousness that brings about future results, it is designated as the member of consciousness.
Question: If that is so, where are the seeds of consciousness themselves included? Answer: The seeds of consciousness are subsumed within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*) encompasses both the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected (*ākṣipta*). This is because karma perfumes consciousness to summon future consciousness;

thus, these two types are designated as the limb of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*). Since the seed of karma is the projector and the seed of consciousness is the projected, both are termed the limb of consciousness.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "This consciousness is merely the support for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), yet it is not itself subsumed under name-and-form."
Because the remaining consciousnesses exist in dependence upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Question:

Since the five kinds of consciousness and so forth arise through being perfumed by karma and its traces within a single moment, and thus have no sequence of priority or posteriority, why is there nevertheless a distinction of before and after?

Answer: Due to the activation by karmic impressions (*karma-vāsanā*), although [the factors] such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) are in reality simultaneous and without priority or sequence, they are conventionally designated as preceding or succeeding based on four characteristics:
namely, that consciousness is the primary factor while the other four are its companions; that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the general category while the other three are the particulars;

that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are predominant while the other two are subordinate; and that the member of contact (*sparśa*) is the cause while the member of sensation (*vedanā*) is the result.

Fruit. Based on these four meanings, "prior" and "subsequent" are provisionally established. Alternatively, because the five factors beginning with consciousness have a sequential order based on their future state of manifesting as fruit, they are said to possess priority and posteriority.
For this reason, these five dharmas beginning with consciousness are also said to be "active" (*samudācāra*) within the state of fruit;
however, when in the state of cause, they definitely lack the meaning of being active. Furthermore, by...

Regarding the future state of fruition, that which is produced and that which is induced can be said to be simultaneous, because the seed and the arising of the manifest fruit must necessarily coexist.

However, if one relies on the capacity to produce and the capacity to induce, they must not be simultaneous, because the stages of being moistened and not yet being moistened do not occur at the same time.
Among these, the single link of ignorance refers exclusively to the afflictions that initiate karma; the single link of formations refers to the karmic latencies (*karmavāsanā*).
These two links are capable of projecting a distant fruit; they are termed the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) and the "predominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya*).

As for the five links beginning with consciousness, they are explained in terms of the stage where the seeds have not yet matured; based on the perspective of the future state of the fruit, five distinct causes are established.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states: "How does one proceed from the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) to the middle limit (*madhyānta*), and having arisen in the middle limit, how does one again enter into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)?

It is said that there is one who, not understanding that the prior consciousness has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its condition, performs and accumulates meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable actions of body, speech, and mind.
By means of this, through the consciousness that follows karma, [the process continues] until life..."
It continues to flow and revolve without interruption, serving as the cause for the consciousness that links to future existence (*punarbhava*).
When this consciousness is about to produce its fruit, having already passed away from the previous limit (*pūrvānta*), it attains birth as a self-body in the present life.
At that time, the karma that induces birth bestows the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) upon name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); by means of this maturation-consciousness, it then relies upon name-and-form.
It revolves because it necessarily depends upon these two supports for its continued functioning; thus, these two supports and consciousness continue in an uninterrupted succession.

For this reason, in the present life, consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form conditions consciousness, like bundles of reeds leaning against one another, continuing in mutual dependence until the end of life.
The three branches that produce [the future] are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).

From the breaking up of the body at the end of life until death itself—these three are called the "branches that produce" because they closely give rise to future birth, aging, and death; therefore, they are termed "producers.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "It refers to how sentient beings, due to their delusion regarding internal maturational results (*vipākaphala*), [engage with] the subsequent..."

There is the suffering of birth. One does not know it as it truly is. Due to delusion regarding future existence and through the predominant power of ignorance concerning the future limit (*aparānta*), one performs and accumulates various formations (*saṃskāra*).

Because of this newly performed karma, this consciousness is called "consciousness following karma. Thus, within the present life itself, it is said that with ignorance as a condition, formations arise; and because formations arise...

Consciousness arises. This consciousness is followed by the seeds of future existence (*punarbhava*), up to the seeds of contact (*sparśa*), which are followed by the seeds of future feeling (*vedanā*).
This is collectively termed the "causal factor for the projection of future existence" within the intermediate state (*madhyāntara*).

Therefore, this consciousness is called the "projecting consciousness" (*ākṣepaka-vijñāna*), because by means of it, [the continuum] is projected up to feeling throughout the course of a single lifetime.
Because of the body. Furthermore, due to the second delusion regarding the objects of experience, there arises the ignorance of feeling; conditioned by the feeling of objects, craving is produced.
Conditioned by this craving, one either gives rise to the quest for sensory pleasure (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) or the quest for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*).

Or, one clings to the grasping of sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*), the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*), the grasping of precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata-upādāna*), and the grasping of the doctrine of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*). To cling to contentious arguments and to cling to future existence—this is the meaning of "grasping" (*upādāna*). Because of...
Bound by the fetters of attachment to sensual desire, with indulgence as the cause, householders engage in mutual strife;
this root of strife is the first *upādāna*. Bound by the fetters of attachment to views, with indulgence as the cause, those who have gone forth engage in mutual strife;
this root of strife consists of the latter three *upādānas*. The sixty-two views are [the category of] view.
Grasping at various distinct prohibitions and ascetic practices constitutes the *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to rules and observances).

The *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity), which serves as their basis, is the *ātmavādopādāna* (clinging to the doctrine of a self). Due to *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) and *śīlavrataparāmarśa*, the various non-Buddhists engage in mutual disputes;
however, due to the *ātmavādopādāna*, the non-Buddhists do not dispute with one another, whereas they do dispute with those who follow the True Dharma.
Contentious debate. Thus, being attached to the root of contentious debate, one further draws forth the ripening of suffering in a future existence;

therefore, it is called "grasping" (*upādāna*). Through the moistening and nourishing of this union of craving and grasping, the seeds of karma belonging to the *saṃskāra* (formative) link are irrigated;

together with the five causes, such as the projected consciousness (*vijñāna*), these are designated as "existence" (*bhava*). This is because both the seeds of karma and the causes are capable of [projecting a future birth].

Because it is proximate and possesses the capacity for future results, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its tenth chapter, refers exclusively to the seeds of karma as "existence" (*bhava*), since these alone can directly induce the ripening result (*vipākaphala*).
Although the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) serve as direct causes, they lack the power to produce [the result].
Because it is in the process of arising as a fruit, it cannot be designated as "existent. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks:

"For what reason is it not said that a self-nature serves as its own condition? The answer is: "Because that self-nature, if it does not encounter other conditions, can neither increase nor diminish its own defilements;
for this reason, it is not so stated. Some say that only five types [of conditions] are taught.

Regarding the term "existence" (*bhava*): it is so called because it serves as the seed for the production of future consciousness and the other factors. In reality, there are eight members (*aṅga*) in total, which are collectively designated by the name "existence.
The seed of karma constitutes one member; consciousness and the others constitute five; and the two factors that provide moisture constitute the essence of the member of existence.
When the subject and object are discussed together, there are said to be eight [links]. These eight combined constitute "existence" (*bhava*), which has no separate essence from them.
The four links that are produced are birth, old age, and death; these three links are so called because they are the immediate results of the preceding three.

That is to say, from the time one seeks parents in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until the point when the fundamental existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) has not yet undergone decay and transformation, all are subsumed under the link of birth. Thus it is remembered.
Reflecting on the transition [of life]: when the vital energy dissipates and the face becomes wrinkled, this state of various decaying transformations is collectively termed "aging.

When the body disintegrates and life comes to an end, this is termed "death. There are four states of existence (*bhava*): first, the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), which occurs after the intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*) and before the fundamental existence (*pūrva-kāla-bhava*).

At the moment of linking the rebirth and continuing the stream of existence, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise in a single instant; this is called birth-existence. Second, the fundamental existence, which follows immediately after birth-existence.
Prior to the existence at death (cyuty-bhava), the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) that exist in the interval between them are called the existence of birth (pūrvakāla-bhava).

The existence at death is the cessation of the five aggregates immediately following the existence of birth and preceding the intermediate existence (antarābhava). The intermediate existence is that which follows the existence at death.
Birth (*jāti*) precedes existence (*bhava*). Within this context, the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are the afflictions that moisten birth;

because they can directly and immediately produce their own fruit, they are the cause for the arising of birth and are termed the "immediate causal condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This is explained in terms of the stage where the seeds have reached maturity.

The single link of existence, moreover, is a provisional designation; it refers to the aforementioned six links of karma and so forth, which, conditioned by craving and grasping, [constitute existence].

That which is moistened is further designated as "existence" (*bhava*), because it has the capacity to produce a fruit. Although the two branches of birth and death (*jāti* and *jarāmaraṇa*) are called the actual fruits of maturation, they too are merely provisional designations.
Thus, the *Śālistamba Sūtra* states: Śāriputra asked Maitreya, "What is meant by 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
He replied, "When there is a cause and there is a condition, this is called the dharma of dependent origination. There is the dharma arisen from causes and conditions."
There are two kinds: first, internal; second, external. From what do external dependent origination phenomena arise?
They are like seeds that can produce sprouts; from the sprout, leaves arise; from the leaves, nodes arise; from the nodes, stems arise; and from the stems, ears arise.
From the ear emerges the flower; from the flower emerges the fruit. Because there is no seed, there is no sprout, and so on, up to the absence of flowers and fruits.
Because there is a seed, the sprout arises, and so on, up to the presence of flowers, the fruit arises.
Yet the seed does not form the thought, "I am able to produce the sprout," nor does the sprout form the thought, "I have arisen from the seed," and so forth. Thus it is.
These are called phenomena produced by external causes. What are called phenomena produced by external conditions?

They are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time. The element of earth provides stability; the element of water provides moisture; the element of fire brings maturation; and the element of wind provides impulsion.
The element of space does not create obstruction. Furthermore, it depends upon time and the harmonious transformations of the seasonal nodes.
When these six conditions are fully present, [the sprout] arises. Yet, the earth does not say, "I am able to support," nor does the water say, "I am able to moisten," and so forth.
The seed does not say, "I have produced the sprout through six conditions," nor does the sprout say, "I have arisen from such a number of conditions.
Yet, in reality, it arises from the convergence of various conditions.
Furthermore, the sprout does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both together, nor from a creator god (Īśvara) and so forth, nor from nothingness.
