This is called the sequence of external dependent origination. As for internal dependent origination, it arises from two kinds [of causes].
What are these causes? From ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). With the cessation of ignorance, formations (*saṃskāra*) cease;
and so on, up to: with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease. Because of ignorance, there are formations; and so on, up to: because of birth, there is [old age and death].
Old age and death. Ignorance does not say, "I can produce volitional formations. Volitional formations also do not say, "I am produced from ignorance.
This continues up to old age and death, which likewise do not say, "I am produced from birth. Yet, when there is actually ignorance, there are volitional formations;
when there is birth, there is old age and death. This is called the sequence of dharmas arising through internal causes. What is meant by "internal"?
Conditioned phenomena refer to the so-called six elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

Earth is able to provide firm support; water is able to moisten and permeate; fire is able to bring to maturity; wind is able to sustain inhalation and exhalation; space is able to provide non-obstruction; and consciousness is able to discern.
The combination of these various factors is called the body. The tainted mind is called consciousness. Thus it is.
When the six conditions are fully assembled, the body is thereby formed. Yet, the earth-element does not think, "I am able to provide stability";

the water-element does not think, "I am able to provide moisture"; and so on, until consciousness does not think, "I am able to bring about growth. Nor does the body think, "I have arisen from these various conditions.
This is called the sequential order of internal dependent origination. Next, [this is explained] in terms of the three periods of time.
There are two layers of cause and effect, clarifying that both "arising" (*utpāda*) and "projecting" (*ākṣepa*) are pervasive. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"To not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called ignorance (*avidyā*). The *Abhidharma* states: "Delusion regarding the true meaning" refers to being confused about the Four Noble Truths.
That which is deluded is the actual object; that which deludes is ignorance (*avidyā*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"All those who are deluded must first be confused regarding the objects to be known, and subsequently initiate wrong conduct toward them.

This ignorance, in terms of a person's confusion regarding the principle, arises perversely from emptiness. The karmic fruit produced by these actions is the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Karma refers to meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma, as these are the fruits arising from that ignorance.

Regarding "the mind at the initial moment is the consciousness upon which the formations depend": this means that the consciousness of the initial moment exists in dependence on the formations; through the perfuming of the mind by the formations, there exist the seeds of future results, leading up to their actual manifestation.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "With what cause as a condition does the resultant consciousness continue in a sequence of prior and posterior moments?"

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the four aggregates of grasping which arise simultaneously with consciousness constitute name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)," the term "consciousness" refers here to the active (*pravṛtti*) member of the causal chain.
From the perspective of being a seed, this consciousness is exclusively the *ālayavijñāna*; however, in its state as an active manifestation, it encompasses all six types of consciousness.

Since the present context distinguishes the active from the seed state, the term "arising simultaneously" is used. As for the four aggregates, since the aggregate of consciousness already belongs to the supporting consciousness (*āśraya-vijñāna*), these [remaining] four aggregates [constitute name].
"Name" refers to [the mental factors], and "form" refers to the *kalala* and so forth. Regarding the growth of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) into the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*):

this means that after four weeks, when the sense faculties have reached full development and the six bases are clearly manifest, the increase of "name" establishes the mind-base (*manāyatana*), while the increase of "form" establishes the other five.

This is because at the time when the four aggregates constituted "name," the characteristics of consciousness were not yet differentiated; now, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is clear and distinct.
This is called "increase," referring to the stage when the flesh has solidified but the five sense organs have not yet differentiated; at that time, it is merely termed "one color.

Now, as the material sense organs gradually become complete, they are opened up into five. Regarding the statement that the conjunction of the three factors—the faculty, the object, and consciousness—constitutes contact, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says:

Contact arises from the conjunction of the three [the sense organ, the object, and consciousness]. Although contact is a single entity, it is divided into six according to the categories of consciousness. These six types of contact are further subsumed into two:
the first five are called "contact by opposition" (pratigha-saṃsparśa), while mental contact is called "contact with designation" (adhivacana-saṃsparśa).

Although contact itself is formless, because its supporting bases—the sense organs and so forth—are characterized by resistance (sapratigha), the five consciousnesses, such as that of the eye, perceive only blue and other such colors, but do not perceive the name "blue. The mental consciousness...

Consciousness can take blue and so forth as its object, and it also takes the name "blue" as its object. Because the name is established based on the object, it is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).
As the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Contact that has not yet understood the distinctions among the causes of the three feelings is called contact.

The "causes of the three feelings" refers to the objects of the three feelings; because these objects can produce feeling, they are termed "causes. This refers to the period from birth until the age of two or three, when one has not yet...

Because it has already ceased, it is not called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Regarding the statement that "feeling is that which arises together with contact" (*sparśa-sahaja*), this refers to the discernment of the three types of feeling and the experiencing of contact;
thus it is called "arising together with contact. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Feeling occurs prior to sensual craving (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*)," meaning from the age of five or six onwards.

From the age of fourteen or fifteen onward, one has already understood the three types of sensation (*vedanā*) through their distinct characteristics; however, as long as sexual desire has not yet arisen, it is merely termed "sensation. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Attachment to a single craving is called sensation," referring here to the craving for food and clothing.

The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says: "From this, six sensations arise: five belong to the body [via contact] and the remaining one belongs to the mind. This means that [sensations] arise from the six types of contact (*sparśa*).

There are six types of feeling (*vedanā*). Among these six, the first five are called bodily feelings (*kāyikī vedanā*), while those produced by mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja*) are called mental feelings (*caitasikī vedanā*), because they are feelings of the mind.
Regarding "attachment to feeling is craving": among the three types of feeling, one is entangled in and yearns for pleasant feeling;

thus it is called "attachment," which refers to greed (*rāga*) of middling or inferior intensity. Although this [craving] generally takes both internal and external fruits as its objects, according to the various treatises...
When one grasps extensively at external objects, craving arises as a dominant fruit. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Craving for requisites and sexual craving—namely, from the age of fifteen or sixteen onwards—one craves exquisite requisites; when sexual craving manifests but has not yet led to extensive seeking, it is merely termed 'craving' (*tṛṣṇā*).

The *Abhidharmakośa* further states: "From these three types of sensation (*vedanā*), three types of craving are induced; that is to say, based on the existence of pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*), [craving] is generated."
One gives rise to craving for sensual desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*). Or, regarding pleasant feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant, one gives rise to craving for the realm of form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*).

Or, regarding only feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant, one gives rise to craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*); these constitute craving of middling and inferior grades. "The increase of craving is grasping" (*tṛṣṇā-vivṛddhir upādānam*):

although this includes other afflictions, because the moistening power of craving is predominant, it is said that the increase of craving constitutes grasping. However, as for the two higher [realms]...
The term *upādāna* (clinging) refers to both its manifest state and its seeds. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "To seek everywhere is called clinging (*upādāna*). Clinging refers to greed.
Once one has grown up, one craves the objects of the five desires and seeks them in all directions, undaunted by toil or fatigue.

Regarding the distinction between craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and clinging: that which first arises is called craving; when it continues and evolves further, it is established separately as clinging. The contaminated karma produced by clinging is called existence (*bhava*).

This is so because the various karmas arising within the mind through grasping (*upādāna*) are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Since these karmas can directly induce their future fruits, they are called "existence" (*bhava*).
This refers to the three time periods; it differs from the previous section where karma was termed "existence" when moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping.
This is because the preceding karma has already been separated [from its result] by the manifest name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Existence..."
This refers to the fact that one who is truly capable of performing karma that draws forth the fruit of future existence accumulates such karma through the process of striving and seeking;
thus, karma is called "existence" (*bhava*). Because it is the cause for the fruit of future existence, the name of the effect is applied to the cause, and so karma is termed "existence.

As for the statement that the aggregates arising from karma constitute "birth" (*jāti*), this is said in terms of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); it means they arise from karma. This begins with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Up until the age of forty, before decline and transformation set in, all these stages are termed "birth" (*jāti*).

This is because karma—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—is the cause of birth, and it is the resultant fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). If one considers the causal conditions: from the seeds of the two types of grasping (*upādāna*), there arises "birth";

the ripening of the aggregates (*skandha*) is "aging" (*jarā*); and the disintegration of the aggregates is "death" (*maraṇa*). Thus, the various states of decline and transformation are called the ripening of the aggregates. After the age of forty...

Subsequently, as the countenance gradually declines, it belongs to old age. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "When one reaches the point of being subject to aging and death, its meaning is subsumed under the branch of birth.
The essence of these latter two branches (aging and death) pervades the five aggregates and consists solely of active manifestations (*samudācāra*), as cited above;

this is explained according to the conventional gate of dependent origination (*saṃvṛti-pratītyasamutpāda*). However, according to the *Yathābhūta-śāstra*, not even a single dharma is seen that is a condition (*pratyaya*) and yet not [subject to] [dependent origination].
Conditioned by what? How much more so for the twelve? Aging is not necessarily present;
it is established as a factor in conjunction with death. (Up to: The Sūtra states that it is not non-existent, yet it is not entirely absent. Question:
Why is birth established as a separate factor, while aging and death are established together? Answer: Because aging is not necessarily present, and there are also cases where it does not exist.

Regarding those who die of old age, the factor of "aging" is therefore established as a dependent link alongside death. Question: For what reason is "sickness" not established as a dependent link? Answer:

Because it does not pervade all realms and destinies, nor is it invariably present; therefore, it is not established as a link. Question: Aging is also not invariably present; why then is it established as a link alongside death? Answer:
Although aging is not invariably present, because it exists universally, it is established as a link alongside death. That is to say, across all realms and destinies...
[Beings] are born, excluding those who die prematurely, because at the time of death there must necessarily be signs of decay and deterioration. Question:

Since name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) does not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), for what reason are [the links of dependent origination] established there? Answer: Although it does not pervade the entire realm, it is nonetheless established as a link because it is determinate.

For example, in the case of one born from a womb, within the mother’s womb, the resultant consciousness (*phalavijñāna*) that continues the stream coexists with name-and-form; even though the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet fully developed.

Because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) necessarily exists, as in the case of womb-birth; the same applies to other modes of birth. Furthermore, the limb of name-and-form not only exists necessarily, but it is also universal.
Even in the case of apparitional birth (upapāduka), at the initial stage of receiving birth, although the five sense-faculties are complete, they have not yet become functional;
and although the mental faculty (manas) is present, it is not yet clear. All of these are subsumed under name-and-form. For this reason...
Therefore, the treatise states that among the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), all [links] have a portion present in the two higher realms. Question:

Since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is not universally present, why is it established as a separate link? For those born in the evil destinies do not give rise to craving for the fruits of suffering therein. Answer: [It is because...]
The members [of dependent origination] are established on the basis of their certainty. Only for one who is free from craving does "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) not exist.
However, for one born in a happy realm, there is necessarily seeking; thus, it is like the noble ones of the three fruits.

At the stage of moistening birth, although they do not give rise to craving due to the strength of their power of antidotes, because the seeds of the member of grasping (*upādāna*) have not been severed, craving likewise possesses its seed with certainty. You...
It is said that the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) does not pervade the miserable realms (*apāya*). This is because it is not understood that the limb of craving also pervades the miserable realms;

for those born in the miserable realms also cherish their own suffering bodies with the thought, "I. However, when the Sūtra states that there is no craving in the miserable realms, it means they do not long for the miserable realms, and thus it says there is no craving;
it does not mean that craving is entirely absent in all those beings.

For what reason are birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) established as the "arisen" (*abhinirvṛtta*), while the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are explained as the "mutually produced" (*anyonya-janman*) states?
Question: Since the "arisen" and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*) are cause and effect, they ought to be identical.

Why is it that the "arisen" consists of only two members, whereas the "projected" consists of five members? Answer: Because the specific characteristics of the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*) are difficult to discern, it is divided into five members and established separately.

The results are easy to understand; they are explained collectively by combining two links. Regarding the three types of suffering—namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)—these correspond respectively to birth, old age, and death. However, there is another specific meaning regarding the two results and five causes.
The two results are established for the purpose of causing future sentient beings to develop weary detachment (*nirveda*). The five causes are established for the purpose of [causing] present...
Because sentient beings recognize the various stages [of existence].

For what reason is ignorance established as the primary factor for the initiation of karma? While craving is superior in its function of moistening [the seeds of rebirth], it is said that craving is predominant [in the stage of birth].
Question: Since both the initiation of karma and the moistening of rebirth are termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*), why is only one—ignorance—established in the stage of initiating karma?

Regarding the specific clarification of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) within the stage of moistening birth (*janmābhiṣyandana*), the answer is as follows: Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of producing moistening, at the stage of initiating karma (*karmotpatti*), the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) is predominant;
therefore, it is said that [ignorance] is the most distinguished among the eleven [factors]. The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states:

First, its object (*ālambana*) is distinguished, because it universally objects to both the defiled and the pure; second, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is distinguished, because it conceals the truth and manifests the false.
1. The excellence of the three causes: because they are the basis for afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth. 2. The excellence of the motivation (*samutthāna*):

because it is able to equally initiate, draw forth, and produce the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). 3. The excellence of the fourfold transformation (*pariṇāma*): because of the four transformations consisting of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), association (*saṃprayoga*), and non-common [factors].
4. The excellence of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti*): because it gives rise to practices of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) based upon the Truths (*satya*).

Therefore: (7) superiority of characteristics, because it manifests as both specific individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that are subtle, and as universal common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) regarding the pleasant and unpleasant;
(8) superiority of activity, because it acts as the basis for the process of saṃsāra and acts as the obstacle to the state of cessation (*śamatha*);
(9) superiority of obstruction, because it obstructs the supreme Dharma; (10) superiority of conformity, because it persists even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because it transforms. Eleventh is the excellence of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-viśeṣa*), because it is that which is to be countered by the two kinds of sublime knowledge (*prajñā*).

At the stage of moistening birth (*upapatti-sneha-avasthā*), the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) increases and becomes predominant; thus, just as seeds such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) require the nourishment, moisture, and irrigation of afflictions (*kleśa*) such as attachment (*rāga*) in order for the sprout of existence (*bhava-aṅkura*) to arise, so too [is this case].
This is because there are six types of co-emergent (*sahaja*) and ten types of conceptual (*vikalpa*) secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Within [the category of] "middle," only the single dharma of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) acts as the primary, central moisture for the middle [existence]. The other five [factors] that arise simultaneously act as auxiliary moisture for the middle.
All others act as auxiliary moisture for the auxiliary middle. Furthermore, based on the initial and final stages, craving and grasping (*upādāna*) are divided into two:

namely, there must be an initial and a final stage in the repeated irrigation [of existence]. Initially, regarding the object produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), it is designated solely by the name "craving. Subsequently...

To give rise to deep defiled attachment toward objects of craving is what is called "clinging" (*upādāna*). As for the production of karma by ignorance (*avidyā*), once it has been produced, that is the end;
there is no sense of repetition, and therefore it is established as a single [link]. Question: Clinging is of four kinds, as previously stated.
The first can only produce the fruit of suffering in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the others pertain to all three realms. Do these four encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*)?

For what reason is it said that only the increase of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called grasping (*upādāna*)? Answer: Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are included within the limb of grasping, the power of the moisture of craving to nourish them is preeminent;
therefore, it is said that craving increases, yet this does not mean that other delusions are absent.
All members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) depend upon their own respective levels (*svabhūmi*). [If they were to extend] beyond this, it would lead to an infinite regress. Question:

Do the various members condition one another while remaining within their own level, or do they also exist in other levels? Answer: All members of dependent origination mutually condition one another by depending upon their own level.
However, when there is karma that has been projected, it also depends upon ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to another level; this is as follows:
The ignorance of a lower stage also gives rise to karma belonging to a higher stage.

If one were to claim that the ignorance of a lower stage does not give rise to karma of a higher stage, then when one first subdues the afflictions of the desire realm and gives rise to the four dhyānas and eight samādhis of the higher realms, these meditative absorptions would not be factors produced by the issuance of ignorance from the lower realm. Why is this? Because of that...
Because ignorance regarding the higher realms has not yet arisen, and because that meditative absorption must first be manifested before it can be attained. Question:
If one descends from a higher plane to a lower plane, or ascends from a lower plane to a higher plane, with respect to which realm’s objects of experience does one give rise to the limb of craving?
Answer: If one descends from a higher plane to a lower plane, one gives rise to the limb of craving by taking the experiences of the lower plane as an object. If [one ascends...]

Regarding those who later descend from a lower stage and are reborn in a higher one: they give rise to the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) by taking the sensations (*vedanā*) of the higher stage as their object.
As for that which is so-objectified, it may take either a currently manifesting state or a latent seed as its object; in both cases, there is no contradiction with reason. Question:

Do these twelve limbs belong to the same lifetime, or to different lifetimes? Answer: The first ten belong to the present, and the latter two belong to the future. They consist of ten causes and two results.

The [links of] existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*) are fixed as belonging to different lifetimes. Among the causes, the first seven links and the three beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) may be either the same or different, because they are both present and absent at the time of moistening and non-moistening [the seeds].

This is because [existence] is fixed as being a result in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), whereas [birth] is fixed as being a result in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*). As for birth and old age/death (*jarāmaraṇa*), these two belong equally to the future;
craving, grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*)—these three—belong to the cause within the present; and the first seven links likewise belong equally to the present. Therefore, each is fixed.
[They exist] in the same world-system. Question: Some say that there are two layers of cause and effect spanning three periods of time; why then do you assert only one? Answer:
These twelve [links] constitute a single layer of cause and effect, which is sufficient to manifest cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

Because the cause ceases as the fruit arises, and the fruit arises as the cause ceases, the arising of the fruit is not annihilation, and the cessation of the cause is not permanence. Thus, this single layer is sufficient to clarify the mutual production of cause and effect.
It is not interrupted. Two layers are established because [more than this] would be useless. Or else, one should exceed this, which would lead to infinity:

if there are those who are ignorant of the prior limit, two past causes are taught; yet for those who are even more ignorant of the prior-prior limit, these two causes would still be too few, and more should be taught.
If there are those who are ignorant of the posterior limit, two future fruits are taught; yet for those who are even more ignorant...
Regarding the "later limit": since the two fruits [of the path] are still few, it is necessary to further explain their abundance.
As for the distinct categories of meaning within these twelve links, [the explanation] up to the arising of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and so forth does not contradict reason.

The following section concerns the classification of the different categories (*paryāya*). First, regarding the conventional (*prajñapti*) and the real (*dravya*): Question: Of these twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), how many are conventional and how many are real? Answer: The first nine are real; the last three are conventional.
That is to say, the six links beginning with "impregnated formations" (*sābhisyandana-saṃskāra*) combine to constitute "existence as karma" (*karmabhava*);

therefore, existence is conventional. Furthermore, the characteristics of birth and old age and death (*jātijarāmaraṇa*) upon the five results—namely, consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth—are designated as "stages" (*avasthā*). Thus, they are conventional.
They are not the same. Therefore, birth, aging, and death are also merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Next, the discussion concerns unity and multiplicity. Question:

How many constitute a single entity as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? Answer: Five constitute a single entity. The seven branches beginning with *saṃskāra* (formative forces) are all not single entities.

This is because *saṃskāra* encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome; *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) consists of two parts; the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) consist of four [groups of] appropriations (*upādāna*); and *bhava* (existence) comprises six factors. Birth...

Regarding the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇāṅga*): because it possesses the five [links] beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is next discussed in terms of being defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).

Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—these three—are exclusively defiled, as their nature is that of affliction (*kleśa*). The five links beginning with consciousness and the two links of birth and aging-and-death are exclusively non-defiled, as they are results of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and are ethically neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Alternatively, it is said that the seven positions may also give rise to defilement; this is a figurative designation (*prajñapti*).

The two links of *bhava* (existence) encompass both the defiled and the undefiled. Next, we discuss the pure and the mixed: three are of a "pure" character because they alone can produce [the subsequent links];

nine are of a "mixed" character because they are intermingled with other links—for instance, the six links already moistened by craving are combined to constitute *bhava*, and the five links beginning with consciousness are designated as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.
Next, we discuss the material and the non-material: six are exclusively non-material.

The six factors beginning with *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) pertain to both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Next, regarding their status as tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):
all of them are exclusively tainted and conditioned, as they are not subsumed under the category of the untainted or the unconditioned. Next, regarding their moral nature (*svabhāva*):

ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus they pertain only to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) have the nature of karma (*karma-svabhāva*) and pertain to both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome. Existence (*bhava*) is karma.
They are produced through the conjunction of various seeds and fruits; therefore, they encompass both the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the non-obscured.

Since consciousness and so forth, as well as arising and so forth, are results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), they are exclusively non-obscured. Within the seven stages [of the life-continuum], they also give rise to the wholesome and the defiled, and thus they encompass all three natures, because the wholesome and defiled arise by taking these as their objects and relying upon them.
Next, regarding their connection to the realms (*dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*): although they all pertain to the three realms, [the specific details follow].
There is partial existence in the higher realms and complete existence in the desire realm. Regarding "partial existence in the higher realms":
in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), there is only the factor of form (*rūpa-aṅga*); in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), there is only the factor of name (*nāma-aṅga*).

Because the practice-factors (*caryā-aṅga*) of the higher stages can suppress those of the lower stages—since those in the lower stages feel weary of the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of their own level, and aspire to the purity, subtlety, and liberation of the higher levels, seeking rebirth therein—they give rise to the practice-factors of the higher stages.

[They are] "limbs" (*aṅga*) because they function by suppressing the lower stages. Next, regarding their inclusion within the [spiritual] levels (*avasthā*): all *bhava-aṅgas* are exclusively comprised within that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).

This is because both learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) are termed "noble ones" (*ārya*). Since the contaminated wholesome karma (*sāsrava-kuśala-karma*) produced by noble ones contradicts the condition of ignorance (*avidyā-pratyaya*), it does not belong to the *bhava-aṅgas*.
Furthermore, such individuals will certainly never again create karma that brings about future existence (*punar-bhava*). Question: Since...

There is no further existence. Why, then, would one be reborn in a higher realm? Answer: Because those who have practiced the mixed cultivation of dhyāna through both tainted and untainted states assist the karma belonging to the lower stages;
thus, it is not logically contradictory for them to be born as non-returners (anāgāmin) in the five [pure abodes].

There is an interpretation that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned solely through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*). (Up to this point, one should understand the various abandonments as previously explained.

Next, the abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is discussed. One master says: "The single member of ignorance is abandoned solely through the path of seeing; it necessarily involves delusion regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*)."

Because they are capable of initiating [karmic action]; because the delusions regarding the principles of the truths are abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*); because noble ones (*ārya*) certainly do not create karma for future existence;

and because there are definitely no afflictions capable of initiating [such karma]. The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), because they moisten rebirth by seeking future existence.
Regarding the nine types of mind at the moment of death, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "There is..."
The nine types of death-minds are associated with self-love (*ātmabhāvaprema*) and cause the continuity [of existence] within each of the three realms;

they are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The remaining nine are all common to both types of abandonment. One master says that it is not only the remaining nine, but all [the ten] are common to both types of abandonment.
The treatise states below to cite proof. "If there were no... and so forth, which directly refutes the previous master. "If one claims there is no... and so forth.
[The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] clarifies: "Only those [afflictions] abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) are [abandoned] within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Since they have already been completely abandoned therein, that treatise should not further state that a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has not abandoned them entirely. If the two members, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), were abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), then they would not be abandoned at all during the stage of the path of seeing;
thus, it should not further state that 'one part of all [afflictions] has been abandoned. Furthermore, that treatise says:"
All afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms are capable of producing rebirth and leading to conduct that goes toward the evil destinies (*durgati*).

This conduct is initiated solely by afflictions consisting of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). He has never stated that the afflictions which moisten rebirth are exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

From this, it is known that ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) also pertain to both types of abandonment. However, there is no lower [affliction] that pervades [all]; this accords with the position of the former master, namely, that [the afflictions] are truly...
That which initiates [rebirth] is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). That which directly moistens and brings about birth is abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Those that assist initiation and assist moistening pertain to both insight and cultivation. Below, it is clarified that all twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) pertain to both types of abandonment.

Furthermore, regarding defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should be abandoned—namely, the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—are abandoned in their intrinsic nature when uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises; this is called "abandonment by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).
"Severed. This is because when clarity arises, darkness departs. All contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome dharmas are not severed by their own nature, for they do not contradict the Path.
Question: If that is so, why are both types [of wholesome dharmas] called "severed"? Answer: There are two senses in which they are said to be severed.

First, because they are separated from bondage; that is to say, due to the seventh [consciousness], the co-emergent afflictions (*kleśa*), which take those [wholesome dharmas] as objects and become associated with them.

Regarding indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas: they cause the wholesome and other states produced by the sixth consciousness to be unable to lose their characteristics when associated with the eighth consciousness’s indeterminate nature, and thus liberation cannot be attained.
Once the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been severed, that [consciousness] is then freed from its bonds. The tenet of this school states: "One merely severs the delusions within the mind;
one does not give rise to greed or hatred toward external objects. Although one may take objects as conditions, one is not defiled by them."

This is called the severance of the bonds of conditions (*pratyaya-bandha-viccheda*), because the two [types of birth] do not arise. That is to say, the resultant phenomena of the three miserable realms (*durgati*) arise based on conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

After entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one can ensure that the suffering results of the evil paths of the three miserable realms never arise again. This is called the severance of the bonds of dependence (*āśraya-bandha-viccheda*).

It is said that contaminated wholesome and neutral [states] are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because those that take them as objects or are mixed with them are innate (*sahaja*).

It is said that the various evil destinies and the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) are abandoned only through seeing (*darśana-heya*), because they serve as the basis for those [states], which arise through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Regarding the aforementioned modes of abandonment, one should understand them as appropriate; this is according to the *Prakaraṇapāda*.

As explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda* (The Treatise on the Auxiliaries). If one follows the general discussion, it is as explained in the *Dharmaskandha* (The Aggregate of Dharmas) regarding the two types of abandonment.

Regarding the ten [mental factors] associated with pleasure and equanimity, and the fact that feeling is not associated with feeling—wise and discerning individuals should reflect upon these according to reason.

Next, the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) are discussed. Ten of the twelve links are associated with the two feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), excluding the two links of feeling and death.
Eleven links are associated with the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha*), excluding the single link of feeling. Next, the three types of suffering (*duḥkhatā*) are discussed.

Eleven [links] are, in part, subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), excluding the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Question: Why is there no suffering of change within the link of old age and death? Answer: Because change...

Suffering is established based on pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), because when pleasure arrives, suffering necessarily arises to destroy it. In the stages of old age and death, there is generally no craving for pleasure;

therefore, they are not mentioned [in that context]. Twelve [of the links] are partially subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), while all twelve in their entirety are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
If one correlates the three types of feeling with the three types of suffering: pleasant feeling corresponds to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and painful feeling corresponds to...

Suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) corresponds to the feeling of pain; the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) corresponds to the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

If one relies on eleven portions of the feeling of equanimity—excluding old age and death—the suffering of conditioned formations is established based on the feeling of equanimity. This is because when old age and death arrive, there is no feeling of equanimity, and thus there is no suffering of conditioned formations. Next, regarding the Four Noble Truths:

all twelve [links] are subsumed under the truth of suffering, for they all have the nature of the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*). [This includes] ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).

The formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) consist of five members and are likewise subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because their nature is that of affliction and karma. Next, the four conditions (*pratyaya*) are discussed.

When the various members are compared with one another, they invariably possess the condition of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*). With the exception of three cases where it is indeterminate, first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is indeterminate:

if the seed of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) gives rise to the active manifestation of grasping (*upādāna*), this is a case of mutual induction among its own kind, and thus possesses the sense of being a causal condition; the seeds of the five resultant consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) likewise give rise to their respective manifestations.
[The phrase] "formations" (saṃskāra) refers to the fact that seeds give rise to manifest activity; thus, there is the sense of being a causal condition.

If one says that the member of consciousness (vijñāna) is the seed of karma, then formations, in relation to consciousness, constitute the sense of being a causal condition for the perfuming of seeds by manifest activity. For anything else, there is no such causal condition. Question:

If that is so, why does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* state that ignorance (avidyā), in relation to formations, has the sense of being a causal condition? Answer: This statement refers to the habitual tendencies of various karmas.

Coexisting with ignorance (*avidyā*), it is conventionally designated as "ignorance. It arises together with the formations (*saṃskāra*) as their concurrent activity; in reality, it is the seeds of the formations that act as the cause for the arising of the formations, rather than ignorance itself giving rise to them. Question:
Why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that when the various members [of dependent origination] are viewed in relation to one another, none possess the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)?

Answer: That [text] considers the active manifestation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to the active manifestation of grasping (*upādāna*) as being a relationship between similar categories; it does not refer to that [other type of causality].

Regarding their own seeds: they possess only the sense of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and lack the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). When considering the seed of karma in relation to the manifest karma of existence, the seed of karma is not consciousness;

it possesses only the sense of predominance and lacks the sense of being a causal condition. Next, the two conditions whose determinacy is indefinite—ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*)—are explained.

Regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), as well as birth (*jāti*) and death (*maraṇa*), there are two types of conditions when they are viewed in relation to one another. If the two are identical, then the former ceases and the latter is induced;

this constitutes the condition of immediate contiguity (*samanantara-pratyaya*). If the two are distinct, then [the former] serves as the object of concern and support; this constitutes the condition of the object (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

If one looks toward birth from the perspective of craving, that which possesses an object consists of the five categories beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), because all of them are capable of cognition; thus, they take the experience of the objective sphere as their object.

Yet when looking back toward "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), it likewise possesses an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but lacks both the equal-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the other conditions.

When the remaining members are viewed in relation to one another, none possess these two conditions. Herein, [the sequence] below concludes; above, the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is established based solely on four meanings.
Otherwise, it would be disjointed, out of order, disordered, or merely a figurative designation.

Regarding how the three—delusion (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*)—encompass the twelve [links]: (up to) "therefore, these can cause the continuity of birth and death. Next, we discuss the three paths.

Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are of the nature of affliction; they are subsumed solely under delusion. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are subsumed under karma.
Seven [links] are subsumed under suffering. Question: The two links of volitional formations and existence belong to karma, while seven all belong to suffering. Why is this so?

It is said that this is subsumed under one portion. In response: some say that the existence-constituent (*bhava-aṅga*) is entirely subsumed under karma; this is based on the teaching that existence arises from karma.

Others say that the consciousness-constituent (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is entirely subsumed under karma and is not subsumed under suffering (*duḥkha*). This is because they regard the seeds of karma as the consciousness-constituent.

Question: Since all twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) should be suffering (*duḥkha*), why are only the seven links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), which are summoned by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma (*karman*), specifically designated as suffering?

Answer: It is because those [seven links] are subsumed exclusively under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and do not extend to the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). This is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to give rise to a mind of revulsion.
[The phrase] "by means of afflictions" and so forth summarizes [the preceding discussion].

Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from internal causes and conditions; because it does not constitute a body resulting from karmic retribution (*vipāka-kāya*), it does not contradict reason.

Next, we shall discuss the two types of death. Since karma is the primary agent of production, it is called the "proximate cause" (*sākṣāt-hetu*); since afflictions (*kleśa*) assist in the production, they are termed "predominant conditions" (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding what is called "segmented birth and death" (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*), this refers to contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karma acting as the proximate cause of production. It initiates—
The moisture of the afflictions acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for their arising. By virtue of this causal condition, it is capable of inducing that which is to be induced:

the maturation (*vipāka*) within the three realms. Regarding the body and life below, [the text] explains the term "segmented" (*paricchinna*). "Segment" (*pari*) refers to temporal divisions; "portion" (*cchinna*) refers to spatial portions.

Because both possess certainty. Regarding the inconceivable transformation: non-outflow (anāsrava) discriminative karma acts as the direct generative cause, while the cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa) acts as the auxiliary generative dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Due to these causes and conditions, it is that which brings about [the result]; the superior maturation (*vipāka*) is that which is brought about.
The passage beginning with "due to compassion" explains the name "transformation. Because of the power of compassion and vows, there is no fixed [limit].
Limitation. Therefore, the body and life-force it manifests are likewise without fixed limits. "Untainted" (*anāsrava*) and below explain the name "inconceivable.
Because untainted meditative concentration and vows are inconceivable, the sublime functions obtained therefrom are also inconceivable.

It is also called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), because it is manifested according to the intentions and vows for the sake of delivering sentient beings. It is the "transformed body" (*nairmāṇika-kāya*), taking compassion and vows as its [basis].
The *dharmakāya* (Body of Essence) has meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and vows (*praṇidhāna*) as its essence.

The *manomayakāya* (Mind-made Body) has the afflictions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conceptualized intention and vow as its essence. Question: If the supporting body varies according to others, it may be described as short or long;
however, life is like the flame of a lamp, arising and ceasing moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*), and is not like the fixed duration of a single lifetime (*kalala-paryanta*).
Question: On what basis is it said that those [lifespans] have no fixed limit? Answer: In reality, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has no distinct boundaries;

rather, boundaries are conventionally designated in accordance with the body upon which it depends. Therefore, the following citation of proof shows that both the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformative) [forms of existence] possess all three bodies.

Just as with the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) acting as conditions and tainted wholesome or unwholesome karma acting as causes, after the death-existence (*maraṇa-bhava*), one takes birth in the three existences—the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), and the basic existence (*pūrvakāla-bhava*). Question: Among these three existences, which body creates karma?
Answer: It is said that the two existences of birth and death cannot initiate karma because they lack mental activity. As for the intermediate and basic [existences]...
There are two types of existence (*bhava*). That which can initiate karma is called the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).

This refers to the body of a sentient being within the five destinies that exists between the two forms of birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) and death-existence (*maraṇabhava*); therefore, it is named intermediate existence. It also has the five aggregates of maturation (*vipākapañcaskandha*) as its substance.
Because this karma draws it forth, the body within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) possesses the physical form and appearance of the "existence at birth" (*upapattibhava*) that is to come.
Just as the intermediate state of humans resembles humans, so too do the intermediate states of the five destinies. The body is the size of a child of five or six years;
although its dimensions are small, its sense faculties (*indriya*) are sharp and keen, and like the body of the existence at birth, it is capable of performing various karmic actions.
Toward one's parents, one gives rise to perverted perceptions and consequently produces feelings of attachment or aversion.

This intermediate state body (antarābhava) is visible only to those of its own kind and to those with the pure divine eye. Within this intermediate state, it subsists solely on fragrant odors. While dwelling in the intermediate state, [it remains there for a time].
Those whose nature is neither unwholesome nor evil, but neutral, will experience rebirth at the slowest rate in no more than forty-seven days;

within this period, there is no instance where the conditions for rebirth do not converge. As for those with extremely wholesome or extremely unwholesome intermediate states (*antarābhava*), it does not matter whether they are near or far.

In but a single kṣaṇa, one proceeds to take birth, giving rise to perverted perceptions; the mind inclines toward the objects of desire. This is precisely the gateway for the eighth consciousness to link with a new existence (*pratisandhi*).
If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belongs to the two modes of birth—womb or egg—one perceives the union of the parents and gives rise to perverted perceptions, whereupon one takes birth.
If the intermediate state belongs to the two modes of birth—moisture or transformation—one does not distinguish between proximity [to the place of birth] due to the power of prior karma.

[The intermediate being] is far away; yet, through attachment that accords with its disposition, it takes rebirth immediately at the place where it is to be perfumed. Question: It is known that those of the same class can see the *antarābhava* body with their eyes;
however, is it not yet known whether the eyes of the *antarābhava* can see the *pūrvakālabhava* (the body of the previous existence)?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Either one sees only a male, or one sees only a female. Thus gradually approaching that location, one eventually no longer sees the parents."

In other places, one sees only the sexual organs of a male or female. If the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is male, it conceives a craving for the mother and gives rise to a mind of desire;
if it is female, it conceives a craving for the father and gives rise to a mind of desire. Once these two kinds of craving have arisen, it unites with the object of its affection.
The discharged impurity flows into the womb, where it is claimed as its own, and thus [the new existence] begins.
Joy arises. Once this mind has arisen, the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) vanishes and one receives a birth-state body (*upapattibhava*). The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

"When that intermediate state body enters the mother’s womb, the mind gives rise to distortions and forms perverted perceptions, conceiving the notions of coldness, great wind and rain, and clouds and mist.
Having formed these notions, according to the excellence or inferiority of one's karma, ten further [perceptions] arise."
Conceiving various deluded thoughts—such as "I am entering a house" or "I am ascending a multi-storied pavilion"—and having formed these notions, they enter the mother's womb.

If one with little merit is in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and is destined to be born into a lowly, poor family, at the time of entering the womb, they hear various unpleasant, clamorous sounds. If, however, one possesses merit...

There are those who are to be born into wealthy and noble families; at that time, they naturally hear exquisite and pleasing sounds, and even as for the objects of smell, taste, and touch, there are likewise gradations.
Question: What is the color of this intermediate state body (*antarābhava*)? Answer:
The intermediate state body of one who has committed evil deeds is like the luster of a black sheep or like a dark, cloudy night; [the body] of one who has performed wholesome deeds...
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of humans is like the radiance of white silk, or like a clear night.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: the intermediate state of hell-beings is like a charred log; that of animals (*tiryagyoni*) is like smoke; that of hungry ghosts (*preta*) is like water;
and that of humans and devas is like white silk. This occurs when ignorance, the latencies (*vāsanā*), the ground, and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) serve as conditions. No...
With outflow-free karma as the cause, one invokes and attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) that experiences the bliss of samādhi, which is the fruit of an Arhat;

the mind-made body that realizes the intrinsic nature of dharmas, which is the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; and the innate, effortless mind-made body attained by Bodhisattvas from the ninth stage upward.
These three bodies all transform the outflowing, originally existing [retribution] through the power of outflow-free concentration, just as...
It is like a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "Swift as one's will, like an illusion, a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror;
neither created nor produced, yet possessing all various forms and limbs, fully adorned, just like a magical transformation.

Question: The treatises state that for a Śrāvaka who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), future existence is forever exhausted and thus they have no physical body. How, then, can they [possess such a form] for long?
At that time, having accumulated merit and cultivated virtue, one realizes and attains Bodhi. Answer:

Although there is no further existence (punarbhava), one relies upon the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to benefit sentient beings and practice the Way until one’s meritorious conduct is perfected and one realizes unsurpassed enlightenment; this is not a body born of karmic retribution (vipākakāya).
If the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) assist untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) in leading one out of the triple world, this is stated according to their auxiliary cause.

Question: If the cognitive obstructions act as conditions that assist untainted karma as its cause to bring about subtle retribution in the form of birth and death, then those of the two vehicles with fixed natures (*niyata-gotra*) would always experience birth and death and could never enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

[The interlocutor] asks: "How is it? [The respondent] answers: "Just as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are constrained by afflictions (*kleśa*), so too those who seek tranquility have minds that incline toward tranquility;
being constrained by *nirvāṇa*, they flow toward the signless (*animitta*) and do not give rise to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

This is no different from ordinary beings having afflictions and being constrained by them such that they do not proceed toward *nirvāṇa*. [The interlocutor] asks: "How does one cultivate the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*)?"
If one asks: "How can a noble being who seeks to extinguish the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*) actually bring about the suffering of birth and death? Answer:

Who says that the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) produced by untainted meditative concentration and vows (*anāsrava-samādhi-praṇidhāna*) actually brings about suffering? Question: If that is not the case, then how is it so? Answer:
It means that once the untainted meditative concentration and vows of the fourth dhyāna have assisted the form and formless realms, they bring about a different [result].
When all contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma has matured, it causes the subtle resultant fruits (*vipākaphala*) obtained thereby to manifest over a long period of time.
Entering the marketplace with hands extended, one receives beings and benefits sentient life, enabling uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) qualities to increase and become ever more excellent.

It is conventionally described as being "able to induce" [results], yet uncontaminated karma does not actually induce suffering. In this way, uncontaminated meditative vows support contaminated karma to induce its results.

At that time, it is not only [the object] itself that can induce [retribution]; rather, it is through the assistance of the conditions provided by what is known as the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that those karmas are then able to induce the subtle, distinct, and superior fruit of maturation (*vipāka*).
Nevertheless, the cognitive obstruction does not obstruct liberation, nor can it induce suffering.

Why is this? Because they lack the capacity to initiate karma (*karmābhinirvṛtti*) or to moisten rebirth (*janmopapatti*); they differ from the afflictions (*kleśa*), which are capable of initiating and moistening. Question: Since birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are of a nature of oppression, they ought to be permanently severed. Why, then, would one employ these [afflictions] to provide the conditions for experiencing the suffering of birth and death? Answer: It is for the sake of accomplishing the two benefits (*dvayārtha*) that one must provide such conditions. That is to say, there is a class of beings who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). If they were to sever the afflictions entirely, they would immediately enter parinirvāṇa; consequently, they would be unable to benefit sentient beings. Therefore, by retaining the afflictions, they can remain in the world for a long time to bring about the welfare of others. Furthermore, because they have already attained mastery over the afflictions, they do not experience the suffering of birth and death as ordinary beings do. Thus, they retain them for the purpose of benefiting others. This is called "retaining the afflictions" (*kleśānupālambha*). It is like a person who, having mastered poison, can consume it without being harmed. It is also like a physician who, having mastered a disease, can contract it without suffering its effects. The two vehicles of fixed nature, as well as the great Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward who have attained mastery over the mind and mastery over form, have already eternally severed and eternally suppressed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Consequently, they cannot again undergo a body of fragmented suffering (*bheda-śarīra*);

fearing that it would interrupt their long-term cultivation of the Bodhisattva practices, they therefore rely upon the power of aspiration and untainted superior meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
It assists the cause of the transformation body (*pariṇāmi-kāya*), causing it to continue yielding its fruit for a long duration without interruption.

Just as the power of medicine prolongs a person's lifespan, so too do meditative concentration and vows repeatedly provide support, increasing in excellence until one finally achieves perfect enlightenment. Question:
The uncontaminated concentration and vows are sufficient to provide the causal impetus for rebirth; what need is there for the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) to act as auxiliary conditions? Answer:
This refers to those of indeterminate lineage among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as great Bodhisattvas.

Since they have not yet fully realized the Dharma of signlessness, great compassion, and the single flavor of equality, if they were not to grasp at the existence of a real bodhi to be realized or real sentient beings to be delivered, how [could they continue their practice]?

By virtue of having generated intense great compassion and intense great vows, and because of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which involve grasping at there being something to be sought or delivered, one is then able to initiate uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karmic activity; thus, it is necessary to rely upon the cognitive objects as auxiliary conditions.
Furthermore, since the cognitive obscurations obstruct Great Enlightenment and are truly difficult to sever abruptly, [one practices] with the desire to permanently eliminate them.

Because it knows the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it takes those very objects of knowledge as its conditions and remains in this body for a long time; this is what is meant by "borrowing them to sever them.
Furthermore, the cognitive obstruction is the cause of all tainted (*sāsrava*) maturation (*vipāka*).

Due to the existence of this obstruction, various karmic actions fail to become untainted (*anāsrava*). If this supporting obstruction were absent, then that which depends upon it—the tainted—would certainly [cease].

There is none. Because that which depends cannot exist apart from its basis, the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) is called the "condition" because it provides great auxiliary power that enables this body to continue in succession for a long duration.
Question: Is this retained body of the nature of *paricchinna* (segmented death) or *pariṇāmika* (transformation)?
Answer: If one is in the four dhyānas or the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), using impure meditative concentration and vows to sustain the present...

The physical body caused by [karmic] factors and its resulting maturation (*vipāka*) are comprised within the *paricchinna-śarīra* (the fragmented body); this is the object known by those of the two vehicles with fixed natures (*niyata-gotra*).

If one supports the physical body caused by such factors and its resulting maturation through the power of aspiration and untainted superior meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), it is comprised within the *pariṇāma-kāya* (the transformation body);
this is the object known by Great Arhats who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] and by autonomous Bodhisattvas, but not by those [of the two vehicles].
The sphere of objects known by those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings is difficult to fathom due to its wondrous function and inconceivability.

From this, one should know that the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*) is by nature contaminated (*sāsrava*), as it is subsumed under the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), being precisely what is induced by contaminated karma.
That which is induced through the support of uncontaminated meditative concentration and vows is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Nevertheless, the holy teachings speak of "transformation..."

The transformation of the body (*kāyaparāvṛtti*) is that which is induced by uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*); this is stated in terms of the contributing conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) and the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), not in terms of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding what is said in the verse concerning "the latencies of various karmas" (*karma-vāsanā*)—up to [the point where it concludes]—"by this one should know that there is only internal consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*)."
Next, the meaning of the verse is set forth. "The seeds of the two types of karma" refers to the seeds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.

Question: In the case of *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death), one abandons this life to take up another; thus it can be said that the former is exhausted and the latter arises. However, since *pariṇāma-cyuti-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth and death) lacks the principle of abandoning this life to proceed to another, how can it be said that the former is exhausted and the latter arises?
Answer: Although transformative birth and death lacks [the process of] abandoning this life and proceeding to another, [it is nonetheless so].

Although there is the exhaustion of one segment and the arising of another distinct segment, through the power of repeated assistance from untainted meditative concentration and vows, that body and life-span are maintained in continuity, becoming progressively more excellent and undergoing successive transformations; thus, there is also the sense that what was previously exhausted arises again.
Question: Since the continuity of birth and death also occurs through active manifestation (*samudācāra*), why does the verse state only this?

Regarding "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā): The answer is that although the continuity of birth and death also depends upon active manifestations (*samudācāra*), the verse specifically mentions habitual tendencies and does not mention active manifestations because seeds are necessarily present while active manifestations are not. Therefore, the verse speaks specifically of them.

Alternatively, it is to demonstrate that both the true and the distinct causes and effects do not depart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); thus, it mentions only the seeds and not the active manifestations.
Question: Since the eighth consciousness in its active state (*pravṛtti*) can also serve as a cause, why do you speak exclusively of seeds? Answer:

Although the eighth consciousness in its active state is indeed a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it necessarily depends upon the perfuming of seeds before it can subsequently yield a fruit; therefore, it is not mentioned [as the primary cause].

Furthermore, because the active states of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are subject to interruption, they are not ripening causes and thus are also not mentioned. It is for this reason that [only seeds are specified].
In the verse, it is stated only that seeds serve as the cause for manifest fruits; thus, there is the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It does not mention the eighth manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti*), nor does it mention the manifest states of the [other] seven.

Because of the three bodies (*kāya*) across the prior, middle, and subsequent limits, the cycle of birth and death proceeds without depending on external conditions, but rather through internal consciousness. By this analogy, one should understand the characteristics of pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma*).

The same applies to the subsequent [stages]. That is to say, within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there have existed from beginningless time, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*).

Through the power of being newly perfumed (*vāsita*) by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and other factors, these seeds gradually increase and become preeminent. This continues until the moment of Buddhahood, when there is a single, uniform maturation (*vipāka*):
one abandons the seeds of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and attains the pure white consciousness (*śuklavidyā*), which sustains all seeds of merit (*guṇa*). By means of this...

By the power of the original vow, throughout the limits of the future, various wondrous functions arise from within pure consciousness, continuing without end and benefiting others without exhaustion.

Based on the principles of defilement and purity explained above, one should know that the continuity of all phenomena consists solely of internal consciousness and lacks external conditions; therefore, know that consciousness is the source of good and evil, and the mind is...
This is the root of suffering and pleasure. Alas! How can one pursue the flow and follow the branches, losing the root and becoming confused about the source?
One may refine their practice for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* in vain, yet remain far removed from the Truth; one may accumulate merit through eternal eons, yet still be distant from the Way.

For this reason, when Sages who have attained the fruit encounter such [circumstances], they willingly declare themselves to be beyond their lot; and when Great Beings who have emerged from the provisional encounter this, they likewise [refuse to claim it].

If even those who have attained realization find it so, how much more so for deceitful and confused teachers, the heretics of Primordial Darkness (*ādikāla*), the haughty officials of the Lacquer Garden (Zhuangzi), and the bewildered followers of vagueness—how could they hope to believe and accept it?
Thus we know that the Mirror of the Source is difficult to comprehend; those who awaken to it are rare and extraordinary.
Not only do they attain the fundamental principle wherever they may be, but they are also able to deeply penetrate the nature of cause and effect.
Therefore, all sentient beings create the causes of good and evil solely through their own minds, thereby inviting the fruits of suffering and joy.

Whether in the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), those who have cultivated virtuous causes perceive pure, radiant light, while those who have committed unwholesome causes behold dark, gloomy forms. Or, when dwelling within the womb...
On the day of entering the womb, those who have accumulated white karma ascend to the heights of palatial towers, while those who have created black karma are cast into the midst of weeds and thorns.
Upon being born into the human world, their primary and secondary bodies likewise distinguish themselves as superior or inferior.

Those with merit possess the features of a prominent chin and a dragon-like countenance, enjoying the splendor of magnificent halls and golden pavilions; whereas those with meager virtue are exposed to the five elements.

Though their physical forms may be minute and humble—dwelling in the dilapidation of jar-windows and mat-doors—it can be said that as the wind is harmonious, the resonance follows; as the form is straight, the shadow is upright.

Cause and effect are simultaneous; when conditions meet, they do not fail. Therefore it is said: "The phenomena of the three realms, from the highest to the lowest, are created solely by this one mind."
If there is only consciousness, for what reason did the World-Honored One [state that objects] are unapprehendable?

From this point downward, the two attachments to self and dharmas are collectively subsumed as the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), and the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) constitute the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

The self-verifying-of-self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) constitutes the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). By thus clarifying the three natures and the three absences of nature, the preceding section is concluded.

This serves as the introductory basis for what follows. First, the question is posed; next, the verse is cited as the answer. Regarding the section beginning with "The treatise says," there is first an explanation:
the first verse concerns that which "universally conceptualizes. This means it engages in various deliberations, leaving nothing uncalculated.

"Many categories" refers to the fact that their types differ and their names are not uniform. This is precisely the nature of the universal conceptualizer (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). By means of this, that...

That false and pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) conceptualizes the various aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as the self-nature (*svabhāva*) and specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*) of both phenomena (*dharma*) and the self (*ātman*).
Regarding "self-nature," it refers to the general grasping of the self and phenomena as having a real intrinsic nature.

Regarding "distinctions," it refers to the specific grasping of the self and phenomena as being existent or non-existent, permanent or impermanent, and so forth, as having a truly existing essence. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Pervasive..."
How many kinds of imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are there? Answer: Briefly, there are five kinds:
first, the imagined nature of objects; second, the imagined nature of names; third, the imagined nature of defilement; fourth, the imagined nature of purity;
and fifth, the imagined nature that is neither defiled nor pure. What is the imagined nature of objects? It is as follows:

There are four kinds: first, the pervasive conceptualization of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which refers to the pervasive conceptualization that "this thing has the intrinsic nature of form," up to "this thing has the intrinsic nature of consciousness," or "this thing has the intrinsic nature of the eye," up to "this thing has the intrinsic nature of mental objects (*dharma*)," and so forth.
Second, the pervasive conceptualization of differentiated characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), which refers to the pervasive conceptualization that "this form is agreeable" or "disagreeable."
This form is visible or invisible; this form is resistant or non-resistant; this form is with outflows or without outflows;
this form is conditioned or unconditioned. As it is with form, so it should be understood for the remaining aggregates as well.

Third is the characteristic of the object grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). This refers to the pervasive conceptualization that "this form is what is grasped by the eye," or "this is what is grasped by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, it is the pervasive conceptualization that "feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are what is grasped by the mind of the desire realm."

This is that which is apprehended by the mind of the form and formless realms; this is that which is apprehended by the unconditioned mind. These are the four types of conceptualization that grasp at signs:
namely, the conceptualization that "this is form" and the grasping at form; and the grasping at sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
Furthermore, one conceptually constructs this feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness as "the grasper of form," and "the grasper of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena.
What is meant by the conceptual construction of names as intrinsic nature? It is of two kinds:
first, the undifferentiated, which refers to all the names applied to all phenomena; second, the differentiated, which refers to the conceptual construction that "this name is for form."
Up to this point, these are called "consciousness. Within such immeasurable varieties of phenomena, each has its own distinct name.

What is the nature of the conceptualization of affliction (*parikalpita-saṃkleśa-svabhāva*)? It refers to the conceptualization of this form as being possessed of greed, possessed of hatred, and possessed of delusion.
They are unable to distance themselves from the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion. Furthermore, they do not associate with all wholesome dharmas such as faith and the like.
Moreover, they conceptually construct that this feeling, this perception, this formation, and this consciousness possess greed, hatred, and delusion;
thus, they cannot distance themselves from the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor do they associate with all wholesome dharmas such as faith and the like. Why is this?
What is the nature of purity regarding the thoroughly imagined? It is that which is the opposite of the aforementioned [nature of defilement].
How should one know that it is not the nature of defilement and purity? It is because one thoroughly imagines this form as the grasped and this as the grasper;
one thoroughly imagines these feelings, perceptions, and so forth as the grasped and the grasper; and furthermore, because one thoroughly imagines everything within all neutral phenomena.
Regarding the indeterminate dharmas, furthermore, one should know that there are five kinds of parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature): first, the imagined nature of objects based on names;

that is, to imagine that "this is form" and that it possesses the real nature of form, or to imagine that "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness" and that they possess the real nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—just as when one has not yet learned the name of an ox, upon hearing the word "ox," [one imagines its existence].
