[First,] the imputation of names: one immediately speculates, "By what principle is this called 'ox' and so forth? Second, the imputation of the intrinsic nature of names based on objects:

that is, one universally imputes that this object is "form" (*rūpa*) or not "form," or that this object is "feeling" (*vedanā*), "perception" (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, or not "feeling," "perception," and so forth.
This is like someone who, not yet knowing the name for an ox, fails to recognize its name upon seeing the ox.

Even if one speculates as to what the name of this thing might be—whether it be "a ghost," "a beast," and so forth—this is the pervasive conceptualization of the self-nature of names based on the three supports.
That is to say, failing to understand the objective reality of form, one conceptually discriminates the name "form" and gives rise to pervasive conceptualization;

failing to understand the objective realities of sensation, perception, and so forth, one conceptually discriminates the names "sensation," "perception," and so forth, and gives rise to pervasive conceptualization. Fourth is the pervasive conceptualization of the self-nature of objects based on their referents.

Nature refers to the failure to understand the names of form; because one fails to understand these names, one engages in conceptualization regarding the entity of form and gives rise to pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*).

One fails to understand the names of sensation, perception, and so forth; because one fails to understand these names, one engages in conceptualization regarding the entities of sensation, perception, and so forth, and gives rise to pervasive imagination.
The fifth [point] concerns the two types of pervasive conceptualization regarding the two natures:

namely, the pervasive conceptualization that "this thing has the nature of form" and thus is designated as "form," and that "this thing has the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness" and is designated as "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is pervasive conceptualization.
In terms of its essence, it does not transcend the two attachments to self and phenomena; in terms of its function, it does not transcend the two types of name and referent.
This falsely grasped nature and its specific characteristics are collectively termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Such a nature is entirely non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit, because when examined one by one through the preceding reasoning and scripture, it cannot be found. This...
Regarding "universal conceptualization" (*parikalpa*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1. There is that which is universal but not conceptualizing.

This refers to the sixth *manovijñāna* acting independently (*mukhya-manovijñāna*), which universally takes all things as its object but does not engage in conceptual clinging. Furthermore, it includes all untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and tainted-but-virtuous (*sāsrava-kuśala*) consciousnesses, which are capable of universal and extensive cognition yet lack conceptual clinging.
Untainted minds refer specifically to those of Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) who, by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), [cognize all objects].
Wisdom (*prajñā*) realizes that all phenomena are empty; although there is no phenomenon that it does not pervade, it is free from conceptual clinging.

As for the contaminated wholesome consciousness (*sāsrava-kuśala-vijñāna*), which refers here to the bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), although they employ a contaminated mind to contemplate non-self and observe all phenomena as being entirely devoid of self, this too is pervasive yet free from clinging.
Second, there is that which involves clinging but is not pervasive, such as the seventh [manas] consciousness when it is contaminated.

Taking the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object, it gives rise to the two types of grasping: the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

When one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) from the sixth consciousness, this seventh consciousness still takes the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as its object and gives rise to the grasping at phenomena; therefore, it is both pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and grasping (*parāmarśa*).
This refers to the sixth defiled mind of sentient beings; because it engages in pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) within the causal state, it is [the first type].

Fourth, that which is neither pervasive nor conceptualizing refers to the five contaminated sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*; because each perceives only its own specific object, they are not pervasive.

Because they possess recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*) but lack conceptualizing conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), they are not conceptualizing. Alternatively, the first [line] is explained again from a lower perspective to clarify the meaning of the verse.
Regarding the first [point], what is the nature of the universal imputer (*parikalpa*)? ... [omitted] ... because the modes of universal imagination differ, it is said to be "this or that.
This is a detailed explanation of the universal imputer. Question: Regarding the first [point], what is the nature of the universal imputer? Sthiramati says:
The eight mind-kings and the fifty-one mental factors, insofar as they are subsumed under the tainted (*sāsrava*), are all *parikalpita* (imagined).
This is because these kings and their attendants are all of the nature of false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) and all manifest with the appearance of the two-fold grasping (*grāhya-grāhaka*).
The treatise states that the eighth [consciousness] also takes the seeds of the *parikalpita* as its object. Thus one master explains.
Zhengyi says: The sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which grasp at a self and grasp at phenomena, are of the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

This is because both of these consciousnesses possess discursive calculation (*vikalpa*) and possess discernment (*pravicaya*). Since the fifth and eighth consciousnesses lack both discursive calculation and discernment, they are not pervasive conceptualization.
Previously, it was established that all mental factors (*caitta*) are exclusively pervasive conceptualization; these two types of grasping are necessarily associated with ignorance (*avidyā*).
They are associated [with ignorance]. Because, due to the delusion of ignorance and folly, one becomes confused regarding the principle of selflessness and gives rise to the two types of grasping.
If all mental factors—whether wholesome or defiled—were universally imagined (*parikalpita*), then the defiled nature of ignorance would have to be associated with a wholesome nature.
However, ignorance belongs to the nature of delusion (*moha*), whereas wholesome states are not deluded; how, then, could they be associated?
Because wholesome mental factors (*caitta*) are free from grasping (*sgrāha*), they are all able to lead to the arising of the wisdom of the two emptinesses (*śūnyatājñāna*).

If ignorance were associated with wholesome states and the like, it would be a grasping ignorance, which would likewise have to be able to lead to the wisdom of emptiness; yet, we do not observe grasping leading [to such wisdom].

Regarding the knower of emptiness: next, the eighth [consciousness] is refuted as being the *parikalpita* (the imagined nature). This means that whatever possesses grasping must necessarily be a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*).

Since there has never been a case where something possessing grasping is not a perfuming agent, and since the eighth consciousness is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and is not a perfuming agent, it is therefore not the *parikalpita*.
Question: If this is so, why does the Sūtra state that the eight consciousnesses, along with all their mental factors (*caitta*), are all false?

[Question: [What is] "discrimination" (vikalpa)? [Answer: All mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) subsumed within the state of being with outflows (sāsrava) are unable to realize the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva);

therefore, they are collectively termed "false discrimination" (abhūta-parikalpa). This does not refer to the imagined nature (parikalpita). [Question: Since it is not the imagined nature, why is it so called?
Why, then, is it said that the characteristics of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) appear? Answer:

Although all mental factors (*caitasika*) manifest as resembling these two types of grasping, there are those that are conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) and those that are not; it is not meant that everything is subsumed under conceptual construction.
If one were to claim that everything is conceptual construction, then even the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) would be conceptual construction. If the untainted mind...

If that which is the parikalpita (the imagined) were such that the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) also possessed conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and also manifested appearances resembling the two types of grasping (*grāhya-grāhaka*), then it too would have to be subsumed under the parikalpita.
However, the sūtras state that the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) manifests bodies and manifests lands.
It is like a bright mirror manifesting various images; it never possesses any grasping, so how could it be called "imagined" (*parikalpita*)?
If one were to claim that the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) of the Tathāgata cannot take vast objects as its range, then it should not be called all-accomplishing wisdom.

Therefore, we know that the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and all wholesome states are able to take vast objects as their range, yet they are devoid of conceptual grasping.
Question: If the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) lacks the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), how can it take the seeds of false attachment as its object? Answer:

Although it is said that the storehouse consciousness can take the seeds of pervasive conceptualization as its objects, it is not said that these are exclusively "pervasively conceptually constructed" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because they lack the activity of discursive deliberation (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, what has been cited does not constitute valid proof. By this principle, one should know that...
The eighth [consciousness] is not of the nature of parikalpita (imagined). Furthermore, not all mental factors (*caitta*) are parikalpita;

rather, it is only those associated with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that grasp at a self and phenomena which are of the nature of parikalpita. Although there are two categories of consciousness, there are those that establish two, three, four, five, and so forth.
Regarding the establishment of two types: first, the name, and second, the object. Regarding the establishment of three: first, the discrimination (*vikalpa*).
1. The basis and object of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). 2. The two views and pride. 3. Greed, hatred, and delusion. 4. These refer to:
(a) specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), (b) distinctions (*viśeṣa*), (c) the apprehended (*grāhya*), and (d) the apprehender (*grāhaka*). 5. These refer to:

(a) imagining an object based on a name, (b) imagining a name based on an object, (c) imagining a name based on a name, (d) imagining an object based on an object, and (e) imagining both based on both. 6. These refer to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
[The first] is differentiation; [the second] is awakening; [the third] is latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); [the fourth] is application (*prayoga*);

and [the fifth] is names—these seven are subsumed within the aforementioned sixth category, "thorough conceptualization" (*parikalpa*), namely: conditioned, unconditioned, permanent, impermanent, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. The eighth consists of:
intrinsic nature, differentiation, retention, self, what belongs to the self, the pleasant, the unpleasant, and that which is contrary to both. The ninth is also the aforementioned...
The sixth is that which is subsumed under pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*). This refers to [the inquiry]: "What is this? How is this thing? What is this?

How is this thing?"—or whether it be the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), or the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The tenth consists of the first five of the aforementioned six types of pervasive conceptualization, and...

Within the five types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), there are again five kinds: namely, attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), union (*saṃyoga*), distinct seeds (*bījāntara*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Next, what is the nature of that which is pervasively conceptualized? [From here until] "the two apprehensions are called the thoroughly imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): [The text continues: ...the two apprehensions are called the thoroughly imagined nature. This refers to the apprehension of the self and the apprehension of phenomena. Among these, the apprehension of the self is further divided into four types: the apprehension of a self as a substance (*dravyātman*), the apprehension of a self as a person (*pudgalātman*), the apprehension of a self as a controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛtman*), and the apprehension of a self as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtman*). The apprehension of phenomena is likewise divided into four types: the apprehension of phenomena as substances, the apprehension of phenomena as characteristics, the apprehension of phenomena as causes, and the apprehension of phenomena as effects. These are collectively termed the thoroughly imagined nature. Why is this so? Because it is produced by the power of false conceptualization; because it is devoid of intrinsic nature; because it is not established by its own characteristics; because it is not perceived by the noble ones; and because it is the basis for all afflictions. For these reasons, it is called the thoroughly imagined nature. Furthermore, regarding the apprehension of the self, since the self does not exist, the apprehension of the self is necessarily non-existent. Since the apprehension of the self is non-existent, the apprehension of phenomena is also necessarily non-existent. Why? Because phenomena are merely designations based upon the self. Therefore, both apprehensions are called the thoroughly imagined nature. This concludes the section on the thoroughly imagined nature. What then is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)? It refers to the mind and mental factors that arise from conditions. Why is this so? Because they arise in dependence upon other conditions and do not arise independently; because they are the basis for the manifestation of the thoroughly imagined nature; because they are the basis for the attainment of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); and because they are the basis for both defilement and purification. For these reasons, it is called the dependent nature. What then is the perfected nature? It refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of the dependent nature, which is eternally free from the thoroughly imagined nature. Why is this so? Because it is unchanging; because it is the object of the noble wisdom; because it is the ultimate reality; because it is the basis for liberation; and because it is the supreme truth. For these reasons, it is called the perfected nature. This concludes the section on the three natures. What then is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? It means that within the dependent nature, the thoroughly imagined nature is non-existent. Why is this so? Because the dependent nature is empty of the thoroughly imagined nature; because the thoroughly imagined nature is empty of the dependent nature; because the perfected nature is empty of the duality of subject and object; and because the perfected nature is empty of the thoroughly imagined nature. For these reasons, it is called emptiness. This concludes the section on emptiness. What then is the meaning of the two truths (*satyadvaya*)? They are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The conventional truth refers to all worldly conventions, names, and designations. The ultimate truth refers to the perfected nature. Why is this so? Because the conventional truth is the gateway to the ultimate truth; because the ultimate truth is realized through the conventional truth; because the conventional truth is the basis for linguistic expression; and because the ultimate truth is the basis for the cessation of all conceptual proliferation. For these reasons, one speaks of the two truths. This concludes the section on the two truths. What then is the meaning of the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*)? They are the door of emptiness, the door of signlessness, and the door of wishlessness. The door of emptiness refers to the realization that the thoroughly imagined nature is non-existent. The door of signlessness refers to the realization that the dependent nature has no fixed signs. The door of wishlessness refers to the realization that the perfected nature is free from all desires. Why is this so? Because by realizing emptiness, one abandons the grasping at a self; because by realizing signlessness, one abandons the grasping at phenomena; and because by realizing wishlessness, one abandons all afflictions. For these reasons, one speaks of the three doors of liberation. This concludes the section on the three doors of liberation. What then is the meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)? They are the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena. The foundation of mindfulness of the body refers to observing the body as impure, impermanent, suffering, and non-self. The foundation of mindfulness of feelings refers to observing feelings as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. The foundation of mindfulness of the mind refers to observing the mind as impermanent, changing, and non-abiding. The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena refers to observing phenomena as arising and ceasing, conditioned, and dependently originated. Why is this so? Because by practicing these four foundations of mindfulness, one attains the correct wisdom; because they counteract the four perversions; because they lead to the path of liberation; and because they are the basis for the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas. For these reasons, one speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness. This concludes the section on the four foundations of mindfulness. What then is the meaning of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*)? They are the effort to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, the effort to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen, the effort to produce wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and the effort to maintain and increase wholesome states that have already arisen. Why is this so? Because by these four right efforts, one abandons all evil and unwholesome dharmas; because one cultivates all pure and wholesome dharmas; because one attains the power of diligence; and because one proceeds toward the goal of nirvana. For these reasons, one speaks of the four right efforts. This concludes the section on the four right efforts. What then is the meaning of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)? They are the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of vigor, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind, and the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation. Why is this so? Because by these four bases of psychic power, one attains mastery over the mind; because one attains the supernormal powers; because one is able to benefit sentient beings; and because one proceeds toward the fruit of arhatship. For these reasons, one speaks of the four bases of psychic power. This concludes the section on the four bases of psychic power. What then is the meaning of the five faculties (*indriya*)? They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Why is this so? Because by these five faculties, one enters the path of seeing; because they counteract the five hindrances; because they lead to the attainment of the fruits of the śramaṇa; and because they are the basis for the cultivation of the powers (*bala*). For these reasons, one speaks of the five faculties. This concludes the section on the five faculties. What then is the meaning of the five powers (*bala*)? They are the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. Why is this so? Because by these five powers, one is not overcome by the five hindrances; because they are firm and unshakable; because they lead to the attainment of the path of cultivation; and because they are the basis for the attainment of the fruits of the śramaṇa. For these reasons, one speaks of the five powers. This concludes the section on the five powers. What then is the meaning of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)? They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of discernment of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of vigor, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. Why is this so? Because by these seven factors of enlightenment, one realizes the true nature of all phenomena; because they counteract the seven perversions; because they lead to the attainment of the path of seeing; and because they are the basis for the cultivation of the noble eightfold path. For these reasons, one speaks of the seven factors of enlightenment. This concludes the section on the seven factors of enlightenment. What then is
Next, the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is explained, which consists of two phrases concerning the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). First, a question is posed;

next, the treatise is cited to show that this is the dependent nature because it arises in dependence upon various conditions. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "That which arises based on a basis and through conditions is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This is because the mind and its associates, which perform pervasive conceptualization, serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). As for the direct image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it necessarily depends [upon the dependent nature].

For this reason, it is asked: "Is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) not the object of perception for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)? The answer is: "The perfected nature is suchness (*tathatā*);
it is the object of perception for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). It is not the object of perception for false attachment, because they are not similar.

If one were to claim that the perfected nature is neither different nor non-different from that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), then if the imagined nature were to grasp the dependent nature, [it would likewise grasp] the perfected nature."

This is also the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Question: If that is so, then the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) should also be an object of the thoroughly imagined nature. Answer:
Although one clings to the dependent nature (*paratantra*) through thorough imagination, and simultaneously takes the perfected nature as an object, it is in reality not its object.

This is because suchness (*tathatā*), by its very nature, is conjoined only with the wisdom of suchness, and is not conjoined with false discrimination (*vikalpa*). Question: Regarding the thoroughly imagined...

What is the difference between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)? Master Sthiramati says: the two parts—the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*)—are the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).
The mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are the dependent nature, because he does not establish a third [part], namely self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).

That is to say, the two parts of aspect and vision transformed by the mind and mental factors exist in the realm of cognition but are non-existent in reality; thus, it is by means of the vision part...

The *parikalpita* (the subject that imaginatively constructs) takes the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect) as its object of construction (*parikalpya*). The substance of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which serve as the basis for both the *nimitta* and *darśana* aspects, truly arises in dependence upon conditions;
this is precisely the *paratantra*. Question: How is this known? Answer: It can be understood by citing the sūtras.
This interpretation is not correct.
There is another interpretation which holds that all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta) are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) within this context.
The master Dignāga stated: "All minds and mental factors are called the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*); by the power of the perfuming of various conditions..."

Within the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), the transformation into the two portions of the image (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) is also of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

To falsely grasp at four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) upon this dependent nature is called the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The following citation provides scriptural proof: "Because objects do not exist, there is only cognition."
"Only two" refers to the existence of the *nimitta* (sign) and the *darśana* (vision). "Only various kinds" refers to the arising of various types of signs.

Furthermore, the *lakṣaṇa* (sign), name, discrimination, correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), and the eleven consciousnesses are all explained in the treatise as being the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Regarding the statement "the eleven consciousnesses," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: first, the body-consciousness, which refers to the five realms such as the eye; second, the body... [text continues]
1. The consciousness of defilement refers to the afflicted consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*). 2. The consciousness of the three feelings refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*). 3.

The consciousness of what is to be experienced refers to the six external objects, such as form and so forth. 4. The consciousness of actual experience refers to the six consciousness-elements (*ṣadvijñānadhātu*). 5. The consciousness of continuity refers to the uninterrupted succession of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
6. The consciousness of number refers to the count from one up to an *asaṃkhyeya*. 7. The consciousness of location refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

9. The consciousness of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-vijñāna*), which refers to seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. 10. The consciousness of the distinction between self and others (*sva-para-viśeṣa-vijñāna*). 11.

The consciousness of birth and death in good and bad destinies (*sugati-durgati-saṃsāra-vijñāna*) and the consciousness of one’s own body (*ātma-bhāva-vijñāna*). From the consciousness of verbal expression down to the nine kinds of consciousness, they arise from seeds perfumed by names and expressions (*nāma-abhilāpa-vāsanā*).
The consciousness of the distinction between self and others arises from seeds perfumed by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi-vāsanā*). [The consciousness of] good and bad destinies...

The consciousness that proceeds toward birth and death arises from the seeds of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the member of existence (*bhava-aṅga*). By means of this nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), all seeds are fully subsumed.

If one does not take the two parts as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), but instead takes the two parts as the conceptually constructed nature, then the object of the untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) at the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) would have to be called the conceptually constructed nature.

In the state of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), if one were to allow that the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) can take the pure portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its object, then the pure portion of the dependent nature would not be an object of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

If that were the case, then the noble wisdom that takes it as an object would likewise not be subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), but would instead have to be subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).
Furthermore, in the untainted state (*anāsrava-avasthā*), it cannot be maintained that both portions [the impure and the pure] are pervasive conceptualization.

According to the [position of] the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), even in the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*), the two parts—the image (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*)—are not admitted to be the imagined nature.

If these two parts were the imagined nature, they would consequently fail to be objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Thus, he sets forth a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute this: "The two parts, the image and the seeing, are the subject (*dharmin*).
They are not objective conditions, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are of the nature of the imagined, their essence does not exist."

It is like the horns of a rabbit and so forth. Furthermore, if the two parts [of consciousness] were themselves the parikalpita (the imagined), then those two parts would not be able to perfume and form seeds, because only dharmas that possess substantial reality can perfume seeds.

If there were no seeds for the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) perfuming into the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), then when subsequent consciousnesses arise, they would lack these two parts. Moreover, all seeds are the image-part of the eighth consciousness.
Since these are comprised [within the dependent nature], are they not entities that can serve as direct productive causes?
If they were non-entities, being merely imagined (parikalpita), then like a rabbit’s horn, how could they possibly function as seeds?

If you insist that the two parts—appearance (nimitta) and seeing (darśana)—produced by various conditions are themselves the imagined nature and not the dependent nature, then those two parts you have described...
Its essence is also not *paratantra* (dependent), because there is no distinction between its aspects (*nimitta*), seeing (*darśana*), and self-realization (*svasaṃvitti*).

From this point downward, it is concluded that [the dependent nature] is *paratantra* and not *parikalpita* (imagined). Question: Since it is *paratantra* and not *parikalpita*, why does the verse state that it is "produced by conditions through discrimination"?
Answer: It should be understood that this refers only to the defiled portion (*kliṣṭa-bhāga*) and does not refer to the pure portion (*viśuddha-bhāga*). This is because...
The other-dependent nature belonging to the pure portion is subsumed within the perfected nature.

Alternatively, some passages state that all defiled and pure minds and mental factors are termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), because all defiled and pure minds and mental factors are capable of taking all objects as their cognitive focus.
This concludes the demonstration below.
Regarding the "perfect accomplishment manifested by the two emptinesses" (up to): thus, the functions of the original and subsequent wisdoms are without distinction.

Next, the perfect nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is explained within those four propositions. Under the heading "the two emptinesses," the name is first explained: "Perfect" (*pari*) means it encompasses the three realms;
"Accomplishment" (*niṣpanna*) means it brings all things to completion; "Real Nature" (*svabhāva*) means its essence is not false or deceptive.
Therefore, from "to manifest this" below, the meaning is explained: it is "complete" because it is exclusively pervasive; it is "accomplished" because it is exclusively eternal;
and it is called "real" because it is exclusively non-deceptive. From "distinguishing from its own" below, there is a detailed analysis:

"specific characteristics" (svalakṣaṇa) refer to the fact that phenomena such as form each have their own essence, such as form having resistance as its specific characteristic. "Common characteristics" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) refer to what is shared among the phenomena of the five aggregates.
Because it is characterized by impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, this [nature] is the dependent (*paratantra*).
"Space" refers to one of the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. "Self" refers to the two types of self grasped through the imagined (*parikalpita*).

When it is said that this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) excludes both the dependent and the imagined, it is equal to the three unconditioned phenomena; although it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is untainted (*anāsrava*).

It receives this name; however, what is explained here in the verse is the true nature (*tathatā*) manifested by the two kinds of emptiness, not the untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).
Untainted conditioned phenomena are precisely the fruits of nirvāṇa and bodhi. This is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Upon that *paratantra-svabhāva*, it is eternally devoid of the aforementioned *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
Because it is the true nature (*tathatā*) revealed by these two kinds of emptiness, the verse states: "The *pariniṣpanna* is, in relation to that, eternally devoid of the former nature.
The verse says "in relation to that" (*tatra*), meaning that the *pariniṣpanna* is neither identical with nor separate from that *paratantra*.
The verse states "always free from," which means that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is free from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The verse states "the former," which means it is merely empty of the imagined nature, but not empty of the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The verse states "nature" (*svabhāva*), which indicates that the two kinds of emptiness are not themselves the perfected nature;
rather, it is the suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by those two kinds of emptiness that is called the perfected nature. By means of suchness...
Because its nature is devoid of parikalpita (imagined construction), it is free from existence. Because it belongs to true suchness (*tathatā*), it is free from non-existence.
For the reasons stated above, the verse says that this [perfected nature] and the *paratantra* (dependent nature) are neither different nor not different.

If one were to say they are different, then true suchness would not be the actual nature of that *paratantra*; for the *paratantra* must necessarily have the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) as its essence. If one were to say...
If they were not different, then this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) would have to be impermanent, because the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is impermanent.
Furthermore, that dependent nature is a conventional, impure object, which is the focal object of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); yet this is the perfected nature.
This is the pure realm of *tathatā* (suchness) and is the object of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

If it were not distinct [from the object of subsequent wisdom] now, then fundamental wisdom would be taking an impure realm as its object, while subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) would likewise take the pure realm of *tathatā* as its object.

In such a case, there would be no difference between the functions of these two wisdoms—fundamental and subsequent—and one could not say that subsequent wisdom takes the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) as its object while fundamental wisdom takes *tathatā* as its object.
"How are the two natures neither different nor identical? (Up to: Therefore, these three are not separate from the mind and so forth.
This explains the latter two lines of the verse. Question: What are the two natures that are neither one nor different? Answer:

For example, the universal characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) such as impermanence, suffering, and emptiness are neither [identical to nor different from] the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of formations (*saṃskāra*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth.

Whether they are different or not different: if impermanence and so forth were different from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and other such dharmas, then those conditioned phenomena and others would be permanent, blissful, self, and pure, rather than being impermanent and so forth.
If they were not different, then this impermanence and so forth would be identical to the conditioned phenomena;

consequently, it would follow that they could not be the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena and the like. By means of this single analogy, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is sufficiently elucidated.

The dependent nature is neither identical to nor different from [the perfected nature]; this is the logical principle for both phenomena (*dharma*) and their true nature (*dharmatā*), because they are neither the same nor separate, and because the ultimate and the conventional necessarily exist in mutual dependence.

Regarding the verse’s statement, "one does not see that [other] without seeing this," it means that there has never been anyone who could perceive that dependent nature without having realized this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); such a thing has never occurred.
Without realizing that the nature of the imagined (*parikalpita*) is empty, one fails to know as it truly is that the dependent (*paratantra*) exists as an illusion. Why is this?

Because the two natures—the imagined and the dependent—arise from one another and both lack intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*). Names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) are established because of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*);

causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are established because of names and characteristics. If false conceptualization does not arise, how could names and characteristics exist? [Names and characteristics...]
There is no arising; causes and conditions do not originate. Thus one knows that all phenomena do not transcend names and marks. Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:

"For example, in the practice of cultivation, various things arise within a single [reality]; yet within that, there is no multiplicity. The characteristics of false conceptualization are just like this."

The commentary states: "For example, when those of the Two Vehicles practice various contemplative exercises, if they perform the visualization of blue, heaven, earth, and the myriad things all appear blue.
This is seeing blue where there is no blue; this breaks through the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). It further states:
"For example, as various colors appear due to diverse visual impairments, though the impairment has neither color nor non-color, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)..."
Jueyan’s commentary explains: It is just as when a person with an eye ailment has a film over their eyes;

they may see floating flowers, hanging hair, or flying flies. These words indicate that the differences in what is seen by the obscured eye do not mean that the hanging hair, flying flies, and so forth actually exist.
This refutes the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). Thus, this is the root of deluded conceptualization.

Emptiness is the absence of intrinsic nature in dependent origination; this is precisely the perfectly established ultimate reality. However, as long as one has not realized that the thoroughly imagined nature is fundamentally empty, one will not understand that dependently arisen phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Therefore, only after attaining non-conceptual wisdom and realizing *tathatā* (suchness) does one subsequently give rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Once subsequently attained wisdom has arisen, one is finally able to fully comprehend dependent phenomena as being like illusions and so forth. Thus, it is necessarily...
Only after realizing the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) can one subsequently perceive the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Question:

Since beginningless time, the mind and mental factors have been able to take the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) as their objects of cognition. Why must one necessarily realize *tathatā* (suchness) before being able to fully comprehend them? Answer:

Although from beginningless time the mind and mental factors have been able to take the two divisions—the object-aspect and the seeing-aspect—transformed by their own consciousness as their objects, nevertheless, those [divisions] are pervasive...
They falsely conceive [them] as real self and real dharmas;

therefore, they do not know them as they truly are—that which is dependent on others is induced by various conditions and is the false manifestation of one's own mind and mental factors, like flowers in a mirror or the moon in water.
That which is non-existent appears as existent; it is not truly existent. Therefore, one must first realize that the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is empty.
Once True Suchness (tathatā) is realized, one can then know the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as it truly is—like an illusory phenomenon. As follows, another verse is cited as proof:
The phrase "In this regard" and so forth explains the meaning of the verse. The intent of this verse is to state that the three natures are all not separate from the mind.

First, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to demonstrate that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is conventionally existent. The argument is stated as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) consists of the mind and mental factors, as well as the dependent nature manifested by them.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are non-existent yet appear to exist. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they are produced by a multitude of conditions."

Therefore, they are likened to illusions and the like. Next, a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is established to demonstrate that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist. The syllogism is stated as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is:
"the self, phenomena, existence, non-existence, both, or neither, which are erroneously imputed by foolish people upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is: "their intrinsic nature and characteristics are entirely non-existent. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because all such things are merely objects grasped through imagination (*parikalpita-ālambana*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: [as with illusions, etc.]
Like flowers in the sky and so forth, it next reveals that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is truly existent.

This means that upon that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), both types of imagined objects—the self and phenomena—are empty. That very reality, such as consciousness, which is revealed by this twofold emptiness, is called the perfected nature.
Therefore, it is said: "That which arises from conditions has no intrinsic nature; having no intrinsic nature, it is emptiness; emptiness is itself the perfected."
Therefore, these three are all not separate from the mind, mental factors, and so forth.
As for space, analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, and so on—up to the remaining four [natures]—they are all subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The following clarifies the classification according to alternative enumerations (*paryāya*). First, the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are subsumed; first the question is posed, then the answer is given. "Mind and so forth" below explains [the conditioned].
"With outflows and without outflows" below subsumes the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). "In this way" below subsumes the seven suchnesses (*tathatā*).

Regarding the "mental engagement with the suchness of cyclic existence" (*pravṛtti-tathatā-manasikāra*): it refers to those bodhisattvas who have already seen the truths and who, through superior Dharma practice, have skillfully cultivated and purified their mental engagement.
Regarding the phenomena of defilement and purification, one contemplates the true nature of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as they have flowed through beginningless time.

Having so contemplated, one becomes free from the view of causelessness and the view of an unequal cause. As for the mental engagement with the two aspects of reality, *tathatā* (suchness), it is as previously described;
furthermore, regarding the phenomena of defilement and purification, through contemplation, there is no [self] among all phenomena or sentient beings.

Having contemplated the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, all views of a self, as well as the mental engagements that conceptualize and differentiate various characteristics, no longer manifest.
Regarding the third, the mental engagement with the suchness of representation-only:
as with the preceding methods, one contemplates that all phenomena, from those that are defiled to those that are purified, have the nature of representation-only. Having [contemplated] this...

Having reflected thus, one understands according to reality that it is solely because the mind is defiled that sentient beings are defiled, and solely because the mind is pure that sentient beings are pure.

Fifth, the mental attention to the fourfold established suchness (*caturvidha-pratiṣṭhita-tathatā-manasikāra*) refers to reflecting upon the truth of suffering regarding the essence of defiled phenomena as previously described;
having so reflected, one explains it to sentient beings in order to bring about their understanding. Fifth.
The mental attention to the *tathatā* of wrong conduct is as previously described.

Up to the point of contemplating the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) regarding defiled phenomena in order to bring about their abandonment, one speaks for the sake of sentient beings. What is called "wrong conduct" refers to the two afflictions of greed and hatred;
being deluded regarding objects and views, they give rise to wrong conduct. Pride, being deluded regarding sentient beings and views, gives rise to wrong conduct. *Sa*... [text fragment].
The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣḥti) give rise to wrong practice by being deluded regarding the objects of knowledge.

False views (mithyādṛṣṭi), the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), and the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) give rise to wrong practice by being deluded regarding various views. Doubt (vicikitsā) gives rise to wrong practice by being deluded regarding the antidotes. Ignorance (avidyā) is deluded regarding everything.

They give rise to wrong practices. Furthermore, the ten afflictions all give rise to various wrong practices by being deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), because these [latter] serve as the causal basis and locus for them.

Moreover, the ten afflictions all give rise to various wrong practices by being deluded regarding cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), because through this they are able to produce fear toward them.
The mental attention (*manasikāra*) to the sixfold purity of suchness (*tathatā*) is as previously described, up to...
The pure dharma-body. Having contemplated the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and desiring to bring about its realization, one teaches it for the sake of sentient beings.

This is the mental attention to the suchness of the sevenfold right practice; that is, as previously described, up to the contemplation of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) regarding pure conduct.
Having contemplated this, and desiring to bring about its cultivation, one teaches it for the sake of sentient beings. These are the seven kinds of reality.

In terms of their nature (*svabhāva*), all are subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), because [the numbers] two, three, seven, and six are all objects of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while one, four,
and five are all objects of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). If categorized according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),

the three— namely, the *pravṛtti* (evolution), *duḥkha* (suffering), and *samudaya* (origination)— are subsumed under both the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures, because they involve false attachment.
Because there is defilement (*saṃkleśa*). The remaining four are all subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
How do the three natures and the six phenomena mutually subsume one another? This should be understood as it is explained in detail in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Next, the six dharmas are subsumed. These are the five aggregates and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); these six dharmas all possess false attachment, are all dependently originated, and all possess the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Thus, they are all subsumed within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Next, the five dharmas are subsumed. These are: name (*nāman*), appearance (*nimitta*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), correct gnosis (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*).

There are four interpretations. According to the first interpretation, some sources state that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) subsumes four of these dharmas, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) subsumes [the remaining one].

Regarding *tathatā* (suchness): it is not included within the five categories of the *parikalpita* (the imagined). The Master [Vasubandhu] explains the meaning as follows: "In this teaching, that which is signified (*lakṣya*) is the 'characteristic' (*nimitta*);
that which signifies (*lakṣaṇa*) is the 'name' (*nāman*); the transforming mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are 'discrimination' (*vikalpa*);

and the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind and mental factors are 'correct wisdom' (*samyag-jñāna*). Since these four types are all dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), they are collectively termed *paratantra* (the dependent). The *parikalpita* is not...
Regarding the subsumption under the five categories: because they are false and lack intrinsic substance. Thus, the *Vyākhyāyukti* states:

"The self-characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent. Why? Because it is not subsumed among the five categories. Apart from these five categories, nothing else exists."
Question: If the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) has no intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*), how can it give rise to the act of thorough imagination?
Answer: Because names operate upon objects. That is to say, following those conventional designations, one circulates among objects.
Worldly fools grasp at the idea that names and objects possess a definitive correspondence and a truly existent intrinsic nature (*tattva-svabhāva*). Question: How should this be understood?
This is a false attachment. Answer: Because the two are mutually guests. Why is this so? Because the name, with respect to the object, does not correspond to its essence;
therefore, it is called a guest. The object, like the name, has no [independent] existence; therefore, it is called a guest.

Regarding the two interpretations, some sources state that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) subsumes both the characteristic (*nimitta*) and the conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because these two—the characteristic and the vision (*darśana*)—[are contained therein].
Because they are categorized separately: the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is subsumed under "names," because it consists only of linguistic designations and lacks any real referent;
correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) subsume the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature), because they are free from error and are characterized by equality.

Regarding the three types of understanding, some sources state that the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is subsumed solely within the *vikalpa* (conceptual construction); the *parikalpita* subsumes names and signs; and correct cognition and suchness subsume the *pariniṣpanna*. Thus says the treatise.

The Master [Xuanzang] explains the meaning as follows: He asserts that the two parts—the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga)—of all contaminated mental states and mental factors are both of the nature of false discrimination and are thus the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*).
This is because the designating names and the designated characteristics are established as these two aspects in accordance with deluded sentiment.

Furthermore, there are four interpretations; some sources state that the name belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra*) while the meaning belongs to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita*).

The Master of the Treatise states the following meaning: He asserts that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), including their objective and subjective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*), are all induced by the power of names;
therefore, names belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*) arises and performs its calculations in accordance with names.

They are provisionally established as "objects" (*artha*); thus, objects belong to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature). Although these five things are taught in four different locations, none of them contradict reason.
Nevertheless, in the first teaching, they are not confused with one another; this should be taken as the standard.

Furthermore, within the Noble Teachings it is said that there are five characteristics (up to) because they have untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and so forth as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Next, the five characteristics are subsumed. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*) states: first, the characteristic of the signifier; second, the characteristic of the signified;

third, the characteristic of mutual relation; fourth, the characteristic of attachment; and fifth, the characteristic of non-attachment. That is to say, the characteristic of the signifier and the characteristic of the signified each—

It possesses the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). That is to say, when one gives rise to false attachment toward the characteristics of the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*), this is subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If the signified is correlated with the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the object-condition, and the signifier is correlated with the subjective aspect (*nāma*) and the discerning consciousness (*vikalpa*), then it belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If the signifier is correlated with correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*), and the signified is correlated with suchness (*tathatā*), then it belongs to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Question: Since correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object and is fundamentally non-conceptual, how can there be any designating expression (*abhilāpa*)? Answer: This is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which manifests as if it were a designating expression.

Although it is not the fundamental [wisdom], it is nonetheless subsumed under correct cognition. The relationship between these two aspects is subsumed solely under the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

Because the two—name and referent—are necessarily associated, the aspect of attachment is conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), which is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The aspect of non-attachment is correct cognition and suchness (*tathatā*), which is subsumed exclusively under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it is taught in the holy scriptures that there are four realities (tattva), which may be either conventional or ultimate; these should be understood according to reason.
Next, the four realities are subsumed as follows: the worldly reality (loka-tattva) and the logical reality (yukti-tattva) are subsumed within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Among the five categories, name, characteristic, and conceptualization are subsumed under three [of the three natures].
Afflictive reality and the reality of purified knowledge are subsumed under the reality of purified objects of knowledge and the reality of correct gnosis and suchness.

The treatise states that mundane reality is subsumed solely under the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is what all sentient beings collectively grasp. The reality of principle (*yukti-tattva*) pertains to all three natures.

Grasping refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature). Non-grasping refers to the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature). Defilement refers to the *paratantra* (dependent nature). Purity refers to the *pariniṣpanna*.

Of these, the latter two realities belong exclusively to the third [nature] and do not extend to the first two. Next, regarding the subsumption of the Four Noble Truths: each of the four truths extends to all three natures.
Within the first, the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), each of the aspects—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—is fully present in all three natures.

The three natures correspond respectively as follows. First, regarding the three types of impermanence: first, the impermanence of non-existence, which means that all natures are fundamentally non-existent;

this pertains to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Second, the impermanence of arising and ceasing, because there is origination and extinction; this pertains to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Third, the impermanence of defilement and purity, because the defiled is transformed into the pure; this pertains to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the three types of suffering, the first is...

First, the suffering of that which is grasped (*grāhya-duḥkha*). This refers to the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*) as being my own phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), because the two types of grasping arise based upon them and lead to attachment.

Second, the suffering of the characteristics of things (*vastu-lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*). This refers to the suffering of birth (*jāti-duḥkha*), the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), which correspond respectively to birth, aging, and death.

Third, the suffering of conjunction (*saṃyoga-duḥkha*). This is because it is through the nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) that the conjunction of all sufferings is attained. Regarding the three aspects of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): first, there is no...
1. Emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*): because it lacks an intrinsic nature. 2. Emptiness of other-nature (*anya-bhāva-śūnyatā*): because it is a mere conventional aggregation;

that is, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) does not coincide with the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), for one exists as an object of cognition while the other is non-existent as an object of cognition.

3. Emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*): the true nature of suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the two [preceding] emptinesses, which is ultimate emptiness. Regarding the three kinds of selflessness:

First, the selflessness of signlessness (*animitta-nairātmya*): this refers to the fact that both the conceptually imputed person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) and phenomenon-self (*dharma-ātman*) are devoid of signs. Second, the selflessness of distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa-nairātmya*):

this refers to the fact that the provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*) taught in the Noble Teachings does not share the same characteristics as the provisional self of the worldly realm. Third, the selflessness of intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-nairātmya*):

this refers to the fact that within the intrinsic characteristic itself, there is fundamentally no self. Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): first is the origination of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-samudaya*), which refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

It is the accumulation (*saṃcaya*). First, the accumulation of the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*): although these seeds are originally dependent on others (*paratantra*), the name "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) is provisionally established based on the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Second, the accumulation of the arising [of afflictions] (*samutthāna*): this refers to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of karma and afflictions, which mutually perfume and incite one another. Third, the accumulation of non-separation from fetters (*asaṃyoga*):

this refers to not being separated from the bonds of the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*) and not having severed the two obscurations (*āvaraṇa*); it is the true suchness (*tathatā*) that is primordially present, which is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The third [category] consists of three types: first, cessation by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*), because intrinsic nature is unarisen; second, cessation through the abandonment of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*), which refers to the permanent severance that extinguishes the two graspings;

and third, cessation by primordial nature (*prakṛti-nirodha*), because it is quiescent from the very beginning and does not depend on further cessation. Regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), there are three types:

first, the path of universal knowledge (*parijñā-mārga*), because it is able to know that the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is definitively non-existent; second, the path of permanent abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*).

Because it can sever the defiled aspect of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is the third: the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*). This is because one realizes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) by severing the obstacles.

"Universal knowledge" (*parijñā*) applies to both of the latter two [truths], because one severs the origin [of suffering] through universal knowledge, and one realizes the truth [of cessation] through universal knowledge.

The seven, three, and three natures refer to the four sets of three within the truth of suffering, and one set of three for each of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path; these together constitute [the total].
73. As with the three sets of seven above, each triad is respectively assigned to one of the three natures; hence it is said they are "assigned and explained in order.

Regarding "either provisional or real": for example, the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is conventional in the world, the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is conventional in the sacred teachings, and only the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) is ultimate reality.
The objective spheres traversed by the three doors of liberation range from the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva (perfected nature), which is the exclusive domain of noble wisdom, down to the other two natures.

Furthermore, these three doors of liberation are subsumed as follows: emptiness belongs to the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature), wishlessness belongs to the paratantra-svabhāva (dependent nature), and signlessness belongs to the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva.

Based on these three natures, there further arise three types of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). First, with respect to the object of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), there arises the patience regarding the fundamental non-arising of intrinsic nature;

this is because one realizes that the imagined nature is fundamentally non-arisen from the very beginning. Second, with respect to the object of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there arises the patience regarding the spontaneous non-arising;
this is because one realizes that the dependent nature is spontaneously non-arisen, like observing a hundred flowers in springtime.

Xiu [states that] the three conditions—such as observing yellow leaves falling in autumn—perfectly accomplish the realized object (*pariniṣpanna-viṣaya*), whereby one gives rise to the patience regarding the non-arising of afflictions and suffering (*kleśa-duḥkha-anutpāda-kṣānti*).

This is because one realizes that afflictions and suffering are, in their very essence, non-arising. Next, the two truths are subsumed. Regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are three types.

First, the "nominal conventional" (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*), which is the worldly conventional (*loka-saṃvṛti*), such as an army or a forest. Second, the "functional conventional" (*pracāra-saṃvṛti*)... which is... [text continues].

The conventional truth of principle refers to such categories as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). The conventional truth of manifestation is the conventional truth of designation, because it designates *tathatā* (suchness).
Regarding the three aspects of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): first, the ultimate as object (*artha-paramārtha*), so called because it is the object of the supreme;

this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Second, the ultimate as attainment (*prāpti-paramārtha*), so called because it is itself the supreme; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Third, the ultimate as practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*)... [the supreme].

This is an etymological explanation based on its proximity [to the subject]. Next, it subsumes two types of knowledge. That which is "thoroughly imagined and grasped" (*parikalpita*) is not an object of cognition;
this is a complete exclusion. If one considers it in terms of whether it exists for ordinary beings or noble ones, it is nonetheless an object of perception for both the mundane and the noble.

The sphere of wisdom. This includes both [the fundamental and the subsequently attained]. The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the object of both the fundamental and the subsequently attained wisdoms.
As for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is the object of the fundamental wisdom alone.
Among these three natures, how many are provisional and how many are real? Fearing that excessive detail would weary the reader, I shall briefly indicate the essential framework.

Next, we shall discuss the provisional and the real. If one maintains that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) exists nominally but lacks substantiality, being established merely by deluded sentiment, it may be described as provisional.
However, if one investigates its essence and characteristics, since it possesses neither a substantial entity nor any defining marks, it cannot be [described]... [as anything].

The conventional (*prajñapti*) cannot be said to be real; it must be like the non-existence of a rabbit’s horns and the existence of a cow’s horns before one can speak of the conventional or the real.
There are three types of conventional [nature] based on the dependent (*paratantra*): first, the conventional of accumulation (*saṃghāta-prajñapti*), such as a jar or a basin.

These are accumulated phenomena because they are formed by the simultaneous integration of many factors. Although the constituting factors are real, that which is constituted is conventional. Second...
Continuity-designation (*saṃtati-prajñapti*): For example, throughout the three periods of time, there is only the continuity of cause and effect;

upon many dharmas and many moments, a single designated dharma is established. As the Buddha said: "The deer king of the past is my present self," and so forth. State-designation (*avasthā-prajñapti*):
For example, the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are of the nature of states; therefore, they are all designations. This occurs within a single moment.
They are established upon a single dharma, just as [the designations] "outflow-tainted," "visible," and "impinging" are applied to a single form (rūpa).
These are all merely provisional designations (prajñapti) made upon a single dharma; if they were real entities, they would necessarily possess multiple substantial bodies.

Such things as anger and resentment are all subsumed under these provisional designations. All mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), as well as material phenomena (rūpa-dharma), arise from causes and conditions.
Therefore, they are said to be real. If real phenomena did not exist, even the conventional would not exist, because the conventional depends upon the real as its cause.

The perfected nature exists because it is not established in dependence upon various conditions. Next, the discussion concerns identity and difference. Question: Regarding these three natures of phenomena...
"Are they different? Or are they not different? Answer: "They are neither identical nor different. "How are they not different? Answer: "Because there is no separate essence.

That is to say, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is without characteristics; the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is without arising; and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is without intrinsic being.

These three natures are thus a single nature, and this single nature is itself the absence of intrinsic being. Furthermore, the perfected true suchness (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā*) has two meanings. The first is...

Unchanging; second, following conditions (*anuparivartin*). The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has two meanings: first, it appears as existent; second, it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) has two meanings:

first, it exists from the perspective of sentient beings' attachments (*sattva-vidyamāna*); second, it is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva-abhāva*). Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is unchanging, because the dependent nature lacks intrinsic nature, and because that which is grasped is non-existent in principle, the three natures are one and the same limit.
If True Suchness follows conditions, the dependent nature appears as existent, and that which is grasped exists from the perspective of sentient beings' attachments.

There are. Because these three meanings are also not different from one another. How, then, are they not identical? Answer: The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is the nature of false attachment;

the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the nature of dependent origination; and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the nature of suchness (*tathatā*). Since these three natures are each distinct, they are not non-different.
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "One with cataracts is like the imagined nature; the appearance of blue and yellow is like the dependent nature."

The pure eye is like the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is like a snake; the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is like a vine.
A verse says: "One perceives a snake arising in a vine; upon seeing the vine, there is no [real] object. Once the parts of the vine are known, there is knowledge of the vine."
It is like the knowledge of a snake; that is, knowing that the nature and parts of the vine are empty. By this analogy, one knows that the false notion of a snake arises upon the vine.
Therefore, an ancient master asked: "If the reflected image perceived by me were dependent on others (paratantra), there would have to be a real self that is dependent on others.
He replied: "This appearance relies upon causes and conditions and is merely a dependent, illusory existence; it is not [a real self]."
"I" is that which is falsely conceptualized as a self by means of that pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*). This has two aspects:

if this phenomenon arises from causes and conditions and possesses the power to produce the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is "existent" and is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Regarding this, the aspect consisting of the object as it is grasped by false attachment is called the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); it is therefore termed "non-existent," just like a person [who does not exist].
In the darkness, one grasps a stone as a cow. While the substance of the stone is not non-existent, the substance of the cow does not exist.
The object perceived by the view of self exists through dependence on others (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), yet the view of self itself does not exist.

Just as the substance of the stone originally has no cow, yet one falsely grasps it as a cow—this grasped cow is entirely non-existent in its essence—so too, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is originally not the self, yet the deluded mind grasps it as the self; this [grasped] self...
The nature of grasping has no substance whatsoever; there is only the mind that grasps, but no self that is grasped.

It is like a stone upon which there is no cow being grasped, yet there is the stone as the object of perception. Upon this objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga), although there is no self that is grasped, [there is still the appearance].
Yet, because there are characteristics of objective referents (*ālambana-nimitta*), one knows that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are not non-distinct.
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight;
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
Composed by Bodhisattvas such as Dharmapāla;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled and annotated by the Śramaṇa Tongrun of Jinting Changshou Monastery.
If there are three natures, how is it that the Blessed One [said] "because all phenomena are the ultimate truth"?
First, he poses the question; next, he provides the answer in verse; then, the commentary explains below:

when the Buddha speaks of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it does not mean that there are three absences of intrinsic nature distinct from these three presences of intrinsic nature. Rather, it is precisely these three presences of intrinsic nature that are intended by his profound intention (*saṃdhāya*).

It is taught that there are three kinds of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). First, based on the imaginary nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is called the "non-nature of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), because its essential characteristic is ultimately non-existent, like a snake [imagined] upon a rope.
Second, based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is called the "non-nature of arising" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), because it arises depending on various conditions;
it is not like the objects grasped by the imaginary nature, which would have their own inherent nature as the cause of their arising. Third, based on...

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is said to be the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), because the single true *dharmadhātu* is the very nature of being without intrinsic nature.

This means that the Buddha spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that all phenomena are entirely without self-nature; it is not an explicit statement (*nītārtha*) that all phenomena are completely devoid of nature.

His intention was precisely to reveal that the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is empty, while the dependent and perfected natures (*paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna*) exist. Question: [Regarding] the dependent and perfected...
If they possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for what reason did the World-Honored One cryptically state that they are non-existent? The answer is:

although the two natures—the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)—exist in substance, there are deluded persons who, regarding the substance of the dependent nature, commit the error of "placing a head upon a head."

Falsely grasping [these] as a real self and real dharmas, the World-Honored One, in order to eliminate this grasping, has stated in general that all dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—are non-existent.
"How so? asks the following question; "It is by relying on this" provides the formal proof (*pramāṇa*) as the answer.

The *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature) is an existent phenomenon (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in terms of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because its essence and characteristics are ultimately non-existent. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like a flower in the sky (*ākāśapuṣpa*), etc. Next, the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

The *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) is an existent phenomenon. The thesis is that it is conventionally designated as lacking intrinsic nature, yet its nature is not entirely non-existent. The reason is: "Because it arises in dependence upon various conditions (*pratyaya*). It is not like the self [imagined] through false attachment.
However, because it is the nature [of things], it is like illusory phenomena and the like. The three measures (pramāṇa) state: "The perfected ultimate reality (pariniṣpanna-paramārtha) is a dharma;
it is conventionally described as being without nature (niḥsvabhāva). The thesis (pakṣa) is that its nature is not entirely non-existent. The reason (hetu) is:

'Because it is free from the previously mentioned nature of the imagined self and dharmas (parikalpita-svabhāva). The example (dṛṣṭānta) is: 'Like space pervading form. This means that although space pervades all forms, it must depend upon those..."
The lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of form (*rūpa*) reveals the lack of intrinsic nature of space (*ākāśa*).
