Although the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is pervasive throughout the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is only by means of the dependent nature’s lack of intrinsic nature that the perfected nature’s lack of intrinsic nature is revealed.

This principle precisely demonstrates that the perfected nature and that dependent nature are neither different nor non-different; both are conventionally designated as being without intrinsic nature. Question: Since the dependent and the perfected natures are neither different nor non-different, [how can they be distinguished?]
Why is it that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is called "the lack of nature in terms of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), while the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is not? Answer:

Although the dependent nature is not the true ultimate nature, it could also be described as "the lack of nature in terms of the ultimate" from the perspective of the provisional teaching (*anuvartana-mukha*).

However, fearing confusion with the third [category], the truly ultimate reality (*tattva-paramārtha*), it is not so described. Nevertheless, this perfected nature is the most [excellent] among all phenomena.
The most excellent ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) cannot be exemplified by that which arises from dependence upon others (paratantra).
Briefly stated, there are four types of ultimate truth, [ranging] from [the conventional ultimate] up to the total negation that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva) whatsoever.

Regarding the ultimate (*paramārtha*), it is contrasted with the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). There are four types of the conventional: first, the worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*), which is the truth of nominal designation without reality, such as an army or a forest;
second, the rational convention (*yukti-saṃvṛti*), which is the truth of the differentiation of phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);
third, the conventional of realization (*adhigama-saṃvṛti*), which is the truth established through skillful means, such as the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and so forth.

The four established conventionalities (*vyavasthāna-saṃvṛti*) are the nominal non-established truths; they are the suchness of the two emptinesses. There are four types of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*):
first, the worldly ultimate (*loka-paramārtha*), which is the truth of the manifestation of essence and function—namely, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Because they possess real essence and function that transcend the conventional, they are called "ultimate. According to their specific distinctions, they are termed "aggregates" and so forth.
Therefore, it is called "manifestation. Second is the ultimate truth of principle (*yukti-paramārtha*), which is the truth of the differentiation of cause and effect;

that is, the Four Noble Truths of suffering and so forth, because they are distinguished as cause and effect through the processes of knowing, abandoning, realizing, and cultivating. Third is the ultimate truth of realization (*adhigama-paramārtha*), which is the truth of manifesting reality by relying on emptiness;

that is, the suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness, because this suchness is manifested by relying upon those two kinds of emptiness. Fourth is the supreme ultimate (*parama-paramārtha*).

Regarding the meaning: this refers to setting aside the conventional expressions to clarify the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), namely the One True Dharma-realm (eka-dharmadhātu), which does not fall within the reach of verbal expression.
This is what is called the "true ultimate nature" within the ultimate. When that conventional truth is contrasted with this ultimate truth, they together constitute the eight truths.

The first is the worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya), which consists merely of the false and illusory nature of self and dharmas; the final one is the ultimate truth, which is simply the One True [Dharma-realm]; and those in between—
The three dharmas correspond to the initial forest army and are called the conventional four truths; they correspond to the final single reality and are called the ultimate four truths.

Herein, "ultimate" (paramārtha) is spoken of according to the final ultimate among ultimates. To distinguish it from the preceding three types of ultimate, it is stated that the ultimate is precisely suchness (tathatā).
"Such" (tathā) means it is not like the falsity of the parikalpita (imagined nature); it is as it truly is.
This is not like the transformation of the dependent nature;
that is to say, although this *tathatā* (suchness) exists amidst all falsely transformed phenomena, it has never been moved or affected by even a single hair’s breadth.

The word "also" indicates that this *tathatā* has many other names, such as *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena), *nirvāṇa*, and the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality). This very nature of *tathatā* is...
The true nature (*tathatā*) of consciousness-only, though it is indeed the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*), is distinguished by two types of differentiation.

First, it is called the "ultimate nature" to distinguish it from false, pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Second, it is called the "ultimate nature" to distinguish it from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
The subsequent exhortation states: "The three verses collectively reveal that the three natures are taught as a secret doctrine; they are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)."
One should not categorically negate all phenomena as being entirely non-existent. These three natures and three absences of nature are the pivotal points for the process of saṃsāra and its cessation.
If one clings to the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), that is saṃsāra; if one realizes the absence of nature in the dependent, that is cessation.
From this point onward, throughout the ten stages (bhūmis), one abandons a portion of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) and realizes...
Because [the nature of] True Suchness is partially realized, five stages are established; these all concern the gradual process of awakening and entry according to the Mahāyāna.
Those of the Hīnayāna cannot participate in this gateway, as they cling to the notion that phenomena exist externally to the mind.
Thus, having established the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), one is finally able to gradually awaken to and enter into consciousness-only.
What follows below clarifies the section on the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) regarding consciousness-only. Question:

Although the preceding text has extensively set forth the two gates of the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only, thereby establishing the meaning of consciousness-only, it is not yet known how one should apply the mind in order to enter this gate.
If one wishes to enter this gate, how many stages are there? Regarding the "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), these refer to the three characteristics of the aforementioned subject-object transformation.
Regarding the "nature" (svabhāva), this refers to the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva). Answer:

One must possess two kinds of Mahāyāna seeds and gradually awaken to and enter [this state] through the five stages. Question: What are the two kinds of Mahāyāna [seeds]? Answer: First, the innate nature (prakṛti).
The seeds abiding by nature refer to those that have been attached to the fundamental consciousness since beginningless time;

they are the seeds of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) which are inherently complete by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and are not obtained from without. Second, the seeds accomplished through practice:

although these possess the original cause, if they lack the power of new perfuming and stimulation provided by external conditions, one cannot attain realization. Therefore, they necessarily depend upon the outflow of the *dharmadhātu*.

The Dharma enters through the gateway of the ear and is followed by hearing, reflection (*cintā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*); that which is accomplished through repeated perfuming at these times is what is meant.

Regarding "that which is accomplished through hearing" (*śrutamaya*) and so forth, the term "and so forth" includes that which is accomplished through reflection and that which is accomplished through cultivation. "Hearing" (*śruta*) refers to listening;

it is the faculty of the ear (*śrotrendriya*) that gives rise to the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*), because one hears the verbal teachings. "Reflection" (*cintā*) refers to contemplation; it is...

"Reflection" (cintā) refers to the generation of wisdom through the analytical discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the practice of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which generates wisdom by cultivating the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
Only when one possesses both of these natures can one gradually enter the gateway of true *vijñapti-mātratā*.
What is meant by "entering the five stages of consciousness-only" (up to: "further causing one to enter the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only")?
Question: What are these five stages? Answer: First is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

This refers to a bodhisattva who, having already perfected the two kinds of lineage (*gotra*), has first resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahā-citta*) and diligently cultivates merit and wisdom as the equipment for entering the noble path (*ārya-mārga*); therefore, it is called "equipment."
The stage of provisions (*sambhāra-avasthā*). Nirvāṇa is termed the "practice of liberation" (*vimukti-caryā*). Regarding the term "conducive factors" (*anuloma-bhāga*):

because one's practice does not contradict [the goal], it is called "conducive" (*anuloma*). Regarding the term "factors" (*bhāga*): it carries the sense of "cause" (*hetu*) and "limb" (*aṅga*). This is because it constitutes one part and one limb of the cause for liberation.
Although one has not yet attained liberation at this stage, because one can accord with the path to liberation, it is called "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).

The stage of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Second, the stage of application (*prayogamārga*): once the path conducive to liberation has been perfected, one further cultivates application in order to enter the path of seeing;

this is also called the "stage conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). It is termed "application" because it is proximate to the path of seeing and subdues and eliminates the two types of grasping.
Following the true path of seeing, that which decisively penetrates the seeds of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is called the "stage of penetration. Although in this stage...

1. The stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*): Even during the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*) before attaining the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one is able to accord with and resolve the two obstacles;
therefore, it is called the "aids to penetration. 2. The stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha*): This refers to when Bodhisattvas enter the first bhūmi and attain the true path of vision.

What are the characteristics of the various sublime practices cultivated in this stage through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)? Answer: They consist of merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).
If one discusses their general characteristics, then each and every perfection (*pāramitā*) possesses both merit and wisdom. If one discusses their specific characteristics, the first five are...

The first three constitute merit (*puṇya*); the last one constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*). Alternatively, the three of giving, ethical discipline, and patience constitute merit, while the last one constitutes wisdom;
diligence and meditative concentration encompass both. Furthermore, if discussed according to their general characteristics, all six perfections pertain to both self-benefit and benefiting others.

If discussed according to their specific characteristics, the six perfections and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are subsumed under the practices for self-benefit. [Specifically,] giving, kind speech, and purposeful action...

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, are all subsumed under the practice of benefiting others. Thus, [the text] concludes below:
although the two obstacles have not yet been suppressed or eliminated at this stage, one firmly and ardently cultivates various supreme practices.
Regarding the three ways of refining through training: first, upon hearing that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is vast, profound, and far-reaching, one may give rise to despondency.
At such a time of despondency, one should refine one’s own mind by citing others who have already realized it, thereby becoming courageous and non-regressive.
"Vast" means boundless; "great" means unsurpassed; "profound" means difficult to fathom; "distant" means long in duration. This is called the first bodhicitta.
It draws upon others to illustrate oneself and refines one's resolve. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* verse says:

"If all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions were to swiftly realize the fruit of the Sugata in every moment of thought, they are already great men, and so am I; I should not [despair]."

First, one becomes discouraged and withdraws. Second, upon hearing that practices such as generosity are difficult to cultivate, one immediately gives rise to discouragement; however, one then reflects:
"I have already attained such an intentionality that is free from all base evils—namely, an intentionality that is far removed from stinginess, greed, malice, and the like.
Because of this, by applying even a small amount of effort to cultivate generosity and the other perfections, I shall attain their fulfillment. This...

The name "Ten Thousand Practices" refers to the difficulty of cultivation and the resulting sense of dejection. One should reflect upon oneself to increase one's training and refinement. A verse says: "In the past, you traversed many eons through evil realms;

though your diligent toil was without benefit, you were still able to arise [from it]. Now, by practicing even a little goodness, you shall attain Bodhi; for this great benefit, you ought not to give rise to dejection.
Third, hearing that the Buddhas' perfect transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is extremely difficult to realize, one may then give rise to dejection.

When one is despondent, one should cite the coarse, shallow, and minor virtues of other humans and devas as a comparison for the superior and sublime causes of the six perfections, thereby refining the mind so that it becomes courageous and does not retreat.
This is called "the difficulty of realizing the transformation of the basis through the refinement of citing the coarse to illustrate the sublime.
The verse says: "Even all ordinary beings on the broad ground Yet aspire to realize the fruit of Bodhi in the distance; you..."
Having already undergone diligent toil through many eons, one should not retreat, become disheartened, or sink back into delusion.

Through these three matters of refinement, one cultivates all supreme practices and severs the obstacles of the four stations: first, by abandoning the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one severs such orientations;
second, by resolving doubts regarding the Mahāyāna, one is able to permanently sever the doubts of divergent wisdom.
Third, by abandoning the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self regarding the dharmas that have been heard and reflected upon, one severs attachment to phenomena.
Fourth, by being without volitional engagement and without conceptual differentiation toward all signs that are manifest, present, and established.

Because of the cessation of conceptual discrimination, what are the characteristics of the subsequent stage of application (*prayoga*)? (Up to: Because the two aspects are identical, they are combined for contemplation.
As for the term "application," it is like a person traveling a long distance who, as they approach their own home, applies further spurts of effort; this is because of this.

The Way is able to relinquish afflictions; therefore, it first poses a question and subsequently provides the answer in verse. Regarding the phrase "few things": ordinary people follow after objects with a deluded mind;
they see objects but do not see the mind, so one cannot say that their objects are few. The Sage realizes that objects are identical to the mind.

One perceives the mind but does not perceive objects; there is no room for even the slightest [object]. One dwells in a state that is still that of an ordinary person while approaching the stage of a sage;
it cannot be called an object, yet it cannot be called non-objective. Therefore, it is said that "a small object is established.
This is the moment when the ancient clay lump is on the verge of being broken but has not yet been broken. By applying effort and practice at this point, one advances until reaching the Way.

The commentary states: This is an explanation. It means that during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, the Bodhisattva has already accumulated the provisions of merit and fulfilled the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Desiring to enter the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), he therefore applies further "whips" [of effort].
One applies effort and practice to suppress and eliminate the seeds and manifest forms of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). What are called the four stages of application (*prayoga*)?
They are the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of Peak (*mūrdhan*), the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), and the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

These four stages are collectively termed the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), because they accord with and lead toward the entry into the true nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Regarding the term "penetration" (*nirveda*): "penetration" (*ni*) means...

"Decisive" (*niścaya*) means discernment (*vicaya*). This refers to the wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which is the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga*).

"Decisive" eliminates the category of doubt (*vicikitsā-pakṣa*), while "discernment" eliminates the category of views (*dṛṣṭi-pakṣa*). The category of doubt is discerned but not decided, because it is characterized by hesitation.

The category of views is decided but not discerned, because they are not correct views. Since the various noble paths (*āryamārga*) are able to sever doubt, [the term] "division" (*vibhāga*) refers to the division and severance of these. This...

The meaning of this statement is to clarify that what is conformed to is exclusively a portion of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), specifically the stage of definitive discernment (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);

therefore, it receives the name "stages conducive to definitive discernment. Those who give rise to the stages conducive to definitive discernment in this life must have previously given rise to the stages conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

It is only those who have initially planted the seeds of the stages conducive to liberation that subsequently attain liberation; that is to say, first one gives rise to the stages conducive to liberation, and next...
One gives rise to the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Upon entering the third [level], one enters the noble state (*ārya*) and attains liberation.

Because this stage is proximate to the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is designated by the name "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). Nevertheless, because there is a prior accumulation of provisions (*sambhāra*), it is also termed "application.

If these preceding stages did not exist, this stage would not be established. Question: Upon what basis are the four stages, beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), established? Answer: They are established based upon the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*).

The first two [applications of mindfulness] are based on the four thorough investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*), while the latter two are established based on the four correct cognitions (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*). The four thorough investigations are:

the investigation of names (*nāmaparyeṣaṇā*), the investigation of objects (*arthaparyeṣaṇā*), the investigation of the false designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaprajñaptiparyeṣaṇā*), and the investigation of the false designation of specific differences (*viśeṣaprajñaptiparyeṣaṇā*). As for the four correct cognitions:

This refers to the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna) induced by the investigation of names (nāma-paryeṣaṇā), the knowledge of reality as it is induced by the investigation of things (vastu-paryeṣaṇā), the knowledge of reality as it is induced by the investigation of the provisional designation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā), and the knowledge of reality as it is induced by the investigation of the provisional designation of distinctions (viśeṣa-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā).

The characteristic of the cause of the means is called the investigation of names; the characteristic of the result of the means is called the knowledge of reality as it is. Regarding the term "name":
"Phenomena" refers to form, sensation, perception, and so forth. When a bodhisattva investigates within names, they see only the linguistic expression and do not see the essence of the name;
thus, they know that these are merely objects of mental discourse, which are provisional and not real. "Meaning" refers to that which is expressed and signified by the name.

This refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), etc. When a bodhisattva investigates these categories of meaning, they perceive only their generic types and do not perceive any further objective referents;

thus one knows that these, too, are merely mental verbalizations (*manojalpa*), being conventional designations rather than realities. Since names and phrases are nothing but the conceptual discrimination of the mind, [they lack external reality].
The referent of a name likewise lacks a distinct substantial entity. Therefore, apart from names and conceptual discrimination, there is no separate referent to be perceived.
Furthermore, when one investigates the intrinsic nature of both name and referent, one finds them to be provisional and not real;

that is to say, the intrinsic natures of names and referents such as "form," "feeling," and "perception" are seen by the bodhisattva through investigation to be merely provisional, and nothing else is seen.
Thus, one knows that in reality nothing exists, and that self-nature is merely a provisional designation, just like the provisional designation of a *pudgala* (person) and so forth.

Furthermore, one investigates the distinction between name and referent; these are provisional and not real. This refers to the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the distinctions between names and referents, such as impermanence, suffering, and so on.
When a bodhisattva investigates these distinctions, they see only their provisionality and do not see anything else.
Thus one knows that in reality nothing exists; these are merely conventional designations for distinctions.

By investigating in this way, one realizes that all four [categories] are of the nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and are entirely non-apprehendable. Knowing them thus, one understands that the four factors, beginning with names, arise in dependence upon consciousness;
if separated from consciousness, they definitely do not exist. Furthermore, it is not only these four factors that are non-existent.
Even the manifesting consciousness itself cannot be apprehended. To understand this thoroughly is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). It is like observing a snake upon a rope;
the snake is not real because it does not exist. If one has already realized that its object is non-existent, [the consciousness likewise ceases].

Although the cognition of a snake has ceased, the cognition of a rope still persists. If one further analyzes this [cognition] into its most subtle categories, it too is found to be false, because its characteristics consist of color, odor, taste, and tangibility;
thus, this cognition serves as the basis for the cognition of the rope, which must then cease.

If the cognition of the rope ceases, one is then able to realize the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Question: Why are the "investigation of names" and "investigation of objects" designated as the stages of this position?

Regarding the distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*): the answer is that there are two kinds, namely name (*nāman*) and object (*artha*), which are precisely the characteristics of names (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
These are the two divisions of the perceived and the perceiver (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*), and they are precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Because these two serve as the essential gateway for delusion and awakening, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* explains the five dharmas, stating: "As for 'characteristic' (*nimitta*): wherever locations, shapes, forms, colors, and images appear, this is called 'characteristic. If that...
There are such characteristics as these, which are designated by names such as "vase" and so forth; to manifest these various characteristics is called *vikalpa* (conceptual construction).
Those names and those characteristics are ultimately unattainable; this is called *tathatā* (suchness). That true, certain, and ultimate self-nature is unattainable;
this is called *samyagjñāna* (correct wisdom). The preceding [section] clarified that delusion regarding these names and characteristics gives rise to conceptual construction.
Perception thus becomes the cycle of transmigration. One clearly understands that these names and characteristics are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

their very essence is suchness (*tathatā*), which is precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Therefore, both delusion and awakening arise from this. Question: Why are names and meanings each separately investigated?

One investigates by combining the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and specific difference (*viśeṣa*) of name and object. Answer: Because the two phenomena of name and object differ in terms of subject and object, they are sought separately.
Because the intrinsic nature and specific difference of name and object are identical, they are investigated in combination.
If one knows that the intrinsic nature and specific difference of the name are unfindable, one then knows that the intrinsic nature and specific difference of the object are likewise unfindable.
Because it can be attained. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "Investigation of names" means that bodhisattvas perceive only names within names.
"Investigation of things" means that bodhisattvas perceive only things within things.
"Investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature" means that bodhisattvas perceive only the designated intrinsic nature within the designated intrinsic nature. [Investigation of] distinctions...

Regarding the investigation of designations (*prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*): it means that when Bodhisattvas encounter designations for specific distinctions, they perceive only those designations for specific distinctions.
These Bodhisattvas, regarding both names and things, either contemplate them as having distinct characteristics or contemplate them as having combined characteristics.

Because they contemplate the combination of name and thing, they thoroughly penetrate the designation of intrinsic nature and the designation of specific distinction; this is called the investigation of names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*).
Regarding the introduction to the knowledge of reality as it is: because Bodhisattvas, having investigated names and found them to be merely names,
understand names as they truly are— namely, that these names are established for the sake of these referents in order to give rise to conceptualization,
views, and verbal expression in the world— if they were not established with respect to the objects of conceptualization, such as form and so forth...
Regarding the establishment of names such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth: there is nothing in the entire world that can be conceptualized as being this "form" or that;
if there were no conceptualization, there would be no arising of superimposed attachment; and if there were no attachment, there would be no verbal expression.
If one understands in this way according to reality, this is called the first "knowledge of reality as it is" (yathābhūta-jñāna) induced by the investigation of things (vastu-paryeṣaṇā).
Regarding the knowledge of reality as it is induced by the investigation of things:

because Bodhisattvas, through the investigation of things, have realized that there is only the thing-in-itself (vastumātra), they understand according to reality that the nature of the imagined things such as form (rūpa) is devoid of all verbal expression and is inexpressible.
This is called the second kind of knowledge of reality derived from the investigation of phenomena (vastu-paryeṣaṇā).
Regarding the knowledge of reality derived from the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā):

it is because bodhisattvas, within the designated intrinsic natures of perceived objects such as form (rūpa), investigate them as being mere designations; thus they penetrate the designated intrinsic nature as it truly is—not as something real.

The intrinsic nature of that object appears as if it were the intrinsic nature of that object, yet one can also understand that the intrinsic nature of that object is like a transformation, a reflection, the moon in water, or a dream—appearing to have an essential nature.

This is called the profound objective domain of the wisdom that accords with reality, which is induced by the investigation into the provisional designation of the third intrinsic nature. Its specific distinction is as follows:
Regarding the "knowledge of reality as it is" induced by the investigation of designations:

because Bodhisattvas investigate the designations of distinctions as being merely of a designated nature, they are well able to penetrate the meaning of non-duality within the designations of distinctions regarding the objects of thought, such as form (*rūpa*).
That is to say, those things are neither of a nature of existence nor of a nature of non-existence, because they can be...

Because its self-nature is not established through verbal expression, it is not of an existent nature; because its self-nature is established as being inexpressible, it is not of a non-existent nature.
Thus, it is neither with form nor without form: from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is not with form;
from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is not without form; yet, within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), form is provisionally established.
Whether there is existence or non-existence, form or formlessness— likewise, all such various conceptual distinctions of dharmas,
such as being visible or invisible, should be understood exhaustively through this principle.
If one can thus understand the meaning of non-duality within these conceptual distinctions, this is called the fourth conceptual distinction.

The wisdom that accords with reality, which is induced by thorough investigation, arises based on the concentration of "attainment of light" (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*) and initiates the lower stage of investigation; because it reaches the culmination of the stage of investigation, it is further named "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

Regarding the concentration of "attainment of light," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Light" refers to the wisdom-light capable of illuminating the absence of objective referents (*anartha*); "attainment" refers to its initial acquisition.

Because there is the illumination of wisdom regarding the absence of objective referents, it is called the *ālokalabdha-samādhi* (the concentration of attaining light). Regarding "arousing inferior investigation":

*ālokalabdha* is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while investigation (*vitarka*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). It is said to be "aroused" because one has for the first time obtained the wisdom of skillful means; by means of this investigation, [one proceeds].
Observing that the grasped phenomena (*grāhya-dharma*) are ultimately unobtainable is called the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

This means that at this stage of Heat, one first observes that the four factors—the name (*nāman*), the object (*artha*), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the specific difference (*viśeṣa*)—of the grasped are all transformations of one's own mind and are thus not truly obtainable.

Question: What is the distinction between the stages of "Attainment of Clarity" (*prāptāloka*) and "Heat"? Answer: They are called "Attainment of Clarity" because one has for the first time attained wisdom (*jñāna*).

The "warmth" stage (*uṣmagata*) is so named because it is the precursor to the sun of wisdom; specifically, it is the precursor to the fire of the Path attained through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The *Saṃgrahaṇī* states: "For example, when drilling for fire, warmth is the precursor;
this is likewise: wisdom is the precursor. Thus, the ancients said: "Studying the Path is like drilling for fire; when smoke is encountered, one should [rejoice]."

Do not cease. Regarding the "increasing clarity" concentration (*vṛddhāloka-samādhi*): because the power of wisdom becomes even more superior and the signs of clarity further increase, one reaches the summit and attains the ultimate peak;
thus it is established as the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdhan*). Fearing that the initial [observation] may not be real, one therefore contemplates again.

Based on the seal-and-conformity concentration (*mudrā-anuloma-samādhi*), one gives rise to the "lower" knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); because this is the most supreme [of all worldly dharmas], it is called the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Regarding "seal-and-conformity concentration": it is so called because it seals what precedes and conforms to what follows. Regarding "giving rise to the lower knowledge of reality": it is called "lower" because it is the first attainment of the fruit of knowledge.
By means of this fruit of knowledge, one seals the two preceding stages as being empty of the apprehended object (*grāhya-śūnya*); therefore, it is so named.

One definitively seals and maintains [the realization] regarding the absence of anything to be grasped. Furthermore, by means of this wisdom, one accords with the subsequent consciousness that grasps, which is likewise empty;
therefore, it is said that within the absence of a grasper, one also accords with joyful patience. The reason for sealing what precedes and then conforming to what follows is as stated.
Since there is nothing to be grasped, the grasper necessarily does not exist; thus, this stage is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). Patience is itself wisdom (*jñāna*);

that patience takes emptiness as its object is explained in the following passage. Regarding "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), it means that by means of this concentration, one immediately and permanently severs the afflictions so that none remain.
It is called "giving rise to superior, suchness-wisdom" because the power of wisdom has become exceedingly intense.
Above, the pair of seals [showing] that both the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) are empty; therefore, this stage is called the first. The remaining text is easy to understand.

Thus, from the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, based on the consciousness that is the grasper, up until the point where the subsequent grasper is also non-existent, one subsequently touches upon the state of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

This summarizes the four stages. That is to say, during the two stages of *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Peak), one relies on the grasping consciousness (*grāhaka-vijñāna*) and contemplates only the emptiness of the object;

however, one cannot seal the object because of a lack of wisdom. When the stage of *kṣānti* (Patience) arises, there are three grades of wisdom: the lower grade is called "sealing patience" (*kṣānti-mudrā*), so named because it seals the emptiness of the grasped object (*grāhya*).
The middle grade is called "patience conforming to joy," so named because one delights in the emptiness of the grasping subject and conforms to its cultivation.

For that reason, the superior grade is called "Seal-Compliance Patience" (*mudrā-anulomikī kṣānti*). This is because it seals the emptiness of the grasper and complies with the contemplation of that [object].

The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) doubly seals both the object and consciousness as empty. Nevertheless, although one thus applies effort and practice, all of these still involve conceptual signs (*sanimitta*).

This has not yet been proven. Although the object and consciousness are empty, the characteristic of emptiness still remains; therefore, it is said that Bodhisattvas at the four stages still establish a small amount of substance before them.
What is this "small amount of substance"? It refers to the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*).

This is because the two characteristics of emptiness and existence have not been eliminated: while the imagined nature is empty, the characteristic of consciousness exists. The *Yanyi* (Exposition of the Meaning) states: "Upon the mind..."

Transformation such as this is called a "minor object. This is not without characteristics; therefore, it is said to "bear characteristics. Because these characteristics exist, one has not yet realized *tathatā* (suchness), for there is still something apprehended.
Only by extinguishing the characteristics of both emptiness and existence does one realize *tathatā*.

As follows, two verses conclude the four stages of application (*prayoga*). Specifically, the first two lines conclude the stage of "heat" (*ūṣmagata*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "That is to say, one contemplates all that exists..."

"Resembling phenomena (dharma) and resembling objects (artha) are the reflections that are the objective domain of meditative concentration; they are solely the internal mind. These two phrases concerning the "conception of objects" conclude the stage of Peak (mūrdhan). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"That is to say, one carefully observes that these things resembling phenomena and resembling objects are merely manifestations produced by one's own concentrated mind.
Thus, the following three phrases conclude the stage of Patience (kṣānti): two phrases for the lower and middle patiences, and one phrase for the higher patience.

The preceding three phrases correspond to the stage of the "Worldly Supreme Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It means that one has already realized that the apprehended object (*grāhya*) is non-existent;
once it is known that the objective realm of the apprehended is non-existent, one then knows that the apprehending mind (*grāhaka*) is likewise non-existent.

The final phrase corresponds to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It means that from this point onward, one realizes the non-existence of the duality of subject and object..."
"Attaining True Suchness (tathatā)" and "contacting" are synonymous with "realizing.

This is because in this stage of preparatory application (prayoga), one has not yet eliminated the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and has not yet realized the true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

This treatise suppresses and severs [the afflictions]. Although this stage is manifest, one still posits a slight degree of substantiality; therefore, the bondage of signs has not yet been relinquished.

That is to say, the seeds of the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of conceptualization have also not yet been eliminated; one can only suppress and remove the manifest activity of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) that arise from conceptualization.
Therefore, it is in opposition to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Regarding the innate (*sahaja*) dual grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), it has not yet been fully suppressed;

nor have the two types of innate grasping at self and phenomena been fully extinguished. This is because what has been attained through the mind of contaminated contemplation (*sāsrava-bhāvanā-citta*) has not yet been forgotten, and conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) has not yet been severed.
Next, concerning the Two Truths: the Bodhisattva at this stage contemplates both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) simultaneously, desiring to induce [realization].

Because it will lead to the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the subsequent path of seeing (*anvayadarśanamārga*), and because it subdues the two obstacles of conceptualizing a self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-āvaraṇa*), although both the ultimate and conventional truths are observed together, the ultimate truth is its primary object of observation.

This is unlike the Hīnayāna, which observes only the four established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "If the established truths are established as truths, for what reason..."
Therefore, the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) is further revealed. Answer:

If one were apart from the non-established truth, the two kinds of liberation would not be tenable—namely, liberation from the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*). Why is this?

If there is any practice regarding the established truths (*pratiṣṭhita-satya*), all such practices are practices characterized by signs. Because they are practices characterized by signs, [one remains bound].

One is bound by various signs and cannot attain liberation. Because one is not liberated from the bondage of signs, one is likewise not liberated from the bondage of coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*).

If one practices in accordance with the unestablished truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) and does not practice in accordance with signs—by not practicing in accordance with signs—one then attains liberation from the bondage of signs.
Because one attains liberation from the bondage of signs, one [is liberated] from coarse...

Even those who are heavily bound can attain liberation. Question: If liberation from all bonds and purification occurs solely through that non-conceptual truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*), for what reason is the conceptual truth (*pratiṣṭhita-satya*) demonstrated?
Answer: It is for the sake of bringing about the purification of the path of provisions (*sambhāra-mārga*) and the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Next, regarding the roots of virtue: this bodhisattva gives rise to these four kinds of meditative concentration and wisdom.

Regarding the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): although during the seven stages of preparation (*saptaprayoga*) they pertain to all four dhyānas, it is only by relying on the fourth dhyāna that the roots of goodness attain full accomplishment and fulfillment.
This is because taking rebirth in that heaven serves as the most excellent basis for entering the Path of True Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Question: From which realm do these roots of goodness arise? Answer: They arise solely based upon the wholesome [states] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It arises within the bodies of the [other] destinies. The other destinies of the desire realm are objects of aversion for them, and they are not superior; therefore, it does not arise there. Next, regarding the inclusion in the stages (*bhūmi*):

this stage is also included within the Stage of Practice through Understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), and is not included within the Stage of Realization (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). This is because one has not yet realized true *vijñapti-mātratā*.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* combines the Stage of Provisions (*sambhāra*) and the Stage of Application (*prayoga*) into the Stage of Practice through Understanding.

Next, what are the characteristics of the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*)? [From "When first illuminating the principle... to "...it is also called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*").
This clarifies the stage of realization and entry. First, a question is posed; next, a verse is cited as the answer. The commentary states:

"This Bodhisattva realizes the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), thoroughly masters the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and attains equality with all sentient beings."
Nature. One attains the equality of all bodhisattvas and the equality of all buddhas;

this is precisely what is called the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the nature of consciousness-only upon the path of seeing. Regarding "simultaneously departing from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped":
this means that both the realizing wisdom and the realized *tathatā* (suchness) are devoid of the dualistic characteristics of subject and object. By means of these two...

Because signs are conceptual constructions, and because they arise as manifestations of the mind that grasps at existence, one now severs conceptualization and realizes non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Since not even the slightest object appears before one, nothing whatsoever is apprehended; therefore, the wisdom that takes the object and the object itself are identical in nature.
All [views] are equal. One master says: "This non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) is devoid of both the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga).

Another master says: "This non-conceptual wisdom possesses both the objective and subjective aspects; for non-conceptual wisdom transforms and carries the aspect of True Suchness (tathatā) as its object.
First, he refutes the view that it is without aspect, stating: "If there were no aspect of True Suchness upon the wisdom of Suchness (tathatā-jñāna)..."

Regarding the statement that "the cognition taking suchness as its object" implies that within the cognition of form and so forth, there is no aspect of sound and so forth, yet it is also called "the cognition taking sound as its object"—this next passage refutes the view of non-existence (*nāstika-dṛṣṭi*), stating:
"If the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) were able to take an object while being non-existent, then the nature of suchness would also be called 'that which takes an object' (*ālambaka*).
To prevent such a consequence—that suchness itself is termed "that which takes an object"—one master sets forth the correct principle, saying: "This cognition... [is the seeing].

Regarding the statement that "the aspect does not exist": it is said that there is no object of apprehension (*grāhya*). Although the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) exists, because it is devoid of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is said that there is no subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*).

This does not mean that the subject of apprehension is entirely non-existent. Although the aspect-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) is absent, [the following] is the text from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 73.
It asks: "If the aspect-portion does not exist, how can it be called 'taking that as an object'? It answers, etc. The commentary explains: "That is to say, this..."

Regarding the wisdom that takes suchness as its object: although it lacks an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), it can arise by directly grasping the characteristic of suchness, and is thus termed an "object-condition" (*ālambana*).
It does not take suchness as its object by means of transforming and carrying along an image-like objective aspect; for the wisdom of suchness is not separate from suchness itself.
The next example clarifies this: "Just as when self-cognition takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) as its object, it is also a direct perception that does not involve the transformation of an image;

so too is it with this wisdom taking suchness (tathatā) as its object. If one were to claim that fundamental wisdom involves the transformation of an image when perceiving suchness, [it would be a misconception].

In that case, fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) would be unable to directly realize *tathatā* (suchness), becoming identical to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which possesses conceptualization.

How then could fundamental wisdom be called "non-conceptual"? Since subsequently attained wisdom necessarily relies upon fundamental wisdom to take its transformed images as objects, one must certainly admit that this [fundamental wisdom] has vision (*darśana*) but no mental aspect (*nimitta*). Question: Why is this stage called "penetration" (*abhisamaya*)?

[The interlocutor] asks: "What is meant by 'attainment'? [The respondent] answers: "When this wisdom arises within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), one realizes and penetrates suchness (*tathatā*);
therefore, it is called 'this wisdom. This wisdom is none other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). 'Body' (*ti*) means penetration; 'realization' (*hui*) means attainment.

Because its principle transcends deluded sentiments, it is termed 'True' (*zhen*); because the essence of all phenomena is identical, it is designated as 'Suchness' (*ru*). Question: For what reason is it also called 'vision' (*jian*)?"
Question: It is the Path (*mārga*). Answer: Because it first illuminates the principle (*tattva*). Illuminating the principle means clear vision; this vision is itself the Path. Question:

If you say it illuminates the principle, do those from the second stage (*bhūmi*) upward not also illuminate the principle? Why then do you specify "the first"? Answer: Because this is the very beginning, it receives this name;
the others follow according to their specific meanings.
However, this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is briefly explained as being twofold... because there is the power of the intention (*āśaya*) and the capacity [to act].

This clarifies the true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*) within a single moment of mind. As for the true path of seeing, it refers to the arising of the wisdom of the double emptiness (*ubhayasūnyatājñāna*).

Within the preceding path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), it simultaneously severs the seeds of the two obstacles—the conceptual obstacles of self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*). Within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), it simultaneously...
One realizes the true suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by the emptiness of both the self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*). Question:

Since the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted [realization] (*ānantarya-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) consist of many moments (*kṣaṇa*), why is it said that a single mind is called the "True Path of Seeing" (*darśana-mārga*)? Answer:

Although the matter is only fully accomplished through many moments, because they are equal in their essential character (*samatā*), they are collectively designated as "one mind. As for the statement that there are many moments, it refers to...
In the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one cultivates it for a single moment; in the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), one abandons it for a single moment;
in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one realizes it for a single moment; and in the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), one enters it for a single moment.

Although it is said that many moments are required for the matter to reach its ultimate completion, the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*) is equal from beginning to end and possesses no dual characteristics; therefore, it is collectively described as "one."
Regarding the mind: one master says that in this stage, there is gradual abandonment and gradual realization.

Because the grasping at a self (*ātman*) is coarse and superficial while the grasping at phenomena (*dharma*) is deep and subtle, one must first abandon the grasping at a self and realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and subsequently abandon the grasping at phenomena to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); thus, it is known that there is gradual abandonment and gradual realization.
Another master says that in this stage, there is sudden abandonment and sudden realization, due to the distinction in the aspirational intention (*āśaya*) during the stage of application (*prayoga*).
[The opponent says: "It is superior, because one necessarily desires to cut them off all at once; this interpretation is correct. [The author replies:

Regarding the second, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are again two types, because true seeing (*bhūtadarśana*) does not take [the objects] individually as its objective support (*ālambana*).
This clarifies the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) consisting of the three minds of the aspectual [view].

As for the "aspectual path of seeing," it refers to attaining the path of seeing by specifically taking the aspects (*lakṣaṇa*) of sentient beings and all phenomena as its object; thus it is called the "aspectual path of seeing. This, in turn, has two types.

The first is that which involves three grades of mind contemplating the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*). The non-established truth is precisely suchness (*tathatā*); that is to say, by means of the three grades of wisdom—

The mind observes suchness (*tathatā*) because it attains the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). What are the three categories? First, the wisdom that internally dispels the conceptual object of sentient beings (*sattva-prajñapti*).

"Internally" refers to the internal body. That which lacks intrinsic substance is called "conceptual. This means that by means of the wisdom capable of dispelling [delusion], one turns back to observe the self (*ātman*) grasped within the internal body and sees that it is not truly existent;
rather, it merely appears as a sentient being through the power of the internal mind. This...

This emulates the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), wherein the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) severs the grasping at a self. Second, regarding "internally dispelling the wisdom that [perceives] the provisional conditions of all phenomena":

"all phenomena" refers to the real dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Furthermore, by means of the wisdom that can dispel them, one observes that even the real dharmas of the five aggregates grasped within one's own body are unobtainable.
This emulates the uninterrupted path, wherein the seeing aspect severs the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Furthermore, the third [wisdom], which dispels the false conditions of all phenomena pertaining to all sentient beings, contemplates all phenomena of all sentient beings as a whole.

This follows the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), wherein the aspect of vision (*darśana-bhāga*) simultaneously abandons the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) and simultaneously realizes the two emptinesses of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*).
Because these three wisdoms abandon [the objects] specifically and realize them collectively, such is the case for the person here.
The dharmas consist of two obstacles, each divided into upper and lower levels; the coarse is the upper, and the subtle is the lower.

If the two coarse levels are removed separately, it is because wisdom is still weak and has not yet severed them both simultaneously. Only when superior wisdom is attained can one sever them both at once.
Thus, these are described according to wisdom as soft, medium, and superior. "Soft" refers to the lower level. The severance by the initial wisdom is termed "soft."
The wisdom that abandons [defilements] next is called "middling," because it is superior to what precedes it and inferior to what follows.

The wisdom that abandons [defilements] last is called "superior," because it can abandon the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) and this wisdom is the most supreme. If categorized according to the weak, middling, and strong grades of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is that which is abandoned last.
That which is abandoned in the intermediate stage is called the medium grade; that which is abandoned at the initial stage is called the superior grade.

However, during the first two moments of knowledge, they are not yet preeminent, as they specifically take as their object the various phenomena within one's own body, excluding the provisional designations of self and dharmas.

Upon reaching the third moment of mind, that knowledge becomes superior, extensively taking as its object all phenomena of all sentient beings, both internal and external, excluding the provisional designations of self and dharmas.
The first two are called the Knowledge of Phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), because they take the various phenomena of sentient beings as their respective objects.

The third is called the Knowledge of Subsequent Similarity (*anvayajñāna*), because it takes them collectively as its object, being similar in nature to the preceding two knowledges. Question: Why is this called the Path of Vision with Characteristics (*lakṣaṇadarśanamārga*)?

Answer: Because within the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the aspect of vision regarding the two emptinesses (*dvayaśūnyatā*) is distinguished by its immediate and liberated [attainments] from the specific obscurations to be abandoned.
Because it establishes [the path] in its entirety. Regarding the term "dharma" (法), it carries the meaning of "emulation.

Within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), although there are the self-witnessing portions (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the two emptinesses, it is the seeing portions (*darśanabhāga*) of those two emptinesses that directly realize *tathatā* (suchness) and thus emulate it. However, within the seeing portion...
There are paths of uninterrupted liberation (*ānantarya-vimukti-mārga*). According to what is abandoned and what is realized, there are four aspects of vision (*darśana-bhāga*).

Because the afflictions are severed individually within the path of uninterruptedness, the aspects of vision regarding the two emptinesses—of persons and of phenomena—are established separately as the first and second moments of mind.

Because the realization of principle is identical within the path of liberation, the aspects of vision regarding the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena are combined together as the third moment.

Because the mind [functions] thus, it is said that the path of seeing is established through both the specific and the general; this is called the "Path of Seeing of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*). One master states:

"These three moments of mind constitute the True Path of Seeing (*bhūtadarśanamārga*), because they do not take the Four Truths as their object. Another master presents the correct position, saying: "These three moments of mind constitute the Path of Seeing of Characteristics, because each takes [the truths] individually as its object."

The path of vision (darśanamārga), which is established through the differentiation of names and characteristics, consists of sixteen moments of mind based on the two types of conventionally established truths (prajñaptisatya).
This passage generally clarifies the path of vision by means of these sixteen moments. As for "conventionally established truths," they are the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).

This further consists of two parts. First, based on the observation of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), one separately establishes sixteen types of mind as dharmas and categories.
That which is called the "grasped" is suchness (*tathatā*); that which is called the "grasper" is correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). "Dharma" refers here to the present dharma.
"Category" (*jāti*) refers to a type. This means that the Dharma-knowledge and Dharma-patience take *tathatā* (suchness) as their object; this *tathatā* is that which is grasped by knowledge.
The subsequent category-patience and category-knowledge take the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of that knowledge as their object; this seeing-portion is the knowledge that performs the grasping.

Therefore, these are called the sixteen moments of mind consisting of the grasper and the grasped. First, regarding "Dharma-patience for the knowledge of suffering": "suffering" refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

"Dharma" refers to the teaching arisen through the predominance of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom that takes the phenomena of suffering as its object during the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
"Receptivity" (*kṣānti*) refers to the arising of untainted insight (*anāsravaprajñā*) that realizes the Truth of Suffering directly, by virtue of the predominant power of prior investigation.
By means of this insight, one permanently abandons all afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering. This...
This is the cause of knowledge (*jñāna*). This "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is the knowledge that arises immediately after patience;

it is able to contemplate the *tathatā* (suchness) within the realm of suffering and is able to sever the twenty-eight types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the three realms.

Specifically, there are ten [latent tendencies] for the suffering of the desire realm, and nine for the suffering of each of the two upper realms—because hatred is excluded from those two realms—the three realms together comprise twenty.
Eight. Second, the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*): the knowledge that takes the suchness (*tathatā*) of suffering as its object is called the dharma-knowledge of suffering.

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the fruit of "patience" (*kṣānti*); because of the preceding patience, this knowledge manifests. When this knowledge manifests, one contemplates suchness and realizes the aforementioned liberation.
Third, the subsequent-knowledge-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*): this refers to that which occurs immediately after the dharma-knowledge of suffering.

There arises untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). This is the third mind, which, in a single moment, individually and internally realizes the patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).

That is to say, one realizes the patience regarding phenomena by means of the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*), and realizes the knowledge of phenomena by means of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
As for the statement that "all subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category," it means that all subsequent noble dharmas rely upon the preceding dharmas. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:

Because the preceding serves as the basis for each subsequent one. That is to say, following those two moments of mind, all the noble dharmas up to those of an Arhat (aśaikṣa) arise in dependence upon these two minds.

As for the "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*), it refers to the fact that when this third "subsequent patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe ’nvayakṣānti*) occurs, an untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) arises;
this knowledge takes only the third "subsequent patience regarding suffering" as its object.
It is said that this refers to the "certainty and approval" (*niścaya-anumodana*) of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*).

Just as there are two knowledges for each of the two truths within the truth of suffering, one should know that it is likewise for the remaining truths; thus, taken together, there are sixteen knowledges.

All of these sever the twenty-eight types of conceptual proclivities (*parikalpa-anuśaya*). Among these sixteen moments of mind, the first two contemplate the *tathatā* (suchness), while the latter two contemplate wisdom—that is, the Dharma-knowledge.

The patience of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) contemplates suchness (*tathatā*), because it awakens to the grasped object (*grāhya*). The subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) contemplate wisdom, because they awaken to the grasper subject (*grāhaka*).
As it is with one truth, so it is with all truths. This patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) takes suchness as its object;

it emulates the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) regarding the truth of suffering. The dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*) takes suchness as its object; it emulates the true [path].
Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the liberation path (*vimuktimārga*) of the insight-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) realizes the principle underlying the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

The subsequent-knowledge-forbearance regarding suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñānakṣānti*) takes the preceding insight-portion as its object; it emulates the self-witnessing (*svasaṃvitti*) of the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) of the first moment by taking the insight-portion as its object. Subsequent-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) takes the preceding insight-portion as its object;
it emulates the self-witnessing of the liberation path of the second moment by taking the insight-portion as its object. Because this is simply the aforementioned knowledge, there is no distinction.
Established separately, it is called the Path of Vision by Way of Names and Characteristics (*nāmalakṣaṇadarśanamārga*).

Second, based on the contemplation of the objects of the lower and upper truths, that which eliminates the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) through discrimination is called the Path of Vision by Way of Names and Characteristics.

This is specifically elucidated as the Path of Vision by Way of Names and Characteristics through sixteen moments of mind. Based on the contemplation of the objects of the lower and upper truths, a distinct system is established.

Regarding the sixteen moments of mind: *dharmakṣānti* and *dharma-jñāna* take the suchness (*tathatā*) of the lower realm as their object; *anvaya-kṣānti* and *anvaya-jñāna* take the suchness of the higher realms as their object.
Because one enters into the vision of the lower realm, it is termed "Dharma" (*dharma*), while the higher realm is termed "Subsequent" (*anvaya*).
Thus, these are called the sixteen moments of mind regarding the objects of the lower and upper truths. The desire realm is the manifest realm, whereas the two upper realms are not.
The present realm takes the Four Truths as its object and gives rise to two types of mind.

That is to say, by contemplating the Four Truths of the desire realm individually, one establishes eight types of mind consisting of the Dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti) and Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna); by contemplating the Four Truths of the higher realms collectively, one establishes eight types of mind consisting of the Subsequent-patience (anvaya-kṣānti) and Subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
This is because within each of the Four Truths of the lower and higher realms, there are respectively two types of mind: patience and knowledge.

Thus, there are sixteen. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Within the twelve truths, sixteen types of knowledge arise; namely, the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
However, one contemplates only the desire realm as the dharma (*dharma*); that is, contemplating the suffering of the desire realm is called dharma-patience and dharma-knowledge.

Next, contemplating the suffering of the two higher realms is called subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), because they are analogous to the desire realm. As it is said:
Regarding "those that correspond," this means: the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* takes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the desire realm as its object;

it emulates the seeing aspect of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) by severing the afflictions of the desire realm. The *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* takes the suchness of the desire realm as its object;

it emulates the seeing aspect of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) within the true path of seeing by realizing the principle of the desire realm. The *duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti* takes the suchness of the higher realms as its object; it emulates...
The seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the afflictions of the upper realms.

If the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) takes the reality of the upper realms as its object, the seeing aspect of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes the principle of the upper realms.

These sixteen moments of mind, combining those of the lower and upper realms, collectively sever one hundred and twelve types of proclivities (*anuśaya*), all of which are afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
If one follows the principle of the extensive dissemination of the holy teachings (up to the point where it says):
"By these nine minds, it is called the Path of Vision characterized by aspects; this is named the Path of Vision characterized by the nine aspects of mind. Regarding the nine types of mind:

they are established based on the distinctions between the two sets of sixteen moments of calm abiding and insight within the previously established truths. As for the phrase "the combination of the forbearances and knowledges of the categories of Dharma and Subsequent": it means...

Dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti) and Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), as well as subsequent patience (anvaya-kṣānti) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)—for each truth (satya), there are four moments of mind. Thus, there are sixteen moments of mind (four sets of four).

Now, if one combines dharma-patience and subsequent patience into a single "patience," and dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge into a single "knowledge," then within the four truths, there is only one patience and one knowledge for each.
Therefore, it is said that patience and knowledge each have four contemplations, which constitute eight [moments].
Mind. There are eight associated cessations (*śamatha*). Because they are unified within a single mind, there are nine minds in total. Question:
In the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cessation and insight (*vipaśyanā*) proceed together. Why, then, is insight divided into eight while cessation is combined into one? Answer:

Although cessation and insight operate in tandem during the path of seeing, within that path, the aspect of "seeing" is primary. Insight accords with the meaning of seeing, whereas cessation does not.

Therefore, the contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) are opened up into eight, while the cessations (*śamatha*) are combined into one; thus they are not the same. Based on these nine mental states, it is called the Path of Seeing with Aspects (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).

All paths of seeing with aspects are conventionally said to rely upon the Truth (*satya*). [This continues] until the final path of seeing with aspects, which is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

This clarifies that the two types of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are established as preceding and succeeding based on the conventional truth, not because they actually exist as preceding and succeeding in reality.
As with the three aforementioned aspects of the path of seeing, both are conventionally described as preceding and succeeding based upon the true path of seeing;

in fact, the path of seeing also arises immediately after the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*). This refers to the path of seeing.
One gives rise to three kinds of mind regarding the non-established truths (apratiṣṭhita-satya), which can suppress the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of conceptualized afflictions.
Then, one gives rise to sixteen kinds of mind within the established truths (pratiṣṭhita-satya), observing them with precise scrutiny so that afflictions no longer arise.

At the stage of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), fundamental wisdom arises, which is able to sever the latent tendencies of conceptualization; this is not what is meant by "true vision" (bhūta-darśana).
Only after the Path of True Seeing (darśanamārga) has arisen can the Path of Subsequent Seeing (anvayadarśanamārga) arise.

If it is claimed that the Path of Subsequent Seeing can only arise after the Path of True Seeing, would this not imply that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are suppressed only after they have already been abandoned?

For it is precisely at the time of the Path of True Seeing that the conceptual latent dispositions are completely severed. Question: Since both paths of seeing proceed simultaneously without contradiction, how is this so?
Why is it that the verse speaks only of "not apprehending anything at all" and does not mention the latter? The answer is:

the preceding true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*) realizes the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), while the subsequent image-path of seeing (*nimittadarśanamārga*) realizes the appearances of consciousness-only. Between these two paths, the former is superior;

therefore, the verse speaks specifically of it. That is to say, the true path of seeing is fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), which directly destroys the ignorance regarding the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

The path of seeing by means of images is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Although it lacks the power to destroy the ignorance that deludes one regarding the principle (*tattva*), it is nonetheless able to destroy the ignorance that deludes one regarding phenomena (*vastu*).
Therefore, both paths of seeing are subsumed under these two types of wisdom.
Do all subsequently attained wisdoms (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) possess two parts? (Up to: By this, both parts of subsequently attained wisdom exist. Question:

Do all subsequently attained wisdoms possess the two parts of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)? One master says: Both the objective and subjective aspects are absent, because they are free from the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*).

Another master says: The subjective aspect exists while the objective aspect is absent; it is said that the subjective aspect exists because it involves conceptualization (*vikalpa*), whereas [the objective aspect is absent] because it is direct [perception].
Because it illuminates the object, its [objective] aspect (*nimitta*) is absent. One master sets forth the correct principle, stating: "Both the aspect and the seeing [faculty] exist.

This contemplation is said to resemble the aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*), because it cannot directly take True Suchness as its object. Contemplation is that which transforms from the seeing-faculty (*darśana-bhāga*) to manifest as an aspect and then takes that as its object;

thus, it is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). As for 'discriminating the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena,' this refers to observing all sentient beings."
Because the Buddha teaches expedient methods according to the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding the statement that he manifests his physical body:

this is for the sake of those whose wisdom is pure and whose faculties are matured, so that he may teach the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*). If the two aspects of the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*) did not exist, how could there be such matters as manifesting a body, manifesting a land, preaching the Dharma, or saving sentient beings?
Question: In the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been transformed; it should not...

Furthermore, [the opponent] manifests the forms of bodies, lands, and so forth. [The respondent] answers: If, in the state of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one were to transform the basis of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) such that form no longer appears, then in that same state of the transformation of the basis, one would also transform the other four aggregates;
consequently, there would be no sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest. Moreover, if there were no sensation and the rest, one would be like earth or wood;

how then could one be called "Greatly Awakened" (*Mahābuddha*)? Furthermore, if this wisdom does not rely upon its own essential substance (*svabhāva*) but transforms into something resembling sound and form...

If it were to take [external objects] as its objective support (*ālambana*), then when perceiving a form (*rūpa*), it would necessarily perceive sound (*śabda*) and so forth, because it would be taking phenomena that are distinct from its own nature as its objective support.

Furthermore, if this cognition were not to manifest a reflected image (*pratibimba*) when taking non-existent phenomena such as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns as its objective support, [it could not perceive them].
It should have no object of cognition (*ālambana*), because its essence is not real and it lacks the function of being an object. The *Zhengjīng* (Mirror of the True Doctrine) asks:
"When the sixth consciousness cognizes the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, does this object of cognition exist or not?

If it exists, the holy teachings should not use these as metaphors for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). If one says it does not exist, then that which is non-existent has no essence and cannot be an object of cognition."

Regarding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): if one says that this mind has no objective condition, how can the treatises state that the "directly perceived objective condition" exists for all cognitions?
