Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the immovable seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one remains unshaken by the winds of the eight worldly concerns (*aṣṭa-loka-dharma*). It is also like the sun, which rises in the east and shines universally upon all lands. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the rising of the sun of Dharma, one brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings without partiality. It is also like the moon, which waxes and wanes yet never abandons its cooling light. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the cycle of rebirth, one continues to provide the cooling relief of the Dharma to all beings throughout the succession of lives. It is also like a great king who, having ascended the throne, issues commands that all subjects must obey. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the sovereignty of the Buddha, one gains mastery over all dharmas. It is also like a master musician who, having tuned the strings of a lute, produces harmonious sounds. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the harmony of the Mahāyāna, one brings about the symphony of the Buddha’s teachings. It is also like a great physician who, having mastered all medical treatises, cures all illnesses. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the medicine of the Dharma, one eradicates the diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*). It is also like a great leader who, having united the people, protects them from all calamities. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the leadership of the Tathāgata, one protects all sentient beings from the perils of the three realms. It is also like a great fire that consumes all fuel and leaves no residue. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the fire of wisdom, one burns away all the fuel of the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). It is also like a great wind that sweeps across the sky without obstruction. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the wind of liberation, one traverses the expanse of the Dharma without hindrance. It is also like a great ship that carries merchants across the vast ocean. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the ship of the Mahāyāna, one ferries all sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death. It is also like a great mountain that cannot be shaken by any force. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the mountain of the Buddha’s body (*dharmakāya*), one remains firm and unshakable. It is also like a great river that flows continuously without interruption. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the flow of the Dharma, one maintains the continuity of the Buddha’s lineage. It is also like a great treasury that holds immeasurable wealth. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the treasury of the Tathāgata, one stores the inexhaustible jewels of the Buddha’s qualities. It is also like a great drum that resounds throughout the world. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the drum of the Dharma, one proclaims the truth to all sentient beings. It is also like a great mirror that reflects all forms without distortion. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the mirror of omniscience, one perceives the true nature of all phenomena as they are. It is also like a great cloud that covers the entire sky. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the cloud of compassion, one pervades all sentient beings with the rain of the Dharma. It is also like a great king who, having conquered all enemies, enjoys peace and prosperity. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the victory of the Buddha, one attains the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa. It is also like a great wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) who possesses the seven treasures and rules over the four continents. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the wheel of the Dharma, one turns the wheel of the teaching and brings all beings under the protection of the Triple Gem. It is also like a great physician who, having prepared a universal remedy, cures all diseases. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the universal medicine of the Dharma, one heals the ailments of all sentient beings. It is also like a great bridge that connects this shore to the other shore. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the bridge of the path, one leads all beings from the shore of saṃsāra to the shore of nirvāṇa. It is also like a great lamp that dispels the darkness of a house. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the lamp of wisdom, one illuminates the inner chamber of the mind. It is also like a great rain that falls equally upon all lands. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the rain of the Dharma, one bestows equal benefit upon all sentient beings. It is also like a great king who, having ascended the throne, grants amnesty to all prisoners. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the throne of the Buddha, one releases all beings from the bonds of the afflictions. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the diagnosis of the afflictions, one applies the medicine of the Dharma according to the needs of each individual. Likewise, by dedicating the roots of virtue toward the fire of the Bodhisattva’s vows, one ensures that the practice of the path is never extinguished. It is also like a great wind that, having arisen, cannot be stopped by any obstacle. This refers to the practice of subsequent vows. Regarding "not being interspersed with the two obstacles," this means practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) in order to abandon the two obstacles.

If even one of the seven [auxiliaries] is lacking, one does not reach the other shore (*pāramitā*). Therefore, these ten perfections should each be analyzed according to four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
first, that which is giving but not a perfection, because it is not associated with the seven excellences; second, that which is a perfection but not giving... [the text continues].

The third is rejoicing in the giving of others; because it possesses the seven excellences, it is both a crossing-over (*tāraṇa*) and a giving (*dāna*), as it practices giving and so forth while possessing the seven excellences.
The fourth is neither a crossing-over nor a giving; it is rejoicing in the giving of others, as it does not correspond with the seven excellences.

Thus, these ten types beginning with giving are comprised within the nature of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and out-flowing (*sāsrava*); the ten *pāramitās*, however, are conditioned and out-flow-free (*anāsrava*).

Because they are subsumed under their essential natures (*svabhāva*), there are only these ten, neither more nor less. This should be understood as it is explained at length in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

"Great body" refers to a noble and dignified physique. "Patience that inspires followers" refers to sentient beings gathering around and submitting to one.
Because of wealth, a superior body, and numerous followers, one becomes preeminent among the realms of existence; this is called the "path of supremacy.

"Diligence that can subdue afflictions" refers to the cultivation of skillful means for practicing virtue. "Concentration that matures sentient beings" means that based on meditative concentration, one manifests supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Therefore, regarding the perfection of wisdom as the Buddha-dharma: because the Buddha-dharma arises from wisdom, it possesses these three virtues and is called "definitively superior.

On the path of the bodhisattvas, there are only these two; if either one is lacking, the path is not accomplished. Thirdly, the six perfections are shown to be neither more nor less than these two benefits for self and others:
giving wealth gathers others in; ethical discipline does not harm them; and patience endures their harm. This...
All three are equally conducive to benefiting sentient beings. Regarding the statement that the latter three involve "diligent cultivation of application," the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"By means of diligence, although one has not yet permanently severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) or permanently destroyed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one is able to apply oneself with courageous effort."
Cultivating all categories of wholesome qualities, those afflictions cannot shake him. Through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he permanently subdues the afflictions;

through wisdom (*prajñā*), he permanently eradicates the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, by means of the first three [perfections], he observes the conventional to benefit sentient beings and thus does not abide in *nirvāṇa*;
and by means of the latter three, he is able to sever the afflictions and thus does not abide in *saṃsāra*. By virtue of these two—
Because they are meaningful, they can serve as the provisions for non-abiding nirvāṇa. Therefore, the first six perfections neither increase nor decrease. Question:
Since the six perfections are thus, what of the latter four? Answer: The latter four assist the former six so that they may be fulfilled.
Skillful means (upāya) assists the first three, such as giving (dāna). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By means of the first three [perfections], sentient beings are gathered..."

Regarding the *saṃgrahavastus* (means of attraction): because they are embraced through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), that is to say, by skillfully employing generosity and the other [perfections] to attract beings.

Regarding "wishing to assist those who exert diligence": the *Mahāśāstra* states that by means of right aspiration (*samyakpraṇidhāna*), one can overcome weak dispositions, so that afflictions (*kleśa*) become thin and subtle, and one gives rise to the cultivation of diligence.
Regarding "assisting those who possess meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)": the *Gambhīrārtha-samuccaya* states that if all...

Because the bodhisattva relies upon virtuous friends, hears the true Dharma, and applies correct mental attention as causes and conditions, their inferior intention is transformed into a superior intention, and they also attain resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the supreme fruit; this is called the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*).
By virtue of this power, the mind abides within and becomes capable of mastery; therefore, it is said that the power-factor assists meditative concentration.

Regarding "wisdom assists prajñā," the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "If bodhisattvas, having already been able to take the hearing of the Dharma as a condition, cultivate it well, they are able to give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
this is called wisdom (*jñāna*). By means of this wisdom, they are further able to induce supramundane insight (*lokottara-prajñā*);
therefore, it is said that wisdom assists prajñā. Thus, one should know that the latter four [perfections] are able to assist the cultivation of the former six.
The perfection of cultivation.
Regarding the ten stages in sequence, this refers to the explanation of their general and specific names from the preceding to the succeeding, as explained elsewhere.

First, according to the sequence of the *Abhinirhāra-śāstra*, the *Gambhīrārtha-samuccaya* states: "Because they serve as the basis for the successive production of each subsequent stage. That is to say:
If bodhisattvas have no regard or attachment for their bodies or possessions, they are able to receive and uphold the pure prohibitive precepts.
To protect these precepts, they cultivate patience. Having cultivated patience, they are able to arouse diligence.
Having aroused diligence, they are able to accomplish meditative concentration. Having accomplished meditative concentration, they are then able to attain supramundane wisdom. Therefore:
The six pāramitās follow this sequence. Furthermore, they are arranged according to the order of the *Saṃgrahaṇī* (Compendium), and because each subsequent one purifies each preceding one:
for instance, while generosity primarily intends to benefit others, ethical discipline ensures that one does not harm them.
Because patience can endure those afflictions and so forth, it further purifies giving. Next, the sequence is established by way of the coarse and the subtle:
giving is coarse, while ethical discipline is subtle; compared to patience, ethical discipline is coarse, whereas patience is subtle, and so on.
Next, the sequence is established by way of the easy and the difficult: giving is easy, while ethical discipline is difficult. Compared to [patience], ethical discipline...
Regarding patience, ethical discipline is easy, whereas patience is difficult; such are the ten cultivations.
These ten cultivations consist of five types of cultivation (up to as explained at length in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts). Their characteristics are described therein.
Regarding the discussion on cultivation: there are four kinds of cultivation based on reliance and sustenance.
First, cultivation based on reliance upon causes, which refers to the correct practice of the pāramitās by means of the power of one’s spiritual lineage (gotra).

Second, cultivation based on reliance upon maturation, which refers to the correct practice of the pāramitās by means of the power of one’s superior physical constitution. Third, cultivation based on reliance upon aspiration, which refers to...
Through the power of the original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*), one practices the correct cultivation of the *pāramitās*.
Through the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), which is the fourth basis, one practices the correct cultivation of the *pāramitās* by means of the power of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, there are four kinds of cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*): first, cultivation based on mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), which [concerns] all the *pāramitās*.

1. Cultivation based on the mental application of superior conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), which gives rise to an exalted and resolute understanding through the teachings of the corresponding sūtras. 2.

Cultivation based on the mental application of relishing (*āsvādana-manasikāra*), which means perceiving the excellent qualities of the perfections already attained and giving rise to a profound sense of attachment and relish for them. 3.

Cultivation based on the mental application of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-manasikāra*), which means generating deep joy toward the acts of giving and so forth performed by all sentient beings throughout all worlds.

Rejoicing. Cultivation through the mental engagement of joy based on the four reliances means generating a profound aspiration and delight toward one's own and others' future, superior perfections (*pāramitā*).
There are six kinds of cultivation based on this intentionality:
namely, by way of the intentionality of insatiability, the intentionality of vastness, the intentionality of joy, the intentionality of gratitude and virtue, and the intentionality of non-attachment.
Because of their virtuous and noble intention, they cultivate the various pāramitās. Furthermore, there are three kinds of cultivation based on skillful means:
namely, observing the three spheres through non-conceptual wisdom so that all are purified. Why is this so?
By means of this expedient, because all practices cultivated through mental engagement are fully perfected, there are also three kinds of cultivation based on mastery:
namely, mastery over the body, mastery over conduct, and mastery over teaching.
Mastery over the body refers to the two bodies of all Tathāgatas—the *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body) and the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body). Mastery over conduct refers to all Tathāgatas...
The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) comes forth; because it can manifest for all sentient beings every kind of practice in accordance with the Dharma, it is called "sovereign.
This means it is able to proclaim all the various distinctions of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Because they are free from obstruction.
Regarding the inclusion of these ten: it means that all ten are subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), as they take conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) as their object.

Regarding the inclusion of their characteristics: it means that each of these ten types includes all ten others, because they are mutually concordant, just like the skillful means of generosity (*dāna*).

Everything can be found therein. Just as one relinquishes both internal and external bodies and wealth, this is the skillful means of giving (*dāna*). Within these skillful means, if one relinquishes everything, this is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

Furthermore, within this very context, if one uses a mind of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) to guard against and ward off all harm, oppression, and affliction toward the nature of others, this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Within this very context...
To endure obstacles, harm, and fatigue is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
To repeatedly arouse a courageous and diligent mind for giving within this very context is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

To have a mind that is purely wholesome within this very context, focused on a single object without wandering outward, is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). Within this very context, [to have] skillful...
To undertake the practice of giving and to not hold divergent views regarding the reality of cause and effect is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
In this manner, up to the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), each should be properly established according to its respective application.

If one explains them based on their mutual induction from preceding to succeeding, then the former necessarily includes the latter, while the latter does not include the former. If, however, one relies on their mutual support from preceding to succeeding...

In this explanation, what follows necessarily subsumes what precedes it, whereas what precedes does not subsume what follows. If categorized according to the pure and the mixed, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
"Pure" refers to cultivation by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); "mixed" refers to cultivation by means of subsequently attained applied wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-prayoga-jñāna*).

This means being pure and not mixed, or mixed and not pure, and so forth. If the ten perfections are subsumed under the six, the sixth [perfection] subsumes the final four, because it encompasses both types of wisdom.

If the ten perfections are subsumed under the ten, the sixth subsumes only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), while the final four are subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
Regarding these ten fruits, there are four that are *sāsrava* (with outflows), which may be explained either individually, in combination with one another, or as a pair.

To establish the argument for the fruits: among the *sāsrava* dharmas, there are four fruits—namely, *vipāka* (maturation), *niṣyanda* (outflow), *adhipati* (dominant), and *puruṣakāra* (human effort)—excluding the *visamyoga* (disjunction) fruit, because within *sāsrava* dharmas, there are no *anāsrava* (without outflows) phenomena. Among the *anāsrava* dharmas, there are four fruits—namely, *visamyoga*.

Regarding the outflow (*niṣyanda*), dominant (*adhipati*), and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) results—excluding the ripening (*vipāka*) result, as there are no contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena within uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena—it is said that these *pāramitās* constitute the result of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) because they can permanently sever their respective opposites.

In this present life, the gathering of oneself and others through giving and the other perfections constitutes the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). In future lives, [this continues] successively...

Increasing and excelling, arising successively, these are the *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruits). A great Bodhisattva is the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit). [The results are: attaining great wealth;
being reborn in happy realms; being without enmity or ruin; possessing much joy and happiness; being honored among sentient beings; having no physical harm;
and belonging to a vast and noble lineage—these are the *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruits) of the perfections such as generosity. Question: What...
Therefore, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [paths] each exclude one fruit. Answer:

This is because these two fruits each belong to a single category, whereas the remaining three are common to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated. Question: If that is so, why is it said elsewhere that all [fruits] are common to the five fruits?
Answer: This is explained either in terms of the mutual assistance between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), or by combining the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
Regarding the mutual inclusion of the ten [factors] with the three trainings (*śikṣā*), their objects (*ālambana*), modes of activity (*ākāra*), and so forth, are as explained elsewhere.
The treatise discusses the three trainings. First, regarding the precepts, there are three types. 1. **The Precept of Restraint (saṃvara-śīla):** Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyā* explains:

"It refers to the guarding and upholding [of oneself] against those unwholesome states that give rise to negligence. Because it restrains all evil and unwholesome actions of body and speech, it is called 'restraint' (*saṃvara*). 2.
**The Precept of Gathering Wholesome Dharmas (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla):** This enables one to realize all qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

Regarding the Buddha-dharma, the precept that benefits others means being able to assist sentient beings by performing, according to the Dharma, impartial and blameless deeds that bring sentient beings to maturity.

Some say that the latter two [precepts] are established based on the first, because by guarding oneself, one is able to cultivate roots of goodness such as making offerings to the Buddhas and benefiting all sentient beings. Therefore, Vasubandhu said:

One who abides in the vow of restraint is able to establish the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas; by means of this, one cultivates and accumulates all Buddha-dharmas and realizes great enlightenment.
Furthermore, one is able to establish the ethical discipline of benefiting others; by means of this, one is able to bring sentient beings to maturity.
Some say that the former two serve to accomplish the fruit of the latter one. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If one is able to abide in the former two kinds..."

Pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) is able to induce and encompass the ethical discipline for benefiting sentient beings. These three categories of ethical discipline are the causes of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Why is this? The first is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*), the second is the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*), and the third is the virtue of beneficence (*anugrahaguṇa*).

Since the four fearlessnesses, the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and so forth, do not transcend these three virtues, it is for this reason that ethical discipline is said to have three categories.
Regarding the fact that this [Mahāyāna] shares and does not share with the Two Vehicles in terms of its profound and vast nature, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"As for the excellence of the shared and unshared training rules (*śikṣāpada*): it means that because Bodhisattvas do not manifest any sinful natures, they share the same characteristics as the Śrāvakas;
yet because they do manifest prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), they are not shared with them. Regarding these training rules..."
What constitutes an offense for a śrāvaka may not constitute an offense for a bodhisattva; what constitutes an offense for a bodhisattva may not constitute an offense for a śrāvaka.

This is because a bodhisattva possesses the precepts of body, speech, and mind, whereas a śrāvaka possesses only the two precepts of body and speech. Therefore, a bodhisattva may commit an offense of the mind, which does not apply to śrāvakas.
To state it briefly: all actions of body and speech that benefit sentient beings and are free from fault [constitute the bodhisattva's path].
Regarding mental action (*manas-karman*), a bodhisattva should practice all of them and should train in all of them.
It should be understood that this is what is called the distinction between the common and the uncommon. As for the distinction of profundity:
it refers to how bodhisattvas, through such categories of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), may perform the ten types of actions, including killing, yet remain without fault and give rise to merit.

Measuring their merit, they swiftly realize Bodhi. For this reason, they may act as kings, manifesting various deeds that afflict sentient beings in order to establish them within the Vinaya; furthermore, they manifest various Jātaka tales.

Manifesting conduct that appears to oppress other sentient beings while truly gathering them in, first causing their minds to give rise to deep pure faith and subsequently bringing them to maturity—this is called the profound and superior ethical discipline (*śīla*) of a bodhisattva.
Regarding its vast and superior nature, there are four aspects: first, by means of various immeasurable training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Greatness: (1) by being vast through the accumulation of immeasurable merit;
(2) by being vast through the intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; and (3) by being vast through the establishment of unsurpassed enlightenment.
By virtue of these excellences, one should know that the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) is most preeminent. There are four types of training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
There are three interpretations. Master Ying states: first, it eliminates the obstacle of unwholesome karma; second, it eliminates the obstacle of attachment to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);

third, it eliminates the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*); and fourth, it eliminates the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Master Xianshou states: first, it can eliminate the obstacle of distracted and defiled karma;
second, it can eliminate the obstacle of attachment to the flavor of concentration and to stillness; third, it can eliminate the obstacle of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*); and fourth—
It is able to eliminate and purify the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa) that hinder the attainment of fruition; this is largely the same as what was previously explained. Qingliang says:

"This means that by means of the wisdom that realizes the truth within phenomena themselves, one remedies the state prior to the [first] stage, accomplishing the first bhūmi and attaining the 'Worthy Guardian' samādhi (*bhadrapāla-samādhi*). By means of this samādhi..."

This is because one is able to maintain the virtuous and wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and the supramundane. The first three stages constitute the mundane; the fourth stage constitutes the supramundane.
This is because, having realized that phenomena are themselves reality (*tathatā*), one is able to remain in meditative concentration even amidst distraction.

Second, by means of the wisdom of the function inherent in the essence, one counteracts the inability to initiate activity on the fourth stage, thereby enabling entry into the conventional world on the fifth stage and bringing it to completion.

The Samādhi of King Accumulated Merit: Third, by means of the wisdom of equality and signlessness, one counteracts the state of the fifth bhūmi where, although one can conform to worldly conventions, true equality has not yet been attained;
this brings about the functional power of the great light of prajñā of the sixth and seventh bhūmis, thereby accomplishing the Mahāyāna Radiance Samādhi.
Fourth, by means of the wisdom of equality and effortlessness, one counteracts the effortful activity of the seventh bhūmi, causing entry into [the eighth bhūmi].
From the eighth stage up to the fruit of Buddhahood, one attains the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and brings all activities to completion.

Since the fruit possesses these four [aspects] and the cause also universally cultivates them, this interpretation is correct. Regarding the objects of focus, the antidotes, the capacities, and the inducements for these four types of activity, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"As for the distinction of the objects of focus, it means that the Mahāyāna Dharma serves as the object of focus."

Therefore, regarding the distinction of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-viśeṣa*): it refers to the wisdom that takes the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as its object, which, by means of the principle of "using a wedge to extract a wedge," eliminates all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the obstructions within the *ālayavijñāna*. Regarding the distinction of capability (*karmanya-viśeṣa*):

it refers to abiding in the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-sukha*) and being able to take rebirth immediately according to one's wish. Regarding the distinction of elicitation (*ākṣepa-viśeṣa*): it refers to the ability to...
Because it triggers unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) throughout all worlds. Regarding the differentiation of its activities:
it is able to cause trembling, blazing, pervasion, manifestation, transformation, coming and going, contraction and expansion; all forms and images enter into its body;
wherever it goes, it appears either hidden or manifest among similar beings; it exercises mastery over what it does, subdues the supernormal powers of others, and bestows [benefits].
He explains mindfulness and joy. Because he emits great radiance and brings forth such supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he is further able to bring forth various difficult practices:
first, the difficult practice of self-vow, because he vows to accept the aspiration for unsurpassed enlightenment;

second, the difficult practice of non-retrogression, because the manifold sufferings of birth and death cannot cause him to turn back; third, the difficult practice of non-repudiation, [toward] all that exists...
1. The difficult practice of affection: because one does not abandon [beings] even when they commit perverse deeds. 2. The difficult practice of presence:

because one manifests all beneficial conduct toward sentient beings who are hostile. 3. The difficult practice of non-defiled conduct: because, though born in the world, one is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
4. The difficult practice of resolute conviction: because, although one has not yet fully realized it within the Mahāyāna, nevertheless—
7. The difficult practice of thorough penetration, because one possesses the capacity to thoroughly penetrate the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
8. The difficult practice of subsequent realization, because one is able to subsequently realize the profound and secret terminology spoken by all Tathāgatas.
9. The difficult practice of non-separation and non-attachment... [not separated from... not stained... [text fragment].
Because one abandons birth and death without being defiled by them. Tenth is the difficult practice of application (*prayoga*), which is able to cultivate the liberation in which all Buddhas abide;
it exhausts the limits of saṃsāra regarding all obstacles, and without effort, constantly initiates all activities for the benefit and welfare of all sentient beings.
Regarding the three types of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*): first is the non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-prajñā*), namely—

First is the superior preparatory wisdom prior to the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness). Second is the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom of the contemplation of *tathatā*.
Third is the non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom, which refers to the wisdom that contemplates conventional reality and is able to initiate various activities.
The *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The three wisdoms refer to those entered through hearing, reflection, and cultivation based on the signless Mahāyāna teachings."
The emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is collectively termed the preparatory wisdom of non-conceptualization (*avikalpa-prayoga-prajñā*).
Because one enters into the three natures of non-substantiality (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*), one attains non-conceptualization; this is termed fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-avikalpa-jñāna*).

Once fundamental non-conceptual wisdom has been attained, if one subsequently enters meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) and either reflects upon it for oneself as it was realized or explains it to others, this is termed [subsequently attained wisdom].
This refers to the post-attainment wisdom of discernment (*prsthalabdha-prajñā*). Because it possesses these meanings, it is said that there are three grades of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Whether in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their basis (*āśraya*), their causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), their objects of focus (*ālambana*), their objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or their support (*upastambha*), these three [grades] are thus established.

One should understand that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is designated as the excellence of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-viśeṣa*) by virtue of its: companions; its maturation (*vipāka*); its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*);
its renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*); its culmination (*niṣṭhāgata*); its benefits consisting of the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent stages;
its distinctions between the fundamental, subsequent, and preparatory stages through analogies; its effortless performance of activity; and its profundity.

Excellent. Within this context, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) takes as its intrinsic nature the departure from five kinds of characteristics: first, the departure from the absence of mental attention (*amanasikāra*);

second, the departure from the stages characterized by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*); and third, the departure from the tranquility of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
Fourth, because it is free from the intrinsic nature of form; fifth, because it is free from conceptualizing what is distinct from the true meaning.
One should know that being free from these five characteristics is called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Thus, regarding the inclusion of these three types of wisdom within the five stages: from the first two stages up to [the stage of] meditative concentration, they are subsumed under the wisdom of *dhyāna*;
the latter five are subsumed under the wisdom of *prajñā*. As for the mutual inclusion of the three wisdoms and the five stages as explained above:

if categorized by way of seeds, provisions, and preparatory application (*prayoga*), all three wisdoms are fully present; however, if categorized by way of actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), there is only the wisdom of preparatory application, because in these two stages [they have not yet arisen].
One attains the path of seeing (darśanamārga). Therefore, there is no fundamental wisdom (mūlaprajñā) nor subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdhaprajñā).

If one is in the stage of penetration (prativedhāvasthā), these three types of wisdom have two modes of manifestation (samudācāra) and possess all three types of seeds (bīja). This is because, in the stage of the path of seeing, both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms are directly realized (pratyakṣa-sākṣātkriyā).
Because there is no wisdom of application (*prayoga-prajñā*), in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), all three types of wisdom exist both as seeds and as manifest activity.

This is because prior to the seventh ground, both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) cognitions arise together; one abandons afflictions and realizes the truth while also giving rise to the wisdom of application.

From the eighth ground up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samudāgama-bodhi*), the two kinds of threefold wisdom exist as manifest activity within the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), for this path is contrary to the wisdom of application. Thus it is said:

There is progress, which is entirely accomplished by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This is because within the state of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-darśana*), no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is made, as one proceeds spontaneously.
Upon reaching the ultimate stage, both the manifest activity and the seeds are of two kinds; [the former] relies solely upon the fundamental [wisdom] that takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.

Subsequently, the attainment of benefit for sentient beings arises spontaneously, without the application of effort (*prayoga*), because both the seeds and the manifest forms of such effort have already been abandoned.

Next, the treatise discusses the inclusion of the three types of wisdom within the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). If they are categorized according to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the three trainings (*śikṣā*), there will be no confusion:

ethical discipline (*śīla*) includes ethical discipline; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) includes meditative concentration; and wisdom (*prajñā*) includes the final five perfections, while not including generosity (*dāna*), patience (*kṣānti*), and diligence (*vīrya*). If...
If one is taken as the primary and the others as its companions, then each of these three trainings is subsumed within the six perfections.
If the three trainings are subsumed according to their specific functions, the training in ethical discipline (śīla) subsumes the first three, taking generosity (dāna) as its requisite.
Ethical discipline (*śīla*) constitutes the essence, while patience (*kṣānti*) serves as its retinue;

therefore, the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) subsumes only meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), whereas the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) subsumes skillful means (*upāya*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). The single factor of diligence (*vīrya*) is subsumed by all three trainings, as it universally exerts them all.

If categorized according to their manifest characteristics, ethical discipline subsumes the first three [trainings] and also subsumes diligence, because it is capable of guarding pure ethical discipline.
Therefore, all other points are as previously stated.
Regarding these ten stages, all five stages possess them; whether manifest or latent, they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for the inclusion within the stages discussed in the treatise, although all ten types are present throughout the five stages, in terms of their cultivation—
Their characteristics are even more manifest in the stages, such as the generosity of the first bhūmi and the ethical discipline of the second bhūmi, and so forth.

However, regarding the two stages of the provisions (sambhāra) and the application (prayoga), for a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment, while their seeds encompass both the out-flowing (sāsrava) and the out-flow-free (anāsrava), they manifest only as out-flowing.

Because their faculties are so sharp and acute, they do not subdue conceptual discrimination; therefore, regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*), no actual manifestation arises, and it is exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*).

If one awakens through a sense of shame, having already subdued the afflictions and attained the four kinds of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), then both the seeds and the manifestations pertain to both the tainted and the untainted.
In the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), the seeds pertain to the tainted.

It is untainted (*anāsrava*), yet its active manifestation (*samudācāra*) is exclusively untainted. This is because, having attained the true Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and realized fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*), one no longer gives rise to the active manifestation of the tainted.
If one is in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), prior to the seventh ground, both the seeds and manifestations of the tainted and untainted are present, as they arise alternately.
From the eighth ground onward, while the seeds are common to both the tainted and untainted, [the manifestations are exclusively untainted].
However, their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because those tainted afflictions (*sāsrava-kleśa*) have been permanently suppressed and do not arise.
In the ultimate state (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), both the seeds and the manifestations are untainted.
These ten stages of the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*) have three designations (up to [the end of the passage]), all of which are subsumed within the ten *pāramitās*.
Regarding the three names for the causal state: the two stages of the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*) each span one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

Furthermore, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage spans another *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. Finally, from the eighth stage up to the stage of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) spans yet another [asaṃkhyeya-kalpa].
Asaṃkhyeya. During the first asaṃkhyeya, at that time, the power of generosity and the other perfections is still slight;
they are subdued by afflictions, and their fruition is still far off. They are merely called *pāramitās* because one practices one practice within a single [perfection].
During the second asaṃkhyeya, at that time, the power of generosity and the others gradually increases; they are able to subdue the afflictions, and the fruition is not far away. Therefore...
It is called "near" because within a single practice one cultivates all practices. In the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, its power increases further, and it is able to definitively subdue all afflictions;
therefore, it is called "great," because through every practice one cultivates all practices.
Question: Since one has reached the stage of Equal Enlightenment (sambodhi), afflictions do not arise and the task is already complete; for what reason is a subsequent stage established?

Regarding the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*): The answer is that although the afflictions (*kleśa*) are permanently suppressed at this stage, there still remain subtle manifest seeds of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) as well as their extremely subtle seeds of affliction which have not yet been fully eliminated;
this continues until the final moment of mind of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, it cuts off and exhausts [the afflictions] without remainder in a single moment;
only then is it called "ultimate. This concludes the ten [perfections]. Question: In which stages (*bhūmi*) are the ten practices cultivated, and what practice is cultivated in each? Answer:

Although all ten practices are indeed cultivated throughout the ten stages, according to their predominant characteristics, one practice is cultivated in each stage. For example, in the first stage, there is giving (*dāna*); in the second, [discipline (*śīla*)]; and so forth.
Regarding the stages, precepts, and so forth: Question: The practice-gates of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) comprise infinite varieties; why, then, are only these ten types explained here?
Answer: Although they are infinite, these ten types encompass them all.
Regarding the tenfold obstructions: the first is the obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is only suddenly severed when one is about to attain Buddhahood.
The following section clarifies these ten types of obstructions; first, the names of the obstructions are listed. The first is the obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being.

In the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) translated during the Liang dynasty, it is called "the nature of an ordinary person" (*bālapṛthagjanatva*) and also "the obstruction of the ordinary person’s mark of self" (*bāla-pudgala-ātma-lakṣaṇa-āvaraṇa*). Because of this grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), it is able to act as an obstruction.
The First Ground. At the time of entering the first ground, these hindrances are severed. Thus, the Great Sūtra says:

"If there are sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness, who have well cultivated various practices, who have well gathered the factors conducive to the path, who have well made offerings to the Buddhas, and who have well accumulated pure and white dharmas;
who, through the guidance of spiritual friends, have well embraced and purified their profound resolve, and have established vast aspirations, they shall give rise to [the first ground]."
Possessing vast understanding, with compassion manifest before them, they act for the sake of seeking the Buddha’s wisdom;
for the sake of attaining the ten powers; for the sake of attaining the great fearlessnesses; for the sake of attaining the equal Dharma of the Buddhas; for the sake of seeking all sentient beings;
for the sake of seeking all worlds; for the sake of purifying great compassion; and for the sake of attaining the non-remaining knowledge of the ten directions.
Therefore, for the sake of purifying all buddha-fields with unimpeded wisdom; for the sake of knowing all three periods of time in a single thought-moment;
and for the sake of turning the great wheel of Dharma with fearlessness—the bodhisattva first gives rise to such a mind.
At that very moment, they transcend the stage of ordinary beings, enter the rank of bodhisattvas, and are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, such that no one can describe their lineage.

Having transcended faults, departed from worldly destinies, entered the supramundane path, attained the dharmas of enlightenment, and dwelt in the station of a bodhisattva, they enter into the equality of the three periods of time.
Within the lineage of the Tathāgatas, they will certainly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
When a bodhisattva abides in such dharmas, it is called dwelling in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). That is to say, they experience joy because they are mindful of all Buddhas.
One gives rise to joy by recollecting the Buddhas’ dharmas; one gives rise to joy by recollecting the bodhisattvas;
one gives rise to joy by recollecting the bodhisattva practices; one gives rise to joy by recollecting the pure pāramitās, and so forth. Question:

On what basis is this designation "ordinary being" (pṛthagjana) established? Answer: It is established based on that which consists of the two kinds of obstacles—the conceptualization of self and phenomena. It is divided [into these categories].
"Distinct" excludes that which is co-emergent (*sahaja*); "seeds" excludes manifest activity (*samudācāra*). Question: By whom are these obstacles abandoned? At what time are they abandoned? Answer:

On the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) abandon only the seeds of conceptualized self (*parikalpita-ātman*); this is called attaining the nature of an Arya. At the time of the Bodhisattva’s Path of Seeing, both the seeds of conceptualized self and phenomena (*dharma*) are abandoned;
this is called attaining the nature of an Arya. Question: Are there also cases where both types are not abandoned, yet one attains [the state of an Arya]?

Question: Are the two types of views present? Answer: When either of the two types of the path of seeing manifests, those two—self and dharmas—are necessarily not established, because when wisdom arises, delusion perishes;
they cannot coexist, just as light and darkness cannot stand together, or like the two ends of a scale, where one goes down as the other rises.
There has never been a case where wisdom arises and delusion does not perish; therefore, these two natures do not exist simultaneously.
This results in a logical fallacy. If wisdom has arisen while delusion still persists, one incurs the fault of both natures being simultaneously established. Question:

If that is so, since the seeds of delusion have already been severed at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), for what purpose does one further give rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)? Answer: At the time of the path of uninterrupted transition, delusions are severed by means of subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
at the time of the path of liberation, the truth is realized by means of the fundamental [wisdom] (*mūla-jñāna*). Since the time limit [for severance] has already been reached...

They are distinct, because the application of the mind is also distinct. Furthermore, although the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), there still remains a state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*).

When the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises, it is precisely for the purpose of abandoning that state of unfitness and realizing a portion of the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: Both afflictions and karma are termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*); why is it that only [the former] is mentioned here?
Question: Are the seeds of afflictions severed, while the seeds of karma are not? Answer:

Although the seeds of karma are also severed at the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), this [text] speaks only of the afflictions that are capable of producing karma, because afflictions are the root of the seeds of karma.
For this reason, it is said in the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*) that two delusions (*moha*) and their two types of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) are severed. What are these two delusions? First—

The delusion of attachment to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa-moha*). This delusion is precisely the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), namely the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the dualistic grasping at self and phenomena.
The delusion of the afflictions of the two miserable realms (*durgati-saṃkleśa-moha*). These are the karmic fruits of the miserable realms; that is, the habitual tendencies of karma. Question:
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is precisely self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), and delusion is precisely folly (*mūḍha*). If karma and its fruit are not ignorance, how can they be called folly?
Answer: It is not only ignorance alone that may be termed folly. One should know that the various categories of folly are collectively designated as "folly."
Although the fruit of karma is not itself ignorance, it is nonetheless a category of ignorance; the subsequent types of ignorance should be understood accordingly.

Alternatively, it is said that "ignorance" refers to the five sharp and five dull afflictions (*kleśa*) among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), all of which arise together with nescience (*avidyā*);
thus, two types of ignorance are spoken of. The term "coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) here serves to manifest those two types of seeds of the sharp and dull afflictions.
"Son, it is either the state of being incapable [of functioning] due to the two types of afflictions—the sharp and the dull. Question:

"If this state of being incapable is neither a manifest activity (*samudācāra*) nor a seed (*bīja*), what is its characteristic? Answer: "It is just as when one has entered the two mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*);

it is said that for such a person, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*) belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*) is severed. Although this faculty of suffering is neither manifest nor a seed, it is termed 'coarseness' (*dauṣṭhulya*)."
The capacity for adaptability (*karmaṇyatā*) should be understood by analogy with this. Question:

Since that which is abandoned in the first stage (*bhūmi*) also pertains to both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), why is it said only that it is the obstacle of the ordinary person’s mark of self (*pṛthagjana-ātma-lakṣaṇa-āvaraṇa*), and not mentioned as the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*)? Answer:

Although that which is abandoned in the first stage actually pertains to both afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obstacles, this obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) specifically takes the cognitive obstacle as its primary object. This is because, throughout these ten stages...
It is said that these ten types of ignorance are abandoned; it is not said that they are abandoned because they are defiled.

That which obstructs the mind with afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is called "defiled," whereas the principle [obstructed by] the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is not called "defiled. These ten ignorances are precisely a portion of the delusion within the ten categories of hindrances.
Question: The two vehicles (*dviyāna*) are also able to abandon the afflictive hindrances; why is this mentioned here?

It is not mentioned. The answer is: that which is abandoned by the two vehicles is also abandoned by the Bodhisattva; however, that which is abandoned by the Bodhisattva is not abandoned by the two vehicles.
Now, it is revealed that this ignorance is abandoned by the Bodhisattva and is not within the scope of the two vehicles; therefore, it is not mentioned.

Furthermore, these ten types of ignorance are abandoned through cultivation by the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); they are not [abandoned] by the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

[They are] abandoned. Therefore, they are not mentioned. Question: Since what is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*) encompasses both afflictions (*kleśa*) and objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), why is it said only that objects of knowledge are abandoned, and not that afflictions are abandoned? Answer:

Although in this state one also simultaneously suppresses the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of innate afflictions and simultaneously abandons their seeds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-bīja*), the primary intention [of the text] does not lie therein.
Because they subdue the active manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and sever the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) of afflictions, these are not mentioned here. Question:
In the first stage (*bhūmi*), does one only sever the conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*) self and phenomena, or does one also sever the innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions]? Answer:

According to the principles of the doctrine, once the conceptually constructed [afflictions] have been severed by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the first stage, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) of that same stage also severs a portion of the innate objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). However, for the time being, this is merely stated as follows:
The innate [afflictions] abandoned at the first stage are abandoned during the subsequent nine stages; this should be understood by analogy. Question:
If it is the case that when the ten stages are abandoned, only the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are abandoned, then at what time are the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa-bīja*) abandoned? Answer:

While dwelling in the final stage, as time has already passed for a long duration, it is logically so that what ought to be abandoned is abandoned. Were it not so, there would be no distinction between the paths of the three periods. This is what is meant by "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*).
"Grounds" (*bhūmi*) refers specifically to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samabhisambodhi*). Regarding the "three periods," these refer to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

The stages of Accumulation (*saṃbhāra*) and Application (*prayoga*) span one *asaṃkhyeya*, which is termed the path of gradual suppression and sudden abandonment; this is because it gradually suppresses innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) while suddenly abandoning intellectually acquired ones (*parikalpita-kleśa*).
The two stages of Penetration (*prativedha*) and Cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—spanning the first seven grounds—also cover one *asaṃkhyeya*, which is termed the path of sudden suppression.

The path of gradual abandonment suppresses afflictions instantaneously and gradually abandons the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Therefore, from the latter three stages of the path of cultivation until the stage of ultimate attainment, one passes through one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*;
this is called the path of permanent suppression and permanent abandonment, because afflictions and the objects of knowledge are ultimately and completely severed.

This is called the distinction of the path according to the three periods. Therefore, it is said that a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) eliminates the two obstacles of conceptualization and attains direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), personally realizing *tathatā*.
Furthermore, within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they sever the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), but do not sever the seeds of innate afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is because they retain the seeds of affliction to assist their vows for rebirth, thereby benefiting sentient beings.
Unlike the followers of the Two Vehicles, who swiftly sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) and hasten toward nirvana, the Bodhisattva, during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),

is urgent in severing the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and slow in severing the afflictions; this is because it is only at the time of the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) that they are suddenly severed.

The second is the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*). This refers to the ignorance within the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*)—either that which gives rise to action or that which fails to comprehend action.

The *Saṃgrahaṇī* states: "It refers to the obstacle of wrong conduct regarding the body and so forth. Because great joy arises in the preceding stage, there may be transgressions of the three types of action;
this is termed 'wrong conduct. The *Yogācārabhūmi* asks: "What is the obstacle of wrong conduct? It should be known briefly as follows..."

It is said that there are eight types of subsequent inducements (*samutthāna*). First is the wrong practice of regressing from wisdom; because of this regression, there is the wrong practice of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*);
because of forgetfulness, there is the wrong practice of the destruction of the hundred dharmas; because of this destruction, there is the wrong practice of the manifestation of malicious intent;

because of malice, there is the wrong practice of being difficult to subdue; because of being difficult to subdue, there is the wrong practice of following a non-path; because of following a non-path, one is not virtuous.
This is improper conduct; because it is unwholesome, it is improper conduct that does not accord with the Dharma. This obstructs the most pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

A Bodhisattva on the second stage (*bhūmi*) gives rise to ten kinds of mind and cultivates the ten wholesome dharmas, whereby they are able to permanently sever one obstruction and two delusions (*moha*).

"Delusion" refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*), while "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) is the seed. Alternatively, regarding the delusion of initiating karma and failing to understand karma: this refers to the former... [text truncated]

This is the delusion regarding the arising of karma, because one does not know that an error has been committed, yet is able to give rise to karma. The latter is the delusion regarding the non-comprehension of karma, because once the karmic act has been committed, one still lacks comprehension.
Question: Since objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) cannot produce or moisten [karma], how can they produce the three types of karma within this context?
Answer: The afflictions that link rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-kleśa*) produce the karma of violating precepts; this applies to both cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This is based on...
This is an inadvertent transgression; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Third, the obstacle of dullness refers to that portion of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which obstructs the dhāraṇīs and the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.

Because one forgets these three types of wisdom, it is called "dullness. This is because in the second stage (*bhūmi*), one practices exclusively the category of ethical discipline (*śīla*), while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are absent.

Therefore, this obstacle [hinders] the superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and dhāraṇīs of the third stage, as well as the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and the wisdoms of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) that are produced by those superior meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs.
A Great Sūtra states: "The Bodhisattva of this stage seeks and practices the True Dharma with redoubled diligence;
day and night they only wish to hear the Dharma, rejoice in the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, rely on the Dharma, follow the Dharma, understand the Dharma, and accord with the Dharma."

"Dharma, reaching Dharma, abiding in Dharma, and practicing Dharma. The commentary explains: "A good mind and a good Dharma are called 'delighting in Dharma' (*dharmārāma*). At the time of its conclusion, the savoring of it is called 'joy in Dharma' (*dharmarati*).
Regarding 'relying on the Dharma,' this means relying on the Mahāyāna teachings so that one's own correct vision is grasped and not lost."
One who follows the Dharma does so by reciting it oneself. One who understands the Dharma does so by explaining it for others.

One who accords with the Dharma does so by contemplating its meaning in a secluded place according to what has been heard. One who reaches the Dharma does so by practicing according to meditative concentration until reaching the ultimate goal.
One who abides in the Dharma does so by dwelling in supramundane wisdom. One who practices the Dharma does so by following the practice of liberation as taught by the Buddha.
These ten are precisely the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). The first three consist solely of hearing (*śruta*); the fourth, fifth, and sixth pertain to both hearing and reflection (*cintā*);

the seventh consists solely of reflection; and the final three consist solely of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). When a bodhisattva thus diligently seeks the Buddha-dharma, they have no precious treasure that they do not give away without stinginess;
there is no act of respect that they cannot perform; and there is no pride that they cannot relinquish.
There is service that he cannot perform, and no hardship that he cannot endure.
If he hears even a single verse of the Dharma never heard before, he gives rise to great joy, which surpasses obtaining the three-thousandfold world system filled with precious jewels and the like.
Thus, the bodhisattva exerts diligent vigor in seeking the Buddha-dharma, contemplating it according to what has been heard.
Investigating Cultivation: Having heard the Dharma, this bodhisattva gathers the mind and dwells in composure.
In a secluded place, they reflect thus: "One attains the Buddha-dharma by practicing as it has been taught; it cannot be purified through mere words alone."
When this bodhisattva dwells in the Radiant Stage (Prabhākārī-bhūmi), they immediately depart from worldly, evil, and unwholesome states;

with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, they dwell in the first dhyāna. The commentary explains: one is called "detached from desire" because of being free from the five sensual pleasures;

"detached from evil" because of having abandoned the ten unwholesome paths of action; and "detached from unwholesome states" because of having removed the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). This clarifies the departure from obstacles. It says "with directed thought... [and so forth].
"Awakening with investigation" (*savitarka*) precisely clarifies the cultivation of the antidote, which is *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).

This means that by means of seeking and examining impurity, loving-kindness, and compassion, one treats the obstacles of sensual desire, ill-will, and harmfulness within the desire realm. As for the phrase "the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion":

This is the benefit of cultivation: by being free from desire, evil, and so forth, one gives rise to joy (*prīti*). Because the body and mind become tranquil and one attains the bliss of liberation, it is called "bliss" (*sukha*).

With the cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), internal purity and single-mindedness arise; without applied or sustained thought, there is the rapture and bliss born of concentration as one dwells in the second dhyāna.
The commentary explains: "The cessation of applied and sustained thought" refers to the obstacles that have been abandoned. Applied thought (*vitarka*)...
Observing coarse movement gives rise to the three consciousnesses, which disturb the second dhyāna;

therefore, it is said that "inner serenity, one-pointedness of mind, and the absence of vitarka and vicāra" constitute the antidote for this practice. Inner serenity has equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension as its essence.

"One-pointedness of mind" means that the mind takes only internal objects as its focal point, unlike the first dhyāna, which possesses the three consciousnesses. This is called "joy and bliss born of concentration."
This refers to the benefit of cultivation. In the first dhyāna, one rejoices in having turned one's back on desire and evil; therefore, it is called "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*).

Now, one rejoices in the cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) within the mind; therefore, it is called "born of concentration" (*samādhija*). It is like a clear mirror or still water; thus, body and mind are at ease and joyful.

Furthermore, while the first dhyāna is secluded from desire and evil, it lacks concentration and is thus called "born of seclusion. The second dhyāna is secluded from applied and sustained thought and possesses concentration; therefore, it is called "born of concentration."

Furthermore, "detached from joy, dwelling in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body—this is what the noble ones describe as 'dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness,' abiding in the third dhyāna.
The commentary explains: "Detached from joy" refers to the obstacle that must be abandoned. The joy of the second dhyāna involves mental discrimination and the agitation of the mind;
in the third dhyāna, these are transformed into stillness, and thus it is necessary to eliminate them. "Dwelling in equanimity" [is explained as follows].

There is mindfulness and clear comprehension; these are the antidotes for cultivation. To speak of "abiding in equanimity" (upekṣā) refers to the mental factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃskāra*), distinguishing it from the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*);

this is precisely the equanimity of the formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*). Regarding "possessing mindfulness," it means that amidst the non-arising of joy, one does not forget and maintains clear recollection.
Regarding "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*): at times, one may lose mindfulness and proceed with delight; one dwells upon this discrimination, which is called "dwelling in equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

The statement that "the body experiences pleasure" and so forth refers to the benefits of cultivation. Because the mind is buoyant with joy (*prīti*) in the second dhyāna, it is said that "the body experiences pleasure.
Even if the mind itself experiences pleasure, it is likewise termed "bodily experience"; thus, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*: [text continues].
It is said: "By means of repeatedly cultivating equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, the mental state of elation accompanied by the feeling of joy is extinguished.
With the subsiding of joy, a mental feeling arises that is tranquil and contrary to joy.
At that time, one experiences physical pleasure and the pleasure of pliancy within both the body and the mind; therefore, it is said that 'one experiences pleasure with the body.'"
Regarding what the Noble Ones have taught—that one who possesses equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) experiences bliss (*sukha*)—this establishes the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
That is to say, in the lower stages there is neither such bliss nor uninterrupted equanimity; in the higher stages there is equanimity but no bliss.

Therefore, the Buddhas and their disciples state that the third dhyāna alone possesses both equanimity and mindfulness with clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), while also experiencing bliss. Thus it is said.

Among all forms of bliss, the bliss of the third dhyāna is supreme. Regarding the phrase "the abandonment of bliss": it refers to the removal of obstacles. Since the superior bliss of the third dhyāna acts as a hindrance to this [fourth dhyāna], it must be eliminated. As for the statement "first abandoning suffering, joy, and grief, and the cessation [of them]":

[The practitioner] dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and mindfulness, and is utterly pure. The commentary explains: The term "abandonment of bliss" refers to the separation from obstacles.
The superior bliss of the third dhyāna is detrimental to this state; therefore, it must be removed. Regarding the phrase "first abandoning suffering, joy, and grief, and their cessation":

This means that in the second dhyāna, painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) has already been eliminated; in the third dhyāna, joyful feeling (*prīti-vedanā*) has already ceased; and in the first dhyāna, sorrowful feeling (*daurmanasya-vedanā*) has already ceased.
Now, with the cessation of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), all four feelings have been extinguished. Regarding the phrase "pure equanimity and mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*):

in the third dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness coexist with a craving for pleasure; because this craving for pleasure is now severed, it is called "pure. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "All lower..."

The afflictions of the stage have been severed—namely, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), suffering (*duḥkha*), pleasure (*sukha*), grief (*daurmanasya*), joy (*saumanasya*), and inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*).
Therefore, within this state, equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are pure and bright. By means of this, the mind of this dhyāna abides immovably.

Transcending all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*), and not attending to perceptions of diversity (*nānātva-saṃjñā*), one enters the sphere of infinite space and dwells in the perception of infinite space.

Regarding the "sphere" (*āyatana*): the commentary explains that this refers to contemplating space as having the aspect of being infinite, thereby being able to extinguish the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and settling the mind in the meditative absorption of space.
This is called the Sphere of Infinite Space. As for the phrase "free from obstacles," it means being free from the three types of obstructive forms.

"Transcending all perceptions of form" means surpassing the characteristics of visual consciousness; this clarifies transcending visible, obstructive objects. "Extinguishing the perception of obstruction" [refers to the same].
Because the perception of the conjunction of the ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses has ceased, this cessation is invisible and non-obstructive.

Regarding "not attending to various perceptions": because one does not attend to the perception of the conjunction of mental consciousness, and because mental consciousness discriminates all phenomena, it is termed "various.
This cessation is invisible and non-obstructive. Although mental consciousness takes as its object that which is non-material...
Regarding the object: here we take only the perception (*saṃjñā*) that conditions form (*rūpa*). This [perception] itself has various types, all of which are called "perception.

In the Hīnayāna, when one cultivates this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) or the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one has not yet abandoned the physical form; therefore, it is said that form is not extinguished, but rather that perception is extinguished.

Since perception grasps the characteristics of form, it is specifically extinguished. If this were the Mahāyāna, even if one were born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one would certainly only extinguish perception.
What is the antidote? The first three [applications of mindfulness] include the antidote, which is the non-conceptualization of objects such as form.
Why is there non-recollection? Because one knows there is no self (*anātman*). This refers to the actual antidote of the Bodhisattva; therefore, it is called "no-self."
If one considers it in terms of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), merely cultivating weariness toward suffering and coarseness constitutes the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

To speak of "entering infinite space" refers to the benefit of this cultivation: namely, when the perceptions of the three realms of form cease, one enters the principle of emptiness, which is vast and boundless.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. The commentary explains:
because the mind takes internal consciousness as its object and forms the mental aspect of infinity, it is so named. First, one transcends the sphere of infinite space.
This is the departure from hindrances. What is it that constitutes the hindrance? It is external mental attention (*bahirdhā-manasikāra*), because it is coarse. How is it counteracted?

By seeing the faults of coarse conceptualization in that external mental attention. One enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); this is the benefit of the practice. As the *Nyāya* states:
That is to say, having correctly grasped the signs within the pure sixfold body of consciousness capable of cognition, one abides in resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Through the power of mental construction (*parikalpa*), one contemplates and examines the sign of infinite consciousness.

Preceded by this preparatory practice, one attains entry into the fundamental state, transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness in its entirety, and enters the sphere of nothingness, abiding therein.
Regarding the "Sphere of Nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*): the commentary states that "nothingness" means that both internally and externally there is nothing at all.

"Transcending the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness" clarifies the departure from hindrances. Why must one transcend it? Because the objects of recollection are coarse. How does one apply the antidote?
By perceiving the faults of conceptualizing coarse objects of recollection. Entering "having nothing whatsoever" clarifies the benefit of cultivation. Previously, by means of equanimity...
Because external conditions enter within, it is termed "coarse mindfulness. Since there is nothing to be grasped, the grasper likewise does not exist;

thus, both internal and external are absent, which constitutes true benefit. The *Nyāya* states: "Seeing that the preceding infinite mental images are coarse and agitated, one initiates this preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, this stage is called 'supreme equanimity' (*upekṣā*), because within it one no longer takes pleasure in practicing those infinite [images]."
Regarding the mode of activity (*ākāra*): the mind, having relinquished all that it possessed with respect to its object, abides in tranquility.

It transcends the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The commentary states: "It transcends the sphere of nothingness."
This is that which is to be abandoned as an obstacle. What is the antidote? It is the absence of that [state] and the absence of anything whatsoever (*akiṃcanya*).

Because one perceives the faults of coarse conceptualization and discursive thought, it serves as the antidote. Since it is already tranquil and devoid of anything whatsoever, why is it called "coarse"?

It is because there still remains the perception of "nothing whatsoever. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "First, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothing whatsoever (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), thereby transcending all that exists."
There is perception. Now, having further transcended the perception of nothingness, it is therefore called "neither-perception.
Furthermore, it is called "not non-perception" because it is not like the state of non-perception or the meditative attainment of cessation, wherein all perceptions are utterly extinguished;

rather, there remains only a subtle perception that functions by taking the object of non-perception as its sphere. Thus, one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding this very state and thereby transcends the proximate.

It is divided and enters into the fundamental [attainment]. The reason why one does not transcend the three realms within this state is that it takes the object of non-conceptualization as its condition;

this is, in fact, a subtle form of conceptualization. The non-Buddhists do not understand this and mistake it for *nirvāṇa*. Since they have not yet attained the state of being without conditions, how could they be free from the mind and its objects?
Moreover, they reckon this state to be a self and further give rise to a relish for its flavor. If one recognizes this affliction, one seeks further advancement. One seeks...
When advancing upward, one seeks the object of focus above but ultimately finds nothing to be obtained. Because nothing is obtained, it ceases and does not evolve;

thus, one attains the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*). If this absorption has not yet been attained, one first develops a distaste for perception, and subsequently, as perception no longer functions, one enters the absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Now, to further briefly indicate the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) according to the primary meaning, [it is said that] form is...
