Emptiness: when the mind rests in emptiness, this is the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Next, knowing that both emptiness and form do not exist outside of the mind, this is the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Next, when both mind and object have perished, there is "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya*). Next, even the perception of nothingness perishes;

abiding by taking non-perception as its object is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). If one does not take this non-perception as an object, then all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever extinguished.
Tranquil is this stage of the Bodhisattva; they act solely in accordance with the Dharma, without any attachment or delight.

It is said that they merely follow the transformative teachings for sentient beings, unlike ordinary beings who possess a craving for sensory flavors. For this reason, it is said in the third stage that two delusions are abandoned:
first, the delusion of desire-attachment, which is precisely the greed of the desire realm. Because of this greed, one frequently dwells in distraction.
It obstructs the concentration and wisdom of the higher realms; now that sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) is severed, the concentration and wisdom of the higher realms can finally manifest.

Question: Since it was stated above that what is to be known (*jñeya*) is severed, how can it coexist with sensual desire? Answer: It is because that which is to be known formerly frequently arose simultaneously with sensual desire;
therefore, it is termed "delusion regarding sensual desire" (*kāmarāga-moha*). Now that concentration and wisdom have been attained, that which was to be known has already [been eliminated].
It is permanently severed, and the desire for it has likewise been subdued, because this desire for it continues to function based upon that which is known.
Second, regarding the delusion concerning the perfection of hearing and retention (*dhāraṇī*): this retention is fourfold: first, retention of the Dharma;

second, retention of the meaning; third, retention of mantras; and fourth, retention capable of attaining patience (*kṣānti*). This is because hearing and reflection are extremely closely related to that retention through hearing.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Regarding the "obstruction of the manifestation of subtle afflictions" (up to the point where) the two cravings of the afflictions also never manifest again:
as for the obstruction of the manifestation of subtle afflictions, because of the craving for meditative concentration and wisdom in the preceding stage, it constitutes an obstruction.
This refers to attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to the Dharma—what is known as "taking medicine and it becoming an illness.

This hindrance is comprised within the innate view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth within the sixth consciousness. The mention of the "sixth" distinguishes this from the seventh; for the innate [afflictions] of the seventh are only subdued at the eighth stage.
It is called "subtle" because it is designated as such in comparison to the preceding stages. First, regarding the sixth consciousness:
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that is conceptually discriminated is called "superior" (*adhimātra*), because it is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Craving (*rāga*) and so forth that arise independently are called "middling" (*madhya*). The innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) associated with these are called "inferior" (*mṛdu*), because they pertain to all three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—and because they arise spontaneously without the application of attention (*amanasikāra-pratyaya*).
Thirdly, they follow the active manifestation from afar, having pursued [the individual] since beginningless time.

Because it arises together with the body, and because it possesses these three characteristics, it is called "subtle. It obstructs the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) of the fourth stage;
upon entering the fourth stage, one is able to sever it forever. What are called the factors conducive to enlightenment are the thirty-seven auxiliaries to the path (*mārga-sambhāra*), namely:
the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and the five...
The faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). A great sūtra states:

"When a bodhisattva dwells in the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), he contemplates the body internally as a body, practicing with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, removing worldly greed and sorrow;

he contemplates the body externally as a body, practicing with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, removing worldly greed and sorrow; he contemplates the body both internally and externally..."

Contemplating, with diligent effort, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow. Thus one contemplates internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings, practicing the contemplation of feelings according to feelings.
One contemplates the internal mind, the external mind, and both internal and external minds, practicing the contemplation of the mind according to the mind.

One contemplates internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena, practicing the contemplation of phenomena according to phenomena. With diligent effort, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, one removes worldly greed and sorrow. The commentary states: "This explains the four foundations of mindfulness."
This is the locus. The body, sensation, mind, and phenomena constitute the objects of focus; mindfulness and wisdom constitute its essential nature. First, one contemplates the body.

Regarding this, there are three types of contemplation: internal and so forth. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Internal sentient forms are the internal body; external insentient forms are the external body;
and other sentient beings are the internal-external body. The first refers to one's own person, which is the object of self-love.

Because of attachment: first, to one's own person; second, to one's requisites and so forth, because they are "mine" and objects of attachment; and finally, to one's kin, wife, and children, because they are both "I" and "mine," and objects of attachment.
By means of these three [objects], one destroys the three types of wrong conduct. However, there are many who possess internal emotional attachments.
One may sacrifice one’s wife and wealth to preserve the body, yet remain full of external attachments; or one may lose one’s life for the sake of wealth, or lose one’s life for the sake of a wife.

These are the three matters regarding which one applies the antidotes. If one contemplates the beginning and end of a single body, it means first observing that within one’s own body, things such as purity cannot be found.
One might then think they exist externally, but next, upon observing the external, they are likewise not to be found.
Next, one observes both the internal and external [bodies] together, yet these too cannot be apprehended. The first [of these two] is specific, while the latter is general;

however, by combining the preceding two, they constitute the internal and external bodies. As for the term "contemplation following the body" (*kāyānupaśyanā*), it generally reveals the characteristics of the practice.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One follows and observes them, knowing them to be impure, and so forth. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "That is to say, by means of the body of conceptualized images, with..."

The essential body (*svabhāvakāya*). One contemplates it with equanimity. What was previously the internal body is the essential reality; what is now called "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupaśyanā*) is the reflected image.
Regarding the phrase "with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension," this reveals the method of cultivation.

Because worldly affairs such as desire and so forth involve beginningless negative habituation, they are extremely difficult to abandon; therefore, one must apply diligence (*vīrya*) before they can be eliminated. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "That is to say..."
Through the cultivation of desire, diligence, exertion, vigor, non-cessation, right mindfulness, right awareness, and heedfulness, there are distinctions in their practice.
Cultivation of desire serves as the remedy for the secondary affliction of lack of attention (*amanasikāra*).

Cultivation of diligence serves as the remedy for the secondary affliction of laziness (*kausīdya*). Cultivation of exertion serves as the remedy for lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Regarding the arousal of the secondary afflictions: for one who exerts effort in cultivation, it serves as the antidote to the secondary affliction of mental inferiority;
for one who cultivates with vigor, it serves as the antidote to the secondary affliction of laxity and fatigue; for one who cultivates without ceasing...
The cultivation of right mindfulness is for the purpose of counteracting the secondary affliction of being satisfied with and taking joy in having acquired only a small amount of wholesome dharmas.
The cultivation of clear comprehension is for the purpose of counteracting the secondary affliction of forgetting the instructions of the Honored One.
The cultivation of heedfulness is for the purpose of counteracting the secondary affliction of neglecting the yoke of all wholesome qualities.
These are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). The phrase "excluding worldly greed and sorrow" refers to the fruit of contemplation, because there is that which has been abandoned.

Since contemplating the impurity of the body is fundamentally intended to counteract those who act out of greed, it universally dispels it. As for sorrow, among the five types of feeling (*vedanā*), [it is the feeling of suffering].

It is specifically capable of obstructing meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Just as when extinguishing evil bandits, one first eliminates the greatest threat, it is therefore mentioned specifically.

When the initial contemplation of the internal body is thus performed, the same applies to the external body and the internal-external body. Regarding the latter three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are the three contemplations beginning with the internal.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Just as one contemplates the internal body, taking the five sense faculties of one's own body as the object; in relation to these, contact (*sparśa*) arises. Because of contact..."

Experiencing what is born, such as impurity and so forth, is called the contemplation of internal feeling (*adhyātma-vedanā-anupaśyanā*). Since internal feeling is thus, external feeling and both internal and external feelings are likewise so.

The same applies to mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*). This leads to the abandonment of the four perversions (*viparyāsa*) and entry into the body of the Four Noble Truths through dissociation (*visamyoga*).
Regarding the abandonment of the four perversions: according to their respective order, one is able to abandon the four types—purity, pleasure, permanence, and self.
[He practices] by means of the four foundations of mindfulness: through the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity, he understands that all sensations (*vedanā*) are suffering;

through the penetration of the distinctions of the bases and conditions of consciousness, he realizes their moment-to-moment transformation; and through the observation of defilement and purity, he perceives that there are only phenomena (*dharma*) and no agent.
Thus, one who enters the Four Truths enters the Truth of Suffering by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), [regarding] all form (*rūpa*).
The body consists entirely of the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha*), as it is manifested by its coarse and heavy nature (*dausthulya*).

Through the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), because feelings such as pleasure are the basis for the arising of craving and other defilements. Through the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*);
by contemplating that consciousness is devoid of a self and will eventually cease to exist, one fears the annihilation of the self and thus gives rise to a dread of nirvāṇa. Forever...

Because of detachment. By means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of the Path. This is for the purpose of abandoning the factors to be countered and cultivating the remedial factors.
Thus, this Bodhisattva, for the sake of ensuring that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise, generates the desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right abandonment.
Furthermore, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, he generates the desire and exerts effort.

Vigorous application of the mind through right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*): for the sake of producing all unarisen wholesome dharmas, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies diligence, and applies the mind with right practice;
and for the sake of maintaining and not losing all already arisen wholesome dharmas, one cultivates them so that they may increase and expand.
"Desiring to give rise to diligence, one arouses vigor and practices correctly. The commentary states: "This clarifies the four right efforts (samyakpradhāna).

Just as the fire of the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) will burn everything without exception when it encounters the wind of diligence, the four right efforts are explained immediately following this. These are the four right efforts.
Vigor constitutes its essential nature. Regarding the cultivation of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), as it is said in the Sūtra:
"One generates desire, exerts effort, initiates right diligence, and strives to uplift and sustain the mind. Herein, these phrases clarify the cultivation of right diligence as well as its basis.
The basis is desire (*chanda*), for it is preceded by the wish [to act] that one initiates diligence (*vīrya*). Right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*) refers to exertion and so forth.

Among the mental attentions (*manasikāra*) regarding the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), when one attends to the signs of tranquility and so forth, disregards the focal object, and practices exclusively the antidote, at that time it is called exertion; this is for the purpose of diminishing [the afflictions].
One applies right effort toward sinking and restlessness. Why is this?
When the secondary affliction of sinking arises, one trains the mind by means of mental orientations (*manasikāra*) such as those that are pure and sublime, in order to diminish it.
When the secondary affliction of restlessness arises, one restrains and sustains the mind through internal methods of withdrawal and concentration. At that time, it is called...
In order to initiate right effort, one employs skillful means to manifest the reduction of lethargy and excitement;

therefore, it is subsequently stated that one "exerts the mind" and "sustains the mind. The fruit of cultivating the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) consists in the complete relinquishing of all factors to be countered (*vipakṣa*).
The attainment or increase of these antidotes is called the fruit of cultivation.

This bodhisattva cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through desire and the exertion for abandonment; it relies on disenchantment, relies on detachment, relies on cessation, and is dedicated toward relinquishment.
Cultivating diligence, concentration of mind, meditative observation, and the formative forces of concentration, one accomplishes the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).

These rely upon disenchantment, rely upon detachment, and rely upon cessation, being dedicated toward equanimity. The commentary states: "This clarifies the four bases of supernormal power. 'Supernormal' (*ṛddhi*) refers to supernatural faculties;
'bases' (*pāda*) refers to concentration. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* says: 'Just as one who has feet is able to go and return, so too [does concentration] enable one to soar.'"
To leap, to be courageous, and to be robust; to be able to attain and realize the supreme mundane dharmas and the extraordinary supramundane dharmas—this is called "divine" (*ṛddhi*).

Because one can reach these [states] through them, they are called "bases of divine power" (*ṛddhipāda*). This is an illustration by means of a metaphor. Because the supramundane dharma is the most excellent mastery, it is the supreme "divine.
Since the four concentrations, such as desire and so forth, are able to realize this, they are called "bases of divine power. Furthermore...

They are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) because they accord with one's desires as intended by the mind. The objective referent (*ālambana*) of the bases of psychic power consists of various miraculous transformations.
The essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the bases of psychic power is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Desire, diligence, mind, and investigation are all their auxiliary companions.

"Desire" refers to intense aspiration; "diligence" refers to uninterrupted exertion; "mind" is concentration, meaning focusing the mind single-pointedly on an object; and "investigation" [refers to discernment].

This is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*), because by means of hearing the teachings, one internally discriminates for oneself; thus, all [these qualities] receive their names from their preparatory application (*prayoga*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Desire" refers to that which can generate a longing; it is the correct and thorough investigation of the intrinsic nature, causes, conditions, disadvantages, and remedies regarding all unwholesome phenomena, which gives rise to one-pointedness of mind and mindfulness; and [it is likewise applied] to the intrinsic nature, causes, and conditions of all wholesome phenomena.
Regarding functional renunciation: one examines and correctly contemplates, dwelling with the mind in a single object and maintaining mindfulness.

Precisely through such repeated cultivation, one touches upon one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*), which is able to destroy active afflictions; therefore, it is called "desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi*).

Regarding "diligence," this refers to the practitioner who exerts themselves and encourages themselves, arousing diligent effort in order to abandon the two types of evil and cultivate the two types of goodness. The mind...

"Being concentrated" means that the mind is single-mindedly guarded; this is what is called "mind. Because this is the attainment of one-pointedness of mind through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it is termed "concentration" (*samādhi*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Mental samādhi refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind by virtue of having previously cultivated the power of concentration.
Why is this so? Because of the repeated cultivation of the power of concentration in previous lives."
This causes the functional capacity of those seeds to increase. By the power of the seeds, the mind spontaneously undergoes a transformation that accords with *samādhi*.
Through this, one swiftly realizes one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
As for the *vipaśyanā-samādhi*, it refers to the arising of one-pointedness of mind through internal discernment based on hearing the teachings of others. These four preparatory practices serve as...

Because it reveals the causes for the arising of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the sequence of the phrases "arousing desire, exerting effort," and so forth within the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) consists of holding the mind and exerting the mind.
This is the order because, within the arousal of the mind, holding the mind can produce the concentration of calm (*śamatha*), since holding [the mind] too loosely leads to agitation;

and exerting the mind can produce the concentration of insight (*vipaśyanā*), since exerting [the mind] too forcefully leads to dullness. Therefore, this follows from each single foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
There are four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*). Each right effort has four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).

When the Sūtra speaks of "cultivating the concentration of desire" (*chanda-samādhi*), it identifies the cultivated auxiliary factors and their essential nature. The two characters "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) generally manifest the characteristics of cultivation.

What are these characteristics of cultivation? There are two kinds: first, by cultivating the concentration of desire, one is able to abandon the active afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*); second, [by cultivating the concentration of energy...]

In order to permanently destroy all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one cultivates the eight formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*): namely, desire (*chanda*), exertion (*vīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), volition (*cetanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
First, regarding desire: it is the aspiration and longing, thinking, "When shall I cultivate meditative concentration to perfection?"

1. Eliminating the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of evil; 2. Exerting oneself and not abandoning the application of effort (*prayoga*); 3. Developing deep faith and understanding regarding what has been realized above; 4.
Giving rise to joy in the mind, thereby gradually removing coarseness and heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);

5. Establishing the mind in *śamatha*; 6. Abiding in the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) of *vipaśyanā*; 7. Ensuring that the mental activities conform to both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; 8. [And so forth.]
Throughout the three periods of time, one is entirely free from defilement. Due to two causes and conditions, one discriminates and understands the abandonment of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):
namely, by means of reflection upon objects that are not currently perceived, and by means of equanimity toward objects that are currently perceived.

The phrase "relying on disenchantment (*nirveda*) and so forth" further clarifies the characteristics of cultivation; that is, cultivation based on the truth of suffering must necessarily rely on disenchantment with suffering. If [one cultivates] based on the truth of origination...
Cultivation must rely on detachment from desire. If one cultivates by taking cessation as the object, one must seek to realize cessation.

If one cultivates by taking the path as the object, one must proceed toward the practice that extinguishes suffering and is able to abandon it. When taking these objects, one must seek to cultivate and must desire to relinquish;
therefore, it is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*). As for the fruit of that cultivation, it refers to having already well-cultivated *samādhi*, such that according to what...
Regarding the dharmas to be realized and thoroughly penetrated, he is able to penetrate and manifest them according to his will.
Furthermore, within each respective category of phenomena, he realizes the capacity for sovereign mastery;

thus, according to his aspirations, he can accomplish various feats such as supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and can further induce superior qualities. This is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

Relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating oneself toward equanimity, one cultivates the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, and the faculty of concentration—relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating oneself toward equanimity. The commentary states:

"This clarifies the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). These five faculties observe the path of skillful means; although they belong to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), they involve the patient acceptance of the principles of the truths."
Cultivating the concentration of the seals (*mudrā*) serves as the preliminary means (*upāya*), and it is also the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Regarding the cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*): the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) refers to the cultivation of the practice of conviction regarding all the faculties.

The faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) refers to the cultivation of the practice of diligence for the sake of awakening, once conviction has arisen regarding all the stages (*bhūmi*). The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) refers to the arousal of diligence regarding the truths (*satya*).

Having done so, one cultivates the faculty of concentration through the practice of non-forgetfulness. Once mindfulness has been established toward the truths, one cultivates the faculty of wisdom through the practice of one-pointedness of mind.
Once the mind has attained concentration upon the truths, one cultivates [the faculty of wisdom] through the practice of discernment.
As for the fruit of cultivating these five faculties, it is that they enable the swift arising of the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), by virtue of their predominance.

Because one will soon be able to give rise to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The objects of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the four noble truths (*catuḥsatya*).

Because they perform this practice by means of being subsumed under the skillful means (*upāya*) of the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), such is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the five faculties."
These are the five faculties, beginning with faith. These five collectively serve as the dominant conditions for the arising of supramundane dharmas;
furthermore, the first four are able to give rise to the latter one, thereby receiving the designation of "dominant. Among them, faith is the foremost, capable of giving rise to the other four.
That is to say: faith gives rise to the latter four; diligence gives rise to the latter three; mindfulness gives rise to the latter two; concentration gives rise to the last one.

As for that final faculty of wisdom, it possesses predominance only with respect to the supramundane. What is now being cultivated is precisely the profound patient acceptance and aspiration toward the reality of the truths;
the remaining four are, respectively, exerting effort based on what was previously believed, clearly recollecting it without forgetting, and so forth.
It is bound to a single object and discriminates between what is right and what is wrong; the rest is as previously explained.

If one considers it in terms of stages, prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), its fruit is the swift manifestation of insight (*vipaśyanā*); now, being in the fourth stage, its fruit is the manifestation of the subsequent stages.

This Bodhisattva’s practice of the power of faith relies upon disenchantment (*nirveda*), relies upon detachment (*virāga*), and relies upon cessation (*nirodha*), and is dedicated toward [enlightenment].
Regarding equanimity (*upekṣā*), one cultivates the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.

These rely upon disenchantment (*nirveda*), rely upon detachment (*virāga*), and rely upon cessation (*nirodha*), being dedicated toward equanimity. The commentary states: "This clarifies the five powers (*pañcabala*).

As for the five powers, they are the growth of the aforementioned five faculties (*pañcendriya*); because Māra, Brahmā, afflictions, and the like cannot subdue them, they are called 'powers. Furthermore, they can diminish..."

Because they extinguish obstacles such as lack of faith, they are further called "powers" (*bala*). The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Because they are able to destroy afflictions and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they are called powers.

When a bodhisattva practices the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), they rely upon disenchantment, rely upon detachment, and rely upon cessation, dedicating [the practice] toward equanimity.
They likewise practice the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

The awakening factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). These rely upon weariness (*nirveda*), rely upon detachment (*virāga*), rely upon cessation (*nirodha*), and are directed toward relinquishment (*vairāgya*).
The commentary states: "This clearly explains the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*). Regarding "awakening" (*bodhi*), it means thorough comprehension (*avabodha*).

If explained according to the stages, it refers to the wisdom that realizes the self-nature of phenomena through direct observation (*abhisamaya*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "All those who have..."

The wisdom of the person (*pudgala*) who has entered the state of rightness and transcendence (*samyaktva-nyāma*) realizes [the truth] as it truly is; taking this as its constituent factor, it is called a "factor of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*).
It is also the object of focus (*ālambana*). The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya* states: "The object of the seven factors of enlightenment is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the four noble truths.
Suchness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because it is the object of purification. This is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the factors of enlightenment.

These are the seven mental factors beginning with mindfulness (*smṛti*). However, regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), all seven constitute its essential nature (*svabhāva*). As for their distinction:

the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) constitutes the essential nature, while the remaining six are branches of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). That is to say, mindfulness is the branch of support, because by means of binding the mind to the object, it ensures that all wholesome factors are not forgotten.
The investigation of phenomena is the branch of essential nature, because it realizes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) [of phenomena].
Vigor is the factor of departure, for by its power one is able to reach the destination. Joy is the factor of benefit, for by its power the body becomes pliant and comfortable.
The triad of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are the factors of non-defilement. Tranquility is indeed pliancy;
it is called "non-defilement" because, through this pliancy, one is free from defilement and can eliminate the fault of heaviness (*dausthulya*). This is due to reliance upon concentration.

It is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*). This means that by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); because it relies on equanimity (*upekṣā*), it is non-defiled, for its essence is non-defilement.
That is to say, through the equanimity of the mental formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), greed and sorrow are forever eliminated;

it takes the state of being non-defiled as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) means relying on seclusion (*viveka*), relying on..."

Desire. Relying on tranquility and dedicating oneself toward relinquishment, one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness. As it is with the awakening factor of mindfulness, so it is for each up to the awakening factor of equanimity.
These four phrases, in their respective order, demonstrate the taking of the objects of the Four Noble Truths as conditions.

One cultivates the factors of enlightenment. Why is this? If one takes the Truth of Suffering as an object when it is being experienced as affliction and suffering, one will certainly seek to distance oneself from that objective sphere.

If one takes the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, characterized by craving, as an object when it is being experienced as the origin of suffering, one will certainly seek detachment from that objective sphere.
If one takes the Cessation of Suffering as an object when it is being experienced as cessation, one will certainly seek to realize it.
Regarding "realization": as for the term "abandonment," it refers to the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Because one abandons suffering through the power of this [practice], when one takes this as an object, one must necessarily seek its cultivation; therefore, it is called "dedication toward abandonment.

Regarding the "fruit of cultivation," it refers to the permanent severance of the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) by means of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). This is because it is [the fruit] of seeing...

Because they constitute the very essence of the Path (*mārga*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are subsumed under three categories. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) permeates both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);

the next three are wisdom; and the final three are comprised within concentration. As elucidated according to their respective stages, their function is to sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) as their fruit.

Although these seven factors operate simultaneously in a single moment, their individual capacities are described according to their specific modes of activity: mindfulness eliminates discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), while discernment (*vīmaṃsā*)...

Excluding improper awareness (*asamprajanya*), the remaining factors exclude indolence (*kausīdya*), lethargy and torpor (*styāna-middha*), coarseness (*dausthulya*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

This is stated according to the general [explanation]. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) in the Mahāyāna: because one does not dwell upon any phenomena; because they cannot be apprehended through definitive discernment (*viniścaya*);

because one is free from diligence and indolence; because one has severed sorrow and joy; and because all other objects for settling the mind are unobtainable—within this intrinsic concentration (*prakṛti-samādhi*), there is none [of these].
Because of the stabilization of distraction, one also does not perceive the subject or object of relinquishment.
This bodhisattva cultivates right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration;

they rely on disenchantment, rely on detachment, and rely on cessation, dedicating [the practice] toward relinquishment. The commentary states: "This clarifies the Eightfold Noble Path. If one relies upon...

Regarding the explanation of the stages: this refers to the path that arises subsequent to clear realization (*abhisamaya*). It is called the "Eightfold Right" because it abandons the eight wrongs for the sake of severing the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is called the "Path" (*mārga*) because it opens the way to *nirvāṇa*. It is also called the "Noble Eightfold Path" (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) because it is the path of the noble ones (*ārya*).
As for "Right View" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), it is the analytical limb; it is the discernment based upon the reality previously realized.

Therefore, right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is the factor of instruction for others; it consists of establishing the names and meanings through skillful means according to what has been realized, thereby giving rise to speech.

The next three are the factors that cause others to have faith. Right speech (*samyag-vāc*) is the skillful reliance upon what has been realized to provide answers and definitive analysis, thereby causing others to believe in the purity of one's view. Right action (*samyak-karmānta*) refers to bodily action...

Regarding progress and withdrawal: it is the perfection of right conduct, because it causes others to believe that one’s ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure. Regarding right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*):

it is like relying on alms-seeking and the noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*) while remaining free from the five types of wrong livelihood; it is for the purpose of causing others to believe that one’s livelihood is pure. Regarding right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*):
it is the factor for purifying the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because by means of it, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are forever severed. Regarding right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*)...

This is the factor for purifying secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), because by not forgetting the characteristics of correct tranquility (*śamatha*) and exertion (*pragraha*), one never admits secondary afflictions such as dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
"Correct concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*) is the factor that can purify the obstacles to the most excellent qualities.

Because this gives rise to immeasurable, supreme qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), if one can provide instruction and guidance through such analytical discernment as described above, this constitutes the fruit of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
The seven preceding categories are collectively illustrated by means of metaphors: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like the great earth;

the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are like seeds; the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are like planting; the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are like the sprouting of shoots; and the five... [five faculties/factors].

The roots are like the growth of roots; the five powers are like the increasing of stems and leaves; one opens the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment and bears the fruit of the eightfold noble path.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, all attachments to the view of a self as primary—including the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—as well as all arising and ceasing, are treated through reflection, observation, and cultivation. This applies to what is regarded as "mine," as well as wealth and possessions.
Therefore, because they are points of attachment, one is detached from all such things. The commentary states: This clarifies the perfection of virtues through the abandonment of hindrances.
First, there is the abandonment of delusions. Within this, the objects abandoned are first presented; among these objects, there arise attachments, emergences, and disappearances.

This is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); all others are specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Attachment to the general characteristic is precisely the pride regarding the understanding of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna-māna*) mentioned in the preceding stage.
The *Śāstra* says: "I know" and "I know greatly. "I know" refers to the attachment to the self as the knower; "knowing greatly" refers to the attachment to the great dharmas that are known.
"Emergence and submergence" refers to the pride regarding meditative absorption (*samāpatti-māna*) in the preceding stage. "Emergence" refers to *samādhi*.

Because it arises from [false] views: that is, one cultivates and gives rise to that meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "Disappearance" (*vyaya*) has the meaning of cessation through meditative absorption;
that is, what is eliminated by the concentration. Now, one conceives: "I am able to cultivate this concentration," and "this concentration is what I have cultivated.

There are five distinct types: first, the root; second, arising; third, activity; fourth, protection; fifth, fault. Regarding the first, the "root": it refers to all forms of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) up to the aggregates (*skandha*).
Regarding the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), among them, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the general category, while "self" (*ātman*) and so forth are the specific instances.

Within the specific instances, the four [views] such as "I" and "person" (*pudgala*) constitute the conceit of self (*ātmamāna*), whereas the aggregates (*skandha*), elements, and bases constitute the conceit of phenomena (*dharmamāna*). Regarding the two types of arising:

the arising through the clarity of reflection refers to the fact that conceit arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). Regarding the three types of practice: the practice through the clarity of observation refers to the mind frequently [engaging] with its objects.

Regarding the observation of what is attained—whether it be a phenomenon (*dharma*) or a meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—it is for the purpose of seeking out superior characteristics so that others may come to know them. Regarding the four protections: they are for the sake of cultivation.
The three phrases clarify protection; "cultivation" refers to repeatedly observing and refining what has been perceived. As for "what belongs to me":

It arises from the notion of self (*ātma-saṃjñā*), because one grasps those superior characteristics as belonging to oneself. Regarding "possessions" (*parigraha*): it is like one who possesses wealth, because of the enjoyment and protection thereof.
By means of these three matters, one guards what has been acquired for oneself. Regarding the five faults: the fault of the locus of attachment is clarified;
that is to say, because the mind is firm and established in two ways within the fixed dharma. In this context, if there is the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)...
Explanation by way of stages: This refers to the abandonment of the innate view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness.

Therefore, it is said that upon entering the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to abandon it forever. Question: Since it is stated that one abandons a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), why is it that afflictions (*kleśa*) are also abandoned?
Answer: These cognitive obstructions, in former times, frequently arose spontaneously as being of the same substance (*ekasvabhāva*) as the afflictions. Therefore...

The name "affliction" (*kleśa*) is established because it acts as an obstacle. Now, since one has attained the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣadharma*) within the fourth stage and has correctly abandoned the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), even that view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not function there. Question: Why were they not abandoned in the three preceding stages?

Answer: The first three [types of self-view] are similar to those of the mundane world; therefore, they cannot sever [the afflictions]. Only when they become identical with the supramundane can they permanently destroy the two types of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-identity) and so forth.
Question: How do we know that this grasping at a self (*ātmagrāhadṛṣṭi*) coexists only with the sixth consciousness and not the seventh?
Answer: The satkāyadṛṣṭi of the seventh consciousness still arises manifestly up through the seventh bhūmi; it is only from the eighth bhūmi onward [that it ceases].
They will never arise again, because their nature is diametrically opposed to that of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

This is because during the five stages, contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) is predominant while contemplation without signs (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is scarce; in the sixth stage, contemplation without signs is predominant while contemplation with signs is scarce;

and upon reaching the seventh stage, it consists purely of the signless. However, because there is still effortful application (*sābhoga*), the eighth stage is designated as the untainted path. There is no [arising of signs] therein.
At the time of entering the path of no-outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*), the co-nascent active manifestation within the seventh consciousness is forever suppressed and does not function;
therefore, it can manifest at all times prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). This is because it takes other co-nascent afflictions as its support.

Furthermore, since this view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) in the sixth and seventh consciousnesses has both coarse and subtle aspects, there is a sequence in its suppression and abandonment. It is by virtue of this principle that...
It is known that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) abandoned at this stage corresponds only with the six consciousnesses, not with the seventh consciousness.
Regarding "the view of a self and so forth," all is explained as previously stated.
Fifth is the obstacle of entering parinirvāṇa via the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna). This refers to those who delight in nirvāṇa and seek to realize it;

they necessarily feel aversion toward saṃsāra. Because they possess this aversion and seeking, it is termed an "obstacle. Specifically, the supramundane mind sought in the preceding four stages is similar to that of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Since this obstacle pertains to the path of non-differentiation in the fifth stage, one enters [the fifth stage] by overcoming it.

On the fifth stage, one is able to sever [these afflictions] forever. This is because a Bodhisattva on the fifth stage gives rise to ten kinds of pure, equanimous minds, and thus knows as they truly are:
this is the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

They skillfully know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), skillfully know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), skillfully know the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), and skillfully know the truth of distinctions (*viśeṣa-satya*).

The distinct truths: he skillfully knows the truth of establishing the truths; the truth of phenomena; the truth of arising; and the truth of non-arising. He skillfully knows the truth of the wisdom that enters the path.
He skillfully knows the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages. He skillfully knows the truth of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Furthermore, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, there are worldly arts and crafts that he does not study; that is to say:
He thoroughly mastered writing, arithmetic, charts, diagrams, seals, and insignia, as well as the various treatises on earth, water, fire, and wind.

Furthermore, he was skilled in medical prescriptions and the treatment of all diseases; he was proficient in composition, praise, and verse, as well as singing, dancing, music, performance, and humorous discourse—all such matters he excelled in.
The commentary states: "The Four Noble Truths are explained as before. As for the phenomena of deluded sentiment..."

That which exists in sentiment but lacks objective reality is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That which is the true dharma, whose characteristics are quiescent yet whose essence exists, is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

For the sake of sentient beings who harbor doubts, one understands the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*); that is to say, there are those who, upon hearing the ultimate truth, remain hesitant and undecided, wondering, "Is this emptiness?

Is it existence? Now, the name itself is the conventional; its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is empty, and thus there is no contradiction with the common-characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore...

This is the Truth of Names and Characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-satya*). It is established for the sake of knowing the distinctions for those sentient beings who are deluded by erroneous interpretations regarding the profound Dharma.

That is to say, when they previously perceived two objects, they immediately claimed them to be different and thus gave rise to doubt; now, hearing that they occupy the same locus, they claim them to be one—this is called "erroneous interpretation.

Now it is clarified that although their essence (*tattva*) is not different, their nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) are clearly and distinctly differentiated, so as to depart from [such] false mindfulness.
Because sentient beings thus know that the truths are established, once they have heard the distinctions [between them], they claim that all possess intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*).

This is called being "separated from right mindfulness. Now, to clarify these distinctions: they are merely established through conditions (*pratyaya*) and lack intrinsic nature; therefore, they are said to be "established" (*siddha*).

Because they are manifested in accordance with words, they are also called "truths established by verbal expression" (*vyavahāra-siddha-satya*). For the sake of sentient beings who possess right view, they know the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*) and the truth of arising (*utpatti-satya*), which are [ultimately] exhausted and non-existent.

The Truth of Arising, the Truth of the Knowledge of the Path, and the Matter—these are the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Arising is the cause of accumulation (*samudaya-hetu*). Non-arising is the cause of cessation (*nirodha-hetu*).

The extinction of the cause is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*), which is the Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). That subsequent results do not arise is called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*); this is the Knowledge of Non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
The four truths of the previously mentioned real dharmas clarify what is to be observed; the four truths herein clarify that one should observe them in this manner.
For the sake of those sentient beings who can be transformed by the Mahāyāna, one should know the stages of the bodhisattva, up to the truth of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Regarding the various treatises on earth, water, fire, and wind, these are subsumed within the context of contentious debate, because of the differing calculations of various false views.
For instance, the Lokāyatikas hold that earth alone is the cause, asserting that everything is composed of atoms; [they likewise claim this for] water and wind.

The two types of non-Buddhist practitioners—the water-and-wind practitioners—take water as their causal basis because the world is formed by water and is sustained by the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
The fire-worshipping non-Buddhists take fire as their causal basis because fire brings things to maturity.

This Bodhisattva, furthermore, teaches and transforms sentient beings through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation; therefore, he does not weary of saṃsāra, nor does he hasten toward nirvāṇa. Thus...
This abandons one hindrance and two delusions.
The sixth is the hindrance of the manifestation of coarse characteristics (the hindrance from "unable to dwell for long periods in signless contemplation" up to "contemplating the Four Truths").
Here, suffering and its origin are termed defiled, while cessation and the path are termed pure. Furthermore, there are ten kinds of equality that accord with suchness.

The Path. This refers only to the description of purity; however, as the characteristics of defilement have not yet been eliminated, there is purity in contrast to defilement, which is also termed "clinging to purity.
Both the presence of defilement and the presence of purity are called coarse characteristics. The Bodhisattvas of this stage employ ten dharmas of equality as their antidote.
That is to say, all phenomena are equal because they are signless; they are equal because they lack substantiality;

they are equal because they are unarisen; they are equal because they are unceasing; they are equal because they are primordially pure; and they are equal because they are free from conceptual proliferation.
It is equal because there is no grasping or rejecting; it is equal because it is quiescent.

It is equal because it is like a dream, like an illusion, like a shadow, like an echo, like the moon in water, like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage, and like a transformation. It is equal because existence and non-existence are non-dual.
The commentary states: "Signless" means that its intrinsic nature is signless; this refers to the fact that all phenomena are dependently originated.

These characteristics are originally non-existent; they are not rendered non-existent through deliberate effort. Therefore, it is said that they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Next, it is explained that all nine types of characteristics lack intrinsic nature.
The following nine are the objects to be remedied (*vipakṣa*), while the single character "non-" (*na*) is the remedy (*pratipakṣa*).

Because there is no substance in this "non-," they are equal. The *Śāstra* states: "The conceptualization of the specific characteristics of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) refers to the six external sense organs grasping the external [objects]."

The characteristics of the six sense objects are collectively termed "perception" (*saṃjñā*); this is the essence of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), because perception takes the grasping of images as its essence.
It is also called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*); all subsequent instances should be understood accordingly. Above, it contradicts the discriminating mind. Regarding the two types of arising:
Contemplating the successive progression of formations: this refers to the various bases (*āyatana*) which are the fruits of suffering, for they have false discrimination as their root.

Third, the cessation of the characteristic of successive progression of birth: this means that birth itself is the fruit of suffering, as it arises from causes based upon those fruits. The two preceding [contemplations] eliminate the defiled aspect of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
by merely citing its conditional formation, they already manifest its lack of arising and lack of cessation. Fourth, the elimination of the pure aspect: this refers to the fundamental...

It is pure by nature; it is not purified by the elimination of delusions. Fifth, the removal of the marks of conceptualization (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the Path, which is able to discern and select in order to eliminate delusions.
If there were conceptualization, there would be proliferation (*prapañca*). Now, since it is fundamentally without proliferation, it is non-conceptual.

The preceding two [points] remove the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) from the perspective of purity. Sixth, the removal of arising and ceasing: this refers to the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which exists within delusion.
Sinking is [the state of] being defiled; emerging is being free from defilement. Now, since the essence of delusion is itself reality, there is nothing to be abandoned;

since the essence of reality is itself emptiness, there is nothing to be grasped. (7) Dispelling the characteristic of defilement follows from the above meaning: defilement is fundamentally quiescent, which is precisely suchness (*tathatā*); there is no separate reality apart from it.
The preceding two [points] dispel the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). (8) Dispelling the characteristic that the self does not exist, it is therefore said: "As... (*yathā*)...

Regarding matters such as illusions and the like, the ninth [point] dispels the characteristics of formation and destruction. Formation is existence; destruction is non-existence. Dependent origination constitutes formation;

the absence of intrinsic nature constitutes destruction. Since that which is dependently formed is itself the absence of intrinsic nature, existence and non-existence are non-dual. This is the stage of the Bodhisattva.

Extensively extending this to the twelve links of dependent origination, one sees that their cyclic flow and cessation are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are equal.
Thus, one eliminates this single hindrance and its two types of delusion.
The obstacle of the manifestation of the seven subtle marks (extending to): being unable to initiate superior practice within emptiness.

In the preceding stage, one delights in Prajñā and contemplates emptiness; this constitutes the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle marks. In this stage, one does not cling to existence as it arises, serving as the antidote.
That is to say, although one was previously able to counteract the mind that delights in emptiness in the preceding stage, because [existence] still...
The immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) involving effort (*sābhoga*) are themselves obstacles. On this stage, one cultivates immeasurable practices free from effort (*anābhoga*) as the antidote;
that is to say, the previous delight in non-action is not called "skillful means" (*upāya*), as it cannot give rise to superior progress and is not the sublime path.
On this stage, one takes the tenfold wisdom regarding the non-abandonment of sentient beings and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) as the antidote.

Therefore, the Great Sūtra states: "When a bodhisattva has fulfilled the practices of the sixth stage and wishes to enter the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), they should cultivate ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom to give rise to the distinguished path. What are these ten? They are:

although they skillfully cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not abandon sentient beings through their compassion; although they have attained [the teachings of] all Buddhas..."
Delighting in the Dharma of equality, they constantly make offerings to the Buddhas; though they enter the gate of wisdom that contemplates emptiness, they diligently accumulate merit and virtue;
though they remain far removed from the triple world, they adorn the triple world;

though they have ultimately extinguished the flames of all afflictions, they are able to give rise to the extinction of the flames of greed, hatred, and delusion for the sake of all sentient beings; though they know all...
The nature of phenomena is non-dual, like illusions, dreams, shadows, and echoes; yet, according to the mind, they manifest in immeasurable varieties of activity.
Although one knows that all lands are like empty space, one can adorn Buddha-lands with pure and wondrous conduct.
Although one knows that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is by nature bodiless, one adorns it with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
Although their bodies know that the nature of the Buddhas' voices is empty, quiescent, and ineffable,
they are able to produce various distinct pure sounds according to all sentient beings. Although they follow the Buddhas in realizing that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment,
they manifest through various signs and various [means] in accordance with the mental inclinations and conceptualizations of sentient beings.
At that time, they cultivate various practices throughout manifold eons.
By means of these ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom, the bodhisattva initiates sublime conduct and enters the seventh stage from the sixth stage.
This bodhisattva attains fulfillment in each and every thought-moment regarding the ten pāramitās, and likewise for all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

In every thought-moment, all are completely fulfilled. What is called the "sublime contemplation of signlessness" (animitta-vipaśyanā) is precisely the entry into meditative absorption (samāpatti) in every thought-moment.
Those who purely and diligently seek through mental attention (manasikāra) that which is signless merely contemplate emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness, and wishlessness (apraṇihita).
Those who have not yet been able to give rise to superior practices within emptiness [should] sport with supernatural powers (ṛddhi-vikrīḍita) in the pure Buddha-lands of the various Bodhisattvas.
It is "penetrating," yet not yet fully perfected.
Regarding the obstacle to applying effort within the eight signless states (up to the fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of persons):

because it does not contradict that [knowledge], the obstacle to applying effort within the signless refers to the superior practice initiated during the aforementioned seventh emptiness, even though...

The mind that initiates superior practice involves deliberate effort (*sābhoga*) and has not yet become spontaneous (*anābhoga*), because on the fifth stage one contemplates both the ultimate and the conventional simultaneously, and thus signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is slight.
On the sixth stage, because defilement and purity are equalized, signless contemplation is predominant.
Although on the seventh stage one enters signless contemplation in every moment of thought, it still involves effort; for the Bodhisattva of the seventh stage acts with such profound wisdom.
They observe with constant diligence the cultivation of skillful means, never ceasing or abandoning them for even a single thought-moment.
Although they are able to manifest bodies and lands, they enter the realms of immeasurable sentient beings and the pure Buddha-lands of immeasurable Buddhas.
Because one has not yet attained spontaneous engagement, this constitutes an obstruction.

Upon reaching the eighth stage, one enters the state where all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, unarisen, signless, unformed, undestroyed, inexhaustible, non-evolving, and characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature as their very nature.
Throughout the beginning, middle, and end, all are entirely equal; it is the sphere entered by the non-conceptual wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*), which is free from all [conceptualization].
The mind, consciousness, and mental discrimination are free from conceptualization and attachment; like space, they enter into all phenomena.
Being of the nature of space, this is called attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

One immediately abandons all effortful application and attains the effortless karma of body, speech, and mind. All mental activities cease, and one abides in the stage of maturation (*vipākacaryā*); thus, this obstacle is severed.

Based on this, it is said that one obstacle and two delusions are abandoned: first, the delusion regarding the activity of signlessness (*animitta*), because at every moment one applies effort to enter the contemplation of signlessness;
second, the delusion regarding lack of mastery within signs, because one is unable to manifest the body and the land spontaneously.
It is only from the eighth stage upward that the purely untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) finally attains spontaneity; it is only at this stage that [one is able to do so].
The name *ālayavijñāna* is relinquished; the afflictions of the three realms never again manifest, and one is freed from birth in discrete segments because one has transcended the three realms.

Only the subtle, co-emergent seventh consciousness (*manas*) may still manifest, because it has realized only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), but has not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), as the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persists.
Question: Why does the clinging to phenomena still persist when the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons has arisen?
Answer: Because the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons does not contradict the seventh [affliction], the clinging to a self of phenomena (*dharmātmagraha*).
Among the nine obstacles to benefiting others, those ranging from "lack of desire to act" up to the end are all subsumed within this ninth obstacle.
Regarding those who do not wish to act for the benefit of others: this refers to Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
All functional efforts cease entirely; furthermore, all activities of mind, thought, and consciousness no longer manifest before them.
Even the mind of a Bodhisattva, the mind of a Buddha, the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and the mind of nirvāṇa do not arise, let alone worldly minds. This is that stage.

By the power of the Bodhisattva’s original vow, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, personally appear before him and bestow upon him the wisdom of the Tathāgata, causing him to enter the gateway of the stream of the Dharma, and speak these words: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
This patience is supreme; it accords with all the Buddha-dharmas. However, son of good family, as for our ten powers and fearlessnesses..."
"You have not yet attained the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. You should apply yourself with diligent vigor and never again let them slip away.
Furthermore, son of good family, although you have attained this liberation of quiescence, ordinary beings have not yet realized it;
their various afflictions are all manifest before them, and their various discursive thoughts constantly assail them."

"Alas! You should take pity upon such sentient beings. Furthermore, son of good family, you should recall your original vow to universally and greatly benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the gate of inconceivable wisdom, and so forth;
for it is through the Buddhas that such immeasurable and boundless gates for the arising of wisdom are bestowed."
The wisdom and activity produced in a single moment [of this stage] surpasses all the practices cultivated from the first aspiration up to the seventh stage;
even a hundredth part, or even a hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta part, cannot equal it.
Why is this? This bodhisattva previously practiced with a single body;
now, dwelling in this stage, he has attained immeasurable bodies, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable births, and immeasurable pure lands, whereby he transforms and guides immeasurable sentient beings.
They make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, enter immeasurable Dharma-gates, and possess immeasurable supernormal powers and so forth.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this eighth stage, they employ the effortless awakening-wisdom (*anābhoga-buddhi*) arising from the skillful wisdom of great expedient means (*mahopāya-kauśalya*).
One contemplates the objective sphere of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), namely, contemplating the formation and destruction of world-systems and so forth.

Thereafter, one enters the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). This Bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the activities of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas, as well as the activities of tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
Having attained mastery over their own mind and dharmas, they transform and benefit sentient beings through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). This is called the dharma.

"Phenomenon" (dharma) refers to the self-nature of things, because it possesses the quality of maintaining its own characteristics; it is the conventional reality subsumed within the two kinds of emptiness, which is the true object.
"Meaning" (artha) refers to the objective aspect of differentiation within the essence of the dharma-realm; that is, the sense of distinct objects upon the substance of phenomena.
"Language" (vyañjana) refers to acquiring the local dialects and explaining them to others. As the Treatise says: "Within the realm of suchness-knowledge, in accordance with others..."

Regarding "speaking what is pleasing": because one gives [speech] with correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*). Fourth, "delight in speaking" (*pratibhāna*) refers to a specific meaning within the category of speech;

it involves subtle discrimination and analysis. The *Śāstra* states: "With respect to those various and immeasurable kinds of speech that accord with what others find pleasing, one speaks with correct knowledge, giving [speech] in accordance with such understanding."
Tenth is the obstacle consisting in not yet having attained mastery over all dharmas (extending to the phrase "the great cloud of dharma-knowledge and that which it contains").
Prior to this, on the eighth stage, the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) does not function at all; this directly obstructs the mental mastery of the ninth stage.
Although one attains mastery of the mind in the ninth stage, one still lacks mastery over all dharmas; therefore, this [obstacle] is also established.
Obstruction. Now, upon reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one finally abandons these two delusions that constitute the obstruction.
Because one has abandoned the delusion regarding great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), this Bodhisattva’s wisdom is clear and penetrating, and their supernormal powers are sovereign.

According to their mental intention, they are able to transform a narrow world into a vast world, a vast world into a narrow world, a defiled world into a pure world, and a pure [world into a defiled world].
Worlds—defiled worlds, those abiding in disorder, those abiding in succession, those abiding inverted, and those abiding upright—all such immeasurable worlds can be mutually transformed.
Or, according to his mental resolve, he may place a single world, including Mount Sumeru and all its mountains and rivers, within a single atom;
yet the characteristics of the atom remain as they were, and the world is not diminished, even up to [the point of] placing [them all therein].
One cannot describe all the Mount Sumerus, mountains, and rivers of world-systems, for the essential nature and characteristics of their atoms remain as they were.
Or, according to the mind's intention, one may manifest within a single pore all the adorned phenomena of the spheres of all Buddhas;
this Bodhisattva is able to manifest such things, as well as other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas.

Through sovereign spiritual power, by virtue of having severed the subtle delusions regarding secrets of abandonment and realization, this bodhisattva knows, exactly as they are, the subtle wisdoms into which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter.
That is to say: the subtle wisdom of cultivation; the subtle wisdom of the end of life; the subtle wisdom of taking birth;
the manifestation of supernatural powers upon leaving the household life; the attainment of perfect enlightenment; the turning of the wheel of Dharma; and their abiding [in the world].
He knows, as they truly are, the lifespan, the parinirvāṇa, and the subtle wisdom regarding the duration of the teaching;
furthermore, he enters the secret spheres of the Tathāgata, namely: the secret of body, the secret of speech, and the secret of mind; the secret of discerning the proper and improper time;
the secret of bestowing predictions upon bodhisattvas; the secret of gathering sentient beings; and the various vehicles.
The secrets: the secret of the differences in the faculties and conduct of all sentient beings; the secret of the workings of karma;
the secret of the practice for attaining bodhi. He knows all such things as they truly are, as well as all the wisdom possessed by all Buddhas.
Vast and immeasurable, this stage is one into which all bodhisattvas are able to enter.

Within a single moment of thought, they are able to settle, receive, gather, and uphold all the immeasurable great Dharma illuminations, great Dharma rains, and Dharma treasuries of the three times belonging to all Buddhas.
For this reason, this stage is named the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi). It bestows the rank of consecration and leads one into the realm of the Buddhas.
Endowed with the ten powers, they are reckoned among the Buddhas;
for on this stage, although they have attained mastery over all phenomena, they proceed until they realize great nirvāṇa and great bodhi.

This reveals the stage of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Regarding these ten stages (*bhūmi*), although one has attained mastery over phenomena (*dharma*), there still remain subtle seeds of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) that have not yet been completely severed;

thus, it is not yet called "ultimate. When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) of a Bodhisattva on this stage manifests, the seeds of the two obstructions are suddenly severed in a single instant, and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata. Only then...
This is called the ultimate limit. Question: What is the difference between the two wisdoms of Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment? Answer:
Just as a person with clear vision perceives various forms and images through a thin silk veil, so too is the sublime wisdom of a Bodhisattva regarding all objects.
Just as a person with clear vision perceives various forms and images without any obstruction, so too is the sublime wisdom of a Tathāgata regarding [all objects].

All objects of perception are likewise so. Furthermore, it is said: although this Bodhisattva has already cultivated the ocean of merit until it is full, because he is still unable to abandon three kinds of dharmas, he is not yet called "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue).
First, because he has not yet abandoned inferior outflow-free (anāsrava) dharmas;
second, because he has not yet abandoned pure neutral (avyākṛta) dharmas; third, because he has not yet abandoned wholesome outflowing (sāsrava) dharmas. Upon reaching Sublime [Enlightenment]...
Because these three are abandoned only at the stage of awakening (*bodhi*).
*Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Nine;
*Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Ten.
Composed by Bodhisattvas such as Dharmapāla;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree;
compiled and annotated by the Śramaṇa Tongrun of Jinting Changshou Monastery.
These eleven hindrances are subsumed within the two hindrances; [this continues] until: "the three stages are made manifest, and for this reason they are specifically mentioned.
Regarding the statement that these eleven hindrances are subsumed within the two hindrances: this means that, in general, the two hindrances encompass and condense the eleven hindrances.
Question: At what stage are the seeds and active manifestations of the afflictions subdued and abandoned? Answer:

If they are the seeds of intellectually acquired afflictions, they are abandoned instantaneously at the moment of the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) in the first bhūmi. If they are the active manifestations of intellectually acquired afflictions, they are gradually subdued during the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*).
If they are the seeds of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), [they are abandoned] at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, all [afflictions] are severed instantaneously.
If it is the case that innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) manifest, these too are gradually subdued from the stage of preparation (*prayoga-avasthā*).

From ascending the first ground (*bhūmi*) up to the eighth, they are completely subdued and no longer function, just as in an Arhat. Question: If they have already been instantaneously subdued at the time of the first ground, for what reason...

Question: Why do greed and other afflictions still arise in the seventh stage? Answer: It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings. By the power of intentional resolve (*cetanā*), they manifest temporarily without committing transgressions.

From the eighth stage upward, these afflictions are never again practiced, because in the eighth stage one attains mastery over signs and lands (*nimitta-bhūmi-vaśitā*), in the ninth stage one attains mastery over the mind (*citta-vaśitā*), and in the tenth stage one attains mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*). Question: Regarding the seeds of the knowable (*jñeya-bīja*)...

Question: At what stage are they suppressed and abandoned? Answer: If they are seeds of the knowable that are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), they are abandoned instantaneously at the same moment as the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) during the True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

If they are the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the conceptually constructed knowable, they are gradually suppressed during the stages of the Requisites (*sambhāra*) and Preparatory Application (*prayoga*). As for the seeds of the innate (*sahaja*) knowable...

Son, these are gradually eliminated throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), until at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests during the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*),
they are forever and utterly severed. If it concerns the manifest activity of innate objects of knowledge (*jñeya*),
these are likewise gradually subdued during the stages of the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), until they are forever [eliminated] at the tenth stage.
[They are] completely severed. Question: Since both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses have objects of cognition (*jñeya*), which stage severs which? Answer:
If the objects of cognition coexist with the six consciousnesses, they no longer manifest from the eighth stage upward.

Because the mind of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-citta*) and the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna-phala*) continue without interruption, they are able to oppose those [objects]. If the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) [coexists] with the seventh...

Regarding those associated with consciousness (*vijñāna*): from the eighth stage upward, they may still manifest until the time when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatājñāna*) becomes present in the tenth stage.

At that point, one attains mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*), and those obstacles are finally suppressed. Question: At which stages are the afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the first five evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) suppressed and abandoned?
Answer: Although the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) associated with the first five evolving consciousnesses exist during the causal stage, [they are suppressed and abandoned as follows:]...

In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), by the power of subduing through that sixth uncontaminated contemplative mind (*anāsrava-citta*), those obstacles do not arise.
If these are attachments to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), they do not exist within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and thus need not be subdued or severed. Question:
