Why is it that during the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one severs only the seeds of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) and does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)? Answer: Although [the afflictions] are present during the stage of the path of cultivation...

Throughout these stages, the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are never severed; rather, it is when the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are severed that the heavy latencies (*dausthulya*) of those afflictions are also gradually eliminated.

For this reason, it is said that all three stages possess the meaning of severing both obstructions. That is to say: in the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), one suddenly severs the seeds of the two obstructions consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one gradually severs the seeds and manifestations of the two obstructions consisting of innate tendencies (*sahaja*).
Upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one completely eradicates the seeds of both innate (*sahaja*) obstacles. Question:

If this is so, do the heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) not persist throughout the stages of Accumulation (*saṃbhāra*) and Application (*prayoga*)? Answer: Although heavy impediments are indeed severed throughout all stages, they are most manifest during these three [stages].
Therefore, it is explained partially.
Regarding the gradual and sudden abandonment of the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), how do they relate? From beginning to end, they may all be present in relation to one another.
Question: Regarding the seeds of the two obstacles, how are they suddenly abandoned and how are they gradually abandoned in both the Great and Small Vehicles? Answer: First...

Regarding the seeds of the innate afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the seven consciousnesses: because those seven cannot enter the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they are not abandoned gradually.
When one is about to realize the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) in any of the three vehicles, they are abandoned all at once within a single moment across the three realms.
As for the seeds of the innate cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness, when a Bodhisattva is about to become a Buddha, [they are abandoned] in a single moment.

All [afflictions] within the intermediate [stages] are abandoned simultaneously. This is because the seventh consciousness, being innate (*sahaja*), spontaneously clings to an internal [object], and being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), its object is of a single category without coarse or subtle distinctions;
therefore, it is abandoned only all at once. As for the seeds of afflictions associated with the six consciousnesses, there are both simultaneous and gradual abandonments.
Regarding the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that are abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), they are abandoned by the vision of the three vehicles.
Within the stages of the Path, all innate seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are suddenly severed.

However, depending on whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, this occurs either instantaneously or gradually. For a certain class of those with dull faculties—the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*)—it takes seven births to sever [these hindrances].

Taking the three realms and dividing them into nine stages (*bhūmi*), each stage is further divided into nine grades (*prakāra*). A person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) severs the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the [first grade of the first stage].

The fifth category is called the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*). Upon abandoning the sixth category, one is named the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), because there remain three categories of residual afflictions through which one must still return to the human realm.
If one abandons up to the eighth category, one is named the candidate for the fruit of non-returning. When the ninth category is abandoned entirely, [one attains the fruit of non-returning].
This is called the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). Because the afflictions of the desire realm are exhausted and one is no longer reborn among humans, it is the fruit of non-returning.
One takes birth in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), and further severs the nine grades of afflictions for each of the upper eight stages until reaching the seventy-first grade;

this is called the stage of the candidate for arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*). Upon severing the final grade, one realizes the fruit of arhatship. Furthermore, there is another class of those with sharp faculties among the two vehicles who, having...
Regarding the nine stages of the three realms, there are eighty-one grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*). These are combined into a single aggregate and divided into nine grades.
Although there are nine grades, they are severed individually within a single lifetime, as they do not require seven lifetimes. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"Furthermore, there are two types of *pudgala* who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*): first, those who attain liberation gradually; second, those who attain liberation all at once. Regarding the gradual [attainment]:

The former case is as previously described. Regarding the "sudden" [attainment], this refers to entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration (the threshold dhyāna) to produce a supramundane path that suddenly severs all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.
Because these are severed category by category, only two fruits are established: namely, the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Regarding the term "sudden abandonment" (*tunduan*) used for an Arhat: this refers to what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). Regarding the term "gradual abandonment" (*bie-duan*):

this refers to first suddenly abandoning the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) across the three realms, followed sequentially down to the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*).
Furthermore, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states: "Whatever form there is, up to consciousness—whether past, future, or present..."
Whether far or near, all these together are condensed into one part, one mass, one accumulation, and one heap.
Having thus condensed them, one should contemplate that all are impermanent, suffering, and empty according to this principle;
however, only the first and last two fruits can be established. If a bodhisattva must reach the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*)...

In the preceding moment, within a single kṣaṇa, the afflictions of the three realms are severed all at once. If these are the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the sixth consciousness, they are not shared by the two vehicles;

only Bodhisattvas sever them. If they are those arising from discrimination (*vikalpaja*) and are to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the Bodhisattva severs them all at once in the first thought-moment of the first bhūmi.
If they are those arising simultaneously with birth (*sahaja*) and are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), from...
The path of cultivation begins at the first bhūmi and proceeds through the ten bhūmis in gradual succession to sever [the afflictions].

When the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, the seeds of the aforementioned afflictions are severed and exhausted in a single moment, and one enters the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*). Question:

For what reason are the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the seventh consciousness severed all at once, whereas the seeds of the cognitive obstructions of the six consciousnesses are severed both suddenly and gradually?

[Question: It is severed [all at once]. [Answer: Because the seventh consciousness spontaneously takes the internal as its object, its objects lack coarseness or subtlety, and its categories lack differentiation;

therefore, it is severed instantaneously. This sixth consciousness, however, universally takes both the internal and external as its objects; its objects possess coarseness and subtlety, and its categories possess differentiation.

Therefore, that which is coarse is abandoned all at once, while that which is subtle is eliminated gradually; that which takes external objects as its condition is abandoned all at once, while that which takes internal objects as its condition is eliminated gradually.
The following clarifies the differences in the application of effort between the two vehicles in abandoning hindrances.

If it concerns those of dull faculties among the two vehicles, when they gradually abandon hindrances, they must each separately give rise to the preparatory (*prayoga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), whether collectively or individually. Thus it is said:

Regarding the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*): when viewed from the perspective of the cause toward the fruit, it is called the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), because it is proximate to the fruit. Regarding the "liberation" (*vimukti*):
when viewed from the perspective of the fruit toward the cause, it is called the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because it is free from the cause.

Because it interrupts the afflictions without interval and realizes the truth through liberation, these two arise separately. All roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) are called the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). The... [text ends]
When each preceding stage is viewed in relation to each succeeding stage, it is called the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). These two paths may arise either collectively or individually.

If a bodhisattva of sharp faculties is in the stage of gradually severing hindrances, although they sever ignorance partially and realize the true reality partially, because delusions are eliminated by the arising of wisdom, it is not necessary for them to separately give rise to an uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever delusions, nor a path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to realize the truth.
Because the four types of paths of abandonment, such as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth, are fully present throughout the preceding and succeeding moments;

thus, regarding the ten aspects of true suchness (*tathatā*), from the first, the universally pervasive true suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), up to the second, one is able to realize the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

This clarifies the ten kinds of true thusness (*tathatā*). Regarding "pervasive true thusness": because one realizes this true thusness by severing the obstacles of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called pervasive.
This means that this true thusness suddenly severs the two kinds of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); there is no phenomenon not subsumed within what is revealed by the two emptinesses.
Therefore, it is called pervasive. In the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is termed "all-pervading" (*paripūrṇa*), meaning it pervades all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because of practice; for there is not a single dharma that is not empty of both [subject and object]. This stage is first and foremost characterized by universal realization and universal pervasion.

Regarding what is called "the most excellent *tathatā*": on the second stage, one abandons the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*) because one is endowed with pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Since ethical discipline is the root of all virtues, and since ethical discipline is the most excellent, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Among great and grievous illnesses, ethical discipline is the efficacious medicine. Great...

In the midst of fear, ethical discipline is the protection. In the darkness of ignorance at the time of death, ethical discipline is the bright lamp. Within the evil realms, ethical discipline is the valiant general.
In the waters of the ocean of death, ethical discipline is the great ship. Therefore, it is called the most supreme, the stream of excellence, and true suchness (*tathatā*).
On the third stage, one abandons the obstacle of dullness and darkness, possesses superior meditative concentration and dhāraṇī, and flows forth boundlessly.

Because of its wondrous wisdom (*suvijñā*). The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya) of the Liang dynasty states: "From *tathatā* flows forth the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); from the fundamental wisdom flows forth the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);
from the subsequently attained wisdom flows forth great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); and from great compassion flow forth the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
Therefore, it is called "the supreme outflow" (*jyeṣṭha-niṣyanda*). The commentary explains: "This teaching, which flows like a stream, is the most supreme. It further states:
If one realizes this suchness, because the teaching is superior, it is called "the suchness without appropriation.

By means of the fourth stage, one abandons the subtle obstacles of the active manifestation of afflictions and partially realizes bodhi; this is termed "supramundane," as one is far removed from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Because it is without any attachment or dependence. Vasubandhu says: Within this suchness (*tathatā*), there is no grasping at "mine," because, like the people of the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), it is without attachment or dependence.

One should explain this suchness as being free from the basis for the grasping of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*), self-love (*ātmasneha*), ignorance (*avidyā*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the statement that "the categories [of suchness] have no distinction," this refers to what is abandoned in the fifth stage.
Because it is the obstacle to the nirvāṇa of the lower vehicles; because the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional, are unified as one; and because saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are both equal.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* names this the "continuously undifferentiated dharmadhātu," meaning that within this, the essence is without distinction.
It is not like the eyes and so forth, which differ according to the individual continuums of various sentient beings. (From the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*).
It is said: Because of this *tathatā*, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are able to continue in succession without difference.

Sentient beings are deluded by it, resulting in the differentiation of the myriad classes of beings; the Buddhas realize it, remaining inherently unchanging. Therefore, regarding what is called "the *tathatā* free from defilement and purity":

in the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmiḥ*), one deeply contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as the equality of defilement and purity, thereby severing the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics and giving rise to [the wisdom of the seventh stage].
There is also the *tathatā* that is neither defiled nor purified, because it attains the fruit of being neither defiled nor purified within the continuums of both self and others.

This means that the intrinsic nature of this *tathatā* is inherently undefiled; it is not something that becomes pure only after having been defiled. Regarding the statement "the *tathatā* in which dharmas have no distinction":

By means of the seventh stage, one abandons the obstacle of the subtle manifestation of signs (*nimitta*) and enters the sublime contemplation of signlessness (*animittadhyāna*), realizing the non-differentiation of phenomena (*dharmābheda*).
This is because one understands that all various teachings are identical to *tathatā* (suchness), as they lack dual characteristics;

that is to say, all teachings are established based upon *tathatā*, and since *tathatā* itself is without variation, one further establishes the various aspects of the true nature of the *dharmadhātu* within those teachings.
These names are identical and without difference. Regarding the statement that *tathatā* (suchness) neither increases nor decreases:

this is because in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the obstacles of preparatory application (*prayoga-āvaraṇa*) and thereby attains that which neither increases nor decreases. This means that although there is defilement when it diminishes, there is no actual diminution;

and although there is purification when it increases, there is no actual increase. Wuxing (Jñānaprabha) says: "There is no function outside of phenomena, therefore it does not increase. All phenomena..."
[It is] destroyed. Therefore, it does not diminish. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of these dharmas remains eternally constant and unchanging. Regarding "mastery over marks and lands," Vasubandhu says:
"To attain mastery among all marks is called mastery over marks (*lakṣaṇavaśitā*), because one can cause them to manifest immediately according to one's desire. [This applies to] the ten...
Because one fashions the physical marks, one attains mastery over the manifested lands; this is called "mastery over the land.
Because one can cause the land to become gold, jewels, and so forth, according to one's wish, it is called "mastery over wisdom. As for *tathatā* (suchness):

because one eliminates the obstacle of non-aspiration in the ninth stage and attains mastery over the mind, the *tathatā* that is realized is called "mastery over wisdom. [End of] *Nirabhilāpya-siddhi*.
It is said: because this stage is the basis for the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), it is the partial realization of the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*).
Regarding all phenomena, one does not follow their mere words, but is skillfully able to understand the underlying meaning and intent of all dharmas.

Thus, one truly accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings, causing them to receive the supreme bliss of the Dharma. The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "There are four kinds of mastery: first, [mastery over non-conceptualization]..."
Mastery over discernment (*vikalpa-vaśitā*) is itself mastery over signs (*nimitta-vaśitā*). Second is mastery over the pure lands (*śuddha-kṣetra-vaśitā*);

third is mastery over gnosis (*jñāna-vaśitā*); and fourth is mastery over karma (*karma-vaśitā*). Because these four serve as the bases for grasping, the eighth stage can only penetrate the first two masteries;
the latter two masteries correspond respectively to the final two stages. Regarding "the *tathatā* of mastery over karma":
On the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), one abandons the obstacle to attaining mastery and realizes mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*).

Because of this attainment of mastery over phenomena, all activities and functions performed are without exception characterized by mastery. Question: Since it is named *tathatā* (suchness), its essence is without differentiation; for what reason [is there a distinction between stages]?

Furthermore, there are various distinctions. The answer is: although the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) has no distinctions, ten kinds of distinct names and so forth are provisionally established according to the supreme qualities (*guṇa*) of *tathatā*; it is not that the essence of *tathatā* actually possesses distinctions.
Question: Since the first stage (*bhūmi*) is already named "Universal True Suchness" (*sarvatraga-tathatā*) and thus pervades all things, why must nine further types be established?
Answer: Although the True Suchness of the first stage already pervades everything, the capacity for its realization has not yet reached fulfillment.
To bring it to completion, the subsequent nine types are established. Thus, [the following] concludes the preceding text proximately and [leads toward the next section] distantly.
When the first fascicle is concluded, if one realizes the two kinds of emptiness, their respective obstacles are accordingly severed.

Regarding the distinctions in the stages of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there are briefly six types. (Up to: because it causes that which is not true to largely no longer manifest.

The following explains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). First, it is explained according to the stages, which are divided into six types. 1. **Transformation through the Diminution of Power and the Augmentation of Capability**:
*Diminution* means reduction; *power* refers to force; *augmentation* means increase; and *capability* refers to functional efficacy.

This refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), wherein one possesses four kinds of power, cultivates six kinds of practice, and gives rise to three kinds of mind, thereby gaining faith and understanding in representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) and its characteristics and nature.

Possessing resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)—that is, during the stage of application (*prayoga*)—one gives rise to the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and brings forth the four cognitions of reality (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).

One contemplates the emptiness of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). Possessing shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), through the power of cultivating resolute conviction and shame during these two stages, one is able to diminish the force of the defiled seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and further augment the functional capacity of the pure seeds within the fundamental consciousness. By means of this...

The transformation of the defiled basis into the pure is called *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis). Question: Since those in the three stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet severed the seeds of the obstacles of conceptualization and have not yet ascended to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), how can they be said to have achieved the transformation of the basis?

Answer: Although they have not yet severed the seeds of the obstacles of conceptualization and have not yet realized the transformation of the basis in its actual sense, because they are able to gradually suppress the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of conceptualization, they may also be said to have realized the transformation of the basis. Second is the transformation through penetration (*prativedha-parāvṛtti*).
This refers to the stage of transformation (āśraya-parivṛtti), which occurs at the time of the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) in the first bhūmi.

At that moment, one suddenly severs the seeds of the two obstacles—those of the self and phenomena—and attains fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), realizing the universally pervasive suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*). Because one truly realizes a portion of the ultimate transformation of the basis, it is called the "stage of transformation.

Regarding the term "transformation through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*): "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means to repair and maintain so as not to allow [the ground] to become overgrown with weeds; "practice" (*abhyāsa*) means to rehearse and familiarize oneself [with the path].

One does not allow [these] to be forgotten or lost. This means that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, one repeatedly cultivates the ten kinds of superior practices (*viśeṣa-caryā*), gradually eliminating the ten kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and progressively realizes the ten kinds of suchness (*tathatā*).

This is called the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*). The following citation from the treatise serves to prove the two meanings of "thorough penetration" (*prativedha*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) regarding this transformation: namely, those of the first six stages. All...

This is called the transformation of thorough penetration, because it penetrates the ultimate and thoroughly understands the conventional. If one penetrates the ultimate through the contemplation of signlessness, then the ultimate appears while the conventional does not appear.
If one thoroughly understands the conventional through the contemplation of signs, then the conventional appears while the ultimate does not appear.
Because the ultimate and the conventional alternate and existence and non-existence intermingle, it is called "thorough penetration.

This refers to the transformation through cultivation in the latter four stages (*bhūmi*), wherein one practices the contemplation of the purely signless for a long duration, thereby severing the remaining coarse latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) so that signs no longer intermingle.
However, the statement that "for the most part, that which is not true does not appear" serves as a counter-illustration, indicating that there still remains a small amount of that which is not true.
This refers to its manifestation at that time.
The "turning" of the four fruits being perfected refers to the ultimate stage (the *niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), wherein benefit and happiness for others continue inexhaustibly until the end of the future.

The former is called "partial realization," while this is called "complete realization. This extends from the path of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) up to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-jñāna*). Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*).
When the ten great samādhis, such as the "Luminous" (Prabhākari), manifest before one, the extremely subtle seeds of the two obstacles that are innate are forever severed.

Upon reaching the Path of Liberation, one suddenly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood and attains the perfect transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti); this is termed the Ultimate Stage (niṣṭhā-bhūmi).
From this point on, having completed the task of self-benefit, one remains solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings throughout the limits of the future.
The five inferior transformations refer to the stage of the two vehicles (up to the point where they) abandon the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and thereby attain realization.
They seek exclusively their own benefit and do not attend to the benefit of others. They loathe suffering and rejoice in quiescence, unable to contemplate [reality] with equanimity.

They realize only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) remains unrealized. They sever the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*) but do not sever the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). They realize true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), but do not realize...
Bodhi [is characterized by] attachment to the bliss of quiescence and a lack of superior capability. Possessing these six meanings is termed "inferior transformation.

The opposite of these six meanings is termed "vast. The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) discussed here refers to this vast [transformation], because it is attained by abandoning the two types of heavy obstructions (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Question: Why is the transformation of the perfection of the fruit not taken up? Answer: In contrast to the Bodhisattva...
Thus it is said. For this reason, it is not accepted. The above discussion regarding the stages does not exceed the two vehicles of the Great and Small;
now, having set aside the Small Vehicle, we exclusively take up the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the Great Vehicle.

The meanings of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) are briefly of four kinds. (Up to: both the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms] are able to correctly sever [the afflictions].
Previously, the transformation of the basis was explained by means of six stages; here, it is explained by means of these four meanings. First, the path that effects the transformation.

Transformation has two meanings: namely, the ability to suppress and the ability to eradicate. Regarding "the ability to suppress," this refers to the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), which possess the power to produce manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
Therefore, one cultivates the wisdom of the six aspects (*ṣaḍākāra*) as well as preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) and so forth to suppress them, ensuring they do not arise manifestly.
This applies to both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths; that is, suppressing them gradually by means of the six aspects pertains only to the contaminated path.

If one gradually subdues [the afflictions] by means of the two types of wisdom—preparatory and subsequently attained—they pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

If one subdues them instantaneously by means of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), it pertains exclusively to the uncontaminated; therefore, that which is said to "sever" refers to the arising of fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Only then can one eternally sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstructions. This path capable of such severance does not include that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*), nor preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*).
That is to say, among the two paths, it excludes the contaminated path; and among the three knowledges, it excludes preparatory knowledge.
It excludes the contaminated because the contaminated path is induced by previously habituated grasping at signs (*nimitta-grāha*), and thus has not yet eliminated those signs. Namely, the first...
The seven consciousnesses grasp at a self moment by moment, causing the sixth consciousness to be unable to eliminate signs (nimitta) regarding its practice of giving and so forth.

Although the paths with outflows (sāsrava-mārga) constantly arise as active manifestations, they neither diminish nor benefit [the grasping at self]; therefore, it is the path that can sever [this grasping].

It refers exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*). The preparatory application (*prayoga*) is excluded because the wisdom of preparatory application (*prayogajñāna*) can only involve diligent effort and the desire to strive toward the superior fruit and its inducing causes;
it has not yet accomplished these. Therefore, the wisdom of preparatory application can only suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for the actual severance of afflictions, this occurs only through the fundamental [wisdom] (*mūla*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*). This is based on the two meanings of "suppressing" and "severing."

This explains the meaning of the term "turning" (*vartana*). One master says: "The fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) directly realizes ultimate truth and is able to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding that truth;

thus, it is the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*). Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) cannot sever the latent tendencies that delude one regarding truth, and therefore it is not the path of abandonment.
Another master states the correct position: "The fundamental non-conceptual wisdom is able to sever [the delusion regarding truth]..."

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are what the path of abandonment severs. Although the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom cannot sever the latent dispositions that delude one regarding principles, it can nonetheless permanently sever the latent dispositions that delude one regarding phenomena;
this too constitutes a path of abandonment. Regarding the terms "deluding one regarding principles" and "deluding one regarding phenomena":
To mistake the self for objects is called delusion regarding principle; to recognize objects as the self is called delusion regarding phenomena. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"On the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is the supramundane path capable of severing [afflictions], and there is the mundane-supramundane path capable of severing them.
The supramundane path capable of severing is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The mundane-supramundane path capable of severing is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)."
Only these two paths are able to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). There has never been a purely mundane path capable of permanently destroying the latent tendencies.
A "purely mundane path" refers to the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*).

Because this wisdom of application only suppresses and removes the active manifestations of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) of conceptual construction while still on the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, it is called "purely mundane wisdom"; it has not yet ascended to the [bodhisattva] stages. Thus it is.

Because they are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), because they have been previously practiced, because they involve conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), because they are induced by the grasping of signs (*nimittagrāha*),

and because the signs have not yet been forgotten— by this principle, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude regarding the nature of reality and are abandoned through seeing and cultivation are exclusively fundamental.
Because one has personally realized the principle, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding deluded phenomena are correctly severed in both their fundamental and subsequently attained aspects.
Regarding the two bases of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) resulting from this, there are two types; however, since the latter is not fundamental, it is not mentioned here.

Second is the basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The term "basis" has two meanings: namely, the support for seeds and the state of delusion or awakening. Regarding the basis as the support for seeds:
this refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which is able to maintain the seeds of all defiled and pure phenomena, because seeds must necessarily have a support.

When one cultivates the Noble Path, the eighth consciousness is transformed such that it abandons defiled seeds and acquires pure seeds; therefore, it is called "transformation of the basis. Question: [Regarding] the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)...
The *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is also the basis for both defilement and purification; why, then, is it not mentioned? Answer:
Although the *paratantra-svabhāva* is indeed the basis for both defilement and purification, it cannot maintain seeds (*bīja*); therefore, it is not mentioned here.

That which is called the "basis of delusion and awakening" is precisely *tathatā* (suchness), because the nature of *tathatā* is the root of both delusion and awakening, and because it serves as the objective support (*ālambana*) for all phenomena of defilement and purification. Cultivation...

At the time of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), it is transformed such that True Suchness (*tathatā*) abandons defilement and becomes pure; therefore, it is also called "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Although the remaining [explanations] are inferior, their resolution of difficulties is the same as the first [case] above. The first basis is the doctrine of the *lakṣaṇavāda* (Characteristics School), while the second basis is the doctrine of the *dharmatāvāda* (Nature School).

Regarding the three things that are relinquished through transformation, there are two [types of] relinquishment up to the eighth stage, because the pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) is not the support for those [three].
There are two senses of "relinquishment": namely, that which is severed and that which is discarded.

What is called "severed" refers to the seeds of the two obstacles—of self and phenomena—which are innate (*sahaja*). Since these seeds are not substantial realities, they can be severed and relinquished; this occurs at the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

In the interim, when the true path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) manifests, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises. This wisdom acts as the antidote to those obstacles; as wisdom arises, delusions perish.
This is termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), meaning they are never again accomplished. This is termed "relinquishment" (*tyāga*).

Since those seeds have been severed, one never again falsely clings to a real self or real dharmas; this is termed "relinquishing the pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpita-tyāga*). The self and dharmas thus grasped no longer confront deluded cognition.
This is called "abandoning what is grasped. By virtue of this meaning, it is called "abandoning that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).

When some say "severing the conceptually constructed," the meaning lies herein. That which is said to be "discarded" refers to the remaining seeds of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the inferior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the remaining contaminated [dharmas]: apart from the seeds of the two aforementioned obstacles, all other contaminated wholesome seeds, as well as the uncontaminated seeds perfumed by inferior indeterminate [states], are no longer the support for those [seeds] at the time when the diamond-like concentration manifests and brings about the most perfectly complete, radiant, purely singular, pure, and stainless fundamental consciousness; they are all forever [extinguished].
Abandonment. Question: For what reason must these two types [of seeds] necessarily be abandoned? Answer: When untainted wholesome states arise, tainted wholesome states naturally cease;
when superior dharmas reach full clarity, inferior dharmas naturally contradict them. This is the natural law (*dharmatā*), not something produced by effort.
Once those seeds have been abandoned, the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of those two will never arise again. It is also called "abandonment" based on this sense of abandonment. Thus it is named.

One abandons the inferior *pariṇāma-vipariṇāma* (transformative) birth-and-death and reaches this state, which is what is meant by the simultaneous disappearance of both good and evil, and the equal casting-off of both existence and non-existence.
Regarding "inferior birth-and-death," it is called inferior because the *pariccheda* (segmented) type is considered superior.
One master says that the remaining contaminated seeds of wholesome [dharmas] and the seeds of inferior uncontaminated dharmas, which remain under the two hindrances, are also [abandoned].
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, it simultaneously abandons the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). One master states the correct position as follows:
when the diamond-like concentration manifests, one merely abandons the seeds of the two obstacles;

the remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome factors and inferior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds have not yet been severed or abandoned, because the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) does not oppose them.

For this reason, if the seeds of other [defilements] were abandoned by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), then the Bodhisattva in the state of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) would have no further birth-and-death;

he would have no further maturation (*vipāka*); he would be designated as a Buddha while abiding in the path of uninterrupted transition; and the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) would be rendered useless.
By this line of reasoning, it is known that the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests within the path of uninterrupted transition.

At that time, although the seeds of the hindrances have been severed, other seeds still remain. It is only upon the arising of the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) at the final moment following the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi) that these remaining seeds are finally severed.
At that point, the maturation-consciousness (vipāka-vijñāna) is transformed into the stainless state, as it is no longer the substratum for those remaining seeds.

Regarding the four [qualities] attained through transformation, there are two further types. Only our World-Honored One can be said to possess all four. "Attainment" (prāpti) is spoken of in contrast to "abandonment" (tyāga);
because one abandons through transformation, one attains through transformation. This attainment is twofold: first, attainment by manifestation (abhivyakti-prāpti);
second, attainment by birth (upapatti-prāpti). What is called "attainment by manifestation" refers to Great Nirvāṇa. As for Nirvāṇa, its meaning is translated as "perfect stillness" (yuanji).

The Way fills the dharma-realm; its virtue extends to as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges—this is called "Perfect" (yuan). To investigate the true nature until it is wondrously transcendent of all phenomenal entanglements is called "Quiescent" (ji).
Question: If the self-nature of nirvana is originally pure, why is it called that which is "revealed through realization"?

Answer: Although this is inherently pure, it is obscured by adventitious defilements and thus cannot manifest. When the path of the truly holy ones eliminates those obstructions, [nirvana] is revealed.
Thus, its characteristics become manifest. This characteristic of *nirvāṇa* is established based on *tathatā* (suchness) once the two obstacles have been eliminated;

its essence is the pure *dharmadhātu*. Nevertheless, while this *nirvāṇa* in principle encompasses all, it is differentiated into four types according to the distinctions between the stages of ordinary beings and sages.
Briefly stated, these are: first, the original self-nature purity...
Pure nirvāṇa does not discriminate between ordinary beings and sages, nor between crawling insects and flying creatures; each and every one is perfectly complete.

This is precisely the true principle of *tathatā* (suchness) inherent within all phenomena. Question: Since this is the true principle of the non-moving *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics), as it is suchness, why...
Why, then, is it also covered by adventitious defilements? The answer is: although there are adventitious stains, its original nature is pure.

It is fully endowed with immeasurable, subtle, and wondrous merits; it is immovable and unchanging, devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, devoid of the characteristics of coming and going, and devoid of the characteristics of high and low.
It is as serene as empty space and is equally shared by all sentient beings—this is the essence of *nirvāṇa*.
It is neither identical to nor separate from all phenomena; it is neither one nor different.

It is free from the marks of existence and non-existence, free from the marks of annihilation and permanence, and free from the marks of mental objects. It transcends the path of thought and the way of language;
therefore, it is called "Suchness" (Tathatā). Although this Suchness exists equally [in all], it is perceived only by the noble ones within the true noble path.
The realization of the realm of self-enjoyment is what the *Laṅkāvatāra* refers to as "nirvāṇa by nature"; it is the realm of the emptiness of phenomena.

Second is nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). This means that although one has emerged from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within true suchness (*tathatā*), there still remains the basis for the suffering of birth and death in its segmented form (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*), because the final body of suffering belonging to the various noble ones (*ārya*) has not yet been extinguished. Yoga...
The Ga said: "Abiding in the state with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa), one still falls within the category of the multitude and still possesses manifold sufferings.

The attained transformation-basis (āśrayaparivṛtti) remains associated with the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana). As for the 'category of the multitude,' it refers to the body of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha); because this body exists,"

Because there are various sufferings. Question: Since there are various sufferings, why is it called *nirvāṇa*? Answer: Although there is still a subtle suffering with which it is associated, because the obstacles have been permanently extinguished, it is also called *nirvāṇa*.
This is because, although the fetters of the fruit (*phala-bandhana*) still exist, the fetters of the seed (*bīja-bandhana*) have already been exhausted.

Regarding the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*): it is called nirvana because there is no longer any suffering of the final *paricchinna-bhava-jāti-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Abiding in the state without remainder, one does not fall into the category of sentient beings; all sufferings are forever absent, and the six sense bases are forever non-correspondent.
Regarding the nirvana without abode (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*): the former two [types] are for the purpose of severing the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
This reveals *nirvāṇa*. This is the *nirvāṇa* manifested by the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding the term "non-abiding": it does not abide in either extreme.
Because it is supported by great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), it does not abide in saṃsāra; because it is supported by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it does not abide in *nirvāṇa*.
If one were to abide in saṃsāra, one would be identical to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); if one were to abide in *nirvāṇa*, [one would be like a śrāvaka].
This would then be identical to the Hīnayāna. Because one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, one is constantly in saṃsāra and yet constantly in nirvāṇa.
Regarding these four types of nirvāṇa, all sentient beings possess the first, but lack the latter three because they dwell in saṃsāra.
Those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning may possess the first three, but lack the final one because they abide in nirvāṇa.
Because of this [non-abiding], only our World-Honored One neither abides in saṃsāra nor abides in nirvāṇa; thus it can be said that he possesses all four [perfections].
This nirvāṇa without abiding is precisely the dwelling place of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
How is it that the Sugata possesses a *sopadhiśeṣa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), rather than being like certain [beings] who have entered *anupadhiśeṣa* (nirvāṇa without remainder)?
Question: Since the Sugata has exhausted the five abodes and forever eliminated the two deaths, how can he still possess *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?

Answer: Although there is no actual basis for suffering (*duḥkhāśraya*), the manifested body appears within the three realms (*tridhātu*) and shows itself as being similar to sentient beings by appearing to be associated with subtle suffering;
or, because the Tathāgata’s body has exhausted the basis for suffering, it is called "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).

That which possesses a remaining basis for bliss (*sukhāśraya*) is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). This is not like the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), where the presence of a basis for suffering is termed "with remainder. Question: Why?
[Question: It is known that the Tathāgata has no basis for suffering, but possesses a basis for bliss. [Answer: By relinquishing impermanent form (*rūpa*), one attains permanent form;

feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise so. Therefore, it is known that there is no basis for suffering, but there is a further basis for bliss.
For this reason, the Blessed One may be said to possess all four [bases]. [Question: If śrāvakas and others also possess the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), why is it that...?
In some places it is said that they have no nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*); in other places it is further said that there is no nirvana at all.
How could there be a remainder? That [remainder] also does not exist. Answer: For the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), there truly exists nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

As for the statement that there is none at all, it is because although the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the śrāvakas and others have been severed, their bodies and cognitions still persist, and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) still remain; thus, the basis for the suffering of birth and death still exists.
It has not yet been exhausted; thus, the meaning of parinirvāṇa cannot be fully manifested. It is with reference to this sense that it is said there is no nirvāṇa.
In reality, the afflictions have already been severed and the state of *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) has been realized; it does not mean that nirvāṇa is entirely non-existent.

Furthermore, there are passages stating there is no *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder), because at that time the bodies and wisdom of the two vehicles still persist and have not yet been realized [as such].
Because there is no further basis for suffering and it is extinguished without remainder, it is said that they possess "no nirvana without remainder.

This does not mean that after their bodies and wisdom have subsequently ceased, they lack nirvana without remainder. Furthermore, it is said that those of the two vehicles do not possess nirvana at all.
There is no fourth [type of] non-abiding nirvāṇa, because this is the ultimate fruit realized by all Buddhas.
It is not that the first three do not exist, for the first three are attainable by the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).

Furthermore, when it is said that the two vehicles lack nirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), this is spoken with reference to those of indeterminate lineage among the two vehicles; for those of indeterminate lineage possess faculties of such sharp capacity.
Having realized the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, they immediately turn their minds toward seeking great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

Without severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) and without being attached to the tranquility of cessation (*śānti*), they utilize the power of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and vows (*praṇidhāna*) to sustain the causes of their current existence, causing the body to remain for a long time.

Thus, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva and deliver sentient beings according to their vows, unlike those śrāvakas of fixed lineage who are determined to sever the afflictions once and for all.
[They] enter the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*). For this reason, it is said that those śrāvakas do not possess [the state of] nirvana without remainder.
This means that because the two vehicles deeply delight in complete quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*), it is stated again that they differ from the Buddha.

Question: How does one realize the entry into the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*)? Answer: It is said that those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who possess a fixed nature have bodies that are solely quiescent and minds that delight in purity and emptiness.
Having attained the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*) and severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), they directly realize True Suchness (*tathatā*).

By permanently extinguishing the cause for rebirth, they realize the state with remainder. When their afflictions that cause rebirth are exhausted and they no longer undergo future existence, [they realize the state without remainder]. Manifestly...
The basis for the suffering of birth and death, as well as the innate, spontaneous afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), have all been extinguished.

Since the remaining material and mental factors that possess functional activity lack a basis, they are simultaneously and instantaneously abandoned along with that basis of suffering, whereby one realizes *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Question: At the time of realizing *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, since the bodies and cognitions of the followers of the Two Vehicles have already ceased, who realizes *nirvāṇa*? Answer: [It is] realization...
Although in the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa* there is neither body nor cognition, it is realized by means of that very body and cognition;

therefore, it can be said that such body and cognition exist. Question: Since one has realized *nirupadhiśeṣa*, one is then equal to a Buddha. Why, then, is there a difference between the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and the Buddha? Answer:
In this stage, having severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and realized the pure *tathatā*, one is free from conceptual marks (*vikalpa-nimitta*). One attains...
Regarding the bliss of quiescent extinction (*śānti-sukha*), because they rely upon this principle, they are no different from the Buddha.

Nevertheless, as they do not seek bodhi above nor deliver sentient beings below, they deviate from the myriad practices; consequently, their fruition lacks the perfection of permanence. For this reason, it is further said that they differ from the Buddha.
Since the various cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) do not induce rebirth [as they do not lead to suffering], only the latter three types are termed "attained through manifestation.
Question: Afflictions (*kleśa*) are of an unwholesome nature and directly induce birth and death; however, the various cognitive obstructions are of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.
They cannot directly induce birth and death; how then can their abandonment lead to the realization of non-abiding nirvāṇa? Answer:

That which is known by them is a cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), not something that directly induces birth. Nevertheless, it is able to obscure the true suchness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmāśūnyatā-tathatā*), preventing them from attaining the union of wisdom and compassion.
Fearing the suffering of birth and death, they abide in a fixed nirvāṇa; therefore, it is abandoned by means of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.

The principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is revealed through that which is known. This principle is precisely *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana), because one does not abide in either this saṃsāra or nirvana.
Question: Since the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) can obstruct nirvana, once the afflictions are severed, one realizes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) also obstruct nirvana, then upon severing those obstructions, one should likewise realize analytical cessation.
[Question: How is it that when those [obstructions] are severed, one does not attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? [Answer: Analytical cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

it can only be realized by becoming free from the bonds of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the nature of those cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is not that of an affliction, when they are severed, one does not attain analytical cessation.

Question: Since that cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is not itself a bond, how can one realize nirvāṇa once it has been severed? Answer: It is said that the various types of nirvāṇa differ from one another; some are comprised within analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), while others are comprised within non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Not all nirvāṇas are comprised within analytical cessation. If you do not accept that the "non-abiding" [nirvāṇa] is comprised within non-analytical cessation, then [your previous position]— [The text continues: ...is self-contradictory. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the afflictions are the bonds": since the afflictions are themselves the bonds, they must be abandoned. If you claim that the afflictions are not abandoned because they are not bonds, then by that same logic, the cognitive obscurations would likewise not be abandoned because they are not bonds. Moreover, if the afflictions were not abandoned because they are not bonds, then even the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) would not be abandoned because it is not a bond. Consequently, the afflictions would never be abandoned, and thus nirvāṇa could never be realized. Therefore, your assertion that the afflictions are not abandoned because they are not bonds is untenable. Furthermore, the afflictions are indeed bonds, for they obstruct the attainment of nirvāṇa. If they did not obstruct its attainment, then even without abandoning them, one would realize nirvāṇa. Thus, it is established that the afflictions are bonds. As for the cognitive obscurations, although they are not bonds in the sense of being afflictions, they are nonetheless obstacles to the realization of nirvāṇa. Therefore, when these are severed, one realizes nirvāṇa. This is like the case where, although the eye and light are not bonds, when they are present, one sees forms; conversely, when they are absent, one does not see. Thus, although the cognitive obscurations are not bonds, they are nonetheless obstacles to the realization of nirvāṇa. Therefore, when they are severed, one realizes nirvāṇa. If intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) were not nirvāṇa, it would follow that it is also not subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
However, one attains analytical cessation by abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), because the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) bind sentient beings and cause them to dwell in saṃsāra;

therefore, by abandoning the afflictions, one immediately attains analytical cessation. As for why one does not attain analytical cessation by abandoning the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is because the cognitive obscurations do not...
Because it perceives birth and death, when those [afflictions] are severed, one does not attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Question:

If analytical cessation is not attained when the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are severed, how can it be called *nirvāṇa*? Answer: Indeed, by severing those objects of knowledge, the true reality of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is revealed.
This characteristic of *nirvāṇa* is primordially quiescent; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*. It is not that this *nirvāṇa* takes analytical cessation as its essence.
This is their nature. Therefore, among the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), the four types of perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*) are either subsumed within them or not.

If one considers the first, *nirvāṇa by nature* (*prakṛti-parinirvāṇa*), and the last, *non-abiding nirvāṇa* (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*), they are subsumed within the unconditioned phenomenon of *tathatā*.

If one considers the middle two—the *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and *nirvāṇa without remainder* (*nirupadhiśeṣa*)—they are subsumed within the unconditioned phenomenon of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through discernment). Question: If it is only the bonds of afflictions (*kleśa*) that are severed...

Regarding that which attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): just as the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asamskṛta*) can sever bonds, so too can the unconditioned state of the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-asamskṛta*).

Within these two—namely, space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and suchness (*tathatā*)—which of the four unconditioned states do they subsume?

Answer: These two are subsumed within the four unconditioned states under the category of the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*). This is because these two types...

Non-arising due to the absence of conditions is called "temporary separation" (*āntarāyika-viveka*); it is not true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because true analytical cessation is ultimate cessation rather than temporary separation.
There is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is temporary separation rather than permanent cessation;

therefore, these two unconditioned phenomena are subsumed under non-analytical cessation. Alternatively, if one holds that the fourth nirvāṇa is also subsumed under analytical cessation, it is because...
Because the power of the discernment of true wisdom extinguishes that which is to be known and brings about the realization of nirvāṇa. Question:

If the fourth nirvāṇa is subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), does it not then become indistinguishable from the two intermediate states—the nirvāṇa with remainder and the nirvāṇa without remainder? Answer:
There are two types of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). First is attainment through the cessation of bonds, namely *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa;
this refers to that which is realized by severing the bonds of afflictions (*kleśa*) that induce rebirth. Second is attainment through the cessation of obstructions, namely the fourth nirvāṇa;

this refers to that which is realized by severing the seeds of the subtle, innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Thus, the four forms of perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*) are contrasted with the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The first type of *nirvāṇa* is subsumed under *tathatā* (suchness). The latter three are all subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The two types beginning with the "immovable" (*āniñjya*) are subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because they merely suppress the afflictions temporarily rather than severing them permanently.

As for what is called analytical cessation, it refers to ultimate cessation, not temporary cessation. Question: Since the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) also obstruct *nirvāṇa*, why is it only [the afflictive obstructions] that are mentioned?
This is an obstacle to bodhi. Answer: As it is said that afflictions (*kleśa*) are obstacles to nirvāṇa, how could those afflictions only obstruct nirvāṇa and not obstruct bodhi?

One should know that when the holy teachings state that afflictions obstruct nirvāṇa and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obstruct bodhi, this is all said in terms of their predominant functions. In reality, afflictions also obstruct bodhi, and the cognitive obstructions also [obstruct nirvāṇa].

It obstructs *nirvāṇa*. Among the four kinds of *nirvāṇa* mentioned above, only the latter three are termed "that which is manifested" (*prabhāsvara-labdha*), as they are realized by severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The *tathatā-svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (the *nirvāṇa* of the intrinsically pure nature of suchness) is immutably quiescent and as profound as empty space; it is universally shared and is not something that is "manifested."
The second [type] of attainment produced is called Great Bodhi (up to this point). This refers to the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-saṃprayukta-citta-varga*).
This explains the second of the attainments produced among those attained through transformation. That is, Great Bodhi.

Although it inherently possesses the seeds capable of producing [it], which are untainted (*anāsrava*), these seeds do not manifest due to the obstructions of the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Through the Noble...
The power of the Path cuts off that which is to be known, causing that bodhi to arise from untainted seeds.
Once arisen, it continues uninterruptedly until the end of the future, benefiting sentient beings without cessation; therefore, it is called "attainment through arising.
This attainment through arising is precisely the mental states associated with the four wisdoms. As for the four kinds mentioned in the preceding text:
Nirvāṇa and True Suchness (*tathatā*) as a single category constitute the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*). They are inherently present from the beginning;
they are not obtained through manifestation, nor are they obtained through arising. The subsequent three types of nirvāṇa and this bodhi are all that which is manifested and that which arises;

they are subsumed within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). The first fascicle states: "By severing the continuous arising of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one realizes true liberation."
Because one has severed the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that hinder understanding, one attains great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*); the meaning is seen here.
What is the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms (up to: a single flavor, continuous until the end of the future)?
The following clarifies the four wisdoms. First, regarding the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*):

when the eighth consciousness has not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is like a clear mirror manifesting various forms and images; upon reaching the stage of the transformation of the basis, it is called the Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

This refers to the mental state that is free from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because in the causal stage there is no discursive calculation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), and in the resultant stage it is likewise free from conceptualization. As for "that which is perceived": [text continues]
Regarding the statement that "the aspects of the causal formations (*saṃskāra*) are subtle and difficult to know":

because the aspects within the causal stage are extremely subtle, and because the internally appropriated objects (*upātta-viṣaya*) are likewise difficult to fathom, it is so for the resultant stage as well. Regarding the phrase "not deluded and not ignorant toward any object":
because in the causal stage one can cognize the three types of natures of objects without cognizing what is false, and because there is no error, it is so for the resultant stage as well.

Regarding "the purity of nature and characteristics": although the characteristics are defiled within the causal stage, the nature remains pure. Now, as the light of wisdom shines forth, both nature and characteristics are pure.

Regarding "being free from all defilements and possessing purely immaculate, perfect virtues": in the causal stage, this is the nature that is perfumed; it becomes defiled through defiled perfuming and pure through pure perfuming.
At the level of the fruit, it transforms into the stainless state, being associated solely with pure, wholesome dharmas.

It is associated [with purity]. Therefore, it is free from defilement (*saṃkleśa*). Because it is free from confusion, it is "pure" (*śuddha*); because it is free from defilement, it is "clean" (*viśuddha*).
Since it is endowed with the complete perfection of the characteristics of pure qualities—being free from both defilement and confusion—it serves as the support for both the manifest and the seeds.

That which can manifest and produce the reflections of the body, the land, and wisdom is that which, within the causal state, can maintain the seeds and can produce the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*), manifesting the sense organs, the physical body, and the receptacle world.
At the stage of fruition, it also serves as the basis for pure conduct; it can also sustain the seeds of that purity;
and it can manifest immeasurable bodies and immeasurable lands, such that even the entire sphere of omniscience is reflected therein.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "Because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is not deluded regarding any object;
because the essence of this wisdom is luminous, clear, and stainless; because it is the sole basis for all untainted virtues;
and because this wisdom can manifest all bodies and lands—whereas the other three wisdoms are its reflections. Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says: "Next, the Sublime..."
The arising of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is designated by way of analogy.
Just as various images appear based upon a perfect mirror, so too do the various objects, sense bases, and consciousnesses appear as reflected images based upon the Tathāgata’s Mirror-like Wisdom.

One should know that the reason only the perfect mirror is used as an analogy is that the Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror is perfectly equal and impartial; therefore, this wisdom-mirror is called "perfect" (pariṇata).
It is like a mirror. As for the second, the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*):
because in the past, during the seventh causal stage, it was grasped as an internal self (*ātman*), one established boundaries and limits by distinguishing between self and other among all phenomena;

thus, various distinctions prevented the attainment of equality, and it was constantly associated with greed, delusion, pride, and views. Now that it has been transformed into the essence of wisdom, [the notions of] self and phenomena...

Once these are eliminated, all things are entirely equal. [This wisdom] is constantly associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it manifests as the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, O Wondrous Birth (*Miaosheng*), the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is fully accomplished through ten aspects. That is to say, it is the realization of the supremacy of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*)."
The equality of the experience of joy; the equality of all perceptions of dependent origination; the equality of being free from distinct characteristics and non-characteristics;

the equality of great compassion that extensively rescues others; the equality of great pity that is without dependence; the equality of manifesting according to the inclinations of all sentient beings;
the equality of what is spoken with the respect and love of all sentient beings; and the equality of the tranquility of the world.
It is of a single flavor and equal. All worldly phenomena—suffering and pleasure—are of a single flavor and equal.
The cultivation and planting of immeasurable merit reach ultimate equality. Because one realizes these ten characteristics, it is named the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

Regarding the statement that the "wonderful observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) has the "unshared support": this means that in the causal stage, the sixth consciousness takes the seventh as its unshared support; [in the resultant stage...]
The former serves as the exclusive support for the *suvicāraṇa-jñāna* (the wisdom of thorough investigation). Regarding that which is established by non-abiding *nirvāṇa*:

during the stage of the cause, one clings to that object of knowledge (*jñeya*) as an internal self, thereby obstructing this *nirvāṇa*. Consequently, when wisdom is transformed, non-abiding *nirvāṇa* manifests from this.
Question: Since both mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and equality wisdom (*samatā-jñāna*) are free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*), upon what do they depend?
There is a distinction in their meanings. Answer: Mirror-like wisdom is non-conceptual; it is like a bright mirror that has no mind.
It is equanimous and non-conceptual, like the sun merging with space, for space has no distinct characteristics.
The third is the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna), which carries out the tasks that should be performed through the power of one's original vows.
Regarding this wisdom of wondrous observation: it refers to the sixth consciousness during the causal stage, which universally cognizes all phenomena; it is likewise so on the resultant stage.

Regarding "wondrous observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*): its divine function is boundless, hence it is called "wondrous. It takes both the specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its objects, hence it is termed "observation.

"Specific" refers to mind, matter, and so forth; "general" refers to impermanence and so forth. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the specific characteristic;

the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the general characteristic. Regarding the term "comprehensive observation" (*saṃgraha-pratyavekṣā*): "comprehensive" (*saṃgraha*) has the meaning of "containing" or "storing," while "observation" refers to discernment.
He immediately observes. By means of this category of wisdom, he is well able to observe the gateways of dhāraṇī and is also able to collect and store them so as not to forget them.
The path-factors of the six perfections constitute the jewels of merit, while the wondrous functions of the supernormal powers constitute the distinctions of their activity.
Having been able to observe both specific and general characteristics, he is further able to collect and contemplate immeasurable dhāraṇīs. Furthermore...
It is able to produce the jewels of merit and virtue, and further manifests infinite diverse activities to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
this clearly demonstrates that there is nothing it does not universally know. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"In this way, the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom sustains all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi, and provides unimpeded eloquence for the Buddhas."

Dharma. It is further said: "It is capable of arising instantaneously as the unimpeded, wondrous wisdom regarding all that is known (*jñeya*), serving as the causal condition for various and immeasurable consciousnesses of marks.

It is also said: "It is adorned by the various delightful *pāramitās*, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), the ten powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*);
it is exceedingly lovely and delightful," and so forth. Fourth is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
This refers to the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s deeds that ought to be performed. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"By means of this, the Tathāgata diligently manifests various fields of craftsmanship through his bodily transformative activities to subdue sentient beings who are arrogant regarding their skills.
Through the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching and brings them to maturity."
Liberation. Through this, the Tathāgata’s transformative activity of auspicious speech proclaims various teachings according to the inclinations of beings;
its phrasing and meaning are so skillful that even sentient beings of limited intelligence will believe upon first hearing them. It is by the power of such skillful means that this is achieved.
He leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching and brings them to maturity and liberation.
For this reason, the Tathāgata’s karma of intentional transformation resolves upon the eighty-four thousand distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings.
By means of the power of such skillful means, he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching and brings them to maturity and liberation. Thus, these three types of karma are accomplished.
The activities performed bring all things to completion without exception.
Thus, because the mental states associated with these four wisdoms [attain this state], it is said that through the eight consciousnesses, the four wisdoms are realized.
The following is a summary of the transformation and attainment associated with the four wisdoms. Question:

If the resulting attainment consists only of mental states associated with the four wisdoms, then do all the seeds and active manifestations of the transforming subject and the transformed object, as well as the associated mental factors, cease to exist?
Answer: When we speak of the "transformation of the mental state associated [with wisdom]," it refers only to the transformation of the twenty afflictions.
Sixth: There are two types of indeterminate [states]. The remaining five universal mental factors, the five object-specific factors, and the eleven wholesome factors are capable of transforming;
the transformation of their seeds and manifest states arises exactly as in the case of the [primary] causes, without any difference. Question:

If this is so, why is it that one speaks only of the "mental complex associated with the four wisdoms" (*caturjñāna-samprayukta-cittapakṣa*), and does not include the others? Answer: Although each [of these complexes] definitely possesses twenty-three dharmas, [the text focuses on the four wisdoms because they are preeminent].

Furthermore, regarding the seeds and active manifestations of both the transforming subject and the transformed object, it is specifically at the stage of the revolution of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) that the function of wisdom increases;
therefore, these are emphasized. Consequently, these four categories encompass all the merits of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*). Question: Regarding these four types of wisdom—

Which consciousness is transformed to obtain which wisdom? Answer: By transforming the contaminated mental states associated with the eighth consciousness, one attains the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
When this wisdom is attained, one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). It illuminates every atom within every land of the ten directions; therefore it is said:

"The great, perfectly round, stainless [wisdom] arises simultaneously, universally illuminating the lands of the atoms throughout the ten directions. By transforming the contaminated... the eighth [consciousness].

The seventh category of mind associated with the mental factors constitutes the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). It manifests the ten kinds of bodies for the enjoyment of others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and preaches the Dharma to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages;
therefore it is said: "The Tathāgata manifests the body for the enjoyment of others, which is the object-capacity (*adhikāra*) of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.

By transforming the sixth consciousness and its associated mental factors, which are characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*), one becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), which universally illumines the great trichiliocosm.
The world. Therefore it is said: "After the Ground of Far-Going, there is pure outflowlessness (*anāsrava*). Observing with perfect clarity, it illuminates the great chiliocosm.

It transforms the five preceding mental states associated with outflows into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), manifesting three types of bodies to benefit sentient beings and engage with all things.
