Answer: The single word "only" (*mātra*) serves to exclude objects external to the mind; it does not negate that which is transformed by internal consciousness.
If internal objects were negated, then even True Suchness (*tathatā*) would have to be non-existent, because True Suchness is likewise an object of cognition. Question:
Question: Since both the internal object and consciousness are substantially real, why do you not say "only the object" but instead say "only consciousness"?
Answer: Consciousness exists solely within and does not extend beyond the mind; objects, however, extend both inside and outside.

Now, fearing that this might be confused with objects existing outside the mind, I do not say "only the object" but rather "only consciousness. Alternatively, it is because foolish people are deludedly attached to external objects.
They give rise to delusions and create karma, thereby undergoing various bitter retributions; yet they do not understand how to contemplate the mind to diligently seek liberation.

Out of compassion for them, I wish to cause them to turn back and contemplate their own minds, so that they do not pursue external objects, detach from their clinging, settle within, and manifest the radiance of their fundamental clarity.
The expression "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) does not mean that internal objects are entirely non-existent like external ones;
rather, it means that the two divisions of appearance and perception, as well as true suchness (tathatā) and so forth, all have consciousness as their intrinsic nature.

Due to the power of perfuming by internal causes and external conditions from time immemorial, they arise in succession and manifest as if many things were produced. It is because these three aspects are taken together [that they are called "consciousness-only"].

Regarding the statement "only consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*): Question. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), whereas consciousness and the like are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Why, then, is True Suchness also subsumed within conditioned consciousness? Answer. Although True Suchness is unconditioned, it is also the actual nature (*dharmatā*) of consciousness.
This means that based upon *tathatā* (suchness), the mind arises through non-awakening, and with the occurrence of thought, it is then designated as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness has no self-nature and is not separate from *tathatā*; therefore, one knows that *tathatā* is also the nature of consciousness. Thus it is said:
"All phenomena within and without the three realms are produced by this single mind alone. Apart from consciousness, there are no other phenomena; therefore, it is simply called "only" (*kevala*).
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is such that there is no phenomenon it does not encompass. Thus, the ancient masters said: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad phenomena are consciousness-only.

Since consciousness is mind-only, when it comes to form and sound—where form does not reach the ear and sound does not touch the eye—how can the eye perceive form and the ear perceive sound? Form and sound [are perceived by] the eye and the ear.
The myriad dharmas are accomplished; yet the myriad dharmas are not dependent on conditions—how could they not be observed as being like illusions?
Of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, what is firm and what changes? It is further said: "There is no dharma before the eyes, yet the meaning lies right before the eyes.

It is also said: "Throughout the entire world-system, all is bright and clear; if there were even a single thread of hair, it would be just that single thread of hair. And again: "Throughout the entire world-system..."
This śramaṇa has but one eye; the entire world of the ten directions is the śramaṇa’s whole body.
The entire world of the ten directions is his own radiance; the entire world of the ten directions is contained within his own radiance.
Within the entire world of the ten directions, there is not a single person who is not himself. Thus we know that mind and mind seal each other, and so it is from patriarch to patriarch.
It is traditionally said that this alone is the single gateway and there are no other dharmas; if one simply cultivates a resolute mind of acceptance, one will certainly not be deceived.
This treatise is established in three parts because it clarifies the principle of Vijñapti-mātra (consciousness-only) until it is perfectly clear and pure.
This is the summary of the names [of the sections]. Regarding the "three parts," it means that while the Sūtra has three parts, the Treatise likewise has three parts.
First, the single verse of prostration is called the "Section on Preliminary Veneration of the Thesis.

Second, the thirty verses and the beginning and end of the Treatise are called the "Section on Extensive Exposition Based on the Teaching. Finally, the single verse following [the previous section] is called the "Section on Bestowing Benedictions. This...

Regarding the three parts of this treatise: some take the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as the three parts; others take the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the mutual manifestation (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* as the basis), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṭa*) as the three parts.

There is nothing incorrect in either approach. That is to say, because the single doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established by means of these three parts, it is called the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
It is also called the "Purification of Consciousness-Only," which precisely reveals the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) within this context. This is [the meaning].

Because within Vijñaptimātra there is the extremely pure, perfectly luminous, and stainless consciousness (amala-vijñāna), this treatise is titled *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-triṃśikā* (Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only); it is thus complete and neither increased nor diminished.
This concluding treatise (vṛtti) reveals the origin from which the author of this work emerged; it attributes the merit to the original master of the treatise (*mūla-śāstrakāra*).

It is said that these thirty verses of the *Mūla-śāstra* were composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu by distilling the essential meanings from within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and condensing them into thirty verses.
Based upon these verses, the principles of the teaching—namely, the nature of cause and effect, and the characteristics of the true and the false—are subsequently established.
All phenomena—whether provisional, real, conditioned, or unconditioned—are solely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

By elucidating the principle of consciousness-only in this manner, it becomes fully perfected; yet this does not involve establishing a separate doctrine outside of this treatise to either augment or diminish its meaning.
Having analyzed the meaning of the nature and characteristics of Consciousness-Only based upon the holy teachings and correct reasoning, I dedicate the merit thus obtained to all living beings;
may we together swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.
The first phrase establishes the principle based on the teachings. The subsequent phrase concerns the beginning and end of this treatise; that is to say, the first eight fascicles reveal—

The aspect of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra-lakṣaṇa*) is presented in the final two fascicles, as they reveal the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). The third line is the dedication [of merit] to sentient beings;
the fourth line is the aspiration to realize the fruit.
